lessons.title: Adaptability — keep the purpose, adjust the plan
lessons.text:
Visual guide Six connected components of adaptability. Short labels summarize the six skill components; numbers match the chapter list. Use the connections in the order the task needs. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. Purpose stays visible as plans change. Six connected components: Take responsibility; Persist and persevere; Regulate emotions when appropriate; Set or adjust goals and expectations; Plan and prioritize; Seek self-improvement. Revisit the component that helps the task.
See it in action · Adaptability
Visual guide The notice and budget both say 26. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
ORIGINAL: 24 participants. UPDATE: 26 participants. Identify what changed. Update affected quantities. Check what stays the same. The notice and budget both say 26. Keep the old version. Do not change the room or time without evidence.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. ORIGINAL: 24 participants. UPDATE: 26 participants.
Try it: Identify what changed. Update affected quantities. Check what stays the same.
Check your result: The notice and budget both say 26. Keep the old version. Do not change the room or time without evidence.
Change the approach with care
Adaptability is the ability to work toward or adjust a goal when circumstances change. It includes noticing what has changed, deciding what still matters, choosing a workable response and learning from the attempt. Sometimes the response is a new method. Sometimes it is a request for support, a revised deadline or a decision to pause until the right information is available.
You may already adapt while balancing training, employment, travel, family responsibilities or community commitments. This chapter does not ask you to disclose those responsibilities. It uses fictional situations so you can practise without putting private information on a worksheet. You can choose a different relevant example with the instructor, provided the same skill can be observed.
Training in B.C. may take place close to home or away from people and places that support you. Your own priorities belong in goal setting when you want them included. You might connect a learning goal with employment, a community role, further study or a practical task that matters to you. The instructor can help make the plan workable without asking you to justify your identity or disclose private commitments.
Being adaptable does not mean accepting every request, hiding frustration or continuing through an unsafe situation. It does not make an individual responsible for barriers outside their control. A useful plan identifies both your next action and any support or decision another person must provide. Asking for an accessible format, clarification or an appropriate adjustment can be part of responsible action.
In this chapter, emotional regulation means choosing a practical way to respond or regain focus when that is useful. It is not a test of whether your feelings are acceptable. The instructor observes the plan and actions you choose, not a diagnosis, a personality trait or a requirement to appear cheerful.
Demonstrate responsibility
Clarify commitments, attend to the task and report relevant changes.
Practise with: “Separate the purpose from the schedule” through “Build a first plan”
Persist and persevere
Try a purposeful next step, use support and recognize when the approach needs changing.
Practise with: “Choose a better second attempt” through “Make a retry record”
Regulate your emotions when appropriate
Choose a task-focused pause or support strategy without required personal disclosure.
Practise with: “Compare useful responses” through “Set a boundary and a next step”
Set or adjust your goals and expectations
Define a meaningful goal and revise it when resources change.
Practise with: “Write a goal you can check”, “Identify what changed” through “Communicate the revised commitment”
Plan and prioritize
Identify dependencies, choose an order and make space for checking.
Practise with: “Build a first plan”, “Identify what changed” through “Prepare for another change”
Seek self-improvement
Use specific feedback, compare attempts and choose further practice.
Practise with: “Turn feedback into actions” through “Review all six components”
Adaptability route card
Practise in four steps
State the purpose, make a workable plan and keep the first version.
Read the changed requirement. Separate what changed from what stays the same.
Choose a useful response, ask for support if needed and carry out the revised plan.
Retrieve and check the result yourself. Use feedback to decide what to keep or try next.
Support route. Use the paper workflow if that suits the focus and available tools. Read the brief together, use a blank “changed / unchanged / next action / check” organizer, or ask for a tool demonstration before the observed attempt. A learner-directed request for an appropriate support can show Adaptability even when the later tool action is assisted. Do not require a personal account of stress or a rehearsed emotional display. If regulation is not needed or chosen, leave that component unobserved in this task.
Retry route. Select the affected step and repeat it after feedback. Use Kit T for a different content requirement when appropriate; record whether it was new. If the first work was accurate, retrieve and verify again or choose another challenge. A retry can confirm a successful process; it need not begin with an invented failure. Track who performs the tool action so a partner's work is not claimed as individual Digital evidence.
What the instructor observes. Keep the first plan, changed requirement and checked result. Discussing a case does not show that the learner carried out the action.
Next-attempt agreement: purpose ; changed requirement ; chosen next action ; paper/digital tool route ; support and boundary ; observer/booking ; check/result ___.
Case document 1 · A plan for the learning folder
Fictional ACCESS-style classroom schedule. A learner is preparing a small learning folder to show three kinds of work: a checked industry table, a short project note and a reflection explaining one improvement. The table uses invented data from the introductory asphalt unit. The project note must distinguish the fictional road owner from the contractor and label the numbers as practice data. The reflection should name a change the learner made after feedback.
The initial goal is to complete the folder by Friday at 12:00. Two supported classroom work periods are available: Tuesday for 60 minutes and Thursday for 90 minutes. These times are classroom planning values, not a requirement of a funded program or a real person's schedule. An instructor can help the learner identify a smaller starting point or an accessible response method.
The learner's Tuesday plan is to read the brief for 20 minutes, practise the table calculation for 25 minutes and check the result for 15 minutes. Thursday's plan is to use the digital tool for 35 minutes, draft the project note for 25 minutes, review the folder for 15 minutes and keep 15 minutes available for questions or revision. The digital task includes entering and checking data, saving a file and finding it again; a paper table alone does not demonstrate those actions.
The folder is a learning record, not a pass-or-fail judgement about the learner's future. A useful record shows what was attempted, what support was used and what still needs practice. If a requirement or resource changes, the learner and instructor will agree the next step. The learner should not silently remove an outcome or claim an unfinished action is complete just to meet the original date.
Separate the purpose from the schedule
Read the case and identify the purpose of the folder, its three products and the initial deadline. Then identify one resource and one support. Explain the difference between “complete the folder” and “demonstrate every skill independently.” Mark one outcome that cannot be demonstrated solely through paper work. Use the case rather than guessing how an actual ACCESS program assesses learners.
Write a goal you can check
Write a goal for one folder product that names the action, evidence and agreed time. Keep it within the resources in the case. For example, “By the end of Tuesday I will have a checked table with units and one recorded check” is more usable than “I will improve my maths.” Add the support you may use and one question to clarify with the instructor.
Build a first plan
Turn the Tuesday and Thursday tasks into a simple plan with time, task, output and check. Confirm that Tuesday totals 60 minutes and Thursday totals 90 minutes. Identify one dependency, such as checking source values before using them in a note. Mark the purpose of Thursday's 15-minute buffer. Explain why a buffer is not evidence that someone is working too slowly.
Stay with the task without judging yourself
When a task changes, your first response may be concern, irritation, curiosity, relief or something else. You do not have to report that response to the class. The useful learning question is, “What action will help me understand the situation and choose a next step?” A strategy can be small: reread the changed instruction, ask for one point at a time, use a written checklist, request a brief pause or speak privately with the instructor.
The strategy should fit you and the setting. A quiet pause is useful for some people and uncomfortable for others. A movement break may be possible in one classroom and require a different arrangement in another. No learner needs to close their eyes, follow a breathing exercise, discuss trauma or participate in a cultural practice to demonstrate adaptability. Choose a task-focused action that supports your work and respects the available setting.
Responsibility also includes communication. If you need a pause, a short message can protect the shared task without giving private reasons: “I need five minutes to review the changed brief. I will come back with one question.” If you cannot make a commitment, state what you can confirm and when you can update the person. Honest uncertainty is more useful than an assurance you cannot keep.
Worked example 1 — pause, clarify, choose. A learner hears, “You have less computer time now,” and starts deleting planned steps. The instructor offers the change in writing. The learner reads it, marks the time restriction and asks whether the completion date can be adjusted. The learner then chooses a revised sequence. The evidence is the clarification, revised plan and next action. The instructor does not need to decide whether the learner looked calm enough or had the “right attitude.”
Compare useful responses
A fictional learner receives a changed task and says, “I will finish everything somehow,” without checking the new conditions. Compare that response with “Let me identify what changed, check the required outcomes and agree what is possible.” Explain what information the second response could reveal. Name one situation in which pausing for clarification would protect the quality of the work.
Rehearse a strategy by choice
Choose one strategy: review the written brief, ask for a short pause, use a three-point checklist or request a private clarification. Rehearse it in a low-pressure role-play with the instructor or a partner. Use a fictional task change, not a personal stress story. Afterwards, describe what the strategy helped you do and one adjustment that would make it more useful.
Set a boundary and a next step
Draft a response to this classroom request: “We are behind, so skip checking the source and mark the table complete.” State what you can do, what you cannot honestly claim and a workable next step. Then explain how setting that boundary can support adaptability. Do not turn the exercise into a debate about whether a learner should tolerate unsafe or dishonest instructions.
Persistence means learning from the attempt
Visual guide Worked-example preview: compare the entry with its source, correct 9 to 90, recalculate and check the paper work. Record the strategy and result. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Four actions compare the source value ninety with an incorrect entry of nine, correct the entry to ninety, recalculate, and compare the new result with the paper work. The strategy, action and new check provide evidence of a useful retry.
Repeating the same action is not always persistence toward the goal. If a saved file cannot be found, opening random folders again may create more confusion. A purposeful next attempt uses information from the first one: check the file name, recall the chosen location, use the application's recent-files list if available, or ask for a demonstration of the search step. The method changes while the learning goal remains visible.
A useful retry has four parts: notice the result → identify one likely gap → choose a different action → check what happened. A likely gap is a working explanation, not a judgement about ability. “I did not record the save location” points toward a practical action. “I am bad with computers” does not tell you what to practise next and may hide the exact step you already know.
Some barriers require another person's action. A broken device, inaccessible file or unavailable support is not solved by telling the learner to try harder. Record the barrier, preserve any completed evidence and agree another opportunity. Persistence may mean returning to the task when the necessary conditions exist. It can also mean deciding with the instructor to change the task while keeping the intended outcome.
Worked example 2 — a retry with evidence. A learner's table total is wrong. Instead of retyping the total, the learner compares the three source rows with the entries. One value was entered as 9 instead of 90. The learner corrects the entry, recalculates and checks the total against the paper working. The useful feedback is, “Comparing each row helped you locate the error.” The record should not say that effort alone guarantees the right answer; it names the strategy and the result.
Choose a better second attempt
Use this fictional record: “The learner entered three rows, saved the file, and later could not find it. They remember the file name but did not note the folder.” Propose two reasonable next actions and choose the one you would try first. Explain what you would check afterwards. Identify what evidence is already available and what remains unobserved.
Keep, change or ask
Sort these responses into a useful next action, an action needing revision or a request for support: repeat an unchanged calculation without checking its inputs; compare each source row with the entry; ask for an accessible copy of a file that cannot be read; claim a partner's saved file as your own; ask the instructor to demonstrate one unfamiliar saving step. Explain each choice using the learning goal.
Make a retry record
Choose a small classroom task you can safely repeat, such as locating a saved practice file, checking a fictional total or explaining a process term. Record the first result, the specific change in method and the second result. You may use a supplied example if you prefer. Identify the support used and what you still need to practise; do not invent a successful result if the retry remains unfinished.
Case document 2 · The time and device access change
Fictional update after Tuesday's work. Tuesday's reading, calculation practice and check are complete. Thursday's work period has been reduced from 90 minutes to 60 minutes. A device is available only during the final 25 minutes of that period. The paper brief and table remain available for the full hour. The initial digital practice was planned for 35 minutes, and the instructor does not expect the learner simply to perform it faster.
The instructor offers a supported 10-minute device appointment on Monday, followed by a separate five-minute paper-review period to update the reflection. Both periods finish before Monday at 12:00. If the learner books this arrangement, the instructor agrees that the remaining digital evidence and reflection update can be added by that deadline. The project note and an interim reflection can still be reviewed on Friday. The learner may instead propose another arrangement, but it must be confirmed; the offer does not mean every possible new deadline is approved.
The folder must continue to distinguish completed work from pending work. The project note should use the already checked paper numbers, so it can be drafted before the Thursday device turn. A paper plan can prepare the headings and file name, but it does not count as the learner using the digital tool. The reflection can explain the revised plan and later be updated after the Monday appointment.
The learner and instructor need to decide how Thursday's first 35 minutes will be used and what will happen during the 25-minute device turn. They also need a clear handover to Monday: what was done, where the practice file is saved and which action remains. The change is a planning problem with support options, not a test of how much personal pressure a learner can withstand.
Revise the plan without losing the goal
Visual guide Worked-example preview: proportional bars show the original 90-minute Thursday, the revised 60-minute session and separate Monday follow-up. This is one feasible plan, subject to confirmation and observed work. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Proportional time bars compare an original ninety-minute Thursday plan with a revised sixty-minute session. The original has thirty-five minutes digital work, twenty-five drafting, fifteen reviewing and fifteen buffer. The revision has twenty-five drafting, ten reviewing and twenty-five digital. Monday adds ten minutes digital and five paper reflection in separate periods before noon. Digital practice remains thirty-five minutes.
Start by separating changed conditions, unchanged outcomes and open decisions. The changed conditions are the shorter Thursday period and limited device access. The outcomes still include accurate information, an authored note, genuine tool use and a reflection based on evidence. The open decision is the agreed completion arrangement. Keeping these categories separate prevents a resource change from silently becoming a lower-quality outcome.
Prioritizing means choosing what must happen before something else. It does not always mean doing the hardest task first. In this case, drafting the note from checked paper information can happen before device access. Saving and locating a file require the actual tool. A final digital check depends on knowing what was entered. Put the tasks in an order that respects those relationships.
Write a revised commitment in plain language. State what will be completed, what remains pending and when the next check will occur. Avoid promising outcomes controlled by someone else. You can commit to attending an agreed appointment or asking for clarification; you cannot guarantee that an unconfirmed device will be available.
Worked example 3 — make the change visible. The learner plans 25 minutes to draft the note and 10 minutes to review its source labels during Thursday's first 35 minutes. During the 25-minute device turn, the learner enters and checks the data and saves the file, recording the location. Monday's 10-minute device appointment is reserved for finding/reopening the file and checking the remaining digital evidence. The separate five-minute paper-review period is used to update the reflection. The exact tool actions must be observed; the plan alone does not prove they occurred. The revised record keeps Friday's partial review and Monday's agreed completion distinct.
Identify what changed
Make three columns: changed condition, unchanged outcome and decision to confirm. Use the update to place at least two details in each relevant column. Calculate the reduction in Thursday work time and the difference between the original digital allocation and Thursday device access. Explain why the 10-minute appointment is a support option, not permission to mark Digital complete before it occurs.
Revise a goal and schedule
Write a revised folder goal that preserves the required evidence and uses the offered arrangement or a clearly labelled proposal. Build a 60-minute Thursday plan and a separate Monday follow-up. Show Thursday's first 35 minutes and final 25 minutes clearly; distinguish Monday's 10-minute device appointment from the separate five-minute paper review. Identify what will be ready for Friday review, what remains pending and the confirmation needed before treating a new deadline as agreed.
Communicate the revised commitment
Write or rehearse a short update to the instructor. Include the changed condition, your proposed order of work, one support request and how you will record unfinished evidence. Ask the listener to restate the plan. Correct any misunderstanding. Keep private reasons out of the message unless you choose to share them; the task is communicating a workable learning arrangement.
Use feedback as information for the next attempt
Feedback is most useful when it names a feature you can inspect and an action you can try. “Your note is unclear” may be true, but it leaves you searching for the problem. “The note names the contractor but does not identify the road owner; add the role from the brief” points to a specific revision. You can ask for that level of detail when feedback is too broad.
Receiving feedback does not require agreeing with every suggestion. Compare the suggestion with the task purpose and evidence. If it seems to conflict with the brief, ask a clarifying question. If it is about preference, consider whether a reader test would help. A reasoned decision to retain accurate wording can show thoughtful review, provided you can explain the decision.
An improvement record should include what changed and what difference it made. Keep the earlier attempt where possible. A before-and-after pair can show learning more clearly than a final polished product alone. It can also show that one strategy did not help and needs replacing. That is useful information for the next lesson, not something to conceal.
Case document 3 · Feedback on the project note
Fictional learner draft. “Pathway Paving owns the Willow Reach road and gets $120,000 profit. We will use all the same rules on every project. My computer work is finished.”
Source facts available for revision. In the practice brief, the Town of Willow Reach owns the road and Pathway Paving Company performs the contracted work. The $120,000 is the total fictional funding, not a profit figure. Applicable requirements depend on the actual project and authorized documents; the historical source labels are not a complete statement of current rules. The learner has entered and saved a practice table but has not yet demonstrated finding and reopening the file.
Instructor feedback. “Your note is brief and names the practice project. Check the owner/contractor distinction, replace the profit claim with the correct funding label, and state which digital action remains. For requirements, name the need to confirm current applicable documents rather than saying all projects use the same rules.”
The learner does not need to defend the first draft as a personal achievement or discard everything in it. The useful next action is to compare each statement with the available facts and revise the misleading parts. Keeping the short format may still serve the reader well.
Turn feedback into actions
Convert the instructor feedback into a revision checklist. For each item, identify the source detail to check and the change needed. Keep one useful feature of the original draft. Explain why “try harder” would provide less guidance than this checklist. The task is to use feedback, not to write a judgement about the fictional learner.
Revise and compare
Write a corrected version of the note using the source facts. Then compare the first and revised versions, naming at least three substantive changes. Include an honest statement about the pending digital action. Ask a partner to identify the owner, the meaning of $120,000 and what remains unfinished. Use their response to check whether your revision worked.
Prepare for another change
The Monday device appointment is confirmed, but the learner will use a different computer with a different folder layout. Create a short preparation plan that preserves the learning goal without assuming the same screen arrangement. Name the information to bring, one step to check with the instructor and how to record the result. Do not put actual passwords or personal records in the plan.
Keep a record of learning over time
One task shows what happened under particular conditions. It does not tell the whole story of your adaptability. A useful record includes the original goal, the change, your selected response, support used, the result and a next step. Several records over time can reveal strategies that help you and situations where different support is needed.
Your goals can also change for good reasons. You may learn more about a role, discover a useful interest or find that an original timeline does not fit available resources. A revised goal should explain what changed and why the new goal remains meaningful. Changing a goal thoughtfully is different from claiming that an unmet goal was completed.
Test a strategy in a new task
Choose a short unfamiliar classroom task with the instructor, such as reorganizing a practice checklist or finding information in a different supplied document. Predict one difficulty and choose a strategy. Try the task, record what happened and decide whether to keep or adjust the strategy. Distinguish your prediction from the observed result and record any support.
Build a one-week practice plan
Plan two short practice opportunities for one skill from this chapter. Give each a task, available resource, check and possible support. Include one reasonable backup if the resource is unavailable. The dates and commitments can be fictional. Explain how you will decide whether to continue the goal, change the method or ask for a different learning arrangement.
Review all six components
Select evidence for each component from your activities. Identify an action you completed, any support used and any component still needing observation or practice. If all intended evidence was collected independently, record that accurately and choose a new practice challenge. Choose a next goal that can be checked through a task. If you plan to use the strategy in work or community life, record that as a transfer plan; do not claim workplace transfer before there is evidence.
Supported practice and extension
For a supported route, use a printed before-and-after plan and work through one changed condition at a time. An instructor can model the first clarification, help record a selected strategy and observe a small retry. For an extension, combine two changed conditions and ask a new partner to check whether your revised commitment is clear. Keep challenge proportionate to learning; surprise, distress and personal disclosure are not required ingredients.
Adaptability practice A · Revise a small pack and carry out the next step
These four original cases give you another opportunity to use a skill after the chapter practice. All people, rooms, events and organizations in these cards are fictional. You can use these cases without sharing personal, family, community or cultural knowledge. They are classroom tasks, not instructions for operating equipment or following an actual workplace procedure.
Your instructor will give you the relevant card when your turn begins. Keep a sender's information separate from the receiver's card until after the exchange. If you have already read the information, say so: the activity remains useful practice, but that attempt cannot show how you receive an unfamiliar message. No one needs to conceal prior practice.
Agree your language, communication mode, tools, access supports and response time before beginning. Speech, sign, text, AAC, a learner-directed scribe and agreed interpretation can be appropriate. The person observing needs a reliable way to understand the meaning of your contribution. Receiving a message in writing shows reception through that mode; it does not automatically show auditory listening. You may decline audio/video recording and use live observation. Ask for a pause or another opportunity if the conditions are not usable. There is no requirement to look cheerful, make eye contact or disclose why you need an arrangement.
Purpose: respond to a changed requirement, choose a workable approach and carry it out. A plan alone is not evidence that a tool or workflow was used. Choose the paper route or an available digital route with the instructor; both can show Adaptability.
“Adaptability practice A · Revise a small pack and carry out the next step” initial brief · Version 1
Prepare one fictional practice pack called Kit R. It needs:
Card label Number of copies
WELCOME 1
EXAMPLE 2
BLANK RESPONSE 2
Use this text for the cards: WELCOME — Kit R, classroom practice; EXAMPLE — Sample response: I checked the label; BLANK RESPONSE — Write, draw or dictate a practice response. The blank-response card contains that instruction but no completed response. There is no private learner information in the pack.
For paper work, copy these labels/text onto separate slips and put them in a folder or envelope labelled Kit R — Version 1. For digital work, create a local document containing one clearly separated section per card and save it with a distinguishable Version 1 name. Use a location and software already agreed with the instructor. Ask for ordinary tool instruction if needed; record who directed the content and who operated the tool.
Before building, make a short plan: goal, order of actions, check and storage or retrieval method. Retain the Version 1 plan or draft so the change can be seen. The next card is a planned classroom change, not a test of how surprised or distressed you appear.
“Adaptability practice A · Revise a small pack and carry out the next step” change card · Instructor releases after the first plan
Fictional coordinator update · Version 2
Kit R now needs one additional EXAMPLE card. The WELCOME and BLANK RESPONSE requirements remain unchanged. Label the revised pack Version 2 and retain a record of what Version 1 required.
The printer is unavailable. A hand-prepared paper pack or a saved on-screen pack is acceptable for this classroom task. Do not wait for a printout or claim that printing has occurred. The next group needs a clear account of what is ready and what, if anything, still needs help.
Identify what changed and what stayed the same. Choose a practical next step, carry it out and check the revised contents against the change card. For a paper pack, close or set aside the labelled pack, retrieve it and check you have the intended version. For a digital pack, save, close and reopen the intended version. This is your own tool/workflow turn; a partner doing it for you cannot become evidence that you did it.
You may choose a brief pause, mark the next action, request clarification, use a checklist or ask for appropriate help. You do not have to explain a feeling or demonstrate a calming routine. If no regulation strategy is needed or chosen, the observer must leave that component unobserved in this attempt rather than infer it from your appearance.
Ask for feedback about one actual feature. If a correction is needed, make it and repeat the affected check. If the check is successful, explain the evidence and repeat the retrieval/check step to confirm the process. A successful result does not require inventing an error. State the revised commitment and any genuine unfinished item or support need.
“Adaptability practice A · Revise a small pack and carry out the next step” fresh retry brief · Kit T
For a later task, the instructor may give this brief after the Kit R attempt. Kit T — Version 1 needs 1 WELCOME, 1 EXAMPLE and 3 BLANK RESPONSE cards, using the same texts but replacing Kit R with Kit T. After you plan, the change is to add 1 REFERENCE card with the text REFERENCE — Check the card list before handing over and mark the pack Version 2. The other counts remain unchanged. Paper or saved on-screen versions remain acceptable; the printer is still unavailable. Perform the same build, retrieve and check steps. Record whether the brief was new to you and which support was used.

lessons.title: Showing up and managing your time on a job site
lessons.text:
Plan your arrival, tell your supervisor early when plans change, and sort your tasks so the important ones get done.
All people and companies in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
On a BC construction site the day often starts with a toolbox talk, a crane lift or a concrete truck booked for a set time. When one person is late, the crew may wait or start short-handed. Showing up on time, and calling early when you cannot, is one of the first things a foreman notices about a new apprentice. It tells them they can count on you.
Key ideas
Work back from the start time
Do not plan from the time you wake up. Plan from the time you must be ready to work, and count backwards.
Start with the time you must be in place (for example, the toolbox talk).
Subtract the time to get your gear on and sign in.
Subtract the walk from the bus stop or parking.
Subtract the travel time.
Subtract a buffer for traffic, a late bus or a slow gate.
Worked example. Dale starts at Riverbend Framing Ltd. The toolbox talk is at 6:50 a.m. He needs 10 minutes to sign in and put on his boots, vest and hard hat. The walk from the bus stop is 12 minutes. The bus ride is 45 minutes. Buses leave his stop at 5:30, 5:50 and 6:10.
Ready by 6:50, so he must reach the gate by 6:50 − 10 min = 6:40.
Off the bus by 6:40 − 12 min = 6:28.
On the bus by 6:28 − 45 min = 5:43.
The 5:50 bus is too late. He takes the 5:30 bus.
The 5:30 bus gets him off at 6:15, to the gate at 6:27 and ready at 6:37. That leaves 13 minutes of buffer before the talk.
Tell your supervisor early
Plans change: a sick child, a flat tire, a fever. What matters is that your supervisor hears it from you, before your shift, in the way your employer asks (a call, a text or an app). A good message says who you are, what is happening, and when you expect to be back or arrive.
In BC, after 90 days with an employer, the Employment Standards Act gives employees up to 5 paid sick days and 3 unpaid sick days each calendar year. Your employer can ask for reasonably sufficient proof that you were ill or injured. For the first two health-related absences of 5 days or less in a calendar year, your employer cannot ask for a note from a doctor or nurse. Some workplaces have union agreements with other rules, so read yours.
Know what your first day should cover
In BC, your employer must give a young or new worker a health and safety orientation before the work starts. It must include your supervisor's name and contact information, your rights and responsibilities (including reporting unsafe conditions and the right to refuse unsafe work) and the workplace health and safety rules. WorkSafeBC's checklist for employers also includes protective equipment, first aid and how to report an injury. If you are not told these things, ask.
Urgent and important are not the same
Urgent means it has to be dealt with soon.
Important means it matters a lot for your work, safety or goals.
Urgent Not urgent
Important A: Do it now. B: Plan a time for it.
Not important C: Deal with it fast or pass it on. D: Leave it for later or drop it.
Many people spend their days in boxes A and C and never get to box B. Box B is where goals like your tickets, your technical training and your health live. Planning time for box B stops those tasks from turning into emergencies later.
Worked example: plan B when the bus is cancelled
Marie is a first-year electrical apprentice at Coastline Electrical Contractors. Her start time is 7:00 a.m. She needs 15 minutes for coffee and to put on her gear at the site. The bus trip, door to door, takes 45 minutes. She wants a 10-minute buffer.
Step 1. Work back from the start.
Ready to work at 7:00.
At the gate by 7:00 − 15 min = 6:45.
Leave home by 6:45 − 45 min = 6:00.
Take off the buffer: leave home at 6:00 − 10 min = 5:50.
Step 2. Set the alarm. Marie needs 40 minutes to get up, eat and get dressed. 5:50 − 40 min = 5:10. Her alarm is set for 5:10.
Step 3. The change. At 5:40 her transit app says her bus is cancelled. The next one means she leaves home 20 minutes later, at 6:10.
At the gate: 6:10 + 45 min = 6:55.
Ready: 6:55 + 15 min = 7:10.
The 10-minute buffer covers half of the 20-minute delay. She would still be 10 minutes late.
Step 4. Look for a better option. Her cousin can drive her. The drive takes 25 minutes, and they can leave at 6:00.
At the gate: 6:00 + 25 min = 6:25.
Ready: 6:25 + 15 min = 6:40, which is 20 minutes early.
Step 5. Tell the supervisor early anyway. At 5:45 Marie texts her foreman: "Hi Lou, it's Marie. My 5:50 bus is cancelled. My cousin is driving me and I'll be on time. If that falls through I'll take the next bus and be about 10 minutes late, and I'll text you again." The foreman knows the plan before 6:00, whatever happens.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Tamara's site safety meeting is at 7:15 a.m. She needs 15 minutes to park, walk to the site trailer and sign in. Her drive takes 35 minutes. She wants a 10-minute buffer. What is the latest time she should leave home? Show each step.
Task 2 (level 1) You wake up at 4:45 a.m. with a fever and cannot work today. Your foreman, Rob, at Riverbend Framing asks crews to text him before 6:00 a.m. Write the text you would send.
Task 3 (level 2) Jesse is a first-year apprentice. Sort each item into box A, B, C or D. Be ready to explain one choice.
The foreman asks Jesse to move the lumber off the access road before the crane truck arrives in 20 minutes.
Jesse's first aid ticket runs out in two months.
A friend texts during work about the weekend hockey pool.
Registration for Jesse's Level 1 technical training opens this week, and seats fill quickly.
A tool borrowed from the tool crib must be returned before the end of today's shift.
A phone number Jesse does not know keeps calling during work.
Jesse wants to study for Thursday's trade math quiz.
Task 4 (level 2) Plan the night before a 6:50 a.m. start. Your alarm is set for 4:45 a.m. Adults are advised to get 7 to 9 hours of sleep.
a. What is the latest bedtime that still gives 8 hours of sleep?
b. List four things you can do the night before so the morning goes smoothly.
Task 5 (level 2) On the first day of this program the group agrees on how it will work together. Write three agreements you want this group to keep. Make each one something people can see or hear, for example "Phones on silent during class."
Check yourself
Why do you plan from the start time instead of from the time you wake up?
What three things should a message about being late or sick include?
Give one example of a task that is important but not urgent for an apprentice.
Name two things your employer must tell you in your first-day orientation.

lessons.title: Owning your work and your mistakes
lessons.text:
Report mistakes early, focus on what you control, and answer criticism without blaming or caving in.
All people and companies in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
Everyone on a crew makes mistakes. A sleeve in the wrong spot or a mislabelled breaker costs little to fix today and a lot to fix after the concrete is poured or the inspector arrives. Foremen trust the apprentice who speaks up early, not the one who never seems to make mistakes. In BC, reporting an unsafe condition or act is also the law.
Key ideas
What accountability looks like
Being accountable means you:
do what you said you would do, or say early that you cannot
tell the truth about where your work is at, including what is not done
report mistakes and hazards as soon as you see them
fix what is yours to fix and learn from it
It does not mean taking the blame for things that were not yours, or saying sorry for everything.
What the law says about reporting
Under BC's Occupational Health and Safety Regulation (section 3.10), anyone who sees what looks like an unsafe or harmful condition or act must report it to a supervisor or the employer as soon as possible. If you are hurt at work, WorkSafeBC says to report it to your employer as soon as possible. Employers are not allowed to punish workers for raising a health and safety issue.
Control, influence and no control
Put your energy where it can make a difference.
You control You can influence You cannot control
Your actions and words What your crew decides The weather
When you leave home How your foreman sees you Other people's moods
How you answer criticism The order of tasks, if you ask A supplier's delivery truck
Reporting a mistake in four parts
What happened. Plain facts, no excuses.
What I have done. Any step you already took to make it safe or stop it getting worse.
What I need. A decision, help or materials.
What I will do next time. One specific change.
Worked example. Marcus is a first-year plumbing apprentice at Salal Creek Mechanical Ltd. At 4:30 p.m. he sees that he set out the floor sleeves on Level 2 from revision B of the drawing. Revision C moved two sleeves. The slab pour is booked for 7:00 a.m. tomorrow. He calls his foreman, Angela, right away:
"Angela, it's Marcus. I set the Level 2 sleeves from revision B. Revision C moved sleeves 4 and 7 about a metre east. I've flagged both with orange tape and haven't moved anything yet. I need to know if I should reset them tonight or first thing at 6. From now on I'll check the revision letter on the drawing before I lay out."
Marcus did not blame the drawing office or say "it's not a big deal". He gave Angela what she needed to decide before the pour.
Worked example: six studs cut short
Jesse is a first-year carpentry apprentice at Riverbend Framing Ltd. The cut list for the Unit 2 kneewall calls for 6 studs at 1200 mm. At 10:30 a.m. Jesse checks the first stud against the wall and sees a gap. He measures all 6. They are 1180 mm, 20 mm short. He read 1180 from the line below on the cut list.
Weak report. "Uh, a few studs came out short. The tape must be off. Not a big deal." This does not say how many, how short, or what Jesse did. It blames the tape. The foreman has to dig for the facts.
Strong report, step by step.
What happened. "I cut the 6 kneewall studs for Unit 2 at 1180 instead of 1200. I read the wrong line on the cut list."
What I have done. "I've set them aside, marked them SHORT and haven't nailed any in."
What I need. "I need 6 more studs from the stack. Do you want the short ones used as blocking?"
What I will do next time. "I'll check the first cut against the cut list and the wall before I cut the rest."
Why speak up now? If the short studs were nailed in, the kneewall would sit 20 mm low and the rafters would not bear on it properly. Fixing it now takes a few minutes. Fixing it after the rafters are on could take hours. The 1180 mm pieces are still useful as blocking, so nothing is wasted.
Answering criticism: the A B C D tools
These four tools come from an ACCESS lesson. Use them alone or together.
Acknowledge: accept a fair point without a long apology. "You're right, I left the gang box open. I'll lock it before I leave."
Boundaries: say how you expect to be treated. "I'd like to talk about this away from the crew. And please drop the name-calling."
Clarify: ask for details so you can fix the real problem. "What part of the cut looks wrong to you?"
Disagree: calmly correct something untrue. "I disagree. I've been on time every day this month. If there's a problem with today, let's talk about it."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Mark each statement O (owning it) or E (excuse or blame).
"The drawing was confusing, so it's not my fault."
"I measured from the wrong gridline. I'll recheck the rest before I cut."
"Nobody told me the pour moved to Thursday."
"I missed the start of the toolbox talk. Can you give me the hazards I missed?"
"Everyone else leaves their tools out too."
Task 2 (level 1) Sort these into control, influence or no control: the bus being late, what time you get up, your foreman's mood, the questions you ask in class, the date of your Level 1 exam, whether you study tonight, what a co-worker says about you, whether you report a frayed extension cord.
Task 3 (level 2) Sam, an electrical apprentice at Coastline Electrical Contractors, finds out at 3:00 p.m. that two circuits on the panel directory in Suite 204 are labelled the wrong way round. The inspector comes tomorrow at 9:00 a.m. Write what Sam should say to the foreman, using the four parts.
Task 4 (level 2) Draw a ripple: a small circle in the middle and three rings around it. In the centre, write a decision, such as "skip Friday's class to work an extra paid shift", or one of your own. In ring 1, write how it affects you (good and bad). In ring 2, the people closest to you. In ring 3, others such as classmates, your sponsor or your crew. You do not have to share a personal decision.
Task 5 (level 2) With a partner, choose a tool (A, B, C or D) for each statement and practise a reply. Write your best reply for one of them.
"You left the gang box open again. Do you even care about this job?"
"This work is sloppy."
"You're always late." (You have been on time all month.)
"Are you stupid? Anyone could do that cut." (Said in front of the crew.)
Check yourself
Under BC law, what must you do when you see what looks like an unsafe condition?
What are the four parts of reporting a mistake?
Name two things that are in your control at work.
Which A B C D tool helps you find out what the real problem is?

lessons.title: Responding to change on a project
lessons.text:
Read a change notice, sort what changed from what stayed the same, and rebuild your plan for the day.
All people, companies and projects in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
No construction project goes exactly to plan. Drawings get revised, deliveries come late, rain moves a pour and crew members change. The workers who do well are not the ones who never get thrown off. They are the ones who find out what changed, keep the parts of the plan that still work, and get back to productive work quickly.
Key ideas
Expected and unexpected change
Some changes you can see coming: a rain forecast, a drawing with a new revision letter, a holiday week. Others hit without warning: a broken pump, a sick foreman, a wrong delivery. You can get ahead of expected change by checking the forecast, the schedule and the revision block on your drawings each day.
Five steps when something changes
Notice. Read or hear the whole change. Check that it is the latest version.
Sort. Make three lists: what changed, what stays the same, what you still do not know.
Ask. Get answers to the "do not know" list from the right person.
Adjust. Rebuild your plan. Keep everything that still works.
Check. At the end, confirm the new plan did what it needed to.
Keep trying, or change the approach?
Ask yourself:
Is it safe? If not, stop and report it. Never "keep trying" at something unsafe.
Is the same method failing again and again? Try a different method or ask for help.
Am I still making progress, even slowly? Keep going.
Is the problem outside my control (weather, a crane down)? Switch to a task you can do and tell your supervisor.
Steady anchors
When a lot is changing, it helps to know what stays steady. The writer Alvin Toffler called these "personal stability zones": the people, places, routines and beliefs that stay the same while other parts of life change. A morning routine, a family call every Sunday or a weekly hockey game can all be anchors. The ACCESS lesson this page replaces put it this way: we need both roots and wings.
Worked example: a plumbing crew's change memo
This memo is for a different crew than the one in the practice tasks.
Salal Creek Mechanical Ltd. · Site memo 9
Project: Harbour Road Clinic Date: Tuesday, May 5, 6:45 a.m. From: Angela Moss, foreman To: Plumbing crew
The Level 2 washroom fixtures arrive Thursday, not Wednesday.
The Level 1 rough-in inspection stays Wednesday at 1:00 p.m.
Drawing P-201 is now revision D. Floor drain FD-3 moves 600 mm north.
Hot work permits now come from the site office, not the trailer.
The crew's plan for Wednesday before the memo:
Time Task
7:00 to 7:15 Toolbox talk
7:15 to 10:00 Set Level 2 washroom fixtures
10:15 to 12:00 Set Level 2 washroom fixtures
12:30 to 1:00 Prepare for the Level 1 inspection
1:00 to 2:00 Level 1 inspection
2:00 to 3:30 Install FD-3
Step 1. Notice. Read all four items. Check that P-201 on the table is revision D.
Step 2. Sort.
Changed Stays the same Still do not know
Fixtures arrive Thursday Inspection Wednesday at 1:00 Is the old FD-3 sleeve already cast in the slab?
FD-3 moves 600 mm north (rev D) Toolbox talk, breaks and lunch
Hot work permits come from the site office
Step 3. Ask. One question for Angela: "Rev D moves FD-3 600 mm north. Is the old sleeve already in the slab, and do we core a new hole or wait for the engineer?"
Step 4. Adjust. Setting fixtures is gone on Wednesday. That frees 7:15 to 10:00 and 10:15 to 12:00. FD-3 waits for an answer. The new plan:
Time Task
7:00 to 7:15 Toolbox talk. Ask Angela about FD-3.
7:15 to 10:00 Prepare the Level 1 inspection: check every joint, test, label
10:15 to 12:00 Stage the Level 2 washrooms for Thursday's fixtures
12:30 to 1:00 Walk the Level 1 rough-in with Angela
1:00 to 2:00 Level 1 inspection
2:00 to 3:30 Install FD-3 at the rev D location if Angela says go. If not, mark the old revision C prints SUPERSEDED and keep staging.
Step 5. Check. At 3:30 the crew checks: inspection done, Level 2 ready for Thursday, FD-3 question answered.
The change notice
Riverbend Framing Ltd. · Site memo 14
Project: Cedar Row Townhomes Date: Tuesday, March 10 From: Rob Lacey, site superintendent To: Framing crew
Drawing A-301 is now revision C. In Unit 4, window W3 on the east wall changes from 1220 mm wide to 1525 mm wide. The header for W3 changes. The new header arrives Thursday morning.
Do not frame the Unit 4 east wall until the new header is on site. All other Unit 4 walls go ahead as planned.
Rain is forecast for Wednesday afternoon. Cover the lumber stack by noon Wednesday.
Mark any printed copy of A-301 revision B "SUPERSEDED" and take it out of the site trailer.
Questions to Rob on radio channel 3.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Read Site memo 14. Make three lists: what changed, what stays the same, and what you still do not know. Put at least two items in each list.
Changed Stays the same Still do not know
Task 2 (level 2) This was the crew's plan for Wednesday before the memo. Lunch is 12:00 to 12:30.
Time Task
7:00 to 7:15 Toolbox talk
7:15 to 10:15 Frame Unit 4 east wall
10:15 to 12:00 Frame Unit 4 north wall
12:30 to 3:30 Frame Unit 4 west wall
a. Which task can no longer happen on Wednesday? b. How many hours of work does that free up? c. Write a new plan for Wednesday that follows the memo. Include covering the lumber (allow 30 minutes). Mark one gap where you would ask Rob what to do.
Task 3 (level 2) For each situation, write keep trying, change the approach, or stop and report, and give a reason.
You have practised converting feet and inches to millimetres twice and still mix them up.
You have phoned the supplier three times about a noon delivery and nobody answers.
The crane is shut down for high wind, and your task needs the crane.
The ladder you were given has a cracked rail.
Your first try at a stair stringer layout was close, and the second try was better.
Task 4 (level 1) List three steady anchors in your own life: people, places, routines or beliefs that stay the same when other things change. This is for you. You do not have to share it.
Task 5 (level 2) Think of a change that was a turning point in your life. You choose how much to write and whether to share it.
a. Did you start the change, or did someone or something else? b. What did you do at first? What did you do later? c. What helped you most?
Check yourself
What are the five steps when something changes?
Name two expected changes you can check for every morning on a job site.
When should you never keep trying?
What is a steady anchor?

lessons.title: Staying calm under pressure and handling anger
lessons.text:
Notice anger early, cool down in ways that work, and say what you need without blowing up or bottling it up.
All people and companies in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
Job sites are full of pressure: deadlines, noise, heat, changing plans and people with strong opinions. Anger is a normal feeling, and it often tells you something matters. But anger near power tools, ladders, moving equipment or traffic can get someone hurt. People who stay calm under pressure, or calm down quickly after a flare-up, are the ones a crew trusts with responsibility.
Key ideas
Notice it early
Anger shows up in the body before it shows up in words. Common signs are a hot face, a fast heartbeat, tight jaw or fists, shallow breathing, a loud voice and racing thoughts. The earlier you notice, the more choices you have.
Anger styles
People learn different ways of dealing with anger from family, culture and past experience. This list comes from an ACCESS lesson.
Style What it looks like
Exploding Yelling, swearing, slamming, threatening.
Holding it in Saying nothing and letting it build.
Withholding Silent treatment, showing up late, "forgetting" a task for the person.
Body Headaches, stomach pain, poor sleep from anger that is not dealt with.
Turning it on yourself "It's all my fault. I'm useless."
Redirecting Taking it out on something or someone else, such as kicking a bin.
Channelling Turning the energy into getting a task done.
Assertive Saying calmly and directly what happened and what you need.
Assertive is usually the most useful style when the situation allows it.
What research says about cooling down
Many people believe that "letting off steam" by hitting something or going for a hard run gets rid of anger. A 2024 review of 154 studies found that activities that calm the body down (slow breathing, relaxing tight muscles, mindfulness, gentle yoga) reduced anger and aggression. Activities that rev the body up (hitting a bag, jogging, cycling) did not reduce anger on average. Exercise is good for your health, but it is not the best cool-down in the moment.
Cool-down options you can choose from:
If it is safe, put the tool down and step away. Say "I need five minutes."
Breathe out slowly, longer than you breathe in, a few times.
Unclench your jaw, drop your shoulders, open your hands.
Get a drink of water or some fresh air.
Talk it through later with someone you trust.
Use what works for you. Nobody has to do a breathing exercise to show they can handle pressure.
Then say what you need
Once you are calmer, an assertive statement has three parts:
"When [what happened], I [how it affected me]. I need [what you are asking for]."
Example: "When my tools went missing from the gang box, I lost half an hour. I need people to sign tools out on the sheet."
If you blew up, recover: own it the way you learned in lesson 2, and fix what you can.
Worked example: shouted at by the saw
Kyle is a first-year carpentry apprentice. At 10:00 a.m. the foreman walks past the saw station and shouts, in front of the crew: "What a mess! Somebody's going to break an ankle on these offcuts. Clean it up!"
1. Notice. Kyle's face goes hot and his hands close into fists. Part of the mess is his. Part is from the other crew. He wants to shout back, "It's not all mine!"
2. Step away from the argument, not the job. The saw is off. Kyle takes one slow breath out and says only: "Okay. I'll clean it up now."
3. Cool down. While he sweeps, he breathes out slowly, longer than he breathes in, and drops his shoulders. After a few minutes his heart rate is down.
4. Check the facts. The foreman's point was fair. Offcuts on the floor by a saw are a trip hazard. The way he said it, in front of the crew, is what stung.
5. Say what you need, at the right time. At break Kyle asks for a minute one-on-one:
"When you shouted at me about the saw station in front of the crew, I felt embarrassed and nearly snapped back. I'll clear my offcuts every hour from now on. I need you to tell me one-on-one next time."
Kyle owned his part, kept the crew safe and said what he needed. He did not blow up, and he did not bottle it up.
When the anger is coming at you
Keep your distance and keep your voice low and even.
Do not argue with someone who is shouting. Say you will talk when things are calmer.
If you feel unsafe, leave the area and tell your supervisor.
WorkSafeBC describes workplace bullying and harassment as actions that the person knew, or should have known, would humiliate or intimidate a worker. A supervisor taking reasonable action to manage and direct workers is not bullying. If you experience or see bullying and harassment, report it to your employer. If your employer does not take reasonable steps, you can call WorkSafeBC's Prevention Information Line at 604-276-3100 or toll-free 1-888-621-7233.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) List three signs in your body that tell you anger is building. Circle the one you usually notice first.
Task 2 (level 1) Name the anger style in each situation.
Trent slams his tool bag down and swears at the apprentice.
Mia is angry at her foreman. She says nothing, then "forgets" to order the parts he asked for.
Leo says nothing all week, but gets headaches every afternoon.
After being yelled at, Ana tells herself, "I'm useless. I always mess up."
At break, Raj tells the foreman, "When the plan changed without notice, I lost an hour. Can you text me changes?"
After a bad call with the supplier, Jo kicks the recycling bin in the lunchroom.
Task 3 (level 2) Rewrite each outburst as an assertive statement using "When , I . I need ___."
"Who keeps taking my tape? I'm sick of you guys!"
"This schedule is garbage. Nobody here knows what they're doing."
"Forget it. I'll just do everything myself."
Task 4 (level 2) Make your own cool-down plan. This is for you. You do not have to share it.
My earliest sign: ____
One calming action I will try: ____
What I will say to step away: ____
Who I can talk to afterwards: ____
Task 5 (level 2) Is each one reasonable direction or possible bullying and harassment? What could the worker do?
The foreman tells you to redo a cut that is the wrong length.
A co-worker hides your tools every day and laughs about it with others.
Your supervisor moves you to clean-up for the day because the crane is down.
A journeyperson calls you names in front of the crew, again and again.
The foreman gives you a written warning after you were late three times without calling.
Check yourself
Why does it help to notice anger early?
Which kind of activity reduced anger in the 2024 review: ones that calm the body or ones that rev it up?
What are the three parts of an assertive statement?
Who should you report workplace bullying and harassment to first?

lessons.title: Setbacks, fear of failure and trying again
lessons.text:
Use fear as a signal, turn a failed attempt into a plan, and know how exam rewrites work for BC apprentices.
All people in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
Every tradesperson has failed something: a weld test, a level exam, an interview, a first try at a stair layout. Apprentices in BC write level exams and a final certification exam, and not everyone passes the first time. What separates people who finish their apprenticeship from those who quit is often not talent. It is what they do in the week after a setback.
Key ideas
Fear can help or hold you back
Fear is a normal reaction to danger or to something new. An ACCESS lesson put it this way: healthy fear gets you moving, unhealthy fear freezes you.
Healthy fear: you are nervous about working at heights, so you check your harness and anchor twice.
Unhealthy fear: you are so afraid of failing the exam that you never register for it.
One label does not define you
"I'm stupid." "I'm bad at math." "I always mess up." A label like this is a whole judgement about you, and it gives you nothing to work on. Swap the label for something specific you can practise.
Label Specific
"I'm bad at math." "I haven't learned to change fractions to decimals yet."
"I'm useless with blueprints." "I mix up the plan view and the elevation view."
Believing you can improve, and doing the work
You may have heard of "growth mindset": the idea that skills grow with practice. That idea is true for trade skills. But the research on growth mindset lessons is more modest than the posters suggest. Large reviews have found that being told about growth mindset, on its own, makes little or no difference to most students' marks. One large study found a small benefit for lower-achieving students, mostly where the people around them backed the message up.
So believing you can get better is a good start, not the whole answer. What moves your results is specific practice, good study methods (lesson 6), feedback, and people who support you.
Five steps after a setback
Feel it. Being disappointed or angry is normal. Give it a little time.
Get the facts. What was the score? Which parts went well and which did not?
Find one or two causes you can work on. For example, "I didn't practise with timed questions."
Make a plan. Write what you will do, when, and who will help.
Try again. Then check what changed.
Worked example. Priya is a first-year carpentry apprentice. On March 3 she writes her Level 1 exam and scores 64 percent. The pass mark is 70 percent.
Facts: she did well on safety and tools, and poorly on the math and drawings questions.
Cause she can work on: she studied by rereading her notes and never practised timed questions.
Plan: practise 30 minutes a day, five days a week, using practice questions. Meet a classmate on Saturdays to quiz each other. Ask her instructor which drawing topics to review.
Rewrite: SkilledTradesBC rewrites have a 30-day waiting period from the last attempt. Thirty days after March 3 is April 2, so April 2 is the earliest she can rewrite.
Worked example: a 4-week plan after missing by 4 percent
Owen is a first-year welding apprentice. On April 10 he writes his Level 1 exam and scores 66 percent. The pass mark is 70 percent, so he missed by 70 − 66 = 4 percentage points.
1. Feel it. Owen is angry for a day. He goes for a long walk with his dog and does not open his notes.
2. Get the facts. His results show he did well on safety and welding processes. He did poorly on drawings and on metric conversions.
3. Find causes he can work on. He studied drawings by rereading. He never practised conversions against the clock.
4. Make a plan. Rewrites have a 30-day waiting period from the last attempt. April has 30 days, so 30 days after April 10 is May 10. That gives Owen about 4 weeks.
Weeks What How often Minutes
1 and 2 Practice questions on drawings and metric only 25 min a day, 6 days a week 25 × 6 × 2 = 300
3 and 4 Mixed practice tests, timed, all topics 45 min, 3 times a week 45 × 3 × 2 = 270
Total 570
570 minutes ÷ 60 = 9.5 hours of practice, spread over 4 weeks. He asks his instructor for a drawing he can practise reading each week.
5. Try again. Owen books the rewrite for May 12 in the SkilledTradesBC Portal. After it, he will check which topics improved.
Exam rewrites for BC apprentices
SkilledTradesBC sets these rules for apprentices who score below 70 percent:
Attempt What you must do first Fee
2nd Schedule the rewrite through the SkilledTradesBC Portal. No fee
3rd Contact your Apprenticeship Advisor for guidance and approval. Certification exam $100. Level exam no fee.
4th Send proof of upgrading. Certification exam $100. Level exam no fee.
5th A member of the Completions Team contacts you for support first. Certification exam $100. Level exam no fee.
Check skilledtradesbc.ca/exam-rewrites before you book, because rules and fees can change.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Rewrite each label as something specific you could practise.
"I'm hopeless at reading a tape measure."
"I'm not a test person."
"I'm too old to learn computers."
"I always freeze up when the foreman watches me."
Task 2 (level 1) Mark each one H (healthy fear) or U (unhealthy fear).
You are nervous about using a new saw, so you ask for a demonstration.
You are worried about speaking at the toolbox talk, so you write two notes on a card.
You are afraid of being laughed at, so you do not ask how the lockout works.
You are scared of failing, so you do not register for technical training.
You feel uneasy about a trench with no shoring, so you stay out and tell the foreman.
Task 3 (level 2) Use Priya's plan.
a. How many minutes will she practise in one week? b. She has 4 weeks before her rewrite. How many hours is that in total? c. Write one more thing she could add to her plan.
Task 4 (level 2) Make a fear action plan. Use a fear of your own, or use this one: "I'm afraid I'll fail my first job interview."
The fear is: ____
Who have I talked to about it? ____
Who can be my buddy for this? ____
What will I agree to do, and by when? ____
What small step will I take each day this week? ____
Task 5 (level 2) Derek is an electrical apprentice. He has scored below 70 percent on his certification exam twice.
a. What must he do before he can book a third attempt? b. What will the third attempt cost? c. If he scores below 70 percent again, what must he send before a fourth attempt?
Check yourself
What is the difference between healthy and unhealthy fear?
Why is "I'm bad at math" less useful than "I haven't learned ratios yet"?
What does research say about growth mindset lessons on their own?
What are the five steps after a setback?

lessons.title: Learning strategies that work
lessons.text:
Find out why "learning styles" do not hold up, and use study methods with strong evidence for trade school and exams.
All people in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
A trade is learned over years: on the job, in technical training, from code books, manuals and drawings. Apprentices in BC write level exams and a certification exam that cover everything from all levels of training. How you study decides how much you still remember on exam day and on the job a year later. Some of the most popular study habits do very little. A few simple ones work much better.
Key ideas
What about learning styles?
You may have been told you are a "visual", "auditory" or "hands-on" learner, and that you learn best when teaching matches your style. Many people believe this. It has been tested.
In 2008, a team of psychologists reviewed the research. They found no good evidence that matching teaching to a person's learning style improves learning. Some well-designed studies found the opposite.
In a 2015 study, adults who said they were "auditory" learners did not learn more from an audiobook, and "visual" learners did not learn more from reading the same book.
People really do have preferences, and that is fine. But the best way to learn something depends mostly on the thing being learned. You learn a knot by tying it, a wiring diagram by looking at it, and the steps of a procedure by doing them and saying them. Good learners use all of these.
Study methods ranked by evidence
A large 2013 review rated ten common study methods.
Evidence Method What it looks like for an apprentice
Strong Practice testing Quiz yourself with flash cards or practice questions instead of rereading.
Strong Spaced practice Study a little on many days instead of all at once the night before.
Moderate Explaining steps Say out loud why each step of a calculation or procedure works.
Moderate Asking why Ask "why is this true?" about a fact or rule, and answer it.
Moderate Mixing problem types Mix area, volume and conversion questions in one practice set.
Weak Rereading Reading the same notes again. Feels good, does little.
Weak Highlighting Colouring the textbook. Feels good, does little.
Worked example
Jordan has two weeks before a Level 1 exam and about 6 hours to study.
Plan A: reread the notes for 6 hours the night before.
Plan B: 30 minutes a day for 12 days. Each session starts with 10 practice questions from memory, then checks the answers, then reviews only what was wrong. The topics are mixed.
Both plans use 6 hours (12 × 30 = 360 minutes). Plan B uses practice testing, spacing and mixing, so Jordan will remember far more on exam day.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Mark each study method S (strong evidence), M (moderate) or W (weak).
Highlighting every important line in the textbook.
Answering practice exam questions, then checking the answers.
Studying 20 minutes a day for two weeks.
Explaining to a classmate why you add the overhang before cutting a rafter.
Reading your notes three times the night before the test.
Mixing fraction, metric conversion and area problems in one practice set.
Asking yourself why a rule in the safety manual exists.
Task 2 (level 1) Pick a topic from this program or your trade (for example, PPE, metric conversion, a tool, or a safety rule). Write five practice questions with the answers. Use them to quiz a partner.
Task 3 (level 2) Your level exam is in two weeks. You can study 25 minutes on 10 of the next 14 days.
a. How many minutes is that in total? How many hours and minutes? b. Choose your 10 days and write them down (for example, "Mon, Tue, Thu ..."). c. For one session, write what you will do in each part of the 25 minutes.
Task 4 (level 2) Explain the steps of this conversion out loud to a partner. Say why each step works. Your partner checks.
Convert 3 feet 6 inches to millimetres.
Task 5 (level 2) A classmate says: "I'm a hands-on learner, so I don't need to read the code book. I'll just learn it on the job." Write what you would say back. Use what you learned today.
Check yourself
What did researchers find when they tested matching teaching to learning styles?
Name the two study methods with the strongest evidence.
Why is rereading your notes a weak method?
What should decide how you learn something new?

lessons.title: Keep learning as an apprentice in BC
lessons.text:
Map the BC apprenticeship path from sponsor to Red Seal, research a trade, and build a learning plan you can check.
All people in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
A Red Seal or Certificate of Qualification is not handed out for time served. You earn it by learning on the job, in the classroom and at the exam table over several years. Apprentices who know the steps, track their hours and plan their training finish. Those who leave it to chance often stall at Level 1 or Level 2. Knowing the path also helps you choose a trade that fits you.
Key ideas
How jobs are grouped in Canada
Canada's National Occupational Classification (NOC 2021) gives every occupation a five-digit code. The second digit is the TEER category (Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities).
TEER What the job usually needs
0 Management experience
1 A university degree
2 A college program of 2 to 3 years, or an apprenticeship of 2 to 5 years, or supervisory or major safety duties
3 A college program or apprenticeship of less than 2 years, or more than 6 months of on-the-job training
4 Secondary school, or several weeks of on-the-job training
5 A short work demonstration and no formal education
Examples: 72310 Carpenters, 72200 Electricians (except industrial and power system) and 72106 Welders and related machine operators are all TEER 2.
WorkBC's 2025 Labour Market Outlook forecasts about 228,400 job openings in TEER 2 and 181,300 in TEER 3 in BC from 2025 to 2035. Every occupation on its High Opportunity Occupations list is in TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3, which means some training after high school.
The BC apprenticeship path
SkilledTradesBC describes an apprenticeship as about 80 percent work-based training with a sponsor and about 20 percent in-class technical training. Across all trades, the average time to finish is 4 years.
Find your trade. SkilledTradesBC has a "find your trade" quiz.
Find a sponsor. A sponsor is often your employer. They make sure you are trained by a certified journeyperson and they report your hours.
Register as an apprentice in the SkilledTradesBC Portal. Your sponsor confirms it.
Register for technical training at a SkilledTradesBC-designated training provider. Classes fill up quickly, so register early. Many apprentices go once a year.
Pass the Standard Level Exams that come with each level of technical training.
Pass the certification exam (70 percent or higher) after all levels are done.
Get a Recommendation for Certification from your sponsor.
Receive your credential: a Certificate of Qualification for BC, with a Red Seal Endorsement in Red Seal trades so you can work across Canada.
Compulsory trades
In BC, seven trades fall under Skilled Trades Certification (compulsory trades): Construction Electrician, Industrial Electrician, Powerline Technician, Steamfitter/Pipefitter, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Mechanic, Gasfitter Class A and Class B, and Sheet Metal Worker. To work in these trades you must be a registered apprentice, a trade qualifier or a certified journeyperson. Employers must keep a ratio of no more than two apprentices to one journeyperson. Mobile Crane Operator and Tower Crane Operator become compulsory trades on July 5, 2027.
Paying for technical training
The Canada Apprentice Loan gives interest-free loans of up to $4,000 per period of technical training to apprentices registered in a Red Seal trade.
SkilledTradesBC advises apprentices to apply for Employment Insurance (EI) for their technical training period.
A learning plan you can check
The old ACCESS Individual Enhancement Plan tracked short, mid and long-term goals. A good plan for each goal names:
what you will do
by when
who or what will help
how you will know it is done
Worked example. Tasha wants to be a construction electrician.
Goal By when Help How I'll know
Short: apply to 5 electrical contractors for an apprentice job End of next month Program staff, online job boards 5 applications sent
Mid: registered apprentice with 1,000 hours logged In 12 months Sponsor, SkilledTradesBC Portal Hours show in the Portal
Long: Red Seal Endorsement In 5 years Sponsor, training provider, study group Certificate received
Worked example: how many weeks to the next level?
Tasha is now a registered construction electrician apprentice. Her sponsor wants her to have 1,500 work-based training hours before she goes to Level 2. This is her sponsor's plan, not a SkilledTradesBC rule. The Portal shows 1,200 hours. She works 38 hours a week.
Step 1. Hours to go. 1,500 − 1,200 = 300 hours.
Step 2. Weeks to go. 300 ÷ 38 = 7.89. Round up to 8 weeks, because after 7 weeks she would have only 7 × 38 = 266 more hours, 34 short.
Step 3. Check. After 8 weeks: 1,200 + 8 × 38 = 1,200 + 304 = 1,504 hours. That is past 1,500.
Step 4. Act now. Classes fill quickly, so Tasha registers for Level 2 technical training today, for a class that starts after week 8. She also writes a goal she can check: "1,500 hours in the Portal in 8 weeks."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Put these apprenticeship steps in order. Number them 1 to 8.
Pass the certification exam.
Find a sponsor.
Register for technical training.
Receive a Certificate of Qualification.
Find your trade.
Get a Recommendation for Certification.
Register as an apprentice in the Portal.
Pass the Standard Level Exams.
Task 2 (level 2) a. In the code 72310, which digit tells you the TEER? What TEER is it? b. What training does a TEER 2 trade usually need? c. Why might a TEER 2 job usually pay more than a TEER 4 job? Give one reason.
Task 3 (level 2) Choose a trade you are interested in. Look it up on WorkBC's career profiles (workbc.ca/plan-career/explore-careers/career-profiles) and on skilledtradesbc.ca. Fill in the table with what you find today, and write where each fact came from.
Item What I found Where I found it
Trade name
NOC code and TEER
Median wage in BC
Job outlook in BC
Levels of technical training
Work-based training hours required
Red Seal trade?
Compulsory trade in BC?
Task 4 (level 2) Your Red Seal trade has 4 levels of technical training. What is the most you could borrow through the Canada Apprentice Loan over the whole apprenticeship? Show your work.
Task 5 (level 3) Write your own learning plan with one short-term goal (next 3 months), one mid-term goal (next year) and one long-term goal (next 5 years). For each goal fill in: what, by when, help, and how you will know it is done.
Goal By when Help How I'll know
Short:
Mid:
Long:
Check yourself
In a NOC code, which digit is the TEER?
About what share of an apprenticeship is work-based training?
What mark do you need on the certification exam?
Name two of BC's compulsory trades.
Who gives the Recommendation for Certification?
Beyond the Red Seal: the route to a BCIT degree
A Red Seal does not have to be the end of your learning. It can also open the door to a degree. BCIT's Bachelor of Technology in Construction Management (BTech CM) has an entry route for certified tradespeople, called Option D. When it was checked in November 2026, BCIT listed these requirements for Option D:
a Red Seal in an approved trade
Math 11 at 60%, or BCIT's BLDT 1011 (Applied Construction Math) at 60%
BCIT's Construction Operations Associate Certificate, with a GPA of at least 67%
at least one year of construction work on top of your apprenticeship hours
English Studies 12 at 73%
a pre-entry assessment with the program head before you apply
Requirements can change. Confirm them with the program at cmgt@bcit.ca before you build a plan around them.
The Construction Operations tab in the Numeracy Hub has more on this route and practice with the construction math it uses.

lessons.title: Looking after yourself with wellness and support in BC
lessons.text:
Look after your sleep, energy and boundaries, map your supports, and know which BC help line to call and when.
All people in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
Trades work is hard on the body and the mind: early starts, long commutes, heavy lifting, noise, pressure to keep up, and sometimes weeks away at camp. WorkSafeBC tells workers never to work while overly tired or under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Looking after yourself is not a luxury. It is part of showing up fit for work, and it is how people last long enough in a trade to get their ticket.
Key ideas
The basics
The Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for adults aged 18 to 64 recommend:
7 to 9 hours of good-quality sleep, with regular bed and wake-up times
at least 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous activity
muscle-strengthening activities at least twice a week
Signs that stress is building up include trouble sleeping, getting irritated quickly, headaches, pulling away from people, and drinking or using more than usual.
A wholistic view of wellness
The First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) in BC shares the First Nations Perspective on Health and Wellness. It shows wellness as circles:
