In the centre is the individual. Wellness starts with each of us taking responsibility for our own health.
The second circle is the mental, emotional, spiritual and physical sides of a healthy, balanced life.
The third circle is the values that hold wellness up: respect, wisdom, responsibility and relationships.
The outer circle is the people and places we come from: Nations, family, community and land.
FNHA says the model is a starting point for discussion. Each Nation has its own teachings about wellness and balance. If you want to learn the teachings of your own Nation, ask an Elder or knowledge keeper from your community, or ask ACCESS staff to help you connect.
Boundaries: saying no without burning bridges
A boundary is a line you draw to protect your time, health or goals. Saying no is hard when you want to help, when it is family, or when it is your boss. A simple pattern:
Say no clearly. "I can't do that."
Give a short reason, if you want to. You do not owe a long explanation.
Offer something else, if you can. "I can help on Sunday instead."
Example: "I can't lend you the truck tonight. I start at 6:30 tomorrow and I need it. I can drive you Saturday."
Worked example: a week plan and one boundary
Amber is a first-year apprentice. She works five 8-hour shifts, drives 1 hour each way to work, and has class two evenings a week for 3 hours. She wants 8 hours of sleep a night and 2 hours a day with her family. Meals and chores take about 3 hours a day.
Add up her week. A week has 7 × 24 = 168 hours.
Item Working Hours
Sleep 8 × 7 56
Work 8 × 5 40
Travel 2 × 5 10
Class 3 × 2 6
Family 2 × 7 14
Meals and chores 3 × 7 21
Total 147
168 − 147 = 21 hours are left for rest, study and everything else.
The ask. Her cousin asks Amber to babysit three evenings a week, 3 hours each, including Tuesday and Thursday, her class nights. That would take 3 × 3 = 9 hours, leaving 21 − 9 = 12 hours, and it clashes with class.
The boundary, said out loud. Amber uses the three steps:
"I can't do three nights. Tuesday and Thursday are my class nights, and I need my sleep for my 6:30 starts. I can do Saturday afternoon."
She gives up 3 hours, not 9, and keeps her class and her sleep. 21 − 3 = 18 hours are still left.
Your worth is not for sale
An ACCESS lesson asked: can money buy self-esteem? Expensive trucks, boots and phones do not decide your worth. Keeping your word, learning your trade and treating people well build respect that lasts, including self-respect.
Your support network
Everyone needs people to turn to. Think of three kinds of support:
Practical help: a ride when your car breaks down, someone to watch the kids.
Someone to talk to: a friend, relative, Elder, mentor or classmate.
Professional and community help: counsellors, health services and help lines.
Have a backup plan for the things most likely to stop you getting to work, such as transportation and child care.
BC supports
If... Call or contact
Someone is in danger right now, or there is a medical emergency 9-1-1
You or someone you know is thinking about suicide or is in crisis Call or text 9-8-8 (Suicide Crisis Helpline), or call 1-800-784-2433 (1-800-SUICIDE), 24/7
You are Indigenous and want culturally aware crisis support in BC KUU-US Crisis Line, 1-800-588-8717, 24/7
You are First Nations, Inuit or Métis and want to talk to a counsellor Hope for Wellness Helpline, 1-855-242-3310, or online chat at hopeforwellness.ca, 24/7
You need emotional support or mental health information, not an emergency 310-6789 (no area code), 24/7
You want health advice from a nurse HealthLink BC, 8-1-1, nurses 24/7
You want same-day help for opioid use Opioid Treatment Access Line, 1-833-804-8111, 9 am to 4 pm
More supports are listed at helpstartshere.gov.bc.ca.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Using the four areas from the FNHA perspective, rate how you are doing this week from 1 (not well) to 5 (very well), and write one small thing you could do for each. This is private. You do not have to share it.
Area Rating 1 to 5 One small thing I could do
Mental
Emotional
Spiritual
Physical
Task 2 (level 1) Which support fits each situation?
Your friend tells you they are thinking about ending their life.
A co-worker collapses and is not breathing.
You cut your hand at home at 11 p.m. It is not bleeding badly, but you are not sure if it needs stitches.
You have felt low for weeks and want to talk to an Indigenous counsellor.
You are stressed and just need to talk to someone tonight.
Your cousin wants help today to get off opioids.
Task 3 (level 2) Write a "no" for each situation using the three steps.
Your cousin asks to borrow your truck the night before your first shift.
Your foreman asks you to stay late every day this week, and you have class on Wednesday night.
Your friends invite you out the night before your Level 1 exam.
Task 4 (level 2) Draw three circles labelled practical help, someone to talk to and professional or community help. Write at least one name or service in each. Then write a backup plan for getting to work if your usual ride falls through. This is private.
Task 5 (level 2) Your shift starts at 6:30 a.m. The drive takes 1 hour. You need 45 minutes to get up, eat and get ready.
a. What time must you wake up? b. What is the latest bedtime that gives you 7 hours of sleep? c. What is the latest bedtime that gives you 8 hours?
Check yourself
How many hours of sleep do the Canadian guidelines recommend for adults?
What are the four areas in the second circle of the FNHA First Nations Perspective on Health and Wellness?
What are the three steps for saying no?
What number can you call or text in Canada if someone is thinking about suicide?
Which line offers culturally aware crisis support for Indigenous people in BC?

lessons.title: Re-plan your day when the job changes
lessons.text:
Read a day plan as a bar chart, find what a change breaks, and build a new plan that keeps everything that still works.
All people, companies and projects in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
A day on site is planned around things that are booked: a crane, a lift, a concrete truck, an inspector. When one of them falls through, the whole plan can stall. Some crews stand around and wait. Good crews spend ten minutes re-planning and keep working. A new apprentice who can say "the lift is down, so here is what I can do until it is back" saves the foreman a headache and shows they can be trusted with more.
Lesson 3 showed you how to sort a change into what changed, what stayed the same and what you still do not know. This lesson goes one step further. You will rebuild the day itself, minute by minute, and check that the new plan works.
Key ideas
A day plan as a bar chart
A bar chart of the day shows time from left to right. Each task is a bar. The longer the bar, the longer the task. You can see at a glance what happens when.
Read a bar chart in three steps:
Read the time scale along the bottom.
Find the start and end of each bar.
Subtract to get the length: end time minus start time.
Example: a bar from 9:45 to 12:00 is 2 hours 15 minutes, or 135 minutes.
Fixed and movable
Fixed items cannot move unless someone else agrees: the toolbox talk, breaks, a booked crane or lift, an inspection, a concrete pour.
Movable items can shift to another time: cleaning up, prefab work at a bench, staging material, sorting fittings.
When a change hits, plan the fixed items first. Then fill the gaps with movable work.
Is the task ready to start?
A task is only ready when all five are in place:
Check Question
Material Is it on site and in the right place?
Information Do I have the right drawing, revision and instructions?
Permit Is any permit needed, such as a hot work permit, and is it issued?
Area Is the area clear and safe, with no other trade in the way?
Tools and equipment Are the tools, lift or crane here and working?
If even one answer is no, the task is not ready. Do not plan it into a gap.
Five questions to re-plan your day
What is fixed now? Mark the breaks, bookings and anything you cannot move.
What can not happen? Cross out every task that needs the thing that changed.
What is ready to start? Use the five checks.
What matters most? Safety first. Then work that other people are waiting on. Then work with a deadline.
Tell and confirm. Tell your foreman what changed, what you plan to do, and what will be late. Start once they agree.
Keep every part of the old plan that still works. A re-plan is not a fresh start.
Worked example
Rae is a first-year steamfitter/pipefitter apprentice with Fraser Bend Piping Ltd. On Tuesday she is hanging copper pipe on Level 3 of a new clinic. All overhead work on Level 3 needs the scissor lift. This is her plan for the day.
At 7:10 a.m., near the end of the toolbox talk, the foreman, Mo, says: "The scissor lift is down. The repair tech will have it running by 1:00." Here is how Rae re-plans.
Step 1. What is fixed now? Toolbox talk 7:00 to 7:15. Coffee break 9:30 to 9:45. Lunch 12:00 to 12:30. The lift is back at 1:00. The shift ends at 3:30.
Step 2. What can not happen? Everything on the lift before 1:00:
install hangers, 7:15 to 9:30 = 135 minutes
hang copper, 9:45 to 12:00 = 135 minutes
part of the afternoon copper, 12:30 to 1:00 = 30 minutes
That is 135 + 135 + 30 = 300 minutes of lift work that cannot happen this morning.
Step 3. What is ready to start? Rae checks three movable tasks.
Task Material Information Permit Area Tools Ready?
Prefab copper assemblies at the bench yes yes none needed yes yes yes
Stage hangers and fittings on Level 3 yes yes none needed yes yes yes
Pressure test prep yes yes none needed no, the pipe is not hung yet yes no
Step 4. What matters most? The hangers must go in first, because the copper hangs from them. So when the lift returns at 1:00, hangers come first.
Step 5. Tell and confirm. At 7:15, right after the toolbox talk, Rae finds Mo and tells him her plan:
"Mo, it's Rae. With the lift down I'll do prefab at the bench until 11:15, then stage the hangers and fittings on Level 3 before lunch. At 1:00 I'll install hangers until 3:15, then lock the lift and clean up. The copper and the test prep will move to Wednesday. Does that work?"
Mo agrees. Here is the new plan. The short blue block from 7:15 to 7:30 is time to talk to Mo and gather what she needs for the bench.
Check the new plan. Add up the minutes from 7:00 to 3:30:
Block Minutes
Toolbox talk, 7:00 to 7:15 15
Talk to Mo and gather material, 7:15 to 7:30 15
Prefab, 7:30 to 9:30 120
Coffee, 9:30 to 9:45 15
Prefab, 9:45 to 11:15 90
Stage parts, 11:15 to 12:00 45
Lunch, 12:00 to 12:30 30
Set up, 12:30 to 1:00 30
Install hangers, 1:00 to 3:15 135
Lock lift and clean up, 3:15 to 3:30 15
Total 510
The shift from 7:00 to 3:30 is 8 hours 30 minutes = 510 minutes. The new plan fills it exactly, with no gaps and no overlaps.
What moves to Wednesday? The old plan had 390 minutes of lift work: 135 + 135 + 120. The new plan has 135. So 390 − 135 = 255 minutes of copper hanging moves to Wednesday, plus the 60-minute test prep. That is 255 + 60 = 315 minutes, or 5 hours 15 minutes. Rae said so when she told Mo her plan, so he can plan Wednesday.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Rae's plan before the change.
a. How long is the first "Install hangers" bar, in minutes?
b. What time does test prep start?
c. How many minutes of lift work were in the old plan?
Task 2 (level 1) Mark each item F (fixed) or M (movable) for a framing crew.
Toolbox talk at 7:00
City inspection booked for 2:00
Sweeping the deck
Lunch at 12:00
Crane lift of roof trusses booked for 10:00
Cutting blocking at the saw station
Sorting hangers and nails for tomorrow
Task 3 (level 2) Riverbend Framing Ltd. plans this day: toolbox talk 7:00 to 7:15, frame walls 7:15 to 9:30, break 9:30 to 9:45, frame walls 9:45 to 12:00, lunch 12:00 to 12:30, frame walls 12:30 to 3:30.
a. How many minutes of wall framing are planned?
b. Write that as hours in decimal form.
c. Draw the day as a bar chart on grid paper. Use one square for 15 minutes.
Task 4 (level 2) Rae has 30 minutes free. Use the five checks. Which task is ready to start now? For each task that is not ready, name the check that fails.
Task Facts
A. Install firestop sleeves on Level 2 Sleeves on site. Drawing on hand. Drywallers are working in that area until 10:00.
B. Weld pipe supports in the mechanical room Supports and welder on site. The hot work permit has not been issued yet.
C. Prefab two valve assemblies at the bench Valves, pipe and fittings at the bench. Drawing on hand. Tools at the bench.
D. Pressure test the Level 1 piping Piping is complete. The test gauge is still at the shop.
Task 5 (level 2) A concrete pour is booked to start at 8:00 and take 2 hours 30 minutes. The batch plant calls: the first truck will be 2 hours 15 minutes late.
a. What time does the pour start now?
b. If the pour runs without a stop, what time does it finish?
c. The crew's lunch is 12:00 to 12:30. Concrete cannot wait. What should the foreman decide about lunch? Give one reasonable plan.
Task 6 (level 2) Write the text you would send your foreman when a change stops your work. Use this case: you are an electrical apprentice, and the drywall crew has not finished the room where you were to pull wire this morning. Include what changed, what you will do instead, what will be late, and one question.
Task 7 (level 3) Sky is an ironworker apprentice with Northshore Steel Erectors Ltd. This was the plan for Thursday:
Time Task
7:00 to 7:15 Toolbox talk
7:15 to 9:30 Set beams with the crane, Level 3
9:30 to 9:45 Break
9:45 to 12:00 Set beams with the crane, Level 3
12:00 to 12:30 Lunch
12:30 to 3:30 Bolt up the beams set in the morning
At 7:05 the crane operator reports a fault. The crane will be back at 11:00. Ready work without the crane: 40 connections on Level 2 still need bolting from yesterday, and the next load of steel needs to be shaken out (sorted and laid out by piece mark) on the ground.
a. Write a new plan from 7:15 to 3:30 that keeps the break and lunch.
b. How many minutes of crane time were planned? How many are in your new plan? How many minutes of beam setting move to another day?
c. Write the two-sentence radio call to the foreman.
Task 8 (level 3) A paving crew with Valley Line Paving Ltd. has two problems on the same morning:
The job spec says no paving in rain. Rain is forecast from 1:00 p.m.
One truck driver is sick, so asphalt will arrive every 40 minutes instead of every 20 minutes.
The plan was to pave the whole parking lot today, starting at 7:30.
a. Which part of the plan should the crew protect first, and why?
b. Name two things the crew could do while waiting between trucks.
c. What should the foreman tell the client, and when?
Task 9 (level 2) Jesse wrote this new plan after the lift broke down. Find three problems.
Time Task
7:15 to 9:30 Hang copper on Level 3 from a ladder
9:30 to 11:00 Prefab at the bench
11:00 to 12:30 Stage parts on Level 3
12:30 to 3:30 Pressure test the Level 3 piping
Jesse did not call the foreman.
Task 10 (level 3) Think of a day at work, school or home when a plan fell apart. Use the five questions to write the plan you wish you had made. Draw it as a bar chart. You choose how much to share.
Check yourself
How do you find the length of a bar on a day chart?
Give two fixed items and two movable items on a job site.
Name the five checks that tell you a task is ready to start.
After safety, what kind of work should go first in a re-plan?
Why do you tell your foreman what will be late, not just what you will do?

lessons.title: Learn a new tool or method fast
lessons.text:
Use a read, watch, try and check loop to learn a new tool safely, track your practice, and ask for the training you are owed.
All people, companies and products in this lesson are fictional, except where a source is named.
Why this matters on the job
Every few months you will meet a tool or method you have never used: a new press tool, a laser level, a different torque wrench, a new app for timesheets. Some apprentices fake it and hope nobody notices. Some freeze and wait to be shown. The ones who move ahead have a simple way to learn a new tool quickly and safely, and they ask for help in the right way.
Key ideas
The learning loop
Read. Start with the manual. Read the safety section first, then the parts and the steps. Reading lesson 8 shows you how to find things in a manual fast.
Watch. Ask a qualified person to show you. Watch their hands, and ask why they do each step.
Try. Do it yourself, slowly, on scrap or a practice piece, with someone nearby.
Check. Compare your result with the spec or the manual. Ask for feedback. Then go round the loop again.
Speed comes last. First get it right every time. Then get faster.
What BC law says about training
Under the BC Occupational Health and Safety Regulation (section 4.3), the employer must make sure each tool is used and operated according to the manufacturer's instructions, if available, safe work practices and the Regulation.
Before a young or new worker starts work, the employer must give an orientation that includes instruction and demonstration of the worker's work task or work process (section 3.23).
If a young or new worker asks for more training, or cannot do the task safely, the employer must provide more orientation and training (section 3.24). A young worker is anyone under 25. A new worker includes anyone new to the workplace, and anyone whose workplace hazards have changed or who moves to a workplace with different hazards.
So asking "Can you show me before I use it?" is not a weakness. It is your right, and it is what the law expects.
Keep a practice log
A practice log is a short record of each try: the time it took and whether it passed the check. It shows you, and your supervisor, when you are ready to work alone. Two things matter:
Pass rate: how many tries passed out of how many tries.
Time: how long each try took.
A fast try that fails the check does not count. Quality first.
Good questions to ask during a demonstration
"What is the most common mistake with this tool?"
"How do you check that it is done right?"
"What do you do if it stops halfway?"
"Where is the manual kept?"
Worked example
Dana is a first-year plumbing apprentice at Salal Creek Mechanical Ltd. Her foreman hands her a PX-20 battery press tool (a fictional tool) for joining copper pipe with press fittings. She has never used one.
Read. Dana opens the manual. She uses the contents page to go straight to what she needs.
Section 1 (page 2): safety warnings. Keep fingers out of the jaws. Wear safety glasses.
Section 3 (page 6): pick the jaw that matches the pipe size stamped on the jaw.
Section 4 (page 8): cut the pipe square, deburr it, mark the insertion depth, push the pipe into the fitting up to the mark, then press.
Section 5 (page 11): check that the mark sits at the edge of the fitting after the press.
Watch. The journeyperson, Ray, makes two joints while Dana watches. She asks, "What's the most common mistake?" Ray says, "Not pushing the pipe all the way in. That's why you mark it."
Try. Dana makes five practice joints on scrap pipe at the bench. Ray stays close by.
Check. After each joint she checks the insertion mark and writes the time and the result in her log.
Try 1 failed the check. The mark showed a gap: the pipe was not all the way into the fitting. Dana marked the next pipes more carefully and pushed them home before pressing. Tries 2 to 5 all passed.
Her numbers:
Pass rate: 4 passes out of 5 tries.
Average time of the four passing tries: (4.5 + 4.0 + 3.5 + 3.0) ÷ 4 = 15.0 ÷ 4 = 3.75 minutes.
Drop in time from try 1 to try 5: 6.0 − 3.0 = 3.0 minutes. As a percent of the first time: 3.0 ÷ 6.0 × 100 = 50%.
Dana tells Ray: "Four passes in a row now. I'm at about 3 minutes a joint. You're at 2. Can I do the next ten on the job with you checking each one?" That is a clear, honest ask.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Put the four steps of the learning loop in order. Then match each action to a step.
Actions:
Ask the journeyperson why they hold the tool that way.
Compare your cut with the line on the drawing.
Read the safety section of the manual.
Make three practice cuts on scrap.
Task 2 (level 1) Use the PX-20 contents page. Which page would you turn to for each question?
a. Which jaw do I need for a 3/4 inch pipe?
b. What does this warning symbol on the tool mean?
c. The tool stopped halfway through a press. What now?
d. How do I mark the insertion depth?
e. How should I store the tool at the end of the day?
Task 3 (level 2) Use Dana's log.
a. What is the average time of all five tries, including the fail?
b. Why is the average of the four passing tries a better number to report?
c. How many minutes slower than the journeyperson was Dana on try 5?
Task 4 (level 2) Choose a tool from your trade that you have not used yet (for example, a rotary laser level, a pipe threader, a powered mitre saw, a bending table or a strut cutter). Write three questions you would ask during a demonstration.
Task 5 (level 2) Sam is 22 and started at a mechanical contractor this week. The foreman hands Sam a cordless band saw and says, "You'll figure it out. Cut that strut to 600 mm." Sam has never used one.
a. Is Sam a young worker, a new worker, or both?
b. What does section 3.23 say Sam's orientation must include about the work task?
c. Write what Sam could say to the foreman.
Task 6 (level 2) Plan a 45-minute session to learn a rotary laser level. Split the time across read, watch, try and check. Show that your times add up to 45 minutes. Say what you will do in each part.
Step Minutes What I will do
Read
Watch
Try
Check
Total 45
Task 7 (level 3) Two apprentices practise the same press joint.
Try 1 2 3 4 5
Jesse, minutes 5.0 3.0 2.5 2.0 1.8
Jesse, check fail fail pass fail pass
Kim, minutes 6.0 5.0 4.5 4.0 3.8
Kim, check pass pass pass pass pass
a. Find each person's pass rate as a fraction and a percent.
b. Who is faster? Who is more ready to work on the job? Explain with numbers.
c. Write one piece of advice for each person.
Task 8 (level 3) You are sent to a job with a gas-powered concrete cut-off saw you have never used. There is no manual on site, and the journeyperson is at another job until noon. Your foreman wants the cuts done this morning.
a. List three things you will do before you start the saw.
b. Write what you will say to the foreman.
c. When would you stop and refuse to go ahead? Explain.
Task 9 (level 2) Explaining steps out loud helps you learn (lesson 6). Pick a task you know well, such as changing a saw blade, tying a bowline or reading a tape measure. Write it as 5 clear steps for a classmate who has never done it. Then read it to a partner and see if they can follow it.
Task 10 (level 3) Look back at Dana's failed first try. Write:
a. what she observed
b. what she changed
c. one more check she could add to her routine so it never happens on the job
Check yourself
Name the four steps of the learning loop.
Which part of a manual should you read first?
What does section 3.23 of the BC OHS Regulation say a new worker's orientation must include about their task?
What two things does a practice log track?
Why does a fast try that fails the check not count?

lessons.title: Keep going after rejected work
lessons.text:
When an inspector or a test rejects your work, stay calm, find the real cause, plan the fix and the re-inspection, and add a check so it does not happen again.
All people, companies and places in this lesson are fictional. The BC Building Code limits are real.
Why this matters on the job
Sooner or later an inspector will fail something you built, or a test will fail on work you did: a stair, a weld, a pressure test, a rough-in. It stings. Some people argue with the inspector, blame the drawings or go quiet for the rest of the day. That makes things worse. The crews that do well treat a rejection as a list of things to fix. They fix it right, check it themselves, and pass the second time.
Key ideas
What a rejection is, and what it is not
A notice of deficiency (or a failed test) says one thing: this work does not meet the rule yet. It is about the work, not about you as a person. Read it as a to-do list.
Six steps after rejected work
Cool down. Use what you learned in lesson 4. Do not argue on site. Say "Thanks. I'll read this and get back to you."
Read it all. What failed? Which rule? What does it ask you to do?
Report it. Tell your foreman, using the four parts from lesson 2.
Find the real cause. Measure. Ask "why?" until you reach something you can fix.
Plan the fix and the re-inspection. What, who, when, and how you will check it yourself first.
Add a check. Change your routine so the same thing does not happen again.
Keep trying or change the approach?
Lesson 3 asked this question. It matters even more after a fail.
If the same fix has failed twice, change the approach or ask for help. A third try of the same thing usually fails the same way.
If each try is closer, keep going.
If it is unsafe, stop and report.
The stair rules in this lesson
The BC Building Code 2024 sets limits for stairs. For a private stair (a stair that serves a single dwelling unit, such as the stair inside a house or townhouse):
Rise is measured from the top of one tread to the top of the next (nosing to nosing). Each rise must be no more than 200 mm and no less than 125 mm (Table 9.8.4.1).
Risers in one flight must be uniform. Two risers next to each other can differ by no more than 5 mm. The tallest and shortest riser in the flight can differ by no more than 10 mm (Sentence 9.8.4.4.(1)).
Lay out a stair from finished floor to finished floor. Flooring changes the top and bottom risers.
Worked example
Riverbend Framing Ltd. built the main stair in Unit 4 of Cedar Row Townhomes. On Monday the city inspector leaves this notice.
Tom, the apprentice who built the stair, feels his face get hot. He wants to say "It was fine on Friday." Instead he says, "Thanks. I'll go through it with my foreman." Then he follows the steps.
Read it all. The stair failed. The rule is Sentence 9.8.4.4.(1) and Table 9.8.4.1. The inspector wants it fixed and a re-inspection booked.
Find the real cause. Tom measures every riser, nosing to nosing, with the finished floors in.
He checks each rule.
Check Rule Unit 4 stair Pass?
Bottom pair of risers differ by 5 mm or less 190 − 184 = 6 no
Top pair of risers differ by 5 mm or less 209 − 190 = 19 no
Middle risers differ by 5 mm or less at most 191 − 189 = 2 yes
Tallest minus shortest in the flight 10 mm or less 209 − 184 = 25 no
Largest rise, private stair 200 mm or less 209 no
Why did this happen? The stringers were cut for 14 equal risers of 190 mm, measured from subfloor to subfloor: 14 × 190 = 2660 mm. Then 6 mm vinyl went on the main floor and 19 mm hardwood went on the upper floor.
The bottom riser lost the vinyl thickness: 190 − 6 = 184 mm.
The top riser gained the hardwood thickness: 190 + 19 = 209 mm.
The real cause is the layout method, not bad cutting.
Report it. Tom calls his foreman, Dana:
"Dana, it's Tom. The Unit 4 stair failed. I laid it out subfloor to subfloor, so the vinyl and hardwood threw off the top and bottom risers. The top one is 209. I've taped off the stair so nobody uses it until it's fixed. I need new stringers and about a day. From now on I'll lay out from finished floor heights."
Plan the fix. The total finished rise is 2660 − 6 + 19 = 2673 mm. Check it against the measured risers: they add up to 2673 mm too. With 14 risers, each rise is 2673 ÷ 14 = 190.9 mm, about 191 mm. That is under 200 mm. To hit 2673 mm exactly, Tom lays out 13 risers at 191 mm and one at 190 mm: 13 × 191 + 190 = 2483 + 190 = 2673 mm. Next to each other they differ by only 1 mm.
Plan the re-inspection. Re-inspections are booked 2 business days ahead.
Tom measures all 14 risers himself on Thursday before he calls the city. That way the inspector checks work he already knows passes.
Add a check. Tom writes a new line on his stair checklist: "Get the finished floor thickness for the top and bottom floors before you lay out the stringers."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Read the notice in the worked example.
a. What failed?
b. Which sentence of the BC Building Code does the notice name?
c. What two things does the notice ask the builder to do?
Task 2 (level 2) These are six risers in one flight, in mm, from the bottom: 190, 190, 196, 190, 189, 190.
a. Find the difference between each pair of risers next to each other.
b. Which pairs break the 5 mm rule?
Task 3 (level 2) A flight has these risers in mm: 182, 185, 186, 184, 183, 187, 189. Does it meet the 10 mm rule for tallest minus shortest? Show your work.
Task 4 (level 2) For a private stair, which of these rises are too tall? 198 mm, 201 mm, 185 mm, 200 mm, 207 mm.
Task 5 (level 3) Another house has a total finished rise of 2745 mm between finished floors.
a. Find the rise for 13, 14 and 15 risers. Round to one decimal place.
b. Which of these numbers of risers give a rise of 200 mm or less?
c. The builder picks 14 risers. Lay out the risers to the nearest whole millimetre so they add up to exactly 2745 mm.
Task 6 (level 2) Mark each reaction H (helpful) or U (unhelpful) after an inspector fails your work.
"This inspector always picks on us."
"Can you show me where you measured?"
Walk away and say nothing to your foreman.
Take a photo of the notice and read it at break.
"I'll fix it tonight and not tell anyone."
Measure the work yourself before the re-inspection.
Task 7 (level 2) Fatima is an electrical apprentice. The inspector fails the rough-in in Suite 3 because two boxes have no support. Write her report to the foreman using the four parts from lesson 2: what happened, what I have done, what I need, what I will do next time.
Task 8 (level 3) Plan the Unit 4 fix as a table with five columns: what, who, when, how long, and how you will check. The notice came Monday morning. Re-inspections are booked 2 business days ahead, and the crew does not work weekends. What is the earliest day the inspector can come back if Tom finishes and checks the stair on Wednesday afternoon and books it right away?
What Who When How long How I will check
Task 9 (level 3) Marco, a plumbing apprentice, is pressure testing a water line. The job spec says the gauge must hold for 15 minutes with no drop. The first test drops after 6 minutes. He tightens every joint he can reach and tests again. It drops after 7 minutes.
a. Should Marco keep trying the same fix, change the approach, or ask for help? Explain.
b. List three things he could do next to find the leak.
c. What should he tell his foreman, and when?
Task 10 (level 3) Think of something you made, wrote or did that was rejected or marked wrong. Write:
a. the real cause, not the first excuse
b. what you did, or wish you had done, to fix it
c. one check you could add to your routine. You choose how much to share.
Check yourself
What does a notice of deficiency say about your work? What does it not say?
Name the six steps after rejected work.
For a private stair in BC, what is the largest allowed rise?
How much can two risers next to each other differ?
Why should you check your own work before you call for a re-inspection?

lessons.title: Set and adjust goals across your apprenticeship
lessons.text:
Turn your trade's hours and levels into dated goals, track your progress, and adjust the plan when a layoff, injury or family need gets in the way.
All people and companies in this lesson are fictional. The SkilledTradesBC program facts are real.
Why this matters on the job
An apprenticeship takes years. Along the way there are layoffs in the slow season, injuries, family needs, a move, a change of employer. Apprentices who finish are not the ones who never hit a bump. They are the ones who know exactly where they stand, in hours and levels, and who adjust the plan instead of dropping it.
Lesson 7 mapped the steps from sponsor to Red Seal. This lesson turns those steps into numbers and dates for you.
Key ideas
Know your program's numbers
Every trade has a SkilledTradesBC program profile. It lists the levels of technical training, the hours in each level, and the work-based training hours you need. For example, the Carpenter program profile (in effect from April 1, 2024) lists:
Requirement Carpenter
Work-based training hours 6,360 hours
Technical training 4 levels, 210 hours each, based on 30 hours a week in school
Pass mark 70% in each level of technical training, and 70% on the Interprovincial Red Seal exam
Usual length about 4 years
At 30 hours a week, one level of 210 hours takes 210 ÷ 30 = 7 weeks.
Look up your own trade's profile on skilledtradesbc.ca. The numbers are different for every trade.
Track your hours
Your sponsor reports your work-based training hours in the SkilledTradesBC Portal. SkilledTradesBC recommends that sponsors report them every 3 to 6 months. Only sponsors can report hours, but you can sign in and check them. Check often.
To track progress:
Hours done as a percent: hours done ÷ hours required × 100
Hours to go: hours required − hours done
Weeks to go: hours to go ÷ hours you work in a week
Goals you can check
A goal you can check names four things: what, by when, who or what will help, and how you will know it is done (lesson 7). "Work hard" cannot be checked. "Reach 3,400 hours by next September, shown in the Portal" can.
When something gets in the way
Plans change. What matters is what you do next.
Laid off or changing employers. Before you leave, check that your hours have been reported in the Portal. When you start with a new employer, make sure the new sponsor and your registration are updated in the Portal.
Lost your sponsor in a non-compulsory trade (such as Carpenter). You can keep working, but your hours do not count toward your apprenticeship until you have a new sponsor.
Lost your sponsor in a compulsory trade (such as Construction Electrician). You cannot keep working in that trade as an apprentice until you have a new sponsor.
Going to technical training. Apply for Employment Insurance (EI) for the training period. Red Seal trade apprentices can apply for the Canada Apprentice Loan (lesson 7).
Not sure what to do. Contact a SkilledTradesBC Apprenticeship Advisor.
A layoff can also be a chance: a time to take a level of technical training, study for an exam or get a ticket you need.
Worked example
Leah is a carpentry apprentice with Sumas Ridge Homes Ltd. She finished Level 1. The Portal shows 1,900 work-based training hours. She averages 38 hours a week on the job.
Step 1. Where am I? 1,900 ÷ 6,360 × 100 = 29.9%. She is just under one third of the way through her hours.
Step 2. How far to go? 6,360 − 1,900 = 4,460 hours.
Step 3. How many working weeks? 4,460 ÷ 38 = 117.4. She rounds up to 118 working weeks, because 117 weeks would leave her short.
Step 4. Add school. Levels 2, 3 and 4 take 7 weeks each: 3 × 7 = 21 weeks. Her plan is 118 + 21 = 139 weeks, about 2.7 years (139 ÷ 52 = 2.67).
Step 5. Set goals. Leah writes three goals:
Goal By when Help How I'll know
Short: save $2,800 to cover rent during Level 2 in 16 weeks $175 a week into savings savings account shows $2,800
Mid: pass Level 2 and reach 3,400 hours in 12 months sponsor, training provider, study group Level 2 mark and Portal hours
Long: Red Seal carpenter in about 3 years sponsor, Apprenticeship Advisor certificate received
Check the savings goal: 16 × $175 = $2,800.
Step 6. Adjust when something changes. In November, Sumas Ridge lays Leah off for the slow season. The layoff lasts 10 weeks. She:
checks the Portal before her last day, and sees all her hours are there
applies for EI
asks the training provider if there is a Level 2 seat this winter
studies for Level 2 using practice questions (lesson 6)
Her plan moves by 10 weeks: 139 + 10 = 149 weeks.
If she gets a winter seat in Level 2, she uses 7 of the layoff weeks for school instead of losing them. Then her finish moves by only 10 − 7 = 3 weeks: 139 + 3 = 142 weeks.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use the Carpenter program facts.
a. How many work-based training hours does a carpenter need?
b. How many levels of technical training are there?
c. How many hours of technical training is that in total?
d. How many weeks of school is that, at 30 hours a week?
Task 2 (level 2) Jordan is a carpentry apprentice with 2,544 hours in the Portal. What percent of the 6,360 hours is that?
Task 3 (level 2) Mia is a carpentry apprentice with 3,100 hours. She works 40 hours a week.
a. How many hours does she have to go?
b. How many working weeks is that? Round up to a whole week.
Task 4 (level 2) Ben wants to save $3,150 before his next level of technical training. He can save $225 a week.
a. How many weeks will it take?
b. His training starts in 12 weeks. Will he make it? If not, how much more a week would he need to save?
Task 5 (level 2) Rewrite each goal so it can be checked. Name what, by when, help, and how you will know.
"Get better at math."
"Find a sponsor soon."
"Do well at school."
Task 6 (level 3) Use Leah's plan. This time her layoff lasts 8 weeks, and she cannot get a Level 2 seat during it.
a. How many weeks is her new plan?
b. During the layoff she does some framing for a neighbour, without a sponsor. Do those hours count toward her apprenticeship? Explain using the rule for her trade.
c. List three useful things she could do during the 8 weeks.
Task 7 (level 2) Andre is a construction electrician apprentice. His employer closes and he loses his sponsor. Construction Electrician is a compulsory trade in BC.
a. Can he keep working as an electrical apprentice for another contractor tomorrow, before a new sponsor is registered?
b. What two things should he check or do in the Portal?
c. Who can he contact for advice?
Task 8 (level 3) Leah can take Level 2 in January (Plan A) or in June (Plan B).
In January, work is slow. She would average 30 hours a week if she stayed on the job.
In June, work is busy. She would average 45 hours a week if she stayed on the job.
Level 2 takes 7 weeks either way.
a. How many work-based hours would she miss with each plan?
b. Which plan costs her fewer hours? By how many?
c. Give one reason someone might still choose the other plan.
Task 9 (level 2) Name two money supports to apply for before a level of technical training, and say who each one is for.
Task 10 (level 3) Look up your own trade's program profile on skilledtradesbc.ca, or use the Carpenter facts. Write a three-year plan with:
one short, one mid and one long goal, each one you can check
the hours or levels each goal needs
one "what if" line: what you will do if you are laid off, injured or needed at home for a month
You choose how much to share.
Check yourself
Where can you check your work-based training hours?
How do you work out the weeks you have to go?
What happens to your hours if you lose your sponsor in a non-compulsory trade?
What happens if you lose your sponsor in a compulsory trade?
What should you check before your last day with an employer?

lessons.title: Is this a good shop to apprentice with?
lessons.text:
Use a five-part checklist to judge whether a shop will support you through your apprenticeship, ask the right questions at an interview, and know what to watch for in your first 90 days.
All people and companies in this lesson are fictional. The facts about apprenticeship completion, PPE, sponsors and bullying policies are real.
Why this matters on the job
Statistics Canada followed apprentices across Canada who registered from 2008 on. At the end of the time their program was supposed to take, only 16% had their certificate. 64% were still in their program and 20% had left it. Apprentices who worked in a job closely related to their trade were also more likely to earn their certificate within one and a half times the expected program time than those who did not (38% compared with 32%).
Where you work is a big part of whether you finish. A shop that gives you a journeyperson, real trade work, gear that fits and a safe place to speak up keeps you moving. A shop that does not can stall you for years. You cannot control everything about a shop, but you can learn to read one before you sign on, and you can spot the warning signs early.
Key ideas
Five things that keep apprentices in a shop
This checklist looks at a shop from your side. It has five areas.
Area What to look for
1. Crew culture and speaking up How the crew treats people. Whether you can report a problem or admit a mistake without being punished for it.
2. Support for your apprenticeship A plan for your first week, a named journeyperson who supervises you, and hours reported to SkilledTradesBC on a schedule.
3. Gear and facilities that fit PPE and tools that fit you. A safe, private washroom and a place to change.
4. The shop's commitment A written bullying and harassment policy, a way to report that works even when the problem is your own boss, and a named person who answers for how apprentices are treated.
5. A path forward Real trade tasks across your program, not just clean-up. A clear pay step as you progress. Time off for technical training.
What BC rules already say
More on these in Collaboration lesson 08 (Respectful workplaces), lesson 07 (Apprenticeship path) and Reading lesson 22 (Employee, apprentice or contractor?).
Some of the checklist is backed by rules a shop must follow:
PPE. Under BC's Occupational Health and Safety Regulation, section 8.2, a worker supplies clothing for the weather, general purpose work gloves, appropriate footwear including safety footwear, and safety headgear. The employer supplies all other PPE the Regulation requires, at no cost to the worker.
Bullying and harassment. WorkSafeBC says every employer, of any size, must have a policy statement that bullying and harassment is not acceptable, procedures for workers to report it (including when the employer or a supervisor is the one doing it), and procedures for dealing with complaints. Workers must be told about the policy and trained on it.
Your sponsor. SkilledTradesBC says a sponsor must make sure you have proper equipment, know which certified journeyperson supervises your work, and get work-based training across the full scope of your trade. Only your sponsor can report your hours, ideally every 3 to 6 months. Under the Apprenticeship Agreement Policy, the sponsor must release you, as far as reasonably possible, to attend technical training.
Four levels for each area
Score each area from 1 to 4.
Level Name What it looks like
1 Reactive Nothing is in place. Things only happen after a problem blows up.
2 Foundational Some good things happen, but nothing is written down. It depends on who is around that day.
3 Established It is written down, most of the crew follows it, and someone is named to make it happen.
4 Leading The shop checks how it is working, fixes gaps and could show another shop how it does it.
Average score = total of the five scores ÷ 5.
Average Band What it means for you
1.0 to 1.7 Reactive Big risk. Your apprenticeship is left to chance.
1.8 to 2.4 Foundational Mixed. Good people, but it depends on who you work with.
2.5 to 3.2 Established Solid. Most of what you need is in place.
3.3 to 4.0 Leading Strong. The shop works at keeping apprentices.
Red flag rule. If any area has a safety or harassment problem, such as "nobody reports anything here" or "the foreman's jokes are part of the job", treat the whole shop as a risk, whatever the average says. Make that area the first thing you deal with or ask about.
Worked example: two job offers
Jesse finished a pre-apprenticeship program and has two offers as a first-year apprentice.
Alder Creek Mechanical. At the interview the owner showed Jesse a one-page first-week plan and named the journeyperson Jesse would work with. Hours go into the Portal every three months. There is a written respect policy and the office manager takes complaints if someone does not want to go to their foreman. Gloves only come in one size, but the owner said they would order Jesse's size. A posted wage sheet shows pay going up at each level, and apprentices rotate through rough-in, service and finishing.
Area Score Why
1. Crew culture 3 A known way to report, and apprentices said mistakes are treated as learning
2. Apprenticeship support 3 Written first-week plan, named journeyperson, hours reported on a schedule
3. Gear and facilities 2 Gloves ordered on request, not stocked
4. Commitment 3 Written policy, a named person outside the foreman
5. Path forward 3 Posted wage steps, rotation through the trade
Total: 3 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 14. Average: 14 ÷ 5 = 2.8. Band: Established (solid).
Stonefield Fabrication. The foreman said, "You'll learn by watching." Nobody could say who would supervise Jesse. When Jesse asked about hours, the foreman said, "We do that when we get around to it." There is no written policy. "If you can't take a joke, this isn't the place for you." Apprentices mostly sweep and grind. A friendly journeyperson sometimes shows the new people things.
Area Score
1. Crew culture 1
2. Apprenticeship support 2
3. Gear and facilities 1
4. Commitment 1
5. Path forward 2
Total: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 7. Average: 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4. Band: Reactive (big risk). The "take a joke" line is also a red flag for area 1.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Sort the signs. Write the area number (1 to 5) for each sign.
a) "Your hours go into the Portal every quarter." ______
b) "We've got smaller harnesses in the trailer." ______
c) "Second years start doing layout with a journeyperson." ______
d) "You can call the office if the problem is your foreman." ______
e) "Nobody gets yelled at for owning a mistake here." ______
f) "You'll work with Maria. She's your journeyperson." ______
g) "Raises go up at each level, and the sheet is posted." ______
h) "There's a lockable porta-potty and a change trailer on every site." ______
Task 2 (level 2) Who supplies it? Under OHS Regulation section 8.2, who supplies each item: the worker or the employer?
a) Safety boots
b) A fall-protection harness the job requires
c) A rain jacket
d) A hard hat
e) A respirator the job requires
Task 3 (level 2) Score a shop. Read about Bayview Electric. Score each area 1 to 4, find the average and the band.
The foreman tells new people, "Speak up if something's wrong," but there is no set way to report and nothing written. Every apprentice gets a written first-week checklist and a named journeyperson, and hours go in every three months. The shop stocks gloves, boots and harnesses in a range of sizes and every site has a lockable washroom. There is a short respect policy in the handbook, but nobody is sure who to go to with a complaint. Raises come up only if you ask, and whether you get varied work depends on your journeyperson.
Area Score
1. Crew culture
2. Apprenticeship support
3. Gear and facilities
4. Commitment
5. Path forward
Total
Average
Band
Task 4 (level 2) Check for red flags. A shop averages 3.0. On your second day, the lead hand says, "Don't take stuff to the office. We handle things on the crew." Is there a red flag? Which area? What does the red flag rule say to do?
Task 5 (level 2) Interview questions. Write three questions you could ask at an interview, each about a different area. Make them polite and specific. For example: "Who would I be working with day to day?"
Task 6 (level 3) Your first 90 days. You took the Alder Creek job. Name two signs you will watch for in your first 90 days that would tell you the shop is not what it seemed. For each one, write who you would talk to first, and who you could go to next if that does not work.
Task 7 (level 2) The numbers. Use the Statistics Canada figures. Out of a class of 50 apprentices who register together, about how many:
a) have their certificate at the end of the expected program time?
b) are still in their program?
c) have left?
Task 8 (level 3) Pay or support? Stonefield offers $1.50 an hour more than Alder Creek.
a) At 40 hours a week, how much more is that a week?
b) Over 2,000 hours in a year, how much more is it?
c) Write two or three sentences on which offer you would take and why. Use the scores from the worked example.
Check yourself
Name the five areas of the checklist.
Under section 8.2, name two items the employer must supply at no cost.
How do you work out the average score?
What does the red flag rule say?
Who reports your work-based training hours to SkilledTradesBC?

lessons.title: Working for yourself in the trades
lessons.text:
Know what changes when you work for yourself in a trade in BC, from business licences and GST to setting money aside for tax and CPP and getting WorkSafeBC coverage, and plan the first steps in order.
All people and companies in this lesson are fictional. The tax, registration and WorkSafeBC facts are real and were checked on government websites in November 2026. Rates and limits change, so check them again before you use them.
Why this matters on the job
Many tradespeople end up working for themselves at some point: a mobile welder with one truck, a finishing carpenter doing renovations, a millwright who takes contract work between plant jobs. Being your own boss means you set your hours and keep the profit. It also means nobody takes tax off your pay, nobody registers you with WorkSafeBC, and nobody sends your invoices for you. People who plan for that from day one do well. People who find out at tax time can owe thousands of dollars they have already spent.
Most people who work for themselves in a trade are already certified. As an apprentice, your hours count only when your sponsor reports them (lesson 12), so this lesson is about a later step on your path.
Key ideas
Employee or self-employed?
Reading lesson 22 (Employee, apprentice or contractor?) goes through the full CRA test. This is the short version.
The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) looks at the whole working relationship, not just what people call it. It asks questions like these:
Question Points to employee Points to self-employed
Who controls how and when the work is done? The payer You
Who supplies the tools and equipment? The payer You, and you pay for repairs and insurance
Can you hire a helper or send someone else? No Yes
Can you make a profit or take a loss on a job? No, you get paid either way Yes
Being told "you're a contractor now, no paperwork" does not make it so. If the boss sets your hours, supplies everything and pays you by the hour, the facts may point to you being an employee.
Set up the business
Step Where What to know
Choose a structure Your own decision, with advice The three common types in BC are a sole proprietorship (one owner), a general partnership (two or more owners) and a corporation (owned by shareholders). A sole proprietor is self-employed and takes on all the business's debts and risks. The Province suggests getting advice from a lawyer or accountant.
Register the name BC Registries If you do business under your own legal name only, you do not need to register with the Province. If you use any other name, such as "Northside Mobile Welding", you need an approved name request and then you register the business. Registration cost $40 when checked.
Get a business licence Each city or town where you work Business licences come from local governments, not the Province. Some regions have an inter-municipal business licence for trades contractors that covers several cities. BizPaL (a free government tool) lists the permits and licences your business may need.
GST: the $30,000 test
You are a small supplier while your taxable sales are $30,000 or less in a single calendar quarter and over the last four calendar quarters in a row. A small supplier does not have to register for GST. You must register once you go over:
Over $30,000 in one quarter: you stop being a small supplier right away and must charge GST on the sale that put you over.
Over $30,000 across four quarters in a row (but not in one quarter): you stop being a small supplier at the end of the month after the quarter you went over. Your registration starts no later than your first sale after that, and you must register within 29 days of that sale.
In BC the GST rate is 5%. The GST you collect is not your money. You send it to the CRA when you file your GST return. You can also register before you reach $30,000 if you choose. If you sell or lease taxable goods or services in BC, you may also need to register to collect Provincial Sales Tax (PST). The Province explains when.
Income tax and CPP
When you work for yourself, nobody takes income tax or Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions off your pay. You pay them yourself:
CPP: a self-employed person pays both the employee and the employer share. For 2026 each share is 5.95%, so you pay 11.9% of your net self-employment earnings between $3,500 and $74,600. (Above that, a second contribution applies. This lesson stays below it.)
Instalments: the CRA may ask you to pay income tax and CPP in instalments during the year instead of all at once.
The safe habit: set money aside from every payment in a separate account, so it is there when the tax is due. How much depends on your income and expenses. Work out your amount with an accountant.
WorkSafeBC
As a sole proprietor or partner, you are not automatically covered if you are hurt at work. You can buy Personal Coverage (it used to be called Personal Optional Protection) for yourself.
If you hire workers, you must register with WorkSafeBC.
General contractors ask subcontractors for a clearance letter. If a GC hires a registered sub who is not paying WorkSafeBC premiums, the GC can be held liable for those premiums. A clearance letter shows your account is in good standing.
Worked example: Dana's first year
Dana is a Red Seal welder. She starts a one-truck mobile welding business as a sole proprietor called Northside Mobile Welding.
Setting up. Because "Northside Mobile Welding" is not her own name, she gets a name approved and registers the business with BC Registries. She gets a business licence where she lives and checks the licence rules in each city she works in. She buys Personal Coverage from WorkSafeBC. A GC she wants to work for asks for a clearance letter and proof of liability insurance before her first job, so she gets both.
The GST test. Dana's taxable sales by quarter:
Quarter Sales
January to March $6,800
April to June $9,400
July to September $8,900
October to December $7,600
Four quarters 6,800 + 9,400 + 8,900 + 7,600 = $32,700
No single quarter is over $30,000. But the four quarters together are over $30,000. Dana stops being a small supplier at the end of January, the month after the October to December quarter, starts charging GST on the first sale after that, and must register within 29 days of that sale.
An invoice with GST. After she registers, Dana does a job: $2,400 labour and $600 materials.
Subtotal: $2,400 + $600 = $3,000
GST: 5% of $3,000 = 0.05 × $3,000 = $150
Total to the customer: $3,000 + $150 = $3,150
Setting money aside. Dana and her accountant agreed on a plan: keep all the GST, plus 25% of each subtotal for income tax and CPP. The 25% is Dana's own plan, not a rule.
Set aside: $150 + 25% of $3,000 = $150 + $750 = $900.
CPP at year end. In 2026 Dana's net self-employment earnings are $52,000. Using BEDMAS, brackets first:
CPP = ($52,000 − $3,500) × 11.9% = $48,500 × 0.119 = $5,771.50
That is money an employer would have paid half of. Now Dana pays all of it.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Employee or self-employed? For each person, say which the facts point to and give one reason.
a) Kim works 7:00 to 3:30 when the boss says, uses the company's welder and truck, is paid by the hour and cannot send someone else in her place.
b) Ray owns his welding truck, quotes each job, picks his own hours, hires a helper for big jobs and lost money on one job last month.
c) Lee's boss says, "You're a contractor now, no paperwork." The boss still sets Lee's hours, supplies all the tools and pays Lee by the hour in cash.
Task 2 (level 1) Which office? Match each item to BC Registries, the city or town, the CRA, or WorkSafeBC.
a) A business licence __
b) Registering a business name that is not your own name __
c) Registering for GST __
d) Personal Coverage if you are hurt at work __
e) A clearance letter for a GC __
Task 3 (level 2) The GST test. Does each person have to register for GST? Show your work.
a) Quarters: $7,200, $8,100, $6,900, $6,700.
b) First quarter $9,000. In the second quarter, one big job brings the quarter to $31,500.
Task 4 (level 2) Write the invoice total. A GST-registered carpenter in BC bills $1,850 labour and $460 materials. Find the subtotal, the GST and the total.
Task 5 (level 2) Set it aside. The carpenter in Task 4 sets aside all the GST plus 25% of the subtotal. How much does he set aside from this job?
Task 6 (level 3) CPP. In 2026 a self-employed millwright has net self-employment earnings of $41,200. Work out her CPP using 11.9% of the earnings between $3,500 and $74,600. Use BEDMAS.
Task 7 (level 2) WorkSafeBC.
a) Dana hires a helper for three months. Does she have to register with WorkSafeBC?
b) Dana falls off a ladder on a job before she bought Personal Coverage. Is she automatically covered as a worker?
c) Why does the GC want a clearance letter from Dana before and after her job?
Task 8 (level 3) Plan your start. You plan to start a one-truck business in your trade. List at least six things to do before your first paid job, in the order you would do them. For each, write where you would go or who you would ask.
Check yourself
Name two things the CRA looks at to decide if someone is an employee or self-employed.
Do you have to register a sole proprietorship with the Province if you use only your own legal name?
What is the GST small supplier limit?
What share of CPP does a self-employed person pay?
Is a sole proprietor automatically covered by WorkSafeBC?

lessons.title: Collaboration — contribute, listen and finish together
lessons.text:
Visual guide Six connected components of collaboration. Short labels summarize the six skill components; numbers match the chapter list. Use the connections in the order the task needs. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. Different strengths. One shared purpose. Six connected components: Work well with others; Value diversity and inclusion; Manage difficult interactions; Support collaboration; Achieve a common goal; Reflect and improve as a team. Revisit the component that helps the task.
See it in action · Collaboration
Visual guide One checked notice; two visible contributions. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
PERSON A: Check the source facts. PERSON B: Build the notice. Agree the goal and roles. Share progress and ask for help. Review together; name next steps. One checked notice; two visible contributions. A shared file alone does not show what each person did.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. PERSON A: Check the source facts. PERSON B: Build the notice.
Try it: Agree the goal and roles. Share progress and ask for help. Review together; name next steps.
Check your result: One checked notice; two visible contributions. A shared file alone does not show what each person did.
Your contribution belongs in the work
Collaboration means contributing and supporting other people toward a shared goal. You may already do this when arranging a ride, working alongside a crew, helping organize an activity or making decisions with people you trust. This chapter gives you language and practice for making that work clearer. It also gives you ways to notice whether everyone has a useful opportunity to contribute.
Working together does not mean everyone must speak in the same way, agree immediately or complete identical tasks. A strong team can include someone who likes to speak while thinking, someone who wants time to read, someone using an assistive tool and someone learning unfamiliar trade vocabulary. The goal is to make those contributions available to the team without deciding in advance what any person can do.
In an ACCESS IS4S classroom, learners may have connections with different First Nations, Métis or Inuit communities, may live away from their home community, or may choose not to discuss those connections. You decide what personal knowledge you share. No classmate is the spokesperson for an entire people. The cases here are fictional classroom situations; they do not describe a Nation's decision-making practices.
You will practise six connected parts of collaboration.
Work well with other people
Make clear agreements, take a role and keep others informed.
Practise with: “Find the shared goal” through “Take a role, then hand it over”, “Build a task board”
Value diversity and inclusivity of others
Ask about useful participation options and use different contributions.
Practise with: “Repair an excluding process” through “Invite knowledge without claiming it”
Manage difficult interactions with other people
Address a disagreement using the task, evidence and a suitable next step.
Practise with: “Sort the disagreement” through “Choose the right support”
Facilitate an environment where you can collaborate with others
Make it easier to contribute, ask questions and receive feedback.
Practise with: “Repair an excluding process”, “Facilitate one short meeting”, “Test one team improvement”
Achieve a common goal with others
Coordinate contributions and check the shared result.
Practise with: “Build a task board” through “Compare result and interaction”
Reflect and improve on how well the team works together
Use observations to choose and try a better team practice.
Practise with: “Compare result and interaction” through “Build your collaboration evidence note”
Collaboration route card
Practise in four steps
Agree the shared goal, each person’s role and a way for everyone to contribute.
Build a task board, complete your part and hand over the information another person needs.
Take a turn inviting contributions and resolving a task question. Ask for support when needed.
Test the shared product and one improvement to the team’s process. Record your own contribution.
Support route. Begin in a pair with the instructor as a practice partner. Use a task board with empty fields for responsibility, handover and check. A facilitation prompt card may say “purpose → invite → hear → dependency → next action → check back.” Record the scaffold and any live prompt separately. A learner can direct a scribe or use a written invitation. Do not assign all decisions permanently to the quickest speaker or keyboard user. Offer private practice and a different partner when needed.
Retry route. Select one observable interaction: wait for the written contribution, restate the handover, name a source discrepancy, or check the next-action summary. Try it with “Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together” Version 2 or another familiar small task. Keep the actual interaction and product result separate. A correct reader test can justify keeping the product; it does not require a manufactured revision. An absent disagreement is Not observed rather than proof of either conflict skill or failure.
What the instructor observes. Observe the contribution, handover and facilitation turn. A future plan does not show that the handover happened.
Next-attempt agreement: shared task ; individual role/action ; contribution mode ; chosen process improvement ; partners and observer ; date/time ; missing evidence ___.
Case document 1 · The visitor information pack
Fictional practice brief — Willow Reach training room, version 1. Four learners are preparing an information pack for six visitors who want to understand introductory asphalt training. The visitors will use the pack in a classroom; it will not authorize anyone to enter a worksite or operate equipment. The pack must include a five-stage process card, a short explanation of road-owner and contractor roles, and a clear session schedule.
The process card must use this order: pit or quarry → plant → haul → place → compact. It must say that real projects include additional preparation, checking and finishing. The project example names the fictional Town of Willow Reach as the road owner and fictional Pathway Paving Company as the contractor. Those are assigned roles in a practice document, not a rule about every B.C. project.
The visitor session starts at 10:00. Welcome and orientation take 10 minutes. The equipment-purpose activity runs from 10:10 to 10:30. Questions run from 10:30 to 10:45. There are six visitors, but a visitor may prefer a large-print copy or a spoken explanation. The coordinator has asked the team to check those preferences before deciding how many copies to produce. No visitor needs to give a reason for a format request.
The team has 45 classroom minutes to prepare a draft. It can use paper, a shared computer or both. One person may coordinate the work, another check source facts, another arrange the draft and another test whether a reader can find the information. These are temporary roles. They may be shared or changed by agreement; the person at the keyboard does not automatically become the decision-maker.
Before work begins, the coordinator asks for one group agreement and one way each member will contribute. At the end, the coordinator will inspect both the pack and how the team worked. A polished pack does not show who had the chance to participate.
Find the shared goal
Read the brief individually, then explain the goal to a partner without listing every instruction. Together, write one sentence beginning, “We will know the pack is ready when…” Include the three required parts and a reader check. Mark two things the brief does not authorize. Compare your goal sentence with the brief and identify the wording you used.
Agree how to begin
In a team of two to four, propose three working agreements that would help this task. Make each agreement observable: “We ask before replacing another person's wording” is clearer than “Be respectful.” Discuss how someone can request thinking time, a different communication mode or help. Keep a short record of one agreement suggested by each member and the final wording the team chose.
Take a role, then hand it over
Choose temporary roles for the first part of the pack. State your responsibility, the information you need and what you will pass to the next person. After a short first attempt, rotate at least one role. Give a handover that explains what is finished, what is uncertain and what needs checking. The receiving person restates the handover before continuing.
Make room for different ways to contribute
A team can look busy while excluding useful knowledge. If one person controls the document, sets every deadline and answers every question, other members may have little influence even when they are present. Inclusion requires a practical change to the process: shared access to the source, a chance to think, an invitation to contribute, and a way to see how a suggestion affected the result.
Ask what would help the task rather than demanding an explanation of a person's needs. “Would a printed copy or a spoken review work better?” offers a choice. “Why can't you read it on the screen?” asks the person to defend themselves. A choice should be genuine. If the team offers a spoken review, it must leave time for that review instead of treating it as an inconvenience.
Different experience can improve a draft. Someone familiar with community events may notice that a schedule needs a clear end time. Someone who has worked around equipment may recognize a confusing term. Someone new to the subject may reveal what a visitor will not understand. Prior knowledge is useful, but everyone still checks the supplied facts. Confidence, age, accent or speed is not a substitute for evidence.
An invitation also includes the option to pass. A learner can contribute through source checking, a written note, a diagram, an accessible communication tool or a later turn. Passing on a personal question is not refusal to learn. If an assigned task prevents meaningful participation, the team and instructor can adjust the task while keeping the intended skill visible.
Worked example 1 — change the invitation. A coordinator says, “You have not said anything, so you can just staple the copies.” This assigns a role without finding out what the person can contribute. A more useful approach is: “We need to check whether the schedule is clear. Would you like to review a printed copy, talk it through with me, or take another part?” The learner chooses a printed review and finds that the question period has no end time. The team adds 10:45 and records the contribution. Inclusion changed the work; it was not just a friendly greeting.
Repair an excluding process
A fictional team shares one small screen. Two people make changes while a third person cannot see the text. The third person asks for a copy and is told, “We are nearly done.” Identify the process problem without guessing anyone's intentions. Propose two workable adjustments, choose one, and explain how the team will know the third person had a meaningful opportunity to contribute.
Use two perspectives
Ask one partner to read the visitor schedule as the person preparing the session and another to read it as a first-time visitor. Use only the fictional brief; no one needs to share personal travel or accessibility information. Record one question from each perspective. Decide whether the existing document answers each question, needs clarification or leaves a decision to the coordinator.
Invite knowledge without claiming it
A teammate suggests adding a local teaching or image they saw online to make the pack “more Indigenous.” Draft a response that values the intention but does not assume permission, ownership or relevance. Offer a useful contribution the team can make immediately using the supplied learning material. Identify who should guide any later addition of specific community knowledge or imagery.
Case document 2 · A disagreement about the draft
Fictional team record. At the halfway point, Morgan has written, “A roller places asphalt.” Sam points to the process card and says the paver places the mixture while rollers compact it. Morgan replies, “I have already finished that section.” The team has not yet decided how corrections are approved. Robin notices the disagreement but is checking the schedule. Alex is using the computer and has not changed the sentence.
The available evidence is short and specific: the supplied process description says a truck transports the mixture, a paver places it and rollers compact it. The group is not being asked to decide operating settings or whether anyone has enough workplace experience. It needs an accurate introductory sentence.
A second issue concerns layout. Morgan prefers a large flow diagram; Sam prefers three question-and-answer boxes. Both layouts could meet the brief. No reader has tested either one. A factual correction and a design preference are different kinds of disagreement. The first can be checked against the supplied source. The second needs criteria and a simple reader test.
The coordinator is available for clarification. If a conversation becomes personal, threatening or discriminatory, learners can stop the interaction and seek instructor support. They are not required to negotiate their way through harmful behaviour as a demonstration of collaboration. For an ordinary task disagreement, the team can slow down, identify the issue and work toward a clear decision.
Disagree about the work without reducing the person
Visual guide Worked-example preview: check the equipment sentence against its source; test the two layouts with a reader. Different issues need different evidence. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Two side-by-side checks distinguish a source fact from a design choice. The equipment statement is checked against the source: a paver places and rollers compact. A flow diagram and question-and-answer layout are both tested with a reader asking who owns the road. Different issues require different evidence.
Use a short sequence: describe the issue → hear each view → check the task or evidence → agree a next action → confirm the decision. Each step protects information that can otherwise get lost. Describing the issue keeps the conversation specific. Hearing each view checks whether people are discussing the same question. Evidence and criteria give the group something more reliable than status or volume.
A useful statement names an observable detail: “Our sentence says the roller places the mixture, but the source gives placement to the paver.” It does not claim, “You never listen.” The first statement can be checked and corrected. The second makes a judgement about the person and invites a different argument. You can be clear about an error without weakening the relationship.
Agreement does not require pretending that every idea was equally useful. A team may reject a proposal because it does not fit the brief. The person who proposed it can still be heard and credited. Record the reason: “We chose the question layout because two readers found the owner information faster,” rather than “The other layout was bad.” Where evidence is incomplete, write down the uncertainty and who will check it.
Worked example 2 — separate fact from preference. Alex pauses editing and says, “First let us settle the equipment sentence.” Sam reads the source wording. Morgan restates the correction, and Alex changes the sentence to “The paver places the mixture; rollers compact it.” The group then draws both layouts on scrap paper. Robin tests each one using the question, “Who owns the road in this example?” The team selects a layout for a stated reason. One evidence check solved the factual issue; a different process addressed the design choice.
Sort the disagreement
For each issue in Case document 2, identify whether it concerns a source fact, a design preference or the team's working process. Write the question that would help resolve it and the evidence or agreement needed. Explain why voting on the equipment fact would be weaker than checking the supplied source, even if most people voted for the same answer.
Practise a useful disagreement
With a partner, use the layout disagreement from the case. Each person explains a reason for a layout; the listener restates it before responding. Use the five-step sequence and finish with a next action rather than a forced winner. Swap roles. An observer or instructor records one exact phrase that helped clarify the issue and one point the pair could improve.
Choose the right support
Consider three situations: a teammate wants a different heading; the source documents appear to conflict; a teammate makes a personal or discriminatory remark. For each, propose an appropriate next step and explain why. Include when to continue a task discussion, when to ask the coordinator for source clarification and when to stop and seek support. Do not invent a workplace reporting policy.
Turn individual tasks into one finished result
Visual guide Worked-example preview: pass along the checked schedule and the unresolved format question. The receiver checks back before printing. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
A checked visitor schedule lists welcome at 10:00, an equipment activity at 10:10, questions at 10:30 and finish at 10:45. The receiving partner retains those confirmed times while readability and copy formats remain pending. The team asks the coordinator before printing.
Shared work needs visible connections. A list of names beside tasks is only a beginning. The team also needs to know what each task produces, who needs that output, how it will be checked and what happens if it is delayed. A handover can be a brief spoken exchange, a labelled paper or a note in a shared document. Its purpose is to prevent someone from guessing whether unfinished work is ready.
A practical task board has four columns: task, person or pair, handover, check. The person named is responsible for making the status clear, not necessarily for doing every step alone. Asking for help early can protect the shared goal. Quietly working past a deadline while others wait makes coordination harder, even when the person is trying very hard.
Check both the product and the process. Product checks ask whether the three required sections are accurate and understandable. Process checks ask whether contributions were invited, information was shared and disagreements were handled using the agreed method. A team can produce an accurate pack while relying unfairly on one person. It can also collaborate thoughtfully and still need instruction to correct an equipment term. Those findings require different feedback.
Worked example 3 — a useful handover. “The schedule is done” leaves several questions unanswered. A clearer handover is: “The times match the brief, including the 10:45 finish. I have marked the visitor-format question as pending. Please check the font and ask the coordinator about copy formats before printing.” The receiver replies, “I will keep the times, check readability and confirm formats; I will not treat the pending question as settled.” The team has transferred both completed work and uncertainty.
Build a task board
Create a four-column board for the three parts of the visitor pack and its final reader check. Use real team members or fictional role names. Include a handover and a check for every task. Identify one point where another person's work depends on yours. Agree how to report a delay or unresolved question before it affects the next task.
Check before combining
Combine the team's three draft sections. Each person checks a section they did not create against Case document 1. Record one confirmed detail, one correction or clarification, and who will make it. If no correction is needed, explain what you checked rather than inventing an error. Each author responds to the check and confirms the final change or decision.
Facilitate one short meeting
Take a turn facilitating a five-minute check-in. State the purpose, invite each person's status, name any dependency and summarize the next actions. Offer a written or supported contribution route. Ask one participant whether your summary reflects their message. The observer records what the facilitator actually did to make participation possible; a confident speaking style is not the criterion.
Case document 3 · The team receives a change
Fictional coordinator update. Two of the six visitors have asked for larger print. One visitor would prefer a spoken review of the process card. The coordinator can provide a second room for the spoken review, but only from 10:10 to 10:30. The main schedule remains unchanged. The team has not been given any personal information explaining the requests, and it does not need that information to prepare the materials.
The computer is now available for only the next ten classroom minutes. Paper copies of the source brief and both draft layouts are available throughout. The team must decide what needs the computer and what can be completed on paper or through a conversation. It can ask the instructor to print a final file later, but must leave clear instructions about the versions and number of copies.
The coordinator does not want the team to promise a separate equipment demonstration. The spoken review is a classroom explanation using the same introductory information.
