Whoever supports it needs an accurate source card and a chance to practise the explanation. The pack should make clear which information belongs to the fictional example.
The task is still shared. The team should revise the plan, confirm the effect on each role and check that no member loses their contribution when the format changes. A good response may retain most of the first draft. Adapting together does not require discarding work that already meets the brief.
Replan together
Read the update separately, then each person identifies one changed requirement and one unchanged requirement. Revise the task board together. Assign the ten minutes of computer access to work that actually needs it and name at least one task that can continue without it. Confirm the new handovers. Keep the original board so the change in coordination is visible.
Produce and test the shared pack
Finish a practice pack using the available classroom tools. Ask another pair or the instructor to find the process order, the road owner and the question-period end time. Also ask how the larger-print and spoken-review requests will be met. Record the reader's answers and either a useful change or the evidence showing that the pack already meets the reader's needs. Each team member explains their contribution without claiming work completed by someone else.
Compare result and interaction
Make two short evidence lists: one about the finished pack and one about how the team worked. Include at least two observations in each. Use a specific moment, document or quoted phrase. Identify one interaction that helped the product and one process improvement for next time. Avoid labelling a person “good at teamwork” without showing the action behind that judgement.
Reflect, retry and carry the skill forward
Reflection is useful when it changes the next attempt. “We should communicate better” is too broad to guide a team. “At our next check-in, the receiver will restate each handover before starting” identifies a practice the team can try and observe. Choose an improvement that is within the team's control and small enough to test during a short task.
Feedback can recognize both contribution and support. “Your source check caught the missing end time” names an action. “You are the organized one” may sound positive, but it can trap a person in the same role and leave others without practice. Share roles over time and allow people to build new strengths. Record support honestly: using a checklist or an instructor prompt is part of the learning evidence, not a reason to hide the attempt.
The local feedback descriptions in this book are Not observed, Not yet demonstrated, Demonstrated with support, and Demonstrated independently. They describe evidence from a particular task, not official proficiency levels or a person's worth. A reflection about using a skill at work is a plan for transfer; actual transfer needs another observed task or a later example with its context recorded.
Test one team improvement
Choose one process improvement from “Compare result and interaction”. Test it while making a four-line summary of the visitor pack for a new classroom partner. Use the same source facts. Before beginning, state what behaviour you will watch for. Afterwards, compare what happened with your expectation and decide whether to keep, adjust or replace the practice.
Transfer to another setting
Choose a fictional setting: a training-room supply handover, a community-room booking task or an office information-sheet update. Explain how the shared goal, roles, contributions and checks would change. Identify one collaboration practice you would retain and one detail you would need to ask about locally. Do not assume a classroom agreement is an actual workplace or community protocol.
Build your collaboration evidence note
Select evidence for all six components from this chapter. Identify an activity, what you did, support used and a next practice step. Choose one component for another attempt and write an observable goal. Ask a partner or instructor whether the evidence describes an action they could recognize. Keep the note with the task board, reader feedback and one revised product.
Choose your next practice
For a supported route, work in a pair, use a partly completed task board and rehearse a handover with the instructor. Focus on two observable actions at a time, such as inviting a contribution and confirming a decision. The goal is a meaningful contribution with appropriate support, not rapid completion of every activity.
For an extension, work with a new partner and a different supplied document. Agree the process before beginning, then compare what transferred and what needed adjustment. More people or less time do not automatically make a better assessment. The task must still allow each learner to contribute and the observer to collect useful evidence.
Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together
These four original cases give you another opportunity to use a skill after the chapter practice. All people, rooms, events and organizations in these cards are fictional. You can use these cases without sharing personal, family, community or cultural knowledge. They are classroom tasks, not instructions for operating equipment or following an actual workplace procedure.
Your instructor will give you the relevant card when your turn begins. Keep a sender's information separate from the receiver's card until after the exchange. If you have already read the information, say so: the activity remains useful practice, but that attempt cannot show how you receive an unfamiliar message. No one needs to conceal prior practice.
Agree your language, communication mode, tools, access supports and response time before beginning. Speech, sign, text, AAC, a learner-directed scribe and agreed interpretation can be appropriate. The person observing needs a reliable way to understand the meaning of your contribution. Receiving a message in writing shows reception through that mode; it does not automatically show auditory listening. You may decline audio/video recording and use live observation. Ask for a pause or another opportunity if the conditions are not usable. There is no requirement to look cheerful, make eye contact or disclose why you need an arrangement.
Purpose: three people prepare and test one accurate handover card. Work with the same source, contribute in an agreed mode and take turns facilitating. The group product and each person's collaboration are different kinds of evidence.
“Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together” shared source · Northbank practice room
Fictional classroom brief · Version 1
The next group begins at 13:20. Your three-person team will hand over the practice resources at a 13:10 check-in.
8 laminated maps have been checked and are ready in Bag A.
6 pencils have been checked and are ready in Box B.
2 clipboards are at Desk C, waiting for the instructor's check. They are not yet ready for handover.
The handover card must identify each resource, quantity, location and ready/pending status. It must state the check-in time and identify what still needs the instructor's decision. No learner is authorized to declare an unchecked clipboard ready.
A receiver should be able to locate the ready resources and explain what to leave pending. The card can use headings, rows, symbols with text, or another agreed accessible layout. It is a practice document and must say so.
An earlier draft says: “All 16 items are ready. Collect everything from Desk C.” Check it against the source. Keep factual checking separate from a preference about how the corrected information should look.
“Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together” role card 1 · Prepare and facilitate the first check-in
Your starting task is to organize the shared work. Invite each person's preferred contribution route and ask what they notice in the brief. At the first check-in, help the team agree the goal, who will do what and how corrections will be confirmed. Ask the others for reasons before the team chooses a layout. You may propose short labelled sections, but you are not required to insist on them or win a vote. Hand a clear next action to another member.
“Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together” role card 2 · Check the source and facilitate the second check-in
Your starting task is to compare the draft with the source. Identify exact facts that need checking. At the second check-in, invite both other members' updates, explain a dependency or unresolved item and ask the group how to address it. You may propose a row for each resource, but listen to the other layout idea. A source fact cannot be decided by preference or majority vote. Confirm who will make the agreed change and who will check it.
“Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together” role card 3 · Act for the receiver and facilitate the third check-in
Your starting task is to consider whether the next group can use the card. Ask where the ready maps and pencils are and how the pending clipboards are identified. At the third check-in, invite each person's review and help the team choose one way to improve the handover process. Test that process while handing the completed card to a reader. The process may involve a receiver restating pending work or a checker naming the source line. If the product is already accurate and usable, retain it with evidence from the test.
“Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together” three check-ins and reader test
Each learner facilitates one check-in, provisionally five minutes with more time agreed when needed. During a check-in, the other members respond in their chosen modes and contribute an actual observation or proposal. Do not act out insults, discrimination or a personal conflict. A respectful disagreement about the draft or layout supplies enough practice. If no disagreement occurs, record that opportunity as absent; do not invent one in the evidence note.
A reader, who may be the instructor, uses only your finished card to answer:
Where are the maps and pencils, and which are ready?
What is still pending, and who can resolve that status?
When is the handover check-in?
Keep the reader's actual answers. Make a useful revision if the check reveals a need, or explain why the result supports keeping the current card. Each person identifies their own contribution. Then try the chosen handover improvement once and record what happened; planning a better interaction does not prove it happened.
“Collaboration practice C · Make a resource handover together” later retry source · Hold until another attempt
For another short handover, use this fictional Version 2 update: one of the two clipboards at Desk C has now been checked and is ready; the second remains pending. The 8 maps, 6 pencils, their locations and the 13:10 check-in stay unchanged. Label the revision Version 2. Check that a receiver can distinguish the two clipboards' statuses without treating the whole location as ready. Use new role allocations where possible. This update is not authority to change any real equipment status.

lessons.title: Doing your share on a crew
lessons.text:
Know your role, know who depends on you, and build trust by doing what you said you would do.
Why this matters on the job
On a BC job site, most work waits on someone else's work. A framer can't stand a wall until the plates are laid out. A drywall crew can't start until the electrical rough-in is done. When one person is late, or quietly skips a step, the whole crew loses time. A crew that trusts each other gets more done and works more safely.
Key ideas
Collaboration is "your ability to contribute and support others to achieve a common goal." That is the Government of Canada's wording in its Skills for Success model. Until 2021 this skill was called Working with Others. The new name covers more: it now includes inclusivity and respect for diversity.
Every crew member has a role. A role is the part of the job that is yours. To do your share, you need to know three things:
What is my job today?
Who is waiting on my work?
Whose work am I waiting on?
Trust is built by small, everyday actions. The Skills for Success model lists "engage in trust building behaviours" and "adhere to social and organizational rules", for example, be on time. On a crew that looks like this:
Show up on time, with your gear.
Do what you said you would do.
If you can't, say so early, before it holds someone up.
Ask when you are not sure, instead of guessing.
Leave your work ready for the next person.
Know your strengths and where you need help. Nobody is good at everything. A strong crew knows who is fast at layout, who is careful with finishing, and who is still learning. Saying "I haven't done this before, can you show me once?" is part of doing your share.
Example: one pole, many hands
Is a totem pole made by one person? Here is one Haida pole project, as Parks Canada describes it.
The Gwaii Haanas Legacy Pole is a 42-foot monumental pole. It was commissioned by the Archipelago Management Board, where the Haida Nation and the Government of Canada have an equal number of members, to mark 20 years of managing Gwaii Haanas together.
A six-person committee (a hereditary Chief, two Haida citizens, a carver and two Gwaii Haanas staff) chose the design. Proposals were judged with no names attached.
The head carver was Jaalen Edenshaw, of the Ts'aahl Eagle clan. He chose the red cedar.
Faller Shaun Peacock worked with him to bring the tree down. The tree was trucked to Skidegate.
Jaalen asked Tyler York and his brother Gwaai Edenshaw to be his assistants. Tyler shaped the log with an Alaska mill. The carving was done in the carving shed at the Haida Heritage Centre.
On August 15, 2013, more than 400 people took part in raising the pole at Hlk'yah G̱awG̱a (Windy Bay) on Lyell Island. Elder Diane Brown blessed the pole. Four lines of people pulled it up, and final directions were given to make sure it stood straight.
So no: this pole took a design committee, a carver, a faller, assistants, an Elder's blessing and hundreds of people pulling on lines. Many parts had to be done before the next could start.
This describes one pole, made with the Haida Nation, as told on the Parks Canada page. It is not a rule for how every Nation or every pole works.
Worked example: a late start
Cedar Flats Framing (a fictional company) has a crew of four building a garage wall.
Person Role today Needs before they can start
Dana Journeyperson and crew lead, lays out the plates Nothing, starts at 7:00
Marcus Apprentice, cuts studs from the cut list The cut list, which is in his truck
Priya Apprentice, nails up the wall Laid-out plates from Dana and cut studs from Marcus
Tomas Labourer, stages material and keeps the area clear Nothing, starts at 7:00
Marcus is stuck in traffic and arrives at 7:20 without texting. For 20 minutes Priya has nothing to nail, and Dana stops her layout to look for the cut list.
A better way: at 6:45 Marcus texts Dana: "Stuck on Highway 1, there by 7:20. Cut list is on the dash of my truck, but I have a photo of it. Sending now." Dana can give the photo to Tomas, who starts cutting. Marcus is still late, but the crew keeps working. He told the lead early, said when he would arrive, and gave the crew what it needed.
The chart shows the same crew from Priya's point of view. Arrows point from the work you wait on to the work that waits on you.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use the Cedar Flats table. For Dana, Marcus and Priya, write who is waiting on that person's work.
Task 2 (level 1) Sort these actions into two lists: builds trust and breaks trust.
a) Texting the lead before start time when you will be late b) Saying "yep, done" when you have not checked the job c) Putting tools back where the crew keeps them d) Taking the last box of screws without telling anyone e) Asking "Can you show me once?" before trying a task you have never done f) Leaving offcuts on the walkway for someone else to pick up g) Finishing your part and asking the lead what is next h) Arriving on time but without your safety boots
Task 3 (level 2) You are Marcus. It is 11:15 and the cut list is due at 12:00. You need 30 minutes beyond that deadline, plus your planned lunch break from 12:00 to 12:30. Your revised finish time is 13:00. You do not know which other materials are ready. Write a text to Dana. Say what is late, when it will be done, and ask Dana to confirm suitable work for the crew in the meantime.
Task 4 (level 2) Name one strength you bring to a crew. Name one task where you would want help the first time. Write the words you would use to ask for that help. You choose what to share.
Task 5 (level 2) Use the Legacy Pole facts. Name four different roles in the project. For each, name a step that had to be done before that person could do their part.
Task 6 (level 2) Use the chart of the Cedar Flats crew.
a) Whose work is Priya waiting on? b) Who is waiting on Priya? c) Marcus is 20 minutes late and does not text. Name everyone who loses time. d) Draw the same kind of chart for a job you know. Put yourself in the middle box.
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. Stoney Creek Concrete (a fictional company) has a pump truck booked for 7:30 to pour two footings. All rebar must be tied before the pump arrives. Your crew today:
Person Strength
Ray, journeyperson Fast at layout and tying rebar
Jess, second-year apprentice Ties rebar, was going to do the north footing
Ali, labourer, first week Moves material, has never tied rebar
At 6:50 Jess texts: "Flat tire. There by 7:40. Sorry."
a) Which task is now at risk, and why does it matter? b) Who takes over the north footing until Jess arrives? Give your reason. c) What job do you give Ali? d) Write the text you send back to Jess.
Check yourself
What is the Skills for Success definition of collaboration?
What was this skill called before 2021?
Name three trust-building actions on a crew.
You find out at 9:00 that you can't finish a task due at 10:00. When should you tell your lead, and what should you tell them?
Does the Legacy Pole example tell you how every Nation makes a pole? Why or why not?

lessons.title: Working styles and style-stepping
lessons.text:
Talk about how you like to work, notice how others like to work, and adjust your approach so the job goes smoothly.
Why this matters on the job
A journeyperson says "clean up the area." To one apprentice that means sweep and stack the offcuts. To another it means tools away, cords coiled, floor swept and garbage hauled. Neither is lazy. They just have different ideas of "done." On a crew you work with people who decide fast and people who check twice, people who talk all day and people who want quiet. Knowing how you like to work, and how others do, saves time and arguments.
Key ideas
A working style is a preference, not a rule. It is how you tend to work when you have a choice. Everyone can work in every style, and most people change with the job, the day and the crew.
This lesson uses two simple questions:
Pace: do you tend to act quickly, or take your time?
Focus: do you tend to think about the task first, or the people first?
Put them together and you get four working styles:
Task first People first
Quick Get it done Get people going
Steady Get it right Keep the crew together
Here is the same grid as a picture. Pace runs down the side. Focus runs across the top.
What each style brings, and what can go wrong when it is overused:
Style Brings to a crew When overused Working with this style
Get it done Speed, decisions, drive Skips steps, gets impatient, talks over others Be brief. Give the bottom line first. Offer choices.
Get people going Energy, ideas, keeps spirits up Talks more than works, loses track of details Start friendly. Give the big picture, then write the details down for them.
Keep the crew together Patience, listening, helps new people Avoids conflict, says yes when they mean no Tell them about changes early. Ask their view directly. Give them time.
Get it right Accuracy, planning, checking Slow, stuck on detail, can sound critical Give facts and numbers. Give time to check. Ask specific questions.
A crew needs all four. The fast one keeps the job moving, the careful one catches mistakes, the friendly one keeps people talking, and the steady one looks after the new hire.
Style-stepping means changing your approach for a moment so the other person can work with you. You don't change who you are. You change how you deliver the message.
Be honest about what this is
The preference check below was written for this lesson. It is not a scientific test and it does not measure your personality. It is a way to start a conversation about how you like to work.
Popular type tests are widely used at work, but researchers still argue about how well they hold up. A 2019 review in Social and Personality Psychology Compass found that the theory behind the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator does not agree well with known data and is hard to test. The company that publishes that test says it should not be used in hiring. If an employer asks you to do a style or type test, it is fair to ask what it will be used for.
Worked example: "Done"
Ridgeline Plumbing (a fictional company) sends apprentice Kai to finish a kitchen sink while journeyperson Lee works in the next unit. Kai is a get it done person. Lee is a get it right person.
Kai texts: "done."
Lee calls back with five questions. Was it tested? Any drips? Where is the box of fittings? Kai is annoyed: "I said it was done."
Style-stepping: Kai sends what a get it right person needs, in one message:
"Kitchen sink in unit 4 is done. Ran the water 5 minutes, no drips under the cabinet. Photo attached. Leftover fittings are back in the van, blue bin."
Lee has no more questions, and Kai gets the next job faster. Kai still works fast. He just added the facts Lee needs.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) For each pair, circle the statement that sounds more like you at work. There are no right or wrong answers.
# A B
1 I like to start right away and figure it out as I go. I like to read the plan before I pick up a tool.
2 I decide fast. I take time to think it over.
3 I talk while I think. I think first, then talk.
4 I like the job to keep moving, even if we fix things later. I would rather slow down than redo work.
5 Change of plan? Fine, let's go. Change of plan? Tell me why first.
6 I get bored on long, repeated tasks. I am happy doing the same task well all day.
7 At lunch I talk about the job. At lunch I talk about people's weekends.
8 A good day is about what got done. A good day is about how the crew got along.
9 I want instructions as a list. I want someone to show me and talk it through.
10 With a problem, I go for the fix first. With a problem, I check how everyone is doing first.
11 I like to work alone on my part. I like to work beside someone.
12 Feedback: just tell me straight. Feedback: tell me what is going well too.
Count your A answers in rows 1 to 6. This is your pace score. 4 or more = Quick. 2 or fewer = Steady. 3 = you use both.
Count your A answers in rows 7 to 12. This is your focus score. 4 or more = Task first. 2 or fewer = People first. 3 = you use both.
My pace: _ My focus: _ My style today: ____
Task 2 (level 1) Which style does each message show most?
a) "Let's just get the forms up. We can square them after." b) "Before we start, can I see the drawing again? I want to check the east side." c) "The new guy is on his own over there. I'll go see if he needs a hand." d) "I've got an idea for the layout. It'll be way faster, let me tell you!"
Task 3 (level 2) You are a get people going person. Your lead is a get it right person. Here is your text:
"Hey!! Great news, the delivery came, we're all set, it's gonna be a good day!"
These are the facts: the delivery came at 7:30. 40 sheets of drywall were ordered and 38 came. The 2 missing sheets will come Thursday. The sheets are stacked in the garage. Rewrite the text for your lead.
Task 4 (level 2) Role play with a partner. Pick a situation (or write one from your own trade):
A homeowner is upset that the electrician is a day late.
A site superintendent wants a progress update right now.
A customer wants to know every detail of a furnace repair quote.
One person plays the customer or superintendent and picks a style card. The other plays the tradesperson. Write a 3 to 5 line conversation where the tradesperson notices the other person's style, style-steps, and the problem gets sorted out. Act it out.
Task 5 (level 2) A crew of four are all get it done people. Name two things that could go wrong. Name two habits the crew could add to cover the gaps.
Task 6 (level 2) Style-step a message. At Tidal Steel Fab (a fictional shop), Lee the lead hand is a "Get it done" person. Mo the fitter is a "Get it right" person. Lee says to Mo:
"Just tack it. We're late. Go."
Rewrite Lee's message so it works for Mo. Use the "Working with this style" column.
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. Two jobs must start at 7:00:
Job 1: lay out anchor bolt locations from the drawing. Every bolt must be within the tolerance on the drawing.
Job 2: unload a steel delivery fast. The truck driver has another drop at 8:00.
Your crew: Kai (Get it done), Rose (Get it right), Sam (Keep the crew together), and Jo (Get people going).
a) Put two people on each job. Explain each choice. b) Write one sentence you would say to brief the Job 1 pair. Style-step it for them. c) What risk do you watch for on Job 2, and what will you do about it?
Check yourself
Is the preference check in Task 1 a test of your personality? Explain.
What does style-stepping mean?
Name one strength of a get it right person and one risk when that style is overused.
A keep the crew together co-worker says "sure, whatever works" to your plan. What could you do to find out what they really think?
Should an employer use a personality type test to decide who to hire? What does the company that publishes the Myers-Briggs test say?

lessons.title: Respecting differences on a job site
lessons.text:
Understand what culture is, work respectfully with people whose ways differ from yours, and know what BC human rights law says about work.
Why this matters on the job
A BC crew can include people from different Nations, countries, faiths and generations, all on the same scaffold. You will eat lunch with them, depend on them for safety and learn the trade from them. If people feel judged or left out, they stop speaking up, and that is when mistakes get missed. Respecting differences is part of doing the job well.
Key ideas
Culture is the shared beliefs, customs and ways of doing things of a group of people. It shows up in language, food, clothing, music, art, how people mark a birth, a marriage or a death, what they value and how they make decisions. There is no single, fixed definition, because the things that make groups different are not the same everywhere.
Everyone has culture, and most people belong to more than one group at once: a family, a community or Nation, maybe a faith, a trade, a sports team, a crew.
Job sites have culture too. Every crew has unwritten rules: who sits where at lunch, how people joke, whether you can ask a "dumb" question, who gets the good jobs. Some of these rules help everyone. Some leave people out.
Indigenous peoples are not one group. The Canadian Constitution recognizes three Indigenous peoples: First Nations, Inuit and Métis. The Government of Canada describes them as distinct peoples with their own histories, languages, cultural practices and spiritual beliefs. In BC alone there are 204 First Nations communities and 36 First Nations languages, according to the First Peoples' Cultural Council. So there is no single "Indigenous way," and no one person can speak for all Indigenous people.
Respect at work, in practice. The Skills for Success model asks you to:
understand that people from different cultures, backgrounds and abilities can have different customs, values and ways of thinking and acting
accept differences in characteristics, abilities, cultures, religions and values
respond without judging people for their different opinions, ideas and views
adapt to different styles of interaction when possible and appropriate
In plain words: ask instead of assuming, let people choose what they share about themselves, and don't make anyone the spokesperson for their group.
The law. BC's Human Rights Code (section 13) says a person must not refuse to employ someone, or discriminate against them about any part of their job, because of their:
Indigenous identity
race, colour, ancestry or place of origin
political belief
religion
marital status or family status
physical or mental disability
sex, sexual orientation, or gender identity or expression
age (19 or older)
a criminal or summary conviction that is unrelated to the job
Employers also have a duty to accommodate. The BC Human Rights Tribunal explains it as a duty to take all reasonable steps to avoid a negative effect on someone because of one of these grounds. For example, a rule to work a certain day can affect a person whose religion does not allow work on that day. The Tribunal advises workers to tell their employer if they can't meet a work requirement because of one of these personal characteristics.
The cards below show the same grounds from section 13. The yellow bar is the duty to accommodate.
Worked example: a call from home
North Arm Electrical (a fictional company) is on a tight schedule. Apprentice Shay gets a call: a family member has died, and the family is gathering in Shay's home community for the funeral. Shay expects to be away for several days.
Response A: "Can't you just come back after the funeral? It's one afternoon, right?" This assumes Shay's family does things the way the speaker's family does. It puts the schedule ahead of the person, and it asks Shay to defend their family's ways.
Response B: "I'm sorry. What do you need? Tell me roughly how long you'll be away, and I'll sort out coverage with the office." This does not ask Shay to explain the ceremony. It asks only what the job needs to know (how long), and it leaves the rest to Shay. The lead then checks the company's leave policy.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Tiny talents. In pairs, teach your partner something new in 3 minutes, then switch. It can be a word or phrase in a language you know, a game, a step in a recipe, a knot, a song line or a trick from your trade. You choose what to share. Then tell the group one thing you learned from your partner.
What I learned: __________
Task 2 (level 1) In a small group, make two lists: - ways people are alike (for example: we all need rest, we all want to be treated fairly) - ways people are different (for example: language, faith, food, age)
Circle two differences that could matter on a crew. Say why.
Task 3 (level 2) Write three unwritten rules from a crew, team or workplace you know. For each, decide: does it help everyone, or could it leave someone out? For one rule that leaves people out, suggest a change.
Task 4 (level 2) What would you say? Write a short, respectful response for each situation. You might be the person involved or someone standing nearby.
a) A co-worker reads the morning safety talk aloud. A few people laugh at his accent. b) A co-worker asks you: "You're Native, right? So what do Indigenous people think about pipelines?" c) At lunch, someone says loudly about a co-worker's food: "What is that? It stinks." d) A new worker asks the lead if she can leave 30 minutes early on Fridays for prayers, and make up the time on another day.
Task 5 (level 2) For each case, decide whether a ground in section 13 of the BC Human Rights Code is involved. If yes, name the ground.
a) Sam, 58, is told "we want someone younger" and is not hired. b) Jo is not hired as a delivery driver because Jo has no driver's licence. c) Ray is refused a labourer job because he is First Nations. d) Lin is let go because she can't work on her religion's holy day. The employer did not look at any other options. e) Alex is not offered overtime because the foreman doesn't like Alex's taste in music. f) Pat is turned down for a framing job because of a conviction 15 years ago that has nothing to do with the work.
Task 6 (level 2) Which ground? For each situation, name the protected ground from the cards, or write "not a protected ground."
a) A foreman says he won't hire a carpenter because she is 58. b) The crew makes fun of a pipefitter's accent and where he grew up. c) An apprentice gets less overtime because he cheers for a different hockey team than the foreman. d) A worker asks to swap her Friday afternoon shift because of her religious practice.
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. Amir (fictional), a second-year pipefitting apprentice, asks you on Monday: "Can I take my lunch at 1:00 on Fridays instead of noon? I go to prayers." The crew always takes lunch together at noon.
a) Which protected ground is part of this request? b) Write what you say to Amir. c) Give two ways to make it work on the crew. d) Who else do you tell, and why?
Check yourself
In your own words, what is culture?
Name the three Indigenous peoples recognized in the Canadian Constitution.
Why should you not ask one person to speak for all Indigenous people?
Name four grounds protected in employment under the BC Human Rights Code.
What is the duty to accommodate?

lessons.title: Checking assumptions before you act
lessons.text:
Separate what you saw from what you assumed, notice your own biases, and check before you judge a co-worker.
Why this matters on the job
A tool goes missing and someone says, "The new guy had it last." A lockout tag is on the panel, so everyone assumes the power is off. A quiet apprentice is passed over for a task because "she probably can't handle it." Each time, someone filled a gap with a guess. Some guesses are only unfair. Some are dangerous. Checking before you act protects people and keeps a crew's trust.
Key ideas
What you saw and what you think are different. You saw the laser level is not in the gang box. You think the apprentice took it home. The first is an observation. The second is an assumption.
An assumption fills a gap in what we know. We all make them. They save time, and many are harmless. They become a problem when we act on them as if they were facts.
A bias is a leaning we already have about a person, a group or a situation, before we have the facts. It comes from our past experience, our family, our friends, the media and the culture around us. Often we don't notice it. Biases can be unfavourable ("people from the city can't work outdoors") or favourable ("he's from my hometown, he'll be a good worker"). Both can lead us wrong.
A stereotype is a belief about a group that we apply to every person in that group. It stops us from seeing the person in front of us.
Four steps before you act on a guess:
Notice that you are making a judgment.
Separate what you saw or heard from what you think it means.
Check: ask, look, read the sign-out sheet, test it.
Decide based on what you found.
Worked example: the missing laser level
Harbour View Builders (a fictional company). At 7:00 the laser level is not in the gang box. Kyle says, "The new apprentice had it last. Bet he took it home."
What Kyle saw or heard What Kyle thinks it means
The laser level is not in the gang box It is missing
The new apprentice used it yesterday He took it home
Check: Kyle reads the sign-out sheet. It says the lead signed the laser out at 3:30 yesterday. The laser is in the second gang box on level 2, where the lead used it last.
If Kyle had told the crew "the new guy took it," the apprentice would have been blamed for something he didn't do. One question would have saved that.
The four steps, with the laser level example written in:
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Read the story once. Then mark each statement T (true), F (false) or ? (the story does not tell you). Do not reread until you have marked them all.
At 6:40 a.m. a white pickup pulled into the Harbour View site. A person in a hard hat and high-vis vest walked to the site trailer, opened the lock box and took out a key. A few minutes later the scissor lift was running. When the site superintendent arrived at 7:05, the lift was parked by the east wall and the trailer door was open. A note on the lift's controls said "Battery low."
# Statement T F ?
1 A pickup arrived at the site before 7:00.
2 The driver of the pickup opened the lock box.
3 A person in a hard hat took a key out of the lock box.
4 The key was for the scissor lift.
5 The superintendent arrived at 7:05.
6 The person in the hard hat moved the lift to the east wall.
7 The trailer door was closed when the superintendent arrived.
8 The person in the hard hat works on this site.
9 A note on the lift's controls said "Battery low."
10 The lift's battery was low.
11 The superintendent is a man.
12 The story mentions only one person.
Task 2 (level 1) Mark each line O (observation: something you can see, hear or measure) or A (assumption).
a) The truck is parked in the fire lane. b) He doesn't care about the rules. c) She has asked three questions this morning. d) She isn't ready for this job. e) The concrete delivery was 40 minutes late. f) The supplier is always unreliable. g) He hasn't said anything at the crew talk. h) He has nothing to add.
Task 3 (level 2) Your instructor will read some statements. Move to the sign that fits what you think: Agree strongly, Agree a little, Disagree a little, Disagree strongly. Stand in the middle if you can't decide. You may stay seated and name your choice, point to a card or write it instead. Then, in groups of four, talk about these questions and have one person take notes:
Where do beliefs like these come from? (family, media, past experience, friends)
Why do people hold on to them?
What harm can they do on a crew?
How does it feel when someone judges you before they know you?
Task 4 (level 2) Rewrite this text so it reports only what was seen and asks for the facts.
"The new apprentice took the lift key and left the trailer open. Typical."
Task 5 (level 2) My plan. This is private. You do not have to hand it in.
One bias I notice in myself (favourable or unfavourable): ____
Where I think it comes from: ____
How it could affect how I treat people at work: ____
One thing I will do to check it: ____
Task 6 (level 2) Saw and think. North Arm Electrical (a fictional company). You walk up and see the panel cover is off and Tyler is on his phone.
a) Write what you saw. b) Write one thing you might think it means. c) Write how you would check before you say anything to the crew.
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. You run an asphalt paving crew. The roller operator, Dale (fictional), has arrived 15 minutes late two days in a row. A crew member says, "He's lazy. Those guys from up north are always like that."
a) Which part of that comment is a stereotype? Which is an assumption? What fact does the scenario give about Dale? b) Name two things you check before you decide what to do. c) Write the first two sentences you say to Dale, in private. d) What do you say to the crew member who made the comment?
Check yourself
What is the difference between an observation and an assumption?
What is a stereotype?
Can a bias be favourable? Give an example.
Name three places biases come from.
A tool is missing. Before you blame someone, name two things you could check.

lessons.title: Preventing and resolving conflict on a crew
lessons.text:
Spot conflict early, listen so the other person feels heard, and say what you need in a way that solves the problem.
Why this matters on the job
Two apprentices need the same tool. A lead and a journeyperson disagree on the order of work. A sub keeps leaving a mess in your area. Conflict happens any time people work together. Left alone, it slows the job, people stop talking to each other, and safety slips. Handled well, it solves a real problem and the crew works better afterward.
Key ideas
Where conflict comes from. Most conflicts come from differences in:
opinions: "We should frame the east wall first."
facts: "The drawing says 16-inch centres." "No, it says 24."
perceptions: how each person sees what happened
values: what each person thinks matters most, such as speed or quality
Conflict also starts when people are not listening, or when they are not working from the same information.
Warning signs. Watch for:
sharp or sarcastic comments
people getting impatient
ideas shot down before the person finishes talking
the same point repeated over and over
people taking sides
lots of talk but no decision
finger pointing, and a lot of "you should"
Prevent it. Many conflicts never happen when the crew shares the same plan and drawings, checks in at the start of the day, knows who makes which decisions, and raises small problems while they are still small.
How people respond to conflict. Most of us have a habit. We might put it off, give in, push until we win, meet halfway, or work it out together. No habit is always right. If the issue is small, letting it go can be fine. If both people care about the result, working it out together usually lasts longest.
The chart places the five habits by how much you push for your own needs and how much you look after the other person's needs. Working it out together is high on both.
Four listening skills:
Attend: stop what you're doing and pay attention to the other person.
Value: show you respect them, even if you disagree with their idea.
Paraphrase: say back what you heard, in your own words. "So you're saying..."
Question: ask open questions. "What would work for you?" Be willing to change your mind.
Look for what makes sense in the other person's view before you push your own.
Say what you need: the W.I.N. method
When you... (describe what happened, not the person)
I... (say how it affects you or the work)
Need... (say what you want to happen)
Keep it natural, not like a script. With a boss, stick to facts and ask for time to talk. For example, instead of "I feel overwhelmed when you give me too much work," say: "I've stayed late four days this week to finish my work. Can we talk about my workload? When is a good time?"
Here is W.I.N. as three boxes, with an example from the rotary hammer conflict below.
Not every problem is a conflict to work out between two people. Threats, harassment and discrimination are not disagreements. You don't have to negotiate with them. Tell your supervisor. Lesson 8 covers this.
Worked example: one rotary hammer
Ridgeview Mechanical (a fictional company) has one rotary hammer on site. Apprentices Ana and Jordan both need it to drill anchor holes.
Jordan keeps picking it up while Ana is partway through a row.
How it went first: Ana: "You always grab it. You're so selfish." Jordan: "I've got work to do too. Get over it." They stop talking, and both rows fall behind.
Using W.I.N. and the listening skills: Ana: "When you take the hammer while I'm partway through a row, I lose my place and have to set up again. I need us to agree on turns. I'll be done my row by 10." Jordan (paraphrasing): "So you need it until 10 to finish the row, then I get it?" Ana: "Yes. What do you need?" Jordan: "I need it by 10 at the latest or I'll hold up the pipefitters." Ana: "Then 10 it is. I'll bring it to you."
The conflict was about the tool and the timing, not about who is selfish. Once each person said what they needed, the fix was easy.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Read this exchange from a fictional crew meeting. Underline every warning sign you find.
Lead: "We need to decide who's on the roof tomorrow." Mo: "Not me again. I'm always on the roof." Rita: "Oh, here we go." Mo: "I'm just saying, I'm always on the roof." Rita: "Well, you should have said something last week instead of..." Mo: "Don't tell me what I should have done." Lead: "Okay, let's..." Rita: "He does this every time."
Task 2 (level 2) My usual response. This is private. When I have a disagreement at work, I usually (tick all that apply):
[ ] put off dealing with it
[ ] try to meet the other person halfway
[ ] point to the rules or the boss to show I'm right
[ ] just give in
[ ] help the other person get what they want
[ ] keep pushing until I get my way
[ ] explain my side and ask for theirs
[ ] keep my ideas to myself
[ ] change the subject
[ ] try to understand the other person's side
[ ] get someone else to decide who's right
[ ] say I'm wrong even when I don't think I am
The kind of person I find easiest to work things out with is ___ because ___.
One thing I would like to change about how I handle conflict: ____
Task 3 (level 2) Paraphrase each statement. Start with "So you're saying..." or "So you need..."
a) "I've been on cleanup three days in a row and nobody else has done it once." b) "The drawings changed yesterday and nobody told the framers, so we built it wrong." c) "I don't mind starting early, but I need to be out by 3:30 to get my kid."
Task 4 (level 2) Write a W.I.N. statement for each situation.
a) A co-worker returns the crew van with the fuel light on, again. b) Your lead has given you all the cleanup for two weeks. (Remember: with a boss, stick to facts and ask for a time to talk.) c) A co-worker keeps talking over you at the morning toolbox talk.
Task 5 (level 2) "You've got it, I want it." Your instructor will give one partner an item from the box. Both partners want it badly for their work. Try to sort it out in 3 minutes, without force. Switch roles and try again. Then do it a third time using W.I.N. and the four listening skills.
What was different the third time? __________
Task 6 (level 2) Think of a conflict you are in now, or make one up. Write:
What I want to happen: ____
My W.I.N. statement: ____
When and where I will say it: ____
Task 7 (level 2) Place it on the chart. A plumber and an electrician both need the same ceiling space for their runs. Name the habit from the chart for each response.
a) The plumber says, "Fine, take it. I'll figure something out." (He is annoyed.) b) The electrician says, "I was here first. My conduit goes in today." c) They agree the plumber goes this morning and the electrician gets the space after lunch. d) They look at the drawing together and find a route where both runs fit. e) Both leave it for tomorrow without talking.
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand. Two of your apprentices, Kim and Raj (fictional), both need the only scissor lift first thing in the morning. They are arguing at the gang box. For this role-play, make up each apprentice's task, deadline and estimated lift time, and write those assumptions down before answering.
a) Write what you say to start, using one of the four listening skills. b) Write one paraphrase you could use for Kim's side. c) Kim uses W.I.N. Write her sentence. d) Write the agreement the three of you reach. Say which habit from the chart it is.
Check yourself
Name four things conflicts are usually about.
Name three warning signs that a conflict is building.
What does it mean to paraphrase? Why does it help?
What do the letters in W.I.N. stand for?
A co-worker threatens to hurt you if you report a safety problem. Is this a conflict to work out with W.I.N.? What should you do?

lessons.title: Plan and build together, then debrief
lessons.text:
Share information, agree on a plan, build a model bridge within a budget, handle a change order and look back on how the team worked.
Why this matters on the job
On a real job, nobody holds every piece of information. The super has the schedule, the engineer has the specs, the estimator has the budget and the client has what they want. The job only comes together when people share what they know, agree on one plan and adjust when a change order lands halfway through. Afterward, good crews ask, "What would we do differently next time?"
Key ideas
Share what you know. If one person keeps part of the information to themselves, the team builds the wrong thing. Say your piece out loud, then check that everyone has it.
Disagree, then decide. Two good ideas can compete. A quick, fair way to decide:
Each side explains its idea in one minute.
The other side says it back in their own words.
Together, pick the best parts of both and agree on one plan.
Agreement does not mean everyone thinks it is the best plan. It means everyone can live with it and will work on it. Problems get solved best when each person takes responsibility for both hearing and being heard.
Give everyone a part. Someone keeps the team on time, someone keeps the budget, someone builds, someone tests. Make sure no one is left watching.
Manage risk and resources. Check the budget before you buy. Test before the client sees it. Think about what could go wrong.
Debrief. After the job, look back on the work and on how the team worked together. Make suggestions that are specific and kind, and use the feedback you get.
The job runs as a loop. A change order sends the team back to the plan.
Worked example: the purchase order
A team plans to buy 8 sheets of paper and 60 cm of tape. Paper costs $2 a sheet. Tape costs $1 for each 10 cm. The budget is $30.
Paper: 8 × $2 = $16
Tape: 60 cm ÷ 10 cm = 6 pieces, and 6 × $1 = $6
Total: $16 + $6 = $22
Left in the budget: $30 − $22 = $8
The team is within budget and has $8 left for a change order.
The job
Client brief. The Lakeside Trail Society (a fictional client) wants a model footbridge to show at a meeting. Your team will design and build it from paper and tape.
Each person on your team gets one spec card from your instructor. Read your card aloud to your team. Do not hand it over. Your team needs every card to meet the brief.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Each person reads their card aloud. Together, write one list of everything the bridge must do. Check that every card is on the list.
Our spec list:
Task 2 (level 2) Sketch two different bridge ideas. Use the three-step method: each side explains for one minute, the other side says it back, then the team agrees on one plan that uses the best parts of both. Write down what you took from each idea.
Task 3 (level 2) a) Write your team's purchase order: how many sheets and how many centimetres of tape. Show that it is within the $30 budget. b) Team Pine buys 9 sheets and 80 cm of tape. Are they within budget? How much is left? c) Team Fir wants 12 sheets and 70 cm of tape. Are they within budget? By how much are they over or under? d) Name your roles: who keeps time, who keeps the budget, who builds, who tests, who talks to the client.
Task 4 (level 2-3) Build your bridge. Partway through, your instructor will hand your team a change order. Decide together how to handle it. At the end, test the bridge and give the client your 30-second explanation.
Number of washers held: _ Did we meet every spec? _
Task 5 (level 3) Debrief as a team. Write short answers:
a) What went well in how we worked together? b) What did not go well? c) Did everyone get a real chance to contribute? How do we know? d) How did we handle the change order? e) One constructive suggestion for next time, starting with "Next time we will..." f) One piece of feedback we got from the observer or instructor, and what we will do with it.
Task 6 (level 2) A real mini-job: the cut list. Your team frames a practice wall in the shop. The wall is 2,400 mm long. Studs go at 400 mm on centre, with a stud at each end. The wall has one bottom plate and one top plate, each 2,400 mm long. Each plate is 38 mm thick, and the wall is 2,400 mm tall overall.
All pieces are cut from 2,440 mm lengths of 2x4 at $5.25 each (a fictional price). The budget is $50.
a) How many studs do you need? b) How long is each stud? c) How many 2,440 mm lengths do you buy? d) What is the total cost? How much of the budget is left? e) Name a person for each role: cutter, layout, nailer, checker, budget keeper.
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. A change order lands. Halfway through, the client asks for one extra stud at 1,200 mm so a shelf can be fixed there. There is already a stud at 1,200 mm on centre, so the client wants a second stud beside it.
a) Can you cut the extra stud from offcuts? Show why or why not. b) How much over budget does the change take you? c) Write what you say to the client.
Check yourself
Why could no one person build a bridge that met the brief using only their own card?
In this lesson, what does "agreement" mean?
A team buys 7 sheets and 90 cm of tape. Are they within the $30 budget? Show your work.
Name two questions a team can ask in a debrief.
What makes a suggestion constructive? Give an example.

lessons.title: Learning from a journeyperson
lessons.text:
Understand how BC apprenticeship puts you beside a journeyperson, ask good questions, take feedback well and pass on what you learn.
Why this matters on the job
In a BC apprenticeship, most of your learning happens on the job, beside a certified journeyperson. How well you learn depends a lot on that working relationship. An apprentice who asks clear questions, listens to feedback and shows progress gets taught more, and gets trusted with more. Later, you will be the one showing someone new.
Key ideas
How apprenticeship works in BC. SkilledTradesBC runs the system. These points come from its website:
About 80% of your training happens at work, under the supervision of a certified journeyperson. About 20% is in-class technical training with a SkilledTradesBC-designated training provider.
Most apprenticeships take four or more years. The average across all trades is about 4 years.
Your sponsor (often your employer) makes sure you get on-the-job training and mentorship from a certified journeyperson. You should know which journeyperson is responsible for supervising you.
Your sponsor reports your work-based training hours in the SkilledTradesBC Portal. SkilledTradesBC recommends every 3 to 6 months. One hour on the job counts as one hour of work-based training.
Sign in to your own Portal account often to check that your hours are there. If they are missing or wrong, contact your sponsor.
At the end, your sponsor and the journeyperson who supervised you give a Recommendation for Certification, confirming you work at a journeyperson's level.
Be easy to teach.
Watch first. Ask to see it done once.
Ask at the right time. Don't interrupt someone in the middle of a cut or a lift, unless it is about safety. Never guess on safety: stop and ask.
Repeat back what you were shown: "So first I check..., then I..."
Write it down. A small notebook in your pocket beats asking the same thing three times.
Try it while they watch, then ask, "What should I change?"
Ask clear questions. "How do I do this?" is hard to answer. "I've measured twice and I get 2 mm different each time. Am I hooking the tape wrong?" shows what you tried and where you are stuck.
Take feedback well.
Listen to the end. Don't start explaining.
Say thanks, even if it stings.
Ask a question to understand: "Can you show me where it goes wrong?"
Do it differently next time.
Follow up: "Is this better?"
The five steps for taking feedback make a loop. Step 5 brings you back to listening.
Mentoring goes both ways. The Skills for Success model includes supporting others through coaching, mentoring and motivating. Once you can do a task well, you can show the next new person. Teaching something is also one of the best ways to check that you really know it.
Worked example: cuts running long
Tidewater Carpentry (a fictional company). Journeyperson Bev tells apprentice Eli: "Your stud cuts are coming out about 3 mm long."
Response A: "That's not on me. The saw's off." Eli defends himself before he knows the cause. Bev is less likely to spend time teaching him.
Response B: "Okay, thanks. Can you watch me do the next one and tell me where it's going wrong?" Bev watches and sees Eli is lining up the blade on the wrong side of his pencil line. She shows him once. Eli's next three cuts are right, and he writes the fix in his notebook. At the end of the day he says, "Checked the last ten, all on the mark."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Is this a good time to ask your journeyperson a question? Write now, wait or stop and ask right away.
a) They are on a ladder in the middle of a cut. b) You are about to start a task you've never done. c) The crane operator is taking signals from your journeyperson. d) It's coffee break, and you have a bigger question about your training plan. e) You are not sure the power to the circuit you are about to touch is off. f) They have just shown you a step, and you didn't catch part of it.
Task 2 (level 1) Make each question clear and specific. Add what you tried or what you see.
a) "How do I do this?" b) "Is this right?" c) "What now?"
Task 3 (level 2) a) Your journeyperson says: "You left the extension cord across the walkway again." Which response is best, and why?
"Everyone does it."
"Sorry. I'll run it along the wall now and check the walkway before I start each task."
"I was going to move it."
b) Your journeyperson says: "You're fast, but you're not checking your work before you call it done." Write your own response using the five feedback steps.
Task 4 (level 2) You started with your sponsor on January 6. You have worked 40 hours a week for 30 weeks. Your Portal account shows 960 work-based training hours.
a) How many hours have you worked? b) How many hours are not showing in the Portal? c) How many 40-hour weeks is that? d) Write a short, polite message to your sponsor about it.
Task 5 (level 2) Coach a partner. Pick a simple task you know well (a knot, folding a shirt for a drawer, a phone setting, a step in your trade). Explain it in 4 steps or fewer. Watch your partner do it. Ask them to say the steps back. Then switch.
What I changed in my explanation after watching my partner: ____
Task 6 (level 2) Use the loop. Your journeyperson looks at your fillet welds on a bracket and says: "These are undercut. Grind them out and redo them."
a) Step 2: what do you say? b) Step 3: write one question to understand. c) Step 5: what do you say after the redo?
Task 7 (level 3) Now you teach. You are a third-year carpentry apprentice. A new first-year, Noor (fictional), needs to learn to mark and cut blocking with a speed square.
a) Write four short teaching steps. Use the "be easy to teach" list from the other side: what will you show, what will Noor try, how will you check? b) Noor's first cut is 3 mm long. Write the feedback you give. Use facts and say what to do next. c) How will you know Noor has really learned it?
Check yourself
About what share of BC apprenticeship training happens at work?
Who reports your work-based training hours, and where?
Name two things you can do to be easy to teach.
What should you do first when you get feedback?
Name one way you can support a newer worker.

lessons.title: Respectful workplaces, bullying and harassment
lessons.text:
Know what counts as workplace bullying and harassment in BC, what employers, supervisors and workers must do, and how to report it.
Why this matters on the job
Some crews still treat hazing and put-downs as part of "paying your dues." WorkSafeBC does not. It treats workplace bullying and harassment as a health and safety hazard, and its policies say it can lead to injury, illness or death. Every BC worker has duties here, including you. Knowing the rules helps you protect yourself, back up a co-worker and keep good people in the trade.
Key ideas
What it is. WorkSafeBC defines bullying and harassment as any inappropriate conduct or comment by a person toward a worker that the person knew, or reasonably ought to have known, would cause that worker to be humiliated or intimidated. It does not include reasonable action by an employer or supervisor to manage and direct workers or the workplace.
The "person" can be anyone at work: a boss, a co-worker, a client or a member of the public.
Can be bullying and harassment Is not bullying and harassment
Verbal aggression or yelling Expressing a different opinion
Humiliating initiation practices or hazing Constructive feedback, guidance or advice about work
Spreading malicious rumours Reasonable management action, such as managing your performance, reasonable discipline or assigning work
Calling someone derogatory names
Any other conduct or comment that would make someone feel humiliated or intimidated
Who must do what. WorkSafeBC policy sets out duties for each person.
Employers must, among other things: - have a policy statement that bullying and harassment is not acceptable or tolerated - take steps to prevent it where possible, or otherwise minimize it - have procedures for workers to report it, including what to do if the employer or supervisor is the one doing it - have procedures for dealing with reports, including investigation - tell workers about the policy, and train supervisors and workers - review the policy and procedures every year - not bully or harass, and follow their own policy
Supervisors must not bully or harass, and must follow the employer's policy and procedures.
Workers must: - not bully or harass anyone at work - report bullying and harassment they see or experience - follow the employer's policy and procedures
How to report. WorkSafeBC lists these steps:
Report it to your employer as soon as possible, following your employer's procedures.
If your employer has no policy or procedures, or has not taken reasonable steps, call WorkSafeBC's Prevention Information Line at 604.276.3100 (1.888.621.7233 toll free) and speak with a prevention officer.
After that, you can send WorkSafeBC a Bullying and Harassment Questionnaire.
WorkSafeBC checks that employers have proper policies and deal with reports. It does not mediate disputes between people.
The chart shows the same three reporting steps as a flow.
Harassment linked to a protected ground, such as Indigenous identity, race, sex or religion, can also be discrimination under the BC Human Rights Code (see lesson 3).
Industry action. The Builders Code, managed by the BC Construction Association, sets a code of conduct for construction sites. Companies sign a pledge for an "Acceptable Worksite" that is free from hazing, harassment, bullying and discrimination.
If you are standing nearby, you can: refuse to join in or laugh, say something short if it is safe ("Not cool, leave it"), check on the person afterward, and report it. Reporting what you see is one of your duties as a worker.
Worked example: the "initiation"
Summit Steel (a fictional company). On Nico's first week, the crew sends him to the tool crib for a "bucket of steam." Everyone laughs, and so does Nico. The next day two crew members tape him to a column during lunch, film it and post the video in the crew group chat with "Welcome, rookie."
The first joke is a well-known gag. Many people would shrug it off. But if Nico is singled out again and again, it can become humiliating.
Taping a worker to a column and posting a video of it is a humiliating initiation practice, or hazing. It fits WorkSafeBC's list.
Every worker who saw the video has a duty to report it. The employer must deal with the report using its procedures.
What does not count: the next week the foreman tells Nico his bolt-up was sloppy and has him redo it. That is reasonable direction of work, as long as it is done reasonably.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) For each situation, decide: likely bullying and harassment or not bullying and harassment. Say which part of WorkSafeBC's lists it matches.
a) The foreman tells you your welds failed inspection and you have to redo them. b) Two crew members yell at a new worker and call him names every morning. c) Two journeypersons disagree about the order of work, then agree on a plan. d) Someone spreads a story that a co-worker only got hired because of who she knows. e) New apprentices are taped to a post as an "initiation." f) Your supervisor assigns you to cleanup for the afternoon. g) A customer keeps making comments about a tradeswoman's body every time she is on site. h) A co-worker shows you a safer way to hold the grinder.
Task 2 (level 2) Who has this duty under WorkSafeBC policy: the employer, the supervisor, the worker, or more than one?
a) Not bullying or harassing anyone b) Reporting bullying and harassment you see or experience c) Training workers and supervisors d) Reviewing the policy every year e) Following the employer's policy and procedures f) Having a way to report when the supervisor is the one doing it
Task 3 (level 2) You are on the Summit Steel crew and you see the video of Nico in the group chat. Write what you will do, in order. Include what you say or don't say in the chat, what you say to Nico, and how you report it.
Task 4 (level 2) Write a short report to your supervisor about the Summit Steel video. Stick to facts. Include what happened, when, where, who was involved, who else saw it, and what you have done so far. If the case does not give a detail, write "not yet known" or use a blank to confirm later. Do not invent witnesses, times or actions already taken.
Task 5 (level 2) Go to WorkSafeBC's page "Responding to workplace bullying and harassment": https://www.worksafebc.com/en/health-safety/hazards-exposures/bullying-harassment/responding-bullying-harassment
a) What is the first thing it says to do? b) What is the toll-free number for the Prevention Information Line? c) What can you submit after you have reported to your employer and spoken with a prevention officer?
Task 6 (level 2) Follow the chart. For each person, write the next step from the chart.
a) Maya (fictional) is called names every day by a co-worker. She has not told anyone. b) Joe reported harassment to his employer two weeks ago. The employer has no policy and has done nothing. c) Ana called the Prevention Information Line and spoke with a prevention officer.
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. For a week, one of your crew has hidden the new apprentice's tools every morning "as a joke." The apprentice laughs, but you can see he is upset, and he is late starting work each day.
a) Could this be bullying and harassment under WorkSafeBC's definition? Explain using the words of the definition. b) As a supervisor, what two things must you do? c) Write what you say to the crew member who hides the tools. d) Write what you say to the apprentice.
Check yourself
In your own words, what is WorkSafeBC's definition of bullying and harassment?
Name two things that are not bullying and harassment.
What are the three duties of a worker?
You see or experience bullying and harassment at work. What do you do first?
What is the Builders Code?
If this topic brings up something hard for you, talk to your instructor or someone you trust. The Hope for Wellness Help Line for Indigenous people in Canada is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, at 1-855-242-3310 or hopeforwellness.ca.

lessons.title: Who does what on a job site
lessons.text:
Know the people on a building site, from the owner to the apprentice, who you ask for what, and how BC law makes one party coordinate safety for everyone.
Why this matters on the job
On your first day on a big site you may meet 40 people from six companies. Some can tell you what to do. Some cannot. If you ask the wrong person, you lose time, or you get an answer that is not theirs to give. If you know who does what, you can find the right person fast, you know whose plan you are following, and you know who to tell when something is unsafe.
Key ideas
The owner pays for the building. The owner might be a person, a company, a First Nation or a school district. On most jobs the owner hires a general contractor to build it.
The general contractor (GC) runs the whole job for the owner. The GC hires subcontractors (subs) for parts of the work, such as plumbing, electrical, drywall or roofing.
The prime contractor is a BC legal role. When workers of two or more employers work at a site at the same time, it is a multiple-employer workplace. The prime contractor must make sure everyone's health and safety work is coordinated. The prime contractor is the contractor named in a written agreement with the owner. With no written agreement, the owner is the prime contractor. On most building sites, the GC is the prime contractor.
Each employer on a multiple-employer site must give the prime contractor the name of the person who supervises its workers there.
On the site, from the top down:
Role What they do Ask them about
Superintendent (super) Runs the whole site for the GC. Plans the order of work across trades. Which trade works where and when, site rules, access
Foreman Runs one company's crew or crews on the site. Your crew's plan for the week, hours, problems with another trade
Lead hand Leads a small crew day to day. Often a journeyperson. Today's task, tools, where to start
Journeyperson A certified tradesperson. Supervises and teaches apprentices. How to do the work right
Apprentice Learning the trade on the job, under a journeyperson. Ask up, help the next new person
Labourer Moves material, cleans up, helps the trades. Where things are on site
Inspector Checks that the work meets the code or permit. Works for a city, Technical Safety BC or another authority. Does not direct crews. Nothing directly. Your foreman deals with inspectors.
Job titles change from company to company. Some sites have a project manager in the office, a site safety coordinator or an engineer. Ask on your first day: "Who is my supervisor here, and who do I go to when they are not around?"
Your supervisor is the person named to supervise you. On most crews that is your foreman or lead hand. Unsafe conditions get reported to a supervisor or the employer as soon as possible. That is a rule in BC's Occupational Health and Safety Regulation, section 3.10.
The chart shows how the roles connect on a typical site.
Ask the right person. Most questions go to the closest person who can answer them. Go up one step when they cannot. Safety goes to your supervisor right away, every time.
Worked example: whose question is it?
Riverside Commons is a fictional three-storey building. The owner is Riverside Housing Society (fictional). Tallgrass Builders (fictional) is the GC and prime contractor. Maria is the superintendent. Coast Mechanical (fictional) has the plumbing sub. Its foreman is Dev. Jordan is a first-year plumbing apprentice working with Lou, a journeyperson.
Jordan has four questions on Monday morning.
Jordan's question Who Jordan asks Why
"How do I support this pipe run?" Lou, the journeyperson It is about how to do the work.
"Can I use the GC's scissor lift?" Dev, the foreman Shared equipment is arranged between companies. Dev asks Maria.
"The guardrail on level 3 is missing." Dev, right away, in person Unsafe condition. Section 3.10 says report it as soon as possible to a supervisor or employer.
"Is the inspector coming today?" Dev Inspections are booked and handled by the foreman and the GC.
Jordan did not go to Maria for every question. Maria runs the whole site. Dev speaks for Coast Mechanical. That keeps one clear line between the two companies.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Match the role. Write the role from the table.
a) Certified in the trade. Supervises and teaches apprentices. __
b) Runs the whole site for the general contractor. __
c) Pays for the building. __
d) Checks work against the code, but does not direct crews. __
e) Runs one company's crew or crews on the site. __
Task 2 (level 1) Read the chart. Use the organization chart.
a) Who does the plumbing subcontractor's crew answer to on site?
b) Where do inspectors sit on the chart, and why are they drawn apart?
c) Who hires the general contractor?
Task 3 (level 1) Ask first. Who do you ask first? Use the "Ask first" chart.
a) Your hours are missing in the SkilledTradesBC Portal. __
b) You don't know how to set the depth on the rotary hammer. __
c) The stair handrail is loose. __
d) You need to know which room to start in today. __
Task 4 (level 2) Prime contractor. Answer from the Key ideas.
a) What makes a site a multiple-employer workplace?
b) Who is the prime contractor if there is no written agreement with the owner?
c) What must each employer give the prime contractor?
Task 5 (level 2) Who speaks for whom? You are an apprentice with an electrical sub. The drywall crew keeps boarding over your boxes before you finish. Who do you tell, and who should talk to the drywall company?
Task 6 (level 2) Draw your site. Draw an organization chart for a job you have worked on or seen, or for the Riverside Commons example. Include at least five roles. Circle yourself.
Task 7 (level 2) First-day question. Write the question you ask on your first morning to find out who your supervisor is and who to go to when they are away.
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand. You lead a four-person framing crew for Tallgrass Builders. Your foreman is off site until 1:00. At 9:30:
The electrical sub's apprentice asks you if he can move your lumber pile to get to a panel.
One of your crew says the temporary stairs to level 2 are wobbling.
A city building inspector asks where the framing for unit 204 is.
For each one, write what you do and who you tell.
Task 9 (level 3) The shortcut. A new apprentice on your crew goes straight to the superintendent every time he needs a tool. The super tells you, "Your guy keeps coming to me." Write what you say to the apprentice. Explain why the line matters without making him feel stupid.
Check yourself
Name the role that runs the whole site for the general contractor.
What is a multiple-employer workplace in BC?
Who must coordinate health and safety on a multiple-employer workplace?
Who do you tell first about an unsafe condition, and how soon?
Why do inspectors not give orders to your crew?

lessons.title: Work around other trades
lessons.text:
Follow the order of trades on a shared job, know who waits on whom, respect inspection hold points and keep the next trade moving.
Why this matters on the job
A washroom renovation can bring seven trades into one small room. The plumber cannot rough in until the framing is done. The drywaller cannot board until the inspector passes the pipes and wires behind the wall. The tiler cannot start until the board is up. If one trade is late, or covers something too soon, every trade after it loses time and money. Good trades know the order, know who is waiting on them and keep the next crew moving.
Key ideas
Trades work in a sequence. Some work must be finished before the next can start. That is called a dependency. "Rough-in" is the work inside the walls and floors: pipes, drains, vents, wires and boxes. "Finish" is what you see at the end: fixtures, cover plates, tile.
Hold points. In many BC cities, rough-in plumbing must be inspected and accepted before it is covered. Electrical rough wiring must be inspected, or the inspection waived by the safety authority, before any part of it is concealed. Many cities also inspect insulation and vapour barrier before drywall goes on. The permit and the inspection list for your job say which inspections apply. Until an inspection passes, nobody covers the work. That point in the job is a hold point.
Who waits on whom. The swimlane chart below shows a fictional 12-day washroom renovation. Each row is a trade. Read across for days. The arrows show who waits on whom.
Read the chart like this: framing is days 1 and 2. The plumber starts on day 3. The electrician overlaps the plumber on day 4. The rough-in inspection is day 6. Insulation, its inspection, drywall and tile follow.
Habits that keep the next trade moving:
Know who is next. Ask your lead hand who follows you in this room.
Say when you are done. Tell your foreman when an area is ready for the next trade or for inspection. Do not let people guess.
Say early when you will be late. One day late for you can be one day late for every trade after you.
Protect other trades' work. Do not step on pipes, bend boxes or lean material on fresh tape.
Do not move another trade's material or tools without asking their crew or your foreman.
Never cover work that has not passed inspection, even if you are told it "passed yesterday." Check with your foreman.
Problems between trades go foreman to foreman. If the drywallers keep boarding over your boxes, tell your foreman. Your foreman talks to their foreman or the superintendent. Arguing in the hallway with another company's crew rarely fixes the schedule.
Worked example: one day late
Use the swimlane chart. The electrician at Northline Electric (fictional) finds a damaged junction box on day 5. The rough-in now finishes at the end of day 6, not day 5.
The rough-in inspection cannot happen until the electrical rough-in is done. It moves from day 6 to day 7.
Insulation moves from day 7 to day 8. Its inspection moves from day 8 to day 9.
Drywall moves from days 9 and 10 to days 10 and 11.
Tile moves from days 11 and 12 to days 12 and 13.
One day late in electrical makes the whole job one day late. The plumber is not affected, because the plumber finished on day 4.
What the electrician's lead hand did right: at 10:00 on day 5 she told her foreman, "Damaged box in the washroom. Rough-in finishes end of day 6, not today. Can you tell the super so the inspection can move?" The super moved the inspection and called the insulator the same morning. Nobody showed up to a room they could not work in.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Rough-in or finish? Write R for rough-in or F for finish.
a) Setting the toilet _ b) Running the drain line in the floor c) Pulling wire to a switch box _ d) Putting cover plates on switches e) Grouting tile ____
Task 2 (level 2) Read the swimlane.
a) Which trades work on day 4? b) On what day is the rough-in inspection? c) Who is the insulator waiting on? d) How many days does the whole job take?
Task 3 (level 2) Hold point. Use the hold point figure.
a) What has to happen before anyone covers rough-in work? b) What happens if the inspection fails?
Task 4 (level 2) Who is affected? The plumber finishes rough-in one day late, at the end of day 5 instead of day 4. The electrician also finishes at the end of day 5, as planned. On what day can the rough-in inspection happen now? Does the finish date change? Explain.
Task 5 (level 2) Two days late. The rough-in inspection fails on day 6. The plumber fixes the problem on day 7, and the inspector comes back on day 8 and passes it. Write the new days for insulation, its inspection, drywall and tile. On what day is the job done?
Work New day(s)
Insulation
Insulation inspection
Drywall
Tile
Task 6 (level 2) The right words. Write the message you send your foreman when your area is ready for inspection.
Task 7 (level 2) Good habit or not? Write G for a good habit or N for not.
a) _ You lean your ladder on the plumber's new copper. b) You tell your foreman at 9:00 that you will be a day late. c) _ You move the tiler's buckets to get to your panel, without asking. d) You ask your lead hand who follows you in unit 3. e) ____ You board a wall because "the electrician said it passed."
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand. You lead the drywall crew for Lakehead Interiors (fictional). It is day 9 in the swimlane plan. You arrive and see the insulation inspection sticker is not posted, and the vapour barrier is torn in two places.
a) Do you start boarding? Why or why not? b) Who do you tell, and what do you say? c) What can your crew do today instead?
Task 9 (level 3) Sequence a job. Put these steps for a new kitchen wall in order, from 1 to 7. Then mark the hold point with an H.
_ Electrical rough-in Drywall _ Framing Rough-in inspection _ Cabinets and finish _ Insulation and vapour barrier ____ Plumbing rough-in
