Task 10 (level 3) Hallway argument. A drywaller from another company says to you, "Your boxes aren't done. We're boarding this wall now, you'll have to cut them out after." You are an electrical apprentice.
a) Write what you say to him, assertively and calmly. b) Who do you tell next? c) Why is boarding over the boxes a problem beyond your extra work?
Check yourself
What is a dependency between trades?
What is a hold point?
Name two habits that keep the next trade moving.
Who should sort out a problem between two companies' crews?
One trade is one day late, and every trade after it waits on it. What happens to the finish date?

lessons.title: Run a pre-task huddle and hand over at shift end
lessons.text:
Run a short huddle before a task so everyone knows the plan, the hazards and their part, and hand over cleanly so the next shift can start safely.
Why this matters on the job
Many incidents start with "I thought you knew." A five-minute huddle before a task puts everyone on the same plan. A clear handover at the end of a shift means the next crew does not walk into an open floor hole, a half-finished anchor or a tool that is not where they think. These two short talks are where collaboration happens every day on a site.
Key ideas
A pre-task huddle is a short talk at the work area, right before a task starts. It is not the same as a toolbox talk. A toolbox talk teaches a topic. A huddle plans one task, today, with this crew. Your site may have its own form and its own name for it. Use theirs.
Five steps for a huddle:
The task. What we are doing, where and by when.
The hazards. What could hurt someone here today. Ask the crew. The newest person often sees something the others stopped noticing.
The controls. What we will do about each hazard.
Who does what. A name for each job. Nobody is left watching.
Questions. Ask for questions. Remind everyone that anyone who sees something unsafe stops and reports it. In BC, a person who sees an unsafe condition must report it as soon as possible to a supervisor or the employer.
Make it a conversation. Ask open questions: "What else could go wrong here?" "Who hasn't done this before?" Let people answer. A huddle where only the lead talks is a speech.
A shift handover passes the work to the next person or crew. Do it face to face if you can, and in writing every time. The handover card covers six things:
Part What it says
Done What is finished, with a count or location.
Not done What is left, and where.
Hazards Anything unsafe or changed: openings, live circuits, lockouts, wet concrete.
Tools and gear Where things are, and their state (charged, tagged out).
Watch for Anything the next crew must know before starting.
Questions to Who to call, with a number.
Write numbers and places exactly. "Most of the anchors" is not a handover. "14 of 20 anchors, grid C to D left" is.
Worked example: the anchor job
Harbourside Concrete Anchors (fictional) is drilling anchors for a steel ledger on level 2. Sam, the day-shift lead hand, runs this huddle at 7:00:
Task: "We're drilling 20 anchors on the east wall of level 2, grid A to D, done by 3:00."
Hazards: "What could hurt us?" The crew names the floor opening at C4, silica dust from drilling, and rebar in the wall.
Controls: "The opening stays covered and tagged. We use the hammer with the dust extractor. We scan before each hole, and if we hit rebar, we stop and call me."
Who does what: "Kai drills. Rose scans and marks. Ben runs the vacuum and moves the lift."
Questions: "Questions? Anyone not done this before? Remember, anyone can stop the job."
At 3:00 the crew has drilled 14 holes. At C3 the scanner found rebar. The engineer said to move that hole 50 mm. Sam fills in the handover card shown above and walks the evening lead hand along the wall.
The evening crew knows exactly how many holes are left, where the opening is, where the hammer is and what to do at C3. Nobody has to call Sam at home.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Huddle or toolbox talk? Write H for huddle or T for toolbox talk.
a) A 5-minute talk on ladder safety at Monday's crew meeting _ b) A 3-minute plan at the trench before today's pipe lay _ c) Who rigs, who signals and who tags out before this afternoon's lift ____
Task 2 (level 1) Name the step. Which of the five huddle steps is each line?
a) "Ali, you're the spotter." __ b) "The grinder sparks could reach the fuel cans." _ c) "We're pouring the north footing by noon." ___ d) "We move the cans 10 metres away and set a fire extinguisher by the grinder." ______
Task 3 (level 2) Find the hazards. You are about to lay asphalt in a parking lot that is still open to cars. List three hazards and one control for each.
Hazard Control
Task 4 (level 2) Fix the handover. Read this handover note. List what is missing or too vague. Then rewrite it.
"Did most of the conduit. Some left. Stuff's in the room. Be careful upstairs."
Missing or vague: __________
Rewrite: __________
Task 5 (level 2) Write your card. Think of the last task you did at work, school or home that someone else had to pick up. Fill in a handover card for it.
Task 6 (level 2) Open questions. Write two open questions a lead hand can ask in a huddle to get the crew talking about hazards.
Task 7 (level 2) Read the card. Use the filled handover card above.
a) How many anchors are left? b) Where is the floor opening, and what state is it in? c) What must the next crew do at C3?
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand. Run the huddle. Your crew of four will hang a steel beam with a mobile crane this afternoon. Write a full five-step huddle. Use real names for your crew (fictional is fine). Include at least three hazards and a control for each.
Task 9 (level 3) The silent crew. You run a huddle and nobody says anything. One apprentice looks worried. What three things do you do differently, right now and next time?
Task 10 (level 3) A handover gone wrong. The night crew on a road job did not tell the day crew that a lane closure sign had blown over at 4:00. At 7:00 a car drove into the work zone. Nobody was hurt.
a) What should the night crew's handover have said? b) Write a rule your crew could add to every handover so this does not happen again. c) Who must be told about the sign and the near miss, and how soon?
Check yourself
How is a pre-task huddle different from a toolbox talk?
Name the five huddle steps.
Why should the newest person be asked about hazards?
Name the six parts of a handover card.
Why is "most of it is done" not a good handover?

lessons.title: Disagree with a lead hand and still get the work done
lessons.text:
Tell a work disagreement from a safety refusal, raise your view once with facts, accept the decision and do the work well, and know how to take a problem further.
Why this matters on the job
You will not agree with every call your lead hand makes. Sometimes you will be right. Sometimes you will not know what they know: the schedule, the engineer's note, the budget, the client. Workers who argue every call, or who go quiet and do sloppy work, lose trust fast. Workers who speak up once, clearly, then do the job well, earn the right to be listened to. And when it is about safety, the rules are different.
Key ideas
First question: is it a safety issue?
Yes. You do not have to argue or "disagree and commit." In BC, if you see an unsafe condition, you must report it as soon as possible to your supervisor or employer (OHS Regulation section 3.10). If you have reasonable cause to believe a task would create an undue hazard, you must not do it, and you must report it right away (section 3.12). Communication lesson 4 teaches the refusal steps.
No. It is a work disagreement: a method, an order of tasks, a tool, a layout. Use the steps below.
Steps for a work disagreement:
Pick the moment. Not in the middle of a lift or a pour. Not in front of the crew if you can avoid it.
Say it once, with facts. Use W.I.N. from lesson 5: when (what you see), I (the effect on the work), need (your idea). "When we run the conduit before the sprinkler lines, I think we'll have to move it twice. Can we wait a day for the sprinkler fitters?"
Ask, then listen. "Is there a reason we're doing it this way?" There may be one you do not know.
The lead hand decides. It is their call and their responsibility.
Disagree and commit. If it is not a safety issue, do it their way, and do it well. No slow work, no "I told you so," no complaining to the crew.
If the problem keeps happening, bring facts to the foreman, in private. "Three times this week we've moved conduit after the sprinkler crew came through. Here are the photos."
Commit means really commit. Doing a job badly to prove a point damages the work, the crew and your name. If your way was better, the results will show it over time.
Going up the chain. Most problems are solved at the lowest step. Go up one step at a time, with facts. Safety concerns that are not fixed can go to your health and safety representative or joint health and safety committee if your workplace has one. If unsafe work is still not resolved after the refusal steps, WorkSafeBC investigates.
Your tone matters as much as your point. Lessons 3 and 5 of the Communication series cover assertive statements and taking criticism. Stay calm and factual. Do not make it personal: "Your plan won't work" invites a fight. "I see a problem with the order. Can I show you?" invites a look.
Worked example: the backfill
Cedar Ridge Civil (fictional) is laying a storm drain. Ravi, a second-year pipelayer apprentice, thinks the crew should compact the backfill in thinner layers than the lead hand, Bo, has asked for.
Is it a safety issue? Not directly. Nobody is in danger from the layer thickness itself. It is a work quality question.
Ravi waits for a pause, then speaks to Bo away from the excavator:
"Bo, can I ask about the backfill? When we lift it in 300 mm layers, I'm not sure the plate tamper gets it all. I need to know we'll pass the compaction test. Could we try 150?"
Bo explains: "Good catch to ask. The engineer's spec for this job says 300 mm lifts with the big roller, not the plate. The roller's coming at 10:00."
Ravi commits: "Got it. 300 with the roller. I'll stage the next load."
Ravi was not wrong to ask. Bo knew something Ravi did not. Ravi spoke once, listened, and got back to work. Next time Bo is more likely to listen to Ravi.
If Bo had said "Just do it" with no reason, Ravi would still do it Bo's way, and well. If the compaction test failed later, Ravi would bring the facts to the foreman calmly, not to the crew.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Safety or work disagreement? Write S for a safety issue or W for a work disagreement.
a) _ The lead hand wants studs at 400 mm on centre. You think 600 mm is enough. b) The lead hand tells you to work on a roof edge with no guardrail and no fall protection. c) _ The lead hand wants you to cut all the pieces first. You would rather cut and install as you go. d) The lead hand tells you to use a grinder with the guard removed. e) ____ The lead hand wants the crew to start on the north side. You think south is faster.
Task 2 (level 2) What do you do? For each S in Task 1, write what you must do and which section of the OHS Regulation says so.
Task 3 (level 2) W.I.N. it. Rewrite this as a W.I.N. statement to a lead hand, in private:
"That's a dumb way to do it. Everyone knows you rough in the drain first."
Task 4 (level 2) Ask for the reason. Write two respectful questions that ask why the lead hand chose a method, without sounding like an attack.
Task 5 (level 3) Disagree and commit. Your lead hand listens and still says, "We do it my way." It is not a safety issue. Write the one sentence you say next. Then list two things you will not do afterward.
Task 6 (level 3) Read the ladder. For each problem, write who you go to first, and who next if it is not fixed.
a) The lead hand keeps giving the best jobs to his cousin. b) The site washroom has been out of order for three days. c) Your lead hand keeps sending you to work under a load that is being lifted, and nothing changes after you report it.
Task 7 (level 3) Facts for the foreman. The same layout mistake has happened three times this month. Each time, the crew tore out and rebuilt a wall. Write what you bring to the foreman, and the first two sentences you say. Use facts, not blame.
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand now. An apprentice disagrees with your plan in front of the crew, loudly. You are fairly sure your plan is right, but you are not certain.
a) What do you say right then? b) What do you do in private afterward? c) Your apprentice turns out to be right. What do you say to the crew?
Task 9 (level 3) Role play. In groups of three, act out one disagreement from your own trade. One person is the lead hand, one is the worker and one observes. Then rotate roles. The observer checks:
[ ] picked a good moment
[ ] said it once, with facts
[ ] asked for the reason and listened
[ ] accepted the decision, or named the safety rule
[ ] stayed calm and kept it about the work
Check yourself
What is the first question to ask yourself when you disagree with a lead hand?
What do sections 3.10 and 3.12 of the OHS Regulation require?
What does "disagree and commit" mean?
Why should you raise a disagreement in private when you can?
When a problem keeps happening, what do you bring to the foreman?

lessons.title: Who does what on this task with a RACI chart
lessons.text:
Use a RACI chart to show who does each task, who answers for it, who to ask first and who to tell after, so nothing falls between two people.
All people and companies in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
Lesson 9 showed who is who on a site: owner, general contractor, foreman, lead hand, journeyperson, apprentice. That tells you people's titles. It does not tell you who books the inspection on Tuesday, or who checks the stair stringers before they go in. When two people each think the other one will do a task, it does not get done. When two people both think they are in charge of it, they argue. A RACI chart fixes that one task at a time.
Key ideas
The four letters
A RACI chart is a grid. Each row is a task. Each column is a person or a role. Each box gets a letter.
Letter Stands for What it means for that task
R Responsible Does the work.
A Accountable Answers for it. Makes the final call and signs off that it is done right.
C Consulted Asked before or during the work. Their advice goes into it. Two-way talk.
I Informed Told after a decision or when the work is done. One-way message.
A box can also be blank. That person has no part in that task.
Three rules for a good chart
Exactly one A on every task. Two A's means two bosses for one task. No A means nobody answers for it.
At least one R on every task. Someone has to do the work.
One person can be A and R on the same task. On a small crew the foreman often orders the lumber and answers for it. Write it as A/R.
C or I?
Ask yourself: do I need this person's answer before the work goes ahead? If yes, they are C. If they only need to know it happened, they are I. Too many C's slow a job down. Too few I's leave people guessing.
A RACI chart is not the org chart
The org chart in lesson 9 shows who answers to whom for the whole job. A RACI chart works task by task. An apprentice can be R on a task. A homeowner can be A on a choice that is theirs to make, such as the railing style.
Worked example: the backyard deck
Riverbend Decks is building a backyard deck for a homeowner, Grace. Sam is the foreman. Ana is the lead hand, a journeyperson carpenter. Kyle is a first-year carpentry apprentice working with Ana. On this job, Sam books all inspections with the city.
Task Grace (homeowner) Sam (foreman) Ana (lead hand) Kyle (apprentice)
1. Order the lumber I A/R C
2. Book the footing inspection I A/R I
3. Dig and pour the footings I A R R
4. Cut the stair stringers I A R
5. Choose the railing style A R C
6. Check the railing before handover I A R I
Read row 4 across. Kyle cuts the stringers (R). Ana answers for them, checks them and signs off (A). Sam is told when they are done (I). Grace has no part in it, so her box is blank.
Read row 5. The railing style is Grace's choice, so she is A. Sam brings her the options and prices (R). He asks Ana first whether each style can be built on this deck (C).
Check the rules. Count the A's in each row: every row has exactly one. Count the R's: every row has at least one. The chart passes.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Match the letter. Write R, A, C or I.
a) Is told after the work is done. ______
b) Does the work. ______
c) Answers for the task and signs off on it. ______
d) Is asked before the work goes ahead. ______
Task 2 (level 1) Read the deck chart. Use the worked example.
a) Who is accountable for digging and pouring the footings?
b) Who must Sam ask before he orders the lumber?
c) Kyle finishes the stringers. Who checks them?
d) On which task is Grace accountable?
Task 3 (level 2) Count the letters. Use the worked example.
a) On how many tasks is Ana R?
b) On how many tasks is Sam A, including A/R?
c) How many boxes in the whole chart are blank?
Task 4 (level 2) Fix the chart. A new foreman drew this chart for a garage slab. Find the three problems and write how you would fix each one.
Task Foreman Lead hand Apprentice Concrete supplier
A. Set the forms A A R
B. Order the concrete C R
C. Place and finish the slab A R R I
D. Strip the forms A I I
Task 5 (level 2) Fill in a shop chart. Ironwood Fabrication is building 10 sections of steel handrail in the shop. Read the notes. Then fill in the chart with R, A, C or I.
Marco, the shop foreman, answers for every step and signs off the finished sections.
Lena, a journeyperson fabricator, fits and welds the sections. She asks Marco before she changes the welding order.
Tyler, an apprentice, cuts the pipe and grinds the welds under Lena.
Lena checks Tyler's cuts before fitting.
The painter primes the finished sections. He is told when each section is ready.
Task Marco (foreman) Lena (journeyperson) Tyler (apprentice) Painter
Cut the pipe
Fit and weld
Grind the welds
Prime
Task 6 (level 2) It fell between two people. On a renovation, the electrical rough-in was covered with drywall before the inspection. Afterwards the foreman said, "I thought the lead hand booked it." The lead hand said, "I thought the foreman did." Which letter was missing from the task "Book the electrical inspection", and how would a RACI chart have stopped this?
Task 7 (level 2) Your own crew. Pick three tasks from your shop class or a job you know (for example, end-of-day clean-up, signing out a tool, the morning safety check). Make a RACI chart with at least three people or roles. Check it with the three rules.
Check yourself
What do the four letters in RACI stand for?
How many A's should each task have?
What is the difference between C and I?
Can the same person be A and R on one task?
How is a RACI chart different from the org chart in lesson 9?

lessons.title: How the job was bought and who answers to whom
lessons.text:
Know the three common ways an owner buys a building, which bonds protect whom, and how a shop drawing travels up the chain and back, so your questions and paperwork go to the right place.
All people, companies and jobs in this lesson are fictional. The facts about contracts, bonds and shop drawings come from the sources your instructor lists.
Why this matters on the job
Lesson 9 showed the people on a site. But the lines between them depend on how the owner bought the job. On one job your design question goes through the general contractor to the architect. On another it stays inside one company. On another, your company's contract is with the owner, but a construction manager runs the site. If you know how the job was bought, you know where a question goes, who pays your company, and why a steel railing cannot be built until its shop drawing comes back stamped.
Key ideas
Three common ways to buy a building
Way to buy How it works Who your company usually signs with Where a design question goes
Design-bid-build The owner hires designers (architect, engineers) first. They finish the drawings and specifications. Contractors bid. The owner signs with one general contractor (GC) to build it. The GC (you are a subcontractor) You, your foreman, the GC, then the consultant (usually by RFI, Communication lesson 12)
Design-build The owner signs one contract with a design-builder, who both designs and builds. The design-builder You, your foreman, the design-builder, whose own designers answer
Construction management The owner hires a construction manager (CM) early to give advice on cost, schedule and how to build it while the design is being done. The work is split into packages and each trade bids its own package. Either the owner (when the CM gives services only) or the CM (when the CM also does the construction) You, your foreman, the CM, then the consultant
The standard Canadian forms of contract come from the Canadian Construction Documents Committee (CCDC). CCDC 2 is the stipulated price (fixed price) contract used on many design-bid-build jobs. CCDC 14 is a design-build stipulated price contract. CCDC 5A and CCDC 5B are construction management contracts.
Safety does not change. In BC, whatever way the job was bought, the prime contractor rule from lesson 9 still applies. If the owner has not named a prime contractor in a written agreement, the owner is the prime contractor.
Bonds: promises backed by a surety
On many jobs, especially public ones, the owner asks contractors for bonds. A bond is a promise from a surety company that backs up the contractor.
Bond When What it protects
Bid bond With the bid That the bidder is serious, will sign the contract at the price it bid, and will provide the performance and payment bonds.
Performance bond After the contract is signed The owner, if the contractor fails to do the work as the contract says.
Labour and material payment bond After the contract is signed Subcontractors and suppliers who have a direct contract with the bonded contractor, if they are not paid. Lower-tier subs and suppliers are not covered by the standard bond.
The Surety Association of Canada says performance bonds and labour and material payment bonds are each typically 50% of the contract amount. The bond amount is the most the surety will pay.
The shop drawing chain
Contract drawings show what the designer wants. A shop drawing is drawn by the fabricator or supplier to show exactly how it will make and install its part: sizes, materials, connections, field dimensions. A steel stair railing, a set of cabinets, a sprinkler layout and a rooftop unit all need shop drawings.
A shop drawing travels up the chain for review, then back down:
Fabricator draws it from the contract drawings and specifications.
Subcontractor checks it (if the fabricator works for a sub).
General contractor checks it: field measurements, quantities, fit with other trades. Then the GC stamps it and sends it on.
Consultant (architect or engineer) reviews it for general conformance with the design, then stamps it.
It goes back down the same way to the fabricator.
The consultant's stamp usually says one of these:
Stamp What the shop does next
Reviewed Build it as drawn.
Reviewed as noted Build it with the consultant's notes added.
Revise and resubmit Do not build. Fix the drawing and send it up the chain again.
Not reviewed The consultant did not review it. Ask your foreman before you build anything.
Two things to remember:
A shop drawing does not replace the contract documents. It adds detail to them.
The consultant's review does not take away the contractor's responsibility for errors in the shop drawing. The shop still owns its measurements.
Worked example: a handrail on a clinic fit-out
The Cedar Lane Health Society (owner) is fitting out a small clinic. It bought the job design-bid-build. Kestrel Architecture designed it. Tallgrass Builders won the bid and is the GC and prime contractor. Ironwood Fabrication has a subcontract with Tallgrass to supply and install the steel stair handrail.
Bonds. Tallgrass's contract is $640,000. On this job the owner asked for a performance bond and a labour and material payment bond, each for 50% of the contract.
50% of $640,000 = 0.5 × $640,000 = $320,000 for each bond.
Ironwood has a direct subcontract with Tallgrass, so it is a claimant the payment bond covers if Tallgrass does not pay it.
Shop drawing timeline. On this job the specification gives the consultant 5 working days to review each shop drawing. The other times are Ironwood's and Tallgrass's own estimates, in working days:
Step Working days
Ironwood draws and checks the shop drawing 4
Tallgrass reviews and stamps it 2
Kestrel reviews and stamps it 5
Back down to Ironwood 1
First pass total 4 + 2 + 5 + 1 = 12
Ironwood needs 8 working days to fabricate after the drawing comes back "Reviewed". Tallgrass needs the handrail on site by working day 25, counting from the day Ironwood starts drawing.
12 + 8 = 20 working days. That is 5 days ahead of day 25.
Where a question goes. Ironwood's fitter sees that the stair stringer on site is 40 mm off the line on the drawing. He tells his foreman. Ironwood's foreman tells Tallgrass. Tallgrass sends an RFI to Kestrel. Nobody from Ironwood calls the architect directly, because Ironwood's contract is with Tallgrass.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Name the way it was bought. Write design-bid-build, design-build or construction management.
a) The owner signs one contract with a company that designs and builds the school. __
b) The architect finishes the drawings, five GCs bid, and the owner signs with the lowest bidder. __
c) The owner hires a firm early to advise on cost and schedule, then each trade bids its own package. __
Task 2 (level 2) Where does the question go? You are an apprentice with a drywall sub. The drawing shows a door where there is a beam. For each way of buying the job, write the chain your question travels.
a) Design-bid-build:
b) Design-build:
c) Construction management, where the CM also does the construction:
Task 3 (level 2) Which bond? Name the bond that applies.
a) The low bidder refuses to sign the contract at its bid price.
b) The GC goes out of business halfway through and the owner needs the work finished.
c) The GC does not pay the electrical sub, which had a direct subcontract with the GC.
d) A supplier sold wire to the electrical sub, not to the GC, and was not paid. Does the standard payment bond on the GC cover the supplier?
Task 4 (level 2) Bond amounts. A GC's contract is $1,250,000. The owner asks for a performance bond and a labour and material payment bond, each for 50% of the contract.
a) How much is each bond?
b) What is the most the surety can pay under the performance bond?
Task 5 (level 1) Put the chain in order. Number these steps 1 to 5 for a cabinet shop drawing on a design-bid-build job.
The GC checks field measurements and stamps it.
The cabinet shop draws it.
The stamped drawing goes back to the cabinet shop.
The architect reviews it for general conformance with the design.
The millwork sub checks the cabinet shop's drawing.
Task 6 (level 2) Count the days. Use the clinic handrail example. Kestrel stamps the first drawing "Revise and resubmit". Ironwood needs 3 working days to revise it. Tallgrass needs 2 days again, Kestrel 5 days again, and 1 day to return it.
a) How many working days does the second pass take?
b) On what working day does the "Reviewed" drawing reach Ironwood?
c) Fabrication still takes 8 days. On what working day is the handrail ready?
d) How many days late is that against working day 25?
Task 7 (level 2) Read the stamp. What does the shop do next?
a) "Reviewed as noted. Add one bracket at the landing."
b) "Revise and resubmit. Post spacing does not match the architectural drawings."
c) "Reviewed." The foreman wants to change the post spacing on site to miss a floor drain.
Task 8 (level 3) Up and back down. You are an apprentice installing the handrail. The stamped shop drawing shows a post exactly where an electrician has just put a floor box. Write what you do, who you tell, and who should talk to whom to settle it. Explain why you do not just move the post.
Check yourself
In design-build, how many contracts does the owner sign for design and construction together?
Which bond protects a sub that the GC did not pay?
Who reviews a shop drawing first: the GC or the consultant?
What does "Revise and resubmit" mean for the shop?
If the owner does not name a prime contractor in writing, who is the prime contractor in BC?

lessons.title: A new crew's rough start with ground rules and conflict styles
lessons.text:
Expect the rough patch when a crew forms, write ground rules people can follow, pick the conflict style that fits, and settle a fight about site paperwork before it costs money.
All people, companies and jobs in this lesson are fictional.
Why this matters on the job
Every new job puts people together who have not worked side by side before. The first week is often polite. Then the friction starts: who sets the pace, how clean is clean, whose way of doing it wins. That rough patch is normal. Crews that get through it fast have a few clear ground rules and know more than one way to handle a disagreement. Crews that do not get through it lose time, lose people and sometimes lose money, as the paperwork fight in this lesson shows.
Key ideas
Crews go through stages
In 1965 a researcher named Bruce Tuckman reviewed 50 studies of small groups. He described four stages that many groups go through. In 1977 he and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth.
Stage What it looks like on a crew
Forming Everyone is polite and careful. People wait to be told what to do and test where the lines are.
Storming Friction. People push back on the plan, the pace or each other. Some take sides.
Norming The crew settles on how it works: who does what, how fast, how problems get raised.
Performing The work flows. People cover for each other and fix problems without drama.
Adjourning The job ends and the crew splits up.
This is a model, not a rule. Some crews skip a stage or slide back when someone new joins. The point is: storming is normal. It does not mean the crew is broken. It means the crew has not agreed how it works yet.
Ground rules get a crew to norming faster
Ground rules are a short list the crew agrees on. Good ground rules are:
specific: you can tell if someone followed them
few: five is plenty
agreed: the crew talks them through, not just the lead hand
visible: written on the gang box lid, the lunchroom wall or the group chat
Weak rule Better rule
Be on time. Be at the gang box, dressed and ready, by 7:00.
Keep it clean. Last 15 minutes of the shift, everyone cleans their own area and puts tools back in the gang box.
Ground rules never replace the law or the company's policies. Safety rules and the bullying and harassment policy (lesson 8) apply whether the crew writes them down or not.
Five ways to handle conflict, and when each fits
Lesson 5 showed five habits people use in a conflict. None of them is always right. Pick the one that fits.
Habit Fits when Does not fit when
Put it off (avoid) The issue is small, or people need to cool down before they talk. It is about safety, or it keeps coming back.
Give in (accommodate) It matters more to them than to you, or you find out you were wrong. You give in every time and start to resent it.
Meet halfway (compromise) Both sides have a fair point, time is short and you have about equal say. Splitting the difference gives a half-done job.
Push until you win (compete) Safety, the law, or an emergency where someone has to decide now. It is just a preference. It damages trust.
Work it out together (collaborate) Both sides care a lot, you will work together for a long time, and there is time to talk. The issue is tiny or there is no time.
Worked example: when paperwork causes a fight
Northgate Construction is the GC on a four-storey rental building. Silverline Mechanical has the plumbing subcontract. Dale is Silverline's foreman. Priya is Northgate's site coordinator. She is newer to the trade than Dale.
The rule on this job. Northgate's quality plan says plumbing in a wall is a hold point. Before drywall covers it, the plumbing crew must take one photo of each wall section with a tag showing the unit and wall, and the lead hand must sign a short checklist. Northgate counts the work as complete on a monthly progress claim only when the photos and the signed checklist are in.
What happened. For two months Dale's crew sent photos with no tags and checklists with no signature. Priya sent the work back. Silverline's progress claims for those two months, $18,400 and $22,600, were held. Dale told his crew, "It's busywork. She's micromanaging us." Priya told her boss, "Silverline doesn't care about quality." Now they barely speak, and there are four more months on the job.
What kind of conflict is it? It started as a disagreement about the process (how much paperwork, in what form), not about the quality of the pipe work. It is sliding into a personal conflict ("she's micromanaging", "they don't care"). Bring it back to the process.
What does each side need?
Dale and Silverline need Priya and Northgate need
To get paid on time Proof the pipe is right before it is hidden
A routine that does not slow the crew down Photos that show which unit and which wall
To be treated as the experienced trade he is Checklists signed by someone who answers for them
Which habit fits? Both care a lot, they have four more months together, and there is time to sit down. That points to work it out together.
What they agreed. Dale and Priya met with their bosses for 20 minutes. They agreed that Silverline's lead hand photographs each wall with a pre-printed tag before he leaves the unit, uploads the photos to the shared folder by the end of the shift, and signs one checklist per unit instead of one per wall. Priya checks the folder each morning and flags gaps the same day, not at month end. Dale's held claims were paid once the required tagged photos and signed checklists for the two months were complete and accepted.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Name the stage. Write forming, storming, norming, performing or adjourning.
a) "Last day on site. Let's grab a photo of the whole crew." __
b) "Nobody told me we start at 6:30. I'm not doing that." __
c) "Okay, we agreed: whoever finishes first starts the clean-up." __
d) "I don't know anyone yet. I'll just do what I'm told today." __
e) "Sonia saw I was short a hand and jumped in without asking." __
Task 2 (level 2) Make the rule better. Rewrite each weak rule so you could tell if someone followed it.
a) Respect each other.
b) Communicate.
c) Look after the tools.
Task 3 (level 2) Your crew's ground rules. Write five ground rules for a new framing crew of four, or for your class crew. Make each one specific. Then check each rule: does it break any safety rule or company policy?
Task 4 (level 2) Pick the habit. Choose the habit that fits best and give one reason.
a) Two apprentices both want the front seat of the crew truck.
b) A crew member wants to skip the guardrail for a 10-minute job at the slab edge.
c) Two lead hands both need the one scissor lift every day this week, and the week starts tomorrow.
d) Your journeyperson wants the stringers cut his way. You think your way is a bit faster, but both ways work.
e) A sub and a GC disagree about a daily paperwork routine they will use for the next four months.
Task 5 (level 2) Both sides. In the Silverline case, Priya's boss says, "Just make them do it." Dale's boss says, "Just ignore her." Write one sentence for each boss explaining why that would not fix the problem.
Task 6 (level 2) What the fight cost.
a) How much money was held from Silverline over the two months?
b) Silverline's next four monthly claims are each about $20,000. If the problem had gone on, about how much more would have been held?
c) Name one cost of this fight that is not money.
Task 7 (level 3) Role-play. Work in threes: Dale, Priya and an observer. Dale and Priya meet for 5 minutes. Each uses one W.I.N. statement from lesson 5 (When you..., I..., Need...) and asks one open question. Together they agree one change to the photo and checklist routine. The observer writes down the W.I.N. statements, the question and the change. Then switch roles.
Task 8 (level 3) Your crew now. Think of a crew, team or class you are in right now. Which stage is it in? Give one sign. Write one suggestion that would help it reach the next stage.
Check yourself
Name the four stages Tuckman described in 1965, in order.
What makes a ground rule a good one?
Which conflict habit fits when someone wants to skip a safety rule?
Which habit fits best when two people care a lot and will work together for months?
In the Silverline case, what was the conflict really about at the start?

lessons.title: Communication • Make room for the message and check understanding
lessons.text:
Communication involves receiving, considering and sharing information so people understand what needs to happen. It includes noticing uncertainty, asking a useful question, explaining the purpose and making room for the other person to respond.
You bring ways of communicating from your experiences, relationships, languages and responsibilities. Other learners bring their own. This classroom does not treat one accent, speaking pace, eye-contact pattern or way of sitting as proof of respect or competence. We will look for understanding and useful interaction. You may use speech, sign, augmentative and alternative communication, text or another agreed accessible mode. Identify the mode and support in the learning record.
In B.C., a training group may include First Nations, Métis and Inuit learners from different places, including people whose Nations are outside the province. No one person can explain how every Indigenous person communicates. Ask about the needs of this conversation and this person. You can share an experience if you choose; you can also use the fictional cases throughout. Personal stories, cultural knowledge and identity explanations are not required contributions.
All cases, people, times and arrangements are invented classroom examples. The asphalt content introduces equipment purposes, not live operating procedures. Practise with a clear purpose and opportunities to pause, receive feedback and try again.
See it in action · Communication
Visual guide Both people can state the same plan. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
SENDER: “Room 2 at 10:00.”. RECEIVER: “Room 2, ten o’clock?”. Agree a usable way to talk. Send the message; check it back. Confirm or clarify, then switch. Both people can state the same plan. Speech, sign, text or AAC can work. Check meaning, not eye contact.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. SENDER: “Room 2 at 10:00.”. RECEIVER: “Room 2, ten o’clock?”.
Try it: Agree a usable way to talk. Send the message; check it back. Confirm or clarify, then switch.
Check your result: Both people can state the same plan. Speech, sign, text or AAC can work. Check meaning, not eye contact.
Six connected components
Visual guide The six Communication components work together around a shared purpose. Agree accessible ways to send, receive and check meaning; the map does not prescribe a fixed order. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. Build shared understanding together. Six connected components: Listen with intention; Listen to understand; Speak with clarity; Speak with purpose; Adapt to audience + context; Adapt modes + tools. Speech · sign · text · AAC · another agreed accessible mode. Observe understanding, not a preferred communication style.
The six components below help you receive and share meaning. Use appropriate communication modes to demonstrate each purpose.
Listen with intention
Prepare to receive the message and attend to its purpose.
Practise with: “Identify what you need to listen for” through “Show attention through a useful response”
Listen to understand
Paraphrase, distinguish facts from assumptions and clarify.
Practise with: “Paraphrase and confirm” through “Resolve a contradictory message”
Speak with clarity
Organize the message and use words the recipient can understand.
Practise with: “Explain a term for a new learner” through “Repair the unclear reference”
Speak with purpose
Make the reason, request or next step clear.
Practise with: “Match purpose and wording” through “Give a useful handover”
Adapt to your audience and contexts
Consider what this audience knows and needs without stereotyping.
Practise with: “Make two audience versions” through “Ask about the conversation, not a stereotype”
Adapt to other people's different communication modes and tools
Agree a usable channel, pace and check-back method.
Practise with: “Practise an agreed accessible exchange” through “Complete a changed-mode handover”
Take both turns: send a message, then receive one. When you receive it, say the key point back in your own words or show the correct next action. Ask a question if something is unclear. Your partner confirms or explains again. Your instructor watches how you reach understanding; you do not need a long written answer or a recording.
Communication route card
Practise in four steps
Agree how to communicate and what the message must achieve.
Send a short instruction or handover. The receiver repeats the essential meaning and asks about any uncertainty.
Confirm or repair the message, then switch sender and receiver roles.
Try a changed audience or communication mode. Keep the actual message, question and confirmation.
Support route. Use a familiar chapter source first, a key-detail organizer with headings but no completed answers, a learner-controlled communication tool, agreed interpretation or an instructor counterpart. Rehearse “What is the current room/time?” or another learner-chosen clarification. If an instructor supplies a phrase or points to the missed answer, record that support on the relevant criterion. Reduce unrelated writing; let the receiver show meaning through a check-back, selected details or an appropriate action. No speed or eye-contact target is added.
Retry route. Choose the missed action, receive feedback and try it again with the familiar source. If the next goal is unfamiliar reception, use held “Communication practice C · Send, receive and check a fresh classroom change” Card C only when it is genuinely unseen by the receiver. Record prior exposure honestly; otherwise arrange another checked message. Compare the essential details and how the uncertainty was resolved, not how confident the learner looked.
What the instructor observes. Observe each learner both sending and receiving. A receiver turn alone does not show how that learner sends a message.
Next-attempt agreement: criterion ; message/version ; sender/receiver role ; mode/language ; access and task support ; observer/date ; evidence still missing ___.
Listen with a reason
Listening with intention begins before the words arrive. Ask what you need to learn from the message. Are you receiving a change in location, hearing a concern, comparing a proposal or deciding what question to ask next? Knowing the purpose helps you identify the important details. It also helps you avoid preparing your own reply while the other person is still explaining the issue.
Check the setting. Background noise, overlapping talk, small text, an unfamiliar term or a weak connection can interrupt understanding. You can ask to move to a quieter classroom position, receive a written key point, use captions, slow the pace or repeat a section. These are communication strategies. They are not admissions that you are incapable of learning. The speaker also shares responsibility for making the message usable.
Attention can be shown in different ways. A person may look at a diagram, use a communication device, take notes, pause before responding or look away while processing. Do not infer attention from eye contact alone. Check understanding through the response. A useful phrase is “I want to make sure I have the change right. Could we go through the time and location once more?”
Case document A • A classroom change that needs to reach everyone
Fictional coordinator message
“For Thursday's classroom session, meet in Room 2 at 10:00, instead of Room 1. The session ends at 10:45. Bring your learner workbook and a pen. The equipment-card activity stays indoors; we are not visiting a worksite. Printed copies of the process map will be available in Room 2. If the room change creates an access issue, tell the instructor through the usual course contact so an arrangement can be discussed. You do not need to explain private details to the whole group.”
Context for the sender: Some learners may have seen an earlier notice showing Room 1. Your immediate purpose is to communicate the current classroom arrangement. You have not been given information about bus departures, parking, meal arrangements or attendance consequences. Do not invent those details when a listener asks.
For an activity focused on receiving a message, the instructor may read the message or provide it in the receiver's agreed accessible mode. A receiver who has already studied the printed version should say so; the instructor can use a different comparable message for a later listening observation. Reading the script is useful preparation, but it is different evidence from understanding a newly received message.
Identify what you need to listen for
Before receiving Case A, identify three kinds of information you would need to carry out its purpose. Then receive the message in your agreed mode and identify the actual purpose. Separate the details supplied from questions you still have. A short spoken response, a few selected labels or a diagram can show your understanding; an extended written paragraph is unnecessary for this listening task.
Prepare a usable conversation
With a partner, identify one possible classroom barrier to receiving Case A and agree one adjustment. For example, take turns without overlapping, provide a clear view of the relevant text, reduce background noise or allow time for a communication device. Practise asking for the adjustment respectfully. State what you will use to check understanding afterward. Do not simulate a disability or assign one to your partner.
Show attention through a useful response
Partner A sends the Case A message in the agreed mode. Partner B receives it, then identifies the main change and asks whether one chosen detail was understood correctly. Swap roles using this second message: “Tomorrow's practice discussion starts at 13:00 in the same classroom. Bring the revised card record. The instructor will provide printed copies for anyone who needs one.” Observe the response, not whether the listener copied a particular posture or expression.
Listen to understand, then check
Visual guide A check-back makes the listener’s understanding visible. Restate the room, day and time, then confirm or correct them and check the remaining details in the full message. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Three speech bubbles demonstrate sending Thursday, Room 2, 10:00–10:45; restating those details; and confirming their accuracy. A dashed return path asks partners to correct a mismatch and check again. The accompanying reminder includes workbook and pen, indoor activity, printed maps and the usual route for access questions.
Understanding means more than remembering isolated words. Connect the details to the speaker's purpose. In Case A, the room change matters because someone following the earlier notice could go to the wrong place. The statement that the activity stays indoors limits what the listener should assume about equipment or travel. The access-contact instruction offers a private route without promising a particular adjustment before it is discussed.
Paraphrasing means expressing the message in your own words while keeping its meaning. It is not adding what you think the speaker should have said. A useful check-back is short enough for the sender to confirm or correct. You can then ask about an unresolved detail. Confirmation is a two-way action: the sender needs to notice whether the paraphrase is accurate, not simply say “yes” to finish the conversation.
Questions can clarify meaning, detail or action. “Which room?” asks for a missing detail. “When you say ‘revised record,’ do you mean version 2?” checks a term. “Should I wait for confirmation before sharing this change?” asks about a next step. Choose the question that would change what you do. Asking ten unrelated questions can make an important uncertainty harder to see.
Worked example 1 • Paraphrase without expanding the promise
A careful listener says: “Thursday's indoor card activity is now in Room 2, from 10:00 to 10:45. I should bring the workbook and a pen, and printed maps will be there. Have I got that right?” The sender checks those details and confirms them. The listener then asks: “Which course contact should someone use to discuss an access issue?” The case says the usual contact, but does not name it, so the sender should identify the approved classroom contact or ask the instructor to confirm it.
An inaccurate paraphrase would be: “Everyone has to arrive early, all access arrangements are already approved, and there will be a bus.” Those claims were not in the message. Good intentions do not make them reliable. Keep a clear boundary between the message received, a reasonable question and an answer that still needs confirmation.
Paraphrase and confirm
Receive Case A or an instructor-provided comparable message. Give a concise paraphrase that preserves the purpose and at least four relevant details. Invite correction. The sender identifies anything changed or missing, and you revise your paraphrase. Record one correction if needed. If the first paraphrase is accurate, explain how the sender checked it against the message rather than merely agreeing politely.
Ask the question that matters
A fictional learner asks, “Will transportation be provided?” The message does not say. Practise a response that distinguishes known information from an unanswered question and identifies who should confirm it. Then ask two useful clarification questions about Case A: one about a practical detail and one about the next action. Avoid a question that asks another learner to disclose a private reason for needing an arrangement.
Resolve a contradictory message
You hear a partner say, “The class is still in Room 1 and goes until 11:00.” Use Case A to check the discrepancy. Respond without labelling the partner careless or dishonest. State the conflicting details, identify the current source you are using, and ask to verify together. End with an agreed message or an explicit unresolved question for the instructor. Do not leave the exchange with two conflicting versions silently circulating.
Speak with clarity: organize before you deliver
A clear message gives the listener a route through the information. Start with the main point, then the details needed to understand or act. Use short groups of related ideas. Explain an unfamiliar word when it first matters. A pause can make room for processing, a question or an accessible response; it does not have to be filled with more information.
Plain language preserves accuracy. “The screed helps control the thickness of the layer being placed” is clearer for a new learner than unexplained specialist language. It does not mean the speaker should invent a simplified operating rule. If the recipient needs technical detail beyond your knowledge or role, identify that boundary and refer the question to the qualified instructor.
Check reference words such as “it,” “that” and “over there.” They may be clear to someone standing beside you and unclear to a person on a phone or using a text version. Name the item or location. If a sequence matters, use numbered steps or clear transition words. Avoid packing a change, an exception and a new request into one long sentence.
Case document B • Two people understood different tasks
Visual guide Six equipment-purpose cards support terminology checking. The screed is a paver component, so six equipment cards are different from the five stage labels in the pair task. Illustrations explain purpose only. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Six original equipment silhouettes show E2 crusher and screen reducing and separating material by size; E3 asphalt plant preparing the specified mixture; E4 haul truck moving paving material; E5 paver receiving mixture and moving it to the screed; E1 screed helping control layer thickness; and E6 roller compacting placed material. The broad flow is pit or quarry, plant, haul, place and compact. The screed is shown with the paver, not as an additional broad stage.
Fictional pair activity
The task sheet says: “Arrange five stage labels in process order. Add one short purpose under each. Both partners explain one connection. Keep the equipment cards beside the map so you can check terminology.”
One partner arranges the stage labels. The other begins sorting the six equipment cards into a separate row. The first says, “You are doing the wrong thing.” The second replies, “I thought you wanted all the cards put in order. You did not say which cards.” Both want to finish the activity, but neither has checked the shared instruction aloud.
The stage labels are pit or quarry, plant, haul, place and compact. The equipment cards describe different pieces of equipment or components; there are six cards, so they are not a second identical five-stage sequence. The task is an introductory classroom explanation, not an equipment operating sequence.
Use these six introductory equipment-purpose cards for the role-play. Copy the rows onto separate cards if helpful.
Card Purpose
E1 · Screed Helps control the thickness of the asphalt layer being placed.
E2 · Crusher or screening plant A crusher reduces material size; a screen separates material by size.
E3 · Asphalt plant Prepares the specified asphalt mixture.
E4 · Haul truck Moves paving material between the supply point and work area.
E5 · Asphalt paver Receives mixture and moves it toward the screed during placement.
E6 · Compaction roller Compacts the placed material.
The immediate communication problem is a different interpretation of the task. A useful response names the shared goal and checks the document: “I think we have understood ‘cards’ differently. The sheet asks us to order the five stage labels and use the equipment cards to check terms. Can we read that line together?” This gives both people a way to revise their understanding without deciding whose personality caused the mismatch.
Explain a term for a new learner
Choose aggregate, haul, paver or compact. Use these introductory meanings: aggregate is mineral material such as sand, gravel or crushed stone; haul means move material between places; a paver places asphalt mixture as part of the paving process; compact means make the placed material denser through the appropriate technical process. Give a short explanation in ordinary language and one classroom example. Invite a question. Do not add operating settings or safety distances.
Give a clear three-step instruction
Use Case B to make a three-step instruction for the pair activity. Identify the correct cards, the expected result and each person's contribution. Send it to a partner who has not arranged the map yet. Ask them to restate the steps before carrying them out. Improve a phrase that could be misunderstood. If both people already know the task, change the card order or use another supplied classroom task for a fresh check.
Repair the unclear reference
Rewrite this message for someone receiving it by phone: “Put those there, use the other ones to check it, and then tell them what it means.” Supply the intended names from Case B and make the recipient and purpose clear. Deliver your revised message in the agreed mode, then ask the listener what they would do. Notice whether your words alone provide enough information without pointing at objects the listener cannot see.
Speak with purpose: what does the listener need to do?
Messages can inform, request, explain, propose, confirm or raise a concern. More than one purpose may appear in a conversation, but the main purpose should be easy to identify. “I am letting you know” differs from “I need your decision.” A listener should not have to guess whether you want action, agreement or simply awareness.
For a request, name what you need, why it matters and when a response would be useful. Avoid promising authority you do not have. “Could the coordinator confirm which version we should use?” is different from “I have approved this version.” For a handover, say what is completed, what remains uncertain and who is taking the next step. This protects continuity when people work at different times or through different channels.
Tone matters, but it does not replace the facts. A calm message can still be unclear, and a person under pressure may have an important concern even if their delivery is uneven. Focus first on understanding the issue and agreed next action. You can ask to pause, involve the instructor or use another channel if the exchange becomes unproductive. Classroom practice should not require reenacting a personal conflict.
Worked example 2 • Turn a vague complaint into a useful request
Vague message: “The files are a mess, and nobody can do this.” The listener may not know which files, what task is blocked or what help is needed. A clearer practice request is: “I am preparing the card-count handout. I found two files labelled version 2 with different totals. Could you confirm the approved file before I print? I have paused the print step and can show both records.”
The revised message gives context, observed problem, requested action and current status. It does not assign blame or guess which file is correct. If the recipient cannot approve the file, the next question is who has that responsibility. The message remains useful even when the answer is “I need to check.”
Match purpose and wording
For each situation, name the main purpose and draft a two-sentence message: tell a partner the room has changed; ask the instructor to confirm a file version; propose a clearer heading for a visitor sheet. Include the response needed, if any. Compare the messages and explain why the same wording would not suit all three. A request should not be disguised as a statement that the decision has already been made.
Practise a short clarification call
In a role-play, one learner calls the fictional training office to ask whether the card activity is indoors and which room is current. The office role has Case A and may answer only from that information. Open with purpose, ask the questions, listen to the answers and check back the key details. Close by identifying any remaining question. Swap roles. No real phone call is required; do not invent transportation, eligibility or attendance rules.
Give a useful handover
Use this invented status: the material-flow cards are printed; the equipment-purpose cards are checked but not printed; the room sign still shows the old location; the instructor needs to confirm who can replace the sign. Give the next learner a handover that separates completed work, remaining work and the decision needing confirmation. Ask them to identify their understood next step. A clear handover should not quietly authorize them to alter a real sign or room arrangement.
Adapt to the audience without making assumptions about them
Audience awareness begins with purpose and relevant knowledge. A new learner may need a term explained. An instructor reviewing the same work may need the evidence and the unresolved question. A visitor may need a short overview and a route to further information. Ask what the person needs rather than assuming it from appearance, age, identity or a guess about their background.
Intercultural communication includes noticing your own interpretations. A pause might mean someone is considering the question, using a communication tool, waiting for their turn, unsure of a term or choosing not to answer. A brief reply might be enough for that task. Describe what happened before explaining what you think it means. Then seek clarification in a way that allows the other person to choose what to share.
A person's cultural knowledge is not a classroom resource automatically available on request. If a project needs a specific community perspective, the instructor or coordinator should arrange an appropriate relationship and permission process with the relevant people. A learner may volunteer a perspective, but that contribution should not be treated as representing an entire Nation or giving permission for public use. For this chapter, the fictional cases provide all the content needed for practice.
Case document C • One message, different access needs
Fictional open-classroom planning note
The group will explain its introductory paving process map to visitors. Some visitors are new to trade vocabulary. One visitor asks for key points in writing before the discussion. Another asks the speaker to face the group and avoid talking over other people so the conversation is easier to follow. A third will join through an online connection and wants the diagram described rather than referred to as “this bit here.”
No visitor has asked learners to guess a medical condition or cultural preference. The group can respond to the stated communication needs. The planned message is: mineral materials can come from pits or quarries; an asphalt plant prepares the specified mixture; hauling moves it to the work area; a paver places it; compaction follows as part of the technical process. The display is introductory learning, not operating guidance.
The coordinator asks the group to keep the explanation to about one minute, leave time for a question and offer a clear next contact for detailed technical questions. The classroom instructor is the appropriate first contact for this exercise. The group may use a written key-point card, the labelled diagram and a spoken or otherwise accessible explanation.
Worked example 3 • Change the delivery, preserve the meaning
For a new visitor, begin: “This map shows five broad stages in a basic paving example. We start with mineral materials, then prepare and move the mixture, place it and compact it.” Point to or describe the numbered stages, explain one unfamiliar word and invite a question. For the instructor, a useful version might begin: “Our map uses five introductory stages. We checked the equipment-purpose wording against the lesson sheet and kept operating settings out of the display.” The core information remains consistent, while the purpose and detail change.
For a remote listener, replace “look at the red box” with “stage three, labelled Haul, means moving the mixture to the work area.” Colour can support the visual but should not carry the only meaning. For someone using a written key-point card, allow time to read and ask whether the sequence is clear. Do not mistake a different response pace for a lack of interest.
Make two audience versions
Prepare a short explanation of the same five-stage map for a new learner and for an instructor reviewing accuracy. Identify the purpose of each version and what knowledge you are assuming. Deliver both versions to a partner taking the relevant role. Ask what was clear and what needed explanation. Revise one feature while keeping the technical meaning and limits consistent.
Separate observation from interpretation
Consider this fictional exchange: a learner pauses for several seconds after a question and looks at the printed map. Someone says, “They are not interested.” State what was actually observed, give three possible interpretations and suggest a respectful clarification. Choose a response that allows time or another mode without diagnosing the person. Explain why a single behaviour cannot establish someone's attitude or a rule about their culture.
Ask about the conversation, not a stereotype
Revise these questions: “People from your community always prefer stories, right?” and “Why won't you look at me when I speak?” Make them relevant to the present task, with room for choice. Then practise asking a partner which information and communication format would help them review the process map. The partner may answer briefly or choose the supplied Case C preferences. No one has to describe their community or personal history.
An approximate one-minute message is a guide to the amount of content, not a speed test. Agree additional time for interpretation, AAC, signing, reading, processing or another access need. Check the intended meaning and the exchange; do not treat a faster response as stronger communication.
Adapt the mode and keep the interaction two-way
A communication mode is a way of exchanging meaning, such as speech, sign, text, symbols or an augmentative communication system. A tool supports that exchange, such as a phone, caption display, shared document or communication device. Ask which mode and tool work for the task and the people involved. Do not assume that access to a tool guarantees that a conversation is accessible.
Allow response time. Speak or present one meaningful section at a time, then make space for a reply. In a text exchange, make the question and requested response visible. In a meeting, identify the speaker and avoid several people speaking at once. If captions or a connection fail, pause and agree a way to continue rather than pretending everyone received the missing information.
Check the message after a change of mode. A phone explanation may need a written reference number; a diagram may need a description; a written update may need a short interaction to resolve ambiguity. Keep only the record needed for the task. Do not record, photograph or circulate another person's contribution without the agreed purpose and permission. A live demonstration can be assessed without storing personal audio or video.
Practise an agreed accessible exchange
Work with a partner using modes each person chooses. One person requests the current room and start time; the other answers from Case A. Agree how each will signal a turn, request repetition and confirm understanding. Demonstrate the exchange, then swap roles. You may use written messages, speech, AAC or another available mode; do not imitate another person's disability. The observer records whether both people could send, receive and clarify the actual message.
Recover a missing part of the message
Simulate a connection interruption by having the sender deliberately omit the room number from this practice message: “The session begins at 10:00 in … and ends at 10:45.” The receiver identifies the missing information and requests it through an agreed alternate route. The sender supplies Room 2 and checks the complete message. Explain how you would distinguish a successful technical connection from actual understanding of the content.
Complete a changed-mode handover
Begin with the “Give a useful handover” handover as a face-to-face or agreed live exchange. The instructor then changes the task: the next learner must receive it through a short written or otherwise accessible remote message, followed by a question-and-response check. Adapt the message, preserve completed/pending/confirmation-needed distinctions and test it. Record one change that helped the recipient. Identify a new work or learning situation where the same strategy might help, without claiming that future transfer has already occurred.
Reflect on evidence, not personality
Keep an example of a paraphrase, a useful clarification, a plain-language explanation, a purpose-focused request and an adapted message. An observer's note should describe what happened: “Asked which version was current and repeated the confirmed room/time.” Avoid labels such as “good attitude,” “natural speaker” or “poor communicator.” Those labels obscure the next practice step.
For supported practice, use a short script, a visual checklist, a private instructor partnership or more response time. For extension, change the audience or introduce one missing detail while preserving a clear purpose. Give specific feedback and repeat the interaction. The local descriptions Not observed, Not yet demonstrated, Demonstrated with support and Demonstrated independently describe evidence under stated conditions; they are not official Communication proficiency scores.
Communication practice C · Send, receive and check a fresh classroom change
These four original cases give you another opportunity to use a skill after the chapter practice. All people, rooms, events and organizations in these cards are fictional. You can use these cases without sharing personal, family, community or cultural knowledge. They are classroom tasks, not instructions for operating equipment or following an actual workplace procedure.
Your instructor will give you the relevant card when your turn begins. Keep a sender's information separate from the receiver's card until after the exchange. If you have already read the information, say so: the activity remains useful practice, but that attempt cannot show how you receive an unfamiliar message. No one needs to conceal prior practice.
Agree your language, communication mode, tools, access supports and response time before beginning. Speech, sign, text, AAC, a learner-directed scribe and agreed interpretation can be appropriate. The person observing needs a reliable way to understand the meaning of your contribution. Receiving a message in writing shows reception through that mode; it does not automatically show auditory listening. You may decline audio/video recording and use live observation. Ask for a pause or another opportunity if the conditions are not usable. There is no requirement to look cheerful, make eye contact or disclose why you need an arrangement.
Purpose: make the practical change clear, receive the other person's meaning and resolve a relevant question. Each person has a sender turn and a receiver turn. Your instructor distributes Card A only to the first sender and Card B only to the second sender. Do not show your source card before your partner has received and checked the message. Sending an agreed written message is allowed; copying the entire source into a receiver's worksheet is a different task and must be recorded as such.
“Communication practice C · Send, receive and check a fresh classroom change” receiver card · Use before either exchange
You are planning to attend a fictional classroom session. An earlier note may be out of date. Ask the sender to explain the current arrangements. Choose how you want to receive the message and how to request repetition or a pause. Find out the activity, current room, start and finish times, and what you need to bring or do. Check your understanding with the sender. Ask one useful question; if the source does not answer it, agree who should check rather than inventing an answer.
You may take notes, select or arrange written details, use your communication tool, or give a spoken check-back. Do not try to memorize the message without access supports you would normally use. After checking, identify the information you can act on and anything still unresolved.
“Communication practice C · Send, receive and check a fresh classroom change” sender card A · Give only to the first sender
Fictional Tuesday update · Current notice A2
The classroom label-making session is now in Room Cedar, from 14:10 to 14:45. The earlier notice A1 said Room Birch and a 14:00 start. The finish time has not changed.
Bring the practice folder supplied in class. The activity uses fictional labels and the classroom provides pens and blank cards. No personal documents are needed. It is an indoor paper activity.
Jo, the classroom coordinator, can check questions that this notice does not answer. The notice gives no parking, travel, food or childcare information.
Explain the current arrangements to your partner, who has not received this notice. State why you are contacting them. Agree a usable mode, invite a check-back and resolve any discrepancy against the notice. Answer only from the supplied information. If something is unknown, identify it and the relevant next contact. A diagram or key-point card can help, but colour or pointing must not carry the only meaning.
“Communication practice C · Send, receive and check a fresh classroom change” sender card B · Give only to the second sender
Fictional Thursday update · Current notice B3
The classroom map-reading session is now in Room Spruce, from 09:35 to 10:05. The earlier notice B2 said Room Pine and a 09:30 start. The finish time has not changed.
Bring one blank practice card from your classroom pack. The classroom provides the maps and pencils. You do not need a phone or a personal address. The activity uses a fictional neighbourhood map indoors.
Rae, the classroom coordinator, can check questions that this notice does not answer. The notice gives no information about transport, refreshments or building access outside class time.
Deliver the update to your partner and complete the same two-way check. This is a new source for the person who received Card A as sender; do not assume that the earlier room or time applies.
“Communication practice C · Send, receive and check a fresh classroom change” retry card C · Hold until a later attempt
Fictional Friday update · Current notice C2
The classroom display-review session is now in Room Alder, from 11:20 to 11:50. The earlier notice C1 said Room Maple and an 11:10 start. The finish time has not changed.
Bring the draft display title card made in class. The classroom supplies the practice display and removable labels. Personal photographs are not needed. This is an indoor classroom review.
Lee, the classroom coordinator, can check questions not answered here. The notice does not identify an actual street address, travel service or meal arrangement.
Use the receiver card again. Record whether this information was new to the receiver. If it was already seen, use it as a supported retry or rehearsal, not an unfamiliar reception check. A later new-message check needs another checked source and corresponding key.
“Communication practice C · Send, receive and check a fresh classroom change” evidence note
Keep the current source identifier, the mode used, one actual check-back or clarification, any remaining unknown, and the support supplied. Identify a phrase or action you would retain or improve. Your partner's correct answer alone does not show which message you sent; the observer needs evidence of each person's turn.

lessons.title: Listening and repeating back instructions
lessons.text:
Catch every detail of a spoken job-site instruction and say it back so you both know you have it right.
Why this matters on the job
On a job site, instructions are often given once, out loud, over noise, by someone who is already walking to the next task. A wrong length, the wrong unit or the wrong material means rework, lost time and sometimes an injury. Saying the instruction back takes about ten seconds. It gives the person who gave it a chance to catch a mistake before you start.
Key ideas
Get ready to listen. Stop what you are doing when it is safe to stop. Move closer, or move both of you out of the noise. Have something to write on when numbers are coming: a notebook, the back of a drawing, a note on your phone.
Listen for the six parts of a job instruction. Most instructions answer some of these:
Part Ask yourself
WHAT What is the task or the material?
WHERE Which floor, unit, gridline, room or pile?
HOW MUCH How many, how long, what size?
WHEN Now, before break, by end of shift?
WHO Who else is involved, or who do I report to?
SAFETY What has to happen first, or what must I not do?
You will not always hear all six. If one you need is missing, ask for it.
Say it back. Keep it short and in the same order. Say every number. End with a question such as "Is that right?" Then wait. The other person confirms or corrects you.
Do not fill gaps with guesses. If you did not hear it, it is not part of the instruction yet. "I think he meant the east side" is a guess. Ask.
Make numbers hard to mishear. Fifteen and fifty, or thirteen and thirty, sound alike over a saw or a generator. Say the number, then the digits: "fifteen, one-five." Say the unit every time: feet, inches, millimetres. This helps on a crew where people speak different first languages, and it helps on a phone or radio.
Attention looks different in different people. Some people look at the speaker, some look at the drawing, some take notes. The proof that you listened is an accurate repeat-back, not where your eyes were.
The read-back loop has four steps. If the other person corrects you, say the change back before you start.
Worked example
Dana, the lead hand at Northbank Framing Ltd. (a fictional company), stops you at the gate:
"Grab six two-by-sixes, twelve footers, from the pile by the east gate and take them up to unit 204 on the second floor. Stack them on the plywood by the window, not on the deck edge. Check with Marco first. He's still cutting in 204."
You say it back:
"Six two-by-sixes, twelve feet, from the east gate pile, to 204 on the second floor. Stack them on the plywood by the window, not the deck edge. Check with Marco first because he's cutting in there. Is that right?"
Dana answers: "Yes. Make it eight, not six."
You confirm the change: "Eight. Got it."
The repeat-back caught a change Dana had not mentioned the first time. If you had only said "okay," you would have made a second trip.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Draw what you hear. Your instructor reads drawing instructions twice. The first time, just draw. The second time, you may ask questions and say steps back. After both rounds, answer:
What made the first round hard?
What did you do differently in the second round?
Task 2 (level 1) Sort the instruction. Work in pairs. One partner reads the card below aloud once while the other listens without looking. The listener then fills in the table from memory. Switch roles with the second card.
Card A. "Take the red extension cord and the work light down to the parkade, level P2, by the elevator. Plug it into the panel marked TEMP 3, not the one marked TEMP 1. I need it set up before the concrete crew gets here at ten."
Card B. "After lunch, help Priya move the scaffold planks from bay 4 to bay 6. Twelve planks. Wear your gloves. Some of them have splinters. Tell me when you're done."
Part What you heard
WHAT
WHERE
HOW MUCH
WHEN
WHO
SAFETY
Task 3 (level 2) Say it back and catch the gap. Your partner reads one card. Say it back. Then ask one question about the part that is missing. Switch roles.
Card C. "Go get the box of three-inch screws and bring it to the stairs."
Card D. "We need forty of the short brackets for the second floor by end of day."
What question did you ask for Card C? For Card D?
Task 4 (level 2) Fact or assumption. Read Card A again. For each statement, write F if Card A said it, or A if it is an assumption.
The work light goes to level P2. ___
The concrete crew will be late. ___
TEMP 1 is broken. ___
The setup has to be done before ten. ___
The lead hand wants the cord plugged into TEMP 3. ___
