Task 5 (level 2) Make it hard to mishear. Rewrite each phrase so it is clear over noise or on a phone.
"Cut it at fifteen."
"Bring the thirteen ones."
"Move it over a bit."
Task 6 (level 2) Find the six parts. Read this paving instruction. Fill in each part, or write "missing."
"Once the tack coat is dry, start the north lane at the first manhole. Fifty-millimetre lift. Roller stays ten metres back. Ken is flagging at the east end. Be done by noon."
Part What the instruction says
WHAT
WHERE
HOW MUCH
WHEN
WHO
SAFETY
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. Catch the errors. You gave the paving instruction in Task 6. Your new roller operator says it back:
"Start the south lane at the first manhole, fifteen-millimetre lift, roller ten metres back, Ken's at the east end, done by noon."
a) Find the two wrong details and the missing condition.
b) Write what you say to correct them. Make the numbers hard to mishear.
c) What do you ask the operator to do next?
Check yourself
Name the six parts of a job instruction.
Why do you end a repeat-back with a question?
You heard "the north side" but you think the speaker meant the south side. What do you do?
Give one way to say a number so that it is not mixed up with a number that sounds like it.
Your partner looked at the floor the whole time you gave an instruction, then repeated it back perfectly. Were they listening? How do you know?

lessons.title: Asking good questions on a new crew
lessons.text:
Introduce yourself, ask open questions to learn and closed questions to confirm, and keep a work conversation going.
Why this matters on the job
Your first week on a new site, you do not know where the tools live, who signs off on what, or how this crew likes things done. The fastest way to learn is to ask. Good questions keep you safe, save rework and show the crew you care about doing it right. Asking is not a weakness. Guessing is the risk.
Key ideas
Start with your name. A short introduction opens the door: "Hi, I'm Jordan. I'm the new first-year apprentice with Sam's crew." Then ask the other person's name and use it once: "Good to meet you, Ken."
Forgetting a name is normal. Most people forget a name right after they hear it, often because they are nervous. Ask again: "Sorry, tell me your name one more time?" Repeat it, use it in the conversation, or write it down later.
Closed questions get a short answer. Yes, no, or one fact. Use them to confirm.
"Is this the panel marked TEMP 3?"
"Do you want them stacked flat?"
Open questions get an explanation. They usually start with what, where, when, who, why or how. Use them to learn.
"How do you want these stacked?"
"What do I need to know about this site before I start?"
Learn with open questions, then confirm with a closed one. "How do you want the hangers spaced?" ... "So every four feet, right?"
Keep a conversation going. A conversation is not a speech. Ask a follow-up question that builds on what the person just said. Let them finish before you ask the next one.
Keep it about the work at first. With someone you have just met, stay on general topics: the job, the site, the weather, the commute. Leave personal questions until you know the person and they have shared first.
Watch how a "why" question sounds. "Why did you do it that way?" can sound like you think they did it wrong. "Can you walk me through how you set that up?" asks the same thing without judgement.
Pick your moment. Do not interrupt someone in the middle of a cut or a lift. Wait for a pause. The exception is safety: if you see a hazard, speak up right away.
Think of questions as a funnel. Start wide with open questions to learn. Finish narrow with closed questions to confirm.
Worked example
First morning at Fraser Bend Mechanical (a fictional company). You meet Ken, a journeyperson plumber.
You: "Hi, I'm Jordan, the new apprentice. Are you Ken?" (closed, to confirm)
Ken: "Yep."
You: "Good to meet you, Ken. What are we working on today?" (open)
Ken: "Roughing in the drains in the duplex on the east side."
You: "How do you want me to help with that?" (open)
Ken: "Carry pipe and fittings from the trailer, then I'll show you how we cut and prep."
You: "Where in the trailer are the fittings?" (open)
Ken: "Back shelf, blue bins."
You: "So pipe first, then the blue bins on the back shelf, then you show me cutting. Is that the order?" (closed, to confirm)
Ken: "That's it."
Four questions gave Jordan the task, the location and the order. One closed question at the end confirmed it all.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Open or closed? Write O for open or C for closed.
"Is the site office in the blue trailer?" ___
"How do you check the levels on this job?" ___
"Do I need a harness up there?" ___
"What's the plan if it rains?" ___
"Who signs my hours?" ___
"Are we done with the forms on the north wall?" ___
Task 2 (level 1) Open it up. Rewrite each closed question as an open question.
"Do you want these here?"
"Is this the right saw?"
"Did the inspector come?"
"Is break at ten?"
Task 3 (level 1) Name circle. Stand or sit in a circle. Say "My name is ..." then turn to the person on your right and say "and this is ..." That person does the same. Keep going until the circle is complete. If you forget a name, ask.
Task 4 (level 2) Your first-day questions. You start tomorrow on a site you have never seen. Write five questions you would ask in your first hour. Use at least two open and two closed questions. Mark each O or C.
Task 5 (level 2) Keep it going. Work in groups of three: a crew member, a new worker and an observer. The crew member picks a card and answers questions about it in character. The new worker keeps the conversation going for two minutes using what, where, when, who, why and how. The observer ticks the checklist. Rotate so everyone plays each role.
Card 1. You run the tool crib on a big commercial site. Tools are signed out with a name and a time. Batteries charge in the cage at the back.
Card 2. You are the site safety coordinator. You are showing a new worker the first aid station, the muster point by the main gate and the sign-in board.
Card 3. You are a journeyperson drywaller. Today you are boarding ceilings in a daycare. Lifts are booked through the lead hand.
Observer checklist:
[ ] introduced themselves and used the other person's name
[ ] asked at least two open questions
[ ] asked a follow-up that built on an answer
[ ] let the crew member finish before asking the next question
[ ] confirmed something with a closed question
[ ] stayed on work topics
Task 6 (level 2) Take out the blame. Rewrite each question so it asks for information without sounding like criticism.
"Why would you put the panel there?"
"Why is this taking so long?"
Task 7 (level 2) Fill the funnel. It is your first morning on a pipefitting crew. Write three open questions to learn about the job, then two closed questions to confirm what you heard.
Open 1: __________
Open 2: __________
Open 3: __________
Closed 1: __________
Closed 2: __________
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand. A new labourer, Tavi (fictional), joins your framing crew today. You have five minutes before work starts.
a) Write three open questions to find out what Tavi has done before and what Tavi is not sure about.
b) Write two closed questions to confirm Tavi is ready to start, such as gear or where to meet.
c) Tavi answers "yes" to everything and looks at the ground. What do you do next?
Check yourself
What is the difference between an open question and a closed question?
When is a closed question the better choice?
You forgot the lead hand's name ten minutes after meeting her. What do you say?
Your journeyperson is halfway through a cut. You have a question about where to stack material. What do you do? What if your question were about a hazard?

lessons.title: Assertive, passive and aggressive responses
lessons.text:
Tell the three ways people respond under pressure apart, speak up assertively on a crew, and set small goals to practise.
Why this matters on the job
Every crew has moments where someone needs to speak up: a trade stacks material in your work area, a co-worker keeps borrowing your tools, someone jokes at your expense, or you need help with a heavy lift. Saying nothing lets the problem grow. Blowing up damages the relationship and can get you sent home. Speaking up clearly and calmly gets the problem fixed and keeps the crew working together.
Key ideas
There are three common ways to respond.
Passive Aggressive Assertive
What it sounds like Says nothing, hints, over-apologizes Yells, threatens, name-calls, sarcasm, gossip Says what is on their mind, calmly and directly
Respect for self Low High High
Respect for others High Low High
What often happens The problem continues. Frustration builds and may blow up later The point may get across, but people feel humiliated or pushed around The problem gets named and there is room to solve it
Assertive and aggressive both speak up. The difference is how. An aggressive response aims to hurt, threaten or put down. An assertive response aims to be clear, with no intention to hurt.
Hinting is passive. "I wish I knew someone who could help me carry this door" leaves the other person guessing. "Can you give me a hand with this door?" is clear.
The three styles on one line, with how each one sounds:
A simple assertive statement has three parts.
What happened, as facts: "When the cords get left across the doorway..."
Why it matters: "...someone could trip carrying sheets."
What you would like: "Can we run them along the wall?"
Use a steady voice and normal volume. Face the person if you can. Assertive does not mean loud.
Assertiveness depends on the situation. Most people are assertive in some situations and not in others. You may find it easy to speak up with friends and hard with a supervisor, or the other way around.
Norms differ. Families, communities and workplaces have different ideas about when and how to speak up, especially to an older person or someone in charge. You choose what fits you and the situation. The goal is to be able to speak up when you decide to.
Practise with small, specific goals. Start small. Take one small risk at a time. Build from easier situations to harder ones. Make the goal specific. "I want to be more assertive at work" is hard to act on. "On Monday I will ask my lead hand to show me the lift plan before I start" is easy to act on and easy to check.
Worked example
On a renovation job at Westridge Interiors (a fictional company), a co-worker named Tyler leaves his offcuts and cords in your work area every afternoon.
Passive: You say nothing and clean up after him every day.
Aggressive: "Are you blind? Clean up your garbage or I'll throw it in the bin with your saw."
Assertive: "Tyler, when your offcuts and cords end up in my area, I lose time and someone could trip. Can you clear them before you head out?"
The assertive version names the facts, says why it matters and asks for one clear action.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Name the response. Read each card. Write P for passive, Ag for aggressive or As for assertive.
A labourer from another trade starts stacking material in the area you just cleaned and set up. You say nothing and move your gear. ___
Your lead hand points out that you put the anchors in the wrong spot. You say, "Get off my back," and walk away. ___
A co-worker calls you "rookie" in front of the crew every time you ask a question. You say, "I don't mind a joke now and then, but I'd like you to use my name in front of the crew." ___
A co-worker borrows your tape measure every day and does not bring it back. Today he asks again. You snap, "What do I look like, the tool crib?" ___

Card ___:

One area where I am already assertive:

Task 5 (level 2) Set three small goals. Choose three statements from Task 4 that you rated 1, 2 or 3. For each, write one specific goal: what you will do, with whom, and when.
Task 6 (level 2) Place it on the line. These lines are from a welding shop. Write P (passive), As (assertive) or Ag (aggressive).
"Whatever. Use my booth, I don't care." ______

Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. An older journeyperson grinds near your apprentice's work area. The sparks spray toward the apprentice and his fuel cans.

b) The journeyperson snaps: "I've been doing this 30 years. Mind your own business." Write your next line. Stay assertive.

Why is hinting a passive response?

lessons.title: Saying no and setting limits at work
lessons.text:
Say no clearly without over-explaining, offer an alternative when you want to, and refuse unsafe work the way BC law sets out.
Why this matters on the job
Work brings a steady stream of requests: stay late, cover a shift, lend your truck, help a friend of the boss move, do a task you have never been shown. Saying yes to everything wears you out and can put you in danger. Saying no well protects your time, your safety and your working relationships. In BC, refusing unsafe work is also a legal duty, and there is a set way to do it.
Key ideas
You can say no. Being assertive does not mean refusing everything. It means you can weigh your own needs and say no when you decide to.
Three ways to say no.
Way Example What often happens
A flat no, no reason "No, I can't." Clear and quick. Can feel abrupt in some situations. Fine for many simple requests.
Over-explaining "Oh, I'd really like to, but my cousin might need the truck, and I think it's making a noise, and I'm not sure about the insurance, and ..." Sounds unsure. The other person argues with each excuse. You often end up feeling guilty or saying yes.
Assertive no "No, I'm not able to stay tonight." Add a short reason only if you want to. Clear and respectful. The other person knows where you stand.
Keep it short. One sentence, maybe one short reason. Use a steady voice. Say "no" or "I'm not able to," not "I don't know, maybe."
Offer an alternative if you want to. "I can't stay tonight, but I can come in an hour early tomorrow." You do not have to offer one.
Notice what stops you. Many people hear an inner voice: "They'll think I'm lazy." "I'll lose the job." "It's rude to say no to someone older or to the boss." Ask: what is the worst that could realistically happen? How would I feel if someone said no to me in the same situation?
Norms differ. Families, communities and workplaces have different ideas about when it is acceptable to say no and to whom. You decide what fits you and the situation.
Refusing unsafe work is different. It is not a favour you can turn down. Under BC's Occupational Health and Safety Regulation, section 3.12, if you have reasonable cause to believe a task, tool or piece of equipment would create an undue hazard to anyone's health and safety, you must not do it. You must report it to your supervisor or employer right away.
How it works, in three steps:
Stop and report. Stop the work and tell your supervisor or employer. Say clearly that you are refusing the work as unsafe, not only that something looks risky. Your supervisor or employer must investigate and fix the problem, or tell you if they do not agree that it is unsafe.
If you still do not agree, your supervisor or employer investigates again with you and a worker member of the joint health and safety committee, a union representative, or another worker you choose.
If it is still not resolved, both you and your supervisor or employer must contact WorkSafeBC. A prevention officer investigates. The Prevention Information Line is 604.276.3100, or toll-free 1.888.621.7233.
You must not be disciplined or penalized for following these steps. Your employer may move you to other work for a while, at no loss in pay. Your employer also may not give the refused task to another worker unless the matter is resolved or that worker is told in writing about the refusal, the hazard, why the employer thinks it is safe, and their own right to refuse.
The same three steps as a flow chart:
Worked example
Rae, the foreman at Clearwater Roofing (a fictional company), asks you on Friday at 3:30: "Can you stay till eight tonight? We're behind."
Over-explaining: "Uh, I'd like to, but I kind of have this thing, my sister might need a ride, and I'm pretty tired, and I didn't bring dinner..."
Assertive no: "I'm not able to stay tonight. I can come in at six tomorrow if that helps."
Rae can plan around a clear answer. She cannot plan around "kind of."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Three rounds. Think of a request that is hard for you to turn down. It can be from work or from your life. Tell your partner the situation. Your partner makes the request three times:
Round 1: say no with no explanation.
Round 2: say no with as many excuses as you can.
Round 3: say no assertively, with a short reason if you want one.
Switch roles. After all three rounds, answer:
Which round felt best to you? Why?
What was your partner's reaction in round 2?
Task 2 (level 2) Cut the excuses. Rewrite this answer as an assertive no in one or two sentences.
Co-worker: "Can I borrow your impact driver for the weekend?"
You: "Oh man, I don't know, I mean, I might need it, my uncle was talking about building a deck, but maybe not, and the battery's kind of weak, and last time someone borrowed it they dropped it, not that you would, but..."
Task 3 (level 2) No, plus an alternative. Write an assertive no for each request. Add an alternative to at least two.
Your lead hand asks you to cover a Sunday shift. You have family plans.
A co-worker asks to borrow $100 until payday.
Your supervisor asks you to help clean the site trailer during your lunch break.
Task 4 (level 2) Refuse unsafe work. Read the situation and answer the questions.
You are an apprentice at Harbourline Fabrication (a fictional company). The guard on an angle grinder is stopping it from fitting into a tight corner. The lead hand says, "Just take the guard off for this one cut. It'll take two seconds."
a) You believe this would create an undue hazard. What exactly do you say to the lead hand?
b) The lead hand checks and says it is fine. You still believe it is unsafe. What happens next?
c) If the matter is still not resolved after that, who must contact WorkSafeBC?
d) Can you be disciplined for refusing?
Task 5 (level 1) What stops me? Write one thought that makes it hard for you to say no. Then write a more realistic way to look at it.
Thought: __________
A more realistic way to look at it: __________
Task 6 (level 2) Put the steps in order. Number these from 1 to 4.
____ You and your supervisor contact WorkSafeBC, and a prevention officer investigates.
____ You stop and tell your supervisor you refuse the work as unsafe.
____ Your supervisor investigates again, with you and a worker you choose.
____ Your supervisor investigates and either fixes the problem or tells you why they think it is safe.
Task 7 (level 3) The trench. You work for a fictional excavation company. The foreman says, "Hop in that trench and grab the tape measure. Two minutes." The walls are wet and bits of soil keep falling in. There is no shoring.
a) Write what you say to refuse. Use the words that start the refusal process.
b) The foreman says, "It's fine. I'll get Sam to do it, then." What does the lesson say about giving refused work to another worker?
c) The foreman still disagrees after looking again. What happens next?
Check yourself
What are the three ways to say no? Which one is assertive?
Why does over-explaining often backfire?
Under section 3.12 of the BC OHS Regulation, what must you do if you have reasonable cause to believe a task would create an undue hazard?
When you refuse unsafe work, why should you say clearly that you are refusing, and not only that something looks risky?
While a refusal is being sorted out, can your employer move you to other work? What about your pay?

lessons.title: Giving and taking feedback and criticism
lessons.text:
Give thanks and corrections that are specific and fair, take criticism without getting defensive, and know when criticism crosses into bullying.
Why this matters on the job
An apprentice is corrected many times a day. That is how a trade is learned. A journeyperson has to correct others without starting a fight. A crew that also notices good work and says thanks gets along better and works safer. Employers notice people who can hear "that's wrong, do it again" and simply do it again.
Key ideas
Giving thanks and compliments
Be specific. "Good job" is nice. "Thanks for holding that ladder steady on the last run. I felt safe up there" tells the person exactly what they did right.
Be sincere. Only say what you mean.
Pick the time and place. Some people like praise in front of the crew. Some would rather hear it one-on-one.
How you say it matters as much as what you say. A flat, rushed "thanks" can sound like the opposite.
When you get a compliment, accept it. "Thanks, I appreciate that" is enough. Brushing it off ("It was nothing, anyone could have done it") tells the person their thanks did not land.
Giving a correction
What I saw, as facts: "The cords were run across the walkway again this morning."
Why it matters: "Someone carrying sheets could trip."
What to do: "Run them along the wall and tape the crossing."
Talk about the work, not the person. Do it in private when you can. Keep your voice steady.
Here is the correction as a card you can carry in your head:
Taking criticism: the A B C D techniques
Fear of criticism is one of the biggest things that stops people from speaking up. These four techniques help you answer criticism directly and honestly. They are taught one at a time, but people often combine them in one reply. They feel stiff at first, like any new skill, and get easier with practice.
Technique What it does Example
Acknowledge Accept a fair point about a mistake, without grovelling. "It was careless of you to leave the gang box open overnight." / "Yes, I left it open. I'll check it before I leave from now on."
Boundaries Say how you expect to be treated. (In front of the crew) "You're an idiot for leaving that box open!" / "Can we talk over here for a minute?" (Away from the crew) "I get that you're frustrated. I left it open and that was careless. I'd appreciate it if you told me in private and dropped the name-calling."
Clarify Ask for details so you can fix the real problem. "Your setup is a mess." / "I want to fix it. Which part of the setup is the problem? Can you show me?"
Disagree Calmly push back on a statement that is not true, and stay open to a fair point. "You're totally disorganized. The box was open and it's your fault!" / "I disagree that I'm disorganized. I keep my area tidy and get my work done. I did leave the box open last night, and I'm happy to talk about a close-up checklist."
Skip the excuses. "The saw's dull," "nobody told me," "it's not my fault" can be true, but leading with an excuse makes it sound like you are not listening. Acknowledge first. Explain after, if it helps fix the problem.
Criticism or bullying?
Fair feedback is part of work. Bullying and harassment is not. WorkSafeBC defines workplace bullying and harassment as any inappropriate conduct or comment by a person toward a worker that the person knew or reasonably ought to have known would cause that worker to be humiliated or intimidated. It does not include reasonable action by an employer or supervisor about managing and directing workers, such as managing performance, reasonable discipline or assigning work.
WorkSafeBC gives examples of bullying and harassing behaviour, including yelling, humiliating initiation practices or hazing, spreading malicious rumours and calling someone derogatory names. It also says that expressing differences of opinion and offering constructive feedback about work-related behaviour are not bullying.
Workers must report bullying and harassment they see or experience, following their employer's procedures. Every employer must have procedures for reporting. More information is at worksafebc.com/bullying.
Worked example
At Kettle Creek Concrete (a fictional company), the lead hand, Maria, says to you in the morning: "You left the gang box open overnight. Somebody could have walked off with the tools."
Defensive reply: "It's not my fault, Jesse was the last one out."
Acknowledge and clarify: "You're right, I didn't check it. Do you want me to be the one who locks up from now on, or should we make a close-up list?"
The second reply takes the point, avoids blame, and moves to fixing it.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Make it specific. Rewrite each compliment so it names exactly what the person did.
"Nice work today."
"You're a good helper."
"Thanks for everything."
Task 2 (level 1) Pass it on. Your instructor passes a wrapped package around the group. When you receive it, give the next person a sincere, specific compliment about something they have done in this course, then hand it over. The receiver accepts the compliment and takes off one layer of wrapping. Keep going until it is unwrapped.
Task 3 (level 2) Which technique? Write A, B, C or D for each reply.
"Hang on. What exactly went wrong with the layout? Show me the measurement that's off." ___
"I hear you. I'd like you to stop calling me 'kid' in front of the other trades." ___
"You're right, I didn't sweep before the inspector came. I'll do it first thing tomorrow." ___
"I don't agree that I never listen. I followed the first three steps exactly. I missed the fourth one and I'll redo it." ___
Task 4 (level 2) Answer the criticism. For each statement, write a reply that uses at least two techniques. Label them.
"You always take forever on the cleanup."
"Did you even look at the drawing? The opening's in the wrong spot."
"You're useless with the transit." (said in front of the crew)
Task 5 (level 2) Give a correction. Your partner on the job keeps leaving the extension cords across the walkway. Write what you would say, using what I saw, why it matters and what to do.
Task 6 (level 2) Feedback or bullying? Using the WorkSafeBC definition, write F for fair feedback or management, or B for bullying and harassment.
Your supervisor says, "Your cuts on that run were off by a quarter inch. Measure twice before you cut the next set." ___
A co-worker calls you a derogatory name every morning in front of the crew. ___
Your foreman assigns you to site clean-up for the afternoon. ___
The crew makes every new apprentice go through a humiliating "initiation." ___
A journeyperson disagrees with your plan for routing the conduit and explains why. ___
Your lead hand yells at you and threatens you after a mistake. ___
Task 7 (level 2) Use the card. Your crew-mate leaves cut rebar ends sticking up by the walkway with no caps on them. Fill in the card.
What I saw: __________
Why it matters: __________
What to do: __________
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand. The superintendent walks by and says, in front of your whole crew: "Your crew's housekeeping is a disgrace. Look at this mess."
a) Write your reply. Use Boundaries and at least one other technique.
b) Later, in private, the superintendent shows you three problems: offcuts in the stairwell, a cord across the doorway and an open pail of screws. Write the correction you give your crew. Use the card.
c) Why do you give your crew the correction as facts, not as "the super is mad at us"?
Check yourself
What makes a compliment specific?
What are the three parts of a fair correction?
Name the four A B C D techniques and say what each one does.
Why is it a good idea to acknowledge before you explain?
Is being assigned a task you do not like bullying? Why or why not?

lessons.title: Body language, tone and talking across a crew
lessons.text:
Notice what people say without words, check what a cue means instead of guessing, and make yourself understood across PPE, noise and different first languages.
Why this matters on the job
A lot of meaning travels without words: a sigh, a shrug, a raised voice, a step back. On a job site, a hard hat, safety glasses, a mask or hearing protection can hide half of those signals. Many BC crews also include people who grew up with different languages and different ways of showing respect. Misreading a cue can start an argument. Checking what it means can prevent one.
Key ideas
We say things without words. Body language, facial expression, eye contact, gestures, tone of voice and how close we stand all send messages. Those messages can be positive or negative, and we often send them without noticing.
Tone can change the meaning of the same words. "Nice work" can be praise or sarcasm depending on how it is said.
Show you are listening. Stop what you are doing when you can. Face the person. Nod or say "okay" or "yep" as they go. Say the key point back. People show attention in different ways, so do not judge someone's listening by where they look. The proof is what they do or say back.
Read the cue, then check it. A cue is a clue, not a fact. Describe what you noticed and ask:
"You went quiet when I said Saturday. Does Saturday not work for you?"
"You're shaking your head. Did I get a measurement wrong?"
Respect personal space. Do not stand too close when you talk to someone. How close is comfortable differs from person to person.
On site, PPE and noise hide cues. Move closer, or both step away from the noise. Use gestures your crew has agreed on. Write numbers down or point to them on the drawing. Then check with a repeat-back.
Across first languages:
Use plain words. Skip slang and sayings such as "eyeball it," "ballpark it" or "call it a day."
Give one idea at a time.
Show as well as tell: point, hold up the part, mark the drawing.
Do not ask "Do you understand?" Many people say yes to be polite. Ask them to say it back or show you.
An accent is not a mistake. The Skills for Success description of speaking clearly includes pronunciation "even with accent." Listen for the meaning.
The two figures below show cues that can look open or closed. They are clues, not facts.
Worked example
A lead hand at Tidewater Mechanical (a fictional company) gives an instruction to Arman, who joined the crew last month and whose first language is not English:
"Just eyeball the hangers, ballpark every four feet or so, and if it looks off, holler and we'll call it a day."
The same instruction in plain words, with showing and checking:
"Put a hanger every 4 feet. Here, I'll mark the first two." (marks the joist) "If the pipe sags between them, stop and tell me. Can you show me where the third one goes?"
Arman points to the next mark at 4 feet. Now the lead hand knows the instruction landed.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) What does this face say? Your instructor posts photos of people around the room. For each photo, write the feeling you think the person is showing. Compare with others.
Photo 1: _ Photo 2: _ Photo 3: _ Photo 4: _ Photo 5: __
Did everyone agree? What does that tell you?
Task 2 (level 1) Change the stress, change the meaning. Say this sentence six times. Each time, stress a different word. Write what it means each time.
"I didn't say you broke it."
I didn't say you broke it: ______
I didn't say you broke it: ______
I didn't say you broke it: ______
I didn't say you broke it: ______
I didn't say you broke it: ______
I didn't say you broke it: ______
Task 3 (level 2) Spot the listener. Your instructor and a helper act out a short conversation twice. Write the cues you see.
Cues that showed poor listening:
Cues that showed good listening:
Task 4 (level 2) Check, do not assume. For each thing you notice, write a question that checks what it means.
You ask a co-worker to help you after break. She sighs and looks away.
You explain a new task. The apprentice nods the whole time but does not ask anything.
Your lead hand frowns at your work and walks off.
You suggest a new way to set up the staging. A co-worker crosses his arms.
Task 5 (level 2) Plain words. Rewrite each instruction for a crew-mate whose first language is not English. Use plain words and add one way to show or check.
"Knock it out before lunch and then we'll hit the next one."
"Just snug it up, don't crank on it."
"That's way out of whack. Tweak it a hair."
Task 6 (level 2) Read the figure. Look at the "can look closed" figure.
a) Name two cues you see.
b) Give two other reasons, not "he isn't listening," that could explain those cues.
c) Write one question that checks.
Task 7 (level 3) You are the lead hand. You give the morning plan to six workers on a slab. A generator is running. Everyone wears hearing protection. Two workers have a first language other than English.
Plan how you will deliver it. Write one line for each:
a) Where you stand and where the crew stands:
b) How you show the numbers (time, grid, quantity):
c) One gesture the crew agrees on, and what it means:
d) How you check each worker understood, without asking "Do you understand?":
Check yourself
Name four ways people communicate without words.
Why is a cue "a clue, not a fact"?
Why is "Do you understand?" a weak way to check understanding? What can you do instead?
You are wearing hearing protection and a mask beside a running compactor. Name two things you can do to get a message across.

lessons.title: Phone calls, voicemail and video calls at work
lessons.text:
Make and answer work calls, leave a voicemail that gets returned, run a video call, and pick the right way to send a message.
Why this matters on the job
You will call in when you are running late, phone a supplier about a missing order, answer a client's questions, and sometimes walk a supervisor through a problem on a video call. On some jobs you will check in by phone because you are working alone. On a call, the other person cannot see you, the drawing or the problem. Your words have to carry the whole message.
Key ideas
Before you call
Know why you are calling, in one sentence.
Have the details in front of you: job address, order or work order number, names, dates.
Have a pen, or a notes app open.
Move somewhere quiet if you can.
Making a call
Greet and say who you are: "Hi, this is Jordan Lee from Clearwater Roofing."
Say why you are calling, right away: "I'm calling about the skylight order for 14 Birch Street."
Give the details, one at a time.
Say back what you agreed: "So you'll deliver Thursday between 8 and 10. Is that right?"
Close with the next step: "I'll be on site to sign for it. Thanks."
Answering a work phone and taking a message
Answer with the company and your name: "Clearwater Roofing, this is Jordan."
If the person they want is not there, take a message with:
who called, and from what company
their number, read back digit by digit
what it is about
when to call back
Calling in late or sick
Follow your employer's rules about who to call and how early. Call before your shift starts. Say who you are, what is happening and when you expect to be in. Keep it short. A call is clearer than a text unless your employer says texting is fine.
Voicemail that gets returned
Your name and company.
Your number, said slowly.
Why you are calling, and what you need.
By when.
Your number again at the end.
Spell your name if it is easy to mishear. Keep it under about 30 seconds.
Video calls
Test your camera and microphone before the call.
Find a quiet spot with light in front of you, not behind you.
Mute when you are not talking. Unmute before you speak.
In a group, say your name before you speak if people cannot see who is talking.
Turn on captions if the app has them and it helps you or someone else.
On a site walk by video, hold the phone steady, say where you are ("This is the north wall, second floor, near gridline C") and describe what the camera is showing.
Group chats and texts
A crew group chat is good for quick updates, photos and times. It is not good for anything urgent or safety-related, because people may not see it for hours. For urgent or safety matters, speak in person or call. After an important phone call, a short text can confirm what was said: "Confirming: delivery Thursday 8 to 10 at 14 Birch." Do not post private information about other people.
Choosing the mode
Situation Best choice Why
Urgent, or about safety In person, or a phone call Fast and two-way
Detailed instruction In person or a call, then a text or email to confirm Two-way first, then a record
Quick update that is not urgent Text or crew chat People can read it when they can
Need to see a problem from far away Video call or photos The other person can see it
The same table as a chart. Start at the top and stop at the first "yes."
Checking in when you work alone
In BC, when a worker is assigned to work alone or in isolation, section 4.21 of the Occupational Health and Safety Regulation requires the employer to have a written procedure for checking the worker's well-being. The procedure must set the time between checks and say what happens if the worker cannot be contacted, including emergency rescue. A designated person makes contact at the set times and records the results. There must also be a check at the end of the shift. The regulation's note says visual or two-way voice contact is the preferred way to check.
That means a check-in call is a real safety call. Answer it, keep it clear and give the information your procedure asks for.
Worked example
You are an apprentice at Clearwater Roofing (a fictional company). You call the client about access to the roof and get voicemail.
"Hi, this is Jordan Lee from Clearwater Roofing. My number is 604-555-0137. I'm calling about the roof repair at 14 Birch Street. We need the side gate unlocked on Thursday morning so we can bring the ladder through. Can you call or text me by Wednesday at 4? Again, it's Jordan at 604-555-0137. Thanks."
It takes about 20 seconds. The client knows who called, why, what is needed, by when, and how to reply.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Open the call. Write the first two sentences you would say for each call: who you are and why you are calling.
You call Peak Glass Supply (fictional) to ask when a window order for the Maple Street job will arrive.
You call your lead hand because the site gate is locked and no one is there.
You call a homeowner to say the crew will be an hour late.
Task 2 (level 1) Take a message. Your partner reads a caller's message. Fill in the message slip. Read the phone number back before you hang up.
Message for
From (name and company)
Phone number
About
Call back by
Task 3 (level 2) Leave a voicemail. Write a voicemail for this call, then say it to a partner. Time it.
You work for Granite Point Electrical (a fictional company). You need the building manager at 220 Harbour Road to confirm whether the power can be shut off on Monday from 9 to noon. You need an answer by Friday at noon.
Time: ______ seconds
Task 4 (level 2) Calling in late. Role play with a partner. Your partner is your supervisor. Your car will not start and you will be 45 minutes late. Make the call. Then switch.
Task 5 (level 2) Pick the mode. For each situation, choose in person, phone call, text or crew chat, email, or video call. Give a reason.
You notice the guardrail on the third floor is loose.
You want to tell the crew that the porta-potty is being serviced at 2.
Your supervisor is at another site and wants to see a crack in a footing.
You agreed on the phone with a supplier to change a delivery date.
You need to explain to a new co-worker how to set up the mixer.
Task 6 (level 2) Working alone check-in. Read the procedure card. Your partner is Lou, the dispatcher. Make the two-hour check-in call. Then switch.
Upland Utility Services (fictional). Working alone procedure, pump station inspections.
Check in with dispatch every 2 hours and at the end of the shift.
Say: your name, the site, the time, "okay" or the problem, and your next stop.
If you miss a check-in, dispatch calls you twice, 10 minutes apart. If there is still no answer, dispatch calls your supervisor, who sends someone to the site.
Dispatch writes down every check-in.
After the role play, answer: what did Lou need to write down?
Task 7 (level 2) Use the chart. Name the mode for each situation.
a) A gas smell in the basement where the plumber is working. __ b) Tomorrow's start moves from 7:00 to 7:30. __ c) Your foreman, at another site, needs to see a crack in a footing. __ d) Long steps for setting up the rental hoist. __
Task 8 (level 3) You are the lead hand. The crane delivery of roof trusses is now 2 hours late. Your crew of six is waiting. The superintendent is in a meeting off site. The truss supplier is waiting to hear when the crane will be ready.
a) Choose a mode for the crew, the superintendent and the supplier. Give a reason for each.
b) Write the message you send to the superintendent.
c) What will you have the crew do for two hours?
Check yourself
What two things should you say in the first two sentences of a work call?
Name the five parts of a good voicemail.
Why is a crew group chat a poor choice for a safety problem?
Under section 4.21 of the BC OHS Regulation, name two things a working alone check-in procedure must include.
Give two things you can do to get ready for a video call.

lessons.title: Giving a short toolbox talk
lessons.text:
Plan and deliver a five-minute safety talk to a crew, with a clear opening, a few key points, something to show, a check and a closing action.
Try it in the visual practice studio
Plan what to show during your talk and put the key points in a useful order.
Plan the visuals for your talk
Why this matters on the job
Most BC crews hold short safety talks, often called toolbox talks or crew talks. In smaller workplaces that do not need a formal safety program, the BC Occupational Health and Safety Regulation (section 3.2) requires the employer to hold regular monthly meetings with workers to discuss health and safety, and to keep a record of them. Sooner or later you will be asked to lead one. A good five-minute talk can be the reason someone goes home without an injury.
Key ideas
A simple shape for a five-minute talk
Open. Name the topic and why it matters here, today. "We're digging the trench for the water line this afternoon, so today's talk is about what's buried under us."
Two or three key points. No more. People remember three things better than ten.
Show something. A tool, a photo, the drawing, the sign on the wall. Showing helps people who learn by seeing and people whose first language is different from yours.
Check. Ask a question that needs more than "yes": "What's the first thing you do if the lead hand asks you to dig before the locates are marked?"
Close with one action. "Before you pick up a shovel today, check the locate marks with me."
Here is the shape as a card you can copy onto an index card:
Preparing
Pick one topic. Tie it to the work happening today or this week.
WorkSafeBC publishes free toolbox meeting guides on many topics at worksafebc.com/toolbox-meeting-guides. Many include a "Record of meeting" form.
Add local details: names, locations, what has happened on this site. WorkSafeBC's guides encourage presenters to add details specific to their own workplace.
Write your points on one card. Do not read a script word for word.
Practise once out loud and time it.
Delivering
Stand where everyone can see and hear you, away from running equipment.
Speak to the person farthest away.
Pause after each key point. Silence gives people time to think.
Keep your hands free to show things.
Look around the whole group as you talk, in the way that is comfortable for you.
Stand steady. Shifting from foot to foot, hands in pockets or arms crossed can make you look unsure, even when you are not.
Know your audience
A crew of experienced journeypeople does not need the basics explained. A crew of first-week apprentices does. Some crew members may have a different first language. Use plain words, show as well as tell, and check with questions.
Keep a record
In a small workplace's monthly safety meeting, the employer must keep a record of the meeting and what was discussed. WorkSafeBC's guideline says this does not have to be formal minutes. A record of when the meeting was held, who attended and the general topics is enough. Many crews use the record form on the back of a toolbox meeting guide for every talk.
Learning from strong speakers
Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech on August 28, 1963, at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. Watch a short excerpt and notice how he uses pauses, repetition and his voice. You may also think of a speaker you respect from your own Nation, family or community, and what makes people listen to them.
Worked example
Rae, the foreman at Clearwater Roofing (a fictional company), plans a talk using WorkSafeBC's toolbox meeting guide "The right to refuse unsafe work."
Open: "Yesterday someone asked me if they could say no to a job they thought was unsafe. Good question. Today's talk is about your right to refuse unsafe work."
Point 1: "If you have reasonable cause to believe a task would create an undue hazard to you or anyone else, you must not do it. Stop and tell me right away. Use the words 'I'm refusing this as unsafe.'"
Point 2: "If we can't agree, we look at it again with our worker rep, Kai."
Point 3: "If it's still not sorted, we both call WorkSafeBC. Nobody gets disciplined for following these steps."
Show: holds up the guide and points to the three steps.
Check: "Who is our worker rep?" and "What are the exact words you use?"
Close: "If something up on that roof doesn't feel right today, stop and come get me."
Rae has everyone sign the record of meeting on the back of the guide. The talk takes about four minutes.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Watch a strong speaker. Watch the excerpt your instructor plays. Write what the speaker does with:
His voice: __________
Pauses: __________
Repetition: __________
His body and face: __________
Task 2 (level 1) Stand three ways. Say this line three times, standing a different way each time: "Today's talk is about ladders." First, slouch with your hands in your pockets. Second, cross your arms and look at the floor. Third, stand steady with your hands free and look around the group. The group says which version made them want to listen, and why.
Task 3 (level 2) Plan your talk. Choose a WorkSafeBC toolbox meeting guide with your instructor. Fill in the planning card.
Part Your plan
Topic
Why it matters here, today
Key point 1
Key point 2
Key point 3
What I will show
My check question
Closing action
Task 4 (level 3) Give your talk. Deliver your talk to your group in three minutes or less. Your group uses this checklist and gives you one thing that worked and one thing to try next time.
[ ] said the topic and why it matters in the first few sentences
[ ] gave no more than three key points
[ ] showed something
[ ] could be heard by everyone
[ ] paused after key points
[ ] asked a check question that needed more than "yes"
[ ] closed with one clear action
[ ] finished in three minutes or less
One thing that worked: __________
One thing to try next time: __________
Task 5 (level 2) Fill in the record. Complete a record for your group's talks today.
Item Entry
Workplace ACCESS classroom practice
Date and time
Topics discussed
Who attended
Safety issues or suggestions raised
Task 6 (level 3) Change the audience. Rewrite the opening of your talk twice: once for a crew of experienced journeypeople, and once for first-week apprentices, two of whom are still learning English.
Experienced crew: __________
First-week apprentices: __________
Task 7 (level 3) Fix the talk. Read this talk. Which of the five parts are missing or weak? Rewrite it.
"Okay, so, ladders. Ladders are important. There are lots of rules. Be careful on them. Three points of contact and all that. Any questions? No? Good. Let's go."
Missing or weak parts: __________
Your rewrite: __________
Task 8 (level 2) Time it. A learner plans these times for a five-minute talk:
Part Time
Open 30 seconds
Key points 3 points × 60 seconds
Show 45 seconds
Check 45 seconds
Close 15 seconds
a) What is the total, in minutes and seconds? b) Is the talk over or under five minutes, and by how much? c) Where would you cut time? Why there?
Check yourself
What are the five parts of a short toolbox talk?
Why should a five-minute talk have no more than three key points?
Under section 3.2 of the BC OHS Regulation, what must the employer in a small workplace do about health and safety meetings?
Give two delivery habits that help a crew hear and follow you.

lessons.title: Hand signals and radio on a job site
lessons.text:
Know the BC rules for crane hand signals and radios, read the official signal chart, and give and confirm a short radio message.
Why this matters on the job
When a crane operator cannot see the load, or the site is too loud to hear, the crew talks with hands and radios. One wrong signal or a missed word can drop a load or swing it into someone. BC's Occupational Health and Safety Regulation sets out who may signal a crane, which signals to use and when a radio must be used instead. Even if you never signal a crane, you will work near lifts, and you need to know what you are seeing and when you can call a stop.
This lesson is an introduction. It does not qualify anyone to signal a crane or rig a load.
Key ideas
Crane and hoist signals: the BC rules
Rule Where it is
When the crane or hoist operator does not have a clear, unobstructed view of the boom, jib, load line, load hook and load through the whole lift, the operator must act only on the directions of a qualified signaller who has a clear view of what the operator cannot see. OHS Regulation section 14.47(1)
The operator must stop when they get a stop signal from any person. Section 14.47(2)
If hand signals are used between a signaller and the operator, the standard signals in Figure 15-1 of the Regulation must be used. Section 15.20
If distance, weather or other conditions make hand signals hazardous or impracticable, a two-way radio or another audio or video system acceptable to WorkSafeBC must be used. Section 14.48(1)
Multi-channel radios are not permitted for directing crane or hoist movement. Section 14.49(2)
Rigging and slinging must be done by, or directly supervised by, qualified workers familiar with the rigging and with the code of signals. Section 15.2
The official chart is in Figure 15-1 of the Regulation. WorkSafeBC also publishes it as a toolbox meeting guide, "Hand signals for hoist and crane operations" (TG 07-29), at worksafebc.com.
What the signals look like
Section 15.20 refers to "Figure 15-1." That figure is in the Regulation, and WorkSafeBC prints the main signals on its toolbox meeting guide TG 07-29. The drawings below show the 12 signals on TG 07-29. Two more signals from the ASME B30.5 standard for mobile cranes are marked with *. Each signaller is drawn from the front, the way the operator sees them. Red marks show movement.
These drawings help you recognize signals. They do not replace the official chart, your site's chart or signaller training.
Why the rules look like this
A qualified signaller with a clear view means the operator acts on directions from someone trained in the signals who can see what the operator cannot, not on waves from whoever happens to be nearby.
Anyone can stop the lift because whoever sees the danger first may not be the signaller.
Standard signals mean any trained operator can read any trained signaller, on any site.
The radio takes over when signals cannot be seen. A signal no one can see is no signal.
Talking on a radio
These habits make any radio call clearer. They are a pattern for practice in this class. Your site may have its own radio rules, and those come first.
Wait for a gap. Do not talk over someone else.
Say who you are calling, then who you are: "Dana, this is Jordan."
Wait for an answer before you give the message.
Keep it short. One message at a time.
Say numbers clearly, digit by digit if needed: "Gate two. Two."
Ask for, or give, a read-back: "Copy that, truck at gate two, you're coming down."
No answer means no message. If you do not hear a reply, the message did not get through. Try again, or go in person.
The radio habits fit on one card:
Worked example
Jordan, a labourer at Harbourline Builders (a fictional company), sees a concrete truck arrive at the wrong gate. Jordan radios the lead hand on the general site channel. This is not a crane call.
Jordan: "Dana, this is Jordan."
Dana: "Go ahead, Jordan."
Jordan: "Concrete truck is at gate two, not gate one. Driver's asking where to set up."
Dana: "Copy. Truck at gate two. Tell him to wait. I'm coming down."
Jordan: "Wait at gate two, you're coming down. Copy."
Each person said back the key fact. Both know the message got through.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Know the rules. Answer from the table above.
Who may give a crane operator a stop signal?
When must the operator act only on the directions of a qualified signaller?
Which hand signals must be used between a signaller and an operator?
When must a two-way radio or other acceptable system be used instead of hand signals?
Task 2 (level 1) Read the chart. Use the printed WorkSafeBC chart "Hand signals for hoist and crane operations." With a partner, take turns: one person makes a signal exactly as the chart shows it, and the other names it without looking at the chart. Do five each, then check against the chart.
Signals I named correctly: ______ out of 5
The one I mixed up, and what it really means: __________
Task 3 (level 2) Radio relay. Your instructor whispers a short site message to the first person in a line. Each person passes it on by "radio": say who you are calling, who you are, wait for "go ahead," give the message, and get a read-back. The last person says it out loud.
What the first person heard: __________
What the last person said: __________
What changed, and why? __________
Task 4 (level 2) Write the call. Write a radio call for this situation, including the other person's read-back.
You are a labourer at Harbourline Builders (fictional). The scissor lift on level 3 has a flat tire. You need to tell the lead hand, Dana, and ask whether to tag it out of service.
Task 5 (level 2) What does the rule say? For each situation, say which rule applies and what must happen.
During a lift, the load will swing behind the building where the operator cannot see it.
Heavy fog rolls in. The operator can no longer see the signaller's hands clearly.
A labourer who is not the signaller sees a worker walk under the load and gives the stop signal.
The crew wants to use their regular multi-channel walkie-talkies to direct the crane.
Task 6 (level 1) Name the signal. Name each signal A to F. Use the drawings above only after you try.
A: __ B: __ C: __
D: __ E: __ F: __
Task 7 (level 2) Which signal? Name the signal or signals a signaller would give.
a) The load needs to go up, slowly. b) Everything must pause while a worker clears the area. c) The load must stop moving. d) The boom must come down while the load stays where it is. e) The telescoping boom must get shorter.
Task 8 (level 3) The blind spot. At Coastline Marine Works (a fictional dock), a mobile crane lifts a pump onto a barge. The load swings behind a shipping container. The operator cannot see the load or the signaller.
a) Which rule applies, and who must the operator take directions from?
b) The signaller can see the load, but the operator cannot see the signaller's hands. What must the crew use, and what kind of radio is not allowed?
c) You are a deckhand, not the signaller. You see a worker step under the load. What do you do, and which rule backs you up?
d) Write the radio call the signaller makes to stop the swing, with the operator's read-back.
Check yourself
Why does BC require a qualified signaller when the operator cannot see the load?
Can you, as a labourer who is not the signaller, stop a crane lift? What rule says so?
Where can you find the official crane hand signals?
On a radio, what does it mean if you do not hear a reply?

lessons.title: Give a clear instruction to a helper
lessons.text:
Give a helper one step at a time, show it, check with a say-back instead of "Do you understand?" and watch them do it before you walk away.
Why this matters on the job
Lesson 1 taught you to listen and say an instruction back. Soon you will be on the other side. A second-year apprentice gives instructions to a first-year. A journeyperson directs a helper. When an instruction goes wrong, it is usually not because the helper was careless. It is because the instruction was too long, too vague or never checked. A clear instruction saves material, time and sometimes a finger.
Key ideas
Before you start, know the job yourself. What is the task? What size, how many, where, by when? What could hurt someone? If you are not sure, ask your lead hand first.
Get their attention. Stop the noise if you can. Face them. Use their name. "Noor, I need you for a minute."
Give one step at a time. People remember a short step better than a long list. Long instructions with six details in one breath lose details. Break the job into short steps and check each one.
Use the four-part loop: tell, show, check, watch.
Tell one step in plain words. Say every number with its unit: "fourteen and a half inches."
Show it once, if it is a hands-on task. Let them see your hands.
Check. Do not ask "Do you understand?" Most people say yes to be polite. Ask: "Tell me back what you're going to do." Or: "Show me where you'll cut."
Watch them do the first one. Then say what was right, and fix anything that was not. Then move to the next step.
Say why when it helps. "Keep the cords along the wall, because the drywallers are carrying sheets through here." A reason helps people remember and helps them make good choices when you are not there.
Safety goes first and stands alone. Do not bury a safety point in the middle of a long instruction. Say it as its own step and check it: "Before you cut, the guard has to snap back. Show me."
Check back later. "I'll be back at 10 to see how it's going." Then come back.
Adapt to the helper. A first-week helper needs more steps and more checks. An experienced helper may only need the goal. A helper whose first language is not English needs plain words, one idea at a time, and something to look at. Lesson 6 covers this.
Worked example: cutting blocking
Tia (fictional) is a third-year carpentry apprentice at Fernhill Framing (fictional). She needs Noor, a first-week helper, to cut blocking.
What Tia used to say:
"Grab the seven-and-a-quarter saw and the speed square, cut twelve blocks at fourteen and a half from the two-by-six offcuts, stack them by bay 3, and sweep the cut-offs into the bin."
Noor cut twelve blocks at fourteen and a quarter and stacked them by bay 2.
What Tia says now:
Tell: "Noor, first step. We need twelve blocks, fourteen and a half inches long, from these two-by-six offcuts."
Show: Tia marks one with the tape and square, and cuts it while Noor watches.
Check: "Tell me back what you're cutting." Noor: "Twelve blocks, fourteen and a half." Tia: "Right. Show me where you'll mark the next one." Noor points to the 14 1/2 mark.
Watch: Noor cuts the second block. Tia checks it with the tape. "That's right on. Keep going. When you've got twelve, come get me and I'll give you the next step."
Tia gave the stacking and sweeping as separate steps after the cutting was done. The job took two extra minutes at the start and saved a stack of wasted blocks.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Good check or not? Write G for a good check or N for not.
a) _ "Do you understand?" b) "Tell me back the three things you're bringing." c) _ "Got it?" d) "Show me where you'll drill the first hole." e) ____ "Makes sense, right?"
Task 2 (level 2) Break it up. Rewrite this as three or four short steps. Put the safety step on its own.
"Take the bender and the half-inch EMT, bend four ninety-degree stubs at ten inches, and watch your hands in the shoe, then lay them out by the panel in room 106."
Task 3 (level 2) Add the why. Add a short reason to each instruction.
a) "Put the cut-offs in the bin, not on the floor." ____ b) "Close the gate behind the truck." ____ c) "Label every cable at both ends." ______
Task 4 (level 2) Find what is missing. Use the six parts from lesson 1 (what, where, how much, when, who, safety). What is missing from this instruction?
"Go get the pipe for the second floor."
Task 5 (level 2) Say it so it can't be misheard. Rewrite each number so it is clear over noise.
a) "Set it at fifteen." ____ b) "Thirteen of them." ____ c) "Two-sixteenths gap." ______
Task 6 (level 2) Tell, show, check, watch. In pairs, one person teaches a simple task with the four parts: tying a bowline, folding a tarp, measuring a board to 23 5/8". The other person is a new helper. Then switch. Write what the teacher's check question was.
Task 7 (level 3) Plain words for a new helper. Your helper, Luis (fictional), is in his first week. His first language is Spanish. You need him to set up cones around a manhole in a parking lot, with 2 m between cones, all the way around. Write your instruction as steps. Say what you will show him and how you will check.
Task 8 (level 3) What went wrong? Your helper laid 40 paving stones in the wrong pattern. You realize you said "Do it like the other side" while pointing at the wrong side.
a) Whose mistake was it? b) What do you say to the helper? c) What would you do differently next time? Use the four-part loop.
Task 9 (level 3) Your trade. Pick a real task from your trade that has at least four steps. Write your instruction for a first-week helper as tell, show, check and watch for each step. Mark the safety step.
Check yourself
Why is one long instruction a problem, even for a careful helper?
Name the four parts of the loop.
Why is "Do you understand?" a weak check? What do you ask instead?
Where does a safety point go in an instruction?
How does an instruction change for a helper in their first week?

lessons.title: Report up the chain
lessons.text:
Know who to tell, how fast and what to say for an unsafe condition, an injury, a delay or a mistake, and give a short report your supervisor can act on.
Why this matters on the job
Every crew has bad news sometimes: a damaged part, a late delivery, a cut that went wrong, a guardrail that is gone. Bad news does not get better with time. A supervisor who hears it early can fix it, move the crew or call the client. A supervisor who hears it late, or from someone else, has fewer choices and less trust in you. Some reports are also the law. In BC, unsafe conditions and injuries must be reported as soon as possible.
Key ideas
Four kinds of report. Each one has a different speed.
Kind Example How fast
Unsafe condition or act Missing guardrail, frayed cord, someone working under a load As soon as possible. Stop the work if it is not safe to continue.
Injury or exposure A cut hand, something in your eye, breathing in a chemical As soon as possible, even if it does not need first aid
Delay Late delivery, broken tool, you will be late As soon as you know
Mistake Wrong length cut, hole in the wrong spot, wrong part ordered Before it gets covered up or built on
The rules for safety and injuries.
Section 3.10 of BC's Occupational Health and Safety Regulation says anyone who sees what appears to be an unsafe or harmful condition or act must report it as soon as possible to a supervisor or the employer. The person who gets the report must investigate and fix it without delay.
WorkSafeBC says workers must report all injuries and exposures to hazardous materials as soon as possible, even if they do not need first aid. Report to your supervisor, and to a first aid attendant if your workplace has one.
Employers must investigate certain incidents, including a near miss that could have caused a serious injury. Your report is where that starts.
Who to tell. Your supervisor first: usually your lead hand or foreman. If they cannot be reached and it is urgent, go to the next person up: the foreman or superintendent. Lesson 9 of the Collaboration series shows who is who on a site.
What to say: the report-up card. Keep it short and in this order:
What happened or what you see.
Where: floor, grid, room, piece of equipment.
When it happened or started.
What I did: made it safe, tagged it out, stopped, nothing yet.
What I need: a decision, a person, a part, a call.
Facts first, no blame. Say what you saw, not who you think caused it. "The guardrail on the east side of level 3 is down" is a report. "The framers knocked the guardrail down again" starts an argument.
Own your mistakes. "I cut the header 20 mm short" is hard to say. It is much easier than explaining why you hid it. Lesson 5 covers taking criticism after.
Pick the mode. Unsafe and urgent: in person or a phone call. A delay that is not urgent: a call or text. Lesson 7 covers choosing the mode. If you text, make sure it was read. No answer means no report.
Worked example: three reports in one morning
Ana (fictional) is a second-year pipefitter at Riverbend Mechanical (fictional). Her foreman is Grant.
7:40, a delay. Ana texts Grant:
"Grant, the 4-inch valves for the boiler room aren't in the delivery. Driver says they're coming tomorrow. I'm starting the 2-inch runs in the meantime. Can you call the supplier?"
What, where, when, what she did and what she needs, in four lines.
9:15, unsafe. The scissor lift's platform gate will not latch. Ana does not text. She lowers the lift, puts a "Do not use" tag on it and walks to Grant:
"Scissor lift number 2 in the boiler room. The gate won't latch, as of 9:15. I lowered it and tagged it out. We need a mechanic, and I need another lift or a ladder plan for the hangers."
11:00, a mistake. Ana finds she cut two hangers 25 mm short. They are not installed yet.
"Grant, I cut two hangers 25 mm short for the line in grid C. They're not up. I've marked them as scrap. I need two more lengths of rod. It was my measurement. I'll measure off the drawing, not the old rod, from now on."
Grant was not happy about the hangers. He was glad to know before they went up.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Which kind? Write U (unsafe), I (injury), D (delay) or M (mistake).
a) _ The concrete truck will be 45 minutes late. b) You drilled a hole in the wrong stud bay. c) _ A labourer is cutting with the grinder guard removed. d) You got a splinter of steel in your thumb. e) ____ The rental generator will not start.
Task 2 (level 1) How fast? For each item in Task 1, write how fast you report it.
Task 3 (level 2) Fill the card. Write a report for this situation using all five parts.
You are an electrician's apprentice. At 2:10 you find a junction box in unit 310 with live wires hanging out and no cover. Nobody else is in the unit.
What: __________
Where: __________
When: __________
What I did: __________
What I need: __________
Task 4 (level 2) Take out the blame. Rewrite each report so it states facts only.
a) "The plumbers left their mess all over the stairs again." b) "Somebody who can't read a tape cut the stringers wrong."
Task 5 (level 2) The rule. Answer from the Key ideas.
a) What does section 3.10 say a person must do? b) Do you report an injury that did not need first aid? To whom?
Task 6 (level 2) Choose the mode. For each report in Task 1, choose in person, phone call or text. Give one reason for two of them.
Task 7 (level 3) Own the mistake. You are a second-year carpentry apprentice. You framed a window opening 50 mm too narrow. The window installer arrives tomorrow at 7:00. Write what you say to your lead hand, and when you say it.
Task 8 (level 3) Your supervisor is not there. You are on a road crew. At 6:30 a.m. you see a trench that was left open overnight, with no barrier, next to the sidewalk. Your foreman does not answer his phone.
a) What do you do first? b) Who do you tell next? c) Write the text you leave for your foreman.
Task 9 (level 3) Near miss. A bundle of rebar slipped from a sling and landed one metre from a worker. Nobody was hurt. The crew says, "No harm done, let's keep going."
a) Should this be reported? Why? b) Write the report you give your supervisor. c) Why does a near miss matter if nobody was hurt?
Task 10 (level 3) Report on a call. Role-play with a partner. You are calling your foreman to report a delay: the crane for this afternoon's lift is broken down, and the rental company says tomorrow. Use the card. Your partner asks two questions. Then switch, with a report of your own choice.
Check yourself
Name the four kinds of report and how fast each one goes.
What does section 3.10 require?
What does WorkSafeBC say about reporting an injury that does not need first aid?
Name the five parts of the report-up card.
Why report a mistake before it is covered up?

lessons.title: Talk about a drawing and ask a good RFI question
lessons.text:
Spot when two drawings disagree, explain the conflict out loud using sheet and detail numbers, and help write a request for information that gets a clear answer.
Why this matters on the job
Drawings are made by people, and people make mistakes. The floor plan says one thing, the schedule says another. If you build what you guess was meant, you may build it twice. If you stop and say "the drawings are wrong," nobody knows what you mean. Trades who can point to the exact sheet, say exactly what does not match and ask one clear question save the job time and money. On most jobs that question becomes a request for information, or RFI.
Key ideas
A request for information (RFI) is a written question asking the designer to clarify the drawings or specifications when something is unclear, wrong or missing. During construction it usually goes from the contractor to the architect or engineer. RFIs are numbered and tracked. An RFI answer, by itself, does not approve extra cost or time. That takes a change order.
Who writes it. As an apprentice or journeyperson you usually do not send RFIs yourself. You find the problem and tell your lead hand or foreman. Your company or the GC's superintendent writes and sends the RFI. Your clear description is what goes in it.
Before you ask, check the set. Many questions are answered somewhere else in the drawings: a detail, a schedule, a general note or the specifications. Look first. Ask your lead hand to look with you. An RFI that is already answered in the documents wastes the designer's time.
Talk like the drawings. Use the sheet numbers, detail numbers, gridlines and tags. Reading lesson 5 covers how a set is organized.
Vague Clear
"The door's wrong." "Door 104. Plan A2.1 shows an 810 opening. The door schedule on A6.1 says 915 wide."
"The drain's in the wrong spot." "Floor drain in room 112. Plumbing plan P2.1 puts it 600 from grid 3. The architectural plan A2.1 shows 900."
"There's no detail." "Section 2 on A3.1 calls up detail 5 on A5.2. Sheet A5.2 only has details 1 to 4."
Say it, then write it. First tell your lead hand, pointing at the sheets. Then help write it down. A good RFI has:
A number and the date.
Who it is to and from.
The drawings and details involved.
One clear question. One question per RFI is easiest to answer.
Your suggested answer, if you have one. It speeds things up, but the designer decides.
The date you need an answer, and why: what work is waiting.
While you wait, do not guess. Do not build the part in question. Work somewhere else and tell your lead hand what is on hold.
Worked example: door 104
At Westridge Clinic (a fictional job), Mika is a third-year carpentry apprentice laying out the corridor walls. Framing the door openings starts on 2026-11-13.
She finds the conflict. The plan shows door 104 with an 810 mm opening. The door schedule says door 104 is 915 mm wide.
She checks the set. No general note, door detail or specification section says which one governs.
She says it to her lead hand, Ty:
"Ty, door 104. Plan A2.1 shows an 810 opening. The door schedule on A6.1 says the door is 915 wide. I checked the general notes and the door details. Nothing says which one wins. Can we get an RFI in? Framing starts on the 13th."
Ty says it back: "So the plan and the schedule don't match on 104, and we need an answer before the 13th. I'll get the super to send it. Frame the other openings and leave 104."
The superintendent writes the RFI using Mika's words:
The architect answers on 2026-11-10: "Schedule governs. Frame for the 915 door. Revised A2.1 to follow." Mika frames 104 on the 13th. Nobody built anything twice.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Clear or vague? Rewrite each one so it uses the sheet, tag or gridline.
a) "The window looks too small." (Plan A2.2 shows window W3 at 1,200 wide. The window schedule on A6.2 says W3 is 1,500 wide.)
b) "The duct hits the beam." (Mechanical plan M2.1 runs a 400 mm duct at grid C-4. Structural drawing S2.1 shows a beam at grid C, 300 mm lower than the duct.)
Task 2 (level 2) Read the figure. Use the door 104 figure.
a) What width does the plan show? b) What width does the schedule show? c) What is the difference, in millimetres?
Task 3 (level 2) Check the set first. Which of these are worth an RFI? Write Y for yes or N for no, and say why.
a) _ The plan does not show the ceiling height, but the room finish schedule lists it. b) _ The electrical plan shows a receptacle where the architectural plan shows a door swing. c) ____ You can't find the stair detail, and the stair section calls up detail 7 on A5.1, which has only 6 details.
Task 4 (level 2) One question. This RFI asks too much. Split it into separate, clear questions.
"What's going on with the bathroom? The tub doesn't fit, the vanity isn't shown and where does the fan go?"
Task 5 (level 3) Say it out loud. In pairs, one person is the apprentice, one is the lead hand. The apprentice explains the window W3 conflict from Task 1a out loud, pointing to imaginary sheets. The lead hand says it back. Switch, using the duct and beam from Task 1b.
Task 6 (level 3) Write the RFI. Write a full RFI for the duct and beam in Task 1b. Use all six parts. Duct work in that area starts on 2026-11-20. Your company needs three working days to change the duct order if the size changes.
Task 7 (level 3) Answer-needed date. For Task 6: duct work starts on Friday 2026-11-20. Your company needs three full working days (Monday to Friday) before the start day to change the duct order. Count back. What is the latest day the answer can arrive, by end of day? Show your count.
Task 8 (level 3) While you wait. The RFI for door 104 is sent. Your lead hand is away. Another carpenter says, "Just frame it at 810. That's what the plan says." Write what you say. Then write what you do instead.
Task 9 (level 3) Your suggestion. For the window W3 conflict, write a suggested answer you could add to the RFI. Why is it only a suggestion?
Task 10 (level 3) The answer arrives. The architect answers the W3 RFI: "Window schedule governs. W3 is 1,500. See revised A2.2, revision 2." Write the short message you send your crew, and say what you check on the new sheet before you build.
Check yourself
What is an RFI, and who usually sends it on a building job?
What should you do before you ask for an RFI?
Name the six parts of a good RFI.
Why is one question per RFI better than three?
Does an RFI answer approve extra cost? What does?

lessons.title: Give a progress update against the schedule
lessons.text:
Read where a job stands on a bar chart, work out how far ahead or behind it is, and give a short update that says where we are, why, the effect, the fix and what you need.
Why this matters on the job
Every morning someone asks, "Where are we?" A foreman asks the lead hand. A superintendent asks the foreman. The owner asks the superintendent. "Going good" does not help anyone plan. "Framing is one day behind because the lumber came late, and here is how we get it back" lets the next person act: book the roofers a day later, or approve the extra crew. A clear update is short, honest and based on the schedule.
Key ideas
A bar chart (Gantt chart) shows each activity as a bar across the days. The plan bar shows when it was supposed to happen. A second bar shows what actually happened or what is now forecast. A today line shows where we are now. Numeracy lessons on scheduling teach how to build these charts. Here you read one and talk about it.
Ahead or behind. Compare what should be done by today with what is done.
Framing was planned for days 5 to 8, which is 4 days of work.
Today is the end of day 7. By plan, 3 of the 4 days of framing should be done. That is 3 ÷ 4 = 75%.
The crew has done 2 days' worth of framing. That is 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.
75% − 50% is a gap of 25 percentage points, representing 25% of the total framing work, or 1 day. Framing is 1 day behind.
The effect. The roof cannot start until framing is done. Windows cannot go in until the roof is on. So if nothing changes, framing ends on day 9, the roof moves to days 10 and 11, and windows move to day 12. The whole job is one day late.
Five parts of a progress update:
Where we are. Ahead, on time or behind, in days. Name the activity.
Why. One sentence. Facts, not blame.
Effect. What else moves if nothing changes.
The fix. Your plan to recover, or two options.
What I need. A decision, a person, money or time, and by when.
Say bad news early and plainly. "We're a bit behind but it should be fine" hides the problem. "We're one day behind on framing" lets people plan. Most supervisors forgive a delay. Few forgive a surprise.
Adapt to the listener. Your foreman wants the detail: which wall, how many framers. The owner wants the effect on move-in day and cost. Same facts, different focus.
Bring options when you can. "We can add four framers tomorrow, or work Saturday. The first costs more but the roofers don't move." Then the person who decides can decide.
Worked example: the garage
Ridgeway Builders (fictional) is building a two-car garage. Kendra is the lead hand. The framing crew is 4 framers. At the end of day 7 her foreman, Paul, calls.
Kendra works it out first.
Framing plan: days 5 to 8. Should be 75% done. It is 50% done. One day behind.
Why: the lumber package came at noon on day 5 instead of 7:00, and the crew lost the afternoon of day 6 to rain.
Work left: 2 days of work for 4 framers = 2 × 4 = 8 framer-days.
Fix: with 4 more framers tomorrow, that is 8 framers for one day = 8 framer-days. Framing would finish at the end of day 8, back on plan.
Kendra's update to Paul:
"Paul, framing is one day behind. The lumber came at noon on day 5 and we lost the afternoon of day 6 to rain. If nothing changes, framing finishes day 9, and the roof and windows each slide a day. If you can send four framers from the Elm St. job tomorrow, we finish framing on day 8 and we're back on plan. I need to know by 3:00 so I can set up the work for eight people."
Paul says it back, then decides: "Okay. Four framers tomorrow. I'll tell the roofers we're still on for day 9."
Kendra used all five parts in under 30 seconds, with numbers from the schedule.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Read the chart. Use the bar chart.
a) What days were planned for the slab? Were they done on plan? b) What day is today? c) On what days are the roof's plan bar and forecast bar? d) Which activity is shown as in progress?
Task 2 (level 2) Percent planned. An activity is planned for 5 days. Today is the end of its day 2. What percent should be done by plan? Show your work.
Task 3 (level 2) Ahead or behind? Siding is planned for 6 days. Today is the end of day 4 of the siding. The crew has done 3 days' worth. How many days ahead or behind is it? Show your work in days and in percent.
Task 4 (level 2) Vague to clear. Rewrite each update so it states where we are in days. You may invent details for this practice, but label them as fictional; a real update needs verified facts.
