a) "Drywall's going okay, a little slow maybe." b) "We're kind of ahead on the paving."
Task 5 (level 3) The effect. In the garage job, the roof is planned for days 9 and 10, and windows for day 11. The roof crew is 2 days late arriving, but framing is back on plan. What are the new days for the roof and windows? What day does the job finish?
Task 6 (level 3) Crew-days. A deck has 3 days of work left for a crew of 2. How many worker-days is that? If you add 1 worker, how many full days will it take now? Is that enough to finish in 2 days?
Task 7 (level 3) Write the update. Electrical rough-in at a fictional duplex was planned for days 10 to 13 (4 days). Today is the end of day 12. The crew is 25% done because the panel was back-ordered. The inspection is booked for day 14 and drywall for day 15. Write a five-part update to the superintendent. Offer two options. For the arithmetic, assume the panel is now available and two crews can work independently at the same rate, so two crews do twice the work in a day. These are exercise assumptions, not a guarantee on a real job. Crew availability, costs, revised inspection bookings and the effect on move-in are not confirmed. Ask for a decision before the start of day 13 if a second crew is to start then.
Task 8 (level 3) Same facts, two listeners. Take your Task 7 update. Rewrite it for the owner of the duplex, who cares about move-in day and cost, not panels and crews.
Task 9 (level 3) Ahead of schedule. Your paving crew finished the base course a day early. Is that worth reporting? Write the update and say what the superintendent might do with the extra day.
Task 10 (level 3) Say it out loud. In pairs, give the Task 7 update out loud in 30 seconds or less. The listener says it back and asks one question. Then switch.
Check yourself
What does the today line on a bar chart show?
An activity planned for 4 days is at the end of its third day. What percent should be done?
Name the five parts of a progress update.
Why report a delay early, even if you might catch up?
How does an update change for the owner compared with your foreman?

lessons.title: Creativity and innovation — notice, make, test and improve
lessons.text:
Visual guide Six connected components of creativity and innovation. Short labels summarize the six skill components; numbers match the chapter list. Use the connections in the order the task needs. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. Make ideas usable. Learn from the trial. Six connected components: Use imagination and curiosity; Find opportunities to innovate; Generate new ideas; Develop your ideas; Apply your ideas; Make room for creativity. Revisit the component that helps the task.
See it in action · Creativity and innovation
Visual guide A tested improvement, with a reason. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
NEED: Find the current card quickly. IDEAS: Divider tabs or a labelled tray. Suggest two useful options. Make a small prototype. Ask a user to try it; improve. A tested improvement, with a reason. Choose a visible measure: correct selection, clear labels or fewer steps.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. NEED: Find the current card quickly. IDEAS: Divider tabs or a labelled tray.
Try it: Suggest two useful options. Make a small prototype. Ask a user to try it; improve.
Check your result: A tested improvement, with a reason. Choose a visible measure: correct selection, clear labels or fewer steps.
Useful ideas can begin with an ordinary question
Creativity and innovation involve imagining possibilities, developing ideas and putting them into use. You do not need to be an artist, invent a product for sale or produce an idea nobody has ever had. An idea can be new to you or useful in a particular setting. A clearer information card, a better way to organize a practice kit or a different explanation of a number can all make learning and work easier.
You may already create solutions when materials are limited, when a familiar approach does not suit a person or when a task needs a different explanation. This chapter makes that process visible. You will practise asking questions, generating several possibilities, selecting one for a reason, making a small version and learning from a reader or user's response.
Creativity also involves care. Changing a classroom filing method is different from changing an approved equipment procedure. Ideas that affect safety, privacy, community knowledge or someone else's work need the appropriate boundaries and permissions. A useful question is, “What can we try safely in this learning task, and who needs to guide a real change?”
In an ACCESS IS4S classroom, learners bring different experiences and ways of making meaning. You may choose to draw on your own experience, but you do not need to provide cultural knowledge, tell a personal story or make an object represent your identity. This chapter uses original fictional classroom cases. It does not supply Nation-specific designs, teachings or claims about a single Indigenous way of being creative.
A useful design is developed with attention to the people who will use it. An urban learning centre and a smaller B.C. community may need different information arrangements, and two learners in the same room may prefer different formats. Ask about the actual task and invite input. The connection to people and place comes through purpose, relationships and appropriate local direction, with learners deciding what they wish to contribute.
Use your imagination and curiosity
Ask questions and explore another possibility before settling on an answer.
Practise with: “Notice before proposing” through “Ask from another viewpoint”
Identify opportunities for you to innovate
Locate a useful change within the task's purpose and boundaries.
Practise with: “Define the useful change” through “Compare two design questions”
Generate ideas that are novel to yourself or others
Make several genuinely different options.
Practise with: “Generate three different options” through “Break one unnecessary assumption”
Develop your ideas
Add details, compare features and prepare a usable prototype.
Practise with: “Compare features with reasons” through “Make a small usable version”
Apply your ideas
Try the prototype, observe results and improve it.
Practise with: “Plan a fair small test” through “Retest and make a limited claim”
Facilitate a creative and innovative environment for yourself and others
Make room for ideas, give useful feedback and share work by agreement.
Practise with: “Help another idea develop”, “Give and receive useful feedback”, “Facilitate a short idea session” through “Assemble your idea-development record”
Creativity and Innovation route card
Practise in four steps
Observe what a user needs to do. State one useful improvement.
Generate different options, compare them and make a small usable version.
Let a partner try it. Record what they actually do and any help they need.
Keep or revise a feature for a stated reason. Give useful feedback without taking over another person’s design.
Support route. Use plain words, movable cards, a spoken specification or a learner-directed scribe. Start with one visible need and practise two approaches before the fuller three-option attempt. A model can support learning; record when it was available and do not call the copied solution independent idea generation. Ask a willing partner or the instructor to be the user. No artistic quality, cultural motif or personal story is required.
Retry route. Change one feature in response to actual evidence, or retain an effective feature with a reason. Try the held status-change card and matching user request. Separate help to the designer from prompts to the user. A repeat with a familiar user shows that repeat under those conditions; it does not establish first-use accessibility or usefulness for everyone. If a truly new user is needed, arrange one rather than claiming a familiar partner is new.
What the instructor observes. Keep the options, prototype, trial observations and reason for the next version. A plan for later use needs a later observation.
Next-attempt agreement: user task ; design decision ; authoring support ; user/role and prior familiarity ; trial prompts ; change/keep reason ; observer/booking ; limit of conclusion .
Case document 1 · The practice-card shelf
Fictional classroom design brief. A training room has three kinds of practice kits. Learners use the kits in pairs, then return the cards to a shared shelf. The next pair sometimes finds a mixed or incomplete kit. The instructor wants a simple classroom system that helps people find the right kit, notice missing pieces and return it without needing to remember every item.
The Paving Process kit, code P, contains five stage cards, six equipment-purpose cards and one instruction card: 12 cards in total. It supports introductory learning about the sequence pit or quarry → plant → haul → place → compact. It does not contain machine-operation instructions. The Number Check kit, code N, contains one fictional data table, one worked example and two blank record sheets: four items. The Communication kit, code C, contains four message cards, two role cards and one check-back checklist: seven cards.
The room has one complete kit of each type. All kit names, counts and observations in this chapter are invented for practice. In four fictional classroom sessions, learners spent 6, 8, 4 and 7 minutes finding or sorting the materials before they could start. Those observations suggest a problem to investigate; they do not prove why it happens or show that every learner has the same difficulty.
The instructor offers plain folders, scrap paper, markers and removable labels for a prototype. A small supply budget may be proposed, but no purchase will be made in this activity. The system must work in black and white, use plain-language labels and avoid putting learners' names or personal information on the shelf. It must fit on one shelf and be easy to reset when a kit changes.
The team can change labels, organization and classroom checking steps. It cannot discard the source cards, invent new equipment facts or require every learner to read small print. A learner should be able to ask for a supported explanation. The design must help people use the materials, not shame someone when an item is missing.
Notice before proposing
Read the brief and list three things you know, three questions still open and one assumption you should avoid. Identify the evidence that suggests an opportunity for improvement. Explain why the four waiting-time observations do not, by themselves, prove that learners are careless or that a particular storage system will solve the problem.
Define the useful change
Write a design question beginning, “How could we help a learner…” Include finding, checking or returning a kit. State the intended user and one limit from the brief. Avoid putting a preferred solution into the question too early. Compare your question with a partner's and explain which wording leaves room for more than one useful approach.
Ask from another viewpoint
Review the shelf from three fictional viewpoints: a first-time learner, a learner who wants larger print and the person resetting the room. Write one question from each viewpoint. Use the brief to identify which questions can be answered now and which need a simple user check. Do not ask a classmate to disclose a disability or represent a whole group of learners.
Curiosity turns an inconvenience into a design question
When a familiar task goes wrong, it is easy to jump to a solution or blame the person nearest the problem. Curiosity creates a pause. Ask what happened, what information was available, what the task required and which part caused difficulty. A missing card might reflect unclear labels, an incomplete starting kit, mixed storage, a changed activity or an uncertain return process. The same visible result can have several explanations.
Observation should be specific. “The kits are a mess” is a broad judgement. “The Number Check folder contains a Paving Process stage card, and its worked example is missing” identifies something a person can inspect. Specific observations help you choose what to test and avoid redesigning everything at once.
An opportunity for innovation is a useful gap between the current situation and the intended result. It does not require a dramatic new invention. If people cannot tell which pieces belong together, a visible contents list may help. If the list is difficult to use, the next idea may involve larger labels, a matching layout or a supported check. Keep asking whose task becomes easier and how you will know.
Worked example 1 — frame the opportunity. A learner first writes, “Make everyone use a better folder.” That statement already chooses a solution and puts the burden on the user. After reading the brief, the learner revises it to: “How could a first-time learner find and check the Number Check kit without remembering its contents?” This question points to a user, a task and a need. It leaves room for a contents card, a matching arrangement or another useful approach.
Compare two design questions
Compare “How can we stop people losing cards?” with “How can the shelf show what belongs in each kit and make a missing piece easy to notice?” Identify an assumption in the first question and a testable feature in the second. Rewrite the first question so it focuses on a useful change without assigning blame. State one thing your revised question still does not establish.
Generate options before choosing one
Idea generation and evaluation are different parts of the work. If you reject every idea as soon as it appears, you may end with only the first familiar approach. If you never evaluate ideas, you may choose something attractive that does not meet the brief. Give each part its own time: first make several possibilities visible, then compare them against the task.
You can generate ideas through lists, sketches, spoken descriptions, a simple model or an accessible tool. The form should help you think, not become a test of drawing skill. Try changing one feature at a time: where the information appears, how pieces are grouped, how a missing item is shown or how a person asks for help. You can also combine useful features from different ideas, while crediting contributions.
“Different” means more than changing the colour of the same design. A folder with a contents list, a board with matching spaces and a small check-out card use different ways to guide the user. Each may have strengths and limits. The goal is not to produce the most ideas at any cost; it is to create enough variety to make a considered choice.
A respectful idea session allows uncertainty. Someone can say, “This is an early thought,” or “I can explain it better with a sketch.” During the first generation round, ask clarifying questions and build on possibilities. Later, give specific feedback against the agreed criteria. Respect for the person does not require accepting an inaccurate fact or an unusable design.
Generate three different options
Create three options for the practice-card shelf. Use any combination of words, sketches or a simple model. For each, explain how a learner would find a kit and notice a missing item. Make the options different in their organization or checking method, not just colour. Mark one question that would need testing before you could recommend each option.
Help another idea develop
With a partner, take turns sharing an unfinished option. The listener asks one clarifying question and offers one possible extension, such as adding a larger label or changing where a contents list appears. The author decides what to use and explains why. Record the contribution with permission. Notice whether the conversation helped the author think, rather than replacing the author's idea with the listener's.
Break one unnecessary assumption
Choose an assumption such as “every kit needs a separate colour,” “instructions must be a full page” or “the first draft has to look finished.” Explain why the brief does not require it. Generate another approach that still meets the actual requirements. Identify one important limit that you must keep, such as accurate source content, no personal data or black-and-white usability.
Case document 2 · Three possible prototypes
Visual guide Case preview: the labelled folder, matching board and shared return tray organize the same task in different ways. The questions beneath them remain to be tested. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Three original prototypes show a labelled Number Check folder, a matching board with data, example and two blank-sheet spaces, and a return tray with N and C kits and a named helper-reset action. Questions ask whether a new user can find instructions, whether cards fit and stay together, and who checks and resets the tray. These are options to test.
Fictional design notes. A group develops three ideas. Option A: labelled folders uses one folder per kit, a large code and name on the front, and a contents list inside. A small “check needed” marker can be placed on a folder when something is missing. The marker identifies the kit status, not the person who last used it.
Option B: a matching board shows an outlined space and label for each kind of item. Learners place returned items beside the corresponding labels. The board makes some gaps visible, but the group is unsure whether it will fit the shelf or whether small cards will stay together when moved.
Option C: a shared return tray has one large sign and a short return checklist. An assigned classroom helper checks the tray at the end of the activity and rebuilds the kits. This may make the learner's immediate return task simple, but it creates a recurring responsibility and a possible delay before another pair can use the materials.
The instructor gives four criteria: the system must show the correct contents; a new user must be able to follow it; it must work without colour; and it must be manageable when the kit changes. The group may add one justified criterion, such as fitting the available shelf. It should not choose a design simply because the most confident member prefers it.
The group has enough scrap materials to make one rough prototype. It is not being asked to buy supplies, publish images or change the real training room permanently. Its recommendation should explain both the useful features and the questions that remain after a small classroom test.
Develop an idea so someone else can use it
Development adds the details that turn a possibility into something testable. Decide what the user sees first, what they do next, how they check the result and what happens when something is missing. A rough prototype can be a folded paper, a labelled folder, a sketch with movable pieces or a short spoken walkthrough supported by an accessible record.
Use the real requirements of the practice brief as your criteria. A beautiful design that relies only on colour does not meet a black-and-white requirement. A complicated tracking sheet may record many details but be harder to use than the task requires. More features are not automatically better. Each feature should help the intended person complete the task or understand the information.
A comparison table can help you choose, but it cannot make the decision for you. Before testing, “easy to use” is a prediction. Label it that way. After testing, you can report what a particular user did under particular conditions. Keep uncertain information visible so a small classroom trial does not become a claim that a design works for everyone.
Worked example 2 — turn an idea into a prototype. The group selects labelled folders for a first test. It writes “N — Number Check” in large text, then lists “1 data table; 1 worked example; 2 blank record sheets; total 4 items.” It adds a “check needed” slip and a short instruction: “If an item is missing, leave this slip with the folder and tell the instructor.” The group has not proved the system works, but another person can now try a clear sequence and report what happened.
Compare features with reasons
Make a comparison table for Options A, B and C using the four given criteria and one criterion you can justify. For each option, record a likely strength, a likely limitation and a question to test. Mark predictions as predictions. Select a first prototype and explain the choice without claiming that the other options have been disproved.
Specify the prototype
Prepare the words, arrangement and checking steps for your selected option. Use the correct kit contents from Case document 1. State what the user should do when something is missing and how the kit will be updated if its contents change. Ask a partner to describe the sequence from your specification. Revise any step they have to guess.
Make a small usable version
Build a prototype with paper or an accessible tool. Include at least one complete kit representation, accurate labels and the missing-item response. You may use dummy cards rather than the original kit. Record which parts are ready to test and which are only suggested for a later version. Artistic polish, expensive supplies and cultural decoration are not required.
Test the task, not the user's worth
A test gives the user a task and observes what happens. For the Number Check prototype, you might ask, “Find this kit, check whether it is complete and show what you would do if the worked example were missing.” Avoid explaining the design while the person is trying it, unless that support is part of the intended use. If you help, record the help so the result is not reported as independent use.
Ask permission before observing or keeping feedback. Use fictional role labels rather than personal information. A user can choose not to take part. The purpose is to learn about the design, not to rank classmates by speed or make someone feel responsible for a confusing instruction. If a person pauses or misinterprets a label, ask what information they were looking for.
Separate observation from interpretation. “The user opened two folders before finding N” is an observation. “The user is careless” is an unsupported judgement. “The code may need to appear on the shelf edge as well as the folder” is a possible design explanation to test. Keeping these separate helps the next revision address the actual difficulty.
Plan a fair small test
Write a task for a willing partner using your prototype. Include what you will observe, what support is available and how you will record feedback without personal data. Add one question that asks about the design rather than the person's ability. Explain why a successful test with one person would still leave limits on your conclusion.
Give and receive useful feedback
Exchange prototypes with another learner or pair. Give one specific observation, one question and one suggestion tied to the brief. The author restates the feedback, decides what to use and explains the decision. If testing is not available, rehearse with the instructor and label the result as a supported walkthrough. Do not present a rehearsal as an independent user test.
Case document 3 · Results and a changed requirement
Visual guide Worked-example preview: the second worked example changes the Number Check kit from four items to five. D = data table; E = worked example; unlettered pages = blank record sheets. Update the version and visible instructions, then retest. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Two Number Check folders show an inspectable revision. Version 1 has four items: one data card, one worked example and two blank sheets. Version 2 has five: one data card, two worked examples and two blanks. A further check must make the slip instruction visible and retest; used sheets stay with the learner and two blank sheets are restocked.
Fictional test record. A first-time user finds the Number Check folder after reading its large name and code. They count the data table, worked example and two blank sheets correctly. When the worked example is removed for the next trial, they notice that there are only three items but do not know where to put the “check needed” slip. The slip's instruction is printed on its reverse side, which the user has not seen.
A second user says the contents list is easy to find but asks whether used record sheets are returned or replaced. The original brief does not answer that question. The instructor clarifies the classroom rule for this fictional case: used record sheets stay with the learner's practice work; the kit is restocked with two blank sheets before reuse. No learner names are written on the folder.
The instructor then changes the kit. The Number Check kit will contain a second worked example, so its new contents are one data table, two worked examples and two blank sheets: five items. The system must show which version is current and prevent an old four-item list from being treated as the new requirement. The group has time for one revision and another small test.
The first prototype has useful features worth keeping. The large name and code helped the first user find the kit. The clear inventory supported counting. The revision should address the slip location, the restocking instruction and the changed contents without making the front of the folder crowded or blaming the users for the original gaps.
Worked example 3 — revise from evidence. The author moves the missing-item instruction to the visible face of the slip, adds a marked pocket for it and writes “Version 2 — five items” beside the new contents list. The author adds, “Keep your used record sheets; ask for two blank sheets before returning the kit ready for reuse.” A second user tries the changed kit and explains the return steps. The record states what that user could do and what support was given. It does not claim the design has solved every future storage problem.
Separate findings from guesses
Make three columns for Case document 3: observed result, possible explanation and next check. Include the hidden instruction, the used-sheet question and the changed item count. Identify a useful feature to retain. Explain why the second user's question reveals missing information in the design rather than proving that the user failed to read carefully.
Revise for the changed kit
Update your prototype or the labelled-folder example for the five-item Number Check kit. Make the version change clear, include the clarified restocking rule and improve the missing-item response. Keep an earlier version or a description of it. Explain how each revision answers evidence from the test or a changed requirement, rather than adding an unrelated feature.
Retest and make a limited claim
Ask a willing user to try the revised version, or use an instructor-supported walkthrough if needed. Record whether the user can find the kit, identify its five required items and explain the missing-item and used-sheet steps. State the conditions and support. Write a conclusion that describes the result accurately and names one question that would need further testing before broader use.
Help ideas grow without taking them over
A creative environment is built through ordinary choices. People need access to the task, materials and time to think. They need to know whether a suggestion is an early possibility or a final decision. They need feedback that can be used and an opportunity to revise. Credit matters too: ask before displaying a person's work or combining it into another product, and name contributions in the way the person agrees.
You can support another learner's idea without treating it as yours to finish. Ask what they are trying to achieve, what is uncertain and what kind of feedback would help. Offer options rather than instructions when the task allows choice. If the idea contains an inaccurate source fact, address that fact clearly while leaving room for a different design solution.
Reflection can also recognize a useful failure. A prototype may reveal that the problem was framed too narrowly or that an important user task was missing. That finding can improve the next attempt. The learning evidence is not simply the number of ideas or whether the finished object looks attractive. It includes how you investigated, developed, applied and improved the idea, and how you made that process possible for others.
Facilitate a short idea session
Lead a small idea session about another classroom improvement, such as making a practice schedule easier to read. State the purpose and limits, offer more than one contribution mode and separate idea generation from evaluation. Invite participants to decide how their contributions may be recorded. Afterwards, ask what helped them think and choose one facilitation improvement.
Transfer the process with boundaries
Choose a fictional office, training or community-room task that could benefit from a clearer form, label or information aid. Describe the user, opportunity, two possible ideas and a small test. Identify who would need to approve a real change and what information or knowledge should not be copied without permission. Do not propose altering live equipment procedures as a classroom creativity exercise.
Assemble your idea-development record
Keep your design question, three options, comparison, prototype, test notes and revision. Use them to identify evidence for all six components. Name one idea contribution from another person and how you used or declined it respectfully. Choose a next practice goal. If a component has not been observed, name the task that could provide evidence instead of claiming the whole skill from the finished object alone.
Supported route and extension
For supported practice, use one kit, a partly completed contents list and an instructor model of a test question. Generate two options first, then add a third by changing one feature. For an extension, test with a different task or revise after a new content requirement. A digital prototype can develop Digital as well, but paper work is a valid route for the creativity outcomes in this chapter.
Use the local evidence descriptions Not observed, Not yet demonstrated, Demonstrated with support, and Demonstrated independently for the stated task. These are not official proficiency levels. A plan to use the design process elsewhere is a transfer intention; a later documented task provides stronger evidence of actual transfer.
Creativity and innovation practice C · Design a clear choose-and-check display
These four original cases give you another opportunity to use a skill after the chapter practice. All people, rooms, events and organizations in these cards are fictional. You can use these cases without sharing personal, family, community or cultural knowledge. They are classroom tasks, not instructions for operating equipment or following an actual workplace procedure.
Your instructor will give you the relevant card when your turn begins. Keep a sender's information separate from the receiver's card until after the exchange. If you have already read the information, say so: the activity remains useful practice, but that attempt cannot show how you receive an unfamiliar message. No one needs to conceal prior practice.
Agree your language, communication mode, tools, access supports and response time before beginning. Speech, sign, text, AAC, a learner-directed scribe and agreed interpretation can be appropriate. The person observing needs a reliable way to understand the meaning of your contribution. Receiving a message in writing shows reception through that mode; it does not automatically show auditory listening. You may decline audio/video recording and use live observation. Ask for a pause or another opportunity if the conditions are not usable. There is no requirement to look cheerful, make eye contact or disclose why you need an arrangement.
Purpose: develop and test a small information design. Artistic polish is not the goal. The design should help someone make a correct choice from the supplied fictional facts.
“Creativity and innovation practice C · Design a clear choose-and-check display” design brief and source cards
A practice shelf has three classroom packs. Users need to check what is ready before choosing. Make a tabletop paper prototype; a screen version is optional if available. Use only these facts:
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Pack Current status What a user may do
MAP Ready Select it for the classroom activity.
WORD Being checked Leave it in place; ask the instructor when it will be ready.
NUMBER Ready Select it for the classroom activity.
The prototype must name all three packs, make each status and next action understandable, and identify itself as classroom practice. It must work without colour as the only status signal. It must not collect names, photographs, cultural knowledge or personal reasons for choosing a pack. Available materials are plain paper, six blank cards, a marker or pencil and removable tape. A learner-directed scribe may prepare the marks you specify. Use descriptive words or simple original shapes; no cultural imagery is required.
Before choosing a design, ask a useful question about the user's task and record at least three different possible approaches. Differences must change how information is found or used, not just the colour. Select one approach with a reason tied to the brief. Make a usable small prototype. Keep a sketch or note of the other options; a finished attractive product alone does not show idea generation.
“Creativity and innovation practice C · Design a clear choose-and-check display” user card · Give to a willing test partner
You want the WORD pack first. If it is not ready, you would use the MAP pack today and ask the instructor about WORD. Using the prototype, identify your first-choice pack's status, say what you will do next and locate the pack you can use today. Explain one point that helped or confused you. Do not pretend to misunderstand a clear display, and do not praise it just to be polite. You can decline or stop the user role; the instructor can take the role or arrange another partner.
“Creativity and innovation practice C · Design a clear choose-and-check display” test and revision
Tell the user the task and agree how they will give feedback. During the first trial, observe rather than coaching the answer. If the user asks for help, you may provide it, but record the actual prompt and treat the trial as supported at that point. A person's support need is not a fault in them. Note whether the display itself made the required information available in the agreed mode.
Ask permission before marking or changing someone else's contribution. Identify a useful change from the trial, make it, and repeat the task. If no change is needed, retain the prototype and explain the evidence from the check. A repeat with the same user is a familiar-task retest; it is not an independent first-use trial with a new person. State what this trial supports and what it cannot establish.
When you take the user role for a partner's design, offer one concrete observation and leave the design decision with its author. Each learner needs a design turn and an opportunity to give feedback. A peer's successful use of your display does not prove you developed it without support.
“Creativity and innovation practice C · Design a clear choose-and-check display” later change card · Hold for a later design attempt
The fictional status changes: WORD is now Ready; MAP is now Being checked; NUMBER remains Ready. The next user's first choice is MAP, with NUMBER as their acceptable alternative. The action for a pack being checked remains “leave it in place and ask the instructor.” Update the prototype, verify all three statuses, and test with this task. If the same person already knows the earlier display, record that familiarity. This is a bounded application in a changed classroom task, not evidence of effectiveness across workplaces or communities.

lessons.title: Picturing yourself in a trade
lessons.text:
Use your imagination and the views of others to try on work you may not have pictured before you choose a trade.
Why this matters on the job
Picking a trade is a big decision. Many people pick the first trade they hear about, or the one a relative works in. If you picture yourself in a few different settings first (a framing crew, a fabrication shop, a pulp mill maintenance crew, a mechanical contractor on a hospital job), you can test how each one fits you before you spend months training for it. Other people often notice strengths you do not see in yourself.
Key ideas
Imagination means picturing "what if." What if I worked outdoors on a high-rise? What if I worked in a quiet shop on one machine?
Curiosity means asking questions about what you pictured. What does a day look like? Do they work alone or on a crew? What tools do they use?
Trying an idea on. You do not have to decide today. You picture an idea, notice how it feels, and keep it open while you learn more. The Skills for Success model calls this being "open to new ideas without judging and setting limitations."
Useful feedback is positive and specific. It says what the person sees and why.
Helpful: "I can picture you as a millwright, because you always want to know how the machine works inside."
Not helpful: "I can't see you doing anything with heights."
You choose what to share. You do not have to talk about your family, your community or your past to take part. You can pass on any turn.
Worked example
Dale is a learner in a fictional trades prep class. He sits in the career chair and says, "I like building things, being outside and working with my hands." The group sits quietly for two minutes and pictures Dale at work.
The scribe writes down what the group says:
"I see you on a framing crew, standing walls with three other people."
"I see you in a fab shop, because you are careful with measurements."
"I see you at a mill, fixing a conveyor. You like figuring out why things break."
Dale had never thought about mill work. He says the conveyor idea surprised him. He keeps the scribe's notes and writes three questions to find out more: What does an industrial mechanic (millwright) do in a day? Is it shift work? Where in BC are the mills?
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Write three work settings you are curious about. For each one, write one thing you picture yourself doing there.
Setting: ___ I picture myself: ___
Setting: ___ I picture myself: ___
Setting: ___ I picture myself: ___
Task 2 (level 1) Take a turn in the career chair if you want to. Tell the group two or three kinds of work you are interested in. Then listen while the group says how they picture you. Do not answer until everyone has spoken. A scribe writes the ideas down for you.
Task 3 (level 1) When someone else is in the career chair, picture them at work. Give one positive, specific comment that starts with "I can picture you … because …".
Task 4 (level 1) When you are the scribe, write each idea in the speaker's own words, then hand the notes to the person in the chair.
Task 5 (level 2) Choose one idea from your scribe notes or your Task 1 list if you did not take a turn in the career chair. The idea may be new to you or one you already know but want to investigate further. Write three questions you would need answered to know if it fits you. Name one place to look for answers, such as a WorkBC career profile (https://www.workbc.ca/plan-career/explore-careers/career-profiles), a SkilledTradesBC trade profile (https://skilledtradesbc.ca/find-your-trade) or a person who works in that trade.
Idea: __________
Where I will look: __________
Check yourself
What is the difference between imagination and curiosity?
Rewrite this comment so it is positive and specific: "You'd hate working in a shop."
Why does the person in the career chair wait until everyone has spoken before answering?
Name one way to check whether a trade you pictured really fits you.

lessons.title: Spotting a better way on the job site
lessons.text:
Look hard at a routine job-site task, question the habits behind it and find where a change could help.
Why this matters on the job
Every crew has routines: where the gang box sits, who gets the fasteners, how material is staged. Some routines are there for a good reason, like site security or safety. Others are just habits nobody has checked in years. A worker who can spot wasted walking, waiting or repeating, and say so clearly, saves the crew time and money. Supervisors notice the people who see a better way.
Key ideas
A norm or habit is "the way we always do it." It is not wrong. It just has not been questioned.
Waste you can see on a site usually looks like one of three things:
walking: trips back and forth for tools, fasteners or drawings
waiting: standing by for a lift, a key, a decision or another trade
repeating: measuring or setting up the same thing over and over
Real limits and possibly artificial limits. A real limit must be kept: a safety rule, a code requirement, a site rule from the prime contractor, the client's drawings. A possibly artificial limit is a rule nobody has checked. It might be there for a reason you do not know yet, so you ask before you change it.
Never treat a safety rule as artificial. If you think a safety rule makes a job slower, bring it to your supervisor. On a larger BC workplace you can also bring it to the joint health and safety committee or the worker health and safety representative. Do not work around it.
An opportunity statement names the problem and who it affects, without giving the answer yet. Start it with "How might we …". For example: "How might we cut the number of trips framers make for fasteners?" This leaves room for many ideas. "How might we buy a rolling gang box?" already picks one answer.
Worked example
Ridgeline Framing Ltd. (a fictional company) is framing townhouses on a Fraser Valley site. The gang box with fasteners and small tools lives in a locked sea-can at the far end of the site. Each of the 4 framers walks to it about 6 times a day. A round trip takes about 4 minutes.
Time spent walking for one day, using BEDMAS (no brackets or exponents here, so multiply left to right):
4 × 6 × 4 = 96 minutes a day
For a 5-day week: 96 × 5 = 480 minutes, which is 480 ÷ 60 = 8 hours. That is a full day of one person's work, every week, spent walking.
Sorting the limits:
Limit Real or possibly artificial? Why
Tools must be locked up at the end of the day Real Site security rule from the prime contractor
The gang box stays in the sea-can all day Possibly artificial Nobody remembers why. Ask the foreman
Only the lead hand hands out fasteners Possibly artificial Started years ago on a different job
Opportunity statement: "How might we get fasteners and small tools closer to the framers during the day, and still lock everything up at night?"
If a rolling gang box near the work cut trips to 2 per framer, the time saved each day would be, brackets first:
(6 − 2) × 4 × 4 = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 minutes a day
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Process walk. Pick a routine you do often in the shop or classroom, such as getting set up for a practical task (sign out tools, put on PPE, get material, set up the bench). List every step in order. Beside each step, mark W for walking, D for waiting or R for repeating, or leave it blank.
Step What I do W, D or R
1
2
3
4
5
6
Task 2 (level 1) Read the Ridgeline Framing example again. List two habits on that site that could be questioned.
Task 3 (level 2) Here are limits on a fictional pipe-trades job. Coldwater Mechanical is running copper on the fourth floor of a new clinic. Mark each one Real or Possibly artificial, and say who you would ask about the ones you are not sure of.
Limit Real or possibly artificial? Who to ask
The gang box stays on the ground floor
Hot work needs a permit from the prime contractor
Fittings are ordered one day at a time
Only the foreman can carry the drawings
Workers wear fall protection near the open slab edge
Task 4 (level 2) On the Coldwater job, 3 pipefitters each make 5 trips a day to the gang box on the ground floor. A round trip takes 6 minutes. Show your work using BEDMAS.
a) How many minutes a day does the crew spend on these trips? __
b) How many hours is that in a 5-day week? __
c) If a box on the fourth floor cut trips to 2 per person, how many minutes a day would the crew save? __
Task 5 (level 2) Write an opportunity statement for the Coldwater job, or for the routine you mapped in Task 1. Start with "How might we …". Do not put a solution in it. Include one real limit that must be kept.
Check yourself
What are the three kinds of waste you can see on a site?
Give one example of a limit that is real and one that might be artificial.
Why should you never treat a safety rule as an artificial limit?
A crew of 2 makes 8 trips each a day. Each trip takes 5 minutes. A change cuts trips to 3 each. How many minutes a day are saved? Use BEDMAS.
What is wrong with this opportunity statement: "How might we buy a second sea-can?"

lessons.title: Many ideas before you choose
lessons.text:
Come up with a wide range of ideas for a repeated shop task, without judging them, then pick one for a reason.
Why this matters on the job
Shops and sites are full of repeated tasks: marking the same hole on 40 plates, cutting 60 pieces of blocking, bending 30 identical brackets. Measuring each one from scratch is slow, and every measurement is a new chance for a mistake. Tradespeople solve this with jigs, templates, stops and story sticks. The first idea that comes to mind is often not the best one. Crews that list many ideas first, then choose, end up with better fixes.
Key ideas
Two phases. Keep them apart.
Generate: get as many ideas out as you can. Do not judge any of them yet. Silly ideas are welcome, because they often lead to good ones.
Choose: now judge. Compare the ideas against what the job needs and pick one to try.
If you judge while you generate, people stop offering ideas and you end up with the first, most familiar one.
Prompts that help you think differently. These come from the Skills for Success description of creativity and innovation:
Do it differently: what if we changed the usual process, the tool, or who does the task?
Ask a question with no obvious answer: why do we mark these at all?
Combine: put two unrelated things together (a bench stop and a template).
Reverse: flip the idea around to see if the opposite works. Instead of moving the tape to each plate, what if the plate moved into a fixed spot?
Expand: take an idea and add to it.
Building on each other's ideas. In a group, say "Yes, and …" to add to someone's idea instead of "No, but …". Write every idea down with the initials of the person who gave it, so credit stays with them.
A jig or template is anything you make once so a repeated task comes out the same every time.
Worked example
North Arm Fabrication (a fictional shop) must mark two hole centres on 40 steel plates. Each plate is 100 mm wide and 150 mm long. Each hole is on the centreline of the width, 25 mm in from each short end. Right now a worker measures every plate with a tape and square. It takes about 2 minutes a plate, and a few marks have been off.
Where the holes are:
across the width: 100 ÷ 2 = 50 mm from either long edge
between the two hole centres: 150 − 25 − 25 = 100 mm
Ideas from a 10-minute generate round, with no judging:
Sheet metal template the size of the plate, with two holes. Lay it on and mark through the holes.
Cardboard template. Quick to make, wears out.
Mark one plate very carefully and use it as a master on top of the others.
Two strips on the bench at a right angle, so every plate sits in the same corner.
Combine 1 and 4: a template hinged to the corner stop that flips down onto each plate.
Reverse: set the measurement once. Lock a combination square at 25 mm instead of reading a tape 80 times.
Story stick with notches at 25 mm and 125 mm.
Do it differently: ask the supplier to send the plates already marked.
Ask a question: can the holes be located by a set-up on the machine instead of by marks? (A question for the shop lead.)
Expand 4: add a stop on the third side so the plate cannot slide.
Then the crew chose, using criteria:
Idea Same every time (1 to 3) Fast (1 to 3) Uses shop scrap (1 to 3) Total
1. Steel template 3 2 3 8
5. Hinged template on corner stop 3 3 2 8
6. Locked combination square 2 2 3 7
Two ideas tied. The crew picked idea 5 to try first, because it locates the plate and marks it in one move. They wrote down what they did not know yet: whether the hinge would wear and let the template move.
Time check: if the new method takes about 0.5 minutes a plate, the time for 40 plates goes from 40 × 2 = 80 minutes to 40 × 0.5 = 20 minutes. That saves 80 − 20 = 60 minutes.
Safety. In this lesson you only sketch and talk. Nothing gets cut, drilled or punched. Any jig you want to build later is checked by your instructor first and built under your shop's safety rules.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Warm-up. In 2 minutes, list as many uses as you can for a C-clamp. Any use counts.
Task 2 (level 2) On your own, generate at least 8 ideas for marking the North Arm plates faster and the same every time. Use words, sketches or both. Do not judge or cross anything out. You may use one idea from the worked example, but the rest must be your own.
Task 3 (level 2) In a group of 3 or 4, run an idea round. One person is the facilitator. The facilitator:
reads out the opportunity: "How might we mark 40 plates the same every time, faster?"
reminds the group of the rules: all ideas count, no judging yet, build with "Yes, and …"
writes every idea with the initials of the person who gave it
makes sure everyone gets a turn
Aim for at least 15 ideas as a group.
Task 4 (level 2) Use two prompts you have not used yet (do it differently, ask a question, combine, reverse, expand). Add one new idea for each prompt and name the prompt you used.
Prompt: __ Idea: ________
Prompt: __ Idea: ________
Task 5 (level 2) Now choose. Pick your group's top 3 ideas. Score each from 1 to 3 against at least three criteria, such as same every time, fast, uses shop scrap, safe, easy to check. Pick one to try first and write one thing you do not know yet about it.
Idea Total
Idea we picked: ___ Why: ___
What we do not know yet: __________
Task 6 (level 2) A new order comes in. The plates are 120 mm wide and 200 mm long. Each hole is on the centreline of the width, 30 mm in from each short end.
a) How far is each hole from a long edge? __
b) How far apart are the hole centres? __
c) Measuring each plate takes 2.5 minutes. A template takes 0.5 minutes. How many minutes does the template save on 40 plates? Use BEDMAS. __
Task 7 (level 3) Northline Electric (a fictional company) must mount 48 receptacle boxes in a new daycare. The drawings call for the bottom of every box to be 450 mm above the finished floor, and the floor is not finished yet. Measuring each box from the subfloor with a tape is slow, and two boxes on the last job were set at the wrong height.
a) Generate at least 6 ideas for setting every box at the same height, faster. Use at least two of the five prompts.
b) Score your top 3 ideas from 1 to 3 against three criteria you choose. Pick one to try first.
c) Write one thing you do not know yet that could change your choice. Who would you ask?
Check yourself
Why do you keep generating ideas separate from choosing ideas?
Name two of the five prompts and give a one-line example of each.
What does the facilitator do in an idea round?
A plate is 180 mm long. Its holes are 20 mm in from each short end. How far apart are the hole centres?

lessons.title: Combining two ideas into something new
lessons.text:
Plan a week of work camp meals that blends two food traditions and still follows Canada's food guide.
Why this matters on the job
Many new ideas in the trades are two old ideas put together: a tape measure with a magnet on the hook, a ladder with a tool tray. Putting two unrelated things together is one of the main ways people come up with something new. This lesson practises it with food. At a remote work camp, the kitchen feeds the same crew for weeks at a time. A good camp menu is healthy, works around allergies, and keeps a tired crew from getting bored. A fusion menu, which blends two food traditions, is one way to do that.
Key ideas
Combining. Take two things that do not usually go together and look for a new mix. Write many combinations first, then judge them.
Canada's food guide plate. Health Canada's food guide uses a plate to show healthy proportions for a meal:
half the plate vegetables and fruits
one-quarter of the plate whole grain foods
one-quarter of the plate protein foods, choosing protein foods that come from plants more often
The food guide also says to make water your drink of choice, to choose foods with little to no added sodium, sugars or saturated fat, and that culture and food traditions can be a part of healthy eating.
Priority food allergens. Health Canada lists these as the priority food allergens: eggs, milk, mustard, peanuts, crustaceans and molluscs, fish, sesame seeds, soy, sulphites, tree nuts, and wheat and triticale. A camp menu should mark which dishes contain them and offer a swap.
Your traditions, your choice. You may use food from your own family or community, food a friend has shared with you, or a style of cooking you like. You do not have to share anything personal. If you use a dish from someone else's tradition, say where it comes from, for example "my co-worker's family recipe for dal."
Worked example
Silverline Camp Services (a fictional company) runs the kitchen at a road-building camp in northern BC. The crew of 30 says the menu is getting boring. Two crew members have allergies: one to peanuts, one to sesame.
Rosa, a camp cook, grew up with her family's Mexican cooking. Her co-worker Harpreet shared his mother's recipe for dal. Rosa lists foods from each:
Rosa's family cooking Harpreet's family dal
tacos, salsa, black beans, corn tortillas, cabbage slaw red lentils, cumin, onion, tomato, spinach
She writes six combinations without judging, then picks lentil dal tacos: spiced red lentil dal with spinach in whole grain corn tortillas, with cabbage slaw, salsa and a side of fruit.
Plate check:
vegetables and fruits (half): slaw, salsa, spinach, fruit
whole grains (one-quarter): whole grain corn tortillas
protein (one-quarter): red lentils, a protein from plants
drink: water on the table
Allergen check: no peanuts or sesame. If she adds a yogurt sauce, it contains milk, so she labels it and serves it on the side.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Choose two food traditions you know: your own, a friend's, or a style you like. List at least five foods or ingredients from each.
Tradition A: __ Tradition B: __
Task 2 (level 2) Pair foods from list A with foods from list B to make at least six fusion dish ideas. Write them all down. Do not judge yet.
Task 3 (level 2) Pick two of your dishes. Check each against the food guide plate. If a dish does not fill half the plate with vegetables and fruits, add a side that does.
Dish Vegetables and fruits (half) Whole grains (one-quarter) Protein (one-quarter) Drink
Task 4 (level 2) For the same two dishes, list any priority food allergens they contain. Remember the Silverline crew has one person with a peanut allergy and one with a sesame allergy. Write one swap or label that keeps the dish safe for them.
Task 5 (level 2) Fill in a Monday to Friday camp menu. Use at least five of your own fusion dishes across the week. Mark each dish that contains a priority allergen with the allergen's name.
Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday
Breakfast
Lunch
Dinner
Task 6 (level 2) Present your menu to the group in 2 minutes. Say:
which two traditions you combined and where they come from
how one dinner follows the food guide plate
how the menu works for the crew: allergies, long shifts, variety
When others present, listen and offer one idea that could make their menu better.
Check yourself
What fraction of the plate does Canada's food guide say should be vegetables and fruits?
Name four of Health Canada's priority food allergens.
Give one example, from a trade or from food, of making something new by combining two things.
What does the food guide say should be your drink of choice?

lessons.title: Building a quick model and explaining it
lessons.text:
Turn an idea into a quick model with building bricks, then give spoken directions clear enough for someone else to build it.
Why this matters on the job
An idea is not much use on a crew until someone else can build it. A lead hand explains a layout. A millwright explains how a guard goes back on. You explain the jig you thought up. A quick, rough model shows the idea faster than words, and trying to explain the model shows you which details you have not worked out yet. Models made from cheap materials let you find problems before you spend real time and material.
Key ideas
A quick model (prototype) is a rough version of an idea, made fast from cheap materials such as building bricks, cardboard or scrap. It does not need to look good. It needs to show how the idea works.
Developing an idea means adding the details other people need to build it:
what: which piece, by size, shape and colour ("the red brick with 2 rows of 4 bumps")
how many: a count, not "some"
where: position from a fixed point ("on the left end, from where you are sitting")
which way: flat or on edge, long side toward you or away
in what order: one step at a time, with words like first, next, then, last
Whose left? When two people sit back to back, your left is their left. When they face each other, your left is their right. Say "from where you are sitting."
Expect it to go wrong the first time. The first set of directions almost always misses something. That is the point of the test. You fix the directions and try again.
Worked example
Tess builds a small model of a tool caddy from 10 bricks. Her partner sits back to back with her and has the same 10 bricks.
First try, no questions allowed: "Put the long red one on top." Her partner puts it on top, but across the caddy instead of along it, and on the wrong end.
What was missing: which way the brick faces, and where on the top it goes.
Second try: "Take the red brick with 2 rows of 8 bumps. Lay it flat with the long side toward you. Put it across the top of the two grey walls so it lines up with the left end, from where you are sitting." This time it matches.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) With your bag of 10 to 12 bricks, build a quick model of something useful on a job site, such as a tool caddy, a sawhorse, a pipe rack or a material cart. Use every brick. Do not show your partner.
Task 2 (level 1) Round 1. Sit back to back with your partner. Give spoken directions so your partner can build a copy of your model. Your partner may not ask questions or look. When you finish, turn around and compare the two models.
Task 3 (level 2) List what went wrong in Round 1. For each problem, write which kind of detail was missing: what, how many, where, which way or in what order.
What went wrong Missing detail
Task 4 (level 2) Round 2. Take your partner's model apart. Give your directions again with the missing details added. This time your partner may ask questions. Compare. Then switch roles and do both rounds with your partner's model.
How close was Round 1? __ How close was Round 2? __
Task 5 (level 2) Write the build steps for your model as a numbered list of 5 to 8 steps. Use order words and the five kinds of detail. Someone who was not in the room should be able to build it from your steps.
Check yourself
What is a quick model, and why make it from cheap materials?
Name the five kinds of detail that help someone build from your directions.
Two people face each other across a bench. You say "on the left." Whose left will your partner probably use?
Why do the first directions usually go wrong, and what do you do about it?

lessons.title: Testing an idea and learning from what fails
lessons.text:
Build a cardboard bracket, load-test it, and use each failure to make the next version better.
Why this matters on the job
On the job, ideas get tested every day: a temporary support, a new way to rig a load, a different layout for a pipe rack. Many first tries do not work. Good tradespeople expect that, find out exactly how and why the idea failed, change one thing, and try again. Learning from a cheap failure on the bench is far better than learning from an expensive one on site.
Key ideas
Expect failures. The Skills for Success description of creativity and innovation says to "expect failures" and "learn from failures to improve." A failed test is information, not a bad mark.
Predict, test, record. Before a test, write what you think will happen. During the test, watch closely. After it, write down what actually happened, in plain words.
Observation and guess are different. "The arm folded at the table edge at 9 washers" is an observation. "The cardboard was too weak" is a guess about why. Write the observation first, then your guess, then how you would check the guess.
Change one thing at a time. If you change three things between versions and the bracket holds more, you do not know which change helped. This is called a fair test.
Reverse the idea. If pushing up from underneath does not work, what if something pulls from above?
Averages. Test each version more than once and take the average. Using BEDMAS, add first because of the brackets, then divide:
average = (trial 1 + trial 2 + trial 3) ÷ 3
Percent improvement = (new − old) ÷ old × 100
The test
Your team builds a bracket from one piece of corrugated cardboard (about 30 cm by 40 cm) and 1 m of masking tape. Tape the base of the bracket to the top of the table. The arm must reach 15 cm past the table edge. Hang a paper cup from the end of the arm. Add washers 2 at a time until the bracket fails. The goal is to hold 20 washers for 10 seconds.
Safety
If you cut cardboard with a utility knife, follow these steps from the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety:
cut on a stable surface, such as a cutting mat
wear safety glasses, which protect your eyes if the blade breaks
cut away from your body, and keep your other hand and your body out of the path the blade could take if it slips
do not use too much pressure when cutting
retract the blade fully right after each cut
do not try to catch a falling knife. Step back and let it fall
put dull or broken blades in a puncture-resistant container
Scissors are a good choice for most cuts. Close them when you put them down.
During the load test, keep the load small and keep your feet and hands out from under the cup. Put a box on the floor under the cup to catch the washers.
Worked example
Marcus's team builds version 1: a flat strip of cardboard taped to the table, sticking out 15 cm. They predict 20 washers. Three trials: 8, 10 and 9 washers. Each time, the arm folds down at the table edge.
Average for version 1: (8 + 10 + 9) ÷ 3 = 27 ÷ 3 = 9 washers.
Observation: the arm bends at the table edge. Guess: a flat strip bends easily. Check: make the arm stiffer and see if the bend moves or stops.
Version 2, one change: they fold the arm into a triangle-shaped tube. Trials: 14, 16 and 15.
Average for version 2: (14 + 16 + 15) ÷ 3 = 45 ÷ 3 = 15 washers.
Percent improvement: (15 − 9) ÷ 9 × 100 = 6 ÷ 9 × 100 ≈ 66.7%
Version 2 still fails, now because the tape peels off the table. For version 3 they reverse the idea: instead of a brace pushing up from below, they run a strip of cardboard from the end of the arm back to a taped spot on the table, so it pulls from above.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Sketch your version 1 bracket. Write how many washers you predict it will hold.
Prediction: __ washers
Task 2 (level 2) Build version 1 within the material limits. Follow the safety steps.
Task 3 (level 2) Test version 1 three times. Rebuild or repair between trials if needed. Record the results.
Version Change made Trial 1 Trial 2 Trial 3 Average How it failed
1 none
2
3
Task 4 (level 2) For version 1, write one observation, one guess about why it happened, and one way to check your guess.
Observation: __________
Guess: __________
How to check: __________
Task 5 (level 2) Change one thing only. Build version 2 and test it three times. Record it in the table. If you have time, build version 3. Try the reverse prompt for at least one version.
Task 6 (level 3) Another team tested two versions.
Version 1: 6, 7 and 8 washers
Version 2: 12, 13 and 14 washers
a) Find the average for each version. Show your work using BEDMAS.
b) Find the percent improvement from version 1 to version 2. Round to one decimal place.
c) Now do the same for your own team's best two versions.
Task 7 (level 2) Write a short test report of 4 to 6 sentences. Say what failed and how, what you changed and why, what you learned, and what you would change next. Then share one tip from your test with another team.
Task 8 (level 3) A pipefitting crew at Coldwater Mechanical (a fictional company) bench-tests two designs for a temporary pipe support on a test rig. Each design is loaded until it slips.
Design A: 180, 175 and 185 kg
Design B, with one change (a second U-bolt): 260, 250 and 270 kg
a) Find the average for each design. Show your work using BEDMAS.
b) Find the percent improvement from A to B. Round to one decimal place.
c) Was this a fair test? What one thing would you check?
d) Why can a bench test like this not decide what goes into a real building?
Check yourself
Why should you change only one thing between versions?
Which of these is an observation and which is a guess? "The tape let go at 14 washers." "The tape was the wrong kind."
Three trials held 10, 11 and 15 washers. What is the average?
Name three safety steps for cutting cardboard with a utility knife.
Why is a failed test still useful?

lessons.title: Pitching an improvement to a supervisor
lessons.text:
Present a tested idea to a supervisor in two minutes, answer their questions, and take their ideas on board.
Why this matters on the job
A good idea that stays in your head does not change anything. On a crew, ideas go through the foreman, the lead hand or the superintendent. They are busy, and they have to think about cost, safety, schedule and the client. A short, clear pitch with numbers and a small test is much more likely to get a yes than "we should do it differently." Being open to the supervisor's questions, and to their ideas, often makes your idea better.
Key ideas
Pick the right moment. Ask for two minutes at a break or at the end of the day, not in the middle of a concrete pour.
A two-minute pitch has six parts:
Problem: what you saw, with a number ("Each of us walks to the sea-can about 6 times a day.")
Idea: what you want to try, in one or two sentences
Test: what you already tried and what happened, including what did not work
Cost and time: what it would take, and what it would save
Safety: how it keeps or improves safety, and how it follows the site rules
Ask: a small, clear request ("Can we try it for one week on Building C?")
Listen to the answer. The supervisor's questions are not an attack. They are checking things you may not have thought of. Answer what you can. If you do not know, say "I don't know yet. I'll find out."
Be open to their ideas. The Skills for Success model describes being "open to new ideas without judging." If the supervisor suggests a change, try it on before you defend your version.
"No" or "not yet" is not the end. Ask, "What would you need to see to try it?" Then go and get that.
Give credit. If others helped with the idea or the test, name them.
Safety ideas have a second path. If your idea is about safety, you can also bring it to the joint health and safety committee or, on a smaller site, the worker health and safety representative. In BC, a workplace with 20 or more workers needs a joint committee. One with 10 to 19 workers needs a worker representative. Part of their job is to deal with workers' health and safety concerns and make recommendations.
Worked example
Jordan is a first-year apprentice at Ridgeline Framing Ltd. (a fictional company). At the end of the day he asks his foreman, Dana, for two minutes.
"Our crew walks to the sea-can for fasteners about 6 times each a day. I timed it at about 4 minutes a round trip, which is about 96 minutes a day for the four of us. I'd like to try a rolling gang box on the deck near where we're working. Yesterday Priya and I moved the small parts bin to the deck for the afternoon, and we only made 2 trips each. A rolling box from the yard would cost nothing, and we'd save about an hour a day. It stays out of the walkways, and I'd roll it back and lock it in the sea-can at the end of every day, so the site lock-up rule is still met. Could we try it for one week on Building C?"
The afternoon trial is a first sign, not proof of a full-day saving. Jordan should compare the same length of time and similar work before and after the change, including time to move and lock up the box. His one-week request lets the crew check the estimate.
Dana asks: "Who's responsible if it gets left out overnight?" Jordan: "Me. I'll do the last trip at 3:30." Dana adds: "Put it on the second floor, not the first. That's where we'll be all week." Jordan says, "Good idea. That cuts more trips," and thanks Priya for helping with the test.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Pick an idea to pitch. Use one from an earlier lesson (the trips in lesson 2, the marking jig in lesson 3, your bracket in lesson 6) or one of your own from a job you know. Fill in the pitch planner.
Part What I will say
Problem (with a number)
Idea
Test (what I tried, what happened)
Cost and time
Safety
Ask
Task 2 (level 2) Work out the saving for your pitch. Show your work using BEDMAS. If your idea saves time, give it in minutes a day and hours a week. If it saves material or money, show that instead.
Task 3 (level 2) Role play. Give your pitch to a partner in 2 minutes or less. Your partner plays the supervisor, using one of the supervisor cards below.
Task 4 (level 2) When you play the supervisor, read your card, then listen to the whole pitch without interrupting. Ask two questions from your card or your own. Offer one idea that could make the pitch better.
Supervisor card A, the busy foreman. You like ideas but the schedule is tight. Ask: "How long will it take to set up?" and "What happens if it doesn't work?"
Supervisor card B, the careful superintendent. Safety and site rules come first. Ask: "How does this fit the site rules?" and "Who checks it every day?"
Supervisor card C, the "we've always done it this way" lead hand. You have done this for 20 years. Ask: "What's wrong with the way we do it now?" and "Who else has tried this?"
Task 5 (level 3) Your supervisor says, "Not yet. Show me it works first." Write what you will do next and what you will bring back to them.
Task 6 (level 2) Write one idea from your supervisor or partner that you will add to your pitch, and how it makes your idea better.
Check yourself
Name the six parts of a two-minute pitch.
Why is "Can we try it for one week?" a better ask than "Can we change how we do this?"
A supervisor asks a question you cannot answer. What do you say?
Your idea is about a safety concern. Besides your supervisor, who else could you bring it to on a BC workplace with 25 workers?

lessons.title: Designing your own personal mark
lessons.text:
Design an original symbol for your toolbox, business card or portfolio, research what it stands for, and present it.
Why this matters on the job
Tradespeople mark their tools so they come home from a shared site. Contractors and small trade businesses need a simple mark for a truck door, a business card or an invoice, so customers remember them. Designing a mark is also a good way to practise creativity: you choose something that says how you work, try many versions, and test whether other people read it the way you meant.
Key ideas
Why this lesson says "personal mark", not "totem" or "crest". The English word "totem" comes from Ojibwe. The Ojibwe People's Dictionary gives the word stem doodem- with the meaning "clan, totem." On the Northwest Coast, the animals carved on totem poles are crests. The Canadian Encyclopedia describes these crests as "the property of specific family lineages." It also says totem poles are specific to certain First Nations, and have been wrongly used as a general symbol of Canada. Clans and crests belong to the families and Nations they come from, and are passed on by their own protocols.
So in this lesson:
you do not design a totem or a crest, and you do not call your mark one
you do not copy designs or art styles that belong to a Nation, such as Northwest Coast formline
if your own family or Nation has clan or crest traditions, those come to you through your family and community. You are not asked to share them or use them here
What a personal mark is. A simple symbol you draw yourself. It can come from an animal, a plant, a tool, an object, a place or a shape that says something about how you work. For example, a level for someone who cares about getting it right, or a bridge for someone who likes connecting people.
What makes a mark work:
simple: a few shapes, no fine detail
readable small and from far away: it still makes sense at 2 cm wide on a hard hat sticker
works in one colour: so it can be stamped, engraved or photocopied
original: your own drawing, not copied from a company logo, clip art or someone else's culture
Research what you chose. If your mark comes from an animal or plant, find out about it from a reliable source, the way the original ACCESS assignment asked:
its attributes (what it looks like and does)
its habitat and range (where it lives)
its role in the food chain
its conservation status
Two official places to look up conservation status:
Species at Risk Public Registry (Government of Canada): https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/services/species-risk-public-registry.html
BC Species and Ecosystems Explorer (Government of BC): https://a100.gov.bc.ca/pub/eswp/
COSEWIC, the national committee that assesses wildlife, uses these status categories: Extinct, Extirpated, Endangered, Threatened, Special Concern, Data Deficient and Not At Risk. Write down where you found each fact and the date you checked it.
Worked example
Kai is training for carpentry. He lists five things that say how he works: a level, a heron, a framing square, a river, a cedar plank. He picks the heron. He has watched herons on the river near his home wait a long time and then move fast, and that is how he likes to measure and cut.
He looks up the great blue heron on the BC Species and Ecosystems Explorer and writes down its status, the source and the date. He uses the same site and a second reliable source for its habitat and what it eats.
He sketches six versions: a full heron, a heron head only, a heron standing on a level line, a heron inside a circle, a heron made from three straight lines, and the letter K shaped like a heron's leg. At 2 cm wide, his partner thinks the full heron is "a bird of some kind" and the three-line heron is "a heron with a level." Kai picks the three-line version. It is simple, works in black only, and is his own drawing.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) List five animals, plants, tools or objects that say something about how you work. Write one word beside each to say why. Circle the one you will use.
____ Why: __
____ Why: __
____ Why: __
____ Why: __
____ Why: __
Task 2 (level 2) Research your choice. If it is an animal or plant, find its attributes, habitat and range, role in the food chain and conservation status. If it is a tool or object, find what it is used for and one fact about how it is made or where it came from. Write the source and the date for each fact.
Fact Source (website name and address) Date checked
Task 3 (level 2) Sketch at least six different versions of your mark. Make them different in shape or idea, not just in colour. Keep every sketch.
Task 4 (level 2) Test two of your sketches. Draw each one about 2 cm wide in black only. Show them to a partner from about 3 m away. Ask, "What do you see?" Write down what they say. Improve the one you like best.
What my partner saw: __________
What I changed: __________
Task 5 (level 2) Make 5 to 8 slides in PowerPoint or Google Slides, or a one-page poster. Include:
a title slide or poster heading with your name, the date and your mark
what your mark comes from
your research facts, each with its source
how the mark relates to you and the way you work
two or three earlier sketches and the final mark, with a sentence on what changed
Task 6 (level 2) Present for 2 minutes. When others present, give one positive, specific comment and ask one question.
Check yourself
Why does this lesson use the words "personal mark" instead of "totem" or "crest"?
Name three things that make a mark work well.
Name the two official places in this lesson where you can look up a species' conservation status.
Why do you test your mark at a small size, from a distance?

lessons.title: Build a jig or template
lessons.text:
Design a drilling jig for a repeated shop task, test it as a cardboard prototype, then work out how much time it saves.
Why this matters on the job
When a task repeats 20, 50 or 200 times, measuring each one from scratch is slow and every measurement is a new chance for a mistake. A jig or template is something you make once so the task comes out the same every time. Cabinetmakers use them for shelf-pin holes. Framers use story sticks and stop blocks. Welders use fixtures to hold parts in the same place. Pipefitters use spacer blocks. In lesson 3 you came up with jig ideas. Today you design one, test it as a cheap prototype, and prove what it saves.
Key ideas
Jig or template. A template shows you where to mark or cut. A jig also holds or guides the tool. Many shop aids do both.
Locate from a fixed edge. A good jig has a fence or stop that sits against an edge of the work. Then every hole is measured from the same place, every time.
Prototype first. Build a quick, cheap version from cardboard or scrap (lesson 5). Test it. Fix what fails. Only then build the real one from plywood or steel.
Know the standard you are working to. Many cabinets are built to the 32 mm system, which is used around the world:
shelf-pin holes are 5 mm in diameter
holes in a row are 32 mm apart, centre to centre
the front row of holes is 37 mm from the front edge of the cabinet side
Is it worth building? Compare the time saved with the time it takes to make the jig.
time saved = (old time per piece − new time per piece) × number of pieces
net time saved = time saved − time to build the jig
break-even = time to build the jig ÷ time saved per piece. Past this number of pieces, the jig has paid for itself.
Safety with a drill and jig. These steps come from the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety:
wear safety glasses
clamp the work and the jig. Never hold small stock with one hand while you drill with the other
tighten the chuck and remove the chuck key before you start
unplug the drill or remove the battery before you change a bit
do not reach under or around the stock being drilled
Worked example
