lessons.title: Choosing and using AI at work
lessons.text:
Compare Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Gemini for trades tasks, keep private information out, follow your employer's AI rules, disclose AI help, and use AI honestly on a job application.
Product facts were checked against each company's own pages, and privacy guidance against the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada and canada.ca, on 2026-11-06. Lessons 11 to 15 come first.
Why this matters on the job
Your employer may already have an AI assistant in Outlook, Teams, Gmail or Docs. You may use a different one on your phone at home. The tool you pick, the account you sign in with and what you paste into it all matter. A client's address or your employer's bid price in the wrong chatbot can break a privacy law or a company rule. A résumé bullet the AI made up can cost you the job when the interviewer asks about it.
Key ideas
The four assistants side by side
Claude ChatGPT Microsoft Copilot Gemini
Made by Anthropic OpenAI Microsoft Google
Personal web address claude.ai chatgpt.com copilot.microsoft.com gemini.google.com
Work version Team, Enterprise Business, Enterprise, Edu Copilot Chat and Microsoft Copilot with a work or school account Google Workspace with Gemini with a work account
Where you meet it at work Its own app, or a work plan Its own app, or a work workspace Teams, Outlook, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, OneNote Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Chat
Minimum age, personal 18 13, with permission under 18 13, older in some countries 13 or your country's age (Google AI plans), 18 for a work account
Personal privacy setting to know Settings > Privacy > Help improve our AI models Settings > Data controls > Improve the model for everyone Settings > Personalization (memory and ads) Settings & help > Activity > Keep activity
Lesson 12 13 14 15
All four can write and explain text and read files or images you give them. All four can be wrong. Features change often, so check the help page before you rely on one.
How to choose for a trades task
At work, use the tool your employer approved, in your work account. Work versions come with data protections your personal account does not have. For example, Microsoft says Copilot Chat prompts and responses are not used to train its foundation models, Google says chats on a Gemini work account are not reviewed by people or used to improve its AI models, and OpenAI says it does not train on business workspace content by default.
Go where your files already are. If your crew uses Outlook and Teams, Copilot is already there. If the company runs on Gmail and Google Docs, Gemini is already there.
Pick by the job. Voice on a phone helps when your hands are busy. File upload helps with a long spec sheet. Web search with links helps with anything that changes.
Check every answer with the check-it loop from Lesson 11.
What never to paste
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada says to limit the personal information you share with AI chatbots, not to share sensitive or identifying information, and not to share information about other people. On a job, that means never paste:
Your Social Insurance Number. The Government of Canada says your SIN is confidential and to share it only when the law requires it. You do not have to give it to fill out a job application.
Health information, yours or anyone else's, including injury or claim details.
Client information: names, addresses, phone numbers, lockbox or door codes, photos that show a house number.
Your employer's private information: bid prices, contracts, drawings marked confidential, passwords, security codes.
Coworkers' information, and never photos or details of children.
Instead, take the details out. Write "Client A" or "a two-storey house in the Fraser Valley". The chatbot does not need the real name to help with the problem.
Employer AI policies
Many employers now have written rules about AI. A policy usually says:
which AI tools are approved
which account to use (work, not personal)
what you may and may not paste
when you must say AI helped
who checks AI work before it goes to a client
If there is no written policy, ask your supervisor before you use AI for work. Using your personal chatbot for company information can break a rule even if the tool is good.
Citing and disclosing AI use
You own what you send. "The AI said so" is not an excuse for a wrong quantity or a wrong rule.
Cite the real source, not the chatbot. Write "WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation s. 11.2", not "ChatGPT".
Say when AI helped if your employer's policy asks, or if the reader would expect to know. A short note is enough: "I used Gemini to help word this handout. I checked the rule on worksafebc.com."
Some product terms say the same. Microsoft's Copilot Terms of Use tell users not to mislead others about whether they used Copilot to create their content.
AI and job applications
AI can help you match your words to a job posting, fix spelling and practise interview answers. It cannot give you experience you do not have.
Everything must be true. Check every skill, ticket, tool and date the AI writes. If you do not hold a ticket, it does not go on the résumé.
Keep private details out. Do not paste your SIN, your references' phone numbers or your full address into a chatbot.
Be ready to explain it. An interviewer will ask about anything on your résumé. If you cannot talk about it, take it off.
Follow the employer's instructions. If an application asks whether you used AI, answer honestly.
Build or update your résumé with the ACCESS résumé builder.
Worked example: tailor a résumé bullet, then check it is true
Kai is applying to Riverside Mechanical Ltd. (a fictional company) for a first-year plumbing apprentice job. The posting asks for "WHMIS training, PEX and copper experience, and the ability to read basic drawings".
Kai's facts (his truth list):
Worked 3 months helping a family friend on a basement renovation
Ran PEX water lines with supervision
Has a WHMIS certificate
Has not worked with copper
Read the floor plan to find fixture locations
Kai's old bullet: "Helped with plumbing on a house reno."
Kai gives a chatbot his truth list and the posting and asks for one stronger bullet that uses only his facts. Suppose it writes:
"Installed PEX and copper water lines on a 3-month residential renovation, reading drawings to place fixtures, with WHMIS training."
Kai checks each claim against his truth list:
Claim in the AI bullet True?
Installed PEX lines Yes, with supervision
Copper lines No
3-month residential renovation Yes
Read drawings to place fixtures Yes, the floor plan
WHMIS training Yes
Kai's final bullet: "Ran PEX water lines under supervision on a 3-month basement renovation, using the floor plan to locate fixtures. WHMIS certified."
The AI made the wording stronger. Kai made it true.
Practice
Use invented details only. Never type a real SIN, client or employer document.
Task 1 (level 2) Which assistant and which account? For each case, write the best choice and one reason.
a. Your employer has approved Copilot Chat for summarizing non-confidential work emails in your work account. Your account shows Copilot Chat in Teams. You need a short summary of a long email from the general contractor.
b. Your employer has approved Gemini in the work Google Workspace account for editing non-confidential notices. You want to shorten a site safety notice in Google Docs.
c. At home, you want to practise for your Level 1 exam by talking, with your phone in your hand.
d. A coworker says to paste the company's bid into your personal chatbot to check the math.
Task 2 (level 1) Write OK if it is safe to paste into a chatbot, or NO if it is not.
a. "How many 1.2 m by 2.4 m sheets cover a 4.8 m by 2.4 m wall?" ___
b. Your SIN, so the AI can fill in a form. ___
c. A client's name, address and door code, to write a schedule. ___
d. The section number of a WorkSafeBC regulation you want explained. ___
e. A coworker's injury details, to write an incident report. ___
f. Invented notes about a late delivery, with no personal, identifying or confidential details. ___
g. A drawing stamped "Confidential" by the owner. ___
h. A job posting from a public job board. ___
Task 3 (level 2) Read this policy from a fictional employer and answer the questions.
Northgate Framing Ltd. AI use policy (fictional) 1. Staff may use Microsoft Copilot Chat signed in with their Northgate work account. No other AI tools may be used for company work. 2. Do not enter client names, addresses or contract prices into any AI tool. 3. Anything written with AI help that goes to a client must be checked by a lead hand first. 4. Safety information must be checked against the WorkSafeBC website before it is shared.
a. Can you use your personal Gemini app to write a client email? Why or why not?
b. You used Copilot Chat to word a note to a client. What must happen before it is sent?
c. Copilot Chat gives you a fall protection rule for a toolbox talk. What do you do first?
d. Can you paste the client's address into Copilot Chat to plan your route? Which rule answers this?
Task 4 (level 2) You used a chatbot to help write a one-page ladder safety handout for your crew. Write (a) a one-line note that says AI helped, and (b) a line that cites the real source of the safety rules.
Task 5 (level 3) Tailor a résumé bullet, then check it.
Posting (fictional): Coastline Electric Ltd., Electrical Apprentice, Level 1. Looking for: completed electrical foundation or pre-apprenticeship, WHMIS, safe use of hand and power tools, and good communication with the crew.
Your truth list (use these facts only):
Finished a 6-month electrical foundation program in 2026
WHMIS certificate
Used drills, saws and fish tape in shop labs
Volunteered setting up lights and power for a community event
No paid electrical work experience yet
Ask an AI assistant to write two résumé bullets that match the posting using only the truth list. Then make a table of every claim in the AI bullets and mark each one true or false. Write your final two bullets. If you use the ACCESS résumé builder, keep these invented bullets in a clearly labelled practice résumé, not your real résumé. Add only your own verified experience to a real application.
Task 6 (level 2) Honest or not? Write H for honest or N for not honest, and give a reason for each N.
a. You use AI to fix the spelling in your cover letter. ___
b. The AI adds "Red Seal" to your résumé. You are a first-year apprentice. You leave it in. ___
c. You practise interview answers with a chatbot, then answer in your own words. ___
d. The application asks if you used AI to write your answers. You did, and you say no. ___
Check yourself
At work, which AI tool and which account should you use?
Name four kinds of information you never paste into a chatbot.
What do you do if your employer has no written AI policy?
When you use a fact an AI gave you, what do you cite?
What must be true of every line on a résumé, even if AI helped write it?

lessons.title: Look up prices, flag a budget and check a loan in Excel
lessons.text:
Pull prices from a supplier price list with VLOOKUP, flag an order that goes over budget with IF, summarize prices with MIN, MAX and MEDIAN, and check a truck loan payment with PMT.
Steps and function rules checked against Microsoft Support pages for Excel for Microsoft 365, 2026-11-08. Lesson 5, Build a materials list in Excel, comes first.
Why this matters on the job
A supplier sends a price list with hundreds of items. Typing each price into an order by hand is slow, and one wrong digit costs money. Excel can look the price up from the item code, total the order and tell you straight away when the order goes over the budget. When you buy a truck or a big tool on credit, Excel can also check the monthly payment a lender quotes you and show how much interest you pay in total.
Key ideas
Open the practice workbook price-list-practice.xlsx. It has three sheets: Prices, Order and Loan. The supplier, Cedar Ridge Supply, and the job for Riverbend Builders are fictional. The prices are practice numbers, not store prices.
A formula can use a cell on another sheet
Prices!D3 means cell D3 on the sheet called Prices. Write the sheet name, an exclamation mark, then the cell.
Absolute references: the dollar sign
When you copy a formula down with the fill handle, Excel changes the row numbers (Lesson 5). Sometimes you do not want that. A dollar sign locks a reference:
A2 changes when copied. Copied one row down it becomes A3.
$A$2 stays $A$2 wherever you copy it.
To add the dollar signs, select the reference in the formula bar and press F4.
VLOOKUP: find a price from a code
VLOOKUP looks for a value in the first column of a table and brings back a value from another column in the same row.
=VLOOKUP(what to find, where to look, which column to bring back, FALSE)
What to find: the item code, for example cell A2.
Where to look: the price table, locked with dollar signs: Prices!$A$2:$D$9. The codes must be in the first column of this range.
Which column: count from the left of the range. Code is column 1, Item 2, Unit 3, Price 4.
FALSE: find an exact match only. Always use FALSE for item codes. If you leave it out, Excel looks for an approximate match and can bring back the wrong price.
If Excel cannot find the code, the cell shows #N/A. Check the code for a typing mistake or an extra space.
Newer versions of Excel also have XLOOKUP, which Microsoft describes as an improved VLOOKUP. VLOOKUP still works, and you will see it in many workplace files.
IF: check a condition
=IF(test, what to show if true, what to show if false)
=IF(E7>E8,"Over budget","OK") shows Over budget when the total in E7 is bigger than the budget in E8. Otherwise it shows OK.
Text in a formula goes inside quotation marks. Numbers do not.
> means greater than, < less than, >= greater than or equal to, <= less than or equal to, = equal to.
MIN, MAX and MEDIAN
=MIN(D2:D9) gives the smallest number in the range.
=MAX(D2:D9) gives the largest.
=MEDIAN(D2:D9) gives the middle number when the numbers are put in order. With an even count of numbers, Excel takes the average of the two middle ones.
=AVERAGE(D2:D9) adds them and divides by how many there are (Lesson 5).
One very expensive item pulls the average up a lot. It moves the median much less.
PMT: the payment on a loan
=PMT(rate per payment, number of payments, amount borrowed)
For this practice loan, assume a fixed nominal annual rate divided by 12, equal payments at the end of each month, no fees and no balance remaining after the last payment. Real loan terms may differ.
Keep the units the same. For monthly payments, divide the yearly rate by 12 and multiply the years by 12.
PMT shows the payment as a negative number, because it is money going out. Put a minus sign in front, =-PMT(...), to show it as a positive number.
PMT includes principal and interest. It does not include taxes or fees.
Payment × number of payments = the total you pay back. Total paid − amount borrowed = the interest.
Worked example
Riverbend Builders orders 10 pieces of code P02. On the Order sheet, cell C2 holds:
=VLOOKUP(A2,Prices!$A$2:$D$9,2,FALSE)
Excel finds P02 in the first column of the price table and brings back column 2: 2x8 pressure-treated, 12 ft. Change the 2 to a 4 and it brings back the price, $32.00. In E2, =B2*D2 gives 10 × 32.00 = $320.00.
Practice
Open price-list-practice.xlsx and save a copy as price-check_riverbend_[initials]_v1.xlsx.
Task 1 (level 2) On the Order sheet, enter a VLOOKUP in C2 that brings back the item name for the code in A2, and one in D2 that brings back the price. Use dollar signs on the price table. Copy both down to row 6. Write the five unit prices.
Task 2 (level 2) In E2, enter a formula for the line total and copy it down to E6. In E7, total the order with SUM. Write the total.
Task 3 (level 2) The budget for this order is in E8. In E9, enter an IF formula that shows Over budget or OK. What does it show? By how much is the order over or under?
Task 4 (level 2) The foreman says one box of deck screws is enough. Save a copy as v2 before editing and confirm it is open. Change the quantity in B4 from 2 to 1. Write the new total and what E9 shows now. Save as v2.
Task 5 (level 2) In F2, enter =IF(B2>10,"Bulk","") and copy it down to F6. Which rows say Bulk? Why does row 2, with exactly 10 pieces, not say Bulk? How would you change the formula so that 10 counts as bulk?
Task 6 (level 2) A co-worker types P10 in A6 by mistake. What do C6, D6 and E6 show? What happens to the total in E7? Fix it back to P06.
Task 7 (level 2) On the Prices sheet, fill G2 to G5 with MIN, MAX, MEDIAN and AVERAGE of the prices in D2:D9. Write the four answers to the nearest cent. Then sort the eight prices by hand from smallest to largest and check the median yourself.
Task 8 (level 3) On the Loan sheet, a small contractor is checking a truck loan: $30,000 at a practice rate of 6% a year for 5 years, paid monthly. In B5 enter =-PMT(B3/12,B4*12,B2). In B6 find the total of all payments, and in B7 the interest paid. Write all three.
Task 9 (level 3) Change B4 to 4 years, then to 3 years. Fill in the table. Which loan costs less in total? Which has the lower monthly payment? Write one sentence about which you would choose for a new business with a tight monthly budget, and why.
Years Monthly payment Total paid Interest paid
5
4
3
Check yourself
In =VLOOKUP(A2,Prices!$A$2:$D$9,4,FALSE), what does the 4 mean?
Why do the dollar signs matter when you copy a VLOOKUP down a column?
What does #N/A from a VLOOKUP usually mean?
Write an IF formula that shows Reorder when the number in C5 is less than 10, and nothing otherwise.
For a 5-year loan paid monthly, what goes in the rate and number-of-payments parts of PMT if the yearly rate is in B3?

lessons.title: Chart crew hours and level the crew in Excel
lessons.text:
Add up the crew needed each day of a deck job, flag the days that need more people than you have, chart it as a resource histogram, and move a task inside its float to fix an over-booked day.
Chart steps checked against Microsoft Support pages for Excel for Microsoft 365 on Windows, 2026-11-08. This lesson uses the Riverbend Decks job from Numeracy lessons 19, 20 and 21, and the IF function from Lesson 17.
Why this matters on the job
A schedule can look fine on paper and still need five carpenters on a day when the company has four. A foreman who spots that the week before can move a task, borrow a helper or warn the client. A foreman who spots it on the day loses the day. A resource histogram is a column chart of how many people the job needs each day. One glance shows the peaks.
Key ideas
The crew loading table
Open deck-crew-loading.xlsx. Riverbend Decks is fictional. The crew sizes are job data for this practice file.
Each row is a working day of the deck job, Day 1 to Day 13.
Columns E to M are the activities A to I from the deck schedule. A number in a cell means that activity has that many people on that day.
Column B will hold the crew on site: the total people needed that day.
Column C holds the crew available: Riverbend Decks has 4 people.
Column D will say OVER or OK.
Days 3 and 4 are empty. That is the fictional schedule's 2-day lag after the footing pour (FS+2 in Numeracy 19). It is not a rule for when real concrete is ready to load; use the job specifications and responsible supervisor's direction.
The activities sit on their early start days from the forward pass in Numeracy 20. An activity that starts at ES 1 is worked on working day 2.
Person-days and person-hours
One person working one day is one person-day. On this job a working day is 8 hours, so person-hours = person-days × 8. Labour cost is usually worked out from person-hours.
A resource histogram is a column chart
To chart it, select the Day labels and the Crew on site numbers (A1:B14), then Insert > Recommended Charts. Pick a Clustered Column chart (look on the All Charts tab if it is not shown) and select OK. Each column is one day. The taller the column, the more people that day.
Excel also has a chart type called Histogram, under Insert > Insert Statistic Chart. Do not use it here. That chart sorts numbers into ranges and counts how many fall in each range. A crew histogram just shows one column per day, so use a column chart.
Levelling with float
Total float is how many days an activity can slip without making the job finish late (Numeracy 21). In the deck job:
Activity Total float
F Cut stair stringers 9 days
G Build stairs 1 day
A, B, C, D, E, H, I 0 days (critical)
Levelling means moving activities that have float to days with fewer people, so no day needs more than the crew you have. A critical activity cannot move without making the job late.
Worked example
Day 1 has only activity A, with 2 people. In B2, =SUM(E2:M2) gives 2. In D2, =IF(B2>C2,"OVER","OK") gives OK, because 2 is not greater than 4. Copy both formulas down to row 14 with the fill handle.
Practice
Save a copy of the file as deck-crew_[initials]_v1.xlsx.
Task 1 (level 1) Read the table before you type anything. On which days does activity C, Posts and beams, have people? How many people? Why are Days 3 and 4 empty?
Task 2 (level 2) Enter the SUM in B2 and the IF in D2 and copy them down to row 14. Which days say OVER, and how many people does each of those days need?
Task 3 (level 2) In row 15, add up each activity column and column B with SUM. In B16 find the peak crew with MAX. In B17 find the person-hours. Write the total person-days, the peak and the person-hours.
Task 4 (level 2) Select A1:B14 and insert a Clustered Column chart. Give it the title Deck crew per day. Which two columns stick up above the others?
Task 5 (level 2) Day 2 is over because B Pour footings (3 people) and F Cut stair stringers (2 people) are both on Day 2. F has 9 days of float. Save a copy as v2 before editing and confirm it is open. Move F's 2 people from Day 2 to Day 3: clear J3 and type 2 in J4. What happens to D3, D4 and the chart? Did the job get longer? Save as v2.
Task 6 (level 3) Day 11 is still over. G Build stairs (2 people) and H Railings (3 people) are both on Day 11. G has 1 day of float, so try moving G to Day 12. What happens? Then explain why this over-booking cannot be fixed with float alone, and write two choices the foreman has, with what each one costs.
Task 7 (level 2) Did levelling in Task 5 change the total person-days or the person-hours? Why or why not?
Check yourself
What does one column in a resource histogram show?
Why should you not use Excel's Histogram chart type for a crew chart?
Which activities can you move to level the crew without making the job late?
A job has 34 person-days and an 8-hour day. How many person-hours is that?
What does =IF(B5>C5,"OVER","OK") show when B5 is 4 and C5 is 4?

lessons.title: Read a GPS fix and share a location
lessons.text:
Convert coordinates between degrees-minutes-seconds and decimal degrees, read how accurate your phone's location is, send a meeting point a crew can find, decide when to share your live location, and read a UTM easting and northing.
Checked against Google Maps Help (computer and Android), Google Earth Help and Natural Resources Canada, 2026-11-08. Lesson 9, Find and measure a site on a map, comes first. The phone steps were checked for Android. On an iPhone, check the iPhone version of the same Google Maps Help pages.
Why this matters on the job
A survey stake, a laydown yard on a logging road or a pipeline right-of-way often has no street address. The foreman sends coordinates, and you have to get them into your phone the right way. Coordinates come in more than one format, and one wrong sign puts you on the wrong side of the world. Your phone's blue dot also has an error you can see, and sharing your live location with a boss or a crew is a choice with privacy on the line.
Key ideas
Three ways to write the same point
Google Maps Help lists all three as formats you can type into the search box. Google Earth Pro can show all three.
Format Example: Vancouver City Hall
Decimal degrees (DD) 49.2608, -123.1139
Degrees, minutes, seconds (DMS) 49°15'39"N 123°06'50"W
Degrees and decimal minutes (DMM) 49°15.650'N 123°06.833'W
One degree has 60 minutes ('), and one minute has 60 seconds ("). So one degree has 60 × 60 = 3600 seconds.
In decimal degrees, north and east are positive, south and west are negative. All of BC is north and west, so BC latitudes are positive and longitudes are negative. In DMS, the letters N and W do that job instead of the minus sign.
Converting DMS to decimal degrees
Decimal degrees = degrees + minutes ÷ 60 + seconds ÷ 3600
BEDMAS: do both divisions first, then add. Then put a minus sign in front if the letter is W (or S).
Worked example
Vancouver City Hall is at 49°15'39"N 123°06'50"W.
Latitude: 49 + 15 ÷ 60 + 39 ÷ 3600 = 49 + 0.25 + 0.010833… = 49.260833… → 49.2608
Longitude: 123 + 6 ÷ 60 + 50 ÷ 3600 = 123 + 0.1 + 0.013888… = 123.113888… → 123.1139. The letter is W, so it is −123.1139.
In Google Maps: 49.2608, -123.1139. Latitude first, a period for the decimal, a comma between the two numbers.
How sure is your phone?
On a phone, the blue dot shows where Google Maps thinks you are.
When Google Maps is not sure, a light blue circle shows around the dot. It is an estimated uncertainty area, not a guaranteed boundary; the actual position can be outside it. The smaller the circle, the more certain the location.
A grey dot, or no dot, means Maps cannot find you and is showing your last known place.
Phone location accuracy varies with conditions; a displayed accuracy estimate is not a guaranteed maximum error. Inside buildings or underground it is often wrong. A location from cell towers alone can be off by a few thousand metres.
A GPS fix on a phone is good for finding a gate or a trailer. It is not a survey, and it does not show buried lines. Before anyone digs, contact BC 1 Call (Lesson 9).
Getting coordinates from your phone
On an Android phone, open Google Maps and touch and hold a spot on the map that has no label. A red pin drops, and the coordinates show in the search box. You can copy them into a text message.
A good meeting-point message has three parts: the coordinates, a landmark a person can see, and the time. For example: Meet 49.2608, -123.1139, City Hall front steps, 6:30. Ask the person to read it back (Communication 1).
Sharing your live location
Google Maps Location sharing sends your real-time location to people you pick. People you share with can see your name and photo, your device's recent location (even when you are not using Google apps), your battery level, and more depending on how you share.
You choose how long: a set time, or until you turn it off.
To stop on an Android phone: tap your profile picture, then Location sharing, tap the person, then Stop.
A share link sent to someone without a Google account works for up to 24 hours.
Before you turn it on for a boss or a crew, ask: who sees it, for how long, and does it stop when my shift stops? Sharing a single meeting point is often all the job needs.
UTM: eastings and northings in metres
Surveyors, forestry crews and engineers often use UTM coordinates instead of degrees. UTM splits the world into 60 zones, each 6 degrees of longitude wide, numbered from 1 at 180° going east. The Vancouver area is in zone 10, which runs from 126°W to 120°W with its centre line at 123°W.
Northing in BC (the northern hemisphere): grid distance in metres north of the equator. Southern-hemisphere UTM uses a different offset, so always record the zone and hemisphere.
Easting: metres from a line set 500 000 m west of the zone's centre line. So the centre line itself has an easting of 500 000. Points west of it have eastings below 500 000, and points east of it have eastings above.
Google Earth Pro on a computer can show UTM: Tools > Options > 3D View, then under Show Lat/Long choose Universal Transverse Mercator. On a Mac it is Google Earth > Preferences > 3D View. The coordinates show in the lower right corner as you move the mouse.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Name the format of each: (a) 49°16.600'N 123°06.717'W (b) 49.2767, -123.1119 (c) 49°16'36"N 123°06'43"W
(a) __ (b) _ (c) ___
Task 2 (level 2) Convert Vancouver City Hall, 49°15'39"N 123°06'50"W, to decimal degrees without looking at the worked example. Show the divisions first, then the additions. Round to 4 decimal places. Type your answer into Google Maps to check it lands on City Hall.
Task 3 (level 2) BC Place stadium is at 49°16'36"N 123°06'43"W. Convert it to decimal degrees to 4 places. Then type the DMS version straight into the Google Maps search box. Do both land in the same place? Which is farther north, BC Place or City Hall? How can you tell from the numbers alone?
Task 4 (level 2) A co-worker types 49.2767, 123.1119 into Google Maps for BC Place. What went wrong, and roughly where in the world does the pin land?
Task 5 (level 1) On your phone, open Google Maps and find your location. Look at the blue dot inside the classroom, then (if you can) by a window or outside. Write what you see around the dot each time and what it tells you.
Task 6 (level 2) Touch and hold a spot near the training site's entrance to drop a pin. Copy the coordinates. Write a meeting-point text for a new crew member with coordinates, a landmark and a time. Send it to your partner (or read it aloud), and have them read it back and find it on their own map.
Task 7 (level 2) Your new foreman says: "Turn on location sharing with me, until you turn it off, so I know where everyone is." Write what the foreman would be able to see, two questions you would ask before saying yes, and how you would stop sharing later.
Task 8 (level 3) In Google Earth Pro, set the coordinate display to UTM. Put the mouse on Vancouver City Hall. Write the zone, the easting and the northing. Is the easting more or less than 500 000? Explain why using City Hall's longitude.
Check yourself
How many seconds are in one degree?
In decimal degrees, why is the longitude of a BC site negative?
What does a large light blue circle around your blue dot mean?
What three things make a good meeting-point text?
In UTM, what does a northing measure?

lessons.title: Put your community on the map
lessons.text:
Find a place that matters to you and the training site on a map, say how far apart they are and in which direction, read a map coloured by numbers, and decide whose data a map shows and who gets to share it.
Checked against Google Maps Help (computer) and the First Nations Information Governance Centre's OCAP® page, 2026-11-08. Lessons 9 and 19 come first.
Why this matters on the job
Many trades jobs are away from home: camp jobs, a pipeline spread, a mill shutdown in another town. Knowing how far a job is from your community, and in which direction, helps you plan travel and talk with an employer about getting home. Reports and funding proposals also use maps coloured by numbers. You should be able to read one and ask two questions: what does it leave out, and whose information is it?
Key ideas
You choose what to share
For this lesson, pick a place that matters to you: your home community, your Nation's community, a town where you grew up or worked, or a public landmark. You decide what goes on the screen. You never have to show where you live, and no home address goes on a shared screen.
Which way is it? Read the coordinates
Right-click a place in Google Maps on a computer to see its latitude and longitude (Lesson 9). Then compare two places:
North or south: the place with the bigger latitude is farther north.
East or west: in BC, longitudes are negative. The more negative longitude is farther west. For example, −124.5 is west of −122.9.
Put the two together: north-west, south-east, and so on. If one of the differences is very small, use only the other direction.
How far is it? Measure a straight line
Right-click the first place, choose Measure distance, and click the second place (Lesson 9). This is the straight-line distance. A road, ferry or flight is longer.
Worked example
Vancouver City Hall is at 49.2608, -123.1139. BC Place stadium is at 49.2767, -123.1119.
Latitude: 49.2767 is bigger than 49.2608, so BC Place is north of City Hall.
Longitude: −123.1119 is a little less negative than −123.1139, so BC Place is a little east. The difference is tiny, only 0.0020 of a degree, compared with 0.0159 of a degree north. So the direction is simply north.
Measure distance from City Hall to BC Place: about 1.8 km.
Sentence: BC Place is about 1.8 km north of Vancouver City Hall.
Maps coloured by numbers
A choropleth map shades each area by a number, such as a count of people. The legend shows which shade means which range of numbers. On the demo map below, more ink means a bigger count.
The map and its data are fictional. Granite Valley is not a real place, and no real people are counted.
What a choropleth map cannot tell you:
where inside an area the people are
anything about one person
whether an area has a big count only because a lot of people live there
To compare areas fairly, divide the count by the population. That gives a rate, for example "per 1,000 people". A big area with many people can have the biggest count and still a low rate.
Whose data is it?
Information about people belongs first to those people. Before you put anyone's community, name or photo on a map that others will see, ask them. Information about learners in a training program is private, which is why this lesson uses fictional data.
For information about First Nations, the First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC) sets out the First Nations principles of OCAP®: ownership, control, access and possession. FNIGC explains that these principles say how First Nations' data and information will be collected, protected, used or shared. FNIGC also says OCAP® is a set of First Nations principles, not general Indigenous ones, and that each First Nation may interpret them in its own way. Read FNIGC's own explanation at https://fnigc.ca/ocap-training/.
OCAP® is a registered trademark of the First Nations Information Governance Centre (FNIGC).
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) In Google Maps on a computer, find the training site and the place you chose. Right-click each one and write its latitude and longitude to 4 decimal places. Write only a place name you are comfortable sharing.
Training site: ___ Your place: ___
Task 2 (level 1) Compare the two latitudes, then the two longitudes. Is your place north or south of the training site? East or west? Write the direction in one or two words.
Task 3 (level 2) Measure the straight-line distance from the training site to your place. Write a sentence like the one in the worked example. Then ask Google Maps for driving directions, or write how people usually travel there if there is no road. Explain why the travel distance is longer than the straight line.
Task 4 (level 1) Use the demo map and its legend. (a) Which district has the most ink, and what is its count? (b) Which two districts are in the 0 to 9 range? (c) Which range is River Bend in?
(a) __ (b) _ (c) ___
Task 5 (level 2) Here are the fictional populations of Granite Valley. Work out the rate per 1,000 people for each district: count ÷ population × 1,000. Which district has the highest rate? Does the map's shading show that?
District Apprentices Population Rate per 1,000
North Ridge 12 4,000
Lake District 27 9,000
East Hills 7 3,500
Cedar Flats 4 1,000
River Bend 18 6,000
Harbour 41 20,500
Task 6 (level 2) A classmate wants to make a graduation slideshow with a map that puts a pin on every learner's home community, with each learner's name and photo beside the pin. Write three things that should happen, or questions that should be asked, before that map is made or shown.
Task 7 (level 2) Tell a partner your sentence from Task 3 and one thing the demo map cannot tell you. Your partner repeats your sentence back.
Check yourself
Two BC places have longitudes −121.9 and −126.3. Which one is farther west?
What does the legend on a choropleth map tell you?
Why is a rate per 1,000 people sometimes fairer than a count?
What do the letters in OCAP® stand for?
Before you put someone's community on a map others will see, what do you do first?

lessons.title: Run and change a Python script
lessons.text:
Open a short Python script that checks the grade between two points, run it, change the inputs and one line of code, break it on purpose and read the error, and check the answer by hand and in Excel.
This is an optional lesson for learners who want a first look at coding. Steps checked against the Python documentation for IDLE, 2026-11-08. The script was tested with Python 3.13. Lessons 5 and 17 (Excel) and 11 to 16 (AI chatbots) help.
Why this matters on the job
Survey crews, estimators and site engineers use small scripts to repeat a calculation hundreds of times. A wrong formula or input can repeat the same mistake hundreds of times too, so testing matters. Machines on site, from a CNC table to a total station, run on code someone wrote. You do not need to become a programmer. Being able to open a short script, read what it does, change a number and see what breaks is a skill that makes new tools less scary.
Key ideas
The script
Download grade_check.py. It asks for two elevations, the horizontal distance between them and the steepest grade the job allows. Then it works out the grade and says whether it is within the limit. The limits you type in are job data for practice, not code rules.
Grade (%) = (end elevation − start elevation) ÷ horizontal distance × 100
BEDMAS: the brackets make the subtraction happen first. Then divide, then multiply by 100.
Reading Python
A line that starts with # is a comment. Python skips it. Comments are notes for people.
input("...") shows a question and waits for you to type.
float(...) turns what you typed into a number with decimals.
start = ... stores a number under the name start, so later lines can use it.
print(...) shows a result.
round(grade, 2) rounds to 2 decimal places.
if, elif and else choose what to do, like IF in Excel. The indented lines under each one run only when its test is true.
abs(...) drops the minus sign, so −2.0 becomes 2.0.
Running it in IDLE
IDLE is the editor that comes with Python from python.org.
Open IDLE. Choose File > Open… and open grade_check.py.
Choose Run > Run Module, or press F5.
The questions appear in the Shell window. Type each number and press Enter.
To change the script, edit it in the editor window, choose File > Save, then run it again.
When it breaks: read the last line
When Python cannot go on, it prints a traceback. Start at the bottom. The last line names the kind of error, for example ValueError or ZeroDivisionError, and a short reason. The lines above it show which line of the script the problem was on.
Worked example
A new footpath runs 18 m from a step at elevation 100.00 m to a landing at 100.45 m. The job allows 5%.
By hand: rise = 100.45 − 100.00 = 0.45 m. Grade = 0.45 ÷ 18 × 100 = 0.025 × 100 = 2.5%.
The script prints:
Rise: 0.45 m Grade: 2.5 % The ground goes uphill from start to end. Within the limit for this job.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Open grade_check.py in IDLE but do not run it yet. Read the comments. Write the four questions the script will ask, and the name it stores each answer under.
Task 2 (level 3) Run the script with the worked example: 100.00, 100.45, 18, 5. Does the output match? Then run it for a drain pipe that drops from 99.80 m to 99.56 m over 12 m, with a 2% limit. Write the output and check the grade by hand.
Task 3 (level 3) On this fictional job, the site super wants the temporary wheelbarrow ramp no steeper than 5%. Run the script for a ramp from 50.00 m to 51.50 m over 20 m with a limit of 5%. What does it say? By hand, what horizontal run would be needed to reach exactly 5%? (This is not the sloping surface length.)
Save a separate practice copy before changing the code. Keep the downloaded original so you can restore it.
Task 4 (level 3) Break it on purpose, three ways. Run the script each time, record the error name and message (or the IDLE error dialog), and fix it before the next one.
(a) Type twelve instead of a number for the distance. (b) Type 0 for the distance. (c) In the line grade = (end - start) / run * 100, delete the closing bracket after start. Save and run.
Task 5 (level 3) BEDMAS test. Change the grade line to grade = end - start / run * 100 (no brackets). Save and run the drain-pipe numbers from Task 2. What grade does it print? Explain the wrong answer step by step, then put the brackets back.
Task 6 (level 3) Add one line of code. Under the line that prints the grade, add:
print("That is about 1 in", round(run / abs(rise), 1))
Run the worked example again. What does the new line print, and what does "1 in 40" mean on site? What happens if you run it for level ground (start and end the same)? Why?
Task 7 (level 2) Ask an AI chatbot (Lessons 12 to 15) to explain this line in plain words: if abs(grade) > limit:. Paste only that line, nothing about the job or yourself. Then check the chatbot's answer against the comment in the script and one test run. Was the chatbot right?
Task 8 (level 2) Do the same calculation in Excel. Put the start elevation in B1, the end elevation in B2 and the distance in B3. Write a formula in B4 for the grade. Check it with the worked example numbers.
Check yourself
What does Python do with a line that starts with #?
Where do you look first in an error message?
Why does the grade line need brackets around end - start?
What does abs(-2.0) give?
Name one thing you would never paste into an AI chatbot when asking about code from work.

lessons.title: Numeracy • Find the quantities, choose a method, explain the result
lessons.text:
See it in action · Numeracy
Visual guide Five folders remain outstanding. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
ISSUED: 18 folders. RETURNED: 13 folders. Name the quantity you need. Calculate: 18 − 13 = 5. Check: 13 + 5 = 18. Five folders remain outstanding. Outstanding does not automatically mean lost or damaged.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. ISSUED: 18 folders. RETURNED: 13 folders.
Try it: Name the quantity you need. Calculate: 18 − 13 = 5. Check: 13 + 5 = 18.
Check your result: Five folders remain outstanding. Outstanding does not automatically mean lost or damaged.
Start with a useful question
Numeracy helps you answer questions that matter: Will the supplies cover everyone? Which travel plan meets the arrival time? How much space is available? What does a table actually tell us? Getting a number is part of the work. Knowing what that number means, checking it and explaining its consequences complete the task.
You may already estimate quantities, compare prices, organize time, follow a score, count materials or share costs. You can build from those strategies. You do not need to describe your finances, household, cultural responsibilities or employment history to practise here. Every project, price, timetable and dataset in this chapter is invented. Use the supplied cases or agree on another non-sensitive classroom example with your instructor.
Try a task before checking the answer guidance. Keep a record of your method, including a sketch or spoken explanation recorded by the instructor if that works better for you. A calculator, counters, larger print or a spreadsheet can support the reasoning. Record the support you used. A correct calculator display still needs the right question, inputs and interpretation.
Six connected parts of numeracy
Visual guide Six connected numeracy actions. Follow the numbered route, and return to the question or inputs when a result needs checking. The icons condense the six component descriptions in the table. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. From a useful question to a checked result Six connected components: Identify the task; Find the information; Connect the facts; Calculate or measure; Interpret and evaluate; Share the result. Recheck the question or inputs. A useful result answers the original question.
Use these six connected components as a working routine. Move between them when a new question or a check changes the task.
Identify the task that requires you to use numeracy
State the decision or question and the form of answer needed.
Identify the mathematical information
Find quantities, units, dates, conditions and missing information.
Make connections between related pieces of mathematical information
Link the available information to the unknown, including information in another table or note.
Apply mathematical operations and tools you will need to answer the question
Choose and carry out a suitable calculation, measurement, comparison or display.
Interpret and evaluate the information
Check whether the result makes sense and what the evidence can support.
Share the mathematical information, results and implications
Explain the result, method, assumptions and consequences clearly enough for another person to use.
You can move back and forth through this routine. A result that seems too large may send you back to the units. An unclear question may require clarification before calculation. That is useful checking, not failure. Separate “I do not yet have this information” from “I have the information but need help choosing a method.” Each calls for a different next step.
Before calculating, make a rough prediction. For example, three packs costing about nine dollars each will cost about twenty-seven dollars. An exact result near that estimate is plausible; a result of two hundred and seventy dollars needs investigation. An estimate does not replace a required exact total, but it gives you an independent check.
Build equal parts, regrouping and unit conversions
Use a calculator if agreed, but first show what the numbers represent. Paper strips, tactile divisions or a drawing can make equal parts visible. Every fraction strip in a comparison must represent the same whole. Drawings support reasoning; they are not calibrated measuring tools.
Begin with a small check
Show one-half and one-quarter of the same whole and explain which is larger. Then decide whether 2/4 and 1/2 can describe the same amount. If this is unclear, fold or mark a strip into equal parts before introducing written operations. If it is already clear, begin with equivalent denominators. Record the step you want to practise, rather than a general label about your maths ability.
Connect equivalent fractions
Work through 3/8 + 5/16. Each eighth can be split into two equal sixteenths, so 3/8 = 6/16. Now the parts have the same size: 6/16 + 5/16 = 11/16. Keep the denominator 16 because it names the size of each counted part. Adding denominators would change that part size incorrectly.
Guided attempt: 1/4 + 3/8. Find how many eighths equal a quarter. Record 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8 and check on equal whole strips. Next try 1½ + 2¾: 1½ = 1 2/4; sum 3 5/4 = 4¼. Discuss why five quarters include a whole and one quarter.
Regroup one whole before subtracting
Visual guide Equivalent parts make addition and regrouping visible. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Three eighths is six sixteenths. Adding five sixteenths gives eleven sixteenths. Four and one eighth is four and two sixteenths, or three and eighteen sixteenths. Subtracting two and three sixteenths leaves one and fifteen sixteenths. Adding the difference to the subtracted quantity returns four and one eighth.
Work through 4⅛ − 2 3/16. First express the smaller parts alike: 4⅛ = 4 2/16. Two sixteenths cannot supply three sixteenths without regrouping. Exchange one of the four wholes for 16/16: 4 2/16 = 3 18/16. The value has not changed. Subtract 2 3/16 to get 1 15/16. Check by adding: 1 15/16 + 2 3/16 = 3 18/16 = 4 2/16 = 4⅛.
Guided attempt: 3¼ − 1⅝. Convert 3¼ to 3 2/8, then regroup as 2 10/8. Subtract 1 5/8 to get 1 5/8. Explain the exchanged whole before checking with addition. If needed, physically exchange one whole strip for eight eighths.
Convert a unit without changing the quantity
1 m = 1,000 mm means each metre contains a thousand millimetres. For example, 0.45 m × 1,000 = 450 mm. Reverse it: 450 mm ÷ 1,000 = 0.45 m. Notice that the numerical value grows when the unit becomes smaller; the described length stays the same. For a nominal classroom input, this does not establish a real measured object's precision.
Guided attempt: 0.32 m to millimetres. The answer is 320 mm. Check whether 32 mm or 3,200 mm could describe the same length, using the known metre relationship to explain the disagreement.
Reconnect the arithmetic to a task
Visual guide Follow a quantity from the target through stock, whole packs, cost and a final check. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
The worked example needs nineteen labels: eight kits times two labels plus three spares. Six labels are available, so thirteen more are needed. Packs contain five labels, so buy three whole packs. Three packs at two dollars and twenty cents cost six dollars and sixty cents. Final stock is twenty-one, two beyond the target. A separate blank record has space for the same five calculation stages using a new agreed example.
Eight practice kits need two labels each, plus three spare labels. Six labels are available. Packs contain five labels and cost $2.20 each, with no other charge in this small example. Follow the record: 8 × 2 + 3 = target 19; 19 − 6 = 13 needed; 13 ÷ 5 = 2.6 packs, so 3 whole packs supply 15. Cost 3 × $2.20 = $6.60. Final available 6 + 15 = 21, two beyond the target. Explain why a pack count is different from a piece count and why rounding down would leave a shortage.
Fresh exit tasks
Add 1⅜ + 2¼. Show equal-sized parts and explain any whole made.
Subtract 4½ − 2¾. Show the exchanged whole and check by addition.
Convert 0.58 m to millimetres and reverse-check it.
Five practice kits need three labels each plus two spares. Four labels are available; packs contain six and cost $3 each with no other charge. Find whole packs, cost and final surplus beyond the target.
Feedback: 1) 3⅝; 2) 1¾, since 4½ = 3 6/4 and 3 6/4 − 2 3/4 = 1 3/4; 3) 580 mm; 4) target 17, shortage 13, 3 packs supply 18, cost $9, final 22, five beyond target. These exit answers are for review after the attempt. A fresh check uses different inputs with the completed example removed.
Continue to the relevant quantity, fraction or unit task when you have a method you can explain with your agreed tools. A partly completed table can support working memory without supplying which operation to choose. Keep calculations and an actual tool-measurement opportunity separate in the learning record.
Case document A • Supplies for a classroom project
Fictional training order: Willow Reach information project, version 1. The Town of Willow Reach is the fictional road owner and Pathway Paving is the fictional contractor in the wider practice case. This order is for classroom materials used to explain that project. It is not an order for road-building equipment or a real purchasing instruction.
Eighteen learners will prepare information folders. Each learner needs one folder, two pens and three labels. The group also wants two spare folders, four spare pens and six spare labels. The supplies cupboard contains seven usable folders, nine usable pens and sixteen usable labels. These counts have already been checked for this invented task. The spare quantities are additional to the learner quantities.
The practice supplier sells complete packs only. The listed prices already include every tax used in this classroom example; do not add another tax. The goods subtotal determines delivery: an order of at least $60 has no delivery charge; an order below $60 has an $8.50 delivery charge. The available budget is $65 for goods and delivery together. No pickup arrangement, discount or alternative supplier has been provided.
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Item Quantity in one pack Price for one pack
Folders 5 $8.75
Pens 12 $6.60
Labels 20 $4.20
The purchasing note must state what is needed, what is already available, how many whole packs to obtain and whether the total fits the budget. An order should not be described as approved merely because someone has calculated it. Where a condition is unresolved, identify the question for the instructor acting as project coordinator.
State the task before calculating
Read document A and write a two-sentence task statement. Identify the decision the coordinator needs and the units your answer will use. Then sort these details into needed now, background or not supplied: learner count, contractor name, usable stock, pack prices, delivery conditions and permission to collect an order. Explain why a missing permission cannot be replaced with a convenient assumption.
Connect learners, spares and stock
Make a table with three rows: folders, pens and labels. Add columns for learner quantity, spare quantity, total target, existing stock and additional quantity needed. Complete the target and additional quantities. Before working exactly, predict which item needs the most individual pieces added. Point to the two parts of document A you had to connect. Explain why subtracting stock before adding the spare target could hide a requirement.
Whole packs, fractions and money
A pack count is different from a piece count. If thirteen more folders are needed and each pack holds five, 13 ÷ 5 = 2.6 packs. The supplier does not sell 0.6 of a pack, so this order needs three whole packs. Rounding down would leave a shortage. In another task, such as counting complete kits that can be made from limited stock, rounding down might be necessary. The purpose decides the rounding direction.
Money calculations need a clear order. First find each line cost, then add the goods subtotal, then apply the stated delivery condition. Do not compare the budget with a subtotal that leaves out a required charge. Keep cents through the calculation. These prices are exact classroom inputs, so round a final money amount to cents only when an operation produces more than two decimal places.
Worked example 1 — folders. Eighteen learners need eighteen folders. Add two spares: 18 + 2 = 20 folders. Seven already exist: 20 − 7 = 13 more folders. Whole packs: 13 ÷ 5 = 2.6, so buy three packs. Cost: 3 × $8.75 = $26.25. Check the quantity: 7 + 3 × 5 = 22 folders, two more than the target of twenty. Check the money: three packs at roughly nine dollars suggest roughly twenty-seven dollars. Both checks support the result. Report “three packs, $26.25, providing two folders beyond the planned target,” not simply “2.6.”
Work out the pen order
Use the folder example as a model, but calculate the pens yourself. Show the learner requirement, spare requirement, target, shortage, whole-pack count, cost and final quantity available. Explain the difference between the four planned spare pens and any additional pens created by buying complete packs. Check the quantity using multiplication and addition after you have calculated the pack count.
Complete and evaluate the order
Calculate the label order independently. Then use the folder, pen and label costs to find the goods subtotal, applicable delivery charge and complete order cost. Compare the complete cost with the $65 budget and state the size of any surplus or shortfall. A note says, “The goods cost less than $65, so the order fits.” Correct that note with evidence. Do not invent a discount or permission to omit required supplies.
A fraction compares a part with a defined whole. Seven existing folders out of a target of twenty is 7/20. Dividing gives 0.35; multiplying by one hundred gives 35%. These are three ways to represent the same share. The denominator must be the relevant whole, not a number chosen because it is nearby in the document. “We already have nine pens and seven folders” does not tell us which requirement is better covered because the target quantities differ.
Visual guide After your attempt, check the worked example: version 1 needs three whole packs of each item. Goods of $58.65 attract $8.50 delivery, making the order $67.15: $2.15 above the $65 budget. All values are fictional. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
A worked whole-pack order needs twenty folders including spares, has seven, and needs thirteen more. Three packs of five bring stock to twenty-two. Folders cost $26.25, pens $19.80 and labels $12.60, making goods $58.65. Because goods are below $60, delivery adds $8.50. The delivered cost is $67.15, or $2.15 over the $65 budget. A scaled budget bar shows the comparison.
Compare shares fairly
Find the share of each target already covered by stock for folders and pens. Give each as a fraction and a percentage. Which target has the larger share covered, even though the other item has more pieces in stock? Explain the role of the whole in your comparison. Use a strip divided into twenty or forty equal parts, a calculator or another clear representation to check your reasoning.
Respond to a changed quantity
Version 2: The learner count rises from eighteen to twenty-two. Each learner's quantities, spare quantities, stock, pack sizes, prices, delivery rule and $65 budget stay the same. Recalculate the three whole-pack counts and total order cost. Identify which lines change and which stay unchanged. Give the coordinator a concise revised report, including the budget consequence and one decision that still needs their direction. Keep version 1 visible so the change can be checked.
Case document B • A training visit timetable
Fictional travel plan, one practice day. A learner is travelling from the fictional South Stop to a training room. Registration must be reached by 08:45. The workshop starts at 09:00 and ends at 15:20. There is an eight-minute walk between Training Stop and the room. The planning instruction adds a ten-minute buffer after the planned walk and before the registration deadline. The buffer is a classroom planning allowance, not a promise about real service reliability.
The learner must change services at Central Stop. Times in the table are for this invented exercise and do not describe a B.C. transport service. A connection is possible only when the first service arrives before the second leaves. No other outbound departures are available in this document.
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Outbound service Leaves Arrives
A: South Stop to Central Stop 07:10 07:45
B: South Stop to Central Stop 07:40 08:15
C: Central Stop to Training Stop 08:00 08:25
D: Central Stop to Training Stop 08:25 08:50
After the workshop, the same eight-minute walk returns the learner to Training Stop. The return service leaves at 15:40 and reaches Central Stop at 16:05. The next service leaves Central at 16:20 and reaches South Stop at 16:55. For the exercise, each vehicle boarding costs $2.50. A fictional $8 day pass covers all four boardings on that day. There are no additional fares or discounts in this case.
The coordinator asks for a workable outward journey, the expected return time and a fare comparison. They also want the learner to identify conditions that a real travel plan would need to confirm, such as current schedules and accessible travel arrangements. No one needs to disclose their actual address or travel needs to solve the case.
Read time as time
Clock minutes use groups of sixty. From 08:25 to 09:00 is thirty-five minutes, not seventy-five. A decimal hour uses a different representation: half an hour is 0.5 h, which is thirty minutes. When a document says 1.30 h, you need to know whether the writer means one hour thirty minutes or 1.30 decimal hours. Clear reporting avoids that ambiguity by writing 1 h 30 min or 1.5 h.
Worked example 2 — a return journey. The workshop ends at 15:20. Add the eight-minute walk to reach Training Stop at 15:28. The wait for 15:40 is twelve minutes. The first vehicle journey takes twenty-five minutes, the Central wait takes fifteen minutes, and the final journey takes thirty-five minutes. Total: 8 + 12 + 25 + 15 + 35 = 95 minutes, or 1 h 35 min. Check directly: 15:20 to 16:20 is sixty minutes, then another thirty-five reaches 16:55. The report should name both the final clock time and the elapsed duration.
Choose a feasible outward journey
Find the latest listed departure from South Stop that allows the learner to meet registration including the eight-minute walk and ten-minute buffer. Name both connecting services. Show arrival at Training Stop, arrival at the room and the end of the buffer. Explain why the later South departure does or does not work. This is a question about stated constraints, not simply about the shortest ride.
Check elapsed time another way
For the feasible outward journey you chose, calculate the Central waiting time and total elapsed time from South departure to room arrival. Add the return journey's elapsed time to find the combined outward-and-return journey time. Include travel and waits within those journeys; exclude all time in the room before the 09:00 workshop, including the planning buffer, and exclude the workshop itself. Report hours and minutes. Correct this claim: “Eighty-three minutes is 1.83 hours.” You may show a timeline, grouped minutes or a calculator conversion.
Compare like-for-like fares
Calculate the cost of four separate boardings and compare it with the day pass. State the saving and the assumptions that make the comparison valid. Then consider a different learner who needs only two boardings that day. Which option costs less for that learner, and by how much? Explain why “the pass is always cheaper” is not supported by the supplied prices.
Update a plan without losing its conditions
New notice: Registration is now due by 09:10 and the workshop starts at 09:20. Everything else in document B stays unchanged, including the ten-minute buffer and the workshop end time. Recheck the later South departure. Prepare a short revised journey note with service letters, room-arrival time, buffer-end time, registration margin and fare choice for four boardings. Identify one real-world fact the fictional timetable cannot verify.
Case document C • A classroom information board
Fictional layout brief. A learning room is preparing an information board using paper cards. The board is a rectangle 600 mm wide and 400 mm high. The first layout requires a clear margin of 25 mm on every edge. Each information card is 180 mm wide and 110 mm high. Cards must keep that orientation. Leave a 20 mm gap between neighbouring cards, horizontally and vertically. The 20 mm rule applies only between neighbouring cards; no additional 20 mm gap is required at an outside edge.
All dimensions are nominal design inputs for this exercise. They are not measurements of the printed page. Printing or screen zoom can change a diagram's physical size. Use the labelled values for calculations. If you practise measuring an actual classroom object, use a suitable real measuring tool and record the unit and precision; do not assume this workbook prints at a particular scale.
The board will explain four fictional practice-session categories. The visitor table counts thirty-six invented visitors, with each person assigned to only one category. It is a complete table for this exercise, not a survey of an actual community. The instructor asks for a neat arrangement, a simple chart and a short explanation of what the chart supports.
Practice-session category Fictional visitors
Orientation 8
Trades preparation 12
Service roles 6
Community project planning 10
Later, the instructor may change the margin requirement. Keep the original layout and calculations so a revision can be compared. The task concerns paper information design. It does not establish structural design, accessibility compliance or a safe installation method for a real board.
Measure the quantity the task actually asks for
Length, perimeter and area answer different questions. Length describes a single dimension. Perimeter is the distance around a shape. Area describes the surface covered. A rectangle's perimeter is 2 × (width + height), while its area is width × height. Label perimeter in a length unit such as metres and area in a square unit such as square metres. The same numbers can produce both calculations, but the results are not interchangeable.
Changing units also requires attention to the quantity. Because 1 m = 1,000 mm, 600 mm is 0.6 m. For area, one square metre contains 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000 square millimetres. Dividing a square-millimetre area by only one thousand produces an incorrect conversion. A sketch of a one-metre square can help explain why two dimensions change.
Worked example 3 — the clear inside rectangle. The board loses a 25 mm margin on both the left and right: 600 − 25 − 25 = 550 mm. It also loses the top and bottom margins: 400 − 25 − 25 = 350 mm. The clear area is 550 × 350 = 192,500 mm². Converting the sides first gives 0.55 × 0.35 = 0.1925 m², which agrees with 192,500 ÷ 1,000,000. Check that the clear area is smaller than the whole board. Do not subtract the margin only once from each dimension.
Identify units and precision
Convert the board width and height to centimetres and metres. Rewrite the 20 mm gap in centimetres. Explain why measuring the drawing on a resized screen would not establish these dimensions. If you have a real ruler, measure a plain classroom sheet's width to the nearest millimetre and record your method; otherwise describe where zero and the endpoint would need to align using the supplied board values. Keep actual measured data separate from nominal case dimensions.
Choose perimeter or area
Calculate the whole board's perimeter in metres and its area in square metres. Then calculate the total area of four information cards and express it as a percentage of the whole board area. Explain which result could describe the amount of surface covered and which describes the distance around the board. Check that the card coverage percentage is below 100% without relying only on the calculator display.
Test fit, not just total area
Using the original margins, work out how many cards fit across and how many fit down. Include only the gaps between cards: two cards have one gap, three cards have two. Find the total number of cards in a rectangular arrangement. Show why a proposed three-column layout fails even if the cards' combined area seems small enough. Draw a labelled sketch that another learner can check without measuring your drawing.
Visual guide After your attempt, check the worked example: 25 mm margins leave 550 × 350 mm. Two columns and two rows fit with 20 mm gaps. Three columns need 580 mm and three rows need 370 mm, so each exceeds the clear space. Use the labels, not the displayed size. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Fictional board 600 by 400 millimetres with 25-millimetre margins has a clear rectangle 550 by 350. Four fixed-orientation cards, each180 by110, fit as two across and two down with20-millimetre gaps. Three across needs580, exceeding550. Three down needs370, exceeding350. The four-card group measures380 by240 millimetres.
Read a different unit system
A separate fictional paper strip is labelled 6½ inches. Use the exact conversion 1 inch = 25.4 mm to calculate its length in millimetres. First rewrite 6½ as a decimal. A second strip is ¼ inch wide; convert that width too. Explain why multiplying by 25 rather than 25.4 would be an approximation. These labels are supplied values, not a claim about the physical size of any printed illustration.
Turn data into a message
A useful graph has a question, a title, clear category labels and a scale. A bar chart compares category amounts well. Start its count axis at zero so the visual lengths represent the quantities fairly. Equal steps on the axis must mean equal numerical changes. A picture with attractive bars but no units may leave the reader unable to tell whether the values represent people, dollars or minutes.
A percentage also needs its population and period. “One third chose trades preparation” means one third of these thirty-six fictional visitors, not one third of all learners or all Indigenous people. A count can describe this dataset without explaining why someone attended or predicting demand next year. Sharing a result includes saying what remains unknown.
Make a chart that can be checked
Total the visitor counts. Create a bar chart on paper or with a digital tool using an axis from zero to twelve in steps of two. Include a title that says the data are fictional. Calculate the share represented by Trades preparation as a fraction and percentage. Write two supported comparisons and one conclusion the table cannot support. If using a tool, check its chart against the original table; paper work demonstrates the numeracy task without claiming Digital evidence.
Recalculate after a layout change
The instructor changes every outside margin from 25 mm to 10 mm. Card orientation, card dimensions and 20 mm between-card gaps stay unchanged. Calculate the new clear width and height. Test the number of cards across and down, then compare capacity with the original arrangement. Explain why increasing clear area alone is not enough to establish that a particular arrangement fits. Report both the new count and its conditions.
Transfer the checking routine to a purchasing choice
Return to document A, version 1 with eighteen learners. The coordinator now permits one extra pack of labels because they will be used at the next session and storage is available. Compare the original minimum-quantity delivered order with an order containing that additional pack. Reapply the delivery rule and find the total difference. Does the revised order fit $65? Explain the trade-off: spending more on goods can sometimes reduce the final charge, but buying unneeded goods is not automatically a saving.
Make a numerical handover
Choose your revised journey, revised board layout or revised supply order. Prepare a handover containing the question, relevant inputs, method, checked result and implication. Include one uncertainty or condition and show how another person could check the result. Your partner or instructor restates the recommendation; correct any misunderstanding. Finally, identify a specific mistake you corrected or a checking strategy you strengthened, using evidence from your working rather than a general claim about being “good” or “bad” at maths.
Practise with a suitable amount of support
Start with a preformatted table, a number line, fraction counters or an instructor modelling one step. Then try a related item with fewer prompts. If a whole case is too much at once, complete its quantities before its costs, or its arrivals before its fares. Keeping the purpose visible helps you reconnect the parts. For an extension, explain a second valid method or show what additional information a real task would require.
A partner can ask questions and compare methods, but keep individual evidence of your reasoning. Explain an operation before entering it into a calculator. When two results differ, compare the task, source values, units and steps in that order. Repeating the same calculation without identifying the disagreement may simply repeat the error. Feedback should name the useful action: “You checked both margins,” or “The delivery condition still needs applying.”
Your local feedback record can distinguish Not observed, Not yet demonstrated, Demonstrated with support and Demonstrated independently. An attempt with an error is different from a task nobody has observed. These descriptions are not official Skills for Success proficiency levels. Application in a different context is recorded separately as transfer, with the new task and evidence named.
Component and evidence map
Identify the task
“State the task before calculating” states the decision; “Choose a feasible outward journey” identifies deadline constraints; “Choose perimeter or area” selects the required quantity.
Identify mathematical information
“Connect learners, spares and stock” extracts quantities; “Choose a feasible outward journey” reads the timetable; “Identify units and precision” identifies units and precision.
Connect related information
“Connect learners, spares and stock” links people, spares and stock; “Complete and evaluate the order” joins pricing and delivery; “Test fit, not just total area” connects dimensions and gaps.
Apply operations and tools
“Work out the pen order” through “Respond to a changed quantity” calculate packs, money and shares; “Check elapsed time another way” through “Compare like-for-like fares” calculate time/fares; “Choose perimeter or area” through “Recalculate after a layout change” calculate and display measurements/data.
Interpret and evaluate
“Complete and evaluate the order” challenges a subtotal claim; “Test fit, not just total area” tests actual fit; “Make a chart that can be checked” limits conclusions; “Transfer the checking routine to a purchasing choice” compares complete costs.
Share results and implications
“Respond to a changed quantity” and “Update a plan without losing its conditions” report revisions; “Make a chart that can be checked” explains a chart; “Make a numerical handover” gives a checkable handover.
Numeracy · fresh quantities, fractions and units
Use the selected form. Show how you chose the quantities, your working, units and a second check. An agreed calculator, fraction strips or accessible number tool may be used. These are nominal classroom values, not dimensions to measure on the page or live purchasing instructions. Prices include all charges except the delivery rule explicitly stated. No purchase is authorized.
Form A · Practice information packs
Fourteen learners each need one folder and three cards. Add two spare folders and six spare cards to those learner quantities. Existing usable stock is five folders and eleven cards. The supplier sells whole packs only.
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Item Pieces per pack Price per pack
Folders 4 $6.40
Cards 12 $3.60
Goods costing at least $35.00 have no delivery charge. Below that threshold, delivery is $4.50. The budget is $37.00 including delivery. No other supplier, discount or pickup option is supplied.
Numeracy practice A · Connect the quantities
For each item, record the learner requirement, spares, total target, existing stock, additional pieces needed, whole packs and pieces available after purchase. Explain your rounding direction. Distinguish planned spares from any additional surplus created by buying whole packs.
Numeracy practice A · Decide from the full cost
Estimate the goods cost, calculate exact line costs and apply the delivery rule. Report the complete cost and its difference from the budget. State whether the order fits and what decision still belongs to the coordinator. Check one result using a different operation, grouping or estimate; identify what your check can detect.
Numeracy practice A · Work with fractional lengths
Two nominal paper strips are 1¾ in and 2⅞ in long. Find their combined length. A separate strip is 4¼ in long and has a marked section 1⅝ in long; find the remaining length. Show equivalent fractions and any regrouping. Check one answer by reversing the operation. These are calculation inputs, not instructions to cut material.
Numeracy practice A · Keep the quantity and unit together
A nominal display strip is 0.64 m long. Use 1 m = 1,000 mm to express it in millimetres. Explain why this conversion does not tell you an actual measured strip's precision. Give a short numerical handover containing the order result, a condition and a method another person could check.
Form B · Practice orientation packs
Eleven learners each need one folder and two cards. Add three spare folders and six spare cards. Existing usable stock is three folders and five cards. Whole packs only are available.
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Item Pieces per pack Price per pack
Folders 4 $6.80
Cards 10 $5.50
Goods costing at least $40.00 have no delivery charge. Below that threshold, delivery is $4.20. The budget is $42.00 including delivery. No other supplier, discount or pickup option is supplied.
Numeracy practice B · Connect the quantities
For each item, record the learner requirement, spares, total target, existing stock, additional pieces needed, whole packs and pieces available after purchase. Explain your rounding direction. Distinguish planned spares from any additional surplus created by buying whole packs.
Numeracy practice B · Decide from the full cost
Estimate the goods cost, calculate exact line costs and apply the delivery rule. Report the complete cost and its difference from the budget. State whether the order fits and what decision still belongs to the coordinator. Check one result using a different operation, grouping or estimate; identify what your check can detect.
Numeracy practice B · Work with fractional lengths
Two nominal paper strips are 2½ in and 1⅞ in long. Find their combined length. A separate strip is 5¼ in long and has a marked section 2⅞ in long; find the remaining length. Show equivalent fractions and any regrouping. Check one answer by reversing the operation. These are calculation inputs, not instructions to cut material.
Numeracy practice B · Keep the quantity and unit together
A nominal display strip is 0.72 m long. Use 1 m = 1,000 mm to express it in millimetres. Explain why this conversion does not tell you an actual measured strip's precision. Give a short numerical handover containing the order result, a condition and a method another person could check.
Working pages for either form
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
