lessons.title: Checking a pay stub and filling in a TD1
lessons.text:
Check the numbers on a pay stub, total your claim on the TD1 and TD1BC forms, and read the banking numbers on a cheque for direct deposit.
Why this matters on the job
On your first day with a new employer in BC, you are usually asked for three things: a TD1 form, a TD1BC form and your banking information for direct deposit. Every payday after that, you get a pay stub. If an hour of overtime is missing or a deduction is wrong, the stub is where you catch it. A few minutes with a calculator can save you money.
Key ideas
Gross pay is what you earned before anything is taken off. Deductions are the amounts taken off, such as Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Employment Insurance (EI), income tax and union dues. Net pay is what lands in your bank account.
Net pay = gross pay − total deductions
In BC, your employer must give you a wage statement (pay stub) every payday. It must show the employer's name and address, your hours, your wage rate, your overtime hours, each deduction and what it is for, and your gross and net pay.
The TD1 (federal) and TD1BC (British Columbia) forms tell your employer which tax credits you will claim. Your employer uses the total to decide how much income tax to take off each pay. You only have to fill in the TD1BC if your federal total on line 13 is more than $16,452.
For direct deposit, your employer needs three numbers from the bottom of a cheque: the branch number (5 digits), the institution number (3 digits) and your account number. The first set of digits on a cheque is the cheque number, which is not needed.
Worked example
Marie works 40 regular hours at $30.00 an hour and 2 overtime hours at 1.5 times her rate.
Regular pay: 40 × $30.00 = $1,200.00
Overtime rate: 1.5 × $30.00 = $45.00 an hour
Overtime pay: 2 × $45.00 = $90.00
Gross pay: $1,200.00 + $90.00 = $1,290.00
Her deductions add up to $290.15. Net pay: $1,290.00 − $290.15 = $999.85.
Check: $999.85 + $290.15 = $1,290.00. The check works, so the subtraction is right.
On the HP 10bII+
The HP 10bII+ is a financial calculator. Out of the box the HP 10bII+ works in Chain mode: it does each operation in the order you key it, not in BEDMAS order. To see the mode, press RCL, then the blue shift key, then ON (marked Alg/Chain above it). CHAIN or ALGEBRAIC flashes on the screen. The keys below press = after each step, so they give the same answer in either mode.
After ×, the % key divides the number by 100. Marie's pay of $1,290.00:
EI: 1290 × 1.63 % = shows 21.03
CPP exemption for one pay: 3500 ÷ 26 = shows 134.62. Press →M to keep it in the M memory.
CPP bracket: 1290 − RM = shows 1,155.38
CPP: × 5.95 % = shows 68.75
The screen rounds to two decimal places, but the calculator keeps 12 digits. →M and RM keep the full exemption, not the rounded 134.62.
Practice
Use the documents below. All people, employers and numbers in them are fictional.
Document A: pay stub
Cedar Ridge Framing Ltd. (fictional employer), 100 Sample Road, Langley, BC Employee: Riley Thomas, apprentice carpenter Pay period: October 5 to October 18, 2026. Payday: October 23, 2026. Paid every two weeks (26 pays a year).
Earnings Hours Rate Amount
Regular 80 $27.50 $2,200.00
Overtime (1.5 × rate) 4 $41.25 $165.00
Gross pay $2,365.00
Deductions Amount
CPP contributions $132.71
EI premiums $38.55
Income tax $312.40
Union dues $48.00
Total deductions $531.66
Net pay (direct deposit) $1,833.34

lessons.title: Working out the monthly cost of a bank account
lessons.text:
Read a fee schedule, count your transactions and work out what each account would cost you in a month and a year.
Why this matters on the job
When you start work, your pay goes into a bank account by direct deposit. Bank fees come out of that pay every month. A tradesperson who buys supplies with a debit card, sends e-transfers to a co-worker for a shared ride and pays a phone bill can make 30 or more transactions a month. The account that looks cheapest is not always the cheapest for the way you bank.
Key ideas
A fee schedule is the list of what a bank charges. Read it like any table: find the row for the account, then the column for the fee.
The monthly cost of an account is:
monthly fee + (extra transactions × fee for each extra transaction) + any other fees
An extra transaction is one over the number included in the account. If 18 are included and you make 23, you have 23 − 18 = 5 extra.
Two rules from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) are worth knowing:
Low-cost and no-cost accounts. Banks that signed the federal commitment offer a low-cost chequing account for no more than $4 a month, with at least 18 debit transactions. The same account has no monthly fee for people 18 or younger, students, seniors receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement, Registered Disability Savings Plan beneficiaries and newcomers in their first year in Canada. Some banks also include Indigenous customers, Disability Tax Credit recipients, or people receiving certain social assistance. Ask the bank which groups it recognizes.
NSF fees. A non-sufficient funds (NSF) fee is charged when a payment bounces because there is not enough money in the account. Since March 12, 2026, federally regulated banks cannot charge more than $10 for it. They cannot charge it when the account would be overdrawn by less than $10, and they cannot charge it again if they already charged one in the last 2 business days.
Worked example
An account costs $6.00 a month and includes 20 debit transactions. Each extra transaction costs $1.00. Sam makes 26 transactions.
Extra transactions: 26 − 20 = 6
Extra fees: 6 × $1.00 = $6.00
Monthly cost: $6.00 + $6.00 = $12.00
Yearly cost: 12 × $12.00 = $144.00

lessons.title: Credit card interest and minimum payments
lessons.text:
Read a credit card information box, work out interest and minimum payments, and see what paying only the minimum costs over time.
Why this matters on the job
Many apprentices buy their first set of tools on credit. A $1,200 tool kit on a card can cost $1,200, or it can cost more than $2,400, depending only on how it is paid back. The difference is arithmetic you can do with a calculator. Knowing it before you buy helps you plan.
Key ideas
Interest rate. A credit card shows a yearly (annual) interest rate. In this lesson we use a simple classroom model for one month of interest:
monthly interest = balance × annual rate ÷ 12
Real cards work out interest on each day's balance, as the cardholder agreement explains. The model gives answers close to that and is easier to follow by hand.
Grace period. Federally regulated financial institutions must give at least 21 days without interest on new purchases, starting from the last day of the billing period (the statement date). You only get it if you pay the full balance by the due date. There is no grace period on cash advances: interest starts the day you take the cash.
Minimum payment. This is the smallest amount you must pay each month to keep the card in good standing. Paying only the minimum keeps the interest growing. Card statements from federally regulated institutions must show an estimate of how long it would take to pay the balance if you paid only the minimum.
Buy now, pay later (BNPL). The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) says that with a BNPL plan "you're financing your purchase with credit." The provider may check your credit, and missed payments can bring fees.
Worked example
A card has a balance of $800 and an annual rate of 18%. The minimum payment is $24.00.
Pay the minimum: $800.00 − $24.00 = $776.00
Interest for one month: $776.00 × 0.18 ÷ 12 = $11.64
New balance: $776.00 + $11.64 = $787.64
After one month and a $24.00 payment, the balance went down by only $12.36. The other $11.64 of the payment covered interest.
On the HP 10bII+
The HP 10bII+ is a financial calculator. Out of the box the HP 10bII+ works in Chain mode: it does each operation in the order you key it, not in BEDMAS order. To see the mode, press RCL, then the blue shift key, then ON (marked Alg/Chain above it). CHAIN or ALGEBRAIC flashes on the screen. The keys below press = after each step, so they give the same answer in either mode.
The worked example on the HP 10bII+:
800 − 24 = shows 776.00
× 18 % ÷ 12 = shows 11.64, the interest
776 = shows 787.64, the new balance
The HP 10bII+ also has time value of money (TVM) keys along its top row: N (number of payments), I/YR (yearly interest rate), PV (present value), PMT (payment) and FV (future value). Enter four of them and it works out the fifth. Money you receive is positive and money you pay out is negative. Task 12 uses these keys to check the spreadsheet in Task 8. "Orange shift, %CHG" means press the orange shift key, then the key with %CHG printed on its edge.

lessons.title: Working out the tax on a simple return
lessons.text:
Follow a T4 slip through the main lines of a 2026 return to find federal and BC tax, then decide whether there is a refund or a balance owing.
Why this matters on the job
Every spring, workers in BC file an income tax and benefit return for the year before. The 2026 return is due by April 30, 2027, for most people. Tax software or a free tax clinic does the arithmetic for you, but knowing how the main lines connect lets you check your return, understand a refund or a balance owing, and spot a T4 slip that is wrong. Filing also matters for benefits: the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) needs a return to work out benefit and credit payments.
Key ideas
Tax brackets. Income tax is charged in slices. Each rate applies only to the part of your taxable income inside its bracket, not to all of it. For 2026:
Federal: each portion of taxable income Rate
$0 to $58,523 14%
$58,523.01 to $117,045 20.5%
$117,045.01 to $181,440 26%
over $181,440 (two more brackets) 29% and 33%
British Columbia: each portion of taxable income Rate
$0 to $50,363 5.6%
$50,363.01 to $100,728 7.7%
$100,728.01 to $115,648 10.5%
over $115,648 (four more brackets) 12.29% to 20.5%
Non-refundable tax credits. These lower your tax, not your income. Add up the credit amounts, then multiply by the lowest rate: 14% federal and 5.6% BC for 2026. If the credits are bigger than the tax, the tax is $0. You do not get the difference back.
CPP is split in two. Box 16 of your T4 holds your CPP contributions. The base part is a credit (line 30800). The additional part is a deduction from income (line 22215). For 2026, the base part is 4.95/5.95 of box 16, and the rest is the additional part. Tax software does this split for you.
Refund or balance owing. Compare the total tax with the tax your employer already took off (T4 box 22, line 43700). If more was taken off than you owe, you get a refund. If less, you have a balance owing, due by April 30.
The main lines used in this lesson
Line What it holds Where the number comes from
10100 Employment income T4 box 14
15000 Total income Add all income lines
22215 Deduction for the additional CPP contributions Additional part of T4 box 16
23600 Net income Line 15000 minus deductions
26000 Taxable income Line 23600 minus other deductions (none in this lesson)
30000 Basic personal amount $16,452 federal, $13,216 BC
30800 Base CPP contributions Base part of T4 box 16
31200 EI premiums T4 box 18
31260 Canada employment amount (federal only) $1,501, or your employment income if less
43700 Total income tax deducted T4 box 22
48400 / 48500 Refund / balance owing Line 43700 compared with total tax
Worked example: tax on two brackets
Taxable income is $70,000. Federal tax before credits:
First bracket: $58,523 × 14% = $8,193.22
Second bracket: ($70,000 − $58,523) × 20.5% = $11,477 × 0.205 = $2,352.79
Total: $8,193.22 + $2,352.79 = $10,546.01
Do the subtraction in the bracket first (BEDMAS), then multiply. Only $11,477 is taxed at 20.5%, not the whole $70,000.
On the HP 10bII+
The HP 10bII+ is a financial calculator. Out of the box the HP 10bII+ works in Chain mode: it does each operation in the order you key it, not in BEDMAS order. To see the mode, press RCL, then the blue shift key, then ON (marked Alg/Chain above it). CHAIN or ALGEBRAIC flashes on the screen. The keys below press = after each step, so they give the same answer in either mode.
After ×, the % key divides the number by 100. The worked example:
First bracket: 58523 × 14 % = shows 8,193.22
Second bracket: 70000 − 58523 = shows 11,477.00, then × 20.5 % = shows 2,352.79
Total: 8193.22 + 2352.79 = shows 10,546.01
Press = after the subtraction. That finishes the bracket before you multiply, in either mode.

lessons.title: Converting money with exchange rates
lessons.text:
Read an exchange rate table, convert between Canadian and other currencies, and work out what a bank, an exchange counter or a credit card adds on.
Why this matters on the job
Tools, parts and safety gear are often priced in US dollars online. Crews from BC travel to job sites in Alberta, but also to Washington State or Alaska, and some workers send money to family abroad. Each time, a dollar amount has to be changed into another currency. Knowing how to convert lets you compare a US price with a Canadian one and see the extra cost a bank or card adds.
Key ideas
The Bank of Canada publishes daily exchange rates once each business day by 16:30 Eastern Time. Each rate shows how many Canadian dollars one unit of the other currency is worth. These rates are indicative only: they are averages, and banks and exchange counters use their own rates.
Two rules cover every conversion with a rate written as "Canadian dollars for 1 unit":
Other currency to Canadian dollars: multiply by the rate.
Canadian dollars to the other currency: divide by the rate.
Check the direction with common sense. One US dollar is worth more than one Canadian dollar on the date used in this lesson, so a US price turns into a bigger Canadian number.
An exchange counter has two rates. It sells you foreign money at a higher rate and buys it back from you at a lower rate. The gap is how the counter earns money.
A credit card used in another currency converts the purchase to Canadian dollars and then adds a foreign currency conversion charge, a percentage of the Canadian amount.
Worked example
On November 5, 2026, the Bank of Canada rate for the US dollar was 1.3989.
A part costs US$80.00. In Canadian dollars: 80.00 × 1.3989 = $111.91
You have $200.00 Canadian. In US dollars: 200.00 ÷ 1.3989 = US$142.97
Check: US$142.97 × 1.3989 = $200.00 (to the nearest cent). The two answers undo each other.
On the HP 10bII+
The HP 10bII+ is a financial calculator. Out of the box the HP 10bII+ works in Chain mode: it does each operation in the order you key it, not in BEDMAS order. To see the mode, press RCL, then the blue shift key, then ON (marked Alg/Chain above it). CHAIN or ALGEBRAIC flashes on the screen. The keys below press = after each step, so they give the same answer in either mode.
US$80.00 in Canadian dollars: 80 × 1.3989 = shows 111.91
$200.00 Canadian in US dollars: 200 ÷ 1.3989 = shows 142.97
Adding a percent: after + the % key works out that percent of the number and adds it. 111.91 + 2.5 % = shows 114.71, the US$80.00 part with a 2.5% card charge.
Percent change: 1.3989, orange shift, %CHG, 1.3600 = shows −2.78. The counter buys US dollars 2.78% below the Bank of Canada rate. A minus sign means the second number is smaller.
"Orange shift, %CHG" means press the orange shift key, then the key with %CHG printed on its edge.
Practice

lessons.title: Reading and making charts of trade wages
lessons.text:
Use real Job Bank wage data for BC trades to read tables, make a fair bar chart, read pie and line graphs, and say what the data can and cannot show.
Why this matters on the job
Choosing a trade, a region to work in or a job offer often comes down to numbers in a table or a chart. Job Bank, run by the Government of Canada, publishes wages for every trade in every region of BC. Charts also show up at work: in safety bulletins, production reports and union newsletters. Reading them well, and making your own fairly, helps you and your crew make decisions on good information.
Key ideas
Read the labels first. Before reading any number, find the title, the units (dollars per hour, percent, hours), the date and the source. Read any notes under the table or chart. They often change what the numbers mean.
Low, median and high wages. On Job Bank:
The low wage is, in most cases, the 10th percentile: 10% of workers earn that much or less.
The median wage is the middle value when wages are ranked from lowest to highest. Job Bank uses it as the prevailing wage.
The high wage is, in most cases, the 90th percentile: 90% of workers earn that much or less.
Job Bank shows wages paid to employees, not wages offered in job postings.
Three common charts.
A bar chart compares amounts across categories. The value axis should start at zero, so the length of each bar matches its value.
A line graph shows how a value changes over time.
A pie chart shows parts of one whole. All the slices add up to 100%, which is 360°.
Percent difference depends on the whole. "A is what percent more than B?" divides by B. "B is what percent less than A?" divides by A. The two answers are different.
Worked example
Job Bank lists the BC median wage for plumbers as $32.00 an hour and for welders and related machine operators as $35.00 an hour.
Difference: $35.00 − $32.00 = $3.00 an hour
The welder median is more than the plumber median by $3.00 ÷ $32.00 × 100 = 9.38%
On the HP 10bII+
The HP 10bII+ is a financial calculator. Out of the box the HP 10bII+ works in Chain mode: it does each operation in the order you key it, not in BEDMAS order. To see the mode, press RCL, then the blue shift key, then ON (marked Alg/Chain above it). CHAIN or ALGEBRAIC flashes on the screen. The keys below press = after each step, so they give the same answer in either mode.
The %CHG key works out a percent change in one step: key the old number, press orange shift, %CHG, key the new number and press =. For the worked example: 32, orange shift, %CHG, 35 = shows 9.38. If the new number is smaller, the answer has a minus sign.
"Orange shift, %CHG" means press the orange shift key, then the key with %CHG printed on its edge.

lessons.title: Metric prefixes from nano to giga
lessons.text:
Read and convert the large and small metric prefixes found on nameplates, bills and data plans, and write their symbols correctly.
Why this matters on the job
A motor nameplate shows kilowatts, a capacitor shows microfarads, a meter reads milliamps, an electricity bill counts kilowatt-hours and a phone plan counts gigabytes. Electricians, millwrights, instrumentation techs and heavy-duty mechanics read these every day. One wrong prefix, or one wrong capital letter, changes a number by a thousand times or more.
Key ideas
In the metric system (the SI), we put a prefix in front of a unit to make a new unit with a precise meaning:
prefix + unit of measurement = new word with a specific meaning
kilo + metre = kilometre, meaning 1,000 metres
milli + litre = millilitre, meaning a thousandth of a litre
mega + watt = megawatt, meaning 1,000,000 watts
Prefix Symbol Written number Power of 10 Trade example
tera T 1 000 000 000 000 10¹² terabyte (TB)
giga G 1 000 000 000 10⁹ gigahertz (GHz)
mega M 1 000 000 10⁶ megawatt (MW), megapascal (MPa)
kilo k 1 000 10³ kilowatt (kW), kilopascal (kPa)
(none) 1 10⁰ watt (W), metre (m)
milli m 0.001 10⁻³ milliampere (mA)
micro µ 0.000 001 10⁻⁶ microfarad (µF), micrometre (µm)
nano n 0.000 000 001 10⁻⁹ nanofarad (nF), nanometre (nm)
pico p 0.000 000 000 001 10⁻¹² picofarad (pF)
Capital letters matter. Prefix symbols for big multiples are capital letters, except k (kilo), h (hecto) and da (deca). Prefixes for small parts are lower-case. So m is milli and M is mega. The symbol goes right against the unit with no space: kW, not k W.
Each step in the table is 1,000 (from pico up to tera). To convert, count the steps and multiply or divide by 1,000 for each one:
going to a smaller unit, the number gets bigger, so multiply
going to a bigger unit, the number gets smaller, so divide
SI prefixes are powers of 10, even for data. One kilobit is 1,000 bits, not 1,024. Computers sometimes count in powers of 2. For those, there are separate binary prefixes, such as kibi (Ki) and gibi (Gi).
Worked example
A heater is rated 1,500 W and runs for 4 hours. How much energy does it use, in kilowatt-hours (kWh)?
Energy in watt-hours: 1,500 W × 4 h = 6,000 Wh
Kilo means 1,000, so divide: 6,000 ÷ 1,000 = 6 kWh
Check: 1,500 W is 1.5 kW, and 1.5 kW × 4 h = 6 kWh. Both ways agree.

lessons.title: Reading the whole task before you calculate
lessons.text:
Practise reading every instruction before you start, then use fractions on a cut list where the last line changes the job.
Why this matters on the job
On a job site, the instruction that changes everything is often at the bottom: "build three of these", "all lengths include the trim", "do not cut until the plans are signed off". People in the trades need to remember and follow procedures with many steps. Every step is a place where things can go wrong. Reading the whole task before you pick up a pencil or a saw is the cheapest check there is.
Key ideas
Before you calculate, read the whole task once from top to bottom. Then ask:
What is the question I have to answer?
What form should the answer take: a number, a length, a list, a yes or no?
Is there anything at the end that changes the start?
Fraction words used on this page:
In 3/8, the numerator is 3 (how many parts) and the denominator is 8 (how many equal parts make the whole).
A proper fraction is less than one whole, such as 3/8.
An improper fraction has a numerator greater than or equal to its denominator, such as 9/8 or 8/8.
A mixed number is a whole number and a fraction, such as 2 3/4.
A fraction is in lowest terms when no number except 1 divides both the top and the bottom.
Worked example
Change 19/8 to a mixed number. 19 ÷ 8 = 2 remainder 3, so 19/8 = 2 3/8. Check: 2 × 8 + 3 = 19.
Practice

lessons.title: Reading a tape measure to the sixteenth
lessons.text:
Read an inch tape to the nearest 1/16 inch, write each reading in lowest terms and compare fractional lengths.
Why this matters on the job
Every cut a carpenter makes starts with a tape reading. On a framing crew in Langley or Kamloops, a stud, a block or a piece of trim is marked from a reading such as 46 7/16 in. A reading that is off by one sixteenth on every piece adds up along a wall. Plumbers, welders and millwrights read the same inch marks on rules and on bolt, drill and wrench sizes.
Key ideas
One inch is split into equal spaces. On most tapes the longest lines mark whole inches. The next longest line marks the half inch, then quarters, then eighths. The shortest lines mark sixteenths, so there are 16 equal spaces in one inch.
The denominator names the size of the space. In 7/16, the 16 says the inch is split into 16 equal spaces. The 7 says how many of those spaces you counted.
Reading a mark, step by step:
Find the last whole inch line before the mark. That is the whole number.
Count the sixteenth spaces from that inch line to the mark.
Write the count over 16.
Put the fraction in lowest terms.
Say the whole reading out loud, whole inches and fraction, so a partner can check it.
Count spaces, not lines. Start counting at the first space after the inch line. If you count the inch line itself as 1, every reading comes out 1/16 in too long.
Lowest terms. Divide the top and the bottom by the same number until no number bigger than 1 goes into both. A quick test for tape fractions: if the numerator is odd, the fraction is already in lowest terms. If it is even, divide the top and the bottom by 2 and test again. Lowest terms change the name of the mark, not where it is: 8/16, 4/8, 2/4 and 1/2 all name the same line.
Comparing lengths. Write both fractions over the same denominator first. For tape fractions, 16 works for halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths. Then the bigger numerator is the longer length.
Let the tool set the precision. A tape marked in sixteenths gives readings to the nearest 1/16 in. Do not write a finer reading than the marks support.
Worked example
A mark is ten sixteenth-inch spaces past the 2 in line.
Whole number: 2
Fraction: 10/16. 10 is even, so divide the top and the bottom by 2: 5/8.
Reading: 2 5/8 in
Check: the mark sits between the 2 1/2 in line and the 2 3/4 in line. 2 5/8 is between them, so the reading makes sense. Writing only "5/8" would lose the two whole inches.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions on a cut list
lessons.text:
Add and subtract fractional lengths and mixed numbers, allow for saw kerf and find the offcut on a cut list.
Why this matters on the job
A cut list tells you how many pieces to cut and how long each one is. Before you cut, you need to know if the pieces fit on the board you have and how long the offcut will be. That means adding and subtracting lengths such as 22 3/8 in and 31 1/2 in, and allowing for the wood the saw blade turns into sawdust. Getting it right saves trips to the lumber rack and wasted boards.
Key ideas
Same denominator: add or subtract the numerators. The denominator stays the same because it names the size of each part. 3/16 + 5/16 = 8/16 = 1/2.
Different denominators: rename first. The parts must be the same size before you add them. For tape fractions, 16 works for halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths. 7/8 − 5/16 = 14/16 − 5/16 = 9/16. Never add the denominators: 1/2 + 1/4 is not 2/6. Rename 1/2 as 2/4, then 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.
Mixed numbers: add the wholes, add the fractions. If the fractions come to one whole or more, carry the whole.
Subtracting mixed numbers: borrow when the top fraction is too small. In 5 1/4 − 2 7/8, you cannot take 7/8 from 2/8. Borrow 1 from the 5 and write it as 8/8: 5 2/8 becomes 4 10/8. Then 4 10/8 − 2 7/8 = 2 3/8.
Repeated pieces: multiply. Four pieces of 11 3/4 in is 4 × 11 3/4 = 47 in.
Saw kerf. Every saw cut turns a strip of wood into sawdust. The width of that strip is the kerf. If the kerf is 1/8 in and you make 3 cuts, 3 × 1/8 = 3/8 in of board is lost. Count the cuts the question describes, and use the kerf it gives.
Check by adding back. Add your answer to the number you took away. You should get the number you started with.
Worked example
Three pieces are on a cut list: 12 3/4 in, 8 5/8 in and 15 1/2 in. What is the total length?
Add the whole numbers: 12 + 8 + 15 = 35.
Rename the fractions in eighths and add: 6/8 + 5/8 + 4/8 = 15/8.
15/8 = 1 7/8. Carry the 1: 35 + 1 = 36.
Total: 36 7/8 in
On the TI-30Xa or the Sharp EL-531XT, key: 12 a b/c 3 a b/c 4 + 8 a b/c 5 a b/c 8 + 15 a b/c 1 a b/c 2 =. The TI-30Xa shows 36⌟7⌟8 and the Sharp shows 36┌7┌8. Both mean 36 7/8.
Tools for this lesson

lessons.title: Converting between fractions, decimals and millimetres
lessons.text:
Change tape fractions to decimal inches and millimetres and back, round a calculator result to the nearest sixteenth, and move between metric units.
Why this matters on the job
BC job sites use both systems. A drawing may give 1,480 mm while your tape reads feet, inches and sixteenths. A cut list may be in feet and inches, a concrete form plan in metres, and a calculator always answers in decimals. Moving between fractions, decimals and millimetres without losing accuracy is part of reading plans and placing orders.
Key ideas
A fraction bar means divide. 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. A size written this way is a decimal inch. For a mixed number, change only the fraction and keep the whole: 2 5/8 in = 2.625 in.
One inch is exactly 25.4 mm. Canadian law defines the yard as 0.9144 m and the inch as 1/36 of a yard, so 1 in = 0.9144 m ÷ 36 = 0.0254 m = 25.4 mm. The factor is exact, not rounded.
Inches to millimetres: multiply by 25.4.
Millimetres to inches: divide by 25.4.
One foot is exactly 0.3048 m, and 12 in = 1 ft.
Check the size of your answer. A millimetre is much smaller than an inch, so a length in millimetres is always the bigger number. If 3/8 in comes out as 0.015 mm, you divided when you should have multiplied.
Fraction Decimal inch Millimetres
1/8 in 0.125 in 3.175 mm
1/4 in 0.25 in 6.35 mm
3/8 in 0.375 in 9.525 mm
1/2 in 0.5 in 12.7 mm
5/8 in 0.625 in 15.875 mm
3/4 in 0.75 in 19.05 mm
7/8 in 0.875 in 22.225 mm
1 in 1 in 25.4 mm
Decimal inches to the nearest sixteenth. A calculator gives an answer such as 2.83 in. Your tape shows sixteenths. To mark it:
Keep the whole inches.
Multiply the decimal part by 16.
Round to the nearest whole number. That is the number of sixteenths.
Write it over 16 and put it in lowest terms.
The fraction key does not round to the tape: 0.83 becomes 83/100, which is not a tape mark. Use the multiply-by-16 method. For finer work on a steel rule, use 32 instead of 16, and say which one you used.
Feet and inches. Change to inches first: multiply the feet by 12 and add the inches. 7 ft 9 1/2 in = 7 × 12 + 9.5 = 93.5 in.
Metric units move by powers of ten. 1 m = 1,000 mm and 1 cm = 10 mm. Going to a smaller unit, the number gets bigger, so multiply. Going to a bigger unit, the number gets smaller, so divide.
Worked example
A metric drawing shows 1,480 mm. You have an inch tape. What do you mark, to the nearest 1/16 in?
Divide by 25.4 to get inches, then multiply by 16 to count sixteenths, in one line: 1,480 ÷ 25.4 × 16 = 932.28 sixteenths.
Round to the nearest whole number: 932 sixteenths.
932 ÷ 16 = 58.25 in = 58 1/4 in, which is 4 ft 10 1/4 in.
Mark 58 1/4 in.

ACCESS Trades Numeracy Textbook, section 5.6, pages 120 to 123, and sections 7.1 to 7.3, pages 164 to 170. Exercise Book, Exercise 7B, Shop problems.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1). Change each fraction to a decimal, or each decimal to a fraction in lowest terms.
a) 3/4 b) 1 7/8 c) 5/16 d) 0.625 e) 0.375
Task 2 (level 1-2). Change to millimetres or metres. Do not round.
a) 12 in to mm b) 3/8 in to mm c) 5/16 in to mm d) 7 ft 9 1/2 in to mm e) 20 ft to m
Task 3 (level 2). Change each length to inches, to the nearest 1/16 in.
a) 762 mm b) 2,000 mm c) 100 mm d) 50 mm e) 1,830 mm (also write it in feet and inches)
Task 4 (level 2). A calculator gives these decimal inches. Change each one to a tape reading.
a) 3.4 in, to the nearest 1/16 in b) 2.83 in, to the nearest 1/16 in c) 0.59 in, to the nearest 1/32 in
Task 5 (level 1). Change the metric units.
a) 2.45 m to mm b) 375 mm to m c) 3.6 m to mm d) 6,096 mm to m e) 42 cm to mm
Task 6 (level 2). Spot the mistake. Explain what went wrong and give the correct answer.
a) A learner changes 3/4 in to millimetres by dividing: 0.75 ÷ 25.4 = 0.03 mm. b) A learner adds 7 ft 9 in as 7 + 9 = 16 in. c) A learner keys 0.83 into the fraction key, gets 83/100 and marks 83/100 in on the tape.

How many millimetres are in one inch? Is that number exact or rounded?
Write 5/8 as a decimal.
You convert a length from inches to millimetres. Should the number get bigger or smaller?
Change 2.83 in to the nearest 1/16 in.
Change 6 ft 8 in to inches.

lessons.title: Order of operations in trade formulas
lessons.text:
Use BEDMAS and the calculator's brackets to work out stud counts, stair totals, perimeters and areas without mixing up the order.
Why this matters on the job
Trade formulas pack several steps into one line: the number of studs in a wall, the total run of a stair, the distance around a frame. If two people work the same line in a different order, they get different answers, and one of them orders the wrong material. BEDMAS is the agreed order, so a formula on a drawing means the same thing to everyone who reads it.
Key ideas
BEDMAS gives the order, from first to last:
Letter Stands for Example
B Brackets ( ) and [ ] (12 + 8) × 3: add 12 + 8 first
E Exponents: squares, powers and roots 100 − 5²: work out 5² first
D and M Division and Multiplication, left to right 24 ÷ 4 × 3: divide first, because ÷ comes first
A and S Addition and Subtraction, left to right 20 − 8 + 2: subtract first, because − comes first
D and M are one step, not two. Work them in the order they appear, left to right. The same goes for A and S.
Rewrite the line after each step. Write the whole calculation again with the part you just worked out replaced by its answer. Each line gets shorter until one number is left.
Brackets inside brackets. Work the innermost pair first, then work outward. On the calculator, every bracket is keyed with the ( and ) keys. Close every bracket you open.
Key the × before a bracket. On paper, 3(4 + 5) means 3 × (4 + 5). On the calculator, always key the × yourself.
Studs in a wall. Studs are set a fixed distance apart, centre to centre, called the spacing on centre (o.c.). There is one more stud than there are spaces:
studs = length ÷ spacing + 1
Divide first, then add 1. If length ÷ spacing is not a whole number, round it up before you add 1, so no space is wider than the spacing. This counts the regular studs only.
Stair totals. In the stairs in this lesson, the upper floor is the top step, so a flight has one tread fewer than it has risers:
total rise = number of risers × unit rise total run = (number of risers − 1) × unit run
The brackets make the subtraction happen before the multiplication.
Worked example
A wall is 4,800 mm long, with studs at 400 mm o.c. How many studs?
BEDMAS divides before it adds: 4,800 ÷ 400 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13 studs.
Brackets in the wrong place change the job: 4,800 ÷ (400 + 1) = 11.97, which is not a stud count.
On the TI-30Xa or the Sharp EL-531XT: 4800 ÷ 400 + 1 = shows 13.
Tools for this lesson
Numeracy Hub, Order of Operations tab: BEDMAS step by step on shape formulas, with the TI-30Xa keys.
ACCESS calculators page: "Watch the keys" presses each key for you.
ACCESS Trades Numeracy Textbook, Chapter 3, pages 67 to 86, and the Exercise Book, Exercise 3K, Carpentry and the BCBC.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1). Work out each line with BEDMAS. Rewrite the line after each step.
a) 6 + 4 × 3 b) 20 − 12 ÷ 4 c) 5 × 6 − 4 × 3 d) 18 ÷ 3 + 2 × 7 e) 8 − 3 × 2 + 1 f) 24 ÷ 4 × 3
Task 2 (level 1-2). Brackets and exponents.
a) (12 + 8) × 3 b) 2 × (450 + 300), the distance around a 450 mm by 300 mm frame c) 2 × [15 − (4 + 6)] d) 100 − 5² e) Nine holes are evenly spaced on a 1,350 mm bar, with the end holes 75 mm from the ends. The spacing is (1,350 − 2 × 75) ÷ 8. Find it.
Task 3 (level 2). Use studs = length ÷ spacing + 1 to count the regular studs.
a) A 3,600 mm wall at 400 mm o.c. b) A 6,000 mm wall at 600 mm o.c. c) A 16 ft wall at 16 in o.c. d) A 4,100 mm wall at 400 mm o.c.
Task 4 (level 2). A stair has 16 risers with a unit rise of 175 mm and a unit run of 255 mm.
a) Find the total rise. b) Find the total run. c) A learner keys 16 − 1 × 255 = and gets −239. What went wrong?
Task 5 (level 2). Work out each formula. Give the area of the ring to two decimal places.
a) A plate is split into two rectangles. Its area in mm² is 300 × 450 + 900 × 250. b) A frame is 600 mm long and 250 mm wide. The distance around it is 2 × (600 + 250). c) A ring has an outside radius of 40 mm and an inside radius of 25 mm. Its area is π × (40² − 25²).
Task 6 (level 2). A pipe run is 7 ft 9 1/2 in long. The length in millimetres is (7 × 12 + 9.5) × 25.4.
a) Write the keys you would press on your calculator, brackets included. b) Work it out. c) What answer do you get if you leave the brackets out? Why is it wrong?
Check yourself
In 24 ÷ 4 × 3, which do you do first, and why?
3(4 + 5) = ?
2 + 3² = ? and (2 + 3)² = ?
Why does the stud formula add 1?

lessons.title: Perimeter and area with openings and cut-outs
lessons.text:
Find the distance around a building or room and the area of walls, floors and plates, take out doors, windows and cut-outs, and count the sheets to order.
Why this matters on the job
Perimeter tells a carpenter how much wall plate, rim joist, fascia or baseboard a job needs. Area tells how many sheets of drywall, sheathing or subfloor to order. On a takeoff, doors and windows come out of the wall area, and holes come out of a plate. Sheets are sold whole, so the count is always rounded up.
Key ideas
Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape. Add the outside edges. For a rectangle:
P = 2 × (length + width)
Area is the flat surface inside a shape, counted in squares. For a rectangle:
A = length × width
Both lengths must be in the same unit. An area always has a small 2 on its unit: mm², m², in², ft².
Square units change by the factor twice. 1 m = 1,000 mm, so 1 m² = 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000 mm². 1 ft = 12 in, so 1 ft² = 12 × 12 = 144 in². To change mm² to m², divide by 1,000,000, not by 1,000. It is often easier to change each length to metres first, then multiply.
Break it down. A composite shape is made of simple shapes.
Split the shape with dashed lines into rectangles, triangles or circles. Label them A, B, C.
Find any missing sizes from the overall sizes.
Find the area of each piece.
Add the pieces. Subtract any opening or cut-out.
When two methods give the same answer, you can trust it. An L shape can be two rectangles added, or one big rectangle with a corner taken away.
Openings and cut-outs. On a wall, subtract the doors and windows the material does not cover. On a plate, subtract the holes. For a round hole, the drawing usually gives the diameter: divide by 2 to get the radius, then use π × r².
Counting sheets. Divide the area by the area one sheet covers, then round up. A result of 3.1 sheets gives a minimum of 4 by area. In this lesson, sheet and stock counts are net-quantity estimates with reusable offcuts and no waste allowance. Before a real order, check the cutting layout, joints, stock lengths, kerf and waste; area alone does not guarantee that the pieces will fit.
Worked example
A wall is 6 m long and 2.4 m high. It has a door 0.9 m by 2.1 m and a window 1.5 m by 1.2 m. Drywall comes in 1.2 m by 2.4 m sheets. How many sheets?
Wall: 6 × 2.4 = 14.4 m²
Door: 0.9 × 2.1 = 1.89 m². Window: 1.5 × 1.2 = 1.8 m²
Net area: 14.4 − 1.89 − 1.8 = 10.71 m²
One sheet: 1.2 × 2.4 = 2.88 m². 10.71 ÷ 2.88 = 3.72
Round up: 4 sheets
Tools for this lesson
Shape Canvas: draw a wall or plate, then draw a shape inside it. A shape that sits inside another starts as a cut-out, and the canvas subtracts its area and shows the cut-outs in red. Use it to check your hand calculations.
Numeracy Hub, Shape Studio tab and Volume, Area, Layout and Measuring tab.
ACCESS Trades Numeracy Textbook, Chapter 9, pages 219 to 231, and Chapter 10, sections 10.1, 10.2, 10.6 and 10.8, pages 242 to 259. Exercise Book, Exercise 10D, Materials takeoff.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1). Perimeter.
a) The outside walls of a house are 12,200 mm by 8,500 mm. Find the perimeter. b) A room is 4.2 m by 3.6 m. Find the perimeter. c) Baseboard runs around the room in part b, except across a door opening 0.9 m wide. How much baseboard is needed?
Task 2 (level 1-2). Area. Give each answer in the units asked.
a) A base plate is 600 mm by 450 mm. Find its area in mm² and in m². b) A sheet is 4 ft by 8 ft. Find its area in ft² and in in². c) A floor is 3.6 m by 2.7 m. Find its area in m².
Task 3 (level 2). Break it down.
a) An L-shaped plate fits in an 800 mm by 600 mm rectangle with a 550 mm by 400 mm corner missing. Find its area two ways: as two rectangles added (250 × 600 and 550 × 200), and as the big rectangle less the corner. Do the answers agree? b) A plate is 400 mm by 300 mm with a hole 160 mm in diameter in the middle. Find its area to two decimal places.
Task 4 (level 2). An exterior wall is 36 ft long and 8 ft high. Take out two windows, each 4 ft by 3 ft, and a door 3 ft by 6 ft 8 in. Sheathing comes in 4 ft by 8 ft sheets.
a) Find the net area in ft². b) How many sheets do you order?
Task 5 (level 2). The house in Task 1a has loadbearing outside walls. The drawings call for one bottom plate and two top plates on every outside wall. Plate stock comes in 4,880 mm lengths. Use the outside perimeter and ignore openings.
a) How much plate is needed? b) How many lengths do you order?
Task 6 (level 2). Open the Shape Canvas. Draw a wall 3,000 mm long and 2,400 mm high. Inside it, draw a door 900 mm wide and 2,100 mm high and a window 1,200 mm wide and 1,000 mm high.
a) Work out the net wall area in m² by hand. b) Compare your answer with the area the canvas shows. If they differ, find out why. c) How many 1.2 m by 2.4 m sheets would cover the net area?
Check yourself
To change an area in mm² to m², what do you divide by?
A calculation gives 3.1 sheets. How many do you buy?
What does "break it down" mean?
Find the area of one 1.2 m by 2.4 m sheet.
Is a 12 m² floor the same as a 12 m perimeter? Explain.

lessons.title: Volume, concrete and waste allowance
lessons.text:
Find the volume of slabs, footings, walls and piers in cubic metres and cubic yards, add a waste allowance and work out how much to order.
Why this matters on the job
Concrete is ordered by volume. If the order is short, the pour has to wait for more concrete. If it is long, the extra is paid for and wasted. A carpenter who forms a garage slab, a footing or deck piers works out the volume from the drawings, adds a waste allowance, and checks the order in cubic metres or cubic yards.
Key ideas
Volume is the space a solid takes up, counted in cubes. The small 3 shows that three lengths were multiplied: mm³, m³, ft³, yd³.
Box or slab: V = length × width × thickness. A slab, a strip footing and a straight wall are all boxes. Round pier (cylinder): V = π × r² × depth.
Change every size to metres first. A slab drawn as 7.2 m by 6 m by 100 mm is 7.2 × 6 × 0.1 m. Mixing metres and millimetres in one line gives an answer 1,000 times too big. 1 m³ = 1,000 L.
Cubic yards. A yard is exactly 0.9144 m, so a cubic yard is 0.9144 × 0.9144 × 0.9144 = 0.764 554 857 984 m³ exactly. A yard is also 3 ft, so 1 yd³ = 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 ft³.
m³ to yd³: divide by 0.9144³ (on the calculator: ÷ 0.9144 x³).
yd³ to m³: multiply by 0.9144³.
ft³ to yd³: divide by 27.
Waste allowance. Some material is always lost on the job. A 10% waste allowance means you order what you need plus 10% of it. In one step, multiply by 1.10. For 8%, multiply by 1.08. For 15%, multiply by 1.15. Apply the allowance once, to the net quantity.
Add the waste before you round. Work out the volume with waste first, then round up once at the end to the unit the supplier sells.
The drawings set the size, and the code sets the minimum. BC Building Code 2024, Division B, Sentence 9.16.4.3.(1) says: "Concrete slabs shall not be less than 75 mm thick exclusive of concrete topping." Take the thickness from the drawings and use the code to check that it is not below the minimum.
Worked example
A garage slab is 7.2 m by 6 m and 100 mm thick. The order adds a 10% waste allowance. How much concrete, in m³ and yd³?
Thickness in metres: 100 mm = 0.1 m.
Volume: 7.2 × 6 × 0.1 = 4.32 m³. In cubic yards: 4.32 ÷ 0.9144³ = 5.65 yd³.
With 10% waste: 4.32 × 1.10 = 4.752 m³, which is 4.752 ÷ 0.9144³ = 6.22 yd³.
Check: 100 mm is not less than the 75 mm minimum in Sentence 9.16.4.3.(1).
Tools for this lesson
Numeracy Hub, Volume, Area, Layout and Measuring tab and Unit Conversions tab.
ACCESS BCBC Part 9 plate for Article 9.16.4.3, slab thickness, and the plate index.
ACCESS Trades Numeracy Textbook, sections 11.1 and 11.2, pages 268 to 270, section 11.8, pages 279 to 286, and section 6.4, pages 142 and 143. Exercise Book, Exercise 11D, Concrete, steel and lumber.
Practice
These are quantity calculations, not structural designs or permission to pour. Sizes and allowances are exercise data. On a real job, use the approved drawings and required checks; satisfying the one quoted slab-thickness clause does not establish full code compliance.
Task 1 (level 1-2). Volume of boxes.
a) A form is 2.4 m by 1.2 m by 0.6 m. Find its volume in m³. b) A tank is 1,200 mm by 600 mm by 500 mm inside. Find its volume in m³ and in litres. c) A mixing tub is 800 mm by 500 mm by 450 mm. How many litres does it hold? How many 20 L pails fill it?
Task 2 (level 2). Convert. Give answers to two decimal places.
a) 3 yd³ to m³ b) 2 m³ to yd³ c) 54 ft³ to yd³
Task 3 (level 2). Waste allowance.
a) A job needs 85 m of pipe. Add a 10% waste allowance. The pipe is sold in 6 m lengths. How many lengths? b) A roof takes 38 sheets of sheathing. Add a 12% waste allowance. How many whole sheets? c) A floor needs 28 m² of plywood. Add a 15% waste allowance. How many m²?
Task 4 (level 2-3). A basement floor is 9.6 m by 7.2 m. The drawings call for a 75 mm slab on 100 mm of granular material.
a) How much concrete, in m³? b) How much granular material, in m³? c) Add a 5% waste allowance to the concrete. The supplier (Fraser Ready-Mix, a fictional company) sells in steps of 0.5 m³. How much do you order? d) Does the slab meet Sentence 9.16.4.3.(1)?
Task 5 (level 2-3). A deck sits on 8 round concrete piers. Each pier is 300 mm across and 1.2 m deep.
a) Find the volume of concrete in m³ and yd³, to two decimal places. b) Add a 10% waste allowance. Give the order in m³ to two decimal places.
Task 6 (level 3). A house has a strip footing 350 mm wide and 100 mm thick under a concrete foundation wall 200 mm thick and 2.4 m high. The footing and the wall each run 40 m.
a) Find the volume of the footing and of the wall in m³. b) Find the total in m³ and in yd³. c) Add an 8% waste allowance. Give the order in m³ and in yd³. d) Write two or three sentences to your crew lead that give the order, say what it includes, and name one thing to check on the drawings before the pour.
Check yourself
How many litres are in 1 m³?
Why do you change millimetres to metres before you multiply?
What do you multiply by to add a 10% waste allowance?
Why do you add the waste before you round up?
A slab is drawn 70 mm thick. What does Sentence 9.16.4.3.(1) say about that?

lessons.title: Right triangles, the 3-4-5 check and squaring a layout
lessons.text:
Use the Pythagorean theorem to find a missing side, check a corner with 3-4-5, and square a frame or a foundation layout with its diagonals.
Why this matters on the job
A wall, a deck or a foundation that is out of square makes every later step harder: sheets and flooring no longer line up with the edges and need tapered cuts. Carpenters check corners with the 3-4-5 method and check whole frames by measuring the diagonals. Both come from one rule about right triangles. The same rule gives the length of a brace or a rafter.
Key ideas
Parts of a right triangle. A right triangle has one 90° corner. The two sides that make the corner are the legs. The side across from the corner is the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is always the longest side.
The Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c², where a and b are the legs and c is the hypotenuse.
To find the hypotenuse, square both legs, add, then take the square root: c = √(a² + b²)
To find a leg, square the hypotenuse and the known leg, subtract, then take the square root: a = √(c² − b²)
If you add the squares when you are looking for a leg, your answer will be longer than the hypotenuse. That cannot happen.
On the calculator, the brackets make it add the squares before the square root. TI-30Xa: ( 400 x² + 250 x² ) √x Sharp EL-531XT: √ ( 400 x² + 250 x² ) =
The 3-4-5 check. 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². If the sides of a triangle are 3, 4 and 5 units, the corner between the 3 and the 4 is square. Any multiple works, in any unit: 300-400-500 mm, 600-800-1,000 mm, 6-8-10 ft. All three numbers must use the same multiple: 3-4-10 is not a 3-4-5 check.
From the corner, mark 3 units along one edge.
From the same corner, mark 4 units along the other edge.
Measure between the marks. If it is exactly 5 units, the corner is square. Longer means the corner is open past 90°. Shorter means it is closed to less than 90°.
Use the largest multiple that fits on the work. A reading error of 1 mm matters less on a long diagonal than on a short one.
Diagonals. A diagonal cuts a rectangle into two right triangles, so d = √(length² + width²). If the opposite sides are equal and both diagonals are equal, every corner is 90°. If the diagonals differ, the two corners at the ends of the longer diagonal are less than 90°. Push those two corners toward each other and measure again until the diagonals match.
Worked example
You mark 600 mm along one side of a wall frame corner and 800 mm along the other. The tape reads 1,006 mm between the marks. Is the corner square?
For a square corner: 600² + 800² = 360,000 + 640,000 = 1,000,000, and √1,000,000 = 1,000 mm.
The tape reads 1,006 mm, which is 6 mm too long.
A diagonal that is too long means the corner is open past 90°.
Not square. Close the corner until the marks are 1,000 mm apart.
Tools for this lesson
Numeracy Hub, Angles, Trig and Chords tab and Carpentry tab.
Shape Canvas: draw a rectangle and read its diagonal, or draw a right triangle with a hidden side.
ACCESS calculators page: "Watch the keys" shows the x² and √ keys.
ACCESS Trades Numeracy Textbook, sections 12.4 to 12.6, pages 301 to 306, and section 12.10, pages 317 to 320. Exercise Book, Exercise 12K, Carpentry and the BCBC.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1-2). Find the hypotenuse. Give answers to two decimal places where needed.
a) Legs 600 mm and 800 mm b) Legs 1,500 mm and 900 mm c) Legs 9 in and 12 in
Task 2 (level 2). Find the missing leg. Give answers to two decimal places where needed.
a) Hypotenuse 1,300 mm, one leg 500 mm b) Hypotenuse 2.5 m, one leg 1.8 m c) A brace 2,000 mm long runs from the floor to a post. Its top end is 1,350 mm above the floor. How far from the post is its bottom end?
Task 3 (level 2). The 3-4-5 check.
a) Marks at 300 mm and 400 mm. What should the diagonal be? b) Marks at 9 ft and 12 ft. What should the diagonal be? c) Marks at 900 mm and 1,200 mm. The diagonal reads 1,494 mm. Is the corner square, open or closed? d) Marks at 1.2 m and 1.6 m. What should the diagonal be? e) Do 5, 12 and 13 make a right triangle? Show the check.
Task 4 (level 2-3). Diagonals.
a) A deck frame is 4,800 mm by 3,600 mm. What should each diagonal measure? b) A frame measures 2,013 mm on one diagonal and 2,020 mm on the other. Is it square? Which corners do you push? c) A door opening is 36 in by 80 in. Find the diagonal to the nearest 1/16 in.
Task 5 (level 2-3). A right triangle has legs of 2 ft 0 in and 1 ft 3 in. Find the hypotenuse to the nearest 1/16 in, in feet and inches.
Task 6 (level 3). A foundation layout for a shop in Prince George is 9,600 mm by 6,000 mm.
a) What 3-4-5 marks would you use at a corner, with 1,200 mm as the unit? b) What should each diagonal measure, to the nearest millimetre? c) The diagonals measure 11,332 mm and 11,309 mm. Is the layout square? d) Write two sentences to the crew telling them what to adjust and how they will know it is right.
Check yourself
Which side of a right triangle is always the longest?
Do you add or subtract the squares to find a leg?
Do 6 ft, 8 ft and 10 ft make a square corner? Show the check.
A frame's diagonals are equal and its opposite sides are equal. What does that tell you?
Why is 3-4-10 not a 3-4-5 check?

lessons.title: Roof slope, stair rise and stair run
lessons.text:
Write a roof slope as a rise in 12 and as 1 in a number, work out the risers, unit rise and total run of a stair, and check them against the BC Building Code.
Why this matters on the job
Roofs and stairs are both about rise and run. A roof slope decides which roofing can go on it. A stair has to fit the height between floors with every step the same, inside the limits of the BC Building Code. Carpenters work these numbers out before cutting a rafter or a stringer.
Key ideas
Slope is a ratio of rise to run. Carpenters write roof slope as a rise in 12: a 4 in 12 roof rises 4 in for every 12 in it runs across. That is the ratio 4 : 12, which simplifies to 1 : 3. The BC Building Code writes the same slope as "1 in 3": 1 unit of rise for 3 units of run.
Rise in 12 to "1 in ?": divide 12 by the rise. 6 in 12 is 1 in 2.
"1 in ?" to rise in 12: divide 12 by the second number. 1 in 4 is 3 in 12.
Rise from run: rise = run × (rise in 12) ÷ 12.
In "1 in ?", a smaller second number means a steeper slope. 1 in 2.4 is steeper than 1 in 3.
What the code says about roof slope. Table 9.26.3.1 of the BC Building Code 2024 sets the minimum slope for each kind of roofing. For asphalt shingles it gives a minimum of 1 in 3 for normal application and 1 in 6 for low slope application, with no maximum.
Stair words. The total rise is the height from finished floor to finished floor. Each step up is a riser. The height of one step is the unit rise and its depth, nosing to nosing, is the unit run. In the stairs in this lesson, the upper floor is the top step, so a flight has one tread fewer than it has risers.
Stair formulas. Work in millimetres.
number of risers = total rise ÷ maximum rise, rounded up to a whole number
unit rise = total rise ÷ number of risers
number of treads = number of risers − 1
total run = number of treads × unit run
Round the number of risers up, never down: rounding down makes each riser taller than the maximum.
What the code says about stairs (BC Building Code 2024, Division B):
What is limited Private stair Public stair Where
Rise, maximum 200 mm 180 mm Table 9.8.4.1
Rise, minimum 125 mm 125 mm Table 9.8.4.1
Run, maximum 355 mm No limit Table 9.8.4.2
Run, minimum 255 mm 280 mm Table 9.8.4.2
Height of one flight not more than 3.7 m not more than 3.7 m Article 9.8.3.3
Risers in one flight 5 mm between adjacent treads or landings, 10 mm between the tallest and shortest the same Sentence 9.8.4.4.(1)
The code measures the rise as "the vertical nosing-to-nosing distance". Private stairs "are exterior and interior stairs that serve" single dwelling units, houses with a secondary suite including their common spaces, and garages that serve those houses. Public stairs "are all stairs not described as service stairs or private stairs." The depth of a rectangular tread "shall be not less than its run and not more than its run plus 25 mm."
Worked example
A private stair in a house has a total rise of 2,690 mm. The drawing gives a unit run of 260 mm.
Risers: 2,690 ÷ 200 = 13.45. Round up to 14 risers.
Unit rise: 2,690 ÷ 14 = 192.14 mm. It is between 125 mm and 200 mm.
Why not 13 risers? 2,690 ÷ 13 = 206.92 mm, taller than the 200 mm maximum.
Treads: 14 − 1 = 13. The unit run of 260 mm is between 255 mm and 355 mm.
Total run: 13 × 260 = 3,380 mm.
Flight height: 2,690 mm is less than 3.7 m (3,700 mm).
Tools for this lesson
Numeracy Hub, Carpentry tab: the math and the BC Building Code.
ACCESS BCBC Part 9 plates: 9.8.3.3 Maximum height of stairs, 9.8.4.1 Rise, 9.8.4.2 Run, 9.8.4.4 Tolerances and 9.26.3.1 Roof slope. The plate index lists all Part 9 plates.
ACCESS Trades Numeracy Textbook, section 6.11, pages 155 to 158, section 8.10, pages 209 to 213, and sections 12.9 and 12.10, pages 312 to 319. Exercise Book, Exercise 12E, Stairs.
Lesson 15 of this set, right triangles, for the length of a rafter or a stringer.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1-2). Roof slope.
a) Write 6 in 12 as "1 in ?". b) Write a slope of 1 in 4 as a rise in 12. c) A roof at 4 in 12 has a run of 4,200 mm. How much does it rise? d) Write 5 in 12 as "1 in ?".
Task 2 (level 2). Use Table 9.26.3.1.
a) Is a 3 in 12 roof steep enough for asphalt shingles in normal application? b) Is a 4 in 12 roof steep enough for asphalt shingles in normal application? c) Is a 3 in 12 roof steep enough for asphalt shingles in low slope application?
Task 3 (level 2). Rafters. The ridge is in the middle of the building, so the run is half the span. Use rafter line length = √(run² + rise²).
a) A building is 7,200 mm wide with a 5 in 12 roof. Find the run, the rise and the rafter line length. b) A building is 9,000 mm wide with an 8 in 12 roof. Find the run, the rise and the rafter line length to two decimal places.
Task 4 (level 2-3). A private stair in a house has a total rise of 2,720 mm. The treads have a unit run of 265 mm.
a) Find the number of risers and the unit rise, to two decimal places. b) Check the unit rise and the unit run against the table. c) Find the number of treads and the total run. d) What would the unit rise be with one riser fewer? Is that allowed?
Task 5 (level 2-3). A public stair has a total rise of 3,150 mm and a unit run of 300 mm.
a) Is one flight allowed for this height? b) Find the number of risers and the unit rise. c) Check the unit run, then find the total run.
Task 6 (level 2). A deck stair has 6 risers of 7 1/4 in and 5 treads with a unit run of 10 1/2 in.
a) Find the total rise and the total run in inches. b) Change the unit rise and the unit run to millimetres (1 in = 25.4 mm). c) Are they inside the private stair limits?
Task 7 (level 3). The risers of a built flight in a house measure, from the bottom: 191, 194, 189, 195, 192 and 190 mm.
a) Find the difference between each pair of neighbouring risers. b) Find the difference between the tallest and the shortest riser. c) Does the flight meet Sentence 9.8.4.4.(1)? d) Write two or three sentences to your supervisor that report what you found and where.
Check yourself
Why do you round the number of risers up, not down?
A flight has 15 risers. How many treads does it have, when the upper floor is the top step?
Write 4 in 12 as "1 in ?".
What is the maximum unit rise for a private stair in the BC Building Code 2024?
A public stair has a unit rise of 185 mm. Is that allowed?

lessons.title: Time math for schedules
lessons.text:
Tell working days from calendar days, add a job's working days to a start date while skipping weekends and BC statutory holidays, work out shift hours on a 24-hour clock, and turn crew-hours into working days.
Why this matters on the job
A schedule counts working days, but people live by the calendar. When a foreman says "the framing takes 8 days", that means 8 days on which the crew works. Weekends and statutory holidays do not count. If you skip that step, you tell the next trade the wrong start date. Crews are also priced and planned in hours, so you need to change hours into days and days into dates.
This is the first of five lessons on project schedules. The next lessons use these skills for Gantt charts, network diagrams, the forward and backward pass, and float.
Key ideas
Calendar days and working days. A calendar day is any day on the calendar. A working day is a day the crew works. In these lessons a working day is Monday to Friday, 8 hours, and not a statutory holiday. Some jobs work other calendars, for example 4 days of 10 hours. Always check which calendar the schedule uses.
BC statutory holidays in 2027. These come from the Province of BC Employment Standards page. Easter Monday and Boxing Day are not statutory holidays in BC.
Holiday 2027 date
New Year's Day Friday, January 1
Family Day Monday, February 15
Good Friday Friday, March 26
Victoria Day Monday, May 24
Canada Day Thursday, July 1
B.C. Day Monday, August 2
Labour Day Monday, September 6
National Day for Truth and Reconciliation Thursday, September 30
Thanksgiving Day Monday, October 11
Remembrance Day Thursday, November 11
Christmas Day Saturday, December 25
Adding working days to a start date. The start day is working day 1. Count forward one working day at a time and skip weekends and holidays. The day you land on for the last number is the finish date. The next activity starts on the next working day.
Duration in working days: count only the working days.
Duration in calendar days: finish date − start date + 1.
The 24-hour clock. Hours run from 00:00 (midnight) to 23:59. For 1 p.m. through 11 p.m., add 12 to the hour: 3:15 p.m. is 15:15. Noon is 12:00 and midnight is 00:00; do not add 12 to the hour in 12 p.m. Many sites, shift logs and equipment hour meters use it.
Elapsed time. Subtract the start time from the end time. If the shift crosses midnight, add 24 hours to the end time first.
Minutes and decimal hours. Divide minutes by 60. 45 min = 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 h, so 7 h 45 min = 7.75 h. To go back, multiply the decimal part by 60: 0.4 h × 60 = 24 min.
Paid hours in a shift. Paid hours = end time − start time − unpaid breaks.
The shift in the picture starts at 06:30 and ends at 17:00. Elapsed time is 17:00 − 06:30 = 10 h 30 min. The unpaid lunch is 30 min, so the worker is paid for 10 h.
Overtime in BC. Under the BC Employment Standards Act, an employee who is not under an averaging agreement gets time-and-a-half for time worked over 8 hours in a day, up to 12 hours, and double time for time over 12 hours in a day. Time over 40 hours in a week is also paid at time-and-a-half, counting only the first 8 hours worked each day. A union contract or an averaging agreement can have different rules, so check yours.
Crew-hours (person-hours). Crew-hours = number of workers × hours each one works.
working days = crew-hours ÷ (workers × hours per day)
If the answer is not a whole number, round up. A part day still ties up the crew for that day.
Worked example 1: a finish date
A crew starts a 10-working-day job on Wednesday, September 1, 2027. When does it finish?
Days 1 to 3 are Wednesday September 1, Thursday September 2 and Friday September 3.
Skip the weekend (September 4 and 5) and Labour Day (Monday, September 6).
Days 4 to 7 are September 7, 8, 9 and 10.
Skip the weekend of September 11 and 12.
Days 8, 9 and 10 are September 13, 14 and 15.
The job finishes on Wednesday, September 15, 2027. The next activity can start on Thursday, September 16.
Calendar days: 15 − 1 + 1 = 15 calendar days for 10 working days.
Worked example 2: crew-hours to days
A drywall crew has 168 crew-hours of board to hang in a suite.
With 3 hangers on 8-hour days: 168 ÷ (3 × 8) = 168 ÷ 24 = 7 working days.
With the same 3 hangers on 10-hour days: 168 ÷ (3 × 10) = 168 ÷ 30 = 5.6. Round up to 6 working days.
On a 10-hour day, each hanger works 2 hours over 8. Unless there is an averaging agreement, those 2 hours are paid at time-and-a-half.
Tools for this lesson
A calculator and a 2027 calendar, or the calendar on your phone.
Lesson 12 of this set, BEDMAS, for formulas with brackets.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1). Time and the 24-hour clock.
a) Write 7 h 45 min as decimal hours.
b) Write 3:15 p.m. on the 24-hour clock.
c) A night paving crew works from 22:40 to 06:10. How long is the shift?
d) Write 0.4 h in minutes.
Task 2 (level 1-2). A crane operator works from 05:45 to 16:15 with a 30-minute unpaid lunch, Monday to Friday.
a) How many paid hours does the operator work each day?
b) How many of those hours each day are overtime under the BC Employment Standards Act? Assume there is no averaging agreement.
c) The operator's regular rate is $42.00 an hour (made up for this task). What is the pay for one week of 5 shifts?
Task 3 (level 2). An electrician starts an 8-working-day rough-in on Thursday, June 24, 2027.
a) On what date does the rough-in finish?
b) How many calendar days is that?
c) On what date can the drywall crew start, if it follows right after?
Task 4 (level 2). A paving crew is booked from Monday, August 2 to Friday, August 13, 2027. How many working days is that? Explain.
Task 5 (level 2). An ironwork crew has 256 crew-hours of rebar to place.
a) How many working days does a crew of 4 need on 8-hour days?
b) How many working days does a crew of 5 need on 8-hour days?
c) The general contractor wants the rebar done in 6 working days of 10 hours. What is the smallest crew that can do it?
Task 6 (level 2-3). The engineer's note on a slab job (fictional) says: "Do not strip forms until at least 7 calendar days after the pour." The slab is poured on Thursday, September 23, 2027.
a) What is the 7th calendar day after the pour?
b) On what date can the crew strip the forms? The crew only works on working days.
c) Why does the note use calendar days and not working days?
Task 7 (level 3). Tidewater Marine Fab (fictional) works a 4-day week: Monday to Thursday, 10 hours a day, with no work on statutory holidays. A job needs 120 welder-hours and 2 welders are on it. It starts on Monday, October 4, 2027.
a) How many working days does the job need?
b) On what date does it finish?
c) Write a two-sentence text to the customer with the finish date and the reason it is later than they expected.
Check yourself
What is the difference between a working day and a calendar day?
A job of 5 working days starts on a Monday with no holidays. On what day does it finish?
Change 30 minutes to decimal hours.
A job needs 90 crew-hours. A crew of 2 works 8-hour days. How many working days does it need?
Is Boxing Day a statutory holiday in BC?

lessons.title: Read and draw a Gantt chart
lessons.text:
Read a Gantt chart's bars, summary bars, milestones, today line and percent complete, compare the baseline with the current schedule, use a three-week look-ahead, and draw your own bars on a time scale.
Why this matters on the job
The Gantt chart is the schedule picture you see most on site. It is pinned up in the site office, shown at the toolbox talk and printed for the weekly coordination meeting. A foreman reads it to know when the crew starts, what must be done first and whether the job is on time. It turns the dates from lesson 17 into bars you can see at a glance.
Key ideas
Parts of a Gantt chart.
Activities are listed down the left side, one per row.
The time scale runs across the top: months, dates and weekdays. Weekends and holidays are shaded because no work is planned on them.
Each bar starts at the start of its first working day and ends at the end of its last working day. A bar that crosses a weekend still counts only the working days.
Critical activities are drawn in a different colour or pattern. If one of them is late, the whole job finishes late. Lesson 21 shows how to find them.
A summary bar is a thick black bar with pointed ends. It runs from the earliest start to the latest finish of the activities under it.
A milestone is a diamond. It marks an event that takes no time, for example "Footings poured" or "Garage complete". Its duration is 0.
The today line is a vertical line at the status date. Everything left of it should be done. Everything right of it is still planned.
Percent complete is shown as a dark strip inside the bar, with a number such as 50%.
The baseline is the plan you saved before work started. A tracking Gantt chart draws a thin grey baseline bar under each current bar, so you can see what has slipped.
A three-week look-ahead is a short Gantt chart taken from the full schedule. It shows only the next three weeks, in more detail, so the foremen can line up crews, material, equipment and inspections.
Reading a bar.
Start date: read the date under the left end of the bar.
Finish date: read the date under the right end of the bar.
Working days: count the unshaded day columns under the bar.
Calendar days: finish date − start date + 1.
Drawing a bar.
Draw the time scale with one column per day. Shade weekends and statutory holidays.
Write the activities down the left in the order the work happens.
For each activity, start the bar at the left edge of the start date and end it at the right edge of the finish date.
Draw milestones as diamonds at the end of the day they happen.
Add a legend so a reader knows what each colour and symbol means.
Worked example: the garage job
Northshore Garage Builders (a fictional company) is building a detached garage with a slab on grade. Work starts on Monday, May 10, 2027. The Gantt chart below shows the plan, with a today line at the start of Thursday, May 20.
Read activity 9, Pour slab:
The bar starts on Friday, May 21 and ends on Tuesday, May 25.
Under the bar are Friday, Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday. Saturday and Sunday are a weekend, and Monday, May 24 is Victoria Day.
Working days: Friday and Tuesday, so 2 working days.
Calendar days: 25 − 21 + 1 = 5 calendar days.
Read the today line:
Activities 1 to 5 and 8 end before the line and show 100%. They are done, as planned.
Activity 7, Under-slab electrical conduit, should have started on May 19, so half of it should be done. It shows 0%. It is critical, so it is a warning sign for the finish date.
Activity 6, the roof trusses, is at 50%. The plan puts it at 6 of its 10 working days, which is 60%. It is a little behind, but trusses are not critical, so there is time to catch up.
The plan for the whole job is in this table.
ID Activity Start Finish
1 Layout and excavate Mon May 10, 2027 Tue May 11, 2027
2 Form footings Wed May 12, 2027 Thu May 13, 2027
3 Place footing rebar Fri May 14, 2027 Fri May 14, 2027
4 Footing inspection Mon May 17, 2027 Mon May 17, 2027
5 Pour footings Tue May 18, 2027 Tue May 18, 2027
6 Order and deliver roof trusses Wed May 12, 2027 Wed May 26, 2027
7 Under-slab electrical conduit Wed May 19, 2027 Thu May 20, 2027
8 Under-slab plumbing Wed May 19, 2027 Wed May 19, 2027
9 Pour slab Fri May 21, 2027 Tue May 25, 2027
10 Frame walls Wed May 26, 2027 Mon May 31, 2027
11 Set trusses and sheathe roof Tue Jun 1, 2027 Thu Jun 3, 2027
12 Shingles Fri Jun 4, 2027 Mon Jun 7, 2027
13 Install overhead door Fri Jun 4, 2027 Fri Jun 4, 2027
M1 Footings poured (milestone) Tue May 18, 2027 Tue May 18, 2027
M2 Garage complete (milestone) Mon Jun 7, 2027 Mon Jun 7, 2027
Practice
Task 1 (level 1). Use the garage Gantt chart.
a) On what date does activity 2, Form footings, start and finish?
b) Frame walls runs from May 26 to May 31. How many working days is that? How many calendar days?
c) On what date is the milestone "Garage complete"?
d) Which date is shaded with hatching, and why?
Task 2 (level 1-2). Summary bars and critical activities.
a) Give the start and finish dates of the Foundations summary bar.
b) Why does the "Framing and roof" summary bar start on May 12, before the walls are framed?
c) List the activities that are not critical.
Task 3 (level 2). The status date is the start of Thursday, May 20.
a) Which activities should be 100% complete?
b) Which activity is behind and on the critical path? What should the site supervisor do today?
c) The trusses show 50%. What percent should they show by the plan? Show your work.
Task 4 (level 2). This tracking Gantt chart shows the same garage job on Monday, May 31. Rain stretched two activities. The grey bars are the baseline.
a) Which two activities took longer than planned, and by how many working days each?
b) "Garage complete" was planned for Monday, June 7. When is it now? How many working days late is that?
c) Frame walls shows 25%. Explain what that means in days.
d) The trusses did not slip. Why did their late finish not matter?
Task 5 (level 2). This is the three-week look-ahead for a parkade foundation, from Monday, June 28 to Friday, July 16, 2027. Its activities and logic come from a real Microsoft Project schedule for a six-storey wood-frame building over a concrete parkade. The dates are set for this lesson.
a) Which activities are planned during the week of July 5 to July 9?
b) On which dates does a concrete pour start in this window? Who needs to know?
c) From June 29 to July 7, two forming activities run at the same time. What does that mean for the forming crews?
d) Why is there no work on July 1?
Task 6 (level 2-3). Riverbend Decks (a fictional company) has this plan for a deck. Draw the bars on the blank grid, or copy the grid onto graph paper. Shade the bars of activities A, B, C, D, E, H and I as critical. Then add a milestone diamond "Deck complete" at the end of the last day.

E Install decking Mon Aug 9, 2027 Tue Aug 10, 2027

Check yourself
What does a diamond mean on a Gantt chart?
What does the today line show?
A bar runs from a Thursday to the next Tuesday with no holidays. How many working days is it?
What is a baseline?
Why do foremen use a three-week look-ahead and not only the full schedule?

lessons.title: Network diagrams and schedule logic
lessons.text:
Draw an activity-on-node network from a predecessor table, name predecessors and successors, and use the four link types (FS, SS, FF, SF) with lag and lead to find when the next activity can start or finish.
Why this matters on the job
A Gantt chart shows when the work happens. A network diagram shows why: which work has to be done before the next work can start. That is called the logic of the schedule. When something changes on site, the logic tells you which other activities move. Planners build the logic first, and the software draws the Gantt chart from it.
Key ideas
Activity. A piece of work with a duration, for example "Pour pier footings, 1 day".
Predecessor and successor. If B cannot start until A is done, A is a predecessor of B and B is a successor of A. A predecessor table lists each activity with its duration and its predecessors.
Activity-on-node (AON). Each activity is a box (a node). Each arrow is a logic link from a predecessor to a successor. Time runs from left to right. AON is the method that scheduling software supports.
Merge and burst. A merge is an activity with two or more arrows coming in. It waits for all of them. A burst is an activity with two or more arrows going out.
Activity-on-arrow (AOA). An older method draws each activity as an arrow between numbered circles (events). When an activity needs two predecessors that do not share an event, AOA needs a dashed dummy arrow that takes no time. AOA cannot show lag, SS or FF links in a clean way, so these lessons use AON.
Day numbers. In these lessons, day numbers count finished working days. Day 0 is the start of the job. "End of day 4" is day 4. An activity that starts at day 4 is worked on during the 5th working day.
The four link types.
Link Short form The rule Example
Finish-to-start FS The successor cannot start until the predecessor finishes. Backfill after waterproofing
Start-to-start SS The successor cannot start until the predecessor starts. Pull wire once conduit has started
Finish-to-finish FF The successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes. Taping finishes after hanging finishes
Start-to-finish SF The successor cannot finish until the predecessor starts. A rented heater runs until the new furnace starts up
FS is by far the most common. SF is rare.
Practice only. Cure, stripping, waterproofing and overlap times on this page are scheduling examples, not safe-work limits. Use the approved specifications, inspections and supervisor or engineer directions on a real job.
Lag and lead. A lag is a wait added to a link, written as a plus number: FS+2 means "start 2 days after the predecessor finishes", for example to let concrete cure. A lead is an overlap, written as a minus number: FS−2 means "start 2 days before the predecessor finishes".
Timing rules for one link. ES is when an activity starts and EF is when it finishes. EF = ES + duration.
FS + lag: successor ES = predecessor EF + lag
SS + lag: successor ES = predecessor ES + lag
FF + lag: successor EF = predecessor EF + lag, so successor ES = that EF − duration
SF + lag: successor EF = predecessor ES + lag
How to draw a network from a predecessor table.
Put the activities with no predecessors on the left.
Place each other activity to the right of all its predecessors.
Draw an arrow from each predecessor to its successor. Write the link type and lag on any arrow that is not plain FS.
Check every intended dependency. A network can have several starting or ending activities, as the garage example does. Connect them to common start/finish milestones when needed, and check that an unlinked activity is intentional rather than missing a dependency.
Check that no arrow path loops back to an earlier box. A loop means "A waits for B and B waits for A", which can never be scheduled.
Worked example 1: the deck network
Riverbend Decks (a fictional company) has this predecessor table for a deck. Durations are in working days.
ID Activity Duration (days) Predecessors
A Lay out and dig post holes 1 none (start)
B Pour pier footings 1 A
C Set posts and beams 2 B FS+2
D Install joists 2 C
E Install decking 2 D
F Cut stair stringers 1 A
G Build stairs 1 E, F
H Install railings 2 E
I Final inspection 1 G, H
A has no predecessors, so it goes on the far left.
B and F both follow A. Put them in the next column. A is a burst.
C follows B with FS+2. The 2-day lag lets the pier concrete cure. Write "FS+2" on that arrow.
D follows C, and E follows D.
G needs E and F. H needs E. Put G and H to the right of E. E is a burst.
I needs G and H, so it is a merge at the far right.
Successors: A → B, F. B → C. C → D. D → E. E → G, H. F → G. G → I. H → I.
Worked example 2: timing each link type
Use the bars in the link type picture.
FS+2. Pour footings finishes at day 1. Strip forms can start at 1 + 2 = day 3.
SS+1. Install conduit starts at day 0. Pull wire can start at 0 + 1 = day 1.
FF+1. Hang drywall finishes at day 4. Tape and mud finishes at 4 + 1 = day 5. It takes 3 days, so it starts at 5 − 3 = day 2.
SF. Start-up of the furnace starts at day 8. The rented heater finishes at day 8 at the earliest. It runs 3 days, so it starts at 8 − 3 = day 5.
Lead, FS−2. Hang drywall finishes at day 4. Tape and mud starts at 4 − 2 = day 2, on the rooms that are already hung.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1). Write the link type (FS, SS, FF or SF) and any lag or lead for each sentence.
a) Paint can start 1 day after the drywall taping is finished.
b) The pipe insulators start 2 days after the pipefitters start, and work behind them.
c) Testing the fire alarm cannot finish until the last device is installed.
d) Backfill starts as soon as the waterproofing is finished.
e) The old electrical service must keep running until the new service is energized.
f) The floor tile setter starts 1 day before the wall tile is finished.
