lessons.title: The forward and backward pass
lessons.text:
Fill in the node box with ES, EF, LS, LF and total float, run the forward pass to find the project duration, run the backward pass to find the latest dates, and handle FS, SS and FF links with lag.
Why this matters on the job
Scheduling software does the forward and backward pass in a split second. You still need to know how it works. When the schedule says your crew can start on day 11 but has until day 14, you need to know where those numbers came from and whether you can trust them. This method is called the critical path method (CPM). It is the math behind every construction schedule.
Key ideas
The node box. Each activity in the network gets a box with six numbers.
ES, early start: the earliest the activity can start.
EF, early finish: ES + Dur.
LF, late finish: the latest it can finish without making the whole job late.
LS, late start: LF − Dur.
TF, total float: LS − ES. It is also LF − EF.
Our day-number rule. In these lessons we count from day 0. A day number means "working days finished so far".
The first activity has ES = 0. That is the start of working day 1.
EF = ES + Dur. An activity with ES 0 and Dur 2 is worked on days 1 and 2 and has EF 2.
With a plain FS link, the successor's ES equals the predecessor's EF. There is no "+1".
To get dates: the activity starts on working day number ES + 1 and finishes on working day number EF.
Some books count from day 1 instead: ES 1, EF = ES + Dur − 1, and the next ES = EF + 1. Both give the same dates. Pick one rule and never mix them on the same schedule.
Forward pass (left to right): find ES and EF.
Activities with no predecessors start at ES = 0.
For each other activity, work out the start that each predecessor allows:
FS + lag: predecessor EF + lag
SS + lag: predecessor ES + lag
FF + lag: predecessor EF + lag − Dur (this comes from EF ≥ predecessor EF + lag)
At a merge, take the largest value. The activity has to wait for the latest predecessor.
EF = ES + Dur.
The project duration is the largest EF of all activities.
Backward pass (right to left): find LF and LS.
Activities with no successors get LF = project duration.
For each other activity, work out the finish that each successor allows:
FS + lag: successor LS − lag
SS + lag: successor LS − lag + Dur (the activity must start by successor LS − lag)
FF + lag: successor LF − lag
At a burst, take the smallest value, including the project duration as an upper limit on every LF. The activity must not hold up any successor or finish after the project. This cap matters with SS links: a successor can start before its predecessor finishes.
LS = LF − Dur. TF = LS − ES.
Checks. The first activities on the longest path have LS = 0. No TF is negative. The activities with TF = 0 join up into an unbroken chain from start to finish. That chain is the critical path.
Worked example 1: the deck (FS links and one lag)
This is the Riverbend Decks (fictional) network from lesson 19. Durations are in working days.
ID Activity Duration (days) Predecessors
A Lay out and dig post holes 1 none (start)
B Pour pier footings 1 A
C Set posts and beams 2 B FS+2
D Install joists 2 C
E Install decking 2 D
F Cut stair stringers 1 A
G Build stairs 1 E, F
H Install railings 2 E
I Final inspection 1 G, H
Forward pass:
A has no predecessor: ES = 0, EF = 0 + 1 = 1.
B follows A: ES = 1, EF = 2. F follows A: ES = 1, EF = 2.
C follows B with FS+2: ES = 2 + 2 = 4, EF = 4 + 2 = 6.
D: ES = 6, EF = 8. E: ES = 8, EF = 10.
G is a merge of E (EF 10) and F (EF 2). Take the largest: ES = 10, EF = 11.
H follows E: ES = 10, EF = 12.
I is a merge of G (EF 11) and H (EF 12). Take the largest: ES = 12, EF = 13.
Project duration = 13 working days.
Backward pass:
I has no successor: LF = 13, LS = 13 − 1 = 12.
G and H both feed I: LF = 12. G: LS = 12 − 1 = 11. H: LS = 12 − 2 = 10.
E is a burst to G (LS 11) and H (LS 10). Take the smallest: LF = 10, LS = 8.
D: LF = 8, LS = 6. C: LF = 6, LS = 4.
B feeds C with FS+2: LF = 4 − 2 = 2, LS = 1.
F feeds G (LS 11): LF = 11, LS = 10.
A is a burst to B (LS 1) and F (LS 10). Take the smallest: LF = 1, LS = 0.
Total float: F has 10 − 1 = 9 days. G has 11 − 10 = 1 day. All the others have 0. The critical path is A, B, C, D, E, H, I.

B Pour pier footings 1 1 2 1 2 0 yes

E Install decking 2 8 10 8 10 0 yes
F Cut stair stringers 1 1 2 10 11 9 no

The deck starts on Tuesday, July 27, 2027. Activity C has ES 4, so it starts on working day 5. Working days 1 to 4 are July 27, 28, 29 and 30. Monday, August 2 is B.C. Day, so working day 5 is Tuesday, August 3.
Worked example 2: SS and FF links with lag
A drywall crew works in a small office (a fictional job). Tape and mud has two links from Hang drywall: SS+1 and FF+1.
ID Activity Duration (days) Predecessors
A Hang drywall 4 none (start)
B Tape and mud 3 A SS+1, A FF+1
C Sand and prime 2 B FS+1
D Install ceiling grid 3 A
E Final clean 1 C, D
Forward pass:
A: ES 0, EF 4.
B: SS+1 gives 0 + 1 = 1. FF+1 gives 4 + 1 − 3 = 2. Take the largest: ES = 2, EF = 5. The FF link controls B. Taping cannot finish until a day after hanging finishes.
C: FS+1 from B gives 5 + 1 = 6. EF = 8.
D: FS from A gives 4. EF = 7.
E: merge of C (EF 8) and D (EF 7). ES = 8, EF = 9. Project duration = 9 days.
Backward pass:
E: LF 9, LS 8. C: LF 8, LS 6. D: LF 8, LS 5.
B feeds C with FS+1: LF = 6 − 1 = 5, LS = 2.
A has three links out. SS+1 to B gives 2 − 1 + 4 = 5. FF+1 to B gives 5 − 1 = 4. FS to D gives 5. Take the smallest: LF = 4, LS = 0.
D has TF = 5 − 4 = 1 day. All the others are critical.

lessons.title: Float and the critical path
lessons.text:
Work out total float and free float, find the critical path and the near-critical activities, predict what a late activity does to the finish date, and shorten a schedule at the lowest cost with cost slopes.
Why this matters on the job
Float is spare time in the schedule. A foreman who knows where the float is can move a crew to where it is needed without making the job late. A foreman who does not know can lose a whole week by holding up one critical activity. When the owner asks "can we finish sooner?", the critical path tells you where extra crews or overtime will help, and where they would only waste money.
Key ideas
Total float (TF). How many days an activity can slip without making the whole job finish late. TF = LS − ES = LF − EF.
Free float (FF). How many days an activity can slip without making any successor start late. Work it out for each successor link, then take the smallest:
FS + lag: successor ES − lag − EF
SS + lag: successor ES − lag − ES
FF + lag: successor EF − lag − EF
No successor: project duration − EF
Free float is never bigger than total float.
Float is shared. Several activities in a row often share the same total float. If the first one uses it up, the ones after it have none left. Free float is the part that belongs to one activity alone.
Critical path. The chain of activities with TF = 0 that runs from the start to the finish. It is the longest path through the network, and its length is the project duration. A critical activity that is 1 day late makes the job 1 day late, unless something else is sped up.
Near-critical. Activities with only a little float, for example 1 or 2 days. Keep an eye on them. A small slip makes them critical.
What happens when an activity slips. Here a slip means shifting an activity's start and finish later together, with its duration and other constraints unchanged. With plain FS links, a duration increase has the same downstream effect. With SS or FF links, it may not: redo the passes when duration changes, as in Task 5b.
If the slip is not more than its TF, the finish date does not move. The float absorbs the delay. The activities after it lose some float.
If the slip is more than its TF, the job finishes late by (slip − TF) days.
The critical path can change. An activity that had float can become critical.
Crashing. Crashing means shortening critical activities by adding crew, equipment or overtime. It costs money.
Cost slope = (crash cost − normal cost) ÷ (normal duration − crash duration). It is the extra cost for each day saved.
For one critical path, compare the feasible one-day reductions on that path. Choose the lowest extra cost for the next day saved, within each activity's crash limit.
With several critical paths, compare combinations that shorten every critical path. A shared activity may shorten several paths at once, but a combination of separate activities may cost less. Count the cost of a shared activity once.
After each proposed change, redo the passes or check all paths. Confirm that the project really finishes sooner: a near-critical path may now control the finish. Repeat until the target is reached or no feasible reduction remains. A cheapest next step is not, by itself, proof of the cheapest complete multi-day plan; compare the full feasible combinations when asked for the overall minimum.
Example: two critical paths share one activity that costs $300 to shorten by a day. Their separate branches can each be shortened by a day for $100 and $150. Either option saves a project day, but the two-activity combination costs $250, less than the shared activity. Shortening just the $100 branch saves no project time.
Never pay to crash an activity that is not critical. The finish date will not move.
Worked example 1: total float and free float
This is the parkade foundation from lesson 19, with the activities and logic of a real Microsoft Project schedule. The dotted lines show total float.
ID Activity Dur ES EF LS LF TF FF Critical?
42 Form footings grid A-D 5 0 5 0 5 0 0 yes
43 Rebar footings grid A-D 4 2 6 4 8 2 0 no
44 Pour footings grid A-D 3 6 9 8 11 2 2 no
45 Form footings grid E-H 4 3 7 3 7 0 0 yes
46 Rebar footings grid E-H 4 5 9 5 9 0 0 yes
47 Pour footings grid E-H 2 9 11 9 11 0 0 yes
48 Footings complete 0 11 11 11 11 0 0 yes
50 Form foundation walls north 6 11 17 11 17 0 0 yes
51 Rebar walls north 5 13 18 13 18 0 0 yes
52 Pour walls north 7 18 25 18 25 0 0 yes
53 Form foundation walls south 6 11 17 13 19 2 0 no
54 Rebar walls south 4 13 17 15 19 2 0 no
55 Pour walls south 6 17 23 19 25 2 0 no
56 Waterproof walls north 7 30 37 30 37 0 0 yes
57 Waterproof walls south 7 28 35 30 37 2 2 no
58 Drainage and protection board 6 32 38 32 38 0 0 yes
59 Backfill foundation walls 6 35 41 35 41 0 0 yes
60 Foundation walls complete 0 41 41 41 41 0 0 yes
Look at activities 43 and 44.
43, Rebar footings A-D: TF = 4 − 2 = 2. Its only successor is 44 (FS). FF = 44's ES − 43's EF = 6 − 6 = 0.
44, Pour footings A-D: TF = 8 − 6 = 2. Its successor is 50 (FS). FF = 50's ES − 44's EF = 11 − 9 = 2.
Both have 2 days of total float, but it is the same 2 days. If the rebar crew takes 2 extra days, the pour also moves 2 days and has no float left. That is why 43 has no free float. The float "belongs" to 44, the last activity before the merge at 50.
The south wall chain, 53 to 57, works the same way: TF 2 on each, and only 57 has FF 2.
The critical path is 42, 45, 46, 47, 48, 50, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 60. Its length is 41 working days.
Worked example 2: crashing the deck
The deck in lessons 19 and 20 takes 13 days, with critical path A, B, C, D, E, H, I. The owner of Riverbend Decks (fictional) wants it done in 10 days. These are the costs (made up for practice):
Activity Normal days Crash days Normal cost Crash cost Cost slope
C Set posts and beams 2 1 $1,400 $2,000 $600 a day
D Install joists 2 1 $1,600 $2,050 $450 a day
E Install decking 2 1 $2,400 $2,750 $350 a day
H Install railings 2 1 $1,800 $2,100 $300 a day
Cost slope of H: ($2,100 − $1,800) ÷ (2 − 1) = $300 a day.
Day 1. The cheapest critical activity is H at $300. Crash H to 1 day. The path through H is now 12 days. The path through G was 1 day shorter, so it is now also 12 days long. The job takes 12 days, and G is now critical too.
Day 2. H cannot go below 1 day. Both paths pass through E, so crash E at $350. The job takes 11 days.
Day 3. Next cheapest is D at $450. The job takes 10 days.
Total extra cost: $300 + $350 + $450 = $1,100.
F, Cut stair stringers, still has float: it went from 9 days to 6 days. Paying to speed it up would save nothing.

Scheduling lab: predict, test and explain

lessons.title: Markup, margin and pricing a job
lessons.text:
Add up what a small job costs, set a price with a markup, and tell markup from margin so the job makes the money you planned.
Why this matters on the job
A lead hand who prices a small repair, a contractor who quotes a set of deck stairs, and a shop that sells a fabricated railing all do the same math. They add up what the job costs, then add enough on top to pay for the business and leave a profit. If the price only covers the cost, the work was done for nothing. If the math mixes up markup and margin, the job can earn less than the owner thinks.
Key ideas
Cost is what the job costs the company: material, labour and equipment. These are the direct costs of the job.
Overhead is what the business pays to stay open whether or not this job happens: the truck, insurance, the phone, the shop, the bookkeeper. Many small companies add overhead to each job as a percent of the direct cost.
Price is what the customer pays. Profit = price − cost.
Markup is the profit as a percent of the cost.
price = cost × (1 + markup). A 20% markup means multiply by 1.20.
markup % = (price − cost) ÷ cost × 100
Margin is the profit as a percent of the price.
price = cost ÷ (1 − margin). A 20% margin means divide by 0.80.
margin % = (price − cost) ÷ price × 100
The same job always has a bigger markup than margin, because the cost is smaller than the price. A 20% markup is only a 16.67% margin. Say which one you mean.
Brackets first (BEDMAS). In (price − cost) ÷ cost × 100, do the subtraction in the brackets first, then divide, then multiply.
Sales tax goes on after the price. In BC the GST is 5%. It is added on top of the price and passed on to the Canada Revenue Agency. It is not part of your profit. Lesson 23 shows how GST works on a construction invoice.
Worked example
Alder Street Renovations (a fictional company) is asked to replace a 6 m section of fence.
Item Cost
Material: posts, rails, boards, screws, concrete $640.00
Labour: 2 workers × 8 h × $45.00 an hour $720.00
Equipment: auger rental for the day $90.00
Direct cost $1,450.00
The company adds 10% for overhead and a 20% markup for profit.
Overhead: $1,450.00 × 0.10 = $145.00
Total cost: $1,450.00 + $145.00 = $1,595.00
Price with a 20% markup: $1,595.00 × 1.20 = $1,914.00
Profit: $1,914.00 − $1,595.00 = $319.00
Margin: $319.00 ÷ $1,914.00 × 100 = 16.67%
The owner asked for a 20% markup and got it. The margin on the same job is 16.67%.
Tools for this lesson
A calculator. On the HP 10bII+ (lesson 3), press = after each step so the order is the same in Chain or Algebraic mode.
Numeracy Hub, Construction Operations tab.
Lesson 3, credit card interest, for more practice with percents of money.
Practice

Task 5 (level 3). A supplier lists a steel gate at $3,450.00. Contractors get 15% off the list price. The contractor installs it and charges the customer the list price for the gate.

lessons.title: Progress claims, holdback and GST
lessons.text:
Work out a monthly progress claim from percent complete, take off the 10% holdback the BC Builders Lien Act requires, add GST, and find when the holdback is paid.
Why this matters on the job
On a building job, a subcontractor does not wait until the end to get paid. Each month it sends a progress claim: a bill for the work done that month. Part of every claim is kept back by law as holdback and paid weeks after the work is finished. A crew lead who can read a claim knows how much money is really coming in, and can spot a mistake before it costs the company.
Key ideas
Schedule of values. The contract price is split into lines, one for each part of the work. Each month the sub estimates how much of each line is done, as a percent.
value to date = line value × percent complete
this month's claim = total value to date − total claimed last month
Change orders. An approved change order adds to (or takes away from) the contract price. Add it to the value to date when the work is done.
Reading lesson 20 (What is in a construction contract) walks through these rules in a contract. Here you do the math. Holdback. The BC Builders Lien Act, section 4, says the person paying on a contract or subcontract must keep back a holdback equal to 10% of the work. So 10% of each claim is held back. Section 4 also says a holdback must not be kept from a worker or a material supplier.
Holdback period. When the work is finished, the payment certifier issues a certificate of completion. Under section 8 the holdback period ends 55 days after that certificate is issued. After the holdback period ends, the holdback can be paid, unless someone has filed a claim of lien. Under section 20, a lien for that work must be filed no later than 45 days after the certificate is issued.
A law that is coming. BC passed the Construction Prompt Payment Act in November 2025. When it comes into force, it will change the 55 days to 46 days. On the date of this lesson it was not yet in force. Check BC Laws before you use the 55 days on a real job.
GST on a progress claim. In BC the GST is 5%. The holdback comes off first. GST is charged on the amount being paid now, the claim less the holdback. The Canada Revenue Agency says the GST on the holdback becomes payable when the holdback is paid or when the holdback period ends, whichever comes first. Do not assume that delayed release also delays the GST: use the earlier of payment and the end of the holdback period stated above.
The claim in four lines (BEDMAS: work out each line before the next):
holdback = this month's claim × 0.10
net claim = this month's claim − holdback
GST = net claim × 0.05
amount due = net claim + GST
Worked example
Coastline Framing Ltd. (a fictional company) has a $120,000 subcontract with Northbank Builders (a fictional general contractor) to frame a small commercial building.
Line Value Done at end of March Value to date
Floor framing $30,000 100% $30,000
Wall framing $45,000 40% $18,000
Roof framing $35,000 0% $0
Sheathing $10,000 0% $0
Total $120,000 $48,000
This is the first claim, so nothing was claimed before. This month's claim is $48,000.00.
Holdback: $48,000.00 × 0.10 = $4,800.00
Net claim: $48,000.00 − $4,800.00 = $43,200.00
GST: $43,200.00 × 0.05 = $2,160.00
Amount due: $43,200.00 + $2,160.00 = $45,360.00
Northbank keeps $4,800.00 as holdback until the holdback period ends.
Tools for this lesson

Practice

Task 3 (level 2-3). Claim 3, end of May. All four lines are 100% done. Northbank also approved change order CO-1 for an extra beam, worth $4,000. The beam is installed.

What is the amount of that invoice? d) If the Construction Prompt Payment Act were in force, the holdback period would be 46 days. On what date would it end?

lessons.title: Loans and interest for a truck or tools
lessons.text:
Work out simple and compound interest, follow a loan payment month by month, and compare the total cost of loans of different lengths before you borrow for a truck or tools.
Why this matters on the job
Many tradespeople borrow to buy a work truck, a trailer or a full set of tools. The dealer or bank shows a monthly payment, and a lower payment looks like a better deal. It often is not. The total you pay back depends on the interest rate, the length of the loan and any fees. This lesson shows you how to work out the real cost before you sign.
Key ideas
Principal is the amount you borrow. Interest is what the lender charges for the loan. The term is how long you have to pay it back.
Simple interest is charged on the principal only:
interest = principal × yearly rate × time in years
Interest on a loan you pay monthly. Each month the lender charges one month of interest on what you still owe:
month's interest = balance × yearly rate ÷ 12
Your payment covers that interest first. The rest of the payment comes off the balance (the principal). Early in the loan, more of each payment goes to interest. As the balance drops, more goes to principal.
Compound interest is interest charged on interest. If you make no payments, each month's interest is added to the balance, and the next month's interest is charged on the bigger balance.
Total cost of a loan.
total paid = monthly payment × number of payments (the last payment may differ by a few cents)
interest paid = total paid − amount borrowed
cost of borrowing = interest + any other charges, such as an admin fee
Longer is not cheaper. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada (FCAC) says that the longer you take to pay off a loan, the more expensive it is. A longer term gives a lower payment but more interest in total. FCAC calls car loans of 72 months (6 years) or more long-term loans.
What the lender must tell you. For a personal loan from a federally regulated lender, such as a bank, FCAC says the lender must disclose the annual interest rate, the annual percentage rate (APR) if it is different, the payments, and the cost of borrowing. FCAC also says that by law lenders may not charge more than 35% interest a year.
Worked example
Sam is buying a used work truck for $28,000.00. Sam puts $3,000.00 down and borrows the rest at 7.9% a year for 60 months. The lender's payment is $505.71 a month.
Loan: $28,000.00 − $3,000.00 = $25,000.00
First month's interest: $25,000.00 × 0.079 ÷ 12 = $164.58
Principal paid in month 1: $505.71 − $164.58 = $341.13
Balance after month 1: $25,000.00 − $341.13 = $24,658.87
Total paid over the loan: $505.71 × 60 = $30,342.60
Interest paid: $30,342.60 − $25,000.00 = $5,342.60
The truck really costs: $28,000.00 + $5,342.60 = $33,342.60
On the HP 10bII+
Lesson 3 introduced the time value of money (TVM) keys: N (number of payments), I/YR (yearly interest rate), PV (present value), PMT (payment) and FV (future value). For a normal loan the payment is at the end of each month, so BEGIN must not show on the screen. Money you receive is positive and money you pay out is negative. Task 8 uses these keys.
Tools for this lesson

lessons.title: Payback and break-even
lessons.text:
Decide whether a tool, an upgrade or a small business pays for itself by working out the payback period, rent-or-buy days and the break-even point.
Why this matters on the job
"Should we buy it or keep renting it?" "Will new lights pay for themselves?" "How many hours do I need to bill each month to keep my truck on the road?" Crews and small contractors ask these questions all the time. Each one has the same kind of answer: how long, or how many, until the money saved or earned covers the money spent. That point is the payback or the break-even.
Key ideas
Payback period. How long until the savings pay back what you spent.
payback period = cost ÷ saving per month (or per year)
If the saving is per month, the answer is in months. If it is per year, the answer is in years.
Net saving. If the new tool also costs something to run, take that off first. Brackets first (BEDMAS):
payback period = cost ÷ (saving per month − extra running cost per month)
Rent or buy. Divide the price to buy by the rental cost per day. That is how many days of rental the price would pay for.
Break-even in units. A business has fixed costs that stay the same however much it makes (a jig, set-up time, a truck payment, insurance) and a variable cost for each unit (material and labour per piece, or wage and fuel per hour). Each unit sold at a price brings in a contribution:
contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit
Below the break-even point the business loses money. Above it, each unit adds its contribution to profit.
When the savings are not even. Add up the savings period by period in a table (a running total). The payback is where the running total reaches the cost.
Assumptions. Every payback answer rests on guesses: how often the tool is used, how long it lasts, what the rental rate will be. Write them down. If a guess is wrong, the answer is wrong.
Worked example
A fabrication crew rents a magnetic drill for $85.00 a day. A new one costs $2,550.00. The crew uses it about 3 days a month.
Rental days the price would pay for: $2,550.00 ÷ $85.00 = 30 days
Months to reach 30 days of use: 30 ÷ 3 = 10 months
If the drill lasts much longer than 10 months, buying pays for itself. The answer assumes the crew keeps using it 3 days a month and the rental rate stays at $85.00.
Tools for this lesson
A calculator.
Creativity and Innovation lesson 11, Measure an improvement, which finds break-even in time saved.
Lesson 22, markup and margin, for price and cost.
Numeracy Hub, Construction Operations tab.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1-2). A shop replaces its old lights with LED fixtures. The job costs $3,600.00. The power bill goes down by $150.00 a month. What is the payback period in months? In years?
Task 2 (level 2). A pipe crew rents a power pipe threader for $120.00 a day. Buying one costs $4,200.00. The crew uses it about 3 days a month.
a) How many days of rental would the price pay for? b) About how many months until buying pays for itself?
Task 3 (level 2). A small shop buys a $2,400.00 air compressor so it no longer has to send work out. It saves 6 hours of labour a month at $45.00 an hour. Power and upkeep for the compressor cost $30.00 a month. What is the payback period?
Task 4 (level 2-3). A shop makes railing brackets. A welding jig and set-up cost $1,800.00. Each bracket costs $14.00 in steel and labour and sells for $26.00.
a) What is the contribution per bracket? b) How many brackets must the shop sell to break even? c) What is the profit if it sells 200 brackets?
Task 5 (level 3). Riley runs a one-truck electrical business. Fixed costs are $6,300.00 a month: truck payment, insurance, phone and shop rent. Riley charges $95.00 for each hour billed. Each billed hour costs $50.00 in wages, payroll costs and fuel.
a) How many hours a month must Riley bill to break even? b) What is the profit in a month with 160 billed hours? c) What happens in a slow month with 120 billed hours?
Task 6 (level 3). A crew lead wants a $10,000.00 trailer-mounted tool crib that saves set-up and travel time. The savings are not the same each year:
Year Saving that year Running total
1 $3,000.00
2 $4,000.00
3 $4,000.00
4 $4,000.00
a) Fill in the running total. b) In which year does the running total pass $10,000.00? c) Find the payback period to two decimal places of a year, assuming savings build up evenly within each year.
Task 7 (level 3). Look back at Task 2. Write two assumptions the answer depends on. For each one, say what happens to the payback if it turns out wrong.
Task 8 (level 3). Write two or three sentences to Riley in Task 5 that give the break-even hours and say what a slow month means in dollars.
Check yourself

Rental is $50.00 a day and buying costs $1,500.00. How many days of rental is that?

In the break-even formula, what do you work out first?
Why should you write down the assumptions behind a payback answer?

lessons.title: What a machine or crew costs per hour
lessons.text:
Work out the owning and operating cost of a machine per hour, add the payroll costs on top of a wage, and build a charge-out rate for a crew.
Why this matters on the job
An estimator prices work by the hour: so many hours of a loader, so many hours of a crew. A machine costs money even when it sits in the yard. A worker costs the company more than the wage on the pay stub. If the hourly cost is too low, every job loses money and nobody can see why. This lesson builds the hourly cost step by step.
Key ideas
Owning cost is what a machine costs just to own.
Depreciation per hour = (purchase price − salvage value) ÷ hours of life. The salvage value is what the machine is worth when it is sold or traded in.
Yearly fixed costs per hour = (insurance + interest on the money + licence + storage) ÷ hours used per year.
Operating cost is what a machine costs to run, per hour.
Fuel = litres per hour × price per litre
Tires or tracks = cost of a set ÷ hours they last
Repairs and maintenance, from the company's records
Machine cost per hour = owning cost + operating cost. The operator is costed separately, as labour.
A machine that sits costs more per hour. The yearly fixed costs are the same whether the machine works 1,200 hours or 600 hours. Fewer hours means each hour carries more of them.
Labour burden. On top of the wage, an employer pays:
vacation pay: in BC, at least 4% of total wages after 5 calendar days of work (Employment Standards Act, section 58)
CPP: the employer pays the same amount as the employee
EI: the employer pays 1.4 times the employee's premium
WorkSafeBC premiums: the company's premium rate × its assessable payroll. The rate depends on the industry (the classification unit). The premium is paid by the business.
A company adds these up as a burden percent on the wage. The CPP and EI amounts depend on the year's rates and maximums, and the WorkSafeBC rate depends on the company, so in this lesson they are given as job data.
Charge-out rate. The company adds overhead and profit on top of the hourly cost, as a markup (lesson 22).
charge-out rate = cost per hour × (1 + markup)
Worked example
Granite Ridge Excavating (a fictional company) owns a compact track loader.
Data Value
Purchase price $96,000.00
Salvage value 35% of the price
Life 6,000 hours
Hours used a year 1,000 hours
Insurance, interest and storage $7,800.00 a year
Fuel 6 L an hour at $1.85 a litre
Tracks $3,600.00 a set, lasts 1,800 hours
Repairs and maintenance $4.50 an hour
Owning cost
Salvage value: $96,000.00 × 0.35 = $33,600.00
Depreciation: ($96,000.00 − $33,600.00) ÷ 6,000 = $62,400.00 ÷ 6,000 = $10.40 an hour
Fixed costs: $7,800.00 ÷ 1,000 = $7.80 an hour
Owning cost: $10.40 + $7.80 = $18.20 an hour
Operating cost
Fuel: 6 × $1.85 = $11.10 an hour
Tracks: $3,600.00 ÷ 1,800 = $2.00 an hour
Operating cost: $11.10 + $2.00 + $4.50 = $17.60 an hour
Machine cost per hour: $18.20 + $17.60 = $35.80 an hour, without the operator.
Crew cost per hour. A crew of a carpenter at $42.00 an hour and an apprentice at $28.00 an hour. On this payroll the burden is 15%: 4% vacation pay, 8.2% employer CPP and EI, and 2.8% WorkSafeBC.
Wages: $42.00 + $28.00 = $70.00 an hour
Crew cost: $70.00 × 1.15 = $80.50 an hour
Charge-out with a 25% markup: $80.50 × 1.25 = $100.625, which rounds to $100.63 an hour
Tools for this lesson
A calculator.
Lesson 22, markup and margin.
Lesson 1, pay stubs, for CPP and EI from the worker's side.
WorkSafeBC, Know how much coverage costs: https://www.worksafebc.com/en/insurance/know-coverage-costs
Numeracy Hub, Construction Operations tab.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1-2). A mini excavator costs $58,000.00. Its salvage value is 30% of the price. It lasts 5,000 hours.
a) What is the salvage value? b) What is the depreciation per hour?
Task 2 (level 2). The mini excavator's insurance, interest and storage come to $6,000.00 a year.
a) What is the fixed cost per hour if it works 1,200 hours a year? b) What if it works only 600 hours a year? c) Explain in one sentence why the answers are different.
Task 3 (level 2). A skid steer burns 4.5 L of fuel an hour at $1.90 a litre. A set of tires costs $1,440.00 and lasts 1,200 hours. Repairs run $3.25 an hour. Find the operating cost per hour.
Task 4 (level 2-3). Back to the mini excavator in Tasks 1 and 2, working 1,200 hours a year. It burns 5 L an hour at $1.90 a litre. Tracks cost $2,400.00 and last 1,500 hours. Repairs run $3.50 an hour.
a) Find the operating cost per hour. b) Find the machine cost per hour (owning plus operating). c) For this fictional comparison, a rental yard charges $380.00 for an 8-hour day, including fuel, maintenance and all machine charges but excluding the operator. What is that per hour? d) Is owning cheaper per hour than renting when the machine works 1,200 hours a year? Name one thing that could change the answer.
Task 5 (level 2). A pipefitter apprentice earns $36.00 an hour. On this payroll the burden is 4% vacation pay, 8.2% employer CPP and EI, and 2.8% WorkSafeBC.
a) Find each burden amount per hour, to the cent. b) What is the total burden percent? c) What does one hour of this apprentice cost the company?
Task 6 (level 3). Granite Ridge prices a 6-hour job: the loader from the worked example and the two-person crew. Use $35.80 an hour for the loader and $80.50 an hour for the crew. The company adds a 25% markup to both.
a) Find the cost of the loader and of the crew for 6 hours, and the total cost. b) Find the price before GST. c) Add 5% GST. What is the total?
Task 7 (level 3). Spot the mistake. A new estimator prices a carpenter at $42.00 an hour × 1.25 markup = $52.50 an hour.
a) What did the estimator leave out? b) With the 15% burden, what does the carpenter cost the company per hour? c) What should the charge-out rate be with a 25% markup? How much was lost on each hour?
Task 8 (level 3). Write two or three sentences to the owner of Granite Ridge. Say what the loader costs per hour, what the crew costs per hour, and why the loader would cost more per hour if it worked fewer hours a year.
Check yourself

lessons.title: Will the job run out of cash
lessons.text:
Lay out the money coming in and going out of a small crew month by month, find the month the bank balance is lowest, and work out how big a line of credit the crew needs.
Why this matters on the job
A small crew can win good work, price it well and still run out of money. The crew is paid every two weeks. The supplier wants its money in 30 days. The general contractor pays 30 days after the claim, keeps 10% as holdback, and pays that weeks after the job is done. A cash flow forecast shows, month by month, whether there will be enough money in the bank. Anyone who wants to run a crew one day needs to read one.
Key ideas
Cash flow is money in and money out of the bank, in the month it actually moves. It is not the same as profit. A job can make a profit over the season and still leave the bank account below zero for some months.
Money in comes when the customer pays, not when the work is done or billed.
Money out goes when the company pays, not when it buys or uses something.
For each month:
total in = all the money in that month
total out = all the money out that month
net cash flow = total in − total out
balance at end of month = balance at start + net cash flow
The balance at the end of one month is the balance at the start of the next.
What moves the timing on a construction job:
Progress claims and holdback (lesson 23). The general contractor keeps 10% of each claim as holdback, as the BC Builders Lien Act requires, and pays it after the holdback period. GST is paid on the claim less holdback.
Supplier terms. "Net 30" means the bill is due 30 days after the invoice.
Payroll remittances. The money an employer takes off pay for income tax, CPP and EI, plus the employer's own CPP and EI, goes to the Canada Revenue Agency. A regular remitter must have it to the CRA by the 15th of the month after the employees were paid.
GST. GST collected on claims belongs to the CRA. A company that files every quarter must file and pay no later than one month after the end of the quarter.
Classroom timing model. For these monthly tables, treat 30-day terms as payment in the following month and 60-day terms as payment two months later. This is a planning simplification, not exact calendar-day counting. Use actual invoice and payment dates for a real forecast. The tables exclude credit interest and fees, and month-end balances can miss a larger cash shortfall earlier in a month.
Line of credit. A bank lets the company go below zero up to a set limit, and charges interest on what it uses. The lowest balance in the forecast shows how big the limit needs to be. Most owners add a cushion for surprises.
Worked example
Kestrel Roofing Ltd. (a fictional company) is a two-person roofing crew. It starts April with $8,000.00 in the bank. In April it claims $24,000.00 of work from the general contractor. The contractor pays in May, 30 days later: it keeps 10% holdback and adds 5% GST to what it pays.
Holdback: $24,000.00 × 0.10 = $2,400.00
Paid now, before GST: $24,000.00 − $2,400.00 = $21,600.00
GST: $21,600.00 × 0.05 = $1,080.00
Money in, May: $21,600.00 + $1,080.00 = $22,680.00
In one step: $24,000.00 × 0.90 × 1.05 = $24,000.00 × 0.945 = $22,680.00.
April has no money in, because nothing is paid until May. April's money out is $11,400.00. So:
April net cash flow: $0.00 − $11,400.00 = −$11,400.00
Balance at end of April: $8,000.00 + (−$11,400.00) = −$3,400.00
Kestrel is already below zero after the first month, on a job that will make money.

lessons.title: Estimate a job's time and cost
lessons.text:
Use a past job, a unit rate or a bottom-up list to estimate a job, work a three-point time estimate with BEDMAS, and build a cost estimate with labour, material and contingency.
Why this matters on the job
Before a crew starts, somebody has to say how long the job will take and what it will cost. The owner uses the time to plan around the work. The company uses the cost to set a price and to check later whether the job made money. A lead hand who can estimate a task well is the person a foreman asks first. A guess that is too low costs the company money. A guess that is too high loses the job to another company.
This lesson comes after the five scheduling lessons (lesson 17 to lesson 21). Those lessons took the durations as given. This lesson shows where durations and costs come from.
Key ideas
Three ways to estimate.
Way How it works Example
From a past job Use what a similar job took or cost before. Quick, but only as good as the match. "The last 8-section handrail cost $6,000."
From a unit rate Multiply or divide a quantity by a rate per unit from your records. 360 m² of wall ÷ 20 m² an hour = 18 hours
Bottom-up Break the job into pieces, estimate each piece, then add them up. Slowest, but the most detailed. Labour + material + consumables + contingency
Good estimators use more than one way and compare the answers. If a bottom-up estimate and a past-job check are far apart, something is missing or wrong.
Three-point estimate. Ask for three numbers for each task:
O, optimistic: the best case, when everything goes well
M, most likely: what usually happens
P, pessimistic: the worst case you can realistically expect
Two ways to combine them:
Simple average: (O + M + P) ÷ 3
PERT average: (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6
PERT counts the most likely number four times, so it leans toward what usually happens. When the worst case is much further from M than the best case is, both averages come out higher than M. On most jobs that is the case: a task can run late by a lot more than it can run early.
BEDMAS in the PERT formula. In (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6, work inside the brackets first. Inside the brackets, multiply 4 × M before you add. Then divide the whole bracket by 6. On a calculator, key the brackets: ( O + 4 × M + P ) ÷ 6 =
Hours to days. A three-point estimate in crew-hours turns into working days the same way as in lesson 17: working days = crew-hours ÷ (workers × hours per day), rounded up.
Bottom-up cost. List each part of the cost:
Labour: hours × hourly rate
Material: from the take-off (lessons 13 and 14)
Consumables: welding wire, gas, discs, blades, fasteners
Equipment: rentals and machine time
Contingency: a percentage added for things that are likely to go wrong but cannot be named yet. Contingency = subtotal × contingency %.
Cost is not price. This lesson stops at cost. The price the customer pays also adds the company's overhead and profit, and tax where it applies. That is a separate step. Lesson 22 (Markup, margin and pricing a job) covers it.
Worked example 1: a three-point time estimate
Riverbend Decks (fictional, from lessons 19 to 21) is estimating "Install decking" on a new deck. The lead hand gives three numbers in crew-hours: O = 20 h, M = 24 h, P = 40 h. The worst case allows for a delivery of warped boards that have to be sorted.
Simple average: (20 + 24 + 40) ÷ 3 = 84 ÷ 3 = 28 crew-hours.
PERT: (20 + 4 × 24 + 40) ÷ 6. Multiply first inside the brackets: 4 × 24 = 96. Then add: 20 + 96 + 40 = 156. Then divide: 156 ÷ 6 = 26 crew-hours.
Both are higher than the most likely 24 h, because the worst case is far from the most likely case.
A crew of 2 on 8-hour days: 26 ÷ (2 × 8) = 26 ÷ 16 = 1.625. Round up: 2 working days.
Worked example 2: a bottom-up cost estimate
Coastline Steel Works (fictional) is estimating a steel handrail of 10 sections, built in the shop and installed on site. All rates and prices are made up for practice.
Line Working Cost
Shop labour 10 sections × 6 h each = 60 h, × $50.00/h $3,000.00
Install labour 2 workers × 2 days × 8 h = 32 h, × $50.00/h $1,600.00
Steel tube and plate from the take-off $1,800.00
Anchors and bolts from the take-off $200.00
Consumables wire, gas, grinding discs $250.00
Primer 2 cans $150.00
Subtotal $7,000.00
Contingency 10% $7,000.00 × 0.10 $700.00
Estimated cost $7,700.00
Check against a past job: the last handrail had 8 sections and cost $6,000. That is $6,000 ÷ 8 = $750 a section. For 10 sections: 10 × $750 = $7,500. The bottom-up estimate of $7,700 is close, so nothing big seems to be missing.
Lesson 29 follows this handrail through the shop and checks whether it stays on budget.
Tools for this lesson
A calculator with brackets.

Lesson 17, Time math for schedules, for crew-hours to days and counting working days.

Practice

c) "We did the same washroom layout on the floor below. It took 9 days."
d) "Our records show what concrete footings cost per metre of footing, so I multiplied that by the length on this drawing."
e) "I priced the stairs, the railing and the decking one at a time, then added 10%."

b) Hang drywall in a suite, in crew-hours: O = 30, M = 36, P = 54

c) The painters work 8-hour days. How many working days is that?

Line Details

Pump $1,240.00
Pipe, fittings and valves $360.00
Consumables $40.00

c) The company adds 15% contingency on pump jobs, because old piping often has to be replaced. Find the contingency and the estimated cost.

Activity O M P
A Dig and pour piers 1 1 4
B Frame posts, beams and joists 2 3 4
C Install decking and railings 2 2 8
a) Find the PERT average for each activity.
b) Add the PERT averages. Add the most likely numbers. Compare the two totals.
c) Round the PERT total up to whole working days.
d) The job starts on Monday, June 7, 2027. Using your answer to c), on what date does it finish? There are no statutory holidays in that part of June.

lessons.title: Is the job on budget?
lessons.text:
Compare percent complete with percent spent, find the actual unit cost and the projected over or under, and use planned value, earned value and actual cost to say whether a job is on budget and on schedule.
Why this matters on the job
An estimate is a promise about money. Once the work starts, someone has to check that promise every week. A crew can be busy all day and still lose money, because the work is costing more per unit than the estimate allowed. The sooner a foreman sees that, the sooner it can be fixed: a better method, a different crew mix, or a talk with the owner about a change. Waiting until the job is done only tells you how much was lost.
This lesson follows lesson 28, Estimate a job's time and cost. It uses the same handrail job.
Key ideas
Part A: unit cost
Estimate. Estimated cost = estimated quantity × estimated unit rate. For example, 800 m² of drywall at $12.00 a square metre.
Two percentages that should match.
Percent complete = quantity done ÷ total quantity × 100
Percent spent = cost to date ÷ estimated cost × 100
If percent spent is bigger than percent complete, the work is costing more than planned.
Actual unit rate. Actual unit rate = cost to date ÷ quantity done.
Projected cost at the finish.
Quantity left = total quantity − quantity done
Cost to finish = quantity left × unit rate
Projected total = cost to date + cost to finish
Projected over or under = projected total − estimated cost. A plus answer is over budget. A minus answer is under budget.
Which rate for the work left? If the reason for the higher cost is over (a one-time delay, a crew learning a new method), price the rest at the estimate rate. If the reason will carry on (the walls are harder than the drawings showed), price the rest at the actual rate. When you are not sure, work out both and report the range.
A wrong quantity. If the take-off was short, the job loses money even when the crew works at the estimate rate. Always check the quantity as well as the rate.
Part B: earned value
Earned value compares three numbers at the same date. All three are in dollars.
Term Short form What it means
Budget at completion BAC The total budget for the job
Planned value PV The budget for the work the schedule says should be done by now
Earned value EV The budget for the work that is actually done by now
Actual cost AC What the work done so far actually cost
Variances (a minus answer is bad news):
Cost variance: CV = EV − AC. Minus means over budget.
Schedule variance: SV = EV − PV. Minus means behind schedule.
Indexes (1 is right on plan, less than 1 is bad news):
Cost performance index: CPI = EV ÷ AC. A CPI of 0.9 means each $1.00 spent earned only $0.90 of work.
Schedule performance index: SPI = EV ÷ PV. An SPI of 0.8 means the crew has done 80% of the work planned by now.
Forecast. If the job keeps costing what it costs now, the estimate at completion is EAC = BAC ÷ CPI. Use the CPI straight from the calculator, not a rounded one. The variance at completion is VAC = BAC − EAC.
Worked example 1: unit cost on drywall
A drywall crew (fictional) has an estimate of 800 m² of board hung at $12.00 a square metre for labour. Made-up rates for practice.
Estimated cost: 800 × $12.00 = $9,600.
After one week, 300 m² is hung and labour has cost $4,200.
Percent complete: 300 ÷ 800 × 100 = 37.5%. Percent spent: $4,200 ÷ $9,600 × 100 = 43.75%. More is spent than is done.
Actual unit rate: $4,200 ÷ 300 = $14.00 a square metre.
Quantity left: 800 − 300 = 500 m².
At the actual rate: 500 × $14.00 = $7,000. Projected total: $4,200 + $7,000 = $11,200. That is $11,200 − $9,600 = $1,600 over.
At the estimate rate: 500 × $12.00 = $6,000. Projected total: $4,200 + $6,000 = $10,200. That is $600 over.
The crew says the slow part is cutting around many small windows, and the rest of the floors are the same. The reason carries on, so $1,600 over is the better forecast.
Then a field measure shows the walls total 900 m², not 800 m². Quantity left: 900 − 300 = 600 m². At $14.00: 600 × $14.00 = $8,400. Projected total: $4,200 + $8,400 = $12,600. That is $3,000 over.
Worked example 2: earned value on the handrail
Coastline Steel Works (fictional) is building the 10-section handrail from lesson 28. The budget is $700 a section, so BAC = 10 × $700 = $7,000. The schedule says 3 sections a week. At the end of week 2:
The plan says 6 sections should be done. PV = 6 × $700 = $4,200.
The crew has finished 5 sections. EV = 5 × $700 = $3,500.
Labour and material so far have cost $4,000. AC = $4,000.
CV = EV − AC = $3,500 − $4,000 = −$500. Over budget.
SV = EV − PV = $3,500 − $4,200 = −$700. Behind schedule, by one section's worth of work.
CPI = EV ÷ AC = $3,500 ÷ $4,000 = 0.875. Each $1.00 spent has earned $0.875 of work.
SPI = EV ÷ PV = $3,500 ÷ $4,200 = 0.83. The crew has done 83% of the work planned by now.
EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = $7,000 ÷ 0.875 = $8,000. VAC = $7,000 − $8,000 = −$1,000.
In one sentence: "The handrail is one section behind and $500 over budget, and if nothing changes it will finish about $1,000 over."
The lesson 28 estimate held $700 of contingency, so a $1,000 overrun would use all of it and $300 more.
Tools for this lesson
A calculator.

Practice

a) What is the estimated labour cost?
b) What is the percent complete?
c) What is the percent spent?
d) Is the job ahead of or behind its budget so far? How can you tell?

a) What is the estimated cost?
b) What is the actual unit rate?

Task 3 (level 3). Use the formwork job from Task 2. A field check finds a wall that was missed in the take-off. The real total is 680 m², not 600 m². The crew keeps working at the actual rate.
a) Find the quantity left, the cost to finish, the projected total and the projected over or under.
b) How much of the overrun comes from the missed 80 m² priced at the estimate rate?
c) How much comes from the crew's higher rate on all 680 m²?

Task 4 (level 2-3). A pipe shop (fictional) is building 8 pipe spools with a budget of $1,500 each. At the end of week 3, the plan says 5 spools should be done. The shop has finished 6, and the actual cost so far is $8,400.
a) Find BAC, PV, EV and AC.
b) Find CV and SV. Say what each one means in words.
c) Find CPI and SPI.
d) Find EAC and VAC.

Task 5 (level 3). A small builder (fictional) tracks a garage with a budget of $40,000. These are the running totals at the end of each week.
End of week PV EV AC
1 $8,000 $8,000 $8,000
2 $18,000 $16,000 $17,000
3 $28,000 $24,000 $25,500
4 $36,000 $32,000 $34,000
a) Find CV, SV, CPI and SPI for each week. Round the indexes to two decimal places.
b) In which week did the job first fall behind and go over budget?
c) Find EAC and VAC at the end of week 4.
d) At the end of week 4, what is the percent complete (EV ÷ BAC) and the percent spent (AC ÷ BAC)?
e) How much money will it take to finish the garage if nothing changes? (EAC − AC)
Task 6 (level 3). Use your week 4 answers from Task 5. Write a two-sentence cost and schedule update for the owner. Say whether the job is on budget and on schedule, and give the forecast cost at the finish.
Check yourself
A job is 40% complete and 50% spent. Is it over or under budget so far?
What does a negative cost variance mean?
A job has 10 sections budgeted at $500 each. Four are done. What is the earned value?
BAC is $10,000 and CPI is 0.8. What is the estimate at completion?
Why is a short take-off quantity a problem even if the crew works at the estimate rate?

lessons.title: Scrap, rework and control charts
lessons.text:
Work out scrap rate, first-pass yield and labour productivity, find what scrap and rework cost, plan how many parts to start, and read a control chart to tell normal variation from a signal.
Why this matters on the job
Every part that goes in the scrap bin was paid for twice: once for the material and once for the hours someone put into it. Every part that has to be fixed costs more hours again. In a fabrication shop, a wall-panel plant or a pipe shop, scrap and rework are often the difference between a job that makes money and one that does not (lesson 29 shows how that loss shows up in the budget). A control chart is a simple picture that tells the crew when a machine or a process has started to drift, before it makes a pile of bad parts.
Key ideas
Scrap, rework and yield
Scrap: a part that cannot be used and is thrown out or recycled.
Rework: a part that fails the first check but can be fixed, then passes.
Scrap rate = scrapped parts ÷ parts made × 100
First-pass yield = parts that passed the first time ÷ parts made × 100. Parts that passed the first time = parts made − scrapped − reworked.
Good parts = parts made − scrapped. Reworked parts count as good once they are fixed, but they cost extra hours.
How many to start. To end up with a number of good parts when you expect some scrap:
parts to start = good parts needed ÷ (1 − scrap rate as a decimal)
Divide first, then round up. Rounding down leaves you short.
Productivity
Labour productivity = good output ÷ labour hours. For example, good brackets per labour hour. Scrap and rework lower productivity, because the hours are spent but fewer good parts come out.
Cost of scrap and rework.
Each scrapped part loses its material cost plus the labour already in it.
Each reworked part costs the extra hours to fix it × the hourly rate.
Control charts
Nothing is ever made exactly the same twice. A saw cuts one stud a little long and the next a little short. That everyday spread is normal variation. A control chart shows whether the process is only showing normal variation, or whether something has changed.
How a common type, the X-bar chart, works:
At set times, measure a small sample, for example 5 parts each hour, and plot the average of the sample as one point.
The centre line is the average of all the sample averages.
The upper control limit (UCL) and lower control limit (LCL) are set 3 standard deviations above and below the centre line. For an X-bar chart, these are standard deviations of the sample averages, not of individual parts. The limits come from the process's own past data, not from the drawing.
Signals that something has changed. Stop and look for a cause when you see:
One point outside a control limit.
A run: 8 points in a row on the same side of the centre line.
Points inside the limits with no pattern are normal variation. Leave the process alone. Adjusting the machine for every small change adds more variation, not less.
Control limits are not the drawing's limits. The drawing or the customer says what size a part must be. Control limits say what this process normally does. A process can be in control and still make parts that miss the drawing. That is a problem for the supervisor to raise, not a reason to move the control limits.
Working out the limits (level 3). For an X-bar chart with a sample of 5 parts:
Find the average and the range (largest − smallest) of each sample.
Centre line = the average of the sample averages.
R̄ (R-bar) = the average of the ranges.
UCL = centre line + 0.577 × R̄ and LCL = centre line − 0.577 × R̄. The number 0.577 is a factor from a quality-control table for samples of 5.
A second chart, the R chart, tracks the ranges. For samples of 5, its upper limit is 2.114 × R̄ and its lower control limit is 0. A range above that limit means the parts are spreading out more than normal.
Worked example 1: scrap and productivity
Northshore Rail Fab (fictional) cut and welded 400 brackets in a week. 20 were scrapped. 30 failed the first check and were reworked. The crew worked 100 labour hours, rework included. All costs are made up for practice.
Scrap rate: 20 ÷ 400 × 100 = 5%.
Passed the first time: 400 − 20 − 30 = 350. First-pass yield: 350 ÷ 400 × 100 = 87.5%.
Good parts: 400 − 20 = 380.
Labour productivity: 380 ÷ 100 = 3.8 good brackets per labour hour. With no scrap it would have been 400 ÷ 100 = 4.0.
Each scrapped bracket had $8 of steel and $12 of labour in it, so $20 each. Cost of scrap: 20 × $20 = $400.
Each rework took 0.5 h at $50.00 an hour. Cost of rework: 30 × 0.5 × $50.00 = $750.
Lost to scrap and rework this week: $400 + $750 = $1,150.
Worked example 2: reading a control chart
Cedar Ridge Panels (fictional) pre-cuts studs for wall panels. The cut list length is 2,400 mm. Each hour the lead hand measures 5 studs and plots their average. From earlier samples, the shop has set the centre line at 2,400.0 mm, the UCL at 2,403.0 mm and the LCL at 2,397.0 mm.
Samples 1 to 8 go up and down around the centre line, all inside the limits. That is normal variation. No action.
Sample 8, at 2,398.6 mm, is the lowest so far, but it is still inside the limits. No action.
Sample 12, at 2,403.8 mm, is above the UCL. That is a signal. Stop and look for a cause.

lessons.title: Setting heights with a builder's level
lessons.text:
Carry an elevation from a benchmark with backsights and foresights, fill in a level book and check it, and work out the rod reading, cut or fill for a footing, a slab or a pipe.
Why this matters on the job
Every footing, slab form, drain and fence top on a site is set to an elevation on the drawings. The heights all come from one fixed point, the benchmark. A carpenter or pipe layer reads a rod through a level, adds and subtracts, and marks the height on a stake or a form. One wrong sum can put a whole footing 100 mm too low, so the work is written down and checked before anyone pours.
Key ideas
Elevation is the height of a point above a reference. In this lesson elevations are in metres to three decimals, for example 100.000. The benchmark (BM) is a fixed point whose elevation is known.
Backsight (BS). The first rod reading after you set up the level, taken on a point of known elevation (the benchmark or a turning point). A backsight is added. It is also called a plus sight.
Height of instrument (HI). The elevation of the line of sight through the level.
HI = known elevation + BS
Foresight (FS). A rod reading on a point whose elevation you want. A foresight is subtracted. It is also called a minus sight.
elevation of the point = HI − FS
A big rod reading means the point is low. A small rod reading means the point is high.
Turning point (TP). When the next point is too far away or out of sight, put the rod on a solid point that will not move, take a foresight on it, move the level, and take a backsight on the same point. The turning point carries the elevation forward.
Intermediate sight (IS). A detail-point reading from the same setup also uses elevation = HI − reading, but does not carry the level run forward. Keep these readings separate from the final foresight at each setup.
The arithmetic check. For a connected level run, add the backsights and the foresights that carry the run through turning points to its final point. Do not add intermediate detail sights. Then:
sum of BS − sum of FS = last elevation − first elevation
If the two sides do not match, there is a mistake in the sums. Find it before anyone builds from the numbers.
Rod reading for a design height. To set a form or a stake to a design elevation:
rod reading needed = HI − design elevation
Raise or lower the form until the rod reads that number on top of it.
Cut and fill. Compare the ground with the design elevation.
ground − design is positive: the ground is too high. That is cut (dig it down).
ground − design is negative: the ground is too low. That is fill (build it up).
Good habits. Keep the backsight and foresight about the same length at each setup. Write every reading in the book the moment you read it. Use BEDMAS: add the backsight first, then subtract the foresight.
Worked example
A gravel pad for a small shop must be at design elevation 99.500. The benchmark is a nail in a power pole, elevation 100.000. The level is set up between the pole and the pad.
Backsight on the BM: 1.425. HI = 100.000 + 1.425 = 101.425
Intermediate sight on corner A: 1.875. Elevation A = 101.425 − 1.875 = 99.550
Foresight on corner B: 2.010. Elevation B = 101.425 − 2.010 = 99.415
Corner A: 99.550 − 99.500 = +0.050. Cut 50 mm.
Corner B: 99.415 − 99.500 = −0.085. Fill 85 mm.
To set a grade stake at 99.500, the rod must read 101.425 − 99.500 = 1.925 on top of the stake.
The level book for this setup:
Point BS HI IS FS Elevation Notes
BM 1.425 101.425 100.000 nail in pole
A 1.875 99.550 cut 0.050
B 2.010 99.415 fill 0.085
Check the run from BM to B: 1.425 − 2.010 = −0.585, and 99.415 − 100.000 = −0.585. The intermediate shot at A is excluded. A passing arithmetic check does not prove the field readings are correct; recheck against known control before building.

lessons.title: Percent grade between two points on a site
lessons.text:
Work out the grade between two elevations as a percent, as 1 in a number and in degrees, find the fall a drain or path needs, check a ramp against the BC Building Code, and change lot areas between hectares and acres.
Why this matters on the job
Driveways, sidewalks, ramps, drain pipes and the ground around a building all slope on purpose. The slope moves water away and lets people and machines move safely. A drawing gives the slope as a grade, such as 2%, or as "1 in 12". On site you work out the grade from two elevations and a distance, or work out how much fall a pipe needs, and check it against the drawing or the code.
Key ideas
Grade compares rise with run. The rise is the difference in elevation. The run is the horizontal distance between the points.
grade (%) = rise ÷ run × 100
1 in n: n = run ÷ rise
rise = run × grade (%) ÷ 100
angle in degrees = tan⁻¹(rise ÷ run), with your calculator in degree mode
Use BEDMAS. Find the difference in elevation first, then divide, then multiply by 100. Keep all the digits until the last step, then round.
From elevations. A point at 48.920 and a point at 48.380 are 27.0 m apart. Rise = 48.920 − 48.380 = 0.540 m. Grade = 0.540 ÷ 27.0 × 100 = 2%. Water runs from the higher point to the lower point, so say which way the grade falls.
Percent and "1 in" are two ways to write the same slope. You met "1 in n" for roofs in lesson 16.
% to 1 in n: n = 100 ÷ percent. 5% is 1 in 20.
1 in n to %: percent = 100 ÷ n. 1 in 12 is 8.33%.
A bigger percent, or a smaller n, is steeper.
Percent is not degrees. A 100% grade rises 1 m for every 1 m of run. That is 45°, not 100°. A 10% grade is only 5.71°.
Horizontal, not along the ground. Grade uses the horizontal distance. A tape laid along a gentle slope reads only a little more. A drive with a rise of 1.200 m that measures 16.045 m along the ground is √(16.045² − 1.200²) = 16.000 m horizontally (lesson 15).
What the BC Building Code 2024 says about ramps and grading (Division B):
What Limit Where
Exterior ramp, Part 9 building not more than 1 in 10 Article 9.8.5.4
Interior ramp serving a residential occupancy, Part 9 not more than 1 in 10 Article 9.8.5.4
Ramp in an industrial occupancy, Part 9 not more than 1 in 6 Article 9.8.5.4
Ramp in any other occupancy, Part 9 not more than 1 in 8 Article 9.8.5.4
Ramp in an accessible path of travel not more than 1 in 12 Clause 3.8.3.5.(1)(b)
Accessible path of travel steeper than 1 in 20 must be designed as a ramp Clause 3.8.3.2.(3)(g)
Ground around a Part 9 building graded "so that water will not accumulate at or near the building" Article 9.14.6.1
Article 9.8.5.4 covers pedestrian ramps that are not in an accessible path of travel. Ramps in an accessible path follow Article 3.8.3.5 (Article 9.8.5.1).
Worked example
A garage slab is at 101.350. The curb at the street is at 100.150. The horizontal distance is 16.0 m.
Rise: 101.350 − 100.150 = 1.200 m
Grade: 1.200 ÷ 16.0 × 100 = 7.5%, falling toward the street
1 in n: 16.0 ÷ 1.200 = 13.33, so 1 in 13.33
Angle: tan⁻¹(1.200 ÷ 16.0) = 4.29°
Areas of lots: hectares and acres
Land is often listed in hectares (ha) or in acres.
1 ha = 10,000 m². A lot 100 m by 100 m is 1 ha.
1 acre = 4,840 square yards = 4,046.856 m² (to three decimals).
m² to ha: divide by 10,000. ha to acres: multiply by 10,000, then divide by 4,046.856.

lessons.title: Reading between the lines of a chart
lessons.text:
Find a value between two rows of a chart with a straight-line estimate, work a chart backwards, round in the safe direction, and know when a chart says you must not estimate between rows.
Why this matters on the job
Trade charts give values in steps: every 10 degrees, every 25 feet, every 4 metres. Your number often falls between two rows. A heater's fuel use, a sealant's cure time or the height of a pipe between two manholes can be estimated from the rows on either side. Some charts, such as crane load charts, say you must not do that. Knowing which is which keeps the job safe.
Key ideas
Interpolation means finding a value between two rows of a chart by assuming a straight line between them.
Find the two rows on either side of your number.
Find how far along the gap you are, as a fraction: fraction = (your number − first row) ÷ (second row − first row).
Find the change in the value between the two rows: change = second value − first value. It can be negative.
Estimate = first value + fraction × change.
Use BEDMAS: work out the brackets, then divide and multiply, then add.
Working a chart backwards. Sometimes you know the value and want the row. Swap the columns: find the fraction from the values, then use it on the rows.
Round in the safe direction. Ask what happens if you are a little off.
Fuel or material to order: round up, so you do not run short.
A time to wait, such as a cure time: round up, so you do not load it too soon.
A largest size allowed, such as the longest hose before the pressure drops too far: round down, so you stay inside the limit.
Exact or estimate? Interpolation is exact only when the thing really changes in a straight line, such as a pipe laid at one steady grade. For most charts it is a close estimate.
When not to interpolate. If the chart's notes tell you how to read between rows, follow the notes. Many crane load charts carry a printed note like this one, from a manufacturer's boom truck chart: "When the boom length or lift radius or both are between values listed, the smallest load shown at either the next larger radius or next longer or shorter boom length shall be used." On a lifting chart, never work out a load between rows yourself. The chart notes and the lift plan decide.
Worked example 1: a heater's fuel use
This practice chart for a site heater was written for this lesson. It is not for any real product.
Outside temperature Fuel use
−20 °C 7.5 L/h
−10 °C 6.0 L/h
0 °C 4.5 L/h
10 °C 3.0 L/h
How much fuel does the heater use at −4 °C?
−4 °C is between −10 °C (6.0 L/h) and 0 °C (4.5 L/h).
Fraction = (−4 − (−10)) ÷ (0 − (−10)) = 6 ÷ 10 = 0.6
Change = 4.5 − 6.0 = −1.5 L/h
Estimate = 6.0 + 0.6 × (−1.5) = 6.0 − 0.9 = 5.1 L/h
For an 8-hour night: 8 × 5.1 = 40.8 L. Round up: bring at least 41 L.
Worked example 2: working backwards, in feet and inches
This practice chart for a sprayer hose was written for this lesson.
Hose length Pressure loss
25 ft 4 psi
50 ft 8 psi
100 ft 15 psi
150 ft 21 psi
The sprayer works if the loss is not more than 12 psi. What is the longest hose you can use?
12 psi is between 8 psi (50 ft) and 15 psi (100 ft).
Fraction = (12 − 8) ÷ (15 − 8) = 4 ÷ 7 = 0.5714
Length = 50 + 0.5714 × (100 − 50) = 50 + 28.571 = 78.571 ft
0.571 ft × 12 = 6.86 in, so 78.571 ft is 78 ft 6.86 in.
This is a largest size allowed, so round down: 78'-6".

lessons.title: Site coordinates with northing, easting and azimuth
lessons.text:
Read site points written as northing and easting, change bearings to azimuths and back, find the distance and direction between two stakes, and work out the coordinates of a new point from a distance and an azimuth.
Why this matters on the job
On a larger site, the surveyor sets control points and gives every corner, pile and pipe a pair of coordinates. A layout crew turns those numbers into stakes in the ground, and checks the stakes before anyone builds. Knowing which number is north and which is east, and how a direction is written, stops a building from going in mirrored, turned or in the wrong place.
Key ideas
Northing and easting. A site grid has a north axis and an east axis. A point's northing (N) is how far north it is on the grid. Its easting (E) is how far east. In this lesson coordinates are in metres to three decimals.
Which comes first? Surveying and most mapping give a point as (North, East). Math graphs give (x, y), with x pointing east, so the east number comes first. Never trust the order. Always read the N and E labels. In this lesson every point is written with labels, for example N 5,030.000 E 2,040.000.
Differences. Going from point 1 to point 2:
ΔN = N of point 2 − N of point 1. Positive means north, negative means south.
ΔE = E of point 2 − E of point 1. Positive means east, negative means west.
Azimuth. The direction of a line, measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°. East is 90°, south is 180°, west is 270°.
Bearing. The direction as an angle of 0° to 90° from north or south, turned toward east or west. N 30° E means: face north, turn 30° toward east. S 40° W means: face south, turn 40° toward west.
Quadrant Bearing Azimuth
NE N β E β
SE S β E 180° − β
SW S β W 180° + β
NW N β W 360° − β
Back direction. The line from point 2 back to point 1 points the other way.
Back azimuth = azimuth + 180°, or − 180° if the azimuth is 180° or more.
Back bearing: the same angle with both letters swapped. N 30° E becomes S 30° W.
Inverse: distance and direction from two points.
Find ΔN and ΔE.
Distance = √(ΔN² + ΔE²). This is the right triangle from lesson 15.
Bearing angle β = tan⁻¹(ΔE ÷ ΔN), using the sizes only (ignore the signs).
The signs give the quadrant: ΔN + is N, ΔN − is S, ΔE + is E, ΔE − is W.
Change the bearing to an azimuth with the table.
If ΔN = 0, do not divide by zero: the direction is due east (90°) when ΔE is positive or due west (270°) when ΔE is negative. If ΔE = 0, use due north (0°) or due south (180°). If both differences are zero, the points coincide and the direction is undefined.
Forward: a new point from a distance and an azimuth.
ΔN = distance × cos(azimuth)
ΔE = distance × sin(azimuth)
new N = N + ΔN, and new E = E + ΔE
With the azimuth, the calculator gives the signs of ΔN and ΔE for you. Keep your calculator in degree mode.
Degrees, minutes and seconds. 1° = 60' (minutes) and 1' = 60" (seconds). To change 53.1301° to degrees and minutes: 0.1301 × 60 = 7.806', and 0.806 × 60 = 48.4". So 53.1301° is about 53°07'48".
Worked example
Control point CP1 is at N 5,000.000 E 2,000.000. Stake A is at N 5,030.000 E 2,040.000.
ΔN = 5,030.000 − 5,000.000 = +30.000. ΔE = 2,040.000 − 2,000.000 = +40.000
Distance = √(30² + 40²) = √2,500 = 50.000 m
β = tan⁻¹(40 ÷ 30) = 53.13°
ΔN is + and ΔE is +, so the line runs NE. Bearing N 53.13° E, azimuth 53.13° (53°07'48").
Back azimuth from A to CP1: 53.13° + 180° = 233.13°, bearing S 53.13° W.
Forward: a pile is 20.000 m from CP1 at an azimuth of 30°.
ΔN = 20.000 × cos(30°) = +17.321. ΔE = 20.000 × sin(30°) = +10.000
The pile is at N 5,017.321 E 2,010.000.
Tools for this lesson

lessons.title: Problem solving • Understand the issue, choose a response, check what happened
lessons.text:
Problem solving is a process for making a decision when the next step is uncertain. It includes finding out what is happening, gathering useful information, considering more than one response, acting within your role and checking the result. It does not require having an instant answer. Sometimes the soundest next step is a specific question, a small test or a request to someone with the right responsibility.
People bring experience from work, learning, family and community responsibilities. That experience can suggest useful possibilities. It can also lead us to expect that a new situation has the same cause as an earlier one. In this chapter, experience is a starting resource, and evidence helps decide how well it fits the present case. You may draw on a personal example if you choose, or use every supplied fictional example without sharing private experiences.
The cases involve classroom scheduling, learning documents and a community information display. They use invented B.C. training situations, not the affairs of a Nation, employer or actual ACCESS cohort. There is no live equipment troubleshooting. When a real problem concerns machine safety, harassment, legal obligations or someone's immediate wellbeing, involve the responsible qualified person or established support process. A classroom decision exercise does not give a learner authority to resolve every kind of problem alone.
See it in action · Problem solving
Visual guide Use the confirmed current instruction. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
OBSERVED: Two notices disagree. UNKNOWN: Which notice is current?. State the problem and unknown. Check dates and authority. Confirm the action; test it. Use the confirmed current instruction. A guess about who made the error is not evidence.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. OBSERVED: Two notices disagree. UNKNOWN: Which notice is current?.
Try it: State the problem and unknown. Check dates and authority. Confirm the action; test it.
Check your result: Use the confirmed current instruction. A guess about who made the error is not evidence.
Six steps that can loop back
Visual guide All six Problem Solving components contribute to a reasoned decision. New evidence can send you back to an earlier action; returning to check a fact is useful progress. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. A decision can improve as the evidence changes. Six connected components: Identify the issue; Gather information; Analyze the issue; Develop multiple routes; Address the issue; Evaluate effectiveness. Keep a record: issue · facts · unknowns · options · action · results. Return when new evidence changes the decision.
You may return to an earlier step when a new fact changes the picture. Returning to gather information is progress when it prevents an unsupported decision. Use the six components to keep both your reasoning and your next action visible.
Identify the issue to be addressed
What is happening, to whom, and what needs to be different?
Practise with: “Write a bounded problem statement” through “Identify people and responsibilities”
Gather information to help you address the issue
What do we know, need to know and need help to establish?
Practise with: “Create an information checklist” through “Organize conflicting information”
Analyze the issue
Which explanations fit the evidence, and which are still guesses?
Practise with: “Build explanations that can be tested” through “Challenge a conclusion”
Develop multiple routes of action
What different responses could meet the actual needs?
Practise with: “Generate three routes” through “Test your preferred option against a drawback”
Address the issue
What will we do, who is responsible and what needs permission?
Practise with: “Write the action plan” through “Make a decision that respects permission”
Evaluate the effectiveness of the solution or decision
Did the response help, for whom, and what should change next?
Practise with: “Define success and inspect the evidence” through “Transfer the method to a new situation”
Use a simple record throughout: issue; known facts; missing information; options; chosen action and reason; result; next step. A drawing, voice note, table or supported written record can help you hold the process in mind. If the instructor is observing Problem solving, the quality of the reasoning matters separately from spelling, handwriting or confidence when speaking.
Turn a concern into a testable next step
A useful decision begins with a situation you can describe. It need not begin with blame or an instant answer. This short practice separates what is known, what is possible and what can be tried within the classroom.
Start with a small observation
Read this fictional note: “A learner opened two practice folders before finding the instructions. Both folders had the label ‘Practice’. We do not know which folder the learner was told to use.” Identify one observation, one unknown and one possible explanation. If you can already distinguish them, move to comparing options. Otherwise, work through the examples below.
Keep the evidence and explanation separate
Example: “Two folders were opened” is an observation supplied by the case. “The labels did not distinguish the folders” is supported by the two identical labels. “The learner did not care” is not established. “Were the intended instructions clear?” is a question, not a known fault.
Try with support: sort both labels say Practice, the wrong folder was opened on purpose, the spoken instruction may have been unclear, and we need to know which folder was requested into fact, unsupported claim, possible explanation and missing information. Discuss why a plausible explanation still needs checking.
Compare two ways to help
Use this goal: a new user should identify the requested folder without the designer choosing it for them. Two possibilities are a distinct name on each folder or a separate index showing which folder contains which material. Explain how each works, one effort or limitation, and what you would observe in a trial. Both could work; do not choose purely because another person prefers one.
Example prediction: “With distinct topic names, the user may select the requested folder by matching its name.” A checkable criterion is “The user selects the named folder and explains the label used.” No timing or emotional reaction is required.
Try a change and inspect its result
Make two dummy folders or folded paper covers named Schedule and Supplies. Ask a willing partner to find Supplies, using an agreed accessible way to read the labels. Record the actual choice and any help. If the partner asks what Supplies means, keep that question: the wording may need teaching or revision. Do not rewrite the result as independent success because the final choice was correct after help.
Ask what to retain, what to change and what another trial could show. A single successful selection does not establish that every future user will understand the arrangement. Record the conditions under which this person used it.
Fresh exit practice
Read a different small case: “Two paper trays are labelled ‘In’ and ‘Out’. A helper does not know which holds checked cards. The coordinator confirms that the tray currently called Out contains checked cards; the other holds cards awaiting a check. Both piles must remain separate.”
State the issue, propose two clearer labelling or checking options, choose one, label two paper areas and ask a willing partner where a checked card belongs. Record the choice, help and next decision. Possible labels are Awaiting check / Checked, or another equally clear arrangement. Do not change the coordinator's assigned status of the piles. The user test can reveal a need to clarify the word checked.
Keep your stated purpose, two options, actual change and honest result in the record. A useful next task is the fresh card-register case, where version information creates a further constraint. Do not claim an observed trial if only the plan was completed.
Define the issue without defining a person as the problem
“The learners do not care” is an interpretation of people. “Four of ten card sets used an older heading” is an observation that can be checked. The second statement gives a starting point for useful questions: which file was available, what instruction was given, how was the version shown, and when was the check made? A clear statement does not pretend people never make mistakes. It makes it possible to investigate the situation without beginning with an unsupported judgement.
Include the gap between present and needed conditions. Name the affected work and a boundary. For example: “The group has three working practice devices for ten learners, and each learner needs an individual tool turn within their available time.” That statement is more useful than “We need more money” because money is only one possible route. It also avoids choosing a solution before understanding the requirements.
A problem statement can acknowledge uncertainty: “We do not yet know whether loan devices will open the practice files.” An unknown is not a failure. Hiding it inside a confident recommendation can create a failure later. Put the unknown beside the decision it affects so the person responsible knows why checking it matters.
Case document A • A tool turn for every learner
Fictional planning brief — Thursday practice session
Ten learners need an individual digital practice turn. Each turn includes 20 minutes controlling a device and 5 minutes saving, reopening and checking the file, so allow 25 minutes per learner. Learners can work simultaneously on separate devices. Allow 5 minutes between groups to reset the classroom practice files. A partner watching does not count as that partner's own turn.
