The original plan uses five devices from 09:00 to 10:00. Two devices have become unavailable for the class. Three remain available. A technician is responsible for the unavailable devices; learners are not asked to repair them.
Three learners must leave at 10:00. The other seven can remain until 11:00. The instructor and room are available until 11:00. Finishing everybody's turn by 10:00 is preferred, but completing a genuine turn within each learner's available time is required. The extra classroom budget is no more than $50.
The training office can reserve two compatible loan devices for $40 total, if confirmed by 08:30. A later room with six devices costs $60 and is available only from 10:00 to 11:00. Paper planning materials cost nothing extra and are already printed. All costs, times and arrangements are invented for this exercise.
Worked example 1 • Separate the issue from the first idea
A first reaction is “Buy two new devices.” Buying is a proposed action, not the issue. Read the brief again. The required outcome is an individual 25-minute device turn for all ten learners within their availability and the $50 extra budget. The original five-device plan needs two groups: 25 + 5 + 25 = 55 minutes, which fits 09:00–10:00.
With only three devices, ten learners need four groups: three, three, three and one. The device time is 4 × 25 = 100 minutes, with three 5-minute changes: 100 + 15 = 115 minutes. A four-group sequence can run 09:00–10:55 if the three learners leaving at 10:00 are in an early group. It does not meet the preferred 10:00 finish for everybody, but it can meet the mandatory availability requirement. That difference keeps a potentially workable option open.
Write a bounded problem statement
Write one or two sentences describing the issue in Case A. Include the learners affected and the required outcome. Leave out a preferred solution. Underline the information that comes directly from the brief and mark anything you are assuming. Explain why “the group is too large” does not yet identify the decision the coordinator needs to make.
Distinguish requirements from preferences
Make two columns: must meet and prefer if possible. Sort the individual tool turn, $50 maximum, each person's availability, everyone's 10:00 finish and use of a familiar device. The brief does not explicitly rank familiarity; identify that as something to discuss rather than quietly making it mandatory. Add one question that would help the coordinator understand learner access needs without asking for private personal explanations.
Identify people and responsibilities
List the learners, instructor, training office and technician. For each, explain one relevant need or responsibility using the brief. Identify who can reserve a loan device and who should address the unavailable equipment. Explain how learners could contribute to the plan without being expected to authorize spending or disclose why they must leave at a particular time.
Gather enough information for the decision
Gathering information is purposeful. You are not required to collect every fact that might exist. Start with the decision and ask which missing facts could change it. A device's colour is unlikely to matter here. Its ability to open the practice file, accessibility settings and reservation deadline may matter. Distinguish confirmed information from a suggestion that still needs checking.
Useful questions are specific and answerable. “Will this work?” can mean several things. “Can the two loan devices open the practice spreadsheet, and can we confirm the needed access settings before the session?” identifies what must be checked. A question about availability can allow a simple yes/no answer without asking someone to explain family, health, transport or community responsibilities.
Keep source and date beside important information. A room that was free yesterday may have been booked today. A remembered price may exclude an additional charge. For a real decision, use the responsible person's current confirmation or the current authorized document. The fictional brief gives fixed facts for this exercise; do not silently import a real provider's prices, policies or rules into it.
Create an information checklist
Make a checklist for comparing the three-device plan with the loan-device plan. Include information already supplied and at least three questions that could matter before real delivery, such as required access settings, how loan devices reach the room and who confirms the reservation. Mark each entry provided, needs confirmation or not relevant to this decision. Do not change the given classroom numbers while identifying real-world checks.
Ask without assuming
Draft three short questions: one to the training office, one to a learner about the usable schedule, and one to the instructor about the required evidence. Use a purpose statement so the person knows why you are asking. Then exchange questions with a partner acting from the brief. Notice any question that asks for information the case does not supply; record it as unresolved rather than inventing an answer.
Organize conflicting information
A fictional sticky note beside the room calendar says, “All learners can stay until 11.” The dated planning brief says three must leave at 10. Explain why choosing whichever statement makes your preferred plan easier is unreliable. Record the conflict, its effect on the schedule, the responsible confirmation route and the temporary assumption you will use until it is resolved. Continue using the brief's three early departures for the remaining classroom calculations.
Analyze causes, patterns and limits
Analysis connects facts without claiming more than they support. It can involve comparing rows, grouping possible causes, noticing a sequence or asking how a process works. A cause-and-effect diagram can group possibilities under headings such as information, tools, time, process and access. Those headings organize questions; they do not prove a cause.
A “why” question is useful when it opens an investigation. It becomes less useful when it forces every answer toward blame. Ask “What made the current version difficult to identify?” rather than “Why did someone ignore the correct version?” Do not keep asking “why” as though a fifth answer must be the truth. Stop at an evidence gap and name what would test the proposed link.
Watch for familiar thinking shortcuts. You might favour the explanation you first heard, notice only examples that support it, or trust the most confident speaker. Counter that by asking what evidence would make you revise your view. Invite a different interpretation before settling on a cause. A partner's question can improve a decision without making either person the winner or loser of a debate.
Case document B • Repeated card-label corrections
Fictional improvement record — classroom print station
During three practice sessions, learners printed ten card sets each session. The review found four sets needing a label correction in Session A, two in Session B and three in Session C. The group did not record each person's name; the purpose was to improve the process, not rank learners.
The instructor observed that both an older practice file and a current practice file were available in the same folder. Their names differed by only one letter. A spoken reminder was given, but no version example was displayed beside the print station. One learner said they selected the first result shown by the file search. Another said they used the file already open on the device. These observations suggest possible links but do not establish the cause of every correction.
For the next two sessions, the instructor placed the current practice file in a clearly named folder and displayed a version-check card. Session D had one corrected set out of ten; Session E had none out of ten. Different learners may have attended, and the record does not measure their prior experience. No comparison group used the old arrangement during the same period.
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Session Sets reviewed Sets needing label correction Arrangement
A 10 4 Earlier arrangement
B 10 2 Earlier arrangement
C 10 3 Earlier arrangement
D 10 1 Revised arrangement
E 10 0 Revised arrangement
Build explanations that can be tested
Identify three possible contributors to the corrections in Case B. For each, point to supporting information and state what remains unknown. Include at least one explanation concerning the information or process, not a learner's attitude. Do not claim that everyone used the older file. The record does not say that. Suggest a respectful way to learn more without collecting unnecessary personal information.
Use a cause-and-effect map
Create a map with the issue in the centre: some printed sets need label corrections. Use at least three headings such as file organization, instructions, display or checking process. Place known observations and untested possibilities in visibly different styles or labelled columns. Choose one proposed link and write a small, low-risk test. Explain which result would support the link and which would make you reconsider it.
Challenge a conclusion
A fictional colleague says, “The new folder proves that people were careless before.” Explain two problems with that conclusion. Then write a statement supported by the record and a question worth investigating. Compare your response with a partner's. Identify one assumption in your own first explanation that you revised after considering the other person's reasoning.
Develop options before selecting one
Visual guide Two routes meet the required individual turns, availability and budget. The shorter route costs $40; the longer route requires the three early departures to go first. Group segments share the same time scale. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Two proportional schedules compare tool turns for ten learners. Borrowing two devices makes five available: two groups of five take twenty-five minutes each plus a five-minute change, ending at 09:55 for $40, with confirmation by 08:30. Using three available devices makes groups of three, three, three and one, taking 115 minutes to 10:55 for no extra cost. The first three finish at 09:25. The maximum extra cost is $50; a later $60 room and paper-only work fail named constraints.
Options should be genuinely different ways to address the issue. “Tell people more firmly,” “give a stronger reminder” and “repeat the instruction louder” may be three versions of the same approach. A different option might change the file arrangement, provide a visible example, add a check before printing or allow a different way to access the instruction. Generate possibilities first, then compare their likely effects and constraints.
Mandatory criteria come before preferences. An option that cannot meet a required access need does not become suitable because it is cheap. An option outside the authorized budget needs a new decision by the responsible person; a learner cannot make the limit disappear by giving cost a low score. After checking requirements, compare useful preferences such as time, simplicity, travel or the amount of new learning needed.
A table can make your reasoning visible, but numbers do not make a judgement objective automatically. If you use ratings, explain their meaning and why a criterion matters. Keep uncertain entries marked as uncertain. A precise-looking total based on guessed ratings can hide the question that most needs discussion.
Worked example 2 • Compare the schedule options
For Case A, compare four routes. Two compatible loan devices cost $40 and restore five simultaneous places, so two groups finish by 09:55. Using only three devices costs no extra money and takes 115 minutes; early departures must be placed before 10:00. The later room costs $60, exceeds the stated budget and begins after three learners must leave. Paper-only work costs nothing but does not supply the required digital tool turn.
Two options remain feasible under the supplied facts: loan devices or a longer rotation with three devices. If the coordinator gives high priority to finishing the whole group before 10:00, the $40 loan plan fits that preference. If minimizing extra spending is the priority and a longer rotation is acceptable, the three-device plan can work. The recommendation must explain the trade-off instead of pretending there is only one possible answer.
Generate three routes
For Case B's label-correction issue, propose three different changes. Explain how each could help and what effort or check it would require. At least one option should change the information or workflow rather than relying only on an extra verbal reminder. Include an option proposed by a partner and identify what you learned from it. Do not select the final response until all three have been described.
Build a decision table
Compare the four Case A routes: loan devices, extended three-device rotation, later six-device room and paper-only replacement. Include extra cost, total device-session duration, early-departure access and whether the actual digital outcome is met. Mark required criteria separately from preferences. Recommend either feasible route with a reason based on the brief. If you recommend a route that needs a changed requirement, name the authorization or new information needed before it could become feasible.
Test your preferred option against a drawback
Take your preferred route from “Build a decision table”. Identify its strongest drawback and one situation that would make it unsuitable. A partner takes the role of a coordinator and asks one challenging but respectful question. Respond using evidence, or change your recommendation if the question reveals a real gap. Record the reason for keeping or revising the choice. Defending a first idea at all costs is not the purpose of this task.
Address the issue with a workable action plan
A decision becomes useful when someone can act on it. Record the action, responsible role, time, required confirmation and check. “We will communicate better” is too broad. “The coordinator will confirm the two loan devices by 08:30; the instructor will check the practice file before learners arrive; the group list will show each person's turn” gives people a clearer shared plan.
Keep within your role. A learner can propose, check classroom data and ask questions. Reserving equipment, spending funds or changing a real schedule may belong to a coordinator. A useful recommendation identifies that boundary rather than presenting a classroom suggestion as an approved decision. The same principle applies to community information: permission to learn about a topic is not automatically permission to publish someone's contribution.
Before acting, decide what would trigger a pause or a fallback. If loan devices do not arrive, when should the coordinator switch to the longer rotation? If a printed display contains an unapproved statement, who checks it before the display is used? A fallback should still meet the required outcome or clearly state which part must be rescheduled. It should not quietly lower the standard and call the work complete.
Case document C • A useful display with an unanswered request
Fictional classroom display brief
A group is preparing a public-information display for an open classroom afternoon. It explains the five-stage introductory paving process and how the nine Skills for Success appear in the learning activities. The display uses original learner diagrams and clearly labelled fictional data. The coordinator has approved a one-page explanation of the classroom project.
A visitor suggests adding a local community story and a photograph of participants to make the display more engaging. The group has no permission to use a particular story or photograph. One learner knows a person who might be willing to contribute, but has not asked them. The deadline is tomorrow. The existing approved diagram can be used without those additions.
The group wants an inviting display and respectful relationships. No learner is expected to speak for a Nation or community, reveal personal identity information, or provide cultural material to improve a class product. The coordinator can discuss a later community-directed contribution if the appropriate people choose to participate.
Write the action plan
Create a plan for your feasible Case A route. Include at least four actions, the responsible role, timing and a check. Make the group sequence clear enough to show how all ten people receive 25 minutes, including the three who must leave at 10:00. Identify the decision that belongs to the training office or coordinator. Your plan is a classroom proposal; do not contact or book anything outside the exercise.
Respond to a changed fact
At 08:35, the fictional office confirms that the loan devices are unavailable. Use the supplied room and learner availability to make a fallback plan. Show the four groups and their times, placing the early-departure learners appropriately. Explain what you would tell the group about the changed finish time and what would need reconfirming in a real class. Paper planning can occupy waiting time, but it cannot replace the required device turn.
Make a decision that respects permission
Apply the six-step process to Case C. Identify the immediate display decision, the facts and missing permissions, at least two possible routes and a justified action before tomorrow. Explain how the group could remain open to a future contribution without treating a possible personal connection as permission. Write a short recommendation to the fictional coordinator. Use the supplied case; no learner needs to provide a real cultural story or photograph.
Evaluate results and learn from them
Visual guide The recorded correction proportion fell from 9/30 (30%) to 1/20 (5%): 25 percentage points. The small before-and-after record supports another check, not a claim that one change alone caused the result. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Dot arrays show nine of thirty sets needing correction before the change, or thirty percent, compared with one of twenty afterward, or five percent. The observed difference is twenty-five percentage points. The current folder and a version-check card were introduced, but different sessions, potentially different learners and no same-time comparison group limit causal claims.
Evaluation asks whether the response achieved its intended purpose, what else happened and what should be done next. Decide what evidence you will collect before trying the change. In Case A, useful evidence includes whether every learner actually controlled a device, whether files were saved and reopened, whether departures were respected and whether the cost stayed within the limit. A full attendance list alone does not answer those questions.
Look at the denominator when comparing counts. One correction out of ten sets is different from one out of a hundred. Keep the observation period and conditions visible. A change seen in a small classroom trial can be promising without proving that the same result will occur in every class. Learner feedback may reveal an access problem that a numerical average hides.
Worked example 3 • Compare the correction record carefully
Before the revised arrangement, Case B records 4 + 2 + 3 = 9 corrections among 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 reviewed sets. The proportion is 9/30 = 0.30 = 30%. After the change, there is 1 + 0 = 1 correction among 20 sets: 1/20 = 0.05 = 5%. The difference is 25 percentage points, because 30% − 5% = 25 percentage points.
A supported statement is: “The recorded correction proportion was lower in the two sessions using the revised arrangement.” It is too strong to say the folder change alone caused the improvement or that the problem can never return. The record includes different sessions and possibly different learners. Continue checking versions, ask whether the process is usable and review another trial before making a broader claim.
Define success and inspect the evidence
For your Case A plan, write four observable success checks. Then consider this invented result: all ten learners attended; nine saved and reopened a file independently or with recorded support; one learner watched a partner but did not control a device. The cost was $40 and everyone left within their availability. State which criteria were met, which remain unmet and what follow-up is needed. Do not turn attendance into proof of the missing individual turn.
Evaluate and improve the print-station trial
Use Case B's data to calculate the before and after correction proportions. Write a two-sentence interpretation that includes one limitation. Add one question for learner feedback and one next observation that would help evaluate the revised process. Explain why asking whether the folder and version card were usable is different from asking who was careless. Preserve both the numerical result and the people affected by the process.
Transfer the method to a new situation
Choose one supplied new issue: a fictional classroom bus-time notice has two different departure times, or a practice supply list contains an item with no quantity. Apply all six steps using a small invented document you label as practice. Identify at least one fact you would need from the responsible person before acting. Explain which step from this chapter helped most and show the record of your reasoning. A planned future workplace use should be recorded as a plan, not as demonstrated transfer at work.
Put a chosen change into practice
Visual guide A prediction becomes useful evidence through a small trial, clear observations and a next decision. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
A four-step cycle begins with a prediction and reason, continues with a small trial under recorded conditions, then records observable actions and help needed before deciding whether to keep, adjust or retest. An example distinguishes an observation, the reader opened two folders, from a possible explanation, the label was hard to find.
Use the kit prototype work in “Make a small usable version” through “Retest and make a limited claim” to carry a problem-solving decision through an actual classroom trial. Before building or revising, keep your own issue statement, two possible responses, chosen action and prediction. State what a useful result would look like. Then identify the change you actually implement, give a willing user the task and record what they do, including any support.
Compare the observation with your criterion. Retain or revise the change for a stated reason and choose another check. Distinguish help you received as the designer from prompts you gave the test user. A supplied case result is an example; your own trial record describes what actually happened. One small trial does not prove that a change works for everyone or that it alone caused a difference. The same work can provide Creativity and Problem solving evidence when the record identifies the individual actions for each.
Your evidence and next practice
Keep the problem statement, information checklist, cause map, options table, action plan and evaluation. These records show how your thinking changed; a final answer alone may hide the strongest part of your learning. You can record a question you left unresolved when the available evidence was insufficient. That is useful evidence of judgement when you also identify an appropriate next step.
For support, work with fewer options, highlight the mandatory criteria, use counters for the learner groups or ask an instructor to model one question. For extension, add one clearly labelled changed fact and test whether the recommendation still holds. Increase the reasoning challenge gradually. The local feedback descriptions are Not observed, Not yet demonstrated, Demonstrated with support and Demonstrated independently; record support and transfer separately rather than awarding a made-up official level.
Problem solving · choose a change, try it and examine the result
Use the form selected by the instructor. These are classroom materials problems. You may make labels, trays or paper arrangements; you may not change the source cards, remove their version information or claim a practice document authorizes a real procedure. Use no personal data. Work on a problem statement and options yourself before discussing them with a partner.
The complete task can use ordinary paper, removable labels and two or three marked spaces on a desk. No computer, purchase or real workplace change is required. If a willing test user is unavailable, arrange an instructor-supported walkthrough and label its support accurately. Do not invent an independent user result.
Form A · Find the current practice pair
A learning room keeps loose practice cards in one mixed pile. A new user must find the current Sheet and Check card for a named kit. Both cards must match the current register. The instructor reports that older cards have sometimes been selected, but supplies no count or proven cause. The user needs a clear arrangement that can be reset after a kit changes.
Current register A
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Kit Current version Required pair
R · Reading practice 2 Sheet and Check
N · Number practice 3 Sheet and Check
C · Conversation practice 1 Sheet and Check
Copy each cell below onto a separate dummy card. The words and codes are the entire card content for this task.
Card Card
R — Sheet — version 2 R — Check — version 2
R — Sheet — version 1 R — Check — version 1
N — Sheet — version 3 N — Check — version 3
N — Sheet — version 2 N — Check — version 2
C — Sheet — version 1 C — Check — version 1
Keep all ten cards; older cards must be retained in a clearly separate practice area rather than destroyed. Any design must work without colour, use the register as the authority, and let a user find the correct pair without the designer choosing it for them. The user may use agreed reading/access supports, recorded in the test.
Problem solving practice A · Define and investigate
State the desired result, observed or reported issue, two constraints and an important unknown. Distinguish the instructor's report from something you have observed yourself. Inspect the cards/register. Identify two possible explanations for wrong selection and what observation could help investigate each.
Problem solving practice A · Compare and predict
Propose at least two distinct organizing or checking methods. Explain how each could help and one drawback. Choose a first change and state your reason. Before building, predict what a user will be able to do. Set a checkable success criterion: selecting both current cards for the requested kit, with any support visible. Do not require speed unless you separately agree a meaningful purpose for measuring time.
Problem solving practice A · Put the decision into use
Build your chosen arrangement using all supplied cards and the current register. Ask a willing user: “Find the current Sheet and Check pair for kit R, then show how you checked the version.” Give them the register and agreed access supports. Observe without choosing the cards for them. Record their actual selection, verification action, questions and any help you supplied. If you intervene, record the point and reason. The trial still provides useful information.
Problem solving practice A · Evaluate, revise and retry
Compare the observation with your criterion. Retain what worked and revise one feature if evidence suggests a need; if the arrangement already works, document the evidence and choose an additional check. Test kit N with a willing user or supported walkthrough. Record the current pair selected and how it was checked. Explain one limitation: a different kit, prior exposure, a different user or changed support may affect the comparison. State a useful next action without claiming your design alone caused all differences.
Form B · Find the approved practice pair
A classroom desk keeps practice cards in one mixed pile. A user must find the approved Brief and Review card for a named kit, using the current register. A helper reports that draft cards have sometimes been mistaken for approved ones, but provides no count or proven explanation. A later version number is not automatically the approved version.
Current register B
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Kit Approved version Required pair
H · Handover practice 1 Brief and Review
T · Time practice 4 Brief and Review
W · Writing practice 2 Brief and Review
Copy each cell onto a separate dummy card.
Card Card
H — Brief — version 1 H — Review — version 1
H — Brief — version 2, draft H — Review — version 2, draft
T — Brief — version 4 T — Review — version 4
T — Brief — version 3 T — Review — version 3
W — Brief — version 2 W — Review — version 2
Retain all ten cards in your arrangement, separating unapproved/older cards clearly. Work without colour-only cues, keep source wording/version labels intact and give the user the register. Use no personal information. The designer must not choose the answer for the user.
Problem solving practice B · Define and investigate
State the desired result, reported issue, two constraints and an unknown. Distinguish report from observation. Identify two possible explanations for wrong selection and an observation that could investigate each.
Problem solving practice B · Compare and predict
Develop two distinct approaches, with a possible benefit and drawback for each. Select one with a reason. Predict the result before building and specify the criterion: both approved cards for the requested kit, with the actual verification method and support recorded.
Problem solving practice B · Put the decision into use
Build the arrangement. Ask a willing user: “Find the approved Brief and Review pair for kit H, then show how you checked its approval.” Give the register and agreed access supports. Record actual selections, checks, questions and any help. Do not silently replace a draft card or supply a correct result in the observation record.
Problem solving practice B · Evaluate, revise and retry
Compare the observation with the criterion. Make an evidenced improvement or document why the arrangement should be retained. Test kit T, observing the selection and approval check. State what happened and one limit on the comparison, including changed kit/user/support or practice effects. Choose a next action rather than promising universal success.
My trial record
Stage My evidence
Issue, required outcome, constraints and unknown Write your response here.
Two options, drawbacks and selected reason Write your response here.
Prediction and criterion written before trial Write your response here.
Action I actually implemented Write your response here.
Trial 1: exact cards selected and check performed Write your response here.
Support to me / support I gave the user Write your response here.
What I retained or revised, and why Write your response here.
Trial 2: exact cards, check and support Write your response here.
Limited conclusion and next action Write your response here.
Sketch the first and revised arrangements, or attach an accessible description. Mark predicted features separately from tested ones.
Reuse an idea-development trial
You can also use the kit prototype work in “Make a small usable version” through “Retest and make a limited claim” as an enacted problem-solving cycle. Keep your own issue statement, two options, choice/prediction and implemented change. Add the actual reader-test record, support, comparison with your criterion and next decision. Cite the precise action that supports each skill; a finished kit alone does not demonstrate the reasoning or the trial. Supplied case results remain examples, separate from observations you collect.

lessons.title: Define the problem before you fix it
lessons.text:
Sort what you are given from what you need to find, and name the goal before you start the work.
Why this matters on the job
A supervisor texts you: "Unit 4 closet door is wrecked, sort it out." If you buy a new door and drive to the site, you may bring the wrong size, the wrong colour, or a fix nobody needed. On BC job sites, a job that starts from a guess costs fuel, materials and hours. A few minutes spent defining the problem first saves trips and arguments later.
Key ideas
Symptom, cause and fix are different things
A symptom is what you notice: "The door won't stay shut."
A cause is why it happens: "The latch does not line up with the strike plate."
A fix is what you do about it: "Move the strike plate so the latch catches."
People often report a symptom and suggest a fix in the same sentence. Your first job is to pull them apart.
Given, required, goal
Given: the facts you already have.
Required: what you must find out or produce.
Goal: what "done" looks like, with its limits: time, money, rules and safety.
Not needed: information that does not change the job. Set it aside, but keep it in case it matters later.
Three questions for any new issue
Is it familiar or new? A familiar problem may already have a procedure. Use it.
Is it simple or complex? A complex problem has many parts or many people. Break it into smaller parts.
Do I need to make a decision, or does someone else? If the issue is unsafe or outside your role, report it to your supervisor.
A one-sentence problem statement
Put four things in one sentence: what is wrong, where, what done looks like, and the limits. Leave the fix out. You do not know the fix yet.
Worked example
A work order from Harbourview Property Services (a fictional company):
Unit 4, 1180 Alder Lane. Tenant reports the bedroom closet door "won't stay shut." Door is a white hollow-core slab, 762 mm wide. Tenant works nights: no entry before 1 p.m. Tenant has a cat. Finish by Friday. Budget for parts: $60.
Given: the unit and address, the tenant's report, the door type and width, entry after 1 p.m., the Friday deadline, $60 for parts.
Not needed for the repair itself: the cat. It still matters for how you work: keep the suite door closed.
Required: the cause, and a repair.
Not yet known: is it the latch, the strike plate, the hinges or the door itself?
Goal: the door closes and stays shut, by Friday, with $60 or less in parts, working after 1 p.m.
Problem statement: "The bedroom closet door in Unit 4 does not stay shut. Find the cause and repair it so it latches, by Friday, with no more than $60 in parts, working after 1 p.m."
The statement does not say "replace the door." That might turn out to be the fix, but nobody knows yet.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Label each statement S (symptom), C (cause) or F (fix).
a. The shop heater blows cold air.
b. The thermostat batteries are dead.
c. Put new batteries in the thermostat.
d. Water is dripping through a ceiling tile in the lunchroom.
e. A roof drain above the lunchroom is plugged with leaves.
f. Clear the leaves out of the roof drain.
g. The chop saw cuts are coming out crooked.
h. The fence on the chop saw has come loose.
Task 2 (level 1) Read this work order. Sort every piece of information into given, not needed or goal, then write what is required.
Coldwater Fabrication (fictional). Customer Silver Creek Farms needs 12 steel brackets like the sample in the bin by the door. The sample is 6 mm plate, 100 mm × 150 mm, with two 14 mm holes. Use plate from the offcut rack first. Paint them black. The customer will pick them up Thursday at 3 p.m. The customer drives a blue truck.
Task 3 (level 2) Your foreman sends this message. Write a one-sentence problem statement. Do not choose a fix.
"Pour is booked for 7 a.m. Thursday. Forecast says heavy rain Wednesday night. Our tarps only cover half the slab forms. The concrete supplier needs 24 hours' notice to change the pour time. Figure out what we do."
Task 4 (level 2) For each case, decide: is it familiar or new, simple or complex, and who should decide what happens next?
a. The staple gun at your station is empty.
b. A guardrail on the second-floor deck is loose.
c. While you install kitchen cabinets, the client asks you to move a wall outlet 300 mm to the left.
d. Two drawings in the site trailer show different widths for the same door opening.
Task 5 (level 2) Go back to the Unit 4 closet door. Write two questions you would ask before you buy any parts. For each question, say how the answer could change what you do.
Check yourself
What is the difference between a symptom and a cause?
In a work order, what does "required" mean?
Why should a problem statement leave out the fix?
You notice a loose guardrail on a deck. What must you do, and who decides on the repair?

lessons.title: Tell facts from opinions and assumptions
lessons.text:
Sort what you know from what you believe or take for granted, and check the assumptions that could hurt the job.
Why this matters on the job
On a site, people pass on information all day: "the lumber's dry," "that supplier is always late," "the power's off in there." Some of it is fact, some is opinion, and some is a guess that nobody has checked. If you act on the wrong kind, you can waste a morning or get hurt. Knowing which is which tells you what to check before you act.
Key ideas
Fact, opinion, assumption
A fact can be checked and shown to be true or false: "The delivery arrived at 9:40." "The tape reads 2440 mm."
An opinion is a belief or a judgement. It can be honest and useful, but it is not proof: "That supplier is useless." "This is the best saw on the market."
An assumption is something taken for granted, usually about what we cannot see or about the future: "The lumber will be dry by tomorrow." "Nobody is working on the other side of this wall."
Assumptions are not bad. We make hundreds a day, and most work out. "I'll be at work tomorrow" is an assumption that saves you planning for every flat tire. The trouble starts when the stakes are high and nobody checks.
Explicit and implicit
Explicit means stated clearly: "The pump truck is stuck at the gate."
Implicit means suggested but not said: the pour will start late, the crew will be standing around, someone needs to call the foreman.
Messages on labels, signs and ads often lean on what is implied. "Industrial strength" sounds like a promise, but it states nothing you can check.
Bias, preconceptions and habits
A bias is a leaning that makes us favour one answer before we look at the facts. It often comes from habit ("we've always done it this way"), from a first impression, or from who is talking. Everyone has biases. The fix is to ask: What fact would change my mind? Have I checked it?
Worked example
Tasha, an apprentice with Lakeview Concrete Forming (fictional), sees a labourer on the deck waving both arms and shouting toward the crane. She thinks: "He's fooling around. Somebody's going to get hurt."
Fact: a worker is waving his arms and shouting toward the crane.
Assumption: he is fooling around.
What she does not know: whether he is the signaller giving signals to the operator.
Check: ask her lead hand who is signalling the crane today, before she reports horseplay.
It turns out he is the assigned signaller and the radio has died. Her first idea was not silly. It just was not checked.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Label each statement F (fact), O (opinion) or A (assumption).
a. The drywall delivery arrived at 9:40 a.m.
b. That supplier is always late.
c. The mud will be dry enough to sand by tomorrow morning.
d. The plan shows the window rough opening at 1220 mm wide.
e. Our old foreman ran a better crew.
f. Nobody is in the mechanical room, so it's fine to start cutting.
g. The thermometer in the trailer reads 4°C.
h. The new hire won't last a month.
Task 2 (level 1) Each sentence states something explicitly. Write one thing each one implies.
a. The pump truck is stuck at the gate.
b. They ran out of 3/8-inch drill bits at the supply store.
c. The SkyTrain isn't running this morning.
d. Everybody passed the fall protection quiz.
e. The forecast says snow overnight.
Task 3 (level 2) A box of safety glasses on a store shelf says:
PRO-SHIELD SPORT. Industrial strength! Meets or exceeds industry standards. As worn by pro riders.
a. What does the box state explicitly?
b. What does it want you to believe?
c. In BC, what must eye protection meet when a worker is required to wear it? Look it up in WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 8.14 at https://www.worksafebc.com/en/law-policy/occupational-health-safety/searchable-ohs-regulation/ohs-regulation/part-08-personal-protective-clothing-and-equipment
d. What would you need to see on this product before you trusted it for grinding?
Task 4 (level 2) Team build. Your instructor gives each team a tray of straws, pins and paper cups with one instruction: "Build the tallest structure you can." After the build, write down every assumption your team made about that instruction. For example: Did you assume it had to stand on its own? That you could only use the tray? That there was a time limit?
Task 5 (level 2) Read the story and answer the questions.
At Fraser Bend Mechanical (fictional), a run of copper pipe on the second floor started leaking at three joints the day after it was installed. The superintendent said, "It's the new apprentice. The new ones never clean their joints." The new apprentice, Devon, had soldered that run. So had Marco, who has 12 years in the trade. Nobody wrote down which joints each person made.
a. Which part of the superintendent's statement is a fact, and which is an assumption?
b. What preconception or habit might be behind it?
c. List two facts you would gather before deciding who or what caused the leaks.
Check yourself
How can you tell a fact from an opinion?
Give one assumption you made today that turned out fine.
What is the difference between explicit and implicit?
What question helps you catch your own bias?

lessons.title: Observe and record what you see
lessons.text:
Scan a work area in order, write down what is really there, and keep what you see apart from what you think it means.
Why this matters on the job
Good problem solving starts with good information, and much of that information comes from your own eyes. A tradesperson walking into a shop or a site in BC has to notice the cord across the floor, the tag on the machine and the wrong part in the delivery, often in a few seconds. What you write down is what your supervisor, the next shift or an inspector will rely on.
Key ideas
Look in an order, not at random
Our eyes jump to whatever is bright or moving. To see everything, scan in a fixed order: left to right, top to bottom, or one zone at a time. Then look again at the floor, because that is where trips and spills hide.
Write what you see, not what you think
Observation: "There is a dark puddle about one metre wide in front of the exit door."
Interpretation: "Someone was careless with the oil."
The observation can be checked by anyone. The interpretation might be wrong: it could be water from a leaking roof. Write the observation first. If you add an interpretation, label it as your opinion.
A useful note answers five questions
What is it? Where is it? How many or how big? When did you see it? Who did you tell? Measure or count when you can instead of guessing.
Report what looks unsafe
In BC, anyone who sees what appears to be an unsafe condition or act must report it to a supervisor or the employer as soon as possible (WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 3.10). You do not have to be sure. "Appears to be" is enough.
Worked example
You notice a hose lying across a doorway.
Weak note: "Hose problem by the door."
Strong note: "Green air hose lying across the doorway to bay 2, at 10:20 a.m. Trip hazard. Told Ray (lead hand) at 10:22."
The shop picture
Coldwater Fabrication (a fictional shop) bay 2 is shown below, split into zones 1 to 4. Your instructor will tell you when to look and when to cover it.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Look at the picture for 60 seconds. Then cover it and answer from memory. For an agreed accessible route, use the instructor's zone-by-zone description, enlarged image or extra viewing time. You may keep that source available: the learning goal is accurate observation, not memory speed. Record the support used.
a. How many boxes are stacked in zone 2?
b. What time does the clock show?
c. What does the whiteboard say?
d. What colour is the extension cord?
e. Which machine has a tag on it, and what does the tag say?
f. How many sawhorses are there?
g. What sign is above the door?
Task 2 (level 1) Uncover the picture. Scan it one zone at a time, from zone 1 to zone 4. List everything you see in each zone, including the floor. Check your Task 1 answers.
Task 3 (level 2) Find four things in the picture that appear to be unsafe. For each one, write a report note that answers what, where, and why it could hurt someone. Is the tagged machine one of them? Explain.
Task 4 (level 2) Rewrite each note so it states only what can be seen. If you want to keep an opinion, label it.
a. "Some idiot left the oil everywhere."
b. "The grinder's broken."
c. "Storage in bay 2 is a disaster."
d. "The job on the board is going to be late."
Task 5 (level 2) Detail in documents. Compare the purchase order with the packing slip that came with the delivery. List every difference.
Purchase order 30871, Coldwater Fabrication to Pacific Metals Supply (both fictional)
6 mm × 1220 mm × 2440 mm hot-rolled plate, qty 2
50 mm × 6 mm flat bar, 6 m lengths, qty 10
14 mm cobalt drill bit, qty 2
Black enamel spray paint, qty 12
Packing slip, Pacific Metals Supply. Your PO: 30817
6 mm × 1220 mm × 2440 mm hot-rolled plate, qty 2
50 mm × 8 mm flat bar, 6 m lengths, qty 10
14 mm cobalt drill bit, qty 1
Black enamel spray paint, qty 12
Check yourself
Why should you scan a work area in a fixed order?
What is the difference between an observation and an interpretation?
What five questions does a useful note answer?
Do you need to be certain something is unsafe before you report it in BC?

lessons.title: Spot patterns and possible causes
lessons.text:
Find what repeats in a log or a layout, break a problem into parts, and test a possible cause before you act on it.
Why this matters on the job
A breaker that trips every morning, welds that fail only on one shift, a crew that always finishes late on Fridays: problems that repeat leave a trail. A tradesperson who can read that trail finds the cause faster and does not waste parts swapping things at random. Patterns also help with everyday work, such as laying out studs or bolt holes.
Key ideas
Look for what repeats
When the same problem shows up more than once, sort the cases and ask what they share:
Time: time of day, day of the week, season, right after a delivery
Place: one machine, one booth, one floor, one side of the building
People and tools: one crew, one shift, one batch of material, one tool
Conditions: cold, wet, busy, after a change
A pattern is a clue, not proof
Two things happening together does not prove one causes the other. If welds fail on the night shift and the night shift always uses booth 3, the cause could be the shift or the booth. To find out, change one thing and keep the rest the same.
Break the problem into parts
A big problem like "the crew keeps finishing late" is easier to analyze in parts. Common headings are people, materials, equipment, method and environment. Put each known fact under a heading. The headings organize your questions. They do not prove a cause.
Possible cause and effect
Write a possible link as: "If ___ is causing , then we should see ." Then go and look for it. If you do not see it, drop that idea or change it.
Worked example
Stud marks on a wall plate at Riverbend Framing (fictional) are laid out every 400 mm, starting at 0: 0, 400, 800, 1200 and so on. Where is the 9th mark?
The 1st mark is at 0, so the 9th mark is 8 spaces along. Using BEDMAS, brackets first, then multiply:
(9 − 1) × 400 = 8 × 400 = 3200 mm
Where the pattern breaks tells you something too. If a plate reads 0, 400, 800, 1220, 1600, the 1220 mark breaks the pattern. Either it is an error, or something is there on purpose, such as an opening on the plan. Check before you cut.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Find the next two numbers and say what the pattern is.
a. 2, 4, 6, 8, __, __
b. 0, 400, 800, 1200, __, __
c. 25, 50, 75, 100, __, __
d. 2, 4, 6, 2, 4, 6, __, __
For a., give a second way the pattern could carry on that still fits the first numbers.
Task 2 (level 2) A wall plate is laid out every 400 mm starting at 0. How far from the start is the 14th mark? Show the steps with BEDMAS. Then find the mark in this list that breaks the pattern, and say what you would check: 0, 400, 800, 1200, 1600, 2000, 2440, 2800.
Task 3 (level 2) Northshore Pipe and Steel (fictional) bend-tests weld samples. Here is the record for the last two weeks.
Shift Booth Welder Samples tested Samples failed
Day 1 Mara 12 1
Day 2 Tyson 12 0
Night 3 Wes 12 4
Night 3 Kiri 12 5
Extra facts: Night shift only uses booth 3. Wes and Kiri both passed all their test samples in booth 1 last month. Booth 3 is next to the big overhead door.
a. Add up the samples tested and failed for each shift. What fraction failed on each shift? Give each as a percentage.
b. What pattern do you see?
c. Does the record show that the welders are the cause? Explain.
d. Name two possible causes the record cannot tell apart.
e. Describe one test that would tell them apart. Change one thing only.
Task 4 (level 2) The site trailer at a fictional job site has a breaker that trips. Here is the log.
Date Day Time Who was in the trailer What was plugged in and on
Nov 2 Monday 7:05 a.m. 6 people heater, kettle, microwave, phone chargers
Nov 3 Tuesday 7:10 a.m. 7 people heater, kettle, microwave, phone chargers
Nov 4 Wednesday none 6 people heater, phone chargers (kettle broken)
Nov 5 Thursday 7:00 a.m. 6 people heater, new kettle, microwave, phone chargers
Nov 7 Saturday none 2 people heater, phone chargers
a. Write the pattern in one sentence.
b. Write one "If ___ is causing , then we should see " statement that fits the log.
c. Who should you give this log to, and why should you not try to fix the electrical system yourself?
Task 5 (level 3) The concrete crew at Lakeview Concrete Forming (fictional) has finished late four Fridays in a row. Sort these facts under the headings people, materials, equipment, method and environment. Then pick the heading you would look into first and explain why.
Concrete is delivered at 10 a.m. on Fridays and 7 a.m. on other days.
Two of the five crew members leave at 2 p.m. on Fridays for a course.
The vibrator broke on two of the four Fridays.
It rained on one of the four Fridays.
On Fridays the crew also strips last week's forms before the pour.
Monday to Thursday the crew finishes on time.
Check yourself
Name four kinds of things to compare when a problem repeats.
Why is a pattern not proof of a cause?
Using BEDMAS, how far along is the 6th mark if marks are 400 mm apart starting at 0?
What does "change one thing at a time" help you find out?

lessons.title: Troubleshoot a fault step by step
lessons.text:
Make the equipment safe, describe the fault exactly, check the likely causes from simplest to hardest, and change one thing at a time.
Why this matters on the job
When a tool or machine stops working, the pressure is on to get the crew going again. Guessing and swapping parts can waste money, and working on equipment that still has power or pressure in it can injure you. A step-by-step method gets the fault found faster and keeps you safe. Employers in every BC trade want apprentices who can troubleshoot calmly and report clearly.
Key ideas
The troubleshooting steps
Stop and make it safe. Stop using the equipment. Tell your supervisor. In BC, anyone who sees what appears to be an unsafe condition must report it to a supervisor or the employer as soon as possible (WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 3.10).
Describe the symptom exactly. What happens, when it started, what changed just before, and what still works.
Read the manual. Most manuals have a troubleshooting table with symptoms, possible causes and who may do each check.
Check from simplest and most likely to hardest. Start with checks that take seconds and need no tools.
Control the energy before you put your hands on it. See the next section.
Change one thing at a time, test, and write it down. Otherwise you will not know what fixed it.
Know where your role stops. If the fix needs covers or guards off, electrical work, or a part the manual says only a service centre may change, the equipment is removed from service and tagged so nobody uses it by mistake (section 12.10), and it goes to the person authorized to repair it.
Energy: unplug, release, lock out
WorkSafeBC counts electrical, mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic, chemical and thermal energy as energy sources (section 10.1). If equipment could start up or release energy unexpectedly and hurt someone, that energy must be isolated and controlled (section 10.2).
Cord or quick-connect equipment (a portable compressor, a corded drill, a tool on a quick-release air line): unplug or disconnect it and keep the plug or connection point under your immediate control the whole time you work on it (section 10.11). Also release any stored pressure, as the manual says.
Hard-wired or fixed machinery (a table saw wired to a wall disconnect, a shop dust collector): lock out the energy isolating device with your own personal lock, following the written lockout procedure, and verify that the energy is locked out before you start (sections 10.3, 10.4 and 10.6). You remove your own lock when your work is done (section 10.7).
Worked example
A shop vac at Coldwater Fabrication (fictional) stops picking up. The symptom: it runs and sounds normal but has almost no suction, starting this morning after it was used on metal filings. The manual's table lists: full tank, clogged filter, blocked hose. Simplest first: unplug it and keep the plug beside you, then check the tank (half full), then look through the hose (a ball of filings and rag is stuck at the bend). Clear the hose, plug in, test: suction is back. Record: "Shop vac, no suction. Cause: hose blocked at the bend. Cleared, tested OK, 9:15 a.m."
The case: a compressor on a framing site
Riverbend Framing (fictional) runs its framing nailers off a portable electric air compressor, the Tidewater PC-20, from the fictional Tidewater Tool Co.
Crew messages, Tuesday
Chris, Monday 4:30 p.m.: Bin truck backed over hose 2 (the long one) this afternoon. Looks ok.
Aaron, Tuesday 2:10 p.m.: Nailer leaving nails sticking up since lunch.
Bri, Tuesday 2:20 p.m.: Compressor never shuts off now.
Aaron, Tuesday 2:25 p.m.: I can hear a hiss by the coupler on hose 2.
Bri, Tuesday 2:40 p.m.: Pump's probably shot, it's old. We should just buy a new one.
Aaron, Tuesday 2:45 p.m.: Regulator gauge says 90 psi.
From the Tidewater PC-20 manual (fictional)
Page 4. Before any maintenance: turn the switch to OFF, unplug the cord and keep the plug with you, then open the tank drain valve until the tank gauge reads 0 psi.
Normal operation: the motor starts when tank pressure drops to 95 psi and stops at 125 psi.
Symptom Possible cause Check Who and how
Runs all the time and never reaches 125 psi Tank drain valve left open See that the drain valve is closed Operator. No tools.
Air leak at a hose, coupler or fitting With tools connected but not firing, listen and look for leaks Operator may replace a damaged hose or coupler only after following page 4
Intake filter blocked Look at the filter Operator, only after following page 4
Worn pump Authorized service centre only. Do not open the pump cover.
Tool weak, but compressor reaches 125 psi and stops Regulator set below the tool's range Read the regulator gauge Operator
The crew's framing nailer label (fictional) says: operating pressure 70 to 120 psi.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Put the troubleshooting steps in order: test and record the result, describe the symptom exactly, stop and tell the supervisor, unplug and release the pressure, read the manual's table, check the simplest likely cause first.
Task 2 (level 2) Use the crew messages to write the symptom description in two or three sentences, with facts only. Then name the message that is an opinion or a guess, and say why you would not act on it yet.
Task 3 (level 2) Using the manual's table and the crew messages, put the four possible causes for "runs all the time" in the order you would check them. Give a reason for your order.
Task 4 (level 2) For each action, write A (operator may do it with the compressor running), B (operator may do it only after page 4: off, unplugged, plug kept with you, tank at 0 psi) or C (not the operator's job: remove from service, tag it, and send it to the authorized service centre).
a. Read the regulator gauge.
b. See whether the tank drain valve is closed.
c. Replace the damaged coupler on hose 2.
d. Take off the pump cover to look at the valves.
e. Look at the intake filter.
f. Listen for leaks with the nailers connected but not firing.
Task 5 (level 3) Here is the crew's test log. Decide whether the fault is fixed, and what should happen next.
Time Change made Test result
3:00 p.m. None. Checked the drain valve. Drain valve was already closed. Compressor still runs nonstop.
3:05 p.m. Followed page 4. Replaced the coupler on hose 2. Plugged back in. Compressor reached 125 psi and stopped.
3:25 p.m. None. Nailers connected, not firing, for 20 minutes. Compressor did not restart. Tank gauge still above 95 psi.
3:30 p.m. Regulator left at 90 psi. Ten test nails into a scrap stud. All ten nails flush.
a. Is the fault fixed? Use the log to explain.
b. Why did the crew check the drain valve even though they could hear the hiss at hose 2?
c. Bri now says, "While we're at it, swap the intake filter and hose 2 too." What do you say, and why?
d. What did the log prove about Bri's 2:40 p.m. message?
Task 6 (level 2) Next week you need to change the blade on the shop's table saw, which is wired to a disconnect switch on the wall. Why does the "unplug and keep the plug with you" method not apply? List what you must do instead before you start, using the sections named in the key ideas.
Check yourself
Why change only one thing at a time?
Name three kinds of energy that WorkSafeBC counts as energy sources.
When may you work on a corded tool without putting a lock on it?
What happens to a tool that is unsafe and cannot be fixed by the operator?

lessons.title: Weigh your options and make a decision
lessons.text:
Know your decision style, build more than one option, check each against what must happen, and choose with if-then thinking.
Why this matters on the job
Every day on a BC site someone has to decide: rent the lift or carry it up, take the job offer now or wait for the apprenticeship, pour today or wait out the rain. A quick decision can be the right one, but a decision made without looking at the options often costs more later. This lesson gives you a way to decide that you can explain to a supervisor, a crew or your family.
Key ideas
Decision styles
Everyone has a usual way of deciding. None is always wrong, but each has a cost. These styles come from the ACCESS lesson this one replaces.
Style What it looks like Motto
Impulsive Little thought, take the first option "Don't look, just leap!"
Fatalistic Let things decide for you "It's out of my hands."
Compliant Let someone else decide, offer no opinion "Whatever you say."
Delaying Put it off, drag it out "What's the rush?"
Agonizing Lost in the details, overwhelmed "I'm so confused!"
Planning Use a process to reach a good result "Let's look at the facts and the consequences."
Intuitive Go with a gut feeling "It just feels right."
Paralysis Accept the decision but cannot act "I can't face it."
Intuition built on years of experience can be fast and good. Compliance is right when the decision really belongs to your supervisor. The planning style is the one to reach for when the stakes are high.
Steps to an effective decision
Define the decision to be made.
List the options you already know about.
Look for new options: ask others, check what worked before.
Sort what must happen from what you would like to happen.
Check each option against the musts first. An option that fails a must is out, however cheap or easy it is.
Compare the options that are left on pros and cons, short term and long term.
Choose, act, and follow up.
If-then thinking
Write what you will do if something changes: "If the boom truck cancels by noon Thursday, then the crew carries the sheets up Thursday afternoon." If-then statements give you a backup before you need one.
People value different things
Two careful people can look at the same facts and decide differently, because they put different weight on safety, money, time, loyalty or fairness. When you disagree, explain what you value and why. That usually gets further than arguing about who is right.
Worked example
Riverbend Framing (fictional) must get 80 sheets of drywall to the third floor of a building by Friday 7 a.m. for the drywall crew.
Musts: on the third floor by Friday 7 a.m., done safely, extra cost no more than $400.
Likes: least crew time, least heavy carrying up stairs.
Option Facts (fictional) Meets the musts?
A. Crew carries it up the stairs Thursday afternoon 4 workers for about 3 hours, no extra cost, lots of carrying on temporary stairs Yes, if done with safe lifting and two-person carries
B. Rent a material hoist Thursday $350 rental. The rental company requires a trained operator. The site's only trained operator is off Thursday. No. Nobody trained can run it on Thursday.
C. Supplier's boom truck places it through third-floor window openings Thursday 2 p.m., $150 extra. Needs the openings clear and two people to receive. Must be booked by Wednesday noon. Yes
D. Leave it on the ground for the drywall crew No cost No. It misses Friday 7 a.m.
Options A and C are left. A costs 4 × 3 = 12 crew hours and a lot of carrying. C costs $150 and about 2 people for a short time. Decision: book the boom truck by Wednesday noon. If the supplier cancels by Thursday noon, then the crew carries the sheets up Thursday afternoon (option A).
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Past decisions. Write three decisions you have made in the last year. You do not have to share them. Beside each, write the letter or letters that describe how you made it.
A. It felt right.
B. I left the decision to someone else.
C. I put off the decision.
D. I did the first thing that came to mind.
E. I took the safest choice.
F. I waited until things got so bad I had to act.
G. I left it up to fate.
H. I decided what mattered most to me and acted on it.
I. I did what I wanted without thinking about what would happen.
Do you see a pattern? Which style from the table is closest to yours?
Task 2 (level 1) Match each saying to a decision style.
a. "Flip a coin, whatever happens happens."
b. "Let me just get through the weekend and I'll think about it."
c. "I've read six reviews of every saw and I still can't pick one."
d. "Let's write down what we need, then compare."
e. "You're the foreman, your call."
f. "Grab that one, it'll do."
Task 3 (level 2) Jordan is finishing a trades prep program and has two offers (both fictional).
Offer 1: labourer with Northline Civil, starts Monday, $26 an hour, no apprenticeship, 90-minute drive each way.
Offer 2: apprentice carpenter with Cedar Flats Builders, starts in 6 weeks, $22 an hour, the employer will sign Jordan up as an apprentice, 20-minute drive each way.
Make a table with pros and cons of each offer, in the short term (next 3 months) and the long term (next 3 years). Then write one question Jordan should answer before choosing.
Task 4 (level 2) The drywall plan in the worked example could still go wrong. Write three more if-then statements that would keep the job on track.
Task 5 (level 3) Read the story, then rank the five people from 1 (most responsible for the lost load) to 5 (least responsible). Write one reason for each. Then compare with a group and try to agree on one ranking.
The rejected load (fictional)
A wall pour at a Lakeview Concrete Forming site was booked for 10:00 a.m. The evening before, superintendent Dale told crew lead Priya to "make sure the forms are checked first thing," then left to manage another site. He did not answer his phone the next morning.
At 6:00 a.m. Priya asked apprentice Sam to check the form bracing. Sam found two loose braces on the north wall. He was not sure it mattered and Priya looked busy, so he told no one.
At the supplier, dispatcher Ray batched the load at 8:45 a.m. to get ahead of traffic, without calling the site. The truck arrived at 9:15. The supplier's ticket says concrete must be placed within 90 minutes of batching.
At 9:30 the pump operator, Gwen, walked the forms, saw the loose braces and refused to pump until they were fixed. The crew finished the repairs at 10:20 a.m. The load was too old to use and was rejected. It cost the company $1,200.
Task 6 (level 2) In the story, Gwen refused to pump. Look up WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 3.12 at https://www.worksafebc.com/en/law-policy/occupational-health-safety/searchable-ohs-regulation/ohs-regulation/part-03-rights-and-responsibilities and explain why her decision was not just her style but her duty. When did the load's 90 minutes run out?
Check yourself
Name two decision styles and one situation where each one works well.
What is the difference between a must and a like?
Write an if-then statement for getting to work on a day the bus might not run.
Why might two careful people rank the people in "The rejected load" differently?
More practice: compare quotes with a weighted decision table
When several options all meet the musts, a weighted decision table helps you compare them on the likes. Give each thing you care about a weight so the weights add up to 100. Score each option from 1 (poor) to 5 (best) on each thing. Multiply each weight by its score, then add the products for each option (BEDMAS: multiply first, then add). The highest total is the best fit for what you said matters.
Task 7 (level 2) Northshore Pipe and Steel (fictional) needs steel pipe for the 10-section handrail job. Every supplier must supply mill certificates (the steel's test reports), because the job specification asks for them. Three fictional suppliers quoted.
Fraser Steel Supply Delta Metals Coastline Steel
Price $4,200 $4,450 $4,900
Delivery 8 working days 3 working days 5 working days
Mill certificates Sent with the steel Only on request, 5 days after delivery Sent with the steel
Distance from the shop 45 km 12 km 30 km
The foreman sets these weights and scores:
What matters Weight Fraser Delta Coastline
Price 40 5 4 2
Delivery 30 3 5 4
Mill certificates 20 5 2 5
Distance 10 3 5 4
a. Check that the weights add up to 100.
b. Work out the weighted total for each supplier. Show the BEDMAS steps for one.
c. Which supplier has the highest total?
d. The general contractor now says the steel must be in the shop within 5 working days. That is a must. Which supplier is out? Of the two left, which has the higher total?
e. Instead of part d, suppose the foreman decides delivery matters most and changes the weights to price 30, delivery 40, certificates 20, distance 10. Work out the new totals. Which supplier wins now?
f. Write two sentences to the foreman defending your choice for the 5-day must in part d.

lessons.title: Plan and organize the work
lessons.text:
Break a job into tasks, put them in order, list what you need, estimate the time, and adjust the plan when something changes.
Why this matters on the job
A job that is not planned turns into trips back to the truck, a crew waiting for material and a finish time nobody can predict. Employers notice the apprentice who shows up on time with the right gear and knows what comes next. Planning is also problem solving: you find the problems before they happen.
Key ideas
Break the job into tasks
Write every task as a short action: "cut shelves," "sand edges." Small tasks are easier to order, time and hand out.
Put the tasks in order
Ask of each task: what has to be done before this can start? Some tasks depend on others: you cannot assemble parts you have not cut. Others can happen at the same time or in any order.
List what you need
From the drawing or cut list, write a checklist of materials, tools and safety gear. Check it before you start, not halfway through.
Estimate the time
Add up the time for each task. Use BEDMAS: brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Add time for setup, cleanup and breaks. Those are the parts people forget.
Use an action planner
This planner comes from the ACCESS lesson this one replaces:
What needs to be done?
When (time frame and deadline)?
Where?
How?
Resources needed: people, materials, tools, money?
Anything else that could get in the way?
Digital tools help, if you check them
A calendar alarm, a checklist app or a photo of the cut list on your phone can keep you organized. Check that the alarm is set for a.m., not p.m., that the date is right, that your phone is charged, and that anyone who needs the plan can see it.
Worked example
You are building two plywood shelf units for the tool crib in a training shop (fictional). Time per task:
Task Time
Set up and check the saw 10 min
Cut parts 25 min per unit
Sand edges 15 min for both
Assemble 20 min per unit
Clean up 15 min
Total time = 10 + 2 × 25 + 15 + 2 × 20 + 15
Multiplication first (BEDMAS): 2 × 25 = 50 and 2 × 20 = 40.
Then add: 10 + 50 + 15 + 40 + 15 = 130 min, which is 2 hours 10 minutes.
Starting at 8:00 a.m. with a 15-minute coffee break, you would finish at 8:00 + 2 h 10 min + 15 min = 10:25 a.m.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Put these tasks for the shelf job in order. Mark any two that could swap places.
Sweep up and put tools away
Cut the parts
Check the cut list against the drawing
Sand the edges
Assemble the units with glue and screws
Get the plywood and screws from the rack
Set up and check the saw
Send the supervisor a photo of the finished units
Task 2 (level 1) Here is the cut list for the two shelf units (fictional). Make a materials and tools checklist.
Cut list, 2 shelf units. 19 mm plywood. Sides: 4 pieces, 300 mm × 1200 mm. Shelves: 8 pieces, 300 mm × 800 mm. Fasten each shelf with 6 screws, 45 mm long. Wood glue on every joint. Sand all edges with 120-grit paper. Wear safety glasses and hearing protection at the saw.
How many screws do you need? Screws come in boxes of 100. How many boxes?
Task 3 (level 2) Plywood comes in sheets 1220 mm × 2440 mm. Each sheet can be ripped into 4 strips 300 mm wide (the leftover allows for saw cuts). From one 2440 mm strip you can cut either 2 sides (1200 mm) or 3 shelves (800 mm). How many strips do you need for 4 sides and 8 shelves? How many sheets is that?
Task 4 (level 2) You start a new job with Cedar Flats Builders (fictional) on Monday. Read the email and fill in an action planner. Work out the latest time you should leave home.
Start time is 7:00 a.m. sharp at 2250 Mountview Road. Please arrive 15 minutes early to sign in and do your site orientation. Bring: hard hat, safety boots, safety glasses, high-visibility vest, work gloves, lunch and water. Parking is on the street. Questions? Reply to this email.
Lena, site office
Your drive takes 45 minutes. You want 15 extra minutes in case of traffic.
Task 5 (level 2) You decide to use your phone to keep the Monday plan. Write the reminder or checklist entries you would set up. Then list three things you would check so the phone does not let you down.
Task 6 (level 2) Back at the shop, the plywood delivery is delayed until 10:00 a.m. You were going to start at 8:00. What can you still do before 10:00? Using the times in the worked example, when will the job now finish if the saw is set up before the plywood arrives and you take no break?
Check yourself
What question helps you put tasks in order?
Using BEDMAS, what is 5 + 3 × 10?
Name two parts of a job that people often forget to include in a time estimate.
What should you check before trusting a phone alarm?

lessons.title: Check whether the fix worked
lessons.text:
Decide what success looks like, test the fix under real conditions, follow up, ask for feedback and record what you learned.
Why this matters on the job
A fix that works for ten minutes is not finished. On BC sites, a leak that comes back, a door that sticks again in winter or a repair that causes a new problem costs a return trip and trust. Checking the result, following up and sharing what you learned is how crews stop solving the same problem twice.
Key ideas
Decide what success looks like before you test
Write checks that anyone can observe. "It works" is not a check. "The compressor reaches 125 psi and shuts off" is.
Test under real conditions
Test the way the work is really done: with the real tools, the real load, for long enough. A door that latches once in the morning may not latch in the afternoon heat.
Watch for side effects
A fix can solve one problem and start another. Ask: Did anything else change?
Follow up
Come back later: the next day, the next week, or after the next cold snap. Problems that return are telling you the first cause was not the whole story.
Count carefully
When you compare before and after, compare rates, not just counts: 2 failures out of 24 is different from 2 out of 200. Small numbers can change a lot by chance, so keep checking before you claim success. If you changed two things at once, you cannot say which one worked.
Ask for feedback and record what you learned
The people who use the fix every day notice things you miss. Ask them. Then write a short lesson learned: what happened, what worked, and what to do next time. The ACCESS decision steps end the same way: follow up, evaluate, and revise if necessary.
Worked example
Back in the shop vac example from the troubleshooting lesson, the hose was cleared and suction came back.
Success checks: picks up a handful of filings from the floor in one pass, runs 10 minutes with no drop in suction, filter not torn.
Follow-up: next morning, the hose blocked again at the same bend.
New question: why does it block there? The crew had been vacuuming filings and rags together.
Revised fix: rags go in the bin by hand, and the shop vac is for filings only.
Lesson learned: "Shop vac hose blocks at the bend when rags are vacuumed. Pick up rags by hand."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) In the troubleshooting lesson, Riverbend Framing (fictional) replaced the coupler on hose 2 of their compressor. Write four checks that would show the fix worked. Each must be something anyone could see or measure.
Task 2 (level 2) Here is the follow-up log for the compressor.
Day What happened
Wednesday 7:30 a.m. Compressor reached 125 psi and shut off. Nailers working normally.
Wednesday 2:00 p.m. Compressor running longer than usual. Hiss at the coupler on hose 3.
Thursday 7:00 a.m. Crew followed page 4 of the manual and replaced the coupler on hose 3. Compressor normal all day.
Friday 7:30 a.m. Chris points out that the couplers on hoses 1 and 4 are the same brand and age as the two that failed.
a. Did the Tuesday fix work? Did it solve the whole problem? Explain.
b. What pattern does the log show?
c. Write one short-term action and one long-term action for the crew.
d. Is there anything from Monday's event (the bin truck backing over hose 2) that should go in the long-term plan?
Task 3 (level 2) Write three questions you would ask the framing crew to get feedback on the compressor and hoses. Then name one other person whose feedback would help, and say why.
Task 4 (level 3) In the patterns lesson, Northshore Pipe and Steel (fictional) found that night-shift welds in booth 3 failed the bend test far more often: 9 out of 24 samples. The supervisor then made two changes to booth 3: a screen was moved to block the draft from the overhead door, and a damaged ground cable was replaced. Here are the next two weeks.
Shift Booth Samples tested Samples failed
Day 1 and 2 24 1
Night 3 24 2
a. What percentage of night-shift samples failed before the changes, and after?
b. By how many percentage points did the night-shift failure rate change?
c. Which of these statements does the record support? Explain each.
"The screen fixed the problem."
"The failure rate in booth 3 was lower in the two weeks after the changes."
"Booth 3 is now as good as booths 1 and 2."
d. What would you do next?
Task 5 (level 2) Write a lesson learned of four or five sentences for the next crew toolbox talk at Riverbend Framing, based on the compressor and hoses. Say what happened, what worked, and what to do next time.
Check yourself
Why should you write success checks before you test?
What is a side effect of a fix?
Why compare rates instead of counts?
What is the problem with making two changes at once?
More practice: close out the job and record lessons learned
A job is not finished when the last board goes down. It is finished when every item on the punch list (the list of small things still to fix or hand over) is closed, the owner has what they need, and the crew has written down what to keep, what to change and what to try next time. That short record is how the next crew starts ahead.
Task 6 (level 2) Riverbend Decks (fictional) is closing out a backyard deck, the same deck used in Numeracy lesson 19. Here is the punch list on Monday morning.
No. Punch list item Status
1 Touch up stain on the stair treads Done
2 Tighten the loose baluster on the east railing Done
3 Replace one cracked deck board Open: new board arrives Thursday
4 Pick up offcuts and loose screws from the lawn Done
5 Give the owner the stain and hardware product sheets Done
6 Final inspection passed Done
7 Fill and re-seed the ruts where the truck drove on the lawn Open
8 Return the rented auger Done
Notes the crew wrote during the job:
"Footing pour got rained out. Lost 2 days." "Ordering lumber a week early meant we never waited for material." "The cracked board came in the first delivery. Nobody checked the pile." "Owner was really happy to get the product sheets." "Truck wrecked the lawn. Should have laid down plywood."
a. How many items are done? What percent of the punch list is complete?
b. Which items stop the job from being closed out? For each one, name an owner (a job title is fine) and a date to have it done.
c. Write a lessons-learned record under three headings: Keep (worked well, do it again), Change (caused a problem, do it differently) and Try next time (a new idea). Put at least one item under each heading, using the crew's notes.
d. Who should get a copy of the record, and why?

lessons.title: Decide whether an online answer can be trusted
lessons.text:
Check who wrote an answer, when, for which place and why, and confirm it against the official BC source before you act on it.
Why this matters on the job
When you get stuck on a job, the fastest answer is usually on your phone: a search, a video, a forum or an AI chatbot. Some of those answers are excellent. Others are out of date, written for another country, or trying to sell you something. In BC trades, acting on the wrong rule can fail an inspection, cost money or hurt someone. Checking takes a few minutes.
Key ideas
Five questions for any answer
Who wrote it? A regulator, a manufacturer, a trade school, a stranger, a company selling something?
When was it written? Codes and rules change. An answer from before the current edition may be wrong now.
