Where does it apply? Rules in another province or country can be different from BC's.
Why was it written? To inform, to sell, to get views?
Can I check it against the official source?
Warning signs
The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security suggests looking for: a web address with typos or one that does not match the organization it claims to represent, no contact information, no physical address and no "About us" page, and information that is out of date. A .net or .org ending alone does not show that a site is unreliable. Compare the full domain with the organization's verified address. Check the story against other sources, and do not assume something is correct just because a friend sent it.
AI chatbots
AI tools can give a confident, well-written answer that is wrong. The Cyber Centre advises being careful with AI content, analyzing it before you act on it, and validating the sources to check whether it is accurate. Use AI to get started or to find the name of the rule, then read the rule itself.
Official BC sources for the trades
Topic Official source
Workplace health and safety WorkSafeBC, Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) Regulation: https://www.worksafebc.com/en/law-policy/occupational-health-safety/searchable-ohs-regulation/ohs-regulation
Building and plumbing Province of BC, BC Building Code 2024: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/construction-industry/building-codes-standards/bc-codes/2024-bc-codes
Electrical Province of BC, BC Electrical Code: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/construction-industry/building-codes-standards/bc-codes/electrical-code
A specific tool or machine The manufacturer's manual for that model
How your employer does it Your supervisor and the employer's written procedures
A few current facts from those pages:
The BC Building Code 2024 came into effect on March 8, 2024. Its earthquake design and adaptable dwelling requirements apply to projects with building permits applied for on or after March 10, 2025.
The BC Electrical Code is the Canadian Electrical Code, Part I, adopted with a few BC changes. The current edition, the 26th edition (2024), came into effect in BC on March 4, 2025. Technical Safety BC enforces it.
Projects permitted before a new edition can fall under transition rules, so check the official page or ask your supervisor which edition applies to your job.
Worked example
Your search for "do I need to lock out an air compressor" finds a forum post: "Nah, just turn it off, it's only air." Check it:
Who: an unnamed forum user. When: no date. Where: unknown. Why: a quick reply.
Official source: WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation Part 10 lists pneumatic energy as an energy source (section 10.1). Where unexpected startup or release of energy could injure someone, it must be isolated and controlled (section 10.2). A corded compressor can be worked on without a lock when it is unplugged and the plug is kept under your immediate control the whole time (section 10.11). The manual will also tell you to release the stored air pressure.
Result: the forum post is wrong. Do not use it.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) You want to know: "What eye protection do I need for grinding at work in BC?" Rank these sources from most to least trustworthy for this question, and give a reason for each.
a. A forum post from 2014 on a United States woodworking site
b. A video by a tool reviewer, paid by a safety glasses brand
c. An AI chatbot answer that names no sources
d. WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 8.14
e. The manual for your grinder
f. Your supervisor and your employer's written safety rules
Task 2 (level 2) An AI chatbot gives you this answer:
"In BC, safety glasses for work must meet ANSI Z87.1. CSA-certified glasses are not accepted."
Open WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 8.14 at https://www.worksafebc.com/en/law-policy/occupational-health-safety/searchable-ohs-regulation/ohs-regulation/part-08-personal-protective-clothing-and-equipment and check the answer. What is right, what is wrong, and what does the chatbot leave out?
Task 3 (level 2) You find this web page. List every warning sign, and check the main claim against WorkSafeBC Part 10.
worksafe-bc-rules.net
BC Safety Rules Made Simple!
Good news: lockout is only needed on machines over 600 volts. Everything else, just hit the off switch. Buy our complete lockout kit today, 50% off!
(No author, no date, no contact page.)
Task 4 (level 2) A blog post from 2022 says:
"Remember, BC builds to the 2018 BC Building Code, and BC electrical work follows the 2021 Canadian Electrical Code."
Use the table above to check both claims. What would you say to an apprentice who quoted this post on a new job today?
Task 5 (level 3) Make your own check card with the five questions. Then pick a real question from your trade, for example about fall protection, a ladder, a stair or a tool. Find the official BC source that answers it, write down its web address, and write the answer in your own words.
Check yourself
What are the five questions to ask about any answer?
Name two warning signs on a web page.
When can an AI chatbot answer be useful, and what must you do before acting on it?
Which organization's regulation covers workplace health and safety in BC?

lessons.title: Recover a late schedule
lessons.text:
Measure a delay with the critical path, build recovery options (resequence, add crew, overtime, fast-track), weigh their days, costs and risks, then decide, justify the choice and check the new schedule.
Why this matters on the job
Every job hits a problem: a failed inspection, a late delivery, a sick crew, a week of rain. The schedule slips. A good lead hand or superintendent does not just say "we'll be late". They work out how late, find ways to buy the time back, weigh the cost and the risk of each, and pick the best one. This lesson uses the critical path skills from Numeracy lessons 17 to 21 and the decision steps from lesson 6 of this set.
Key ideas
Six steps to recover a late schedule
Measure the delay. Put the delay into the network and redo the passes. How many working days late is the finish? What date is that?
Find the new critical path. Only time saved on the critical path moves the finish date.
List your options. Look for all four kinds below. Write down how many days each saves, what it costs and what could go wrong.
Check the musts. Drop any option, or mix of options, that does not meet a must, for example the date the owner needs.
Choose and justify. From the options that meet the musts, pick the one with the best mix of cost, risk and effort. Plan a backup with if-then thinking.
Check the result and tell people. Redo the passes with your choice. Look at the float that is left. Tell the owner and every trade whose dates change.
Four ways to buy time back
Option What you do Why it saves time Costs and risks
Resequence Change the order of the work or split it, so crews keep working around the problem. Work that was waiting starts sooner. Low cost. Needs planning. Crews may set up twice. Some changes need the inspector or engineer to agree.
Add crew (crashing) Put more workers or equipment on a critical activity. The activity takes fewer days. Extra labour cost. Only helps if there is room to work and the work can be shared. New workers need an orientation.
Overtime Work longer days or a Saturday. More working hours fit into the same calendar days. Overtime pay or a premium from the subcontractor. Fatigue raises the risk of mistakes and injuries.
Fast-track Overlap activities that were planned one after the other. The second activity starts before the first one finishes. Little direct cost. Higher risk of rework, damage and crowding.
Shorten the critical path only. Buying time on an activity with float does not move the finish date. After each change, check the critical path again. A new path may become critical.
Worked example: late roof trusses on the garage
Northshore Garage Builders (fictional) planned the garage in Numeracy lessons 18 to 21 at 20 working days, finishing on Monday, June 7, 2027.
Measure. The truss supplier says the trusses will take 14 working days instead of 10. The trusses had 3 days of total float, so the job is 14 − 10 − 3 = 1 day late: 21 days, Tuesday, June 8.
New critical path. 1, 6 (trusses), 11, 12. The trusses are now critical. The footing, slab and framing work (activities 2 to 5 and 7 to 10) now has 1 or 2 days of float.
Options.
Resequence: nothing useful. The roof cannot go on before the trusses arrive.
Add crew: a second roofer cuts Shingles from 2 days to 1 for $350 (from lesson 21). Saves 1 day.
Overtime: the framing crew works a Saturday. But framing is no longer critical, so it saves nothing.
Fast-track: start shingling while sheathing is still going on. Risky on a small roof with two crews on it.
Musts. The owner needs June 7. Only the extra roofer meets it with low risk.
Choose. Add the second roofer for $350. If the supplier slips again, then ask about a Saturday for the roof crew.
Check. With trusses at 14 days and shingles at 1 day, the passes give 20 days, Monday, June 7. Every activity from 11 on is critical, so the roof crew must not lose a day.
Musts and wants
From lesson 6: a must is a requirement that an option has to meet, or it is out. A want is something you would like, used to compare the options that are left, for example lowest cost, lowest risk or no weekend work.
The situation
Cedar Flats Builders (a fictional company from lesson 7) is renovating a washroom in a rental suite for Harbourview Property Management (fictional). The network is the washroom job from Numeracy lessons 19 to 21. Work started on Monday, September 13, 2027. The plan finishes with the final inspection on Wednesday, October 6. The new tenant's lease starts on Thursday, October 7. The property manager has said that date is a must: if the washroom is not done, Harbourview pays $350 a night for a hotel for the tenant (made up for this lesson).
The delay. On Tuesday, September 21, the rough-in inspection fails at the shower drain. The plumber needs 2 working days to redo the drain. Then the inspector comes back for a re-inspection, 1 working day. The insulation cannot start on the plan until the re-inspection passes. The planner adds the two new activities to the network and redoes the passes:
ID Activity Start Finish
6 Rough-in inspection Tue Sep 21, 2027 Tue Sep 21, 2027
6a Rework shower drain Wed Sep 22, 2027 Thu Sep 23, 2027
6b Re-inspection Fri Sep 24, 2027 Fri Sep 24, 2027
7 Insulation and vapour barrier Mon Sep 27, 2027 Mon Sep 27, 2027
8 Hang drywall and cement board Tue Sep 28, 2027 Wed Sep 29, 2027
9 Tape and mud Wed Sep 29, 2027 Mon Oct 4, 2027
10 Waterproof membrane Fri Oct 1, 2027 Fri Oct 1, 2027

The options. The site supervisor and the trades suggest four ideas. Costs are made up for this lesson.
Option A. The inspector agrees that the walls without plumbing passed. The crew insulates and boards those walls during the drain repair, and does the shower wall after the re-inspection. Tape and mud can start on the finished walls. Extra cost: the crews set up twice, about $240.
Option B. A second plumber joins the drain repair, so it takes 1 day instead of 2. Extra cost: 8 hours at $95 an hour = $760.
Option C. The crew on site works on Saturday, October 2. Each trade crew charges a $450 Saturday premium.

The planner redid the passes for each option and for some mixes. A Saturday does not change the day numbers. It adds one working day to the calendar, so the dates move earlier.

a) How many working days late is the job with no action?

c) Which activities moved, and which did not move? Use the tables and charts.

Task 3 (level 2-3). Copy and finish this table. Hotel nights: count each night from October 7 up to and including the final inspection date. If the final inspection is on October 6 or earlier, there are 0 nights.
Plan Extra cost Hotel nights Hotel cost Total cost Meets the must?
No action $0

a) Option D saves 1 day on its own. Why does A + D save no more than A alone? Hint: after Option A, both the tile path and the paint path are critical.
b) A + C has 2 Saturday crews, but C alone has only 1. Why?
Task 5 (level 3). Decide.
a) Which plans meet the must?

What are the four ways to buy time back on a schedule?

lessons.title: Break a job into a work breakdown structure
lessons.text:
Split a whole job into the pieces you will hand over, number them, check that nothing is missing or extra, and write a work package card for each piece.
Why this matters on the job
Before anyone orders lumber or books a crew, someone has to answer one question: what exactly are we building? A job that is broken into clear pieces is easier to price, schedule, hand out and check. A piece that nobody wrote down, like the stairs or the cleanup, is the piece that gets forgotten and costs money at the end. On BC sites, lead hands, estimators and superintendents break jobs down this way every week. This lesson comes before the activity lists in Numeracy lesson 19 and the planning steps in lesson 7.
Key ideas
A work breakdown structure is a family tree for the job
A work breakdown structure (WBS) starts with the whole job at the top. Under it are the big pieces. Under each big piece are smaller pieces. You keep splitting until each piece is small enough to hand to one person or one crew.
Pieces, not actions
A WBS lists the pieces you will hand over (the deliverables). Write them as things, not actions:
Piece in the WBS (a thing) Activity in the schedule (an action)
Pier footings Pour pier footings
Stair stringers Cut stair stringers
Railings Install railings
The activities come later, when you plan the order and the days. Start with the pieces so you do not miss any.
Number every piece
The whole job is 1. The big pieces are 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 and so on. The pieces under 1.2 are 1.2.1, 1.2.2 and so on. The number tells you where a piece sits in the tree. Some companies write the top as 1.0. Use whatever your company uses, the same way every time.
The 100 percent check
Ask three questions of every WBS:
Is everything in the job somewhere in the list? Include the pieces people forget: permits and inspections, cleanup, handover.
Is anything in the list that is not part of this job? If the owner did not pay for it, it does not belong.
Is any piece in two places? Each piece has one home. If the door is under "walls" and also under "openings", it gets counted, priced and built twice on paper.
Stop when a piece is a work package
Stop splitting when one person or crew can do the piece, you can say how long it takes and what it costs, and someone can check that it is done. That lowest piece is a work package. Write a card for it:
Number and name
Who does it
How long it takes
Cost (labour and material)
Done when: what anyone can see or measure to know it is finished
Worked example: the backyard deck
Riverbend Decks (a fictional company) is building the backyard deck you will meet again in Numeracy lesson 19.
The lines show which pieces belong to the whole deck. They do not show task order or construction details. Read the complete text outline below. Open the full-size diagram.
1 Backyard deck 1.1 Footings 1.1.1 Layout and post holes 1.1.2 Pier footings 1.2 Frame 1.2.1 Posts and beams 1.2.2 Joists 1.3 Decking 1.4 Stairs 1.4.1 Stair stringers 1.4.2 Finished stairs 1.5 Railings 1.6 Close-out 1.6.1 Final inspection 1.6.2 Cleanup and handover
100 percent check. Everything the owner is paying for is there, including the inspection and the cleanup. Nothing extra is there: the owner's new hot tub is not in this contract, so it is not in the list. Each piece has one home.
Work package card, 1.1.2 Pier footings (job data for this fictional deck):
Who: Marcus and one labourer
How long: 1 day to pour, then 2 days for the concrete to cure before posts go on
Cost: labour 2 workers × 6 hours × $40 an hour = $480, plus concrete, tubes and anchors $360, total $840
Done when: 6 piers poured at the layout marks, tops at the marked height, anchors set, and the inspector's footing approval recorded (on this job the city checks the holes before the pour)
Notice the BEDMAS in the cost: multiply first (2 × 6 × 40 = 480), then add (480 + 360 = 840).
From work packages to activities
Each lowest piece becomes one or more activities, written as a verb and a thing: 1.1.2 Pier footings becomes "Pour pier footings". When every work package has its activities, you have the activity list for the schedule. For more practice with job planning numbers, open the Numeracy Hub Construction Operations tab.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Sort these into pieces (things you hand over) and activities (actions).
Install joists
Decking
Railings
Cut stair stringers
Final inspection
Dig post holes
Posts and beams
Sweep the yard
Task 2 (level 2) Riverbend Decks is also building a small garden shed (fictional). Put these pieces into a WBS with numbers. The whole job is 1 Garden shed. There are four big pieces: base, walls, roof and close-out.
Floor framing, roof sheathing and shingles, gravel pad, wall framing, roof trusses, door and window, floor sheathing, siding, final cleanup, concrete deck blocks
Task 3 (level 2) A new estimator wrote this WBS for the shed. Find three problems using the 100 percent check. Say which question each one fails.
1 Garden shed 1.1 Base 1.1.1 Gravel pad 1.1.2 Floor framing and sheathing 1.2 Walls 1.2.1 Wall framing 1.2.2 Siding 1.2.3 Door and window 1.3 Openings 1.3.1 Door and window 1.4 Close-out 1.4.1 Paint the owner's fence 1.4.2 Final cleanup
Task 4 (level 3) Northshore Pipe and Steel (fictional) has a job to build and install 10 sections of steel handrail for a stair in a small commercial building. Read the job notes.
Shop drawings must be approved by the general contractor before we cut. Steel comes from our supplier. Each section takes 3 hours to cut and fit, 2 hours to weld and 1 hour to grind. Each section is then primed in the shop (half an hour each). Install on site takes 1.5 hours a section. After install, the general contractor checks the rail and we touch up any scratched primer. On this job, labour is costed at $50 an hour.
a. Write a WBS with the whole job as 1 and at least five big pieces.
b. Write a work package card for the piece that covers the 10 fabricated sections (cut, fit, weld, grind). Work out the hours and the labour cost with BEDMAS.
c. How many hours of shop priming and site install are there for all 10 sections?
Task 5 (level 2) Look at the backyard deck WBS in the worked example. For each lowest piece (the ones with three-part numbers, plus 1.3 and 1.5), write one activity as a verb and a thing. Then compare your list with the deck table in Numeracy lesson 19. Which piece in the WBS has no activity in that table? Why does it still belong in the WBS?
Check yourself
What is the difference between a piece in a WBS and an activity in a schedule?
What number would the second piece under 1.4 get?
Name the three questions of the 100 percent check.
When do you stop splitting a piece into smaller pieces?
What goes on a work package card?

lessons.title: Rate job risks in a risk register
lessons.text:
List what could go wrong on a job, score how likely and how bad each risk is, rank them, and give each one an owner, a response and a warning sign to watch for.
Why this matters on the job
Every job has things that might go wrong: rain on pour day, steel that arrives late, a wall that is not where the drawing says it is. A crew that has thought about these ahead of time has a backup ready. A crew that has not finds out at 7 a.m. with a truck waiting. Lead hands and superintendents keep a list of these risks, called a risk register, and check it at every planning meeting. This lesson uses the deck and handrail jobs from lesson 11.
Key ideas
A risk has not happened yet
A risk is something that might happen and would hurt the job: its time, cost, quality or someone's safety. "The lumber delivery could be late."
An issue is something that has happened. "The lumber delivery did not come." Issues need action now, like the schedule recovery in lesson 10.
A good risk register turns risks into plans before they become issues.
Write a risk as cause, event, effect
"Weather" is not a risk you can act on. Write three parts:
Because the forecast shows rain on Tuesday (cause), the footing pour may be put off (event), which pushes every later task back (effect).
Score the likelihood and the impact
Use a 1 to 3 scale. A job sets its own scale. This is the one used in this lesson:
Score Likelihood Impact
1 Unlikely Small: less than half a day, or under $200
2 Could happen Medium: half a day to 2 days, or $200 to $1,000
3 Likely Serious: more than 2 days, or over $1,000, or the work must be torn out
Choose the highest applicable impact across time, cost and rework. For example, a delay of one day with a cost over $1,000 has impact 3, not 2.
Risk score = likelihood × impact. Scores run from 1 to 9.
6 or 9: high. Plan a response now and watch it every day.
3 or 4: medium. Plan a response and check it at each planning meeting.
1 or 2: low. Write it down and keep an eye on it.
Read across impact 1, 2, 3. Likelihood 3 gives 3 medium, 6 high, 9 high. Likelihood 2 gives 2 low, 4 medium, 6 high. Likelihood 1 gives 1 low, 2 low, 3 medium. These are the lesson’s practice categories, not a universal risk standard. Open the full-size diagram.
Safety comes first
A risk register is for the job's time, cost and quality. It does not replace the safety hazard checks you learn in safety training. If anything on your list could hurt someone, do not wait for a meeting: in BC, anyone who sees what appears to be an unsafe or harmful condition must report it as soon as possible to a supervisor or the employer (WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 3.10).
Four ways to respond
Response What you do Example
Avoid Change the plan so the risk cannot happen. Measure on site before cutting steel, so the rail cannot be built to wrong numbers.
Reduce Make it less likely or less serious. Order lumber a week early. Book a backup pump.
Share Give it to someone better placed to handle it, by agreement. The supplier agrees in writing to a delivery date.
Accept Live with it and keep an if-then backup ready. If a crew member is off sick, then the lead hand moves a worker from the other site.
Give each risk an owner and a warning sign
Owner: one named person who watches the risk and starts the response. "Everyone" means nobody.
Trigger: the warning sign that the risk is starting to happen. "Supplier has not sent a shipping notice by Wednesday noon."
Worked example: the backyard deck
Riverbend Decks (fictional) listed five risks for the deck. L is likelihood and I is impact.
No. Risk (cause, event, effect) L I Score Response Owner Trigger
R1 Rain is forecast this week, so the footing pour may be put off and the whole job slides. 3 2 6 Reduce: book the pour for the driest day and have tarps on site. Marcus Forecast over 60% chance of rain the evening before
R2 The lumber yard is busy, so the delivery may be late and framing waits. 2 2 4 Reduce: order a week early and confirm by phone. Lena (office) No delivery confirmation by Thursday
R3 A hole may not reach firm soil, so the footing inspection may fail and the holes are redug. 1 3 3 Reduce: check depth and soil before calling the inspector. Marcus Soft soil at the bottom of any hole
R4 A crew member may be off sick, so framing slows. 2 1 2 Accept: if someone is off, then move a worker from the other site. Marcus A sick call before 6:30 a.m.
R5 The supplier may send the wrong size joist hangers, so joists wait. 2 1 2 Reduce: check the hardware against the order when it arrives. Apprentice Packing slip does not match the order
Ranked: R1 (6), R2 (4), R3 (3), R4 and R5 (2). R1 is the only high risk, so Marcus checks the forecast every evening this week.
Learners who want more practice with job numbers can open the Numeracy Hub Construction Operations tab.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Risk or issue? Write R or I beside each.
a. The crane could be booked by another job that day.
b. The inspector failed the framing this morning.
c. The concrete truck might get stuck in traffic on the bridge.
d. Two sheets of plywood arrived cracked.
e. The new apprentice may not have steel-toe boots by Monday.
f. The client changed the paint colour yesterday.
Task 2 (level 2) Rewrite each vague risk as cause, event, effect. You may make up a sensible cause.
a. "Steel."
b. "The inspector."
c. "Parking."
Task 3 (level 2) Northshore Pipe and Steel (fictional) listed these risks for the 10-section handrail job from lesson 11. Work out each score, rank the risks from highest to lowest, and label each high, medium or low.
No. Risk L I
H1 The stair was built a little different from the drawings, so rails built only to drawing numbers may not fit and must be rebuilt. 3 3
H2 The steel supplier is short of pipe, so the material may come late and fabrication waits. 2 3
H3 Drywall in the stairwell may not be finished on install day, so the install crew is sent home. 2 2
H4 The only certified welder may be off sick, so welding waits. 1 2
H5 The primer may be the wrong colour, so the painter complains. 1 1
Task 4 (level 3) For the two highest risks in Task 3:
a. Choose a response (avoid, reduce, share or accept) and say what the crew will do.
b. Name an owner (a job title is fine).
c. Write a trigger.
d. Write one if-then backup.
Task 5 (level 2) Here are parts of a small commercial job (fictional). For each one, describe what could go wrong and state your assumptions about the delay, cost or rework. Use those assumptions to rate its impact: 1 (small), 2 (medium) or 3 (serious). Explain your rating. There is no single impact rating without those details. You cannot assign an overall risk score until you also know the likelihood. If your example could hurt someone, follow the safety reporting rule above rather than using this grid to decide whether to act.
a. Concrete slab pour
b. Roof membrane
c. Sprinkler pressure test
d. Painting the office walls
e. Planting the front garden
Task 6 (level 2) Back at the deck. It rained on Tuesday, as R1 warned, and the pour moved to Thursday.
a. Is R1 still a risk, or is it now an issue?
b. Write a one-line status update for the register.
c. Does any other risk change because of the two-day move? Explain.
Check yourself
What is the difference between a risk and an issue?
A risk has likelihood 2 and impact 3. What is its score, and is it high, medium or low?
Name the four ways to respond to a risk.
Why does each risk need one named owner?
What should you do right away if a risk on your list could hurt someone?

lessons.title: Find the biggest problem first
lessons.text:
Tally problems from a list, sort them in a Pareto chart, draw a fishbone diagram for the biggest one, and test a fix with Plan, Do, Check, Act.
Why this matters on the job
At the end of a job, the deficiency list can run to dozens of items. In a shop, the reject bin fills with parts that failed for all sorts of reasons. A crew cannot fix everything at once. The trick is to find the one or two problems that cause most of the trouble and fix those first. Builders and fabricators across BC use four simple tools for this: a tally sheet, a Pareto chart, a fishbone diagram and Plan, Do, Check, Act. This lesson builds on the patterns in lesson 4 and the before-and-after rates in lesson 8.
Key ideas
1. Tally the problems
Sort each problem into a type and make a mark for each one. Count the marks. A tally sheet turns a long, messy list into a few numbers.
2. Sort them in a Pareto chart
A Pareto chart is a bar chart with the tallest bar on the left and the shortest on the right. "Other" always goes last. A line above the bars shows the running total percent: the first bar, then the first two together, and so on.
Very often a few types make up most of the problems. The chart shows them at a glance, so the crew works on those first.
3. Draw a fishbone for the biggest one
A fishbone diagram (also called a cause-and-effect diagram) puts the problem at the head of the fish. Each bone is a family of possible causes:
People: training, experience, rushing, communication
Method: the order of the work, the procedure, the checklist
Material: what was delivered, stored or used
Equipment: tools, machines, carts, blades
Environment: space, light, weather, noise
Write every possible cause on a bone. Then pick the one or two most likely and check them. A fishbone gives you ideas to test, not answers.
4. Test a fix with Plan, Do, Check, Act
Plan: choose one change, say what you expect, and decide how you will measure it.
Do: try it on a small scale, such as one area or one week.
Check: compare the results with the plan. Use rates, not just counts (lesson 8).
Act: if it worked, make it the new standard way. If not, learn from it and plan the next try.
Then go round again with the next biggest problem.
Some factories have a cord or a button any worker can use to stop the line and call a lead hand when something is wrong. The idea is the same: fix the problem where it starts instead of passing it down the line.
Worked example: a deficiency list
Harbourline Interiors (a fictional company) finished a small office fit-out. The walk-through found 80 deficiencies. The site lead tallied them.
Type Count Percent of total Running total
Drywall dents and gouges 32 40% 40%
Paint touch-ups 20 25% 65%
Missing or loose trim 12 15% 80%
Doors that do not latch 8 10% 90%
Missing cover plates 4 5% 95%
Other 4 5% 100%
Total 80 100%
Percent of total = count ÷ 80 × 100. For drywall: 32 ÷ 80 × 100 = 40%.
Drywall and paint together are 65% of the list. The site lead draws a fishbone for drywall dents:
People: new labourers carry material through finished halls.
Method: drywall is finished before the doors and trim go in, so carts pass bare corners for weeks.
Material: no corner guards were ordered.
Equipment: the material carts have hard steel edges.
Environment: the main hallway is narrow, and one end is badly lit.
The crew thinks carts hitting outside corners is the most likely cause. Plan: put plastic corner guards on every outside corner in hallway A only, and count new dents for two weeks in hallway A and in hallway B, which is the same length. Do: install the guards. Check: hallway A had 3 new dents, hallway B had 11. Act: keep the guards in place and compare dents per material movement over another period before extending the practice. Equal hallway length does not guarantee equal traffic or exposure; the early counts are encouraging, not proof that the guards caused the difference.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Northshore Pipe and Steel (fictional) kept a log of 40 rejected parts over two weeks. The codes are: B = burrs not ground off, L = wrong length, H = hole in the wrong place, U = weld undercut, P = paint runs. Make a tally sheet and count each code.
Parts Reject codes
1 to 10 B, U, B, L, L, B, H, L, B, B
11 to 20 P, B, H, L, P, L, L, H, H, H
21 to 30 L, U, B, H, P, B, B, B, U, L
31 to 40 H, U, L, B, U, B, B, H, B, L
Task 2 (level 2) Use your counts from Task 1.
a. Make a Pareto table with count, percent of total and running total.
b. Sketch the Pareto chart.
c. Which two types make up more than half of the rejects?
Task 3 (level 2) The shop chose burrs not ground off for a fishbone. Here are notes from a crew huddle. Put each note on the right bone: people, method, material, equipment or environment.
a. "The new apprentices were never shown how to check an edge for burrs."
b. "We grind at the end of the day when everyone is rushing to pack up."
c. "Flap discs run out by Wednesday, so people use worn ones."
d. "The cold saw blade is dull, so every cut leaves a big burr."
e. "The light over the grinding bench has been out for a month."
f. "The cut list does not say to deburr."
g. "The grinder at station 2 is missing its side handle."
One of these notes needs action today, before any fishbone work. Which one, and why?
Task 4 (level 3) The shop runs one Plan, Do, Check, Act cycle on burrs.
Plan: replace the dull cold saw blade, change nothing else, and count burr rejects for two weeks.
Do: before the change, 14 of 200 parts made were rejected for burrs. In the two weeks after, 3 of 150 parts made were rejected for burrs.
a. Work out the burr reject rate before and after, as percentages.
b. What improvement does the record show? Why is the blade a plausible explanation, and what still needs checking before claiming it caused the difference?
c. Write the Act step.
Task 5 (level 3) Go back to Harbourline's 80 deficiencies. The site lead now looks at cost to fix instead of count. On this job the average cost to fix each one is: drywall $15, paint $10, trim $20, doors $90, cover plates $5, other $25.
a. Work out the total cost for each type and the total for all 80.
b. Which type is the biggest problem by cost? What percent of the total cost is it, to one decimal place?
c. Should the crew fix drywall first or doors first? Explain in two sentences.
Check yourself
Why does the tallest bar go on the left of a Pareto chart?
Name the five bones of the fishbone used in this lesson.
What does each letter of PDCA stand for?
Why should you change only one thing in the Do step?
Can the "biggest" problem change depending on what you count? Give an example.

lessons.title: Plan a site layout and log your assumptions
lessons.text:
Place the gate, crane, trailers, storage, bins and safety points on a building lot, check the crane reach with the Pythagorean theorem, and write an assumption log that says why each choice was made.
Why this matters on the job
Before the first truck arrives, someone decides where the gate goes, where the crane stands, where the lumber is stacked and where everyone meets if the alarm sounds. A bad layout means trucks blocking a busy street, material moved three times, a crane that cannot reach the far corner, and workers walking under loads. A good layout comes with an assumption log: a short list of every choice and the reason for it, so the superintendent, the crane company and the city can check it. Superintendents and site coordinators on BC jobs do this at the start of every build.
Key ideas
Start with what you cannot change
Read the job information and sort it into two lists:
Fixed: the lot lines, the building footprint, the streets, the hydrant, the power line, the neighbours, the permit rules.
Your choices: the gate, the crane spot, the trailers, the laydown area, the bins, the walkways, the muster point.
Plan your choices around the fixed things.
Think about how things move
Follow a delivery truck from the street to where it unloads and back out. Follow a worker from the gate to the lunch trailer and to the muster point. Follow a load from the laydown area up to the building. Where those paths cross, there is a risk.
Check the crane reach with the Pythagorean theorem
Put the lot on a grid. Measure each point as x metres east and y metres north of one corner. The straight-line distance between two points is
distance = √(difference in x² + difference in y²)
Square the differences first, then add, then take the square root (BEDMAS). This is the same right triangle as in Numeracy lesson 15. Check the crane against the farthest point it must reach, and leave a margin: round in the safe direction, never the hopeful one.
Write an assumption log
Each line has five parts:
No. Decision or assumption Why How we will check it Who confirms
An assumption is something you are treating as true that nobody has confirmed yet, such as "the lumber truck can turn into the lane". Writing it down tells everyone what to check.
Example log lines
These lines come from the job below. They are examples only. Your layout may be different.
No. Decision or assumption Why How we will check it Who confirms
A1 Keep a clear space at least as wide as a fire truck in front of the hydrant. Nothing is stored there. Fire crews must reach the hydrant at any time. Walk the frontage each morning. Site super
A2 Waste bins go away from the neighbour's windows. Bins are noisy and dusty when they are loaded and swapped. Ask the neighbour after the first week. Site super
A3 Assume deliveries arrive between 7 a.m. and 3 p.m. That is what the suppliers quoted. Confirm each delivery time when it is booked. Site office
The job
Kestrel Ridge Construction (a fictional company) is building a three-storey wood-frame building with shops at street level and apartments above. Here is the job sheet. Every rule in it is job data for this fictional site.
Lot: 40 m east to west by 30 m north to south. The south-west corner is point (0, 0). x is metres east, y is metres north.
Building footprint: 24 m by 14 m, from (4, 4) to (28, 18).
Cedar Street runs along the south side. It is busy, it is a bus route, and there is a school across the street. A bus stop sits on the sidewalk at the south-west corner. A fire hydrant is on the sidewalk near x = 36. A storm drain catch basin is in the curb near x = 20.
Mill Lane runs along the west side. It is a quiet two-way lane. An overhead power line runs along Mill Lane on the lot side, with a pole near the north-west corner.
The neighbour's house is on the east side, with windows facing the lot.
City permit for this job: Cedar Street and its sidewalk stay open. Solid hoarding (fencing) goes along both street sides. A covered walkway protects the Cedar Street sidewalk while the building is framed. No deliveries on Cedar Street from 8:00 to 9:00 a.m. or from 2:30 to 3:30 p.m. (school times). Wash water from the wheel wash must not run into the Cedar Street catch basin.
Crane: a self-erecting tower crane with a 30 m jib. The supplier says it can lift the heaviest planned load (a 1,000 kg bundle of wall panels) out to 30 m. Kestrel's rule: plan every lift no farther than 28 m from the crane centre, for a margin. The crane stands on a 6 m by 6 m pad on flat ground, at least 2 m from the building. Loads must not be swung over Cedar Street, the covered walkway, the school or the neighbour's house. The crane supplier and the power utility decide how far the crane must stay from the power line.
Things to place: one vehicle gate 6 m wide, one pedestrian gate, a wheel wash at the vehicle gate, a site office trailer 3 m by 12 m (with the first aid room), a lunch and washroom trailer 3 m by 6 m, a lockable storage container 2.5 m by 6 m, a lumber laydown area 6 m by 10 m, two waste bins 2.5 m by 6 m each, a muster point and the crane pad.
Parking: workers park off site, in a lot two blocks away.
Before digging the foundation, every underground utility service must be located (WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 20.79).
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) From the job sheet, make two lists: fixed (what you cannot move or change) and your choices (what you decide). Then list three things you would ask the superintendent before you start.
Task 2 (level 2) Where should the vehicle gate go: on Mill Lane or on Cedar Street? Give three reasons from the job sheet. Write it as line 1 of your assumption log.
Task 3 (level 3) The crew marked three possible crane spots: P1 (34, 22), P2 (16, 26) and P3 (2, 26). The crane must reach every corner of the building and the centre of the lumber laydown, L (34, 10). The building corners are (4, 4), (28, 4), (4, 18) and (28, 18).
a. For each crane spot, find the distance to the farthest building corner and to L. Show the BEDMAS steps for at least one.
b. Which spots meet Kestrel's 28 m rule for every point?
c. Which spot has another problem, not about distance? What is it?
d. Choose a spot and write it as a line in your assumption log.
Task 4 (level 3) Make your full layout. Sketch the lot on grid paper (one square = 2 m) or on a printed copy of the plan. Place every item in item 8 of the job sheet, plus the hoarding and the covered walkway. Draw the truck route in one colour and the walking route from the pedestrian gate to the trailers in another. Then complete your assumption log with at least 8 lines.
Task 5 (level 2) Swap layouts with a partner. Check theirs with these questions and write down any no answers.
Can a fire truck reach the hydrant, with nothing parked or stored in front of it?
Do trucks turn in and out without backing onto Cedar Street?
Does any lift pass over a trailer, the walkway, the street or the neighbour's house?
Can every worker walk from the pedestrian gate to the trailers without crossing the truck route or walking under a lift?
Can everyone reach the muster point quickly, and can a supervisor count people there?
Does wash water from the wheel wash stay away from the Cedar Street catch basin?
Are the waste bins away from the neighbour's windows?
Is the crane pad at least 2 m from the building and well away from the power line?
Task 6 (level 2) Two days before the first lumber delivery, the supplier calls: their truck is 16 m long and cannot make the turn from Mill Lane into the gate. What are two options? Which do you choose? Write the new or changed lines in your assumption log.
Check yourself
What is the difference between a fixed thing and a choice on a site plan?
What is an assumption, and why write it down?
A crane at (10, 20) must reach a corner at (34, 2). What is the distance?
Why check the farthest point instead of the nearest?
Name the five parts of an assumption log line.

lessons.title: Make an ethical decision on the job
lessons.text:
Name the dilemma, list who is affected and the pressures on you, then decide and explain why, using four steps that work for gifts, timesheets and safety shortcuts.
Why this matters on the job
Sooner or later someone on a job will ask you to do something that does not sit right: sign for hours nobody worked, take a gift from a supplier, skip a step "just this once". Saying yes can feel easier in the moment, especially when you are new and want to fit in. But your name, your ticket and other people's safety can be on the line. A clear way to think it through helps you make a choice you can stand behind, and explain it calmly.
Key ideas
What makes it an ethical dilemma
An ethical dilemma is a choice where doing what is right pulls against something else you care about: keeping your job, getting along with the crew, saving time, earning more. A choice is not a dilemma just because it is hard. "Which saw blade?" is a hard choice. "Do I sign a timesheet I know is wrong?" is a dilemma.
Four steps
Name the dilemma. In one sentence: what is right, and what is pulling against it?
List who is affected. You, the crew, your employer, the client, the public, your family. Who gains and who pays?
List the pressures. Sort them into three kinds:
Personal: your values, your money, your fear of looking bad
Company: your boss, the crew, deadlines, company policy
Outside: the law, safety rules, the client, the community
Decide, act and say why. Choose, then check your choice with three questions:
Is it legal, and does it follow the safety rules and company policy?
Would I be comfortable if my crew, my family and the news knew?
Is it fair to everyone it affects?
If you are stuck, ask for help: a supervisor you trust, the safety representative, your union, an instructor or a mentor.
Some answers are already set by law
For some dilemmas the rule decides for you. In BC:
Anyone who sees what appears to be an unsafe or harmful condition or act must report it as soon as possible to a supervisor or the employer (WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 3.10).
A person must not carry out work or run equipment if they have reasonable cause to believe it would create an undue hazard to anyone's health and safety. A worker who refuses must report it right away to the supervisor or employer (section 3.12).
A worker must not be subject to prohibited action (such as being disciplined or fired) for refusing unsafe work under section 3.12 (section 3.13).
A personal lock may only be removed by the worker who put it on. If that is not possible, the supervisor or manager in charge takes over. They must make every reasonable effort to reach that worker and must make sure the equipment can be run safely before removing the lock (section 10.8).
Worked example: the free impact driver
Dez is an apprentice who checks in deliveries for Cedar Flats Builders (fictional). Last week the company chose Coastline Fasteners (fictional) for a big hardware order. Today the Coastline driver hands Dez a new impact driver still in the box: "From the rep. A thank-you for the business. Keep it."
Name the dilemma. Taking a $300 gift is tempting, but it could look like Dez is being paid to favour this supplier.
Who is affected. Dez. The company, which needs fair prices on future orders. Other suppliers. The foreman, who trusts Dez to check deliveries honestly.
Pressures. Personal: Dez needs tools and the gift is free. Company: Dez does not know the company's gift policy. Outside: the supplier wants more business.
Decide and say why. Dez does not keep it. Dez thanks the driver, says the gift has to go through the office, and tells the foreman the same day. Dez can explain it: "I check their deliveries. If I keep a gift from them, nobody can trust my count."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Which of these are ethical dilemmas? Write D for dilemma or C for just a hard choice.
a. Choosing between two brands of safety boots that both meet the job's rules.
b. Your cousin asks you to say he worked on the site last week so he can get paid.
c. Deciding whether to take the bus or drive to the site.
d. You find the extra 20 sheets of plywood on the delivery were not on the invoice.
e. Choosing which day to book your level 1 exam.
f. The lead hand tells you not to report a small spill of fuel near the storm drain.
Task 2 (level 2) Read the case and use the four steps.
On a renovation job for Harbourline Interiors (fictional), the crew of 4 works 8 hours a day. The lead hand asks you to sign the weekly timesheet showing 10 hours a day for everyone. "The general contractor never checks. Everyone does it. You want to stay on this crew, right?" On this job the company bills the client $45 an hour for each worker.
a. Write the dilemma in one sentence.
b. How many hours a week would be billed that nobody worked (5 days)? How many dollars a week is that?
c. List who is affected and the three kinds of pressure.
d. What do you decide, and what exactly do you say to the lead hand?
Task 3 (level 2) Read the case, then answer.
At 3:30 p.m. on a shop floor at Northshore Pipe and Steel (fictional), the lead hand says: "Jay left his lock on the saw disconnect and went home. Grab the bolt cutters and cut it off so the next shift can start."
a. What does WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 10.8 say about removing a personal lock? Look it up at https://www.worksafebc.com/en/law-policy/occupational-health-safety/searchable-ohs-regulation/ohs-regulation/part-10-de-energization-and-lockout
b. Is this an ethical dilemma, or has the rule already decided it? Explain.
c. What do you say to the lead hand, and what should happen next?
Task 4 (level 3) Read the case and use all four steps.
Priya is an estimator for a small contractor (fictional). This week she is comparing three supplier quotes for a large lumber order. One supplier invites her on a free fishing weekend. She knows her own boss went on the same trip last year. The supplier's quote is the second lowest.
Task 5 (level 2) You are new on a framing crew. To save 20 minutes before lunch, the crew does not put the guardrail back after a lift and keeps working at the open edge on the second floor.
a. Which sections from the Key ideas apply?
b. Write what you would say to the lead hand in two or three calm sentences.
c. Why can you speak up without fear of being punished for refusing the unsafe work?
Task 6 (level 3) Think of a dilemma you have faced at work, at school or that you could face in the trade you are heading into. You do not have to share it. Write it out with the four steps. At the end, write who you could ask for help if it happened again.
Check yourself
What makes a choice an ethical dilemma and not just a hard choice?
Name the four steps.
Name the three kinds of pressure.
In BC, who may remove a personal lock, and what happens if they are not there?
What three questions can you use to check your decision?

lessons.title: Decide whether a map or data is good enough to act on
lessons.text:
Tell accuracy from precision, ask whether a map or a set of numbers is fit for the job, find out why a map pin can be wrong, and confirm buried lines on site before anyone digs.
Why this matters on the job
Trades work runs on maps, drawings and numbers: a site address on a phone, a drawing that shows where a gas line runs, a GPS point for a sign post. Most of the time they are close enough. Sometimes they are not, and the cost can be a wasted trip or a punctured pipe. This lesson takes the checking questions from lesson 9 and applies them to maps and data. It builds on Digital lesson 9, where you found and measured a site on a map.
Key ideas
Accuracy and precision are different
Accurate means close to the true value.
Precise means repeated measurements agree closely. A display with many digits has fine displayed resolution, which does not by itself prove precision or accuracy.
A tape measure with a bent hook can read 2 mm long on every cut. It is precise (the same every time) but not accurate. A number like 49.204517 looks exact because of all the digits, but the digits do not prove it is right. Always ask: how close to the truth is this, and how do I know?
Fit for the job
Data does not have to be perfect. It has to be good enough for what you are about to do.
Source Good enough for Not good enough for
A phone map Driving to the site Finding the property line
A city's online utility map Planning which utility owners to contact Deciding where it is safe to dig
A written dimension on an approved drawing Laying out a wall Proving where a buried line is
A phone GPS point Telling a crew which gate to meet at Setting a survey corner
Why a map pin can be wrong
The address was typed without the city, so the map picked a street with the same name in another town.
A number or street type is wrong (Road instead of Street, 1450 instead of 1540).
The street or subdivision is new and is not on the map yet.
The pin sits at the middle of the lot or the middle of the road, not at the gate.
Fix it by sending the full address with the city and postal code, checking the pin on the map before you leave, and adding a landmark or a dropped pin.
Drawings show the best records, not the ground
Drawings of buried lines are often based on older records. A line can be off by metres from where the drawing shows it. A real case from BC shows what that can cost.
In July 2007, a contractor in Burnaby was digging a trench for a new storm sewer. The design drawings, based on a 1957 drawing, showed a crude oil pipeline at a constant 8.5 m from the property line. After the strike, a survey found the pipeline was really between 4 m and 9.8 m from that line. Where it was hit, it was only 1.5 m from the centre of the trench instead of the 2.8 m on the drawings. The excavator bucket punctured the pipe and about 234 cubic metres of crude oil was released. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada found that the pipeline's location had not been verified along the street before construction, as the crossing agreement and the federal crossing rules required, so the difference between the drawing and the ground was not found in time.
In BC, locate before you dig
WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 20.79: before excavating or drilling with powered tools and equipment, the location of all underground utility services in the area must be accurately determined, and any danger to workers from them must be controlled. Work near a utility service must follow that owner's requirements. Pointed tools must not be used to probe for underground petroleum and electrical services.
BC 1 Call passes your locate request to its members, the owners of buried lines in the area. A request is free. Submit it online at bc1c.ca or call 1-800-474-6886. For a regular request, the owners have 3 business days to respond. BC 1 Call itself does not confirm that it is clear to dig, so follow each owner's response.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) For each case, write accurate, precise, both or neither.
a. A laser level that is out of adjustment reads 6 mm high every time, at every spot.
b. Three workers measure a wall and get 3048 mm, 3048 mm and 3049 mm. The wall really is 3048 mm.
c. Someone guesses a room is "about 20 feet". It is really 14 feet.
d. A scale reads 25.03 kg, then 24.71 kg, then 25.38 kg for the same 25 kg bag.
Task 2 (level 2) Is the source fit for the job? Write yes or no and one reason.
a. Using a phone map to find a new subdivision that was finished last month.
b. Using a city's online sewer map to decide where to drive fence posts with a post driver.
c. Using the written dimension 3600 on an approved floor plan to lay out a wall.
d. Using your phone's GPS point to tell a delivery driver which side of a farm to come to.
Task 3 (level 2) Riverbend Decks (fictional) booked a lumber delivery to "1540 Mill Rd". The truck went to 1540 Mill Road in Cedarvale, 40 minutes away. The real site is 1540 Mill Road in Fernhill, the next town over. (Both towns are fictional.)
a. What most likely went wrong?
b. Write the delivery address and instructions the way they should have been sent.
c. Name two things the office can check before the next delivery.
Task 4 (level 2) Use the Burnaby case in the Key ideas.
a. The drawings showed 2.8 m between the pipeline and the centre of the trench. The real distance where it was hit was 1.5 m. How much closer was the pipe than the drawing showed?
b. One cubic metre is 1000 litres. How many litres of crude oil were released?
c. The pipeline was between 4 m and 9.8 m from the property line. What is the difference between the closest and farthest?
d. Which question from lesson 9 ("who, when, where, why, can I check it") would have caught the problem? Explain.
Task 5 (level 3) A phone app shows a point as 49.204517, −122.910812 and says "accuracy ±12 m". (Digital lesson 19, GPS and location sharing, explains what that accuracy number means.)
a. Treat 12 m as the app's estimated error radius. What is the radius and the diameter of that estimated area? Is that estimate a guarantee that the true point lies inside it?
b. A driveway is 3 m wide. Could the app tell you which side of the driveway a buried line is on?
c. What does this show about the number of decimal places?
Task 6 (level 2) Cedar Flats Builders (fictional) will set 12 fence posts along a back lot line with a powered auger. Write the steps, in order, from planning to the first hole. Include who you contact, how long you wait, and what you check on site.
Check yourself
What is the difference between accurate and precise?
What does "fit for the job" mean for data?
Give two reasons a map pin can land in the wrong place.
Under WorkSafeBC OHS Regulation section 20.79, what must happen before excavating with powered equipment?
Is a drawing of buried lines proof of where they are? Why or why not?

lessons.title: Reading: find what you need and use it well
lessons.text:
Reading helps you turn a document into a useful action. You might check the room for a training session, compare two travel choices, understand a project notice or find out what a form is asking. Reading includes words, symbols, pictures, tables and diagrams. It also includes deciding that a document does not provide enough information to act.
You already bring ways of making sense of information. You may recognize a familiar route, notice an unclear instruction, remember a useful heading or ask someone to explain a new term. This chapter builds a repeatable process around those strengths. You can use the fictional situations throughout. You do not need to share personal records, family information or knowledge that you prefer to keep private.
All organizations, timetables, messages and project arrangements in this chapter are invented teaching cases. They are complete enough for the activities, but they are not live travel advice, workplace procedures or announcements. Read them as practice documents. For real decisions, obtain the actual current document and check its applicability.
See it in action · Reading
Visual guide Meet in Room 2 at 10:00. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
NOTICE 1: Room 1 at 10:00. UPDATE: Room 2; time unchanged. Find the current message. Compare what changed. Say the room and the time. Meet in Room 2 at 10:00. Use both messages. The room changes; the time does not.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. NOTICE 1: Room 1 at 10:00. UPDATE: Room 2; time unchanged.
Try it: Find the current message. Compare what changed. Say the room and the time.
Check your result: Meet in Room 2 at 10:00. Use both messages. The room changes; the time does not.
Six parts of a useful reading process
Visual guide Use the component numbers as an index, not a compulsory sequence. A missing date, unfamiliar word or changed question can send you back to another action. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. Let the question and document guide your next move. Six connected components: Identify the reading task; Find the information; Connect related details; Understand and apply; Evaluate the document; Reflect on the document. Return to any action when you need to check meaning or evidence.
The Skills for Success Reading components are:
Identify the task that requires you to read. What are you trying to find out or do?
Identify the information contained in the document(s). What is here, and how is it organized?
Make connections between different parts of the document(s). Which details belong together?
Understand and apply the information. What does it mean for this particular task?
Evaluate the document(s). Is the information suitable, clear, credible and sufficient?
Reflect on the document(s). Who is it written for, how does it work, and what should you carry forward?
These are connected actions, not six boxes you must complete in a fixed order. A confusing footnote may send you back to the heading. A missing date may stop you from using an otherwise clear instruction. The aim is an accurate understanding, with a reason you can explain.
Choose supports that let you work with the text: larger print, a ruler under a line, a glossary, text-to-speech, a reading partner or extra time. Keep track of the support used. You can demonstrate comprehension by pointing to evidence, explaining aloud, using an accessible communication method or writing. This chapter does not require polished writing to prove that you understood a reading.
Build a word, read a phrase, use its meaning
Practise privately, with a partner or through an agreed accessible format. No one needs to read aloud to the group. Keep track of whether you recognized the printed word yourself, used audio access or received help with its meaning. These are useful but different observations.
Start with a small observation
Look at return, returned, check, checked, available. Identify a familiar word, use it in a classroom sentence and read a short phrase. If these words are already familiar, move to the notice practice. If a word becomes clear after someone says it, compare the spoken word with its letters and practise it in a useful phrase.
See a useful word part
Compare check → checked. Point to the shared letters. Adding -ed here shows a completed action. In this word the ending sounds like /t/; the spelling still records -ed. Compare return → returned, where the ending sounds like /d/. The same spelling can have different sounds; use the whole word to check its pronunciation. Read “the helper checked the kit” and explain which action is complete.
Break unavailable into un + available: in this notice, un- reverses the meaning. Say the base word, read the whole word, then test its meaning in “The kit is unavailable today.” A word part is a clue; the sentence confirms whether that meaning fits.
Try with support: choose from checked / check / unavailable / available. Complete “Please ___ the code before the loan” and “The kit is ___ because it is already lent.” Explain your choice. Then compare “return pending” with “returned and checked.” Identify which record still needs an action.
Read a short passage in meaningful phrases
The practice desk opens at ten. / A helper checks the kit code / before handing over a folder. / The learner checks the return time. / If the folder is unavailable, / ask about another suitable resource. / Do not assume that a reserved item is free to take. / A learner can ask for a printed reminder / without explaining private reasons. / Keep the agreed return point / with the practice record.
Listen to one sentence read by your instructor if helpful, then explain its meaning. Read it together or reread a short chosen part, using the slashes as optional phrase guides. Answer: What happens before a folder is handed over? What should happen if it is unavailable? Return to the words that support the answers. Fluency here means readable phrasing that supports meaning; faster reading is not the goal.
Fresh exit passage
Remove the model passage while using this new text:
A learning pack is ready for collection at two. The helper must check its code before recording the loan. The pack includes a return slip. If a requested pack is unavailable, ask the helper to check another option. A reserved pack belongs to an agreed booking. Do not remove it without confirmation.
Identify check, unavailable and reserved. Explain the collection condition and what to do if the requested pack is unavailable. Reread after feedback if useful. Keep word help, phrasing help and comprehension help separate in your note.
Check after your attempt: collection is at two, subject to the helper's code check before the loan is recorded; ask the helper to check another option if unavailable; reserved is not unrestricted availability. If a word needs more practice, name it and ask for a useful example. When you can locate the condition with your agreed supports, continue to “Build useful vocabulary” and connect information from a short paragraph and table. You can agree more focused word-reading practice without repeating a whole long case.
Begin with the task, then preview the document
Before reading every word, finish this sentence: “I need this document so that I can….” A precise purpose narrows the search. “Find the check-in room for a first visit” is more useful than “read the schedule.” A person looking for lunch arrangements may use the same document differently.
Preview the title, date, sender, headings and document type. A table usually lets you compare categories. A paragraph may explain a condition. A diagram shows relationships or location. Skimming gives you the general message. Scanning helps you locate a specific item. Close reading checks the exact wording around that item. Strong reading often uses all three.
Case document A: a first visit to the training room
Fictional Northside Learning Room • Welcome note • Version 2, issued for Practice Day 1
Purpose. This note explains the classroom visit for people attending the introductory learning session. It replaces the earlier draft that named Room 3. All activities described here take place in classrooms. There is no equipment operation or worksite tour during this visit.
Arrival. Please arrive at the reception desk between 08:40 and 08:55. Reception is beside the main entrance. A staff member will check your learning ID and direct you to Room 2. If you do not have a learning ID, reception will provide a temporary classroom label. You do not need to bring identity documents for this fictional practice activity.
What to bring. Bring a pen or use one supplied in the room. Printed workbooks and calculators will be available. A phone is optional. The activities can begin on paper, and a shared device will be available for the later digital task. Tell the instructor if you would like enlarged print, a quiet reading space or another available support. You can ask privately.
Changes. The introductory session ends at 11:30. An optional resource-table visit follows until 11:50. The resource table is not part of the required session. A separate afternoon session appears on the building schedule, but it is for a different group. If two documents seem to disagree, ask reception which version applies to your group before changing your plan.
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Time Introductory group activity Place
08:40–08:55 Check in Reception
09:00–10:10 Welcome and learning tasks Room 2
10:10–10:20 Break Classroom or nearby seating
10:20–11:30 Practice and review Room 2
11:30–11:50 Optional resource table Room 1
State the reading task
You are helping a fictional learner prepare for their first visit. They ask, “Where do I go first, and do I have to stay after 11:30?” State two precise reading goals. Locate the part of document A that answers each goal. Explain why the afternoon session mentioned in the note is not relevant to this person's plan.
Preview before you search
Identify the document's audience, purpose and version. Name two features that help you find information. Then choose how you would begin each task: skim for an overview, scan for a time, or read a paragraph closely for a condition. Use these tasks: understanding the visit generally; finding the break time; deciding whether a phone is required. Explain one choice.
Worked example 1: a word that changes the answer
Question: Must every introductory learner attend the resource table?
First identify the requested information. “Must every learner” asks about a requirement, not whether the table exists. Scan for “resource table.” Read both the table row and the paragraph headed Changes. The row says “Optional,” and the paragraph says it is not part of the required session. Together they support: No. The required session ends at 11:30; the resource table is optional.
The competing detail is its appearance on the schedule. A scheduled event is not automatically compulsory. Reading the label prevents that mistake. Words such as optional, required, before, after, except, only and unless deserve close attention because they limit a general statement.
Build useful vocabulary
Use document A to explain optional, replaces, temporary and applies in this context. Give the nearby words that helped you. Choose one term and make a new classroom example using it accurately. If you know a useful equivalent in another language, you may add it for your own use; sharing it is optional. Check uncertain meanings with a glossary, partner or instructor rather than guessing silently.
Find the information, including its limits
A good search follows the question. Who usually asks for a person or role. Where asks for a place. When asks for time or a condition. Which asks you to select between options. Why often needs a reason across more than one sentence. Underline the requested information and any limits before searching.
Tables need the same care as sentences. Read the title, column headings, row labels and notes. Keep a finger or pointer on the row while moving across it. Do not take a number from a nearby row because it looks familiar. A symbol's meaning comes from its legend, not its shape alone. An asterisk might identify a footnote; it does not always mean a warning.
Case document B: choosing a classroom journey
Fictional practice journey planner • Day 1 only
The learner starts at Cedar Stop and needs to reach the Northside Learning Room reception by 08:55. This is a fictional route exercise. The timetable does not describe a real service. All listed journeys run on the practice day. The learner can choose either route, and no fare calculation is needed.
Route A is direct. It arrives at Northside Stop, which is beside the learning room's main entrance. Allow five minutes between the listed arrival and reaching reception. That allowance is a task assumption, not a measured travel time for a real person. If a learner needs a different allowance, the plan must be reconsidered using that requirement.
Route B involves a connection at Market Stop. A connection is usable in this exercise only if the first vehicle arrives at least five minutes before the next departure. The second vehicle also arrives at Northside Stop. Add the same five-minute reception allowance. The table shows the individual services; it does not promise that every combination makes a connection.
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Service Leaves Cedar Arrives Market Leaves Market Arrives Northside
A1, direct 08:05 — — 08:35
A2, direct 08:25 — — 08:55
B1, first leg 08:10 08:25 — —
B2, second leg — — 08:28 08:43
B3, second leg — — 08:32 08:47
Legend: A dash means the field does not apply to that service. It does not mean a cancelled trip. A service number identifies one row, not a whole journey with a connection.
Scan accurately
Find the departure and arrival for direct service A1. Identify which service leaves Market at 08:32. Explain what the dashes in that row mean. Point to the heading and legend that support your answers. You may say the answer aloud while marking the row instead of copying the whole timetable.
Read the condition
A classmate says, “B1 arrives before B2 leaves, so the connection works.” Find the exact condition that must be checked. Does the statement meet it? Explain using the times and the minimum connection allowance. Then identify a different second-leg service that can be combined with B1.
Visual guide After your attempt, use this worked visual check. Arriving before departure is not enough: this timetable also requires a five-minute connection. Read the condition with the row. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
A proportional timetable shows B1 arriving at Market at 08:25. The required connection allowance is five minutes. B2 leaves at 08:28, giving only three minutes; B3 leaves at 08:32, giving seven. The earliest usable departure is 08:30. B1 plus B3 reaches Northside at 08:47; five minutes to reception gives 08:52, before the 08:55 deadline.
Worked example 2: combine a table and a paragraph
Question: Does direct service A2 meet the reception deadline?
The row gives an arrival at Northside of 08:55. The paragraph requires a further five-minute allowance to reception. Therefore the task's reception time would be 09:00. That is later than the 08:55 deadline. A2 does not meet the requirement in this exercise.
The reading challenge is to connect “arrives Northside” with “reaches reception.” They name different points. The arithmetic is small, but finding the relevant rule is essential. If the table's heading had already been “Arrives reception,” adding the allowance again would be wrong. Check what a number represents before calculating.
Choose with evidence
Choose two journeys from document B that meet the reception deadline. For each, identify the service or services, Northside arrival, reception allowance and planned reception time. Explain a difference between the two choices without claiming that one is best for every learner. Now change the reception allowance to ten minutes: which of your choices still meets the deadline?
Connect details without inventing missing facts
Some information is stated directly. Other information can be inferred by combining details. An inference is a reasoned conclusion, not a free guess. “The project needs both a place and a time” can follow from an invitation that asks people to attend. “The project is behind schedule” does not follow merely because an invitation was revised.
Use four labels while reading: stated, supported inference, contradicted, and not established. A contradicted statement conflicts with the document. An unestablished claim needs information the document does not provide. Keeping those separate helps you notice the exact question that still needs an answer. You do not have to force every document into a complete story.
Case document C: who is responsible for what?
Fictional Willow Reach access project • Public learning brief, version 1
The fictional Town of Willow Reach owns an access route serving a recreation centre and a delivery area. The Town's project team describes what the project must achieve, manages the agreement with the contractor and checks the delivered work against that agreement. The fictional Pathway Paving Company is the contractor. It carries out the work it has been engaged to deliver. The roles of owner and contractor are different even when both are working toward the same project outcome.
The practice funding plan contains $60,000 from the Town, $40,000 from the fictional Regional Access Fund and $20,000 from the fictional Community Route Fund. These names and amounts are invented. Contributing money does not, by itself, make a funder the road owner. The funding amounts also do not tell us a contractor's profit, a worker's pay or the cost of each activity.
This learning brief is about roles and questions. It does not supply a work schedule, a traffic plan, operating instructions, environmental findings or legal permissions. The project team would need current applicable documents for a real project. For this classroom exercise, questions about ownership go to the Town's project contact; questions about the contractor's proposed classroom display go to Pathway's training contact. Neither contact has been given authority here to answer for the other organization.
Notice for learners. A classroom information display will explain where paving material comes from and how the project roles differ. Visitors are asked to identify questions they would want answered before a real project begins. No visitor should treat this practice display as a notice of actual construction.
Town of Willow Reach: owner and project team │ engages a contractor for described work ▼ Pathway Paving: contractor Town contribution + two fictional funds: funding plan Funding contribution alone does not establish ownership.
Follow the role, not the familiar name
Who owns the route? Who carries out the contracted work? Which contact would receive a question about ownership? Which would receive a question about the contractor's classroom display? Cite a sentence for each decision. Explain why the funding paragraph is insufficient to identify a contractor's profit.
Separate evidence from assumption
Label each statement stated, supported inference, contradicted, or not established: “The Town and contractor have different roles”; “More than one organization contributes to the practice funding”; “The contractor owns the road”; “Construction starts next Monday”; “The brief is suitable for deciding the legal permits for a real job.” For a statement that is not established, name the missing document or detail rather than simply saying “wrong.”
Use both forms of the message
Compare the diagram and paragraphs in document C. Identify one fact both forms communicate, one qualification that is clearer in the paragraphs and one question neither form answers. Then choose which form you would use for a quick introduction and which you would consult for a responsibility question. Your choice must refer to the information needed, not only to personal preference.
Evaluate a document before relying on it
A clear-looking document can still be unsuitable. Ask who produced it, when and for what audience. Check whether it names its sources and explains its limits. Consider the difference between a sales claim, an official project instruction, a personal opinion and a classroom example. These can all be useful for different purposes; their authority is not interchangeable.
Check the actual claim, too. “Always” requires much stronger evidence than “in this example.” A photograph may show an item without proving how it performs. A newer date helps identify a version, but newer does not automatically mean accurate or applicable. A document needs both a traceable source and relevant content.
Case document D: two environmental messages
D1 • Fictional promotional card. “Our nearer supply source proves asphalt is always greener than concrete. Save time: there is no need to compare alternatives.” The card supplies no author, study, date, quantities, transport assumptions or definition of “greener.”
D2 • Fictional classroom comparison note. “The example lists one source for an asphalt option at 20 km from the work area and one source for a concrete option at 50 km. The distances are invented. They describe one-way routes, not total travel. Quantities, number of trips, vehicle loads, production impacts, maintenance and design-life information are missing. The note cannot rank the total environmental impact of the two options. A fair comparison would need the same project purpose and comparable service requirements, together with relevant evidence for the impacts being considered.”
Judge what a claim can support
Identify D1's main claim and two features that make it unreliable for a whole-project environmental conclusion. State the limited comparison D2 permits. Name two missing facts that would matter before making a broader comparison. Explain how D2's admission of limits affects its usefulness for this reading task.
Worked example 3: resolve a version conflict
Visual guide Use the matching audience and explicit replacement statement, then follow the check-in instruction. This shows Welcome Note version 2 before the later “Apply a precise update” update. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
Two document specimens show an earlier introductory-group draft with Room 3 and a version 2 notice that explicitly replaces it, names Room 2 and requires check-in first. A route below moves from the entrance to reception during 08:40–08:55, then to Room 2 after check-in.
An old classroom notice says, “Introductory group: Room 3.” Document A says “Version 2,” identifies the introductory audience and explicitly replaces the earlier Room 3 draft. It directs learners to Room 2 after reception. For this fictional visit, use the Room 2 instruction and check in first. This conclusion depends on the replacement statement and matching group, not only on a bigger version number.
If the second document were for a different group, its newness would not settle the conflict. If neither document identified which one applied, the next action would be clarification. Reading well includes knowing when a comparison cannot be resolved from the available evidence.
Inspect a source record
Compare these supplied records: Record X: “Equipment guide,” screenshot, no issuer or edition. Record Y: “Classroom equipment-purpose cards,” prepared for this workbook, labelled introductory, no operating instructions. Which could support identifying the intended purpose of this workbook's card activity? Could either justify operating equipment? List three additional details you would seek before relying on an actual technical document. Do not invent those details.
Apply a precise update
Read this fictional update: “Practice Day 1, introductory group only: check-in remains at reception. The 10:20–11:30 practice block moves to Room 4. The 09:00 welcome remains in Room 2. Issued as an update to Welcome Note version 2.” Identify exactly which table entry changes and which entries stay the same. Explain why rewriting the entire day as “Room 4” would be inaccurate.
Reflect on how the document works
