Reflection includes looking back at the document, not only judging yourself. Who needs the information? What does the writer emphasize? What evidence is offered, and what is left out? Does the structure help the intended audience? A short notice can be effective because it removes unnecessary detail, yet become misleading if it removes an essential condition.
Your reading process also matters. Notice where you first looked, what slowed you down and what helped you recover. “I am bad at tables” is a broad judgement with no next action. “I skipped the heading, so I compared workers with employers” identifies a habit you can change. Keep the observation connected to an actual example.
Case document E: borrowing a classroom resource
Fictional resource desk guide • Current classroom copy
The resource desk lends practice books and calculators during the learning block. A learner may borrow one calculator and up to two books at a time. Each item has an item code. The code identifies the item, not the borrower. The classroom borrowing sheet uses learning IDs so that personal details do not need to appear in the activity.
To borrow an available item, tell the desk helper its code and your learning ID. The helper records the item and the agreed return point. “Available” means the desk can lend it now. “Reserved” means the item is set aside for another booking. “In use” means it has already been lent. These labels can change, so the desk helper checks the current sheet before agreeing to a loan.
The guide is written for learners who want a resource during the classroom block. It does not describe a public library account or a charge. If an item is unavailable, choose another suitable resource or ask when it may become available. The guide does not promise a return time for an item marked “In use.”
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Item code Item Status at the time of this exercise
C04 Basic calculator Available
C05 Large-display calculator Reserved
B12 Measurement practice book In use
B16 Document-reading practice book Available
Read for audience and purpose
Who is document E written for? What practical decision does it help them make? Identify one feature that helps a first-time borrower and one detail deliberately outside its scope. Explain why the sentence about learning IDs belongs in this document even though it does not describe the equipment.
Apply the conditions
A learner wants C04 and B16 immediately. Another wants C05 and needs a specific display feature. Use the guide and status table to explain the next step for each. Do not tell the second learner that an unsuitable alternative must meet their needs. What can the document establish, and what should the desk helper clarify?
Notice what a summary loses
A proposed sign reads, “Borrow any calculator and two books. Give your details to the helper.” Compare it with document E. Identify three ways the sign could mislead a reader or remove a useful protection. Explain the information that a corrected sign should retain. You may annotate the sign and explain aloud; writing a polished replacement is optional.
Transfer the process to a different setting
The same reading habits work across trades, service work, study and everyday planning. The document changes; the need to identify purpose, conditions, evidence and gaps remains. Transfer does not mean assuming that a rule from one setting applies somewhere else. It means bringing the process of checking.
Independent transfer: booking a practice room
Use this complete fictional booking note: “Room East holds up to eight people and is available 13:00–14:00. Room West holds up to twelve and is available 13:30–15:00. Bookings need a ten-minute setup period before the meeting, within the room's available time. A group of ten wants a 45-minute meeting starting at 14:00. Ask the desk to confirm any booking; this note is not a reservation.” Select a suitable room, explain how the size and time conditions connect, and identify the remaining action. Then explain what changes if the meeting must start at 13:30.
Show your reading route
Choose document A, B, C or E. Ask a partner to choose a new detail question using only that document. Before answering, state the information you need, show where you look and explain any condition you checked. Then swap roles. If the answer is missing, identify that clearly. Keep the partner's question and the evidence you used so the instructor can observe your reading, not merely your memory.
Compare and reflect
Compare the promotional card D1 with the resource guide E. Explain their audiences, purposes and use of evidence. Point to language that attempts to influence the reader. Select one reading strategy that helped you in an earlier activity and one situation where it was insufficient on its own. Choose a next practice task from this chapter, naming the detail you will check more deliberately. You can provide your reflection orally with marked documents.
Keep evidence of what you can do
Identify the task that requires you to read
“State the reading task”, “Preview before you search”, “Show your reading route”: clear purpose and requested information.
Identify information in documents
“Build useful vocabulary” through “Read the condition”: vocabulary, headings, rows and conditions.
Connect parts of documents
“Choose with evidence” through “Use both forms of the message”, “Apply a precise update”: paragraphs, tables, diagrams and updates used together.
Understand and apply information
“Follow the role, not the familiar name”, “Apply the conditions”, “Independent transfer: booking a practice room”: a justified decision for the specified case.
Evaluate documents
“Judge what a claim can support” through “Apply a precise update”, “Notice what a summary loses”: source, scope, version and adequacy checked.
Reflect on documents
“Read for audience and purpose”, “Compare and reflect”: audience, purpose, language and evidence considered.
Use the local feedback descriptions Not observed, Not yet demonstrated, Demonstrated with support and Demonstrated independently. Record transfer separately when you use the process in a new situation. These descriptions are not official proficiency levels. Keep a marked document, a short explanation and the support used. Together they give a more useful picture than speed alone.
Reading · fresh document checks
Use the form selected by your instructor. Read the supplied documents and show which words, rows or conditions support your answers. You may mark the document and explain through an agreed communication mode. Writing polish is not the focus. Ask for the agreed access tools before starting. All information is fictional; do not visit or contact a real service.
Form A · Pick up a practice kit
A1 · Earlier notice, issued Practice Monday
The introductory learning group can collect its reserved practice kits at Counter East on Practice Friday, 13:00–13:30. Bring the kit code and your learning ID. This is a classroom collection arrangement.
A2 · Correction, issued Practice Tuesday
For the same introductory learning group and Practice Friday collection: Counter West replaces Counter East. The collection window remains 13:00–13:30. Bring the kit code and learning ID as previously stated. A helper must check the current counter record before handing over a kit. This correction replaces A1's location only. A separate evening group uses Counter East at 17:00; that arrangement does not apply to this group. Ask the course coordinator when information cannot be confirmed.
A3 · Counter record for the exercise
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Kit code Resource Status Collection condition
P14 Large-print process cards Reserved for the introductory group Helper checks code and learning ID.
P18 Standard process cards In use No return time has been supplied.
N22 Number practice kit Available Helper checks the current record and agrees a loan.
“Reserved” means set aside for the named group. “Available” means a loan can be discussed now, not that the item has already been booked. “In use” means currently lent. A request for a particular format does not require a learner to explain private reasons. The counter record says nothing about transport or a charge.
Reading practice A · Find the current instruction
Where and when should the introductory learner collect P14? What must they bring, and what must the helper do? Mark the source for the location, unchanged time and collection condition.
Reading practice A · Connect the records
A peer says, “I will go to Counter East at 17:00 because the correction mentions it.” Explain the problem using the audience and replacement wording. Then explain whether P14 and P18 can both be promised for collection at 13:00.
Reading practice A · Check a summary
A proposed summary says, “All kits are ready. Bring identity documents to Counter West any time Friday. Transport is included.” Identify four unsupported or contradicted claims. For one claim, distinguish “the documents say something different” from “the documents do not say.”
Reading practice A · Explain your next step
You receive an undated cropped image saying only “Counter East.” Explain what it cannot establish, where you would seek confirmation and one part of your reading process that helped you. Do not invent the coordinator's answer.
My evidence notes: write the task ID, answer, source and any unresolved question. An additional sheet or recorded oral response can be used.
Form B · Return a practice resource
B1 · Earlier notice, issued Practice Wednesday
The afternoon learning group returns borrowed folders on Practice Monday, 11:15–11:45, at the Materials Desk. Bring the folder code and your learning ID. Do not write a personal phone number on a folder.
B2 · Correction, issued Practice Thursday
For the same afternoon learning group and Practice Monday returns: use the Library Desk instead of the Materials Desk. The 11:15–11:45 window and code/learning-ID requirement stay the same. The desk helper checks the folder against the loan record and records its return; placing it on a desk alone does not confirm a return. This correction replaces B1's location only. The evening group's return to the Materials Desk at 18:00 is a separate arrangement. Ask the course coordinator about information that cannot be confirmed.
B3 · Loan record for the exercise
If needed, scroll across this table. Keyboard: focus the table, then use the arrow keys.
Folder code Record status Required next step
F32 Loaned to afternoon group; return due Practice Monday Present to helper for return check.
F35 Returned and checked No second return is required.
F39 Return reported, check pending Helper must confirm against the loan record.
“Check pending” means a necessary check has not yet been confirmed. It is different from a completed return. No penalty, charge or delivery service is specified. Learners can ask privately for an accessible way to identify the folder code.
Reading practice B · Find the current instruction
Where and when should the afternoon learner return F32? What must they bring, and what must the helper do? Mark the source for the location, unchanged time and return condition.
Reading practice B · Connect the records
A peer says, “I will go to the Materials Desk at 18:00 because the correction mentions it.” Explain the problem using the audience and replacement wording. Then explain whether F35 and F39 can both be recorded as checked returns.
Reading practice B · Check a summary
A proposed summary says, “Every folder is checked in. Leave F32 at the Library Desk any time Monday. Bring your personal phone number; late returns cost $5.” Identify four unsupported or contradicted claims. For one claim, distinguish “the documents say something different” from “the documents do not say.”
Reading practice B · Explain your next step
You receive an undated cropped image saying only “Materials Desk.” Explain what it cannot establish, where you would seek confirmation and one part of your reading process that helped you. Do not invent the coordinator's answer.
My evidence notes: write the task ID, answer, source and any unresolved question. An additional sheet or recorded oral response can be used.

lessons.title: Skim, scan and read closely
lessons.text:
Decide why you are reading, then choose the fastest way to find what you need in a workplace safety document.
Why this matters on the job
On a BC job site you are handed safety bulletins, toolbox talk sheets, site rules and incident guides. Most of the time you do not need every word. You need one answer, and you need it right: who to tell, how long you have, what to bring. Knowing why you are reading tells you how to read.
Key ideas
1. Start with your purpose. Finish this sentence before you read: "I am reading this so that I can…". For example: "…find out who I report a near miss to."
2. Choose a way of reading.
Way of reading What you do Use it when
Skim Read the title, headings, bold words and the first sentence under each heading. Move fast. You want the general idea, or you want to know where things are.
Scan Hold one key word or number in your head. Run your eyes down the page until you see it. Stop there. You know what you are looking for: a name, a number, a time, a word.
Read closely Read every word of the sentence or two around what you found. Watch for small words that change the meaning: must, only, not, within, before, unless. You have found the right place and the details matter.
3. Scan, locate, decide. This is the ACCESS routine. Scan for your key word. Locate the sentence that holds it. Decide whether that sentence answers your question, or whether you need to keep looking.
Worked example
Question: Who does a supervisor tell first after an incident?
Purpose: I need a person or role ("who").
Skim the guide below. The heading 3. Report first looks right.
Scan under that heading for a role. You find "the site superintendent".
Read closely: "Tell the site superintendent right away, by phone or in person. Do not wait to finish your notes."
Decide: The answer is the site superintendent, right away, by phone or in person.
You did not read the whole guide. You read about 25 words closely.
Practice document
Kestrel Point Builders Ltd. (fictional company) Incident Investigation Guide for Site Supervisors Version 3 · Issued March 2026 · Replaces Version 2
1. Purpose of this guide This guide helps site supervisors investigate incidents on Kestrel Point job sites. It explains what to do, in what order, and what records to keep. The goal of every investigation is to find out why an incident happened and to stop it from happening again. An investigation is not about finding someone to blame.
2. What counts as an incident For this guide, an incident is any event at work that injured a worker so that the worker needed medical treatment. It is also any event that did not hurt anyone, or caused only a minor injury, but could have caused a serious injury. We call that a near miss. Treat near misses as seriously as injuries.
3. Report first Tell the site superintendent right away, by phone or in person. Do not wait to finish your notes. If a worker is hurt, first aid comes before everything else.
4. Preliminary investigation Start the preliminary investigation right away. WorkSafeBC requires the employer to complete the preliminary investigation and its report within 48 hours of the incident. Use Kestrel Point form KP-12. Fix any unsafe condition you find before work starts again in that area.
5. Full investigation The full investigation looks for the underlying causes. WorkSafeBC requires the full investigation report to be submitted within 30 days of the incident. The safety coordinator submits it. You give the safety coordinator your notes, sketches and photos.
6. Mapping the scene Before anything is moved, sketch the area. Note, measure and mark: - where people, equipment and materials were - anything broken, bent or out of place - marks on the ground, such as tire tracks or drag marks - spills, wet spots or loose material on walking surfaces - lighting, noise and weather at the time - guards, rails and other safety devices, and whether they were in place
7. Talking to witnesses Talk to each witness alone, as soon as you can. Ask what they saw, not what they think caused it. Write down their words. Thank them.
8. Corrective actions For each cause you find, write one action that will fix it, the person responsible and a date.
9. Records Keep a copy of every form, sketch and photo in the project's safety binder. The safety coordinator keeps the electronic copies.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Skim the guide for one minute only. Then cover it and answer. a) How many numbered headings does the guide have? b) Who is the guide written for? c) Which version is it?
Task 2 (level 1) Scan for the number of hours the employer has to complete the preliminary investigation report. What key word or number did you scan for?
Task 3 (level 1) Scan for the section on mapping the scene. List three things a supervisor must note, measure and mark.
Task 4 (level 2) Read closely. A labourer trips on an extension cord at the top of a stairwell. She grabs the rail and is not hurt. Does this count as an incident under this guide? Point to the words that decide it.
Task 5 (level 2) For each purpose below, say whether you would skim, scan or read closely first. Give a reason for one of them. a) You want to know what the guide covers before a safety meeting. b) You need the form number for the preliminary investigation. c) You need to know exactly who submits the full investigation report and what you hand over.
Task 6 (level 2) A co-worker says: "We have a week to write up the preliminary report, and the supervisor sends the full report to WorkSafeBC." Use the guide to correct both parts of this statement.
Check yourself
What sentence should you finish before you start reading?
You need one phone number from a two-page notice. Do you skim, scan or read closely first?
Name three small words that can change the meaning of a sentence and that tell you to read closely.
What are the three steps of the ACCESS routine?

lessons.title: Break down the question first
lessons.text:
Use the question word, the key words and the limit words in a question to know exactly what answer to look for.
Why this matters on the job
A lead hand asks, "How many of the new hires have been signed off on the lift?" A wrong answer here can put an untrained worker on a machine. Many reading mistakes happen before you even look at the document, because the question was not clear in your head. A few seconds spent breaking down the question saves time and gets the right answer.
Key ideas
1. The question word tells you what kind of answer to look for.
Question word Look for
Who a person, a role or a group
What a thing, an action or an event
Where a place or a location
When a time, a date or a condition ("when the gate does not close")
Why a reason
How a way or a method
How many / How much a number or an amount
How often a frequency, such as daily or every 30 days
Which one choice out of several
2. Key words carry the meaning. Underline them. Cross out the words that only hold the sentence together. If the sentence still makes sense with only the key words, you found them.
~~What should~~ you do ~~if the~~ entry gate ~~on the lift~~ does not close ~~by itself~~?
3. Given and requested. The question gives you some information (the given) and asks for other information (the requested). The given tells you where to look. The requested tells you when to stop.
4. Limit words narrow the answer. Watch for only, except, not, before, after, first, last, at least, no more than, both, either.
5. The document may use a different word. The question says "inspect", but the document says "check". The question says "number", but the document says "quantity". If you cannot find your key word, think of other words that mean the same thing.
Worked example
Question: Where must the lift be charged?
Question word: where, so look for a place.
Key words: lift, charged.
Given: it is about charging the lift.
Requested: the place.
Scan the document for "charge". Item 4 says: "Charge it in the charging bay only."
Limit word: only. So the answer is the charging bay, and nowhere else.
Practice document
Northline Fabrication Ltd. (fictional company) Shop Procedure SP-07: Scissor lift pre-use check · Revision B
Do this check at the start of every shift before you raise the platform. Only workers trained on this model may operate it. The shop supervisor keeps the training records. The lead hand does not.
Guardrails and gate. Check the platform guardrails and the entry gate. The gate must close and latch by itself. If it does not, tag the lift DO NOT USE and tell the lead hand.
Tires and wheels. Look for cuts, bulges and loose wheel nuts.
Hydraulic fluid. Check the level with the platform fully lowered. Top up only with the fluid named on the decal on the machine.
Battery. Look at the charge indicator. Do not start work if fewer than 2 bars show. Charge it in the charging bay only.
Emergency stops. Test the emergency stop button at the platform controls and at the base controls. Both must stop all movement.
Emergency lowering. Test the emergency lowering valve at the base.
Record. Write the check on the daily log card in the holder on the base. Print your full name, sign, and write the date.
If any item fails, do not use the lift. Tag it and tell the lead hand. The lead hand books the repair.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) For each question, write the question word and the kind of answer you will look for.
Question Question word Kind of answer
a) Who keeps the training records?
b) When should you do the pre-use check?
c) How many bars must show before you start work?
d) Where is the daily log card kept?
e) Why do you think the platform must be fully lowered before you check the fluid?
Task 2 (level 1) Cross out the supporting words and leave only the key words. a) What should you do if a tire on the lift has a deep cut in it? b) Which fluid can you use to top up the hydraulic tank?
Task 3 (level 2) For each question, write the given and the requested. Then answer it from the procedure.
a) If the gate does not latch by itself, what tag goes on the lift? Given: ___ Requested: ___ Answer: _____
b) What three things must you write on the daily log card? Given: ___ Requested: ___ Answer: _____
c) Who books the repair when an item fails? Given: ___ Requested: ___ Answer: _____
Task 4 (level 2) A new worker asks you: "Who do I ask to find out if I've been signed off on this lift?" The words "signed off" are not in the procedure. Which words in the procedure mean the same thing, and what is the answer?
Task 5 (level 2) Use the limit words to answer. a) The charging bay is full. Can you charge the lift at your workstation? b) The emergency stop works at the base controls but not at the platform controls. Can you use the lift? c) The indicator shows exactly 2 bars. Can you start work?
Task 6 (level 1) Here is an old riddle. Read the question at the end very carefully.
As I was going to St Ives, I met a man with seven wives. Each wife had seven sacks, each sack had seven cats, each cat had seven kits. Kits, cats, sacks, wives: how many were going to St Ives?
What exactly does the question ask? What is your answer, and why might someone who starts multiplying get a different one?
Task 7 (level 2) Each answer below does not match its question. Say what is wrong, then write an answer that does match. Use the procedure where you can.
a) Q: When did you last test the emergency stops? A: The red button is on the base. b) Q: Why is the lift tagged? A: The lead hand tagged it. c) Q: How many workers are trained on this model? A: The shop supervisor keeps that.
Check yourself
What kind of answer does a "how often" question ask for?
What is the difference between the given and the requested?
You scan for the word "inspect" and cannot find it. What do you try next?
Name three limit words.

lessons.title: Follow written instructions step by step
lessons.text:
Read a set of instructions all the way through, find the order, the numbers and the conditions, and carry them out without skipping a step.
Why this matters on the job
A plumber gluing ABS drain pipe, a carpenter staining a rail, a millwright changing a filter: each job comes with written steps. Every step you skip or do out of order is a place where the job can fail. A joint that is pressure tested too soon can leak inside a finished wall. Reading instructions well is a safety skill and a money skill.
Key ideas
1. Read all the steps before you start. You may find a warning at the end that changes step 1, or a tool you need to get first.
2. Find the order. Numbers and letters show order. So do these words: first, next, then, after, before, while, until, finally, last. Watch for "but first", which moves a step earlier.
3. Find the numbers. Times, temperatures, sizes and amounts. Write them down or circle them. Check the unit: seconds or minutes, mm or inches.
4. Find the conditions. "If…", "when…", "only if…", "unless…". A condition tells you when a step applies, or when to stop.
5. Find the warnings. "Do not", "never", "discard". These are steps too.
6. One numbered step can hold two actions. "Hold the joint for 30 seconds and wipe off the extra" is two actions. Do both.
7. Keep your place. Tick each step as you finish it.
Worked example
"Apply a thin coat of cement to the fitting, then a heavier coat to the pipe. Assemble quickly while the cement is still wet."
Order words: then. Fitting first, pipe second.
Two actions in the first sentence: thin coat on fitting, heavier coat on pipe.
Condition: while the cement is still wet. If it has dried, you are too late.
Practice documents
Document A: Read everything first
Read all of these steps before you do anything. 1. Write your name at the top of this page. 2. Circle the word "bolt" in step 4. 3. Write today's date under your name. 4. Count the bolts in the box on your table and write the number here: ____ 5. Draw a small square in the margin. 6. Now that you have read all the steps, do only step 1. Then put your pencil down.
Document B: Practice label for a solvent cement
This practice label is adapted from an older ACCESS handout. It is for a fictional product. Real products differ, so always follow the label on the can you are using.
Coastline ABS Cement, Medium Bodied, Black (fictional product) General directions for making a solvent cement joint - Look at the cement before using it. If it has turned to jelly, throw it out. Do not use primer or cleaner to thin the cement. - Cut the pipe square and remove all dirt and burrs. - Check the dry fit. The pipe should go easily into the fitting about 1/4 of the way. - Apply a thin coat of cement inside the fitting. Do not let it puddle. - Apply a heavier coat of cement to the pipe. Leave no bare spots. - Assemble quickly while the cement is still wet. Push the pipe into the fitting with a 1/4 turn until it bottoms out. - Hold the pipe and fitting together for 30 seconds. Wipe off the extra cement at the joint. - Allow 15 minutes before handling the joint. - Allow 24 to 48 hours before applying pressure to the joint. - Stir the cement often while using it. Use an applicator about 1/2 the diameter of the pipe. Keep the can tightly closed when not in use.
Document C: Toolbox card
Kestrel Point Builders Ltd. (fictional company) · Toolbox card TC-04: Staining the new deck rails Stain the rails only when all of these are true: - the wood is dry to the touch - the air temperature is at least 10 °C now, and the forecast keeps it at or above 10 °C until the stain is dry to the touch (see the drying time on the can) - no rain is forecast for the next 24 hours
If any one of these is not true, do other work and tell the foreman.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Follow Document A exactly.
Task 2 (level 1) These steps from Document B are mixed up. Put the letters in the correct order.
A. Hold the pipe and fitting together for 30 seconds. B. Cut the pipe square and remove burrs. C. Apply a heavier coat to the pipe. D. Look at the cement and throw it out if it has turned to jelly. E. Push the pipe in with a 1/4 turn until it bottoms out. F. Check the dry fit. G. Apply a thin coat inside the fitting. H. Wait 24 to 48 hours before applying pressure.
Order: ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___
Task 3 (level 2) Use Document B. a) How long do you hold the joint together? b) How long before you can handle the joint? c) How long before you can apply pressure? d) How far should the pipe go into the fitting on a dry fit? e) You are joining 3-inch pipe. About what size applicator should you use?
Task 4 (level 2) A co-worker describes how he made a joint. Find three things he did that go against Document B.
"The cement was getting thick so I thinned it with a bit of primer. I put cement on the pipe and the fitting, then went and grabbed a coffee while it set up a bit. Then I pushed them together. I pressure tested the line an hour later."
Task 5 (level 2) Use Document C. The can of stain says "dry to the touch in 4 hours". a) It is 9:00 a.m. The rails are dry. It is 14 °C now. The forecast says 12 °C at 1:00 p.m. and 6 °C overnight. Rain is forecast to start in 30 hours. Can you stain the rails this morning? Explain. b) Same day, but rain is now forecast to start in 12 hours. Can you stain? What do you do instead?
Task 6 (level 2) Turn this paragraph into numbered steps, in the right order.
Before you leave the area at the end of the day, close every can of cement and primer tightly. Put the cans back in the flammables cabinet, but first wipe any cement off the outside of each can with a dry rag. Used rags go in the metal rag bin with the lid closed, not in the regular garbage. Last, write on the job board which joints are less than 24 hours old so that nobody pressure tests them in the morning.
Check yourself
Why should you read all the steps before starting?
Name four words that show the order of steps.
What does "but first" do to the order of steps?
In Document C, how many conditions must be true before you stain, and what do you do if one is not?

lessons.title: Find it in a table, log or form
lessons.text:
Read lists, tables and logs by their titles, headings and notes, find the cell where a row meets a column, and fill in a work form correctly.
Why this matters on the job
Parts lists, bin labels, maintenance logs, time sheets, material requests and inspection forms are made of lists and tables. You do not read them from top to bottom like a story. You go straight to the row and column you need. A wrong row means the wrong bolt, a missed oil change or a time sheet that does not get paid.
Key ideas
1. A simple list is a group of items under one label. All the items have something in common. Lists are put in an order: by number, by letter, by date, or by the order you do things. Knowing the order helps you find things fast.
2. A table puts lists side by side. The first column usually names the thing. The other columns tell you more about it. Read it in this order: 1. Title: what is this table about, and for what date or job? 2. Column headings across the top, and row labels down the side. 3. Notes and symbols: an asterisk (*), a dash (–) or a footnote can change the meaning of a cell. 4. Find your row. Keep a finger or a ruler on it while you move across.
3. Where a row meets a column. Some tables need two pieces of information to find a third. "How many hours did compressor 2 run on Wednesday?" needs the row (Wednesday) and the column (compressor 2, hours run today). The answer is in the cell where they meet.
4. A form is a table you fill in. Before you write, check: - Who fills in which part? Some parts say "Office use only". - Which fields are required? They are often marked with an asterisk (*). - What format is asked for? For example, a date written as YYYY-MM-DD. - Who signs? Never sign for someone else.
Worked example
Question: What is the box quantity for 1/2" flat washers?
Title: Fastener bin list. Good.
Headings: Bin, Item, Size, Material, Box quantity.
Scan the Item column for "Flat washer". Two rows. Check the Size column: B07 is 1/2".
Move across row B07 to Box quantity: 100.
Practice documents
Document A
Northline Fabrication Ltd. (fictional company) · Fastener bin list · Rack 2

B02 Hex bolt 3/8" × 2" Stainless steel 25
B03 Hex bolt 1/2" × 3" Zinc-plated steel 25
B04 Hex nut 3/8" Zinc-plated steel 100
B05 Hex nut 3/8" Stainless steel 100
B06 Flat washer 3/8" Zinc-plated steel 100
B07 Flat washer 1/2" Zinc-plated steel 100
B08 Lock washer 3/8" Stainless steel 100
Note: Stainless steel items are for outdoor railings. Ask the lead hand before using them for anything else.
Document B
Northline Fabrication Ltd. (fictional company) · Shop air compressors: daily hours log Week of 2026-10-05 · Change the oil every 500 hours run
Day C1 hours run today C1 hours since last oil change C1 oil level OK? C2 hours run today C2 hours since last oil change C2 oil level OK?
Mon 8 470 Yes 6 212 Yes
Tue 9 479 Yes 7 219 Yes*
Wed 7 Yes 8 227 Yes
Thu 9 495 Yes 0 227 –
Fri 8 503 No 7 234 Yes
* Oil was topped up that day. – The compressor was not run that day.
Document C
Northline Fabrication Ltd. (fictional company) · MATERIAL REQUEST · Form MR-1 Fields marked * are required. Print clearly.
*Date (YYYY-MM-DD) *Job number *Requested by (print name) Crew (tick one)
☐ Fab ☐ Install ☐ Maintenance
*Bin *Item *Size *Quantity *Unit (each or box)
Needed by (YYYY-MM-DD) *Approved by (lead hand signature)

Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Document A. a) In what order are the rows listed? b) Which bin holds 1/2" × 3" hex bolts? c) How many bolts are in one box from bin B02?
Task 2 (level 1) Use Document A. You are fixing a railing outdoors. Which bins hold a matching 3/8" stainless bolt, nut and lock washer?
Task 3 (level 2) Use Document B. a) How many hours did compressor C2 run on Wednesday? b) The cell for C1 hours since last oil change on Wednesday is blank. What number belongs there? Show how you worked it out. c) What does the dash in the C2 oil column on Thursday mean?
Task 4 (level 2) Use Document B. a) On which day did C1 go past the oil change limit? b) Name two things in Friday's row for C1 that need action. c) On which day was oil added to C2? How do you know? d) Which compressor ran more hours this week, and by how many?
Task 5 (level 2) Fill in Document C for this request.
You are Sam Ward on the install crew. Your job number is 26-114. Today is 6 November 2026. You need 2 boxes of 3/8" × 2" stainless hex bolts and 2 boxes of matching stainless hex nuts for an outdoor railing. You need them by Monday 9 November 2026. Your lead hand is Priya Desai.
Task 6 (level 3) Here is a form another worker handed in. Find five problems with it.

Check yourself
Name the three things to read in a table before you look for your answer.
In a table where you need a row and a column, where is the answer?
What does an asterisk (*) next to a form field often mean?
A form has a box for your lead hand's signature. Your lead hand is not here. What do you do?

lessons.title: Read a floor plan and its notes
lessons.text:
Use the title block, legend, schedules, notes and detail references on a construction drawing to find what to build and where.
Why this matters on the job
Carpenters, tilesetters, plumbers and electricians all work from the same set of drawings. The drawing shows the shape of the job, but most of the answers are in the words around it: the title block, the legend, the schedules and the notes. Missing a revision or a note can mean tearing out finished work.
Key ideas
1. Kinds of views. - A plan (floor plan) looks straight down on the building, as if the roof were lifted off. - An elevation looks straight at a wall from the side. - A section shows what you would see if you sliced through a wall or floor. - A detail is a close-up, drawn bigger, of one small part.
2. The title block sits in a corner of every sheet. It names the project, the drawing, the drawing number, the scale and the date. It lists the revisions: each change to the drawing, with a number and a date. Always check that you have the latest revision.
3. The legend explains the symbols and abbreviations used on that set of drawings. Abbreviations are not the same on every job, so read the legend for each set.
4. Schedules are tables on the drawing. A room finish schedule says what goes on each floor, base, wall and ceiling. A door schedule gives the size and type of each door. The plan shows a door number. The schedule tells you about that door.
5. Notes are rules written on the drawing. A general note applies to the whole drawing unless it says otherwise. Notes often say "TYP" (typical), meaning the same thing applies in all similar places.
6. Detail references look like (1/A5.1): detail number 1, found on drawing A5.1. Go to that drawing for the close-up.
7. Scale. "Scale 1:50" means 1 mm on the drawing stands for 50 mm in real life. A wall 2250 mm long is drawn 2250 ÷ 50 = 45 mm long. Paper prints can shrink or stretch, so most drawings tell you to use the written dimensions, not a ruler. A ruler is only for a rough check.
Worked example
Question: What size is door D1?
Find D1 on the plan. It is in the wall between room 104 and the corridor.
The legend says D1 is a door number: see the door schedule.
In the door schedule, row D1 says 915 × 2135.
The legend says dimensions are in millimetres, so the door is 915 mm wide and 2135 mm high.
Practice documents
All documents below are for a fictional project.
Drawing A2.1 · Floor plan: washrooms 104 and 105 (not to scale on this page)

Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use the title block. a) What is the drawing number and the scale? b) What is the latest revision, and what was its date? c) What changed in that revision?
Task 2 (level 1) Use the plan and the legend. a) How many toilets (WC) are there in room 104? In room 105? b) How many hand sinks (LAV) are there in total? c) Which room is the corridor? d) Which wall of room 105 is on the north side?
Task 3 (level 2) a) How high does the wall tile go on most walls in room 105? b) How high does it go behind a hand sink? c) Where do you look for a close-up of the wall at a hand sink?
Task 4 (level 2) a) On a full-size print of drawing A2.1 (scale 1:50), the north wall of room 104 measures 45 mm with a ruler. How long is the wall in real life? b) A helper uses a ruler on a reduced photocopy and gets a different length. Which number do you trust, and which note tells you so?
Task 5 (level 2) The east wall of room 105 has no fixtures on it. It is 3000 mm long. Using the room finish schedule, how many square metres of wall tile go on that wall? (Ignore the cove base.)
Task 6 (level 2) A supplier sends a quote for door D2 at 865 mm wide. Is that correct? Which part of the drawing tells you?
Task 7 (level 2) What does P&MG mean, and where does note 4 say it applies?
Task 8 (level 3) Read general note 2 and detail 1 on A5.1 together. Is there a problem? If so, explain it and say what you should do before you set the tile and mirror.
Check yourself
What is the difference between a plan and an elevation?
Where on a drawing do you check that you have the latest revision?
A plan shows "(3/A6.2)". What does it mean?
At a scale of 1:50, how many millimetres in real life does 1 mm on the drawing stand for?
What should you do when two parts of a drawing set do not agree?

lessons.title: Find a rule in the BC Building Code
lessons.text:
Use the edition, the index and the numbering system of the BC Building Code 2024 to find the exact rule that applies, and read it word by word.
Why this matters on the job
On a house, a small building or a renovation in BC, the BC Building Code sets the minimum rules: how high a stair can go, what goes under floor tile, how far a handrail can stick out. A foreman may say "Code says…" and you need to check it yourself. The Code is thousands of pages, so nobody reads it front to back. You find a rule by its number and by the index, and then you read it very closely.
Key ideas
1. Use the current edition. The BC Building Code 2024 came into effect on March 8, 2024. It applies to projects with building permits applied for after that date. It is based on the National Building Code of Canada 2020. The Province posts it as a free PDF, and says that the PDF does not include every later update. Check the revisions and bulletins on the same web page.
BC Building Code 2024 page: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/construction-industry/building-codes-standards/bc-codes/2024-bc-codes
2. How the Code is organized.
Part of the Code What it holds
Division A Compliance, objectives and functional statements
Division B Acceptable solutions: the technical rules
Division C Administrative provisions
Division B, Part 9 Housing and Small Buildings. Most residential work is here. It is in Volume 2.
Index At the back of each volume. Topics in alphabetical order, with Code numbers.
3. How a Code number works. Each extra number goes one level deeper.
Level Example What it is
Part 9 Housing and Small Buildings
Section 9.30. Flooring
Subsection 9.30.2. Panel-Type Underlay
Article 9.30.2.1. Required Underlay
Sentence 9.30.2.1.(3) one numbered rule in that article
Clause (a), (b) … one part of a sentence
Subclause (i), (ii) … one part of a clause
4. Words in italics have a special meaning. Part 9 says: "Words in italics are defined in Article 1.4.1.2. of Division A." If a word is in italics, look it up there. Do not guess. In the index, "1.4.1.2.[A]" means Article 1.4.1.2. of Division A.
5. "Shall" means must. BC's Interpretation Act says "shall" is to be read as imperative, and "may" as permissive. Watch the limit words too: not less than (at least), not more than (no more than), except, only.
6. Tables and notes. Under each table, the Code tells you which rule uses it, for example "Forming Part of Sentence 9.23.3.4.(1)". Notes to Part 9 are labelled with "A-" and a Code number, such as "Note A-9.8.4." They explain the rule in more detail.
Worked example
Question: Over a lumber subfloor, does ceramic tile need panel-type underlay?
Look in the index under Flooring. It lists "underlay, 9.30.2."
Go to Subsection 9.30.2. Panel-Type Underlay. The first article is 9.30.2.1. Required Underlay.
Read Sentence (1) closely. It says a panel-type underlay shall be provided under resilient flooring, parquet flooring, ceramic tile, felted-synthetic-fibre floor coverings or carpeting laid over lumber subflooring.
Answer: yes. The rule is Sentence 9.30.2.1.(1).
Practice
For Tasks 2 to 7 you need the BC Building Code 2024 PDF open on a phone, tablet or computer. Use the web page in Key idea 1. Part 9 is in Volume 2.
Task 1 (level 1) Name each part of this Code number: 9.8.7.6. And of this one: 9.30.2.1.(3)
Task 2 (level 2) Open the BC Building Code 2024 web page. a) When did the BC Building Code 2024 come into effect? b) The page warns that the PDF may not include everything. What else does it tell you to check?
Task 3 (level 2) Use the index at the back of Volume 2. a) Under "Flooring", what Code number is listed for ceramic tile flooring in houses and small buildings? (Look for the number that starts with 9.30.) b) Under "Ceramic tile", what Code number is listed for installing ceramic tile as an interior wall finish?
Task 4 (level 2) Go to Article 9.30.2.1. Required Underlay. a) Read Sentence (3). Must panel-type underlay go under ceramic tile that is applied with adhesive? b) Which Code number would you quote to your foreman for that rule?
Task 5 (level 2) Go to Article 9.30.2.4. Joints Offset. a) How far must the joints in the underlay be offset from the joints in the subfloor below? b) Is that a minimum or a maximum? Which words tell you?
Task 6 (level 2) Go to Article 9.30.6.1. Substrate, in Subsection 9.30.6. Ceramic Tile. Read Sentence (1). What are the two ways ceramic tile may be set?
Task 7 (level 3) Go to Section 9.8. Stairs, Ramps, Landings, Handrails and Guards. a) In Subsection 9.8.3., find the greatest vertical height allowed for any one flight of stairs. b) Go to Article 9.8.7.6. Projections into Stairs and Ramps. How far can handrails and their supports stick out into the required width of a stair? c) In these articles, some words are in italics, such as ramp and flight. Where do you find what they mean?
Task 8 (level 3) An old ACCESS handout from about 2010 gives a Code number and a rule for the slump of concrete. Your co-worker wants to use it to settle an argument on site today. What would you tell them, and why?
Check yourself
In 9.30.2.1.(3), which number is the Sentence?
Where in the Code do you find the meaning of a word in italics?
What does "shall" mean in a Code rule?
What does "not less than 200 mm" mean in plain words?
Why should you check the revisions page as well as the PDF?

lessons.title: Read a WHMIS label and a safety data sheet
lessons.text:
Find the hazard, the protection and the emergency steps on a WHMIS supplier label and its 16-section safety data sheet, and know when a workplace label is needed.
Why this matters on the job
Degreasers, solvent cement, spray paint, cutting fluid, concrete additives and welding gas all come with a WHMIS label and a safety data sheet (SDS). In BC, your employer must make the SDS readily available to workers who may be exposed to the product. The label tells you the main hazards in seconds. The SDS tells you the details: which gloves, how to store it, what to do if it splashes in your eye. Reading them well protects you and your crew.
This lesson is reading practice. It does not replace the WHMIS education and training your employer must give you for the products at your workplace.
Key ideas
1. WHMIS is the Workplace Hazardous Materials Information System. A hazardous product at work has a label and a safety data sheet. Canada updated the WHMIS supplier rules in December 2022. The transition period ended on December 14, 2025, so labels and SDSs should now meet the updated rules.
2. A supplier label comes on the product from the supplier. It must be in English and French. It has these parts:
Label part What it tells you
Product identifier the name of the product, which must match the SDS
Initial supplier identifier the name, address and phone number of the Canadian maker or importer
Pictogram(s) a symbol inside a red diamond border that shows the type of hazard
Signal word Danger for more severe hazards, Warning for less severe ones
Hazard statement(s) standard sentences that say what the hazard is
Precautionary statement(s) standard sentences that say how to protect yourself, store the product and respond to an emergency, including first aid
Supplemental label information other information, such as an instruction to read the SDS
3. A workplace label is needed when a product is made at the workplace, when it is poured or pumped into another container (decanted), or when the supplier label is lost or cannot be read. A workplace label gives: - the product identifier (the name, matching the SDS) - safe handling information - a reference to the SDS
4. The SDS has 16 sections, always in the same order. That makes it easy to scan.
Section Heading
1 Identification
2 Hazard identification
3 Composition/Information on ingredients
4 First-aid measures
5 Fire-fighting measures
6 Accidental release measures
7 Handling and storage
8 Exposure controls/Personal protection
9 Physical and chemical properties
10 Stability and reactivity
11 Toxicological information
12 Ecological information
13 Disposal considerations
14 Transport information
15 Regulatory information
16 Other information (includes the date of the latest revision)
For most jobs, read Sections 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8 first.
5. In BC, SDSs are checked every three years. WorkSafeBC says SDSs must be checked every three years to make sure they have the most current information. Look at the revision date in Section 16.
Worked example
Question: What should you do if ShopClean Degreaser 40 splashes in your eye?
Purpose: first aid for the eye.
On the label, scan the precautionary statements for "IF IN EYES". It says to rinse cautiously with water for several minutes, remove contact lenses if present and easy to do, and continue rinsing.
For more detail, go to SDS Section 4, First-aid measures, and read "Eye contact".
Practice documents
All documents below are for a fictional product from a fictional supplier. Only the English part of the label is shown.
Document A: Supplier label
ShopClean Degreaser 40
[Pictogram: flame] [Pictogram: exclamation mark]
WARNING
Flammable liquid and vapour. Causes serious eye irritation.
Keep away from heat, hot surfaces, sparks, open flames and other ignition sources. No smoking. Keep container tightly closed. Wear protective gloves and eye protection. IF IN EYES: Rinse cautiously with water for several minutes. Remove contact lenses, if present and easy to do. Continue rinsing. If eye irritation persists: Get medical attention. Store in a well-ventilated place. Keep cool.
Read the safety data sheet before use.
Tidewater Chemical Supply Ltd., 1200 Harbour Road, Port Kestrel, BC · 604-555-0142
Document B: Safety data sheet (excerpt)
SAFETY DATA SHEET · ShopClean Degreaser 40
Section 1. Identification Product identifier: ShopClean Degreaser 40 Recommended use: removing grease and oil from metal parts Restrictions on use: do not use on hot surfaces or near open flames Supplier: Tidewater Chemical Supply Ltd., 1200 Harbour Road, Port Kestrel, BC · 604-555-0142 Emergency telephone: 604-555-0199 (24 hours)
Section 2. Hazard identification Classification: Flammable liquids, Category 3. Eye irritation, Category 2A. Pictograms: flame, exclamation mark. Signal word: Warning. Hazard statements: Flammable liquid and vapour. Causes serious eye irritation.
Section 4. First-aid measures Eye contact: Rinse cautiously with water for several minutes. Remove contact lenses, if present and easy to do. Continue rinsing. If eye irritation persists, get medical attention. Skin contact: Wash with soap and water. Inhalation: Move the person to fresh air. Ingestion: Rinse mouth. Call a poison centre or doctor.
Section 5. Fire-fighting measures Suitable extinguishing media: dry chemical, carbon dioxide, foam. Unsuitable extinguishing media: direct water jet.
Section 7. Handling and storage Keep the container closed when not in use. Store in a cool, well-ventilated area away from heat and ignition sources, such as a flammables cabinet. Keep away from strong oxidizers.
Section 8. Exposure controls/Personal protection Engineering controls: use with good general ventilation. Eye protection: safety glasses with side shields, or goggles. Hand protection: nitrile gloves.
Section 16. Other information Date of latest revision: 2024-02-12
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Find each of the seven supplier label parts on Document A. Write what each one says.
Task 2 (level 1) What is the signal word on Document A? Would a product with the signal word "Danger" be more or less hazardous?
Task 3 (level 2) Which SDS section would you go to for each question? Then answer it from Document B. a) What kind of gloves should you wear? b) What should you do if it splashes on your skin? c) Where should the product be stored? d) What kind of fire extinguisher can be used on it? e) What is the product meant to be used for? f) When was the SDS last revised?
Task 4 (level 2) Name three things the SDS tells you that the label does not.
Task 5 (level 2) You pour some degreaser into a spray bottle. The crew will use it all week. Write the workplace label for the spray bottle.
Task 6 (level 3) Today is 2026-11-06. In BC, SDSs are checked every three years. Using Section 16 of Document B, when is this SDS next due to be checked? Is it overdue?
Task 7 (level 3) A new jug arrives. Its label says "ShopClean 40 Citrus" and gives a different supplier. The SDS in the binder is for "ShopClean Degreaser 40" from Tidewater. A co-worker says, "Same stuff, just use the binder SDS." What do you do, and why?
Task 8 (level 3) You work the night shift. Your foreman says the SDS binder is kept in the site office, which is locked after 4:00 p.m. Is that good enough? What would you do?
Check yourself
What are the two signal words, and which one is for the more severe hazard?
Name the three things a workplace label must show.
Which SDS section tells you about personal protective equipment?
Which SDS section has the date of the latest revision?
Name one time when a workplace label is needed.

lessons.title: Use an equipment manual
lessons.text:
Find specifications, safety warnings, troubleshooting steps and part numbers in a tool manual by using its contents page, index and tables.
Why this matters on the job
Every grinder, saw, pump and compressor comes with a manual. Millwrights, fabricators and service techs use manuals to set up equipment, fix faults and order parts. A manual is not read like a book. You jump to the page you need using the contents page, the index and the tables. The safety warnings at the front apply to every page after them.
Key ideas
1. Contents page or index? - The contents page at the front lists the sections in order. Use it when you know the general topic, such as "maintenance". - The index at the back lists small topics in alphabetical order, with page numbers. Use it when you are looking for one thing, such as "brushes", that does not have its own section.
2. Read the safety warnings first. They are at the front, and they apply to the whole manual. Words like always, never, do not and only matter.
3. The specifications table lists the numbers for the tool: voltage, current, speed, size, weight. The same numbers are usually on the nameplate (the rating label on the tool). Check that they match.
4. The troubleshooting table has three columns: the problem, the possible cause and what to do. Find your problem in the first column, then read across. A problem can have more than one possible cause. Try the simple, safe fixes first.
5. The parts list connects a reference number on a drawing to a part number you can order. Order by the part number, not the reference number.
6. A manual can disagree with what you see online. The manual for your model and edition is written for that tool. If a video, a forum or a co-worker says something different, follow the manual and ask your supervisor.
Worked example
Question: What size disc does the AG-125 take?
It is a number about the tool, so go to the specifications table.
The contents page says Specifications is on page 4.
Read across the row "Disc diameter": 125 mm.
Practice document
Westbrook Tools (fictional company) · AG-125 Angle Grinder · Operator's Manual · Edition 2, 2025
Contents 1 Safety warnings ............ 2 2 Specifications ............. 4 3 Know your grinder .......... 5 4 Fitting a disc ............. 6 5 Operating .................. 8 6 Maintenance ................ 10 7 Troubleshooting ............ 11 8 Parts list ................. 12 Index ........................ 14
1 Safety warnings (page 2, excerpt) - Always use the wheel guard. Never use the grinder if the guard is missing or damaged. - Use only discs and accessories with a maximum speed marked on them that is equal to or greater than the no-load speed marked on this grinder. - Unplug the grinder before you fit or change a disc. - Wear eye protection and hearing protection.
2 Specifications (page 4)
Item Value

lessons.title: Read a workplace policy or agreement
lessons.text:
Use the index, definitions and must, should and may to understand an employee handbook, and check an agreement against BC employment standards before you sign.
Why this matters on the job
On your first day with a new employer you may get an employee handbook and a stack of forms to sign. The handbook tells you how to report an absence, when time sheets are due and what happens with your own tools. An agreement you sign can affect your pay. In BC, the Employment Standards Act sets minimum standards. An agreement cannot take them away, even if you sign it. Reading before you sign protects you.
Key ideas
1. Use the index and the definitions first. A handbook is a reference book. Find your topic in the index or contents. Then read the definitions section: a word like "employee" or "supervisor" may have a special meaning in this document.
2. Must, should and may. - Must (or shall): required. No choice. - Should: expected. Check what the document says about exceptions. - May: allowed, not required. "The supervisor may ask for a note" means they can, but do not have to.
Many handbooks define these words. Use the handbook's own definitions if it has them.
3. Watch who does what. Underline the person in each rule: "you must call your supervisor". A message to the wrong person may not count.
4. Look for limits and conditions. Only if, unless, including, except, in a row, before.
5. Check an agreement against the law. In BC, section 4 of the Employment Standards Act says its requirements are minimum requirements, and an agreement to waive any of them has no effect. The Province also says it is illegal to make employees pay for business expenses, such as stolen or damaged company property, even if they agree to it. If something in a handbook or agreement looks like it takes away a minimum standard, ask before you sign. The BC Employment Standards website is https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/employment-business/employment-standards-advice/employment-standards
6. Ask who wrote it and why. A handbook is written by the employer, for employees, to set rules and protect the business. That is normal. Knowing who wrote it helps you read it fairly and notice what it leaves out.
Worked example
Question: Do part-time workers have a probation period?
Index: "Probation ... 5". Go to page 5.
Read section 3 closely: "All new employees, including part-time employees, are on probation for the first 3 months."
"Including part-time employees" answers it: yes, 3 months.
Practice documents
All documents below are for a fictional employer.
Document A: Employee handbook (excerpt)
Kestrel Point Builders Ltd. (fictional company) · Employee Handbook · Edition 4, January 2026
Index Absence, reporting ........ 7 Cell phones ............... 12 Definitions ............... 3 Overtime .................. 9 Probation ................. 5 Time sheets ............... 8 Tools, company ............ 13 Tools, personal ........... 13
Section 1. Definitions (page 3) "Employee" means anyone on Kestrel Point's payroll, including apprentices and part-time employees. "Supervisor" means the foreman or site superintendent you report to. "Must" means required. "Should" means expected unless there is a good reason. "May" means allowed but not required.
Section 3. Probation (page 5) All new employees, including part-time employees, are on probation for the first 3 months. Your supervisor will review your work before the probation ends.
Section 4. Reporting an absence (page 7) If you will be absent or late, you must call or text your supervisor before your shift starts. A message left with a co-worker does not count. If you are absent because of illness for more than 2 shifts in a row, your supervisor may ask for a note.
Section 5. Time sheets (page 8) You must submit your time sheet in the company app by 10:00 a.m. Monday for the week before. If you miss the deadline, tell the office right away.
Section 6. Overtime (page 9) Employees who want extra hours may agree in writing to be paid their regular rate for those hours instead of overtime rates.
Section 8. Cell phones (page 12) Personal phone use should be kept to breaks. You must not use a phone while operating equipment or while working on a ladder or scaffold.
Section 9. Tools (page 13) Kestrel Point supplies power tools. You must supply your own hand tools from the basic list for your trade. You may use your own power tools only if your supervisor has inspected them and you have signed the Personal Tool Form (KP-30).
Document B: An agreement handed to a new worker
Kestrel Point Builders Ltd. (fictional company) · Company Tool Sign-out Agreement I agree to take good care of any company tool I sign out. I agree that the cost of any company tool that is lost, stolen or damaged while signed out to me may be deducted from my pay. Name: __ Signature: __ Date: __
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use the index in Document A. On what page would you find: a) the rules for using your own power tools? b) what to do if you will be late? c) when time sheets are due?
Task 2 (level 1) Use the definitions in Document A. Label each rule as must, should or may, and say what it means for you. a) "Personal phone use should be kept to breaks." b) "Your supervisor may ask for a note." c) "You must not use a phone while operating equipment."
Task 3 (level 2) Is an apprentice an "employee" under this handbook? Point to the words that show it.
Task 4 (level 2) You wake up sick at 5:30 a.m. Your shift starts at 7:00. You text a co-worker on your crew and ask him to tell the foreman. Have you followed section 4? What should you have done?
Task 5 (level 2) You want to bring your own cordless circular saw to work. What two things must happen first?
Task 6 (level 3) Read section 6, Overtime. Then read Key idea 5. Is there a problem with section 6? Explain.
Task 7 (level 3) You are handed Document B on your first day and told to sign it. Read it closely. a) What does it allow the employer to do? b) How does that compare with what the Province of BC says about business expenses? c) What could you do before you sign?
Task 8 (level 3) Think about Document A as a whole. a) Who wrote it, and who is it written for? b) What does it want the reader to do? c) Name one thing a new worker might want to know that this excerpt does not say.
Check yourself
What is the difference between "must" and "may"?
Why read the definitions section before the rules?
Can you sign away a minimum standard under BC's Employment Standards Act?
Name one question to ask yourself about who wrote a document.

lessons.title: Read on a screen and check the source
lessons.text:
Find information fast on a phone, and decide whether a web page, post or search summary can be trusted before you act on it.
Why this matters on the job
On a BC job site, the SDS, the building code, a WorkSafeBC rule or a tool manual is often read on a phone. Searching online is fast, but anyone can post anything. A forum post, an ad or a quick search summary can be wrong, out of date, or from another province or country. Before you act on something you read online, check who wrote it and whether it is current.
Key ideas
1. Make the screen work for you. - Pinch to zoom in on small print. Turn the phone sideways for wide tables. - Use find on page to jump to a word instead of scrolling. - Chrome on Android: tap More (top right), then Find in page. - Chrome on iPhone: tap More, then Find in Page… - Safari on iPhone: tap the Page Menu button, then the Search Document button. - Phone menus change with updates. If yours looks different, check the help page for your browser.
2. Check who published it. Look at the web address. Official BC and federal sources include worksafebc.com, gov.bc.ca, bclaws.gov.bc.ca and canada.ca. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security advises checking that the address matches the organization, with no typos and no different ending such as .net or .org. Check for contact information, a physical address and an "About us" page.
3. Check the date and version. Look for a date, a version or a "last updated" note. A rule from 2010 may not be the rule today. Some official documents warn you themselves. For example, the BC Building Code page says its PDF does not include every later update.
4. Check the evidence. Does it name its source? Can you find the same thing on an official page? Be careful with headlines and claims that make you feel strongly or seem too good to be true.
5. Check the purpose. Is the page trying to inform you, or sell you something? A page that sells SDS binders has a reason to say your SDSs are out of date.
6. Summaries are not sources. A search summary, a social media post or an AI answer can be wrong. Use it only as a lead. Go to the original, official page and read the actual words.
7. Never log in from a link you were sent. If a page asks for your password or payment, type the official address yourself instead of tapping the link.
Worked example
Question: How often must SDSs be checked in BC?
A search result from a site called "safetyanswers-bc.example" says every 5 years. The address is not an official one, and it sells binders. Treat it as a lead only.
Go to worksafebc.com and open the WHMIS 2015 page. Use find on page to search for "three years".
It says: "In British Columbia, SDSs must be checked every three years to ensure they include the most current information."
Answer: every three years, from WorkSafeBC.
Practice documents
Document A: Four search results (results 2, 3 and 4 are fictional)
1. WHMIS 2015 - WorkSafeBC worksafebc.com/en/health-safety/hazards-exposures/whmis/whmis-2015 "…In British Columbia, SDSs must be checked every three years to ensure they include the most current information…"
2. SDS Sheets EXPIRE After 5 Years, Expert Warns! Is Your Binder Legal? safetyanswers-bc.example · Sponsored "Don't get fined! Order our 2026 SDS Binder Kit today, only $89.99…" No author. No date.
3. TradesTalk Forum: "anyone actually check their SDS sheets??" tradestalk-forum.example · posted by user "rebar_rick" "never heard of checking them lol, we just keep the ones that came with the stuff"
4. WorkSafeBC: Download your updated SDS pack now. Log in to continue. worksafebc-update.example "Your account needs updating. Enter your WorkSafeBC password to download."
Document B: Search summary (fictional)
Quick answer: In BC, safety data sheets expire every 5 years and must be replaced by the supplier.
Practice
For Tasks 1, 2 and 5 you need a phone, tablet or computer with internet.
Task 1 (level 1) On your phone, open the WorkSafeBC WHMIS 2015 page: https://www.worksafebc.com/en/health-safety/hazards-exposures/whmis/whmis-2015 Use find on page to search for "workplace label". What three pieces of information does a workplace label provide?
Task 2 (level 1) On your phone, open the CCOHS SDS page: https://www.ccohs.ca/oshanswers/chemicals/whmis_ghs/sds.html Find the table of SDS sections. Zoom in or turn your phone sideways. What is the heading of Section 8?
Task 3 (level 2) Look at the four results in Document A. For each one, answer: Who published it? Is there a date? What is its purpose? Would you trust it for a safety rule? Fill in the table.
Result Who published it Date shown? Purpose Trust it?
1
2
3
4
Task 4 (level 2) Look closely at the address of result 4. What is wrong with it? What should you do instead of logging in?
Task 5 (level 2) Open the BC Building Code 2024 page: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/construction-industry/building-codes-standards/bc-codes/2024-bc-codes Find the warning about the PDF. What does it say you must also check, and why does this matter?
Task 6 (level 3) Your foreman reads Document B out loud and says, "Good, ours are only four years old, so we're fine." Is the summary right? Using an official source, write what you would say to the foreman. Name your source.
Task 7 (level 3) Compare result 1 and result 2 in Document A. a) Who is each one written for? b) How does each one try to get you to act? c) Why does that matter when you decide what to believe?
Check yourself
How do you jump to a word on a long web page on your phone?
Name two official websites for BC workplace rules.
Name three things to check before you trust a web page.
A search summary gives you an answer. What do you do before you act on it?
A page you reached from a text message asks for your password. What do you do?

lessons.title: Orthographic projection: read the views of an object
lessons.text:
Read the front, top and right side views of an object drawn in third-angle projection, find hidden features, and match a set of views to the object it shows.
Why this matters on the job
A shop drawing for a steel bracket, a pipe spool or a stair part rarely shows a picture of the object. It shows flat views: the object seen straight on from the front, from above and from the side. A welder, pipefitter or carpenter has to put those views together in their head to see the real shape. If you read a view from the wrong side, a hole ends up on the wrong leg or a notch is cut on the wrong face. This lesson is the first in a set of drawing lessons. Reading lesson 5 showed the words on a floor plan. These lessons show how the lines work.
Key ideas
1. A view is the object seen straight on. In a front view you look straight at the front. In a top view you look straight down. In a right side view you look straight at the right end. Each view shows only two of the three sizes:
The front view shows width and height.
The top view shows width and depth.
The right side view shows depth and height.
Drawing an object as a set of flat views is called orthographic projection (or multiview drawing). Most objects need only three views. A flat plate may need only one or two.
2. Third-angle projection is used in Canada and the USA. The views always sit in the same places:
The top view goes directly above the front view.
The right side view goes directly to the right of the front view.
A simple way to remember it: each view sits on the side it was looked at from.
3. The views line up. The front and top views share the same width, so their left and right edges line up. The front and right side views share the same height, so their top and bottom edges line up. The top and right side views share the same depth. Thin lines that carry a point from one view to the next are called projection lines. A 45° mitre line turns depth in the top view into depth in the side view.
4. In the top view and the side view, the front of the object faces the front view. In the top view the front edge is at the bottom, next to the front view. In the right side view the front edge is on the left, next to the front view.
5. Three kinds of line do most of the work.
An object line (thick, solid) is an edge you can see.
A hidden line (thin, short dashes) is an edge you cannot see from that side, because it is behind or inside the object.
A centre line (thin, long and short dashes) marks the centre of a hole, a pipe or a round part.
6. First-angle projection puts the views on the other side. Much of Europe and Asia uses first-angle projection. The views look the same, but the top view goes below the front view and the right side view goes to the left. A drawing should show a projection symbol near the title block. It is a cone drawn in two views. In the third-angle symbol the narrow end of the cone points at the circles. In the first-angle symbol it points away from them.
7. Read one feature at a time. Pick a line in one view. Follow the projection lines to find the same feature in the other two views. One view alone can fool you. A line in the front view could be a step, a groove or the edge of a hole. The other views tell you which.
Figure 1. A notched wood block (fictional), 150 mm wide, 90 mm deep and 100 mm high. The top view is above the front view, and the right side view is to the right. Dotted projection lines and the 45° mitre line link the views. The step at the top right shows as object lines. A groove in the back face shows as hidden lines in the front view and the side view.
Figure 2. The same step block in third-angle projection (left) and first-angle projection (right). The shapes of the views do not change. Only their places change. The projection symbol tells you which method was used.
Worked example 1: find a hole in all three views
Figure 3 shows a bracket cut from steel angle. It is 100 mm long. Both legs are 75 mm and the steel is 10 mm thick. One hole, Ø18 (18 mm across), goes through the upright leg. Its centre is 50 mm from the left end and 45 mm above the bottom.
Figure 3. Steel angle bracket with one Ø18 hole, shown as a pictorial and in three views. The front view shows the hole as a circle with centre lines. The top view and the right side view show it as two hidden lines with a centre line.
Question: Where does the hole show in each view, and why?
Front view. You look straight at the face with the hole. You see a circle. Centre lines cross at its centre.
Top view. You look down on the top edge of the upright leg. That edge is the strip 10 mm deep at the back of the view. The hole runs through the leg, under that strip, so you cannot see it. It shows as two hidden lines 18 mm apart, one on each side of a centre line.
Right side view. You look at the end of the angle. The upright leg is on the right of this view, because it is at the back of the object and the front of the object faces the front view. The hole is inside the leg, so it shows as two hidden lines across the leg.
Each hidden line is half the hole size from the centre: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 mm. So the lines are at 45 − 9 = 36 mm and 45 + 9 = 54 mm above the bottom.
Answer: a circle in the front view, and two hidden lines (with a centre line) in the top view and the right side view. The hidden lines in the side view are 36 mm and 54 mm above the bottom.
Worked example 2: read a pipe tee
Figure 4 shows a pipe tee. The straight part is the run. The part that goes up is the branch. The outside diameter (OD) is 60 mm and the inside, or bore, is 50 mm.
Figure 4. An equal pipe tee in three views. In the front view the branch rises from the middle of the run. In the top view you look down into the branch and see two circles. In the right side view you look into the open end of the run and see two circles, with the branch above. Dashed lines show the bore.
Question: Which way does the branch point, and how thick is the pipe wall?
In the front view the branch goes up from the run. The top view shows two circles in the middle. Two circles mean you are looking straight into a round opening. So the branch opening faces up.
The right side view shows two circles for the end of the run, and the branch above it. This agrees with step 1.
The wall thickness is half the difference between OD and bore: (60 − 50) ÷ 2 = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 mm. Do the subtraction in the brackets first (BEDMAS).
Answer: the branch points up, and the wall is 5 mm thick.
Practice
Figure 5. Three blocks (A, B and C) shown as pictorials, and three sets of views (1, 2 and 3) in third-angle projection. The sets of views are in a different order from the blocks.
Figure 6. Grid exercise. The front view and the top view of a notched wood sill block are drawn on a grid. One square is 25 mm. The right side view is missing.
Task 1 (level 1) Use Figure 1. a) Which view is directly above the front view? b) Which view is directly to the right of the front view? c) Which projection method is this, and how can you tell from the symbol?
Task 2 (level 1) Use Figure 1. Name the size (width, height or depth) that each pair of views shares. a) Front view and top view b) Front view and right side view c) Top view and right side view
Task 3 (level 1) Use Figure 1. a) What kind of line shows the groove in the front view? b) Why is it drawn that way? c) In which view can you see the groove as object lines?
Task 4 (level 2) The notched block in Figure 1 is 150 mm wide, 90 mm deep and 100 mm high. A carpenter wants to check the step at the top right before cutting. a) In which two views can you see the height of the step? b) In which view can you see the width of the groove as object lines? c) The groove is at the back. In the right side view, is it on the left or the right? Explain using Key idea 4.
Task 5 (level 2) Use Figure 3 and Worked example 1. An ironworker is checking the bracket before welding. a) How long is the bracket, and how thick is the steel? b) In the top view, how far apart are the two hidden lines? c) Why does the hole show as a circle in only one of the three views?
Task 6 (level 2) Use Figure 5. Match each block (A, B and C) to its set of views (1, 2 or 3). For each match, name one line or shape that helped you decide.
Task 7 (level 2) Use Figure 2. A shop drawing for a pump base comes from a supplier in Germany (fictional). The top view is drawn below the front view. a) Which projection method was used? b) What should the projection symbol look like? c) What could go wrong if a fabricator read it as third-angle?
Task 8 (level 2) Use Figure 4. A plumber is checking a tee on a drawing. a) In which view do you look straight into the branch? b) What do the dashed lines in the front view show? c) A reducing tee has a run with a 60 mm OD and a 48 mm bore. How thick is the wall?
Task 9 (level 3) Use Figure 6. The block is 6 squares wide, 4 squares deep and 4 squares high. a) Give the width, depth and height in millimetres. b) The front view has a line across it, and the top view has a hidden line. Explain what shape makes these two lines. c) Sketch the right side view on grid paper, in the right place. Use projection lines from the front view.
Task 10 (level 3) A helper on a welding crew (fictional) sketched the right side view of the bracket in Figure 3. The sketch shows the upright leg on the left side of the view. Is the sketch right? Explain the rule you used, and say what could happen in the shop if nobody caught it.
Task 11 (level 3) Your foreman asks you to text a co-worker how to cut the notched block in Figure 1 from a solid piece 150 mm wide, 90 mm deep and 100 mm high. Use the views and the sizes below. Write the instructions in short steps. Say where each cut is, how big it is, and which face it is on.
