Groove: 20 mm wide and 20 mm deep, in the back face, starting 40 mm from the left end, the full height of the block.
Check yourself
In third-angle projection, where does the top view go? Where does the right side view go?
Which two sizes does a front view show?
What does a hidden line look like, and what does it mean?
In the top view, which edge of the object is next to the front view?
How can you tell a first-angle drawing from a third-angle drawing?

lessons.title: Pictorial drawings: isometric, oblique and perspective
lessons.text:
Tell isometric, oblique and perspective drawings apart, know which lines you can measure on each, read a single-line piping isometric, and sketch an object on isometric grid paper.
Why this matters on the job
A pictorial drawing shows an object in 3D, in one picture. It is easier to understand at a glance than a set of flat views. Pipefitters work from piping isometrics every day. Welders and carpenters sketch parts in oblique to show a co-worker what they mean. Builders show customers a perspective rendering of a new house or deck. Each kind has its own rules. You need to know which lines you can measure and which you cannot. In Reading lesson 11 you read flat views. This lesson turns flat views into pictures and back.
Key ideas
1. Isometric drawing. Height is drawn vertical. Width and depth go up and away at 30° from horizontal, one to the left and one to the right. The three axes are 120° apart. You can see this at the top front corner of a box: one edge goes straight down and the other two go up at 30°, and each pair is 120° apart. In an isometric drawing, lengths along the three axes are drawn at full size (or at the drawing scale).
2. Isometric lines and non-isometric lines. A line parallel to one of the three axes is an isometric line. You can measure it. A sloped line that is not parallel to an axis is a non-isometric line. It is drawn too long or too short, so you cannot measure it. To draw it, find its two end points along isometric lines, then join them.
3. Circles become ellipses in isometric. A round hole or pipe end on any face of an isometric drawing is drawn as an ellipse.
4. Oblique drawing. The front face is drawn true shape, just like a front view. Depth goes back at an angle, most often 45°.
Cavalier oblique: depth drawn at full length.
Cabinet oblique: depth drawn at half length. It looks less stretched. Furniture and cabinet makers use it.
Because the front face is true shape, a circle on the front face stays a true circle. That makes oblique quick for shop sketches. Put the face with the holes or curves at the front.
5. Perspective drawing. Perspective looks the most real. Lines that go away from you get closer together and meet at a vanishing point (VP). The vanishing points sit on the horizon line (HL), which is at the viewer's eye level.
One-point perspective: you look straight at one face. Receding lines meet at one VP.
Two-point perspective: you look at a corner. Horizontal edges go to two VPs on the horizon line. Vertical edges stay vertical.
Things farther away are drawn smaller, so you cannot measure a perspective drawing.
6. Which one is used where.
Isometric: piping drawings, assembly sketches and grid-paper sketches. Piping isometrics are drawn with a single line for the pipe and are not to scale. They carry written dimensions.
Oblique: quick shop sketches of a part with holes or curves on one face.
Perspective: renderings that show a customer what the finished job will look like.
Figure 1. One pipe support block, 80 mm wide, 60 mm deep and 50 mm high, with a Ø30 hole from front to back, drawn three ways. In the isometric drawing the hole is an ellipse. In the two oblique drawings the front face is true shape, so the hole is a true circle. The cavalier drawing shows the depth at full length. The cabinet drawing shows it at half length.
Figure 2. Left: the isometric axes. Height is vertical. Width and depth are at 30° from horizontal. The axes are 120° apart. Right: a block 80 mm wide and 60 mm deep, 20 mm high at the front and 50 mm high at the back. The bottom front edge is an isometric line. The sloped edge on the right face (in red) is a non-isometric line.
Figure 3. A cube in isometric with a circle drawn on the top, the front and the right side. Each circle shows as an ellipse.
Figure 4. Left: one-point perspective of a box seen straight on. Its front face is a true rectangle and its receding edges meet at one vanishing point (VP) on the horizon line (HL). Right: two-point perspective of a shed seen from a corner, with a door on the right wall. Its horizontal edges meet at two vanishing points on the horizon line. Its vertical edges stay vertical.
Worked example 1: why you cannot measure a sloped line in isometric
Question: In Figure 2, the sloped edge on the right face goes from 20 mm high at the front to 50 mm high at the back, over a depth of 60 mm. How long is it really, and how long is it drawn in a full-size isometric?
The real edge is the long side of a right triangle. One side is the depth, 60 mm. The other side is the rise, 50 − 20 = 30 mm.
Real length = √(60² + 30²) = √(3600 + 900) = √4500 = 67.08 mm, about 67 mm.
On the isometric drawing, the 60 mm depth goes up and across at 30°, and the 30 mm rise goes straight up. Worked out on the drawing, the line comes out about 79 mm long.
The drawn line is about 12 mm too long.
Answer: about 67 mm in real life, but about 79 mm on the drawing. Only lines along the three axes can be measured. To draw the sloped edge, mark 20 mm up at the front and 50 mm up at the back, then join the two points.
Figure 5. A single-line piping isometric, ISO-101 (fictional), not to scale. Starting at a flange, the pipe rises 1200, runs east 2400 to a tee, runs east another 1500, drops 600, then runs north 1800 to a flange. A gate valve is on the first east run. The tee branch runs north 900 to a cap. The north arrow points up and to the right. Dimensions are in millimetres to pipe centre lines.
Worked example 2: read a piping isometric
Question: Using Figure 5, how much pipe (centre line length) is in the main run, and how many elbows are there?
Find the north arrow. North is up and to the right. So east is down and to the right, and vertical lines are up or down.
Follow the pipe from START: up 1200, east 2400 (through the valve to the tee), east 1500, down 600, north 1800 to END.
Add the main run: 1200 + 2400 + 1500 + 600 + 1800 = 7500 mm = 7.5 m.
Count the changes of direction on the main run: up to east, east to down, down to north. That is 3 elbows. The tee is where the branch leaves. It is not an elbow.
Answer: 7500 mm of pipe in the main run, with 3 elbows. Real fitters take off allowances for fittings. The centre line total is the starting point.
Worked example 3: cabinet oblique at a scale
Question: A cabinetmaker sketches a base cabinet 900 mm wide, 750 mm high and 600 mm deep in cabinet oblique at a scale of 1:10. How long is each line on the paper?
At 1:10, divide each real size by 10.
Width: 900 ÷ 10 = 90 mm. Height: 750 ÷ 10 = 75 mm. These form the true-shape front face.
Depth: cabinet oblique uses half depth. 600 ÷ 2 = 300 mm, then 300 ÷ 10 = 30 mm, drawn back at 45°.
Answer: a 90 mm by 75 mm front rectangle, with 30 mm depth lines at 45°.
Practice
Figure 6. Grid exercise. Left: the front, top and right side views of a step block on a square grid (third-angle projection). The block is 8 squares wide, 5 deep and 6 high. A step 3 squares wide and 3 squares down is cut from the top right. Right: isometric grid paper with a red dot at the front left bottom corner.
Task 1 (level 1) Use Figure 1. a) In which drawings is the hole a true circle? b) Why is it a true circle in those drawings? c) What shape is the hole in the isometric drawing?
Task 2 (level 1) Use Figure 2. a) At what angle from horizontal are the width and depth axes drawn? b) How many degrees apart are the three axes? c) Which axis is drawn straight up?
Task 3 (level 1) Use Figure 4. a) What do the letters HL and VP stand for? b) How many vanishing points does each drawing have? c) In the two-point drawing, what happens to the vertical edges?
Task 4 (level 2) The block in Figure 1 is 60 mm deep. All three drawings are full size. a) How long is the depth line in the cavalier drawing? b) How long is it in the cabinet drawing? c) A welder wants to sketch a 600 mm deep tool cart so it does not look stretched. Which kind of oblique should they use, and how long is the depth line at full size?
Task 5 (level 2) Use Figure 2. You have a full-size isometric drawing of the sloped block and a ruler. a) Can you measure the 80 mm bottom front edge? Why? b) Can you measure the 50 mm height at the back corner? Why? c) Can you measure the sloped edge? Why?
Task 6 (level 2) Use Figure 5. A pipefitter is walking the line. Starting at START, list each run of the main line in order. For each run, give the direction (up, down, north, south, east or west) and the length.
Task 7 (level 2) Use Figure 5. a) How many tees and how many valves are on the drawing? b) What is the total centre line length of pipe, main run plus branch, in millimetres and in metres? c) What does the note NOT TO SCALE tell you?
Task 8 (level 2) Pick the best kind of pictorial drawing for each job: isometric, oblique or perspective. Give one reason for each. a) A welder sketches a steel base plate with four bolt holes on its face. b) A homeowner wants to see what a new deck will look like from the yard. c) A pipefitter needs the route of a pipe spool with every elbow and dimension. d) A carpenter sketches a cabinet on grid paper and wants to show all three sizes with no stretching.
Task 9 (level 3) Use Figure 6. Sketch the step block on isometric grid paper. Start at the red dot. Use one grid step for each square. Draw the three box edges first (width 8, depth 5, height 6), then cut away the step. Do not draw hidden edges.
Task 10 (level 3) On a photocopy of ISO-101, the 1800 dimension is smudged. A helper measures the north run on the paper with a tape, compares it with the 2400 run, and says, "It's about 1800, close enough." Is this a safe way to get the length? Explain why or why not, and say what you would do.
Task 11 (level 3) A framer is handed only the two-point perspective of the shed in Figure 4 and asked to cut the door header. Explain why the framer cannot get sizes from this drawing. Name the kind of drawing they need instead, and say what it should show.
Check yourself
In an isometric drawing, which lines can you measure?
What happens to a circle on the face of an isometric drawing?
What is the difference between cavalier and cabinet oblique?
Where are the vanishing points in a perspective drawing?
Why is a piping isometric not drawn to scale, and where do you get the lengths?

lessons.title: The alphabet of lines and reading dimensions
lessons.text:
Name each kind of line on a drawing and what it means, read feet-and-inch and millimetre dimensions, and add up chain and baseline dimension strings to find a missing size.
Why this matters on the job
Every line on a drawing means something. A thick line is an edge you can see. A dashed line is an edge you cannot see. A thin line with arrows is a size. If you mix them up, you can drill a hole that is not there or cut a part to the wrong length. Most of the numbers you build from are in dimension strings: rows of sizes that add up to an overall size. Checking that a string adds up is one of the quickest ways to catch a mistake before it is built. This lesson follows Reading lesson 11 (views) and Reading lesson 12 (pictorial drawings).
Key ideas
1. The alphabet of lines. Drawings use a standard set of lines so that everyone reads them the same way. Each line has a pattern and a weight (thick or thin). See Figure 1.
Object line (thick, solid): an edge you can see.
Hidden line (thin, short dashes): an edge you cannot see from that side.
Centre line (thin, long and short dashes): the centre of a hole, pipe or round part, or a line of symmetry.
Dimension line (thin, arrowhead at each end): shows the distance that a size applies to.
Extension line (thin): carries an edge out to the dimension line. It starts with a small gap from the object and runs a little past the dimension line.
Leader (thin, one arrowhead): points to a feature and carries a note, such as "Ø14 2 HOLES".
Cutting-plane line (thick, a long dash and two short dashes): shows where a part is cut to make a section view. The arrows show which way you look.
Section lines (thin, usually at 45°): fill the cut surface in a section view. Lesson 15 covers them.
Break lines: show that a long part has been shortened to fit the sheet. A long break is thin with a zigzag. A short break is thick and wavy.
Phantom line (thin, a long dash and two short dashes): shows a part next to the one being drawn, or another position of a moving part.
2. Line weights. Thick lines are about twice as wide as thin lines. The ASME Y14.2 standard uses at least 0.6 mm for thick lines and 0.3 mm for thin lines. Thick lines jump out first: the object and where it is cut.
3. A break does not change the size. When a long part is drawn with break lines, the written dimension still gives the full real length.
4. Feet and inches. On construction drawings, imperial sizes are written in feet and inches with a dash between them: 12'-6" is twelve feet six inches. Zero feet is still written: 0'-9". Fractions of an inch follow the inches: 3'-4 1/2".
5. Millimetres. Metric construction and shop drawings give sizes in millimetres with no unit after the number: 2400 means 2400 mm. The drawing should have a note that says dimensions are in millimetres.
6. Chain dimensions run from one feature to the next, like links in a chain. Add the links to get a distance from the end. Baseline dimensions all start from the same line (the baseline or datum), such as one end of a wall. Each one is a distance from that line.
7. Dimension strings add up. The sizes in a chain should add up to the overall dimension. If one size is left out, you can find it: overall minus the sum of the others. If a string does not add up, do not guess. Ask in writing.
Figure 1. The alphabet of lines, with a sample of each line, its name and its weight (thick or thin).
Figure 2. A steel gate hinge strap (fictional), 1200 mm long, 75 mm wide and 10 mm thick, with two Ø14 holes, 40 mm from each end. The top view is at the top and the front view is below it. Break lines leave out the middle of the strap. A phantom line shows the gate post. A cutting-plane line A-A passes through the right hole, and SECTION A-A is drawn at the right. Blue numbered bubbles 1 to 10 point to ten different kinds of line.
Figure 3. The parts of a dimension: extension lines with a small gap at the object, a dimension line with arrowheads, the number in feet and inches, and a leader with a note.
Worked example 1: check a chain against the overall
Figure 4. A sill plate 20'-6" long with four anchor bolts, dimensioned two ways. Above the plate, chain dimensions run 1'-0", 5'-0", 6'-0", 6'-0" and 2'-6", with an overall of 20'-6". Below the plate, baseline dimensions all start at the left end: 1'-0", 6'-0", 12'-0", 18'-0" and 20'-6".
Question: Do the chain dimensions in Figure 4 add up to the overall 20'-6"?
Add the feet: 1 + 5 + 6 + 6 + 2 = 20 feet.
Add the inches: 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 6 = 6 inches.
Total: 20'-6". It matches the overall dimension.
Answer: yes. Check with the baseline dimensions too. The last bolt is 18'-0" from the left end, and 18'-0" + 2'-6" = 20'-6".
Worked example 2: add feet and inches with a carry
Question: A carpenter adds two sizes from a drawing: 3'-8 1/2" and 4'-6 3/4". What is the total?
Add the feet: 3 + 4 = 7 feet.
Add the inches: 8 1/2 + 6 3/4 = 15 1/4 inches.
15 1/4 inches is more than a foot. 15 1/4 − 12 = 3 1/4. Carry 1 foot.
Total: 7 + 1 = 8 feet and 3 1/4 inches.
Answer: 8'-3 1/4".
Worked example 3: find a missing metric dimension
Figure 5. Plan of a 7200 mm wall with a window W1 and a door D1. The dimension string reads 900, 1200, X, 900, 2400. The overall dimension is 7200. Dimensions are in millimetres.
Question: How long is the wall section marked X in Figure 5?
Add the sizes you know: 900 + 1200 + 900 + 2400 = 5400.
Take that from the overall: 7200 − 5400 = 1800.
Check: 900 + 1200 + 1800 + 900 + 2400 = 7200. It adds up.
Answer: X = 1800 mm.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Figure 1. a) Name the three thick lines. b) Which line shows an edge you cannot see? c) Which line shows a part next to the one being drawn?
Task 2 (level 1) Use Figure 2. Name the kind of line that each blue bubble (1 to 10) points to.
Task 3 (level 1) Write each size the way it appears on a construction drawing. a) twelve feet six inches b) nine inches c) three feet four and a half inches d) two thousand four hundred millimetres, on a metric drawing
Task 4 (level 2) Use Figure 2. A welder is laying out the hinge strap. a) The middle of the strap is not drawn. How long is the real strap? How do you know? b) How far apart are the centres of the two holes? c) What does "Ø14 2 HOLES" tell the welder?
Task 5 (level 2) Use Figure 2. a) Which way do you look to see SECTION A-A? How do you know? b) Why is there a gap in the middle of the hatching in SECTION A-A? c) Why is the gate post drawn with a phantom line instead of an object line?
Task 6 (level 2) Use Figure 4. A carpenter is marking anchor bolt holes on a sill plate. a) Using only the chain dimensions, how far is the third bolt from the left end? b) Check your answer with the baseline dimensions. c) Using only the baseline dimensions, how far apart are bolt 3 and bolt 4?
Task 7 (level 2) Use Figure 5. a) Find X. b) How far is it from the left end of the wall to the left side of door D1? c) How wide is the window opening W1?
Task 8 (level 2) A framing elevation has this chain string along a wall: 2'-3 1/2", 3'-0", 5'-10 1/2", 4'-8". The overall dimension is 15'-10". Does the string add up? Show your work.
Task 9 (level 3) A concrete slab drawing (metric) shows a chain string of 1500, 2750, 3000, 1250 and an overall dimension of 8600. Does it add up? If not, by how much is it out, and what should the form setter do before setting forms?
Task 10 (level 3) An apprentice lays out the four anchor bolts in Figure 4 by measuring each chain dimension from the last mark. Each mark ends up 3 mm too long. a) How far off is the last bolt? b) Another apprentice hooks the tape on the left end once and marks each bolt from the baseline dimensions. Each mark is off by up to 3 mm. How far off can the last bolt be? c) Which method is better for anchor bolts that must line up with holes in a steel base plate? Explain.
Task 11 (level 3) A shop drawing from one supplier says a panel is 2400 (metric drawing). A drawing from another supplier says 8'-0". A co-worker says, "Same thing." Work out 8'-0" in millimetres (1 inch = 25.4 mm). Is your co-worker right? What would you say before anything is ordered?
Check yourself
What does a thin dashed line mean on a drawing?
Which lines are drawn thick?
A drawing shortens a 6 m beam with break lines. Which do you trust, the drawn length or the written dimension?
How is four feet and zero inches written on a drawing?
A chain string does not add up to the overall dimension. What do you do?

lessons.title: Drawing scales and the scale rule
lessons.text:
Read imperial architectural scales, engineer's scales and metric ratio scales, use a scale rule, change a measured drawing length into a real size and back, and know when a drawing must not be scaled.
Why this matters on the job
A house does not fit on a sheet of paper, so it is drawn smaller, to scale. On site you need to know what scale a drawing uses, how to read a scale rule, and how to turn a length on paper into a real length. You also need to know when not to measure a drawing. Prints shrink, copies get resized, and a dimension can be changed without the line being redrawn. A carpenter who scales a reduced copy can be off by a metre. Reading lesson 5 introduced "Scale 1:50" and the note "Do not scale this drawing". This lesson goes deeper.
Key ideas
1. What a scale is. A scale compares a length on the drawing with the real length. It is written in the title block, or under the title of a view. One sheet can have more than one scale. A detail is often drawn bigger than the plan.
2. Imperial architectural scales. These are written as a length on paper equals one foot: 1/4" = 1'-0" means every 1/4 inch on the paper stands for 1 foot in real life. Common architectural scales are 1/8" = 1'-0", 3/16" = 1'-0", 1/4" = 1'-0", 1/2" = 1'-0", 3/4" = 1'-0", 1 1/2" = 1'-0" and 3" = 1'-0". The bigger the fraction, the bigger the drawing. Plans are often 1/4" or 1/8". Details are often 3/4", 1 1/2" or 3".
3. Change paper inches to real feet. Divide the measured inches by the scale fraction. That is the same as multiplying by a number:
Scale Multiply paper inches by Ratio
1/8" = 1'-0" 8 1:96
3/16" = 1'-0" 16/3 1:64
1/4" = 1'-0" 4 1:48
1/2" = 1'-0" 2 1:24
3/4" = 1'-0" 4/3 1:16
1 1/2" = 1'-0" 2/3 1:8
3" = 1'-0" 1/3 1:4
The answer is in feet. To go the other way (real feet to paper inches), multiply the feet by the scale fraction.
4. The architect's scale rule. It has three sides and six edges. Most edges carry two scales that read in opposite directions, such as 1/8 from one end and 1/4 from the other. The zero is not at the very end. Past the zero is one foot cut into inches. To measure: put a whole-foot mark on one end of the line, so the other end falls in the inch part past zero. Read feet, then inches.
5. Engineer's scale (civil scale). It divides an inch into 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 60 parts. It is used for site plans, roads and water mains, with scales such as 1" = 20' or 1" = 50'. Lengths are in feet and tenths of a foot, not feet and inches.
6. Metric ratio scales. 1:50 means 1 mm on paper stands for 50 mm in real life. Common metric scales are 1:200 or 1:500 for site plans, 1:100 and 1:50 for plans, 1:20 for wall sections, and 1:10, 1:5 or 1:1 for details.
Real size = paper length × the scale number.
Paper length = real size ÷ the scale number.
A metric scale rule has one ratio on each edge. It reads real lengths straight off, in metres.
7. Scale bars and NTS. A scale bar (graphic scale) is a small ruler printed on the sheet. If the print is copied bigger or smaller, the bar changes size with the drawing, so it stays right. The written scale does not. NTS means "not to scale". Never measure an NTS drawing.
8. Written dimensions win. If a dimension is written, use it. Do not measure the drawing. Copies can shrink, paper can stretch, and a changed dimension may not have been redrawn. Scale a drawing only when no dimension is given or for a rough check. Treat the answer as approximate, use the scale bar if you can, and confirm it before you cut, drill or pour anything.
Figure 1. The 1/4" = 1'-0" edge of an architect's scale, enlarged. Zero is near the right end. Feet are numbered to the left of zero, every 2 feet. To the right of zero, one foot is cut into 12 inches. A wall on a drawing has its left end on the 13 mark and its right end on the 6-inch mark. It reads 13'-6".
Figure 2. Two edges of a metric scale rule, enlarged. The 1:50 edge reads 0 to 3 m. The 1:100 edge reads 0 to 6 m. A line 47 mm long on the paper reads 2.35 m at 1:50 and 4.7 m at 1:100.
Worked example 1: paper to real, imperial
Question: On a floor plan at 1/4" = 1'-0", a wall measures 3 3/8" with a ruler. How long is the wall? Then check it on the scale rule (Figure 1).
At 1/4" = 1'-0", multiply paper inches by 4.
3 3/8 × 4 = 13 1/2 feet. (3 × 4 = 12, and 3/8 × 4 = 1 1/2.)
1/2 foot = 6 inches. So 13 1/2 feet = 13'-6".
On the scale rule, the line runs from the 13 mark to 6 inches past zero. It reads 13'-6". The two methods agree.
Answer: 13'-6".
Worked example 2: real to paper, imperial
Question: A 22'-6" wall is drawn at 1/4" = 1'-0". How long is it on the paper?
22'-6" = 22 1/2 feet.
Paper length = feet × 1/4 = 22 1/2 × 1/4 = 5 5/8 inches.
Answer: 5 5/8" on the paper.
Worked example 3: metric both ways
Question: a) On a 1:50 plan a line measures 47 mm. How long is it in real life? b) A shed is 3600 mm by 2400 mm. How big is it on paper at 1:50 and at 1:100?
a) Real = 47 × 50 = 2350 mm (2.35 m). This matches the 1:50 edge in Figure 2.
b) At 1:50: 3600 ÷ 50 = 72 mm and 2400 ÷ 50 = 48 mm.
At 1:100: 3600 ÷ 100 = 36 mm and 2400 ÷ 100 = 24 mm. The 1:100 drawing is half as big.
Answer: a) 2350 mm. b) 72 mm by 48 mm at 1:50, 36 mm by 24 mm at 1:100.
Figure 3. The same shed plan, 3600 by 2400 mm, at 1:50 (left) and 1:100 (right). On paper it is 72 by 48 mm at 1:50 and 36 by 24 mm at 1:100. The dimensions written on both are the same.
Figure 4. Left: a sheet at the written scale 1:100 with a scale bar from 0 to 5 m. Right: the same sheet copied at 70%. Everything shrinks, including the scale bar. The written scale still says 1:100, but it is now wrong. The scale bar still measures correctly.
Figure 5. Detail 4, marked NTS. The landing is dimensioned 1200 and the opening 3000, but the opening is drawn shorter than the landing. Build to the written dimensions.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) a) Where on a drawing do you find the scale? b) What does NTS mean? c) Can one sheet have more than one scale? Give an example.
Task 2 (level 1) a) What does 1/4" = 1'-0" mean in your own words? b) Which drawing of the same house is bigger on paper: 1/8" = 1'-0" or 1/4" = 1'-0"? c) Which is bigger on paper: 1:50 or 1:100?
Task 3 (level 1) Use Figure 1. a) Where is the zero on this edge? b) Which way do the feet numbers count from zero? c) What is the small section to the right of zero for?
Task 4 (level 2) A framer measures a wall on a plan drawn at 1/4" = 1'-0". It is 5 5/8" long on the paper. How long is the real wall? Give your answer in feet and inches.
Task 5 (level 2) Find the real size. Give each answer in feet and inches. a) A stair section at 1/2" = 1'-0". A line measures 5 3/4". b) A cabinet detail at 3/4" = 1'-0". A line measures 2 1/4". c) A trim detail at 3" = 1'-0". A line measures 7 1/2".
Task 6 (level 2) A drafter is drawing metric details. How long is each line on the paper? a) A wall section at 1:20. The wall is 1150 mm high. b) A flashing detail at 1:5. The flashing leg is 140 mm long. c) A plan at 1:100. A room is 4200 mm long.
Task 7 (level 2) a) A site plan is drawn at 1" = 20'. An excavator operator measures a trench route at 3.4". How long is the trench? b) A metric site plan is at 1:100. A line measures 85 mm. How long is it in millimetres and in metres?
Task 8 (level 2) Use Figure 4. A plan is drawn at 1:50 on a large sheet. The office prints a half-size copy for the site. A helper measures a wall on the copy at 30 mm and says, "30 × 50 = 1500 mm." a) What is the real length? b) What should the helper have used instead of the written scale?
Task 9 (level 3) Use Figure 5. A carpenter lays a ruler on Detail 4 and sees the opening is drawn shorter than the landing. She thinks the 3000 dimension is a typing mistake. a) What does NTS tell her? b) Which size should she build to? c) If she still thinks something is wrong, what should she do?
Task 10 (level 3) An electrician needs to place a ceiling light. The 1:50 plan shows the light but gives no dimension to it. The light measures 63 mm from the north wall on the plan. a) About how far from the wall is the light? b) Is it OK to scale the drawing here? Explain. c) What should the electrician do before cutting the hole in the ceiling?
Task 11 (level 3) You must draw a deck 4800 mm by 3600 mm in a space on the sheet that is 150 mm by 100 mm. a) Will it fit at 1:20? Show your work. b) Will it fit at 1:50? Show your work. c) A different deck is 16'-0" by 12'-0". Will it fit at 1/4" = 1'-0" in a space 6" by 4"?
Check yourself
At 1:100, how many millimetres in real life does 1 mm on the paper stand for?
At 1/8" = 1'-0", what do you multiply paper inches by to get feet?
On an architect's scale, where are the inch marks?
Why does a scale bar stay right on a reduced copy when the written scale does not?
A dimension is written on the drawing, but your scaled measurement is different. Which do you use?

lessons.title: Sections, details and callouts
lessons.text:
Read cutting-plane lines and section views, name common material hatch patterns, and follow section marks and detail callouts from one sheet to another.
Why this matters on the job
Plans and elevations show the outside of things. To see how a wall, a footing or a pipe fitting is built inside, drawings cut through it and show the cut face. These cut views are called sections. Small, tricky areas, such as where a wall sits on a foundation, are drawn bigger as details. Small symbols on the drawings, called callouts, tell you which sheet to turn to. A drawing set can have hundreds of sheets. If you can follow a callout, you can find the one detail that answers your question. This lesson follows Reading lesson 13 (lines) and Reading lesson 14 (scales).
Key ideas
1. Cutting plane and section view. A cutting-plane line (thick, with a long dash and two short dashes) shows where the object is cut. The arrows at its ends show which way you look at the cut. The letters at the ends, such as A-A, name the section. The section view is labelled with the same letters, such as SECTION A-A.
2. Section lines (hatching). In a section view, the surfaces the cut passes through are filled with thin lines or a pattern. Holes and empty spaces are left blank. Edges you see beyond the cut are drawn as object lines. Hidden lines are usually not needed.
3. Kinds of section.
Full section: the cut goes all the way through the object.
Half section: one quarter of the object is cut away. Half the view shows the outside and half shows the inside. It is used for round, matching parts such as bushings and flanges.
Broken-out section: only a small area is cut open, bounded by a thick, wavy break line. It shows one feature, such as a drilled hole, without cutting the whole part.
4. Material hatch patterns. On building drawings, the pattern tells you the material. Common ones are concrete (dots and small triangles), earth, gravel, brick (45° lines), concrete block, wood framing cut across the grain (a box with an X), finish wood, steel, batt insulation (a looping line) and rigid insulation (a crosshatch). Patterns are not the same in every office. Always check the legend of the drawing set.
5. Section marks. On a plan, a section is shown by a cut line with a bubble at the end. The bubble is split by a line. The top number is the section number. The bottom is the sheet it is drawn on. 1 over A-301 means section 1 on sheet A-301. A solid triangle on the bubble points the way you look.
6. Detail callouts. A circle or box drawn around an area, with a bubble such as 3 over A-501, means that area is drawn bigger as detail 3 on sheet A-501. Elevation markers use the same kind of bubble, with a triangle pointing at the wall that is shown.
7. Drawing titles close the loop. Under each section or detail is a title with the same bubble, its name and its scale. When you arrive at sheet A-501, look for the title bubble 3 over A-501. Details are drawn at a bigger scale (such as 1:5 or 3" = 1'-0") so small parts can be read.
8. Sheet numbers. The letter at the front of a sheet number often tells you the discipline, such as A for architectural or S for structural. The number tells you where the sheet sits in the set. Real drawing sets are covered in Reading lesson 16.
Figure 1. Section views of a flanged steel bushing. Top left: the top view, with cutting-plane line A-A through the middle and arrows pointing up (toward the back). Bottom left: SECTION A-A, a full section, with the cut steel hatched and the bore and two bolt holes left blank. Top right: a half section, with the outside on the left half and the cut on the right half. Bottom right: a steel shaft with a broken-out section at one end showing a drilled hole.
Figure 2. Common material symbols in section. Concrete: dots and small triangles. Earth: short strokes in clusters. Gravel: small open circles. Brick masonry: 45° lines. Concrete block: diagonal lines with dots. Wood framing cut across the grain: a box with a diagonal cross. Finish wood: wavy grain lines. Steel or general use: close diagonal lines. Batt insulation: a looping line. Rigid insulation: a crosshatch.
Worked example 1: read a section view
Question: In Figure 1, the bushing flange is 100 mm across, the hub is 60 mm across, and the bore is 30 mm across. How thick is the hub wall, and why are there blank gaps in the flange in SECTION A-A?
The cutting-plane line goes straight through the centre, so the section shows the full width of each part.
Hub wall thickness = (hub diameter − bore) ÷ 2 = (60 − 30) ÷ 2 = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 mm. Brackets first (BEDMAS).
In the top view, the cutting-plane line passes through the two small bolt holes. A hole has no steel to cut, so in the section it is left blank. The lines across the top and bottom of each gap are the far side of the hole.
Answer: the hub wall is 15 mm thick. The gaps are the two bolt holes, cut through their centres.
Figure 3. Wall section 1 on sheet A-301 (fictional, for reading practice), scale 1:20. Letters A to F mark hatched areas. A: dots and small triangles, in the footing, the foundation wall and the floor slab. B: short strokes in clusters, outside the foundation. C: small open circles, under the slab. D: a crosshatch, under the slab and on the inside face of the foundation wall. E: a box with a diagonal cross, on top of the foundation wall. F: a looping line, in the wall cavity. A detail callout circle around the sill area points to a bubble reading 3 over A-501.
Figure 4. Reference symbols. 1: a section mark with a bubble reading 1 over A-301 and a triangle showing the viewing direction. 2: a detail callout, a dashed circle with a bubble reading 3 over A-501. 3: an elevation marker reading 2 over A-201, with a triangle pointing at the wall to be shown. 4: an interior elevation marker with four triangles, numbered 1 to 4, on sheet A-401. 5: a drawing title: bubble 3 over A-501, SILL DETAIL, SCALE 1:5.
Figure 5. Three sheets that point to each other. A-101 (floor plan, 1:50) has a section mark 1 over A-301 across an outside wall. A-301 (wall sections, 1:20) shows section 1, with a detail callout 3 over A-501 at the sill. A-501 (details, 1:5) shows detail 3, the sill, drawn larger.
Worked example 2: follow the callouts
Question: A carpenter on the floor plan (A-101) needs to know how the sill plate sits on the foundation wall. Where does she look?
On A-101, she finds the section mark on the outside wall. The bubble reads 1 over A-301.
She turns to sheet A-301 and finds the title bubble 1 over A-301: WALL SECTION, 1:20 (Figure 3).
On the wall section, the sill area is circled. The bubble reads 3 over A-501.
She turns to sheet A-501 and finds the title bubble 3 over A-501: SILL DETAIL, 1:5.
Answer: detail 3 on sheet A-501, reached from A-101 through section 1 on A-301.
Worked example 3: how much bigger is the detail?
Question: The wall section is at 1:20 and the sill detail is at 1:5. The sill plate is 38 mm thick. How thick is it drawn on each sheet, and how many times bigger is the detail?
At 1:20: 38 ÷ 20 = 1.9 mm on paper.
At 1:5: 38 ÷ 5 = 7.6 mm on paper.
20 ÷ 5 = 4. The detail is drawn 4 times bigger. Check: 1.9 × 4 = 7.6.
Answer: 1.9 mm on the wall section, 7.6 mm on the detail. The detail is 4 times bigger.

lessons.title: Title blocks, sheet sets and the drawing index
lessons.text:
Read the title block on a real sheet, find any sheet in a full drawing set with the drawing list, and check the issue, the revision and the date before you build.
Why this matters on the job
A building is not drawn on one sheet. It is drawn on a set of 50, 100 or 200 sheets, split up by trade. Before you can read a dimension, you have to find the right sheet. Then you have to be sure it is the latest one. A crew that builds from an old issue of a sheet builds the wrong thing, and the work gets torn out. The title block, the drawing list and the revision marks are how you find the right sheet and prove it is current.
This lesson uses three real drawing sets. You will see that every office does things a little differently.
Set What it is Stage and year Units Notes
London Square Mixed-use building: 2 levels of parking, shops, 2 office floors Issued for tender Imperial (feet and inches) A teaching set. Firm names on it, such as Athena Architecture Ltd., are made up (fictional).
leləm̓ Community Centre Two-storey community centre with a gym, University Endowment Lands, BC Issued for construction, 2022 Metric (millimetres) A full set from six consultants, drawn on a computer
Fire Hall No. 3 A Vancouver fire hall at 2801 Quebec Street Construction set, 1999 Metric Paper prints that were scanned. A past reader added check marks and notes.
Key ideas
1. A drawing set is a book of sheets, sorted by trade. Each trade's sheets start with a discipline letter.
Letter Discipline What you find there
A Architectural Floor plans, elevations, sections, doors, windows, finishes
S Structural Footings, columns, beams, slabs, rebar
M Mechanical Heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC). Some offices put plumbing and fire protection here too.
P Plumbing Fixtures, drains, vents, water piping
E Electrical Lighting, power, panels, fire alarm, communications
L Landscaping Planting, trees, paving, irrigation
C Civil Site grading, storm and sanitary services, roads
F or FP Fire protection Sprinklers, standpipes, fire department connections
The US National CAD Standard gives F to fire protection. Many offices still write FP. In all three sets in this lesson, fire protection sits inside the mechanical sheets. In leləm̓, plumbing does too (M2.00 to M2.03). London Square has its own P sheets.
2. Sheet numbers. A sheet number is the discipline letter plus a number, such as A-201. Many offices use the first digit for the kind of drawing: 1 for plans, 2 for elevations, 3 for sections, 5 for details, 6 for schedules. But every office has its own habit.
Kind of sheet London Square leləm̓ Fire Hall No. 3
Floor plans A-211 to A-251 A-201, A-202 A1-03 to A1-05
Elevations A-301, A-302 A-401, A-402 A2-01
Building sections A-401, A-402 A-501, A-502 A3-01
Door schedule A-901 A-081 A5-01
So A-401 is a section in London Square but an elevation in leləm̓. Never guess a sheet from its number. Look it up in the drawing list.
3. The cover sheet and drawing list. The first sheet of a set (or of each discipline) holds the drawing list, also called the drawing index or sheet list. It gives every sheet number and sheet name. It is the table of contents of the set.
4. The title block. Every sheet has a title block, usually down the right side or along the bottom. It tells you: - the project name and the firm that drew the sheet - the sheet title (what is on it) and the sheet number - the scale ("As indicated" means each view has its own scale under its title) - who drew and checked it, and the project number - the issue block or revision block, and often a plot date (when the file was printed)
5. Issues and revisions. Each time a sheet goes out, the issue block gets a new line: a number or letter, a date and a reason. Common reasons are "issued for building permit" (BP), "issued for tender" (IFT, for pricing), an addendum during tender, and "issued for construction" (IFC). Only build from the issue meant for construction.
When an area of a drawing changes, the drafter draws a wavy revision cloud around it. A small triangle called a delta sits beside the cloud. The number in the delta matches a line in the revision block. That line tells you when and why it changed.
6. Dates are written many ways. The three sets write dates like this: 2022.05.06, 21 11 26, Feb 10 14, Nov 8/99 and 08/11/99. A date such as 08/11/99 could mean August 11 or November 8. Read the other dates on the sheet to decide. When you write a date yourself, the safe all-number form in Canada is year-month-day, for example 2022-05-06.
7. General notes. General notes apply to the whole sheet or the whole set unless a note on the drawing says otherwise. They often tell you the units, how dimensions are measured, and not to scale the drawing.
8. How to find a sheet. 1. Decide which trade the question belongs to. 2. Open the drawing list. Find the sheet name that matches. 3. Go to that sheet. Check the sheet number in the title block. 4. Check the issue block. Is this the latest issue, and is it for construction? 5. Read the general notes on that sheet before you take a number from it.
Worked example
Question: In London Square, which sheet shows the Level 4 floor plan, and what is its latest issue?
A floor plan is architectural, so look in the Architectural Drawings list on the cover sheet A-100 (Figure 1).
The list shows A-241 FLOOR PLAN - LEVEL L3 & L4 OFFICE PLAN.
Go to A-241 (Figure 4). The title block says drawing number A-241 and sheet title "Floor plan - Level L3 & L4 office plan".
The revision block has three lines. The top line is the latest: C, Feb 10 14, issued for tender.
Answer: A-241. Its latest issue is C, issued for tender. That is a pricing issue, not a construction issue. Ask for the construction issue before you build from it.

Figure 7. Fire Hall No. 3, Volume III cover sheet, drawing list. The check marks and the hand-written M09 to M11 were on the print when it was scanned.

Practice

Which sheet is it on? d) An electrician wants the electrical floor plan for Levels 3 and 4. Which sheet?

What date? b) The E-000 list jumps from issue 7 to issue 9. What is missing? c) An electrician has an E-000 print marked issue 7. Can they build from it? Why or why not?

Note 4 says dimensions are measured to what? d) What does N.I.C. mean on the Fire Hall drawings?
Task 9 (level 3) You are a plumber pricing the Fire Hall job. You need the ground floor plumbing plan. Use Figure 7. a) Look at sheets M05 to M08. What problem do you see in the sheet names? b) Which floor seems to be missing from the plumbing names, and why can you not be sure from the list? c) What would you do before you order pipe and fittings?
Task 10 (level 3) The leləm̓ A-001 sheet (the sheet with the list in Figure 2) has 7 lines in its issue block: 1 to 4 are drafts and the building permit issue, 5 is 2021.12.10 Issued for Tender, 6 is 2022.02.15 Issued for BP Minor Amendment and 7 is 2022.05.06 Issued for IFC. Compare it with the A-201 issue block in Figure 3. a) Which issue does A-201 have that A-001 does not? Give its date and description. b) What does that tell you about each sheet's issue block? c) Why must you check the issue block on every sheet you use, not only on the cover sheet?
Task 11 (level 3) Use Figures 3 and 11 (leləm̓ A-201). a) What does the title block say for Scale and for Graphic Scale? b) Look at the whole sheet in Figure 11. Is a scale written under the plan? c) A labourer wants to measure the gym with a ruler on a half-size print. What would you tell them? Use the notes on the sheet in your answer.
Check yourself
What does the discipline letter at the start of a sheet number tell you?
Why should you look up a sheet in the drawing list instead of guessing from its number?
Name five things you can find in a title block.
What do a revision cloud and a delta tell you, and where do you read the reason for the change?
How do you write the date November 8, 1999 in all numbers?
Extra: what a CAD drawing is
Most drawing sets today are made on a computer with CAD (computer-aided design) software. AutoCAD is one common program. You do not need to use CAD to read the prints, but four CAD ideas explain things you will see on the sheets.
1. Drawn full size, printed to scale. In AutoCAD, the drafter draws in model space at full size (1:1), after deciding what one unit stands for, such as one millimetre. To print, they set up a layout in paper space with the title block and notes. On the layout, viewports show views of the full-size model, each at its own scale. That is how one sheet can show a plan at 1:100 and a detail at 1:20. Both views come from the same full-size drawing.
2. Layers. Every object is put on a layer, such as walls, doors or electrical wiring. Autodesk compares layers to clear plastic sheets. A layer can be turned off or frozen to hide everything on it. So two sheets made from the same file can show different things. If something you expect is missing from a print, it may be on a layer that was turned off. Ask before you assume it is not there.
3. Blocks. A block is a group of objects joined into one named object, such as a door symbol, a receptacle symbol or a title block. The drafter inserts the same block again and again. That is why every receptacle symbol on a set looks exactly the same.
4. External references (xrefs). An xref links one drawing file into another. For example, the architect's floor plan can be linked into the electrical drawing so the electrical engineer draws on top of the walls. Changes made to the linked file show up in the drawing when it is opened or the xref is reloaded. So a sheet can change because a file it links to changed. This is one more reason to build only from an issued sheet and to check its issue block.
Task 12 (level 2) a) A sheet shows a floor plan at 1:100 and a stair detail at 1:20. Did the drafter draw the stair twice, at two sizes? Explain with model space and layouts. b) An electrician's print shows the walls of a floor, but no doors. Which CAD idea could explain this? What should the electrician do? c) Every receptacle symbol on the electrical sheets looks exactly the same. Which CAD idea explains this? d) The architect moved a wall on Monday. On Tuesday, someone in the office prints an electrical sheet, and the wall is in its new place. The issue block on the print has not changed. Which CAD idea explains why the wall moved? Why must the electrician still build from the issued sheet?

lessons.title: Symbols, legends, grids and schedules
lessons.text:
Use grid lines, markers, tags, schedules and each trade's legend to look up what a symbol on a real sheet means, then follow it to the right table.
Why this matters on the job
A drawing is mostly symbols. A small circle with "C / A-502" in it sends you to another sheet. An oval with "119" in it is a door you will hang. A circle with two lines is a receptacle an electrician will rough in. None of these make sense until you look them up. Every set has a legend for its symbols and a list of its abbreviations, and they are not the same from job to job. Good tradespeople do not memorize every symbol. They know where to look it up.
This lesson uses real sheets from the same three sets as lesson 16: London Square (imperial teaching set), leləm̓ Community Centre (metric, 2022) and, through lesson 16, Fire Hall No. 3 (1999).
Key ideas
1. The legend is the dictionary for that set. Look for sheets with names like "Legends", "Symbols" or "Abbreviations", often the first sheet of each trade. In this lesson: - London Square A-100 has a drawing symbols legend and an abbreviation legend for the architectural sheets. - leləm̓ E-001 is the electrical symbol legend. M0.01 holds the mechanical legends: pipes, valves, plumbing, ducts, fire protection and abbreviations. - leləm̓ S200 has a small structural legend. S101 has the structural abbreviations. - Floor plans often have a small legend of their own, such as the fire rating legend on leləm̓ A-201.
2. Grid lines and grid bubbles. Long thin lines with a bubble at the end are grid lines. They run through the columns and main walls. One direction is numbered (1, 2, 3...) and the other is lettered (A, B, C...). Crews use them to say where something is: "the door near grid C-2". Dimension strings measure between grid lines, so grids are where layout starts.
3. North arrow. A north arrow shows which way north is on the sheet. Some sets show true north (on the earth) and project north (a direction picked to keep the drawing square on the page).
4. Markers that send you to another sheet. A circle split by a line holds two numbers: the view number on top and the sheet number below. So "C over A-502" means view C on sheet A-502. - A section marker sits at the end of a cut line. The solid triangle or arrow points the way you are looking. - A wall section marker works the same way, for a cut through one wall. - An elevation marker points at a wall to show which way the elevation looks. - A detail callout circles a small area and sends you to a bigger drawing of it.
5. Tags point to schedules. A tag is a small shape with a mark in it. - Room tag: room number (and often the name). - Door tag: door mark. Look it up in the door schedule. - Wall tag: wall type. Look it up in the wall assembly schedule. - Window tag: window type. Look it up in the window schedule. - Equipment or fixture tag: for example WC-1 or EF-1. Look it up in that trade's schedule.
The shape of each tag is set in the legend. It changes from office to office.
6. Schedules are tables. A schedule lists every item of one kind with its size, type and material. A door schedule lists each door mark. A room finish schedule lists each room's floor, base, wall and ceiling finish. A footing schedule lists footing sizes and rebar. A panel schedule lists each electrical circuit and its breaker. The tag on the plan is the key that opens the right row.
7. Trade symbols. Electrical plans use symbols for receptacles, switches and lights, plus a circuit label such as 2A:24 (panel 2A, circuit 24). Plumbing plans use fixture tags and line types for each kind of pipe. HVAC plans show ducts with their size and what air they carry. Structural plans use footing, column and wall marks.
8. Abbreviations change meaning. The same letters can mean different things in different trades, or even on the same sheet. Always read the abbreviation list for the trade you are working from. If something in the legend looks wrong, ask.
Worked example
Question: On leləm̓ A-201, what does the marker labelled B in Figure 3 mean, and where do you go next?
Look at the marker: a circle split by a line, with C on top and A-502 below, and a solid black triangle behind the circle. The triangle points up the sheet, the way you look at the cut.
The London Square legend (Figure 1) shows this kind of marker for building sections and wall sections. The leləm̓ set uses the same idea. The top is the view, the bottom is the sheet.
In the leləm̓ drawing list (lesson 16, Figure 2), A-502 is "Building sections".
Answer: it is building section C, drawn on sheet A-502. Go to A-502 and find the view titled C.

(Hint: look at the ceiling tag in Figure 1.) c) What would you do on a London Square job if a note said "outlet at 18" A.F.F."?
Task 13 (level 3) Put Figures 3, 5 and 6 together. You are setting the floor transition at door 119. a) What floor finish is on each side of the door? b) Why does that matter to the carpenter and the flooring installer? c) Which three documents did you use, and what key (tag or mark) linked them?
Check yourself
Where do you look first when you do not know what a symbol means?
On a section marker, what is the top number and what is the bottom number?
What do grid lines help a crew do?

lessons.title: Capstone: read a real drawing set
lessons.text:
Work a real job through one drawing set, from the drawing list to the plan, section, wall section, schedules and plumbing sheets, then do the math and flag the problems you find.
Why this matters on the job
On a real job nobody hands you one tidy drawing. You get a set, a question and a deadline. You have to find the right sheets, follow the marks from one sheet to the next, read the schedules, do the math with the written dimensions, and notice when two sheets do not agree. That is what this capstone asks you to do, on a real set.
This lesson pulls together: - Reading lesson 05: title block, legend, schedules, notes and "do not scale" - Reading lessons 11 (views), 12 (pictorial drawings), 13 (lines and dimensions), 14 (scales) and 15 (sections, details and callouts) - Reading lesson 16: title blocks, sheet sets and the drawing list - Reading lesson 17: symbols, legends, grids and schedules - Numeracy lesson 11 and Numeracy lesson 13: fractions, converting to metric, and area
The job
You are on the crew that will fit out the Level 4 washrooms at London Square, a mixed-use building at 828 Kingston Blvd. The set is imperial (feet and inches). The firm names on it, such as Athena Architecture Ltd. and Oslo Mechanical, are made up (fictional). The drawings are real.
Your foreman wants a short report before the crew starts: - which sheets you need - the grid layout and one bay area - the floor heights and the wall build-up at the east wall - the washroom doors and fixtures - anything on the drawings that does not add up
How to work through a set
Start at the drawing list. Write down every sheet you think you need.
Check each title block. Note the scale and the latest issue.
Find your area on the plan by grid lines. Read the written dimensions.
Follow every marker. A section mark sends you to a section. A callout on the section sends you to a wall section or detail.
Follow every tag to its schedule. Door tags to the door schedule, wall tags to the wall types, fixture tags to the plumbing sheets.
Check the trades against each other. The plumbing plan and the architectural plan should show the same fixtures.
Write down anything that does not agree, and ask in writing before you build.
Worked example
Question: What is the scale of the Level 4 plan, and how long would the 25'-6" bay between grids 4 and 3 be on a full-size print?
The A-241 title block says "As indicated" (lesson 16, Figure 4). So look under the plan. The view title in Figure 2 says LEVEL 4, 1/8" = 1'-0".
At 1/8" = 1'-0", every foot is drawn 1/8" long.
25'-6" = 25.5 feet. 25.5 × 1/8" = 25.5 ÷ 8 = 3.1875".
0.1875" = 3/16" (3 ÷ 16 = 0.1875). So the bay is drawn 3 3/16" long on a full-size print.
That is only a check. London Square project note 3 says no dimension shall be taken (scaled) from the drawings. Build to the written 25'-6".
The drawing set
Tap a figure to open it full size, then zoom in. Figure 1 is the same drawing list used in lesson 16.
Figure 1. London Square, sheet A-100 Cover sheet and code review, drawing list. Athena Architecture Ltd. (fictional).
Figure 2. London Square, sheet A-241 Floor plan Level L3 and L4 office plan, the Level 4 plan (view 1). Athena Architecture Ltd. (fictional).
Figure 3. London Square, sheet A-241, Level 4 plan, dimension strings at grids 5 to 2.
Figure 4. London Square, sheet A-241, Level 4 plan, dimension string between grids C and B.
Figure 5. London Square, sheet A-241, Level 4 plan, the washroom core and the east wall.
Figure 6. London Square, sheet A-401 Building sections, Building Section 1, east part (title moved under the view to fit). Athena Architecture Ltd. (fictional).
Figure 7. London Square, sheet A-602 Wall sections, wall section 07, top part with its title. Athena Architecture Ltd. (fictional).
Figure 8. London Square, sheet A-101 "Construction schedule" (a schedule of wall, floor and roof assemblies), wall type W2. Athena Architecture Ltd. (fictional).
Figure 9. London Square, sheet A-901 Door schedule, header and the rows from 3ST2 to 404 on Levels 3 and 4 (the rows in between are left out). Athena Architecture Ltd. (fictional).

Tasks

Write the sheet number for each thing the crew needs. a) The Level 4 floor plan b) The building sections c) The door schedule d) The wall, floor and roof assemblies (careful: look at the name of A-101) e) The plumbing plan for Levels 3 and 4 f) The plumbing washroom details g) The electrical floor plan for Levels 3 and 4

Of Level 3? c) What is the floor-to-floor height from Level 3 to Level 4? Check it by subtracting the two elevations. d) What is the floor-to-floor height from Level 4 to the roof?

On which sheet? b) What is the full title and scale of that wall section? c) Which wall type tag is on the wall between Level 3 and Level 4? d) List the layers of that wall type from outside to inside. What do you think that means?

b) Does the architectural plan (Figure 5) show the same fixtures as the plumbing plan (Figure 11)? c) What kind of floor drain is FD-1, and what size is its strainer? (Figure 13)

Which unit numbers and which floor elevation does it show? b) Which level does that floor elevation belong to on Building Section 1? (276.17 feet = 276'-2".) c) What is wrong on P-6, and why does it matter to a plumber? d) Write a short request for information (RFI) to the mechanical engineer. Check yourself
Where do you start when you get a new drawing set?
A plan shows "07 over A-602". What do you do next?

lessons.title: Read a scope of work
lessons.text:
Find what the crew must do, what is left out and when the work counts as done, and spot extra work that was never in the scope.
Why this matters on the job
Before a crew starts, the company agrees on a scope of work: a list of exactly what it will do for the price. On site, people ask for "one more quick thing" all the time. If the crew says yes to work that was never in the scope, the company pays for the hours and the material, and the job runs late. Knowing what is in and what is out lets you answer the request politely and send it to the right person.
Key ideas
1. The four parts of a scope. Most scopes of work have: - Work included: what the crew will do. Often a numbered list. - Exclusions: what the crew will not do, often marked "by others" or "by owner". - Assumptions: things the price depends on, such as "the stair is finished before we install". - Acceptance criteria: how everyone will know the work is done. Think of it as a "done when" list.
2. Read the included list as a checklist. Each numbered item is one piece of the job. If a piece of work is not on the list, it is not in the price.
3. Exclusions tell you who does it. "Finish paint by others" means another trade paints. "Permit by owner" means the owner gets the permit. Your crew does not.
4. Assumptions can break. If an assumption turns out to be false (the stair is not ready, there is no power), tell your supervisor the same day. The price or the schedule may have to change.
5. "Done" means every acceptance item is met. Finishing the install is not the same as the work being accepted. Check each item on the "done when" list.
6. Scope creep. Small extra requests on site add up. This is called scope creep. Do not refuse rudely, and do not just do it. Point to the scope, say who decides, and ask for a written change order. If something in the scope is unclear, ask a question in writing: see Communication lesson 12. For how to say no politely, see Communication lesson 04.
Worked example
Question: Does Fraser Bend have to paint the new handrail black?
Look in Work included (section 2). Item 2.4 says "Shop prime all steel with one coat of grey primer." Item 2.6 says touch up the primer. Nothing about a finish colour.
Look in Exclusions (section 3). It says "Finish paint. By others (painting contractor)."
No. Fraser Bend primes the steel grey. The painting contractor does the finish paint.
Practice documents
All documents below are for fictional companies.
Document A: Scope of work
Fraser Bend Metalworks Ltd. (fictional company) · Subcontract SC-14 · Scope of work For: Kestrel Point Builders Ltd. (fictional company), general contractor Job: Tool library fit-out, Unit 4 (fictional building) Date: March 2
1. Purpose Kestrel Point needs a handrail on the new mezzanine stair and a guard along the mezzanine edge so the tool library can open.
2. Work included 2.1 Prepare shop drawings of the handrail and guard. Send them to Kestrel Point for review before fabrication starts. 2.2 Fabricate two steel stair handrails: one 4.2 m long and one 3.6 m long. 2.3 Fabricate one steel guard, 6.0 m long, for the mezzanine edge. 2.4 Shop prime all steel with one coat of grey primer. 2.5 Deliver to site. Install and anchor the handrails and guard. 2.6 Touch up the primer on site after installation. 2.7 Remove our own cut-offs, scrap and packaging from site at the end of each day.
3. Exclusions - Finish paint. By others (painting contractor). - Building permit. By owner. - Removing the existing wood railing. By Kestrel Point. - Handrails at the exterior ramp. - Structural design of the stair and mezzanine. By owner's engineer.
4. Assumptions - The stair and mezzanine are complete and ready for anchors on install day. - 120 V power is available within 15 m of the work. - Access is through the rear loading door. - Work is done on day shift, Monday to Friday.
5. Acceptance criteria (done when) - Installed as shown on the reviewed shop drawings. - All anchors in place and tight. - No sharp edges or weld spatter. - Primer touched up. - Kestrel Point's site superintendent has walked the work and signed the checklist.
6. Changes Any work not listed in section 2 needs a written change order signed by Kestrel Point's project manager before the work starts. A verbal request does not count.
Document B: Texts and requests on site during install week
a) Site superintendent: Can you guys put a handrail on the outside ramp while you're here? Quick job. b) Site superintendent: Painter starts Friday. Make sure your primer touch-ups are done Thursday. c) Kestrel Point lead hand: Heads up, the stair treads aren't set yet. You can't anchor to it until Monday. d) Site superintendent: Can you throw the old wood railing in your bin when you leave? e) Owner's rep: Can you paint it black instead of grey? It would look better. f) Site superintendent: Please sweep up your cut-offs before you go tonight.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Document A. a) Who is doing the work, and who hired them? b) What is the total length of steel rail and guard Fraser Bend will make, in metres?
Task 2 (level 1) Name two things in the Exclusions, and who does each one.
Task 3 (level 2) Read each message in Document B. Sort it into one of three groups, and give the section of Document A that tells you. - In scope: the crew should do it. - Out of scope: it needs a written change order first, or it belongs to someone else. - Assumption problem: something the price depends on is not true. Tell the supervisor.
Task 4 (level 2) The crew finishes installing on Wednesday. The anchors are tight, the edges are clean and the primer is touched up. The site superintendent is away until Friday. Is the work done and accepted? Explain using section 5.
Task 5 (level 3) Answer message (a) from the site superintendent. Be polite. Name the section of the scope, say what is needed before your crew can do it, and who has to sign.
Task 6 (level 3) Read Document A as a whole. Find one thing it does not say that could cause an argument later. Say why.
Check yourself
What does "by others" mean in an exclusion?
What is an acceptance criterion?
A request for extra work arrives by text. What does it need before you start?
Why read the assumptions, not just the work included?

lessons.title: What is in a construction contract
lessons.text:
Find the parties, the work, the price, payments, changes, warranty and holdback in a short subcontract, and learn what a builders lien protects in BC.
Why this matters on the job
Every job runs on a contract, even a small one. The contract says what the work is, what it pays, when the money comes and what happens when something changes. Lead hands, foremen and small contractors read contracts all the time. One day you may sign one for your own crew. In BC, a law called the Builders Lien Act also decides part of how money moves on a job, so some of the money is held back until the end. Knowing where to look saves arguments and lost pay.
This lesson teaches reading. It is not legal advice. For a real contract or a real unpaid bill, talk to a lawyer.
Key ideas
1. Find the nine parts. Most construction contracts and subcontracts cover:
Part The question it answers
Parties Who is agreeing with whom?
The work What exactly will be done? (see Reading lesson 19)
Price How much, for all of it?
Schedule When does it start and finish?
Payment When do you invoice, and when are you paid?
Changes How is extra work agreed and priced?
Holdback How much is kept back until the end?
Warranty What do you fix later, and for how long?
Signatures and dates Who agreed, and when?
2. Get it in writing. If something was agreed out loud, ask for it to be added in writing before you start. A contract that says "changes must be in writing" means a handshake on site will not count.
3. Holdback in BC. Under section 4 of the Builders Lien Act, the person paying on a construction contract or subcontract must keep back a holdback of 10% of the work done. The holdback must not be kept back from a worker's wages or from a material supplier.
Work done this month: $10,000 Holdback: 10% of $10,000 = $1,000 Payment now: $10,000 − $1,000 = $9,000
4. When holdback is paid out. When the work is complete, the contractor can ask for a certificate of completion. "Complete" in this Act means substantially complete, not every last item. The holdback period ends 55 days after that certificate is issued (section 8). After the holdback period, the holdback can be paid out if no liens have been filed.
5. What a builders lien is. Under section 2 of the Act, a contractor, subcontractor or worker who does work or supplies material on a building or land has a lien for the price that is still unpaid. The lien is a claim on the owner's interest in the building, the building itself, the land it stands on, and material delivered to that land. - Deadline: when a certificate of completion has been issued, a lien must be filed no later than 45 days after the date it was issued (section 20). - A lien cannot be filed for less than $200 (section 17). - You cannot sign your lien rights away. Section 42 says an agreement that the Act will not apply, or that its remedies will not be available to a person, is void (it has no effect).
6. The law can change. BC passed a new law, the Construction Prompt Payment Act, in November 2025. When this lesson was checked, it was not yet in force. When it comes into force, some payment and lien rules will change. Always check the current Act on BC Laws: https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca
Worked example
Question: Who supplies the lumber on the garage job?
Find the section about the work: section 2 of Document A.
Read it closely: "Cedar Line supplies all framing labour and fasteners. Kestrel Point supplies all lumber."
Kestrel Point supplies the lumber. Cedar Line supplies labour and fasteners.
Practice documents
Document A: A short subcontract
Subcontract KP-G7 (fictional)
1. Parties. This subcontract is between Kestrel Point Builders Ltd. (fictional company), the contractor, and Cedar Line Framing Ltd. (fictional company), the subcontractor.
2. The work. Cedar Line will frame the walls and roof of a detached garage, 6.0 m by 7.2 m, at Lot 7 (fictional), as shown on drawings A1 to A4, revision 2. Cedar Line supplies all framing labour and fasteners. Kestrel Point supplies all lumber. Not included: roofing, siding, installing windows and doors, and electrical.
3. Price. A fixed price of $18,000 for the work in section 2.
4. Schedule. Cedar Line will start within 3 working days after Kestrel Point signs off the slab, and finish within 15 working days after starting.
5. Payment. Cedar Line invoices on the last working day of each month for work done that month. Kestrel Point pays within 30 days of receiving the invoice, less the 10% holdback required by the BC Builders Lien Act. Kestrel Point pays the holdback after the holdback period ends, if no liens have been filed.
6. Changes. Cedar Line will not do extra work without a written change order signed by both parties. The change order states the price of the extra work.
7. Safety. Cedar Line follows the WorkSafeBC regulation and Kestrel Point's site safety plan. Before starting, Cedar Line gives Kestrel Point a WorkSafeBC clearance letter.
8. Warranty. Cedar Line will fix, at no charge, any defect in its work that is reported within 1 year after the work is complete.
9. Clean-up. Cedar Line keeps its work area clean. If it does not, Kestrel Point may give 24 hours' written notice, then clean the area and deduct the cost from Cedar Line's next payment.
10. Liens. Cedar Line agrees not to file a builders lien on this job for any reason.
Signed: __ for Kestrel Point Signed: __ for Cedar Line Date: _
Document B: What happened on the job
End of month 1: Cedar Line has done $10,000 of the work.
Month 2: The owner asks for an extra window opening in the back wall. Both companies sign change order CO-1 for $1,500. Cedar Line frames it.
End of month 2: Cedar Line finishes the rest of the original work, worth $8,000, plus CO-1.
June 10: A certificate of completion is issued for Cedar Line's subcontract.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Document A. a) Who are the two parties? b) What is the price? c) Name two things that are not included in the work.
Task 2 (level 1) When does Cedar Line send an invoice, and how long does Kestrel Point have to pay it?
Task 3 (level 2) The owner walks up to the Cedar Line foreman and says, "Can you frame an extra window in the back wall?" What must happen before the crew frames it? Name the section.
Task 4 (level 2) Use Document B and section 5. a) How much holdback is kept from the month 1 invoice, and how much is Cedar Line paid? b) The month 2 invoice is for the $8,000 of original work plus change order CO-1. What is the invoice total, the holdback and the payment? c) What is the total holdback kept on the job?
Task 5 (level 2) The certificate of completion is issued on June 10. a) On what date does the holdback period end? b) What is the last day a lien could be filed for this subcontract?
Task 6 (level 3) Read section 10 of Document A. Is it valid in BC? Explain using Key idea 5.
Task 7 (level 3) A framer employed by Cedar Line has not been paid wages for his last two weeks on the garage. a) Does the Builders Lien Act give a worker lien rights? b) Can a holdback be kept back from his wages?
Task 8 (level 3) Look at Document A as a whole. a) Who probably wrote it, and whose side does section 9 favour? Explain. b) Name one thing the contract does not say that Cedar Line should ask about before signing.
Check yourself
What is a holdback?
In BC, what percent is the holdback under the Builders Lien Act?
Name two things a builders lien is a claim on.
Can you sign away your right to file a lien in BC?
Where do you check the current version of a BC law?

lessons.title: Read a tender package
lessons.text:
Find your way through the drawings, specifications and addenda in a bid package, and use the order of precedence to decide which document wins when they disagree.
Why this matters on the job
Before a company bids on a job, an estimator reads the whole tender package and prices exactly what it asks for. On site, the crew builds from the same documents. Sometimes a drawing says one thing and the specification says another. If you guess, you may build it wrong, tear it out and do it again on your own time. A tender package tells you which document wins. This lesson builds on the drawing lessons (Reading lessons 11 to 18).
Key ideas
1. What is in a tender package. A tender (or bid) package is the set of documents a contractor uses to price a job. It usually has: - Instructions to bidders: the rules for the bid, such as the closing date and how to ask questions. - A bid form: where the contractor writes the price and lists the addenda it received. - The contract and its conditions. - Drawings. - Specifications ("specs"). - Addenda: changes issued before the bid closes.
2. Drawings and specs do different jobs. - Drawings show what and where: the location, shape and size of the work. - Specifications are written requirements: which materials and products, what quality, and how the work is done.
3. Specs are filed by number. Most specs in Canada are organized with MasterFormat numbers: three pairs of digits. The first pair is the division. For example, the London Square spec from Reading lesson 18 lists: - Division 01: General Requirements (rules for every trade on the job) - 05 50 00: Metal Fabrications - 06 10 00: Rough Carpentry - 09 91 00: Painting
To find a rule, start at the spec's table of contents, find the section, then read it.
4. Addenda change the package. An addendum is a formal written change issued during bidding. Once issued, it becomes part of the bid documents, and the price must include it. A later addendum replaces anything earlier that it changes. List every addendum on the bid form. A phone call or a chat on site does not change the documents. Only a written addendum does.
5. Order of precedence. When two documents disagree, the package says which one wins. This list is called the order of precedence. Standard Canadian contracts, such as CCDC 2 (2020), set an order like this. Common rules: - Specifications win over drawings. - On drawings of the same date, the larger-scale drawing wins (a 1:10 detail beats a 1:50 plan). - A written dimension wins over a dimension you measure with a scale rule. - A later document wins over an earlier one of the same type.
Always read the order of precedence in your package. Do not assume.
6. When the rules do not settle it, ask. If two documents disagree and the order of precedence does not decide it, ask the design team in writing before the question deadline: see Communication lesson 12.
Worked example
Question: What colour is the finish paint on the guard?
Go to the spec table of contents (Document C). Paint is in section 09 91 00 Painting.
Section 09 91 00 says: finish colour "Charcoal".
Check the addenda (Document D). Addendum 2, dated March 3, says: "09 91 00 Painting. Change finish colour from Charcoal to Slate Blue."
A later document wins over an earlier one (Document A, item 5d). Slate Blue.
Practice documents
All documents below are for a fictional job.
Document A: Instructions to bidders (excerpt)
Tool library fit-out, Unit 4 (fictional building) Issued by: Alder & Moss Architects (fictional company), for the owner, the Riverside Tool Library (fictional) Issued for tender: February 10
Bids close at 2:00 p.m. on March 12. Late bids are not opened.
Send all questions in writing to the architect by March 5. No questions are answered after that date.
Any change to the bid documents is made only by a written addendum from the architect. No other answer, written or spoken, changes the documents.
List every addendum you received on the bid form.
If the documents disagree, this order applies: a) Addenda, the latest first b) Specifications c) Drawings. On drawings of the same date, the larger-scale drawing governs. d) A later-dated document governs over an earlier one of the same type. e) Written dimensions govern. Do not scale the drawings.
Document B: Drawing list (all dated February 10)
Sheet Title Scale
A-101 Floor plan 1:50
A-301 Details 1:10
A-401 Door schedule none
Document C: Specifications (excerpts)
Table of contents Division 01 · 01 11 00 Summary of Work Division 05 · 05 50 00 Metal Fabrications Division 06 · 06 10 00 Rough Carpentry Division 09 · 09 91 00 Painting
05 50 00 Metal Fabrications. Steel guard at mezzanine: steel pipe rails, shop primed with one coat of grey primer by the fabricator. 06 10 00 Rough Carpentry. Plywood backing for wall-mounted tool racks: 19 mm plywood, fastened to every stud. 09 91 00 Painting. Finish colour: Charcoal. Painter primes all bare steel on site before finish coats.
Document D: Addenda
Addendum 1 · February 24 A-401 Door schedule. Door D2: change width from 900 mm to 1000 mm.
Addendum 2 · March 3 09 91 00 Painting. Change finish colour from Charcoal to Slate Blue.
Document E: What the drawings show
A-101 (1:50): The workbench wall has a written dimension of 3000 mm. Measured with a scale rule on the printed sheet, the wall is 62 mm long.
A-101 (1:50): A note says "Tool counter 600 mm deep."
A-301 Detail 2 (1:10): The section through the tool counter shows the counter 650 mm deep.
A-301 Detail 4 (1:10): A note says "12 mm plywood backing behind tool racks."
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Document A. a) When do bids close? b) What is the last day to send a question? c) Who can change the bid documents, and how?
Task 2 (level 1) Use the table of contents in Document C. Which spec section would you open to find: a) the plywood for the tool racks? b) the steel guard? c) the paint?
Task 3 (level 2) Would you look on a drawing or in the specifications first for each of these? Use Key idea 2. a) where the tool counter goes in the room b) the thickness of the plywood backing c) how many coats of primer the steel gets d) the shape of the guard at the top of the stair e) the paint colour
Task 4 (level 2) The workbench wall on A-101 has a written dimension of 3000 mm. Someone measures the printed sheet with a scale rule and gets 62 mm at 1:50. a) What length does 62 mm at 1:50 stand for? b) Which length do you build to? Name the rule in Document A.
Task 5 (level 2) A-101 says the tool counter is 600 mm deep. Detail 2 on A-301 shows it 650 mm deep. Both sheets are dated February 10. Which depth do you price and build? Why?
Task 6 (level 2) Detail 4 on A-301 says 12 mm plywood backing. Spec section 06 10 00 says 19 mm. Which wins? Why?
Task 7 (level 3) a) How wide is door D2 now? Which document tells you? b) An estimator fills in the bid form and lists only Addendum 1. What is wrong, and what could it cost the company? c) On March 4, a site visitor tells the estimator, "Don't worry about the paint, the owner said grey is fine." Does this change the documents? Why or why not?
Task 8 (level 3) Section 05 50 00 says the fabricator shop primes the guard. Section 09 91 00 says the painter primes all bare steel on site. a) Do these instructions necessarily conflict? What handover detail about bare or damaged areas would you clarify before pricing? b) Today is March 2. Write the question you would send to the architect.
