lessons.title: Employee, apprentice or contractor
lessons.text:
Read a job offer and judge whether it makes you an employee or a self-employed contractor, and what that means for deductions, WorkSafeBC coverage and your apprenticeship hours.
Why this matters on the job
Some offers come on letterhead. Some come by text: "cash, no paperwork, you're a contractor". The words in an offer change a lot: who takes off tax, whether BC's employment standards protect you, how WorkSafeBC treats you, and whether your hours count toward your apprenticeship. Reading the offer closely before you start protects your pay and your path to a ticket.
This lesson teaches reading. It is not legal or tax advice. The places to ask are at the end of the Key ideas.
Key ideas
1. Two kinds of working relationship. - An employee works in someone else's business. The employer directs the work and pays wages. - A self-employed person (an independent contractor) runs their own business and sells a service to a customer.
2. The label does not decide it. The facts do. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) says the facts of the whole working relationship decide your status. The Province of BC says that calling a worker an independent contractor, even if the worker agrees, does not decide it. A good question to ask is: whose business is it?
3. The CRA's six questions. The CRA looks at:
Question Points to employee Points to self-employed
Control: who decides what work you do, when and how? The payer decides You decide and can turn work down
Tools and equipment: who supplies them and pays to repair and insure them? The payer supplies most of them You supply them and have a big investment in them
Helpers: can you hire someone or send someone in your place? You must do the work yourself You can hire and pay a helper
Financial risk: do you pay costs that are not paid back? No ongoing costs of your own You pay fixed costs even when there is no work
Investment and management: do you run a business? No business of your own You have money in the business and manage it
Chance of profit: can you make a profit or a loss? Paid by the hour, no profit or loss Paid a flat price for a job, and you carry the costs
No single answer decides it. The CRA looks at each one, then at all of them together.
4. Why it matters. - Employee: the employer takes Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions, Employment Insurance (EI) premiums and income tax off your pay and sends them to the CRA, with its own share of CPP and EI. BC's Employment Standards Act protects you. WorkSafeBC says BC workers are covered automatically, and an employer who hires workers must register. - Self-employed: nobody takes deductions off what you are paid. You run a business and look after its tax. The Employment Standards Act does not apply to independent contractors. A self-employed sole proprietor is not automatically covered by WorkSafeBC, but can buy optional Personal Coverage. - Apprentice: you register with SkilledTradesBC, and your employer is your sponsor. Sponsors submit your work-based training hours to SkilledTradesBC. A new sponsor can credit hours from an earlier job, but must collect enough proof first. Cash work with no paperwork leaves you with no proof.
5. Things that do not prove you are a contractor. The Province of BC lists things that, on their own, do not make a worker an independent contractor. You may still be an employee even if you agree to be called a contractor, charge GST, send invoices instead of time cards, have no deductions taken off, work without much supervision, drive your own car, bring your own tools, or are paid by the piece.
6. Where to ask. - CRA: either you or the payer can ask the CRA for a ruling on whether you are an employee or self-employed. You can ask in My Account or with form CPT1. Ask by June 29 of the year after the work. - BC Employment Standards: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/employment-business/employment-standards-advice/employment-standards - SkilledTradesBC, for questions about your apprenticeship and hours: https://skilledtradesbc.ca
Worked example
Question: A framer brings her own hammer, tool belt and nail gun to work. Does that make her a contractor?
Key idea 3, tools: supplying tools can point to self-employed, but the CRA also notes that many tradespeople, such as mechanics, must supply their own tools even when they are full-time employees.
Key idea 5: "provides their own tools" is on the Province's list of things that do not decide it on their own.
No, not on its own. Look at the other questions too: who controls her work, who pays her, and whose business it is.
Practice documents
Document A: An offer letter
Granite Ridge Mechanical Ltd. (fictional company) Dear Jordan, We are pleased to offer you a position as a first-year plumbing apprentice. - Pay: $24.00 an hour, paid every second Friday by direct deposit. - Hours: 40 hours a week, Monday to Friday, 7:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. - Probation: the first 3 months. - Tools: Granite Ridge supplies all power tools, the work truck and fittings. You supply the basic hand tools on the attached list. - Deductions: CPP, EI and income tax are deducted from each pay. - Apprenticeship: Granite Ridge will be your sponsor. We will help you register with SkilledTradesBC and we submit your work-based training hours each month. - Safety: Granite Ridge is registered with WorkSafeBC. You will attend our site safety orientation on your first day. Please sign and return this letter by May 15. Signed: Dana K., Operations Manager
Document B: A text message
Ray (Ray's Renos, fictional): Hey Jordan, got lots of work for you. $30 an hour cash, no paperwork. You're a contractor so no deductions, more money in your pocket. I'll tell you where and when each day. Use my tools and my van. Start Monday 7 am. Don't worry about your apprentice hours, I'll sign something later.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Document A. Find: a) the hourly pay b) the hours each week c) the length of the probation d) who supplies the power tools
Task 2 (level 1) For a 40-hour week, before any deductions: a) What does Document A pay? b) What does Document B pay? c) How much more does Document B pay each week?
Task 3 (level 2) Use the CRA's six questions in Key idea 3. For Document B, write what the text says (or does not say) for each question, and whether it points to employee or self-employed. Then decide: does Ray's offer look like employee work or contractor work?
Question What Document B says Points to
Control
Tools and equipment
Helpers
Financial risk
Investment and management
Chance of profit
Task 4 (level 2) Ray says, "You're a contractor so no deductions." Use Key ideas 2 and 5. Does having no deductions make Jordan a contractor? Explain.
Task 5 (level 3) Jordan wants to become a journeyperson plumber. Ray's offer pays more each week. Name three things Jordan could lose or risk by taking Document B. Use Key idea 4.
Task 6 (level 3) Jordan is not sure what Ray's offer really is. Name two places Jordan could ask, and what each one can help with.
Task 7 (level 3) a) Who wrote each document, and what does each writer want? b) Name one thing a new apprentice might want to know that Document A does not say.
Check yourself
If you sign a paper saying "I am an independent contractor", does that make you one?
Name three of the CRA's six questions.
Who submits an apprentice's work-based training hours to SkilledTradesBC?
Does BC's Employment Standards Act protect independent contractors?
Who can ask the CRA for a ruling on employment status?

lessons.title: Part 3 or Part 9 and the occupant load
lessons.text:
Read the BC Building Code articles that decide whether a building falls under Part 3 or Part 9, classify a building by its major occupancy, and work out an occupant load from Table 3.1.17.1.
Why this matters on the job
The BC Building Code has two different sets of rules for buildings. Part 9 covers houses and small buildings. Part 3 covers bigger buildings and buildings where people gather, sleep in care or are held. A garage, a corner store and a four-storey apartment building do not follow the same rules, so the first question on any job is "which Part are we under?" The designer answers it before the drawings are made, and it is often written on a code review sheet at the front of the set, like the London Square cover sheet in Reading lesson 16. The occupant load, the number of people a room or floor is designed for, is the number that many fire and exit rules are built on. You may have seen it on a sign beside the door of a restaurant.
This lesson builds on Reading lesson 6, Find a rule in the BC Building Code. Have the BC Building Code 2024 PDF open:
BC Building Code 2024 page: https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/industry/construction-industry/building-codes-standards/bc-codes/2024-bc-codes
Key ideas
1. Where the answer is. Which Part applies is set in Division A, Subsection 1.3.3. Application of Division B. Two articles do the work: - Article 1.3.3.3. Application of Part 9 - Article 1.3.3.2. Application of Parts 3, 4, 5 and 6
2. Part 9 needs three things, all at once. Sentence 1.3.3.3.(1) says Part 9 applies to buildings - of 3 storeys or less in building height, and - with a building area not exceeding 600 m², and - used for major occupancies in Group C (residential), Group D (business and personal services), Group E (mercantile) or Group F, Division 2 or 3 (medium- and low-hazard industrial).
If even one of the three is not true, the building is not a Part 9 building.
3. Some buildings are always Part 3. Sentence 1.3.3.2.(1) says Part 3 applies to buildings that are - post-disaster buildings, or - used for Group A (assembly), Group B (care, treatment or detention) or Group F, Division 1 (high-hazard industrial), of any size, or - Group C, D, E, F2 or F3 buildings that are over 600 m² in building area or over 3 storeys in building height.
4. The words in italics have exact meanings. They are defined in Article 1.4.1.2. of Division A.
Defined word What the Code says, in short
Building area the greatest horizontal area of the building above grade, measured to the outside surface of the exterior walls. It is not all the floors added together.
Storey the space from the top of one floor to the top of the floor above
First storey the uppermost storey whose floor is not more than 2 m above grade
Basement a storey below the first storey
Building height (in storeys) the number of storeys from the floor of the first storey up to the roof. A basement is below the first storey, so it does not count.
Grade the lowest of the average levels of finished ground along each exterior wall
5. Major occupancy groups. Table 3.1.2.1. lists the groups. Note A-3.1.2.1.(1), in the notes at the end of Part 3, gives examples of each one.
Group Division Major occupancy Examples from Note A-3.1.2.1.(1)
A 1 Assembly, performing arts theatres, motion picture theatres
A 2 Assembly not classed elsewhere in Group A restaurants, churches, community halls, gymnasia, schools
A 3 Assembly, arena type arenas, rinks, indoor swimming pools
A 4 Assembly in the open air bleachers, grandstands, stadia
B 1 Detention jails, prisons
B 2 Treatment hospitals
B 3 Care group homes, care facilities without treatment
C – Residential houses, apartments, hotels, motels
D – Business and personal services offices, banks, dental offices, barber shops
E – Mercantile shops, stores, supermarkets
F 1 High-hazard industrial paint factories, spray painting operations
F 2 Medium-hazard industrial repair garages, woodworking factories, warehouses
F 3 Low-hazard industrial storage garages, creameries
Some uses show up in more than one list, such as warehouses and workshops in both F2 and F3. Then the designer decides from what is stored or done there. A building with more than one major occupancy is classified by all of them (Sentence 3.1.2.1.(2)).
The Code also has a few special cases. For example, Article 3.1.2.7. lets a small Group A, Division 2 suite (not more than 30 persons, and not a daycare) be classified as Group D if it meets the conditions in that Article. Special cases like this are the designer's call. In this lesson, use the main tables.
6. Occupant load. Article 3.1.17.1. (Part 3) and Article 9.9.1.3. (Part 9) both send you to Table 3.1.17.1. Occupant Load. For most areas, the table gives an area per person in m². Divide the floor area by that number:
occupant load = floor area ÷ area per person
The Code says the occupant load is not less than what the table gives, unless it can be shown that fewer people will use the area. Dwelling units are different: Part 9 uses 2 persons per bedroom or sleeping area. If a room is used for different things at different times, Sentence 3.1.17.1.(4) says to use the value that gives the greatest number of people. The numbers in this lesson are chosen so that every answer comes out to whole people.
7. Check the revisions. The Code changes. Revision 3 (in effect August 27, 2024) replaced Article 1.3.3.3. Sentence (1) kept the same three tests, and a new Sentence (2) says Part 9 does not apply to buildings designed under Subsection 3.2.10., a new set of rules for some residential buildings with a single exit stair. The PDF on the government page may not include every revision, so always check the revisions page too.
Worked example
Question: A small survey company is building a one-storey office with no basement. It measures 15.5 m by 12 m to the outside of the walls. Is it Part 3 or Part 9, and what is the occupant load of the 186 m² office floor?
Occupancy. Offices are Group D (Table 3.1.2.1. and Note A-3.1.2.1.(1)). Group D is on the Part 9 list.
Building height. One storey. That is 3 storeys or less.
Building area. 15.5 × 12 = 186 m². That does not exceed 600 m².
All three tests pass, so Sentence 1.3.3.3.(1) puts it under Part 9.
Occupant load. Part 9 sends you to Table 3.1.17.1. (Article 9.9.1.3.). Under "Business and personal services uses", offices are 9.30 m² per person.
186 ÷ 9.30 = 20 persons.
Practice
For Tasks 1, 2, 5, 6, 8 and 9 you need the BC Building Code 2024 PDF open. All buildings in this lesson are fictional.
Task 1 (level 2) Go to Article 1.3.3.3. in Division A. a) Write the three things that must all be true for Part 9 to apply. b) Which words in the Sentence tell you that a building of exactly 600 m² can still be Part 9?
Task 2 (level 2) Use Table 3.1.2.1. and Note A-3.1.2.1.(1). Give the Group (and Division, if there is one) for each use. a) a hair salon b) a supermarket c) a motel d) a church e) an arena f) a hospital g) a repair garage h) a paint factory
Task 3 (level 2) Part 3 or Part 9? For each building, give your answer, the reason, and the Sentence you used.
Building Use Storeys (building height) Building area
A House 2 120 m²
B Restaurant 1 240 m²
C Hardware store 1 900 m²
D Apartment building 4 550 m²
E Repair garage 1 450 m²
F Daycare for children 1 200 m²
G Office building 3 600 m²
For building F, also read Article 3.1.2.8.
Task 4 (level 2) A two-storey house measures 140 m² on the main floor and 110 m² on the upper floor, both measured to the outside of the walls. There is no basement. a) What is its building area? b) A co-worker says the building area is 250 m². What mistake did they make?
Task 5 (level 3) A building has four floors. Their levels, measured from grade, are: - Floor 1: 2.4 m below grade - Floor 2: 0.3 m above grade - Floor 3: 3.3 m above grade - Floor 4: 6.3 m above grade
a) Which floor is the first storey? Use the definition. b) What is Floor 1 called? c) What is the building height in storeys? d) The building is an office with a building area of 480 m². Part 3 or Part 9?
Task 6 (level 2) Use Table 3.1.17.1. Find the occupant load of each area. a) an office floor of 279 m² b) a classroom of 74 m² c) a cafeteria (dining space) of 96 m² d) a store on the first storey, 185 m² of sales floor e) a storage room of 92 m²
Task 7 (level 3) A two-storey building has a building area of 400 m². The ground floor is a store with 370 m² of sales floor. The second floor is offices, 372 m². a) What are its major occupancies? b) Part 3 or Part 9? Why? c) What is the occupant load of each floor, and of the whole building?
Task 8 (level 3) A 30 m² hall in a Part 3 building is set up with loose chairs for meetings. On some nights it is used for standing-room events. a) What area per person does Table 3.1.17.1. give for each use? b) What is the occupant load for each use? c) Which number must the designer use, and which Sentence says so?
Task 9 (level 3) A co-worker says: "Part 9 is anything three storeys or less. Everybody knows that." a) Name two kinds of building that are three storeys or less and still fall under Part 3. b) Open the BC Code revisions page from the BC Building Code 2024 page. What did Revision 3 do to Article 1.3.3.3.? c) What would you tell your co-worker?
Check yourself
Which Division and Subsection of the Code decide whether Part 3 or Part 9 applies?
Name the three tests in Sentence 1.3.3.3.(1).
Is a restaurant of 150 m² a Part 9 building? Why or why not?
Is building area the total of all the floors? What is it?
How do you find the occupant load of an office floor?

lessons.title: Deficiency reports and punch lists
lessons.text:
Read a deficiency report, a deficiency log and a punch list, find who has to fix what, where and by when, and know what you may and may not do until the work is closed.
Why this matters on the job
Near the end of every job, and often in the middle, someone walks the building and writes down what is wrong or not finished. Each item becomes a deficiency report, and the list of them becomes a log. If an item has your trade's name on it, the report tells you exactly what to fix, where it is and when it is due. Fixing it right the first time saves a second trip. Covering it up before it is checked can mean tearing out finished work. Being able to read these documents quickly is part of being trusted on a crew.
Key ideas
1. A deficiency is work that is missing, damaged, or not built the way the drawings and specifications show. A blocked drain, a dented corner, a missing piece of blocking and the wrong door handle are all deficiencies.
2. A deficiency report answers who, what, where and when. Look for these parts:
Part What it tells you
Number Each report has its own number, such as DR-021. Use it when you talk about the item.
Date found and found by When it was seen, and who to ask about it
Location Level, room number and name, and often a grid line, as in Reading lesson 17
Reference The drawing, detail or specification section that shows how it should be
Description What is wrong, in words
Photo A photo number, so you can see it before you go
Trade responsible Whose crew fixes it
Target date When it must be fixed
Status Where the item is in the process
3. Status words. Every company uses its own words. In this lesson: - Open: not fixed yet. - Ready for re-inspection: the trade says it is fixed. Nobody has checked yet. - Closed: checked and accepted, with a date and initials. - Reopened: it was checked and it was still not right, so it is open again.
4. A non-conformance report (NCR) is used for a bigger problem: one that cannot be fixed just by redoing the work the way the drawings show. Something built in the wrong place, or the wrong material, needs a decision from the designer before anyone touches it.
5. A punch list is the list of small items still to finish or fix, room by room, before the owner takes over the building. It is written on a walk-through near the end of the job.
6. Reading a log. A deficiency log is a table, so read it the way Reading lesson 4 taught: title and date first, then the column headings, then your row. To find what is late, compare each target date with today's date.
Worked example
Question: Use Document B. What is wrong, where, who fixes it, and by when?
Number and date: DR-021, found 2026-11-03 by T. Morin, the superintendent.
Where: Level 1, Room 104 (Staff room), east wall at grid C-3.
What: the blocking for the upper cabinets is missing. Detail 4 on sheet A-501 shows it.
Who and when: Framing, by 2026-11-05.
What to look at before going: photo P-021, plan A-201 and detail 4 on A-501.
Why it is urgent: the wall is still open. Once it is boarded, adding blocking means cutting the drywall.
Practice documents
All documents in this lesson are fictional. They were written for this lesson.
Document A: The company procedure
Ridgeline Builders Ltd. (fictional company) · Quality procedure QP-03: Deficiencies and the punch list
Words used in this procedure - Deficiency: work that is missing, damaged, or not built the way the drawings and specifications show. - Deficiency report (DR): the form used to record one deficiency. Each DR has its own number. - Non-conformance report (NCR): used instead of a DR when the problem cannot be fixed just by redoing the work the way the drawings show, for example work built in the wrong place or with a material that is not the one specified. The superintendent sends every NCR to the consultant. Nobody fixes, moves or covers NCR work until the consultant answers in writing. - Punch list: the list of small items still to finish or fix in each room before the owner takes over.
Steps 1. Anyone who finds a deficiency tells the superintendent the same day. 2. The superintendent writes a DR within one working day. It gives the location (level, room, grid), the drawing or specification reference, what is wrong, a photo, the trade responsible and a target date. The DR goes on the deficiency log as Open. 3. The superintendent gives a copy of the DR to the foreman of the trade responsible. 4. The trade fixes the work by the target date. If the date cannot be met, the foreman tells the superintendent before the date, and a new date is written on the log. 5. When the work is fixed, the foreman signs the DR, and the log status changes to Ready for re-inspection. Do not cover the work with drywall, ceiling tile, paint or concrete until it has been re-inspected. 6. The superintendent re-inspects. If the work is right, the DR is Closed, with the date and initials. If it is not right, the DR is Reopened, with a note saying why. 7. Two weeks before handover, the superintendent and the consultant walk every room and write the punch list. Any DR that is still open goes on the punch list.

Which item, and which step of the procedure put it there? c) The walk-through was two weeks before handover. What is the handover date?
