lessons.title: Follow a commissioning procedure
lessons.text:
Read a written procedure for starting up a new motor, find who does each step, the hold points and the lockout steps, and decide what to do when something goes wrong.
Why this matters on the job
Commissioning means proving that a new machine is installed right and runs safely before it is handed over to the people who will use it every day. On a new conveyor, pump or fan, the electrician, the millwright and the supervisor each have steps to do, in a set order. The steps are written down, because starting a machine that is wired wrong, misaligned or unguarded can wreck the machine or hurt someone. Millwrights and electricians read procedures like this one on every install. This lesson uses a fictional procedure. On a real job you follow your employer's written procedure, the manufacturer's manual and your supervisor.
This lesson builds on Reading lesson 3, Follow written instructions and Reading lesson 8, Use an equipment manual.
Key ideas
1. Read the whole procedure first. A procedure for a machine is long and split into sections. A warning in Section 4 can change what you do in Section 2.
2. Role tags tell you who does each step. Many procedures put a letter or a word at the start of each step, such as [E] for electrician, [M] for millwright or [S] for supervisor. Only do the steps that are yours. Some steps are for everyone.
3. Hold points. A hold point is a step you must not go past until something is done or someone signs. Look for words like "Do not go on to…", "Stop", "until" and "only then".
4. Conditions and loops. "If…" steps tell you what to do when something is not normal. Often they send you back to an earlier step, such as locking out again.
5. Lockout appears more than once. In BC, the Occupational Health and Safety Regulation (Part 10) says that when machinery is shut down for maintenance, which includes installing, the energy isolating devices must be locked out before work is done. Lockout means using locks to make the machine inoperable or to isolate the energy, following a written procedure. Each worker's personal lock must be marked or tagged with who put it on. Each worker checks that the lockout works before starting, and removes their own lock when their work is done. In a commissioning procedure, lockout shows up every time someone works on the machine, and it comes off only for the tests. Always follow your employer's own lockout procedure.
6. Records. Commissioning steps often say "record" or "sign". The readings written down at start-up become the starting point for maintenance later.
Worked example
Question: In Document A, who does step 2.1, and what must be true before Section 2 starts?
Step 2.1 starts with [E]. The key at the top says [E] is the licensed electrician.
Look back at Section 1. Step 1.3 says everyone locks out the conveyor following procedure LO-01 and checks the lockout before any work starts.
Answer: the electrician does step 2.1, and only after the start-up meeting (1.1), reading the procedure and manual (1.2) and the lockout and check (1.3) are done.
Practice document
Document A
Fraserline Process Ltd. (fictional company) · Procedure CP-12: Commissioning a new conveyor drive motor
Who does what: [E] licensed electrician · [M] millwright · [S] supervisor · [All] everyone on the job This is a training procedure for a fictional company. It does not replace your employer's procedures or the manufacturer's manual.
Section 1. Before you start 1.1 [S] Hold a start-up meeting. Check that the motor nameplate matches the drawing and the purchase order. 1.2 [All] Read this whole procedure and the motor manufacturer's manual. 1.3 [All] Lock out the conveyor following Fraserline lockout procedure LO-01. Each worker puts on their own tagged lock. Check that the lockout works before any work starts.
Section 2. Power path 2.1 [E] Check that the overload relay and the fuses or breaker in the starter are the ones shown on the electrical drawing for this motor. 2.2 [E] Connect the motor leads as shown on the wiring diagram. Close and latch the panel. 2.3 [E] Rotation check. The motor must not be coupled to the gearbox yet, so a wrong direction cannot drive the conveyor backward. Clear everyone from the motor. Remove locks following LO-01. Start the motor for one second and stop it. Watch which way the shaft turns. 2.4 [E] If the direction is wrong, lock out again following LO-01 before you change any wiring. Then repeat 2.3.
Section 3. Alignment 3.1 [All] Lock out again following LO-01. Check that the lockout works. 3.2 [M] Set the motor on its base. Check each foot for soft foot (a foot that does not sit flat on the base) and correct it with shims before you start aligning. 3.3 [M] Align the motor to the gearbox: up and down with shims, side to side with the jack screws. Align to the limits in the manufacturer's manual. Record the final readings on form CP-12A. 3.4 [M] Install the coupling and the coupling guard. Do not go on to Section 4 until the guard is installed.
Section 4. Test run 4.1 [S] Check that everyone is clear of the conveyor. Each worker removes their own lock following LO-01. 4.2 [S] One person stands at the emergency stop and stays within reach of it for the whole test. 4.3 [S] Bump test: start the motor and stop it right away. Everyone watches and listens for the wrong direction, noise, vibration or rubbing. 4.4 [All] If anything is not normal, press the emergency stop, lock out following LO-01 and tell the supervisor. Do not start the motor again until the cause is found and fixed. 4.5 [S] If the bump test is normal, run the conveyor empty for the time the supervisor writes on form CP-12A. Check for heat, noise and vibration, and record what you find.
Section 5. Hand-over 5.1 [S] Sign form CP-12A. The readings on it are the starting point for future maintenance. 5.2 [S] Only then may production staff run the conveyor.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Use Document A. a) What does [M] stand for? b) Which steps does the electrician do? c) Which step tells the supervisor to check the nameplate?
Task 2 (level 2) These steps are mixed up. Put the letters in the order they happen in Document A.
A. Install the coupling and the guard. B. Connect the motor leads. C. Bump test. D. Hold a start-up meeting. E. Check for soft foot. F. Rotation check, with the motor not coupled. G. Sign form CP-12A.
Order: ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___
Task 3 (level 2) Find the hold points. a) Which step says not to go on to the next section until something is done? What must be done? b) Which step says production staff may run the conveyor only after something has happened? What?
Task 4 (level 2) a) List every step in Document A where workers lock out. b) List every step where locks come off. c) Why do the locks come off in those steps?
Task 5 (level 2) a) In step 2.3, why must the motor not be coupled to the gearbox yet? Use the words in the step. b) In step 3.2, what is soft foot, and when must it be fixed?
Task 6 (level 3) During the bump test in step 4.3, you hear a rubbing noise from the coupling. Write the steps you take, in order, using Document A.
Task 7 (level 3) A co-worker says: "Leave the coupling guard off for the test run. That way we can see the coupling turn." a) Which step does this break? b) What would you say to your co-worker?
Task 8 (level 3) a) Why does the bump test (4.3) come after the alignment (Section 3), and not before? b) Why does step 4.2 put a person at the emergency stop? c) Key idea 5 says the BC Regulation requires lockout to follow a written procedure. Which document in this lesson is that written procedure, and where would you find it on a real job?
Check yourself
What does commissioning mean?
What is a role tag, and why does it matter?
Name two words or phrases that tell you a step is a hold point.
When a worker is done working on locked-out equipment, whose job is it to remove that worker's lock?
Why do the readings recorded at commissioning matter later?

lessons.title: Topographic maps and site plans
lessons.text:
Read the scale, contour lines, spot elevations, grid and legend on a topographic map and a site plan, and use them to find heights, distances, slope and which way water will run.
Why this matters on the job
Before a crew digs, sets forms or plans a drain, someone has to know how the ground lies. Which corner of the lot is high? Where will rain water run? How steep is the road into a remote camp job? A topographic map shows the land around a job over many kilometres. A site plan shows one lot, close up. Both use the same ideas: a scale, contour lines, spot elevations, a north direction and a legend. This lesson follows Reading lesson 14, Drawing scales, and Reading lesson 17, Symbols, legends, grids and schedules.
Key ideas
1. Scale at map sizes. A map scale compares a distance on the map with the real distance on the ground. The most-used Canadian topographic map is 1:50 000. On it, 2 cm on the map is 1 km on the ground, so 1 cm is 500 m (half a kilometre). Natural Resources Canada (NRCan) also makes 1:250 000 maps, where 1 cm is 2.5 km. One 1:250 000 sheet covers the same area as sixteen 1:50 000 sheets.
Real distance = map distance × the scale number. Then change the units: 100 cm = 1 m, and 1000 m = 1 km.
Map distance = real distance ÷ the scale number.
A scale bar is printed at the bottom of the map. Use it on a screen or a copy, because a copy may not be printed at true size.
2. Contour lines. A contour line joins points of the same elevation above mean sea level. - The contour interval is the difference in elevation between two lines next to each other. It is printed in the margin of the map. - On many maps, every fourth or fifth line is a heavier index contour with its elevation written on it. - Lines close together mean a steep slope. Lines far apart mean a gentle slope. Very far apart means flat ground. - Contour numbers are printed so that they read uphill. - Where a contour line crosses a creek, it bends into a V that points upstream. - Water runs downhill, from a higher line toward a lower line, straight across the lines.
3. Spot elevations. A spot elevation is a point with its height written beside it, usually a dot and a number. Topographic maps show them at places like hilltops, road crossings and lakes. Site plans show them at lot corners and other key points.
4. Which way is north. On an NRCan topographic map, north is always at the top. On a site plan, look for the north arrow. Do not assume.
5. The grid and grid references. A topographic map has a square grid. On NRCan maps it is the UTM grid, measured in metres. Eastings are written along the top and bottom edges. Northings are written along the sides. To give a six-figure grid reference: 1. Easting first. Read the number of the grid line to the left of the feature. Then estimate how many tenths of a square the feature is to the east of it. 2. Then northing. Read the number of the grid line below the feature. Then estimate how many tenths of a square it is to the north.
NRCan's memory trick: "In the house, then up the stairs." Go along first, then up.
6. The legend and the margin. The legend tells you what each symbol means. The margin also gives the scale, the contour interval, and the year and edition of the map. NRCan says to check the map data and publication date in the bottom left corner. Roads, buildings and clearings made after that date may not be on the map.
A map never shows what is buried. Before any digging, follow the BC 1 Call steps in Digital lesson 9.
Worked example
Question: Use Figure 1. What is the six-figure grid reference of the cabin, and is the cabin higher or lower than 400 m?
Easting. The grid line to the left of the cabin is 52. The cabin is about 3 tenths of a square east of it. Easting 523.
Northing. The grid line below the cabin is 62. The cabin is about 7 tenths of a square north of it. Northing 627.
Grid reference: 523627.
Height. The heavy line labelled 400 is south of the cabin. The ground rises to the north (the numbers get bigger going north, and the V shapes point north, upstream). So the cabin is higher than 400 m.
Practice documents
Both figures are fictional. They were drawn for this lesson. Figure 1 is drawn in the style of a topographic map, but it is not a real NRCan map.
Figure 1. A fictional topographic map extract at 1:50 000, with Cedar Creek, a road, a bridge, a cabin and two spot elevations. Contour interval 20 m. The blue grid squares are 1 km.
Figure 2. A fictional site plan of Lot 12, Alder Lane, at 1:200, with corner spot elevations, existing contours at a 0.5 m interval and a proposed house.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Use Figure 1. a) What is the scale? b) What is the contour interval? c) How many kilometres wide is one grid square? d) What elevations are written on the two heavy contour lines?
Task 2 (level 1) Use Figure 1. a) What are the two spot elevations? b) How much higher is the higher one than the lower one?
Task 3 (level 2) Use Figure 1. Which way does Cedar Creek flow, north or south? Give two clues from the map.
Task 4 (level 2) Use Figure 1, west of the creek. Each grid square is 1 km, so a tenth of a square is 0.1 km (100 m). a) About how far apart are the 380 and 400 contour lines? b) About how far apart are the 260 and 280 contour lines? c) Which part of the map is steeper, the north or the south? How do you know?
Task 5 (level 2) Use Figure 1. a) Give the six-figure grid reference of the bridge. b) What is at grid reference 523627?
Task 6 (level 2) Use Figure 1. The road crosses the creek on the bridge. Between which two contour elevations is the bridge?
Task 7 (level 2) Use Figure 1. a) How far is it along the road from the west edge of the map (easting 52) to the bridge? b) On a real paper map printed at 1:50 000, how many centimetres long would that stretch of road be? c) On a real 1:50 000 map, you measure 7 cm between two lakes. How far apart are they on the ground?
Task 8 (level 1) Use Figure 2. a) Which corner of the lot is highest? Give its elevation. b) Which corner is lowest? Give its elevation. c) What is the contour interval? d) Which side of the lot faces Alder Lane?
Task 9 (level 2) Use Figure 2. a) How much does the ground fall from the highest corner to the lowest corner? b) Which way will rain water run across the lot? c) What is the existing ground elevation at the middle of the west lot line? How do you know? d) How big is the proposed house, and how far is it from the south lot line?
Task 10 (level 3) Use Figure 2. Work out the percent grade along the west lot line, from the north-west corner to the south-west corner.
percent grade = (fall ÷ distance) × 100
Show your steps. More practice with grades and elevations is in the Construction Operations tab of the Numeracy Hub and in Numeracy lesson 32 (Percent grade between two points on a site).
Task 11 (level 3) Choose a scale. a) You need to print an area 10 km wide and 14 km tall. The map space on the sheet is 20 cm wide and 28 cm tall. Which of these scales shows the area as big as possible and still fits: 1:25 000, 1:50 000 or 1:250 000? Show your working. b) A lot is 20 m wide and 25 m deep. The space on the sheet is 12 cm wide and 15 cm tall. Does it fit at 1:100? Does it fit at 1:200?
Task 12 (level 3) a) Your crew is heading to a job up a logging road. The foreman printed a topographic map. The margin says the map data is from 1985. A new road to the site was built two years ago, and it is not on the map. Is the map wrong? What does this tell you about using the map, and what would you check? b) A labourer wants to measure the distance from the house to the east lot line in Figure 2 by holding a ruler to the screen. What does the note on the plan say? Work out the distance from the written dimensions instead.
Check yourself
On a 1:50 000 map, how far on the ground is 2 cm on the map?
What does a contour line join?
What do contour lines that are close together tell you?
In a grid reference, which do you read first, the easting or the northing?
Where is north on an NRCan topographic map? Where do you look on a site plan?

lessons.title: Writing: make a message another person can use
lessons.text:
Writing helps a reader understand, decide, remember or act. A useful piece of writing might be a two-line request, a completed form, a clear label, a table or a longer explanation. Its success depends on the task. A short note can be effective when it includes exactly what the reader needs. A longer document can fail when its important point is difficult to find.
You can build writing through practice, feedback and revision. You may already organize information for work, study, appointments or activities you choose to support. This chapter gives those actions a visible process. You can use the supplied fictional cases rather than personal experiences. No activity requires a real message to be sent, a real account to be opened or private information to be shared.
All people, organizations, schedules, quantities and funding arrangements below are invented for learning. The documents resemble useful workplace and classroom formats, but they are original simulations. They do not establish a legal reporting requirement or a workplace procedure. The focus is writing that is accurate for the information you have.
See it in action · Writing
Visual guide Please confirm a loan of two calculators. ACCESS IS4S. (2026). Original fictional teaching diagram. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
NEED: 2 calculators by 09:00. RETURN: 11:45; loan not confirmed. Name the reader and request. Include quantity and timing. Ask for confirmation; revise. Please confirm a loan of two calculators. Include collection and return times. A request is not a confirmed loan.
This small fictional example shows the skill in use. NEED: 2 calculators by 09:00. RETURN: 11:45; loan not confirmed.
Try it: Name the reader and request. Include quantity and timing. Ask for confirmation; revise.
Check your result: Please confirm a loan of two calculators. Include collection and return times. A request is not a confirmed loan.
Six parts of writing with a purpose
Visual guide Writing moves between planning, wording, format and review. The learner controls the wording and the revisions, using any agreed access tools. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An original task illustration occupies the left panel; six numbered actions appear on the right. Keep the reader and purpose at the centre. Six connected components: Identify purpose and reader; Plan the writing task; Use words to convey meaning; Choose language and style; Choose a useful format; Review and revise. Revisit a plan, wording or format when feedback reveals a better choice.
The Skills for Success Writing components are:
Identify the task that requires you to write. Name the purpose and intended reader.
Plan the writing task. Gather information, decide what matters and organize it.
Use written words and phrases so you can achieve the purpose of the writing task. Make the meaning clear enough to use.
Choose the appropriate language and style for the writing task. Match the reader, relationship and context.
Choose the appropriate format for the writing task. Use a message, form, list, table or another useful structure.
Review and revise your writing. Check facts, meaning, tone and presentation, then improve them.
Writing is not always a straight line through these components. You may discover a missing fact while drafting. A reader's question may show that your chosen format hides the answer. Going back to the plan is part of writing, not proof that you failed.
You may handwrite, type, use speech-to-text or work with a scribe. To show your Writing skill, you need to control the words, review the resulting text and decide on revisions. A discussion that produces no learner-authored text does not show this chapter's writing outcome. Record supports so the evidence describes what you actually did.
Make the actor, action and time clear
You can think through a sentence aloud, sign it, type it or use another authoring method. Keep control of its words and review the result. Begin with a clear sentence, then use it in a useful whole message.
Start with one sentence
Write or dictate a sentence for this task: “Tell a helper that four blank sheets are needed before two o'clock.” Ask a reader to identify the item, quantity and time. If all are clear, move to the writing case. Otherwise, choose one feature below to practise first.
Name who does what
Read this example: The helper / checks / the folder code / before recording the loan. Mark actor, action, object and condition. Compare “They do it first.” In that version, the reader must guess both actor and action.
Guided task: expand “They need them tomorrow” using these facts: the classroom coordinator needs five blank record sheets by 09:30 Practice Friday. Choose a complete sentence. Check which words prevent guessing. A valid sentence is “The classroom coordinator needs five blank record sheets by 09:30 Practice Friday.” Other word orders work.
Put a boundary between complete ideas
Consider: “The file is saved the location still needs checking.” Say each idea separately: The file is saved. The location still needs checking. Each has an actor/topic and an action/state. A full stop makes the boundary visible. Another valid choice is “The file is saved, but its location still needs checking.” Notice what but connects: one completed action and one pending check.
Guided repairs:
“The helper counted eight sheets the note lists ten.”
“I wrote the heading it still needs a date.”
“Please check the code before the loan is recorded.”
Check: the first two need boundaries or suitable connecting words; the third is already usable and need not be changed. A long sentence is not automatically wrong. Keep wording that carries the meaning clearly.
Put the reader's action where it can be found
Given “Please confirm. We may need a second box. The count is not complete,” identify what must be confirmed and what remains unknown. The agreed confirmation time is 11:00. Here is a clearer request: Please confirm the completed count by 11:00 before deciding whether another box is needed. Compare the two versions. A clearer sentence must not turn an uncertain need into a confirmed order.
Fresh exit task
Use only these new facts: The practice instructor needs three large-print labels by 14:00 Practice Monday. Two labels are prepared. The remaining label has not been checked. Ask the materials helper to confirm when it will be ready. Write two or three sentences for the helper. Keep prepared, checked and ready distinct; do not claim the whole set is ready. Underline the requested action and mark sentence endings.
Ask a reader to say how many labels are needed and what action they would take. Revise if their reading differs, or explain why the text works. A possible complete response is: “The practice instructor needs three large-print labels by 14:00 Practice Monday. Two are prepared; the remaining label has not been checked. Please confirm when it will be ready.” Your wording can differ while preserving these facts. Record any wording supplied by another person.
Continue to “Repair ambiguity” for several ambiguities, or “Complete the form” for a factual record. For the fresh handover checks, remove these models and use different supplied information. Ask for further sentence, spelling or paragraph practice when that would help you communicate your meaning.
Start with the reader and the needed action
Before drafting, answer four questions: Who will read this? What do they need to know? What should they do next? What information do I have the authority and evidence to state? These questions prevent two common problems: writing everything you know, and leaving out the one detail that makes action possible.
A useful request often begins with the request, followed by the context needed to answer it. A factual record often begins with what happened and when. A public notice often begins with the event and essential arrangements. “Formal” does not have to mean complicated. Respectful, direct wording usually helps readers across roles.
Case document A: a resource request with a deadline
Fictional classroom planning record • Introductory learning session
The Northside Learning Room is preparing a classroom session for twelve learners. The session begins at 09:00 on Practice Thursday. The learning tasks include reading a short project brief, checking a small number table and recording a result. Paper workbooks are already available for every learner. Learners may work in pairs for the calculator activity, so the plan calls for six calculators at the start of the session.
The resource cupboard currently contains four working practice calculators. The desk helper can check whether two more can be lent from another classroom. The helper needs the item, quantity, required time and return plan. They cannot promise a loan until the other classroom's booking has been checked. The intended recipient of your message is the resource desk helper, not the learners attending the session.
The session ends at 11:30. The instructor has offered to return the borrowed calculators to the resource desk by 11:45. The helper asks to receive the request by 15:00 on Practice Wednesday so they can check availability. If the extra calculators cannot be supplied, the instructor will adapt the activity. Your role is to request the items and ask for confirmation, not to claim they are already booked.
The planning record also mentions that one staff member prefers tea and that the room's old storage labels were blue. Neither fact affects the calculator request. The names and needs of individual learners are not required. Use the group size only if it helps explain the quantity. This is a practice message; do not send it to a real service.
Define the writing task
Write a planning note that names the reader, purpose, requested action and information you must avoid presenting as confirmed. Give the note a useful title. Include one sentence explaining why the learners' personal details are unnecessary for this task.
Select the information
Make a two-column planning table: Include and Leave out. Sort at least eight details from case A. For two choices, explain how the detail helps or distracts from the reader's decision. Check that your Include column contains the exact extra quantity, required time, return plan and request deadline.
Organize before drafting
Plan a four-part request: subject line, request, supporting context and confirmation question. Write short notes under each part. Arrange the information so the helper can answer without searching the whole paragraph. If a fact is missing, mark the question you would ask rather than inventing an answer.
Worked example 1: turn the plan into a useful request
Visual guide A useful request separates the reader, needed facts and action. “Please confirm” keeps a proposed loan distinct from a completed booking. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
An annotated request asks the resource helper for two calculators by 09:00 on Practice Thursday. Four available plus two requested would make six for pairs. The loan is pending, borrowed items are to return by 11:45, and the request is due by 15:00 on Practice Wednesday. The callouts identify reader, needed facts and requested confirmation.
Subject: Request for two calculators for Practice Thursday
“Hello resource desk team. Could we borrow two calculators for the Northside Learning Room session starting at 09:00 on Practice Thursday? We have four calculators and need six for paired activities. The instructor can return the borrowed items by 11:45. Please confirm whether two are available. This request is being prepared before the 15:00 Practice Wednesday deadline. Thank you.”
The message states the extra quantity rather than the total quantity. It includes when the items are needed and when they will return. “Could we borrow” and “please confirm” show that this is a request, not an established booking. The subject lets the recipient understand the topic before opening the message.
The model is one valid version, not wording to memorize. A shorter message could work if it retained the decision-making details. A more familiar greeting could also be appropriate. The test is whether the intended reader can understand and respond accurately.
Write your request
Using your plan, write a complete practice message of about 70–110 words. Include a subject and an explicit question the helper can answer. Check the quantity against case A. Then underline the words that show availability is not yet confirmed. Keep your own wording rather than copying the worked example sentence by sentence.
Choose words that carry a clear meaning
Readers should not have to guess who “they” are, what “it” refers to or whether “later” means today or next week. Specific nouns and times can solve these problems. “Return the two borrowed calculators by 11:45” is clearer than “Bring them back later.” Repeating a key noun can be useful when several items or people are involved.
Sentence boundaries also carry meaning. Use one sentence for an action and another for its condition when that makes the instruction easier to follow. Put closely related information together. A comma or full stop is not merely a marking rule; it helps the reader separate ideas. Check names, quantities and units with particular care because an otherwise smooth sentence can still communicate the wrong action.
Repair ambiguity
Revise this practice message using case A: “They need them Thursday. Bring it before the class and give them back after. We need six more, I think. It should be fine.” Make the recipient, item, extra quantity, timing and unconfirmed status clear. Then explain two changes you made and the misunderstanding each prevents.
Change the reader
Now write a short classroom notice for the twelve learners. They need to know that the activity can begin with supplied paper workbooks and that they do not need to bring a personal calculator. The borrowing request is still pending. Write 40–70 words that explain what learners should bring or do without promising that six calculators have been secured. Identify one detail from your request that this audience does not need.
Plan a factual record before interpreting it
A record is useful when another person can understand what was observed, what was reported by someone else and what remains unknown. Separate those categories. “The box contained 22 workbooks when counted” is an observation in the case below. “The supplier deliberately removed two” is an accusation that the case does not support.
Use who, what, when and where as prompts, then add the action taken and the unresolved question. Not every form needs all possible details. A classroom materials record should not include personal learner information simply because there is room on the page. A blank field may mean information is missing; use “not provided in the case” where appropriate rather than making up a name or code.
Case document B: the workbook delivery
Fictional materials-desk case • Practice Tuesday
At 09:10, a classroom helper receives a sealed box at the Northside resource desk. The delivery note lists 24 copies of the introductory workbook. The outside label reads “Introductory workbooks, box 1 of 1.” The case gives no order number or supplier contact name. The helper opens the box on the desk and counts 22 workbooks. A second classroom helper independently counts the same 22 copies at 09:15.
The helpers keep the delivery note and put the 22 workbooks together on the resource shelf. At 09:20, they tell the instructor that the note and count differ. The instructor asks for a short written record so the resource coordinator can check the order. The coordinator has not yet contacted the supplier. No explanation for the difference has been confirmed.
The class needs the workbooks for a later session, and existing spare copies may be available. The instructor will decide how to prepare that session after checking the cupboard. The helpers should not promise replacement delivery, describe a refund, change the supplier's paperwork or claim that anyone caused the discrepancy. Their immediate writing task is to preserve a clear account and request the appropriate check.
One draft note on the desk says, “The supplier messed up again and left us short. Someone should fix this right away.” That draft contains an unsupported claim about a repeated problem, gives no quantities and does not identify who should take the next step. You have enough information to produce a more useful record.
Complete the form
Create and complete this practice form using case B: Practice day; location; item; receipt time; quantity on delivery note; quantity counted; count-check time; action already taken; information still missing; requested follow-up. Use short entries where they are sufficient. Do not invent an order number or contact name. Keep the difference between the receipt time and recount time visible.
Replace judgement with evidence
Rewrite the draft note from case B as three or four factual sentences. Include the quantities, the independent recount, the action already taken and the next check. Mark one phrase you removed because it was unsupported. Explain how the revision lets the resource coordinator investigate without accepting an accusation as fact.
Worked example 2: order the record for the reader
Visual guide Record the quantities and sequence before interpreting the cause. Receipt, recount and notification are different events. Open full-size visual
Read the visual description
A factual record compares a delivery note of twenty-four copies with an independent count of twenty-two, a difference of two with no confirmed cause. The timeline records receipt at 09:10, recount at 09:15 and informing the instructor at 09:20.
An unordered note reads: “Instructor told. Twenty-two books. It said twenty-four. Counted again at 09:15. Box arrived 09:10.” A useful revision is:
“At 09:10 on Practice Tuesday, a box of introductory workbooks arrived at the Northside resource desk. The delivery note listed 24 copies. Two helpers counted 22 copies, with the independent recount completed at 09:15. The instructor was informed at 09:20. The resource coordinator is asked to check the order and the discrepancy. The cause has not been confirmed.”
The revision organizes events in time order, names the item and distinguishes the listed quantity from the observed count. It does not hide the uncertainty. It also does not add a conclusion about who is responsible. The reader can now see both the evidence and the action requested.
Write a short record for a handover
Write a 100–140-word handover record for the resource coordinator using case B. Include a heading, a factual account and a separate Follow-up needed line. State what happened to the delivered workbooks and delivery note. Review your wording for a claim that goes beyond the evidence. A partner should be able to identify the discrepancy and the next step from your text alone.
Choose a format that supports the task
Different formats do different work. A numbered list is useful when order matters. Bullets suit a set of items without a required sequence. A table helps readers compare the same categories across several items. A paragraph explains a relationship or reason. A form helps collect a consistent set of fields.
You can combine formats, but every extra element should serve the reader. A large title cannot repair an inaccurate table. A colour highlight should not be the only way a reader knows which item matters. Clear labels and words should preserve the meaning in black-and-white print or an accessible text version.
Write an ordinary classroom procedure
Use these complete fictional borrowing rules: a learner chooses an available practice item; tells the desk helper the item code and learning ID; the helper checks the current sheet and agrees a return point; the learner checks the recorded item and return point; the item is returned to the helper at that point. If the item is unavailable, the learner asks about a suitable alternative. Write five numbered steps and a separate sentence for the unavailable-item condition. This is a classroom-resource procedure, not equipment-operation guidance.
Turn notes into a readable table
Convert these supplied notes into a table with a clear title and headings: “C04 basic calculator available; C05 large-display calculator reserved; B12 measurement practice book in use; B16 document-reading practice book available. Statuses are for this classroom exercise only. The helper checks the current sheet before agreeing to a loan.” Include the status limitation and checking instruction below the table. Explain why item codes and status labels need separate columns.
Match style to the reader without losing respect
Style includes tone, vocabulary, sentence length and how directly you state the action. A familiar team message can be brief without becoming vague. A message to someone you have not met can be courteous without using elaborate phrases. Avoid labelling readers as careless or assuming why they have not responded. Describe the information needed and make the next step clear.
Plain language does not mean removing every technical term. Some terms are necessary. Explain them when the audience may not know them, and use the same term consistently. A notice for visitors may say “the organization that owns the route” before using “owner.” An internal record may use the established role title without repeating the explanation.
Case document C: a classroom information display
Fictional Willow Reach project-learning display • Planning brief
The learning group is preparing a classroom display called “From materials to a finished road.” It introduces the pit-or-quarry, plant, haul, place and compact stages and explains that equipment items have different purposes. The display contains no operating instructions and is not a public construction notice. It uses the fictional Willow Reach access project to help visitors ask useful questions about responsibilities and information sources.
In the example, the Town of Willow Reach owns the route and manages the project agreement. Pathway Paving is the contractor engaged to deliver described work. Practice funding is $60,000 from the Town, $40,000 from the fictional Regional Access Fund and $20,000 from the fictional Community Route Fund. The labels and amounts must remain identified as fictional. The brief does not establish any real grant eligibility, permit, schedule or environmental result.
The classroom display visit is on Practice Friday, 13:00–13:40, in Room 2 at the Northside Learning Room. This is an invented session, not an actual invitation. Visitors first check in at reception. They do not need to bring tools or personal devices. Printed explanations are provided. The planning team can prepare enlarged copies if requested by 15:00 on Practice Thursday. Questions and requests are directed to the classroom coordinator in this simulation. Do not invent a phone number or email address.
The group needs two documents: a visitor notice that gives the essential arrangements and an internal planning note identifying who will prepare the materials. The visitor does not need individual learner names or private support information. The internal note should record agreed tasks, not make assumptions about what someone can do based on their background.
Write a visitor notice
Write a notice of 90–130 words using case C. Include a title, purpose, practice day, time, room, first arrival point, what visitors need to bring and how to request enlarged copies. Keep the fictional status visible. Use a structure that helps a reader find the arrangements quickly. Do not add a contact address that was not supplied.
Make the tone useful
Revise this internal draft: “You never follow the plan. Just put the stuff in the room and make it nice. Everyone knows what to do. Don't bother the coordinator.” Use only case C to replace it with a respectful request that identifies a useful task and asks for confirmation where responsibility is not assigned. Explain which details you cannot honestly supply yet. Then write a different opening suitable for the visitor notice rather than the internal team.
Review meaning before polishing sentences
Revision changes the substance: the facts, organization, missing information or suitability for the reader. Proofreading checks the final surface: spelling, punctuation, formatting and small copying errors. Both matter, but polishing an unsupported claim does not make it true. Start with purpose and facts, then work toward presentation.
Read as if you were receiving the message for the first time. Can you locate the action? Are names, dates, times, quantities and units correct? Does “confirmed” actually have evidence? Is the scope clear? Finally, read the text aloud or listen through a tool to notice awkward phrasing. You remain responsible for checking the output of a spelling or writing tool against the source.
Worked example 3: a small edit can change the promise
Draft: “Join our real roadwork tour Friday at 1. Bring your tools. All special copies are ready.”
Case C does not support a real worksite tour, a tools requirement or the claim that requested copies are ready. A substantive revision is: “Visit our fictional project-learning display on Practice Friday, 13:00–13:40, in Room 2. Check in at reception first. Tools are not needed. Ask the classroom coordinator for enlarged copies by 15:00 on Practice Thursday.”
Only after those corrections does proofreading become useful. Check the hyphenation or punctuation if needed, but do not spend the whole review making the wrong event description look polished. The revised wording makes the action possible and keeps promises within the brief.
Check against the source
Review this new draft: “The Willow Reach display runs 13:00–14:00 in Room 3 on Practice Friday. Go straight to the room. Bring a calculator. Enlarged copies can be requested any time. The $120,000 funding comes entirely from the contractor.” Identify every factual conflict with case C, then write a corrected version. Label one correction about time, one about access/instructions and one about project roles or money.
Use reader feedback while keeping authorship
Give your “Write a visitor notice” notice to a partner. Ask them to underline the time, first arrival point and copy-request deadline, then identify one phrase that could be clearer. Listen to their interpretation. Complete at least two purposeful review actions: make one justified change that improves clarity, and check one important fact against case C. If that fact is already correct, retain it and record the verification rather than inventing an error. Keep the first version, revised version and a short change note. You can explain why you declined a suggestion if it would remove accurate information.
Write independently in a new context
Case document D: reserving a practice room
Fictional group-planning brief
Ten learners need a room for a 45-minute peer-learning meeting starting at 14:00 on Practice Monday. They need ten minutes in the room beforehand to arrange paper resources. Room East holds eight people and is available 13:00–14:00. Room West holds twelve and is available 13:30–15:00. These are classroom planning values, not a real booking system.
The desk coordinator handles requests. A room is not reserved until the coordinator confirms it. The message should identify the group size, desired meeting time, setup period, selected room and requested confirmation. It should not include learners' names or reasons for individual support requests. The coordinator will clarify access arrangements with the group if needed.
The group can return the room to its ordinary classroom layout by the end of its requested booking. If a room cannot meet all conditions, the writer should identify the conflict and request an alternative rather than change a requirement silently. Keep copies of the request and any reply so later changes can be traced.
Independent request and record
Write a complete room request using case D. State the whole period you need, including setup, and ask for confirmation. Then make a one-row planning record with request status, room, date label, group size and requested time. The status must match a request that has not yet received a reply. Check that your message and table agree.
Revise when the requirement changes
After drafting “Independent request and record”, read this fictional change: “The group now needs to start at 13:30. All other needs stay the same. No new room availability has been supplied.” Write a follow-up that refers to the previous request, explains the changed need and identifies why the original plan no longer meets all conditions. Ask a precise question instead of claiming an alternative is available. Update the planning record without erasing the history of the first request.
Show what changed in your writing
Choose two pieces you wrote for different audiences or purposes. Add a brief writer's note to each explaining the purpose, chosen format and one important wording decision. Select a before-and-after passage and explain how the revision improved accuracy or usefulness. Finish with a specific next practice goal, such as making confirmation questions clearer or checking times against the source. Use actual text as evidence rather than judging yourself as a “good” or “bad” writer.
A practical check before sharing
Use this final sequence on your own draft: purpose → facts → reader → format → wording → proofread. For a practice message, sharing means giving it to your instructor or partner, not sending it to the fictional organization. For a real message later, check the actual recipient and your authority to share the information.
Identify the writing task
“Define the writing task”, “Change the reader”, “Write a visitor notice”: purpose and audience guide the text.
Plan the writing task
“Select the information”, “Organize before drafting”, “Complete the form”: selected facts and a useful organization.
Use written words and phrases to achieve the purpose
“Write your request”, “Repair ambiguity”, “Replace judgement with evidence”, “Write a short record for a handover”: usable requests and factual records.
Choose appropriate language and style
“Change the reader”, “Write a visitor notice”, “Make the tone useful”: tone and detail fit the reader.
Choose appropriate format
“Complete the form”, “Write an ordinary classroom procedure”, “Turn notes into a readable table”, “Independent request and record”: forms, steps, tables and messages support the task.
Review and revise
“Check against the source”, “Use reader feedback while keeping authorship”, “Revise when the requirement changes”, “Show what changed in your writing”: source checks, feedback and traceable changes.
Local feedback can be Not observed, Not yet demonstrated, Demonstrated with support or Demonstrated independently. Record transfer to a new situation separately. These are learning descriptions, not official proficiency levels. Preserve your draft and revision so the progress is visible, including the support that helped you make it.
Writing · fresh factual handovers
Use the selected form. Produce text that you control, using handwriting, typing, speech-to-text or a scribe under your direction. The reader needs a useful record and a clear next action. No message will be sent. All roles, quantities and events are fictional. Keep the first draft and review notes; a correct first draft does not need an invented error.
Form A · Display posters
Source brief
At 08:45 on Practice Tuesday, a helper received a flat package at the Riverside learning-room desk. Its delivery note listed 12 introductory display posters. The first count found 9 posters. A second helper independently counted 9 at 08:50. The label says Poster package 1 of 1. No order number or supplier contact is supplied.
At 08:55, the helper informed the instructor. The nine posters and delivery note are together in the labelled Display materials tray. The instructor asks for a factual handover to the resource coordinator, who will check the order and tell the instructor the next step before 12:00 Practice Tuesday. The coordinator has not contacted the supplier. No cause, replacement, refund or delivery promise is confirmed.
The posters are for a later classroom display. The instructor will decide whether existing display materials can be used. The helper does not decide that arrangement. A personal phone number written on the outer packaging is not relevant to the handover and must not be copied. The desk's blue pen and a visitor's comment that “deliveries are always wrong” are not evidence about this order.
Writing practice A · Plan for the reader
Make a brief plan naming the reader, purpose, necessary facts and requested next action. Identify two details you will leave out and why. Distinguish completed actions from the decision still pending.
Writing practice A · Write the handover
Write about 80–130 words, with a useful heading and a separate Follow-up needed line. Include the quantities, independent check, sequence, location of the materials and record, unresolved cause and coordinator's next step/deadline. Use your own wording. Do not add a contact address or promise a solution.
Writing practice A · Review meaning
Give the draft to a reader. Ask them to identify the discrepancy, what is already done, where the materials are and who must do what next. Check their interpretation against the brief. Revise a misleading or unclear detail, or record why the tested wording already works. Also check one sentence boundary and one pronoun/reference. Keep the reader's actual response and your decision.
My plan and draft — use another sheet or an accessible document if helpful.
Form B · Orientation cards
Source brief
At 14:05 on Practice Thursday, a helper received a box at the Harbour learning-room desk. The packing record listed 30 orientation cards, but the first count found 26. Another helper independently counted 26 at 14:10. The label says Orientation cards, box 1 of 1. No order number or supplier contact is supplied.
At 14:15, the instructor was informed. The 26 cards and packing record are together in the labelled Orientation materials tray. The materials coordinator needs a factual handover so they can check the order and tell the instructor the next step before 16:00 Practice Thursday. The coordinator has not contacted the supplier. No explanation, replacement, refund or delivery promise is confirmed.
The cards are for a later classroom session. The instructor will decide whether to adapt that session after checking other resources. The helper cannot announce that decision. A personal address written on the box is unnecessary for the handover and must not be copied. The colour of the box and a colleague's remark that “someone must have taken them” do not establish the cause of the discrepancy.
Writing practice B · Plan for the reader
Make a brief plan naming the reader, purpose, necessary facts and requested next action. Identify two details you will leave out and why. Distinguish completed actions from the decision still pending.
Writing practice B · Write the handover
Write about 80–130 words, with a useful heading and a separate Follow-up needed line. Include the quantities, independent check, sequence, location of the materials and record, unresolved cause and coordinator's next step/deadline. Use your own wording. Do not add a contact address or promise a solution.
Writing practice B · Review meaning
Give the draft to a reader. Ask them to identify the discrepancy, what is already done, where the materials are and who must do what next. Check their interpretation against the brief. Revise a misleading or unclear detail, or record why the tested wording already works. Also check one sentence boundary and one pronoun/reference. Keep the reader's actual response and your decision.
My plan and draft — use another sheet or an accessible document if helpful.

lessons.title: Keep a daily work log
lessons.text:
Write short, factual log entries that tell the next person what was done, when, by whom and what still needs doing.
Why this matters on the job
On a BC job site or in a shop, the person who reads your log is often not there when you write it: the next shift, your foreman, the office that does payroll, or you, three weeks later. A good log says what happened in plain facts. It backs up your timesheet, warns the next crew about a problem, and gives a clear record if anyone asks later what was done.
Key ideas
1. Write it soon. Memory fades fast. Write your log at breaks or at the end of the shift, not the next morning.
2. Answer the reporter's questions. Each line should answer as many of these as it can:
Question Example
When? 10:15 am
Where? Bay 3, east wall
Who? J. Moon and I
What was done or seen? cut and tacked 6 brackets
How much or how many? 6 of 10 brackets
What is still open? 4 brackets left, waiting on 3/8" flat bar
3. Facts first. Keep guesses and opinions out, or label them. A fact is something you saw, heard, measured or did. An opinion or guess is what you think about it.
Fact: "Grinder guard on grinder #2 is cracked. Tagged it out of service at 1:40 pm."
Opinion: "Somebody wrecked the grinder again."
If you need to give a reason you are not sure of, say so: "Possible cause: guard was hit during the lunch move. Not confirmed."
4. Use the date and time formats your workplace uses. For all-number dates, the Government of Canada's Language Portal recommends year-month-day with hyphens: 2026-11-06 means November 6, 2026. It cannot be confused with June 11.
5. Short lines are fine. A log is not an essay. Each line can be a short sentence or a phrase, but every line must make sense to someone who was not there. "Done" is not enough. "Pump base bolts torqued and marked, Bay 2" is.
6. Read it once as a stranger. Before you close the log, read it as if you were the next shift. Can they start work from it? Is anything only clear inside your own head?
Worked example
These are an apprentice's rough notes for one shift at Fraser Bend Fabrication (a fictional shop):
brackets bay 3 / 6 done / flat bar out / grinder guard busted, tagged / told Dale / Moon helped am
Here is the same information as a log entry:
Date: 2026-11-06 Shift: 7:00 am to 3:30 pm Written by: R. Thomas
7:15 am. Bay 3. J. Moon and I cut and tacked 6 of 10 wall brackets.
11:30 am. Ran out of 3/8" flat bar. 4 brackets not started.
1:40 pm. Grinder #2 guard cracked. Tagged out of service. Told Dale (lead hand) at 1:45 pm.
Still open: 4 brackets, flat bar order, grinder #2 repair.
What changed:
The date, times and names are added.
"Busted" became what was actually seen.
"Told Dale" now says when, and who Dale is.
The open items are listed at the end, so the next shift finds them fast.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Rewrite each rough note as one clear log line. Use the time, place and details in the brackets.
a) "pipe rack done" (2:10 pm, Unit 4 mechanical room)
b) "leak again" (9:05 am, hose bib on the north side, small drip at the fitting)
c) "boss says wait" (10:40 am, foreman M. Joe said not to pour until the inspector signs off)
Task 2 (level 1) Mark each line F (fact) or O (opinion or guess). Then rewrite the two opinion lines as facts, using only what the line tells you, or say what you would need to find out.
The east stairs were wet at 6:50 am. ___
The night crew is lazy and never cleans up. ___
Delivered: 40 sheets of 5/8" drywall, stacked in Room 112. ___
The forklift is probably going to break down soon. ___
Forklift alarm sounded twice when reversing, then stopped working at 2:20 pm. ___
Task 3 (level 2) During today's class, something will happen that you are not told about in advance. When your instructor asks, write a log entry about it. Include the time, where in the room it happened, who was involved (describe them if you do not know their name), what they did, what they said, and anything they brought in or took out. Write only what you saw and heard.
Task 4 (level 2) Use the worked example log above. Write a handover note of three to five sentences to the next shift lead, Tanya. Tell her what is finished, what is not, and what she needs to know about the grinder. Do not add facts that are not in the log.
Check yourself
Write November 6, 2026 as an all-number date in the order the Language Portal of Canada recommends.
Why is "Done" a weak log line?
Is "The welder looked tired" a fact or an opinion? How could you write what you actually saw?
Name three readers, other than yourself, who might read your work log.
Where in a log entry should you put the jobs that are still open, and why there?

lessons.title: Write sentences that say who does what
lessons.text:
Build clear sentences with a doer, an action and an object, choose active or passive voice on purpose, and keep pronouns and verb tenses from confusing the reader.
Why this matters on the job
"The valve was left open." Who left it open? When? A sentence like this can start an argument on site, or stall a safety investigation. In logs, reports, texts and emails, the reader needs to know who did what, to what, and when. A clear sentence protects you, your crew and the people reading it later.
Key ideas
1. Most sentences have a doer, an action and an object
Doer (subject) Action (verb) Object
The crew laid the pipe.
The gas fitter is connecting the meter.
The apprentice will clean the welding booth.
To find each part, ask questions:
Who or what did it? That is the subject.
Did what? That is the verb. Look for the action word.
To what or whom? That is the object.
Where, when, how, how many? These add detail: "...laid the pipe in the trench on Tuesday."
2. Kinds of words
Kind of word What it does Trade examples
Noun names a person, thing or place welder, flange, shop, Bay 3
Verb shows an action or state cut, torque, is, will check
Adjective describes a noun cracked guard, 3/4" pipe
Adverb describes how, when or where an action happens tighten evenly, reported immediately
3. Pronouns must point to one clear thing
Pronouns are short words like it, they, he, she, this, that. They save space, but only if the reader knows what they stand for.
Unclear: "The forklift hit the trailer. It was damaged." (The forklift or the trailer?)
Clear: "The forklift hit the trailer. The trailer's rear light was damaged."
When something matters, name it. "Unit 14, the yellow skid steer" is clearer than "the machine", which is clearer than "it".
4. Active and passive voice
Active voice puts the doer first. Passive voice puts the object first and often drops the doer.
Active Passive
Ken shut the valve. The valve was shut (by Ken).
The crew is excavating at Bear Creek. Excavation is being done at Bear Creek.
We will charge a late fee. A late fee will be charged.
Passive voice uses a form of be (is, was, were, has been, will be) plus the action word.
When to use which:
Use active when the reader needs to know who did it. In incident reports, logs and messages about your own work, this is almost always.
Passive is fine when the doer is unknown or does not matter: "The slab was poured on 2026-10-14."
Passive can sound like you are hiding something. "Mistakes were made" sounds worse to a foreman than "I measured from the wrong line. I've re-marked it."
5. Keep the time steady, and match the doer to the verb
A report about what happened is in the past tense: "I checked the gauge, saw 0 psi and opened the valve." Do not switch to "I check... I see..." halfway.
One doer takes the singular form, more than one takes the plural form: "The bolt is loose." "The bolts are loose." "One of the bolts is loose." (The doer is "one", not "bolts".)
Worked example
A lead hand at Salmonberry Framing (a fictional contractor) wrote this note:
The ladder was moved and the area was not taped off. Then the box was dropped and it broke.
These are the facts from the site:
At 10:20 am, Sam moved the ladder to the north wall.
Nobody taped off the area under the scaffold.
At 10:25 am, a box of fittings fell from the second level and split open on the ground. Nobody was hurt.
Rewritten with doers, past tense and clear nouns:
At 10:20 am, Sam moved the ladder to the north wall. Nobody had taped off the area under the scaffold. At 10:25 am, a box of fittings fell from the second level. The box split open on the ground. Nobody was hurt.
Notice: "the box was dropped" became "a box of fittings fell", because the facts do not say anyone dropped it. "It broke" became "The box split open", so the reader is not left guessing. The writer did not add blame that the facts do not support.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) For each sentence, write the subject (S), verb (V) and object (O).
a) The millwright aligned the coupling. b) Our crew will frame the east wall tomorrow. c) The supplier delivered forty studs. d) Maria is grinding the welds on the handrail. e) The inspector checked the firestopping in Room 204.
Task 2 (level 1) Each sentence has a pronoun that could mean two things. Rewrite it so the meaning is clear. Make your own choice where needed and say which you chose.
a) The pipe rolled into the trench box and it was dented. b) Jordan told Lee that he left the van keys in the shop. c) The grinder and the extension cord were both on the floor. Put it away. d) The client called about the invoice and the schedule. This needs an answer by Friday.
Task 3 (level 2) Change each active sentence to passive and each passive sentence to active. For passive sentences with no doer, use the doer in brackets. Then circle the version you would use in an incident report, and say why.
a) The apprentice left the guard off the bench grinder. b) The scaffold was inspected this morning. (doer: the foreman) c) Someone moved the barricade. d) The trench was entered before it was shored. (doer: two labourers) e) I tagged the saw out of service. f) The delivery was signed for. (doer: Priya)
Task 4 (level 2) Fix the verb tense and the doer-verb matches in this log entry. There are five errors.
At 8:00 am I check the tank level and it was low. I call the supplier. The trucks is coming at noon. One of the fill caps are cracked, so I tag it and told the foreman.
Task 5 (level 2) Rewrite this note in active voice using the facts below it. Use past tense and clear nouns. Do not add anything the facts do not say.
The breaker was turned off and the panel was opened. The work was started before the lock was put on.
Facts: At 1:15 pm Darren switched off breaker 12. At 1:17 pm Darren opened panel P2. At 1:18 pm Kim started pulling wire. Darren put his lock on breaker 12 at 1:25 pm.
Check yourself
In "The apprentice swept the shop floor", what is the subject, the verb and the object?
Change "The forms were stripped" into active voice, using "the carpenters" as the doer.
Give one situation where passive voice is fine to use.
Which is correct: "One of the welds are cracked" or "One of the welds is cracked"? Why?
Why can the word "it" cause problems in a report?

lessons.title: Write steps and conditions a crew can follow
lessons.text:
Turn a task into numbered steps, put each condition before the action it controls, and use words like if, unless, and, or and all so they mean exactly what you intend.
Why this matters on the job
Shops and sites run on written steps: how to sign out a tool, how to close up at the end of a shift, what to do if a machine makes a strange noise. When steps are out of order, or a condition is hidden at the end of a sentence, people do the action first and read the warning second. Clear steps let a new apprentice do the job right the first time.
Key ideas
1. One action per step, in order, starting with the action word
Weak: "The grinder should be unplugged and checked and the wheel looked at for cracks."
Clear: 1. Unplug the grinder. 2. Check the wheel for cracks. 3. Check that the guard is in place.
Start each step with a verb (unplug, check, sign, return). Number the steps when the order matters. Use bullets when it does not.
2. Put the condition before the action it controls
People act on the first words they read.
Risky: "Give the tool to the crib attendant if it is damaged."
Better: "If the tool is damaged, give it to the crib attendant."
3. Condition words have exact meanings
Word Meaning Example
if ... then when the first part is true, do the second If the cord is cut, then tag the tool out.
unless do this, except when the condition is true Lock the gate unless the foreman is still on site.
and every part must be true You need boots and a hard hat. (Both.)
or any one part is enough Bring a pay stub or a letter from your employer. (Either one.)
only this and nothing else Crib staff only.
except everything, leaving one out Return all tools except your own hand tools.
"And" is all-or-nothing. If a job posting asks for three things joined by "and", you need all three. If it says "or", one is enough.
4. Short signs are conditions too
A sign packs a whole sentence into a few words.
"Hard hats required beyond this point" means "If you go past this point, wear a hard hat."
"Authorized personnel only" means "If you are not authorized, do not enter."
5. "All" means every single one
A statement with "all" is false if you can find even one case that does not fit. That case is called a counter-example.
"All the pipe in this building is copper." One PEX line proves it false.
If you are not sure every case fits, write "most", "some" or the exact number.
Worked example
A lead hand at Cedar Ridge Mechanical (a fictional company) wrote this for new hires:
Tools come from the crib and you sign the sheet with your name and the tool number and the time, and if it's broken when you bring it back tell the attendant, and everything has to be back by 3:15 unless you're on overtime, then leave it in the overnight bin.
Rewritten as steps:
Signing tools out and in
Take the tool from the crib.
Write your name, the tool number and the time on the sign-out sheet.
Return the tool by 3:15 pm. - If you are on overtime, put the tool in the overnight bin instead.
If the tool is damaged when you return it, tell the crib attendant.
What changed: one action per step, each step starts with a verb, the two conditions ("on overtime", "damaged") are placed where the reader will need them, and "everything" became "the tool", because the steps are about one tool at a time.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Read this fictional job notice. Then answer the questions.
Cedar Ridge Mechanical: Shop helper (fictional posting) To apply, you must be 18 or older and live in Surrey or Langley. You must have a valid BC driver's licence or your own way to get to our Surrey and Langley shops. You need steel-toed boots. If you have not taken a fall protection course, we will provide one in your first week.
a) List every condition an applicant must meet.
b) Which requirement can be met in two different ways? What are the two ways?
c) An applicant is 19, lives in Langley, has no driver's licence, takes the bus to both shops and owns steel-toed boots. She has never taken a fall protection course. Does she qualify? Explain.
Task 2 (level 2) Rewrite each sign as a full "If ... then" sentence.
a) No hot work without a permit. b) Ear protection required when the planer is running. c) Visitors must sign in at the office. d) Do not enter. Confined space.
Task 3 (level 2) Mark each statement True or False. For each false statement, give one counter-example.
a) All fasteners are made of steel. ___ b) Some fittings have threads. ___ c) All squares are rectangles. ___ d) All rectangles are squares. ___ e) All apprentices are under 25 years old. ___
Task 4 (level 3) Use these notes from the shop foreman at Fraser Bend Fabrication (fictional) to write a numbered end-of-shift procedure. Give it a title. Put each condition before its action.
Notes: sweep your bay. Put offcuts in the scrap bin, but aluminum goes in the blue bin, not the steel bin. Shut off the welder and close the gas cylinder. If you used the plasma table, empty the dross tray if it's more than half full. Coil the extension cords and hang them. Last person out turns off the compressor and locks the side door. Write anything broken in the shop log.
Task 5 (level 3) Give your Task 4 procedure to a partner. Your partner reads it aloud and acts out each step exactly as written, without guessing. Note every place where they had to stop and ask. Revise your procedure so those questions do not come up.
Check yourself
Rewrite with the condition first: "Shut down the pump if the pressure drops below the red line."
A sign says "Gloves and safety glasses required." Do you need one or both?
What is a counter-example?
Why should each step begin with an action word?
When should you use a numbered list instead of bullets?

lessons.title: Fill in a workplace form correctly
lessons.text:
Read a form before you write, put each fact in the right box, calculate hours with BEDMAS, report facts without accusing anyone, and check before you sign.
Why this matters on the job
Timesheets, tool sign-outs, material requests and report forms decide whether you get paid right, whether the right parts show up, and whether a problem gets fixed. A form is a piece of writing with the structure already built for you. Your job is to put the right fact in the right box, clearly, so the person who reads it does not have to come and find you.
Key ideas
1. Read the whole form before you write anything. Look for:
who fills in each part. Boxes marked "Supervisor" or "Office use only" are not for you.
the format each box wants. WorkSafeBC forms, for example, print (yyyy-mm-dd) beside date boxes.
where your signature goes, and what you are signing for.
2. Fill every box that applies to you. If a box does not apply, write N/A (not applicable) so the reader knows you did not skip it.
3. Print so a stranger can read it. If you write by hand, use pen and print clearly. If the form asks for capital letters, use them.
4. Numbers need units, and the maths must check. Write "38.5 h", "3 coils", "20 m". Then check every total.
5. Calculate hours with BEDMAS. Hours worked = (finish time − start time) − unpaid break. Do the bracket first.
Finish 5:00 pm, start 7:00 am, 30 min unpaid lunch. Change 5:00 pm to 17:00 so you can subtract. (17.0 − 7.0) − 0.5 = 10.0 − 0.5 = 9.5 h
Common mistake: doing the break first. 17.0 − (7.0 − 0.5) = 10.5 h is wrong. BEDMAS says brackets first, so write the bracket where it belongs.
6. Report facts, not accusations. Follow your workplace's reporting rule. The fictional company in this lesson has this one: report a problem to your supervisor, do not confront anyone yourself, and let the supervisor investigate. On a report form, write what you saw. Leave out who you think did it unless you saw it happen.
7. Check, then sign. Your signature says the form is true and complete. Never sign a blank form or one you have not read. Keep a copy or a photo if your workplace allows it.
Worked example
Cedar Ridge Mechanical (a fictional company) uses this timesheet. Here is Monday for an apprentice:
Day Date (yyyy-mm-dd) Job # Start Finish Unpaid break Hours
Mon 2026-11-02 26-118 7:00 am 3:30 pm 0.5 h 8.0
Working: 3:30 pm is 15:30, or 15.5 in decimal hours. (15.5 − 7.0) − 0.5 = 8.5 − 0.5 = 8.0 h.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Fill in the Cedar Ridge Mechanical timesheet below for Alex Paul, employee number 4471, for the week ending Friday, November 6, 2026. Use these facts:
Monday to Thursday: job 26-118 (Langley townhouses). Friday: job 26-120 (Surrey warehouse).
Monday and Tuesday: 7:00 am to 3:30 pm, 30 min unpaid lunch.
Wednesday: 7:00 am to 5:00 pm, 30 min unpaid lunch.
Thursday: 7:30 am to 3:30 pm, 30 min unpaid lunch.
Friday: 7:00 am to 1:00 pm, 30 min unpaid break.

Day Date (yyyy-mm-dd) Job # Start Finish Unpaid break Hours
Mon __ ______ ______ ______ ______ ______
Tue __ ______ ______ ______ ______ ______
Wed __ ______ ______ ______ ______ ______
Thu __ ______ ______ ______ ______ ______
Fri __ ______ ______ ______ ______ ______
Total ______

Task 2 (level 1) Show your working for Wednesday and Thursday using BEDMAS, then add the week's total.
Task 3 (level 2) Read the case, then fill in the report form.
Case. Cedar Ridge Mechanical has a rule: report missing or damaged material to your supervisor the same day, do not confront anyone, and let the supervisor investigate.
On Tuesday, 2026-11-03, at 3:30 pm, apprentice Jesse Lim (employee #4502) counted 8 coils of 3/4" PEX pipe in the locked cage at the Langley townhouse site (job 26-118). On Wednesday, 2026-11-04, he arrived at 6:50 am. A white pickup truck was parked beside the cage. It left at 7:00 am. Jesse did not see the licence plate or the driver. At 7:10 am he saw that the cage lock was hanging open and only 5 coils were left. At 7:20 am he told his supervisor, Carla Ng (site foreman), and filled in the form.
