lessons.title: Report a workplace injury in BC
lessons.text:
Know who writes which injury report in BC, and write a clear, factual description of how an injury happened.
Why this matters on the job
If you are hurt at work in BC, several people may have to write about it: you, the first aid attendant and your employer. What you write affects your WorkSafeBC claim, and it helps the employer find out what went wrong so the next worker does not get hurt. A clear, factual description of how it happened is one of the most important things you will ever write at work.
Key ideas
1. Who writes what (WorkSafeBC, checked November 2026)
Who What they write or do
You, the worker Tell your employer as soon as it is safe to do so. If you get medical care, tell the clinic or hospital you were hurt at work. Report the injury to WorkSafeBC online (24 hours a day, 7 days a week) or by phone through Teleclaim: 604.231.8888 in the Lower Mainland, 1.888.967.5377 toll-free in Canada, Monday to Friday, 8 am to 6 pm. The paper Form 6 for fax or mail is no longer available. You have up to one year from the date of the injury to report, but WorkSafeBC asks you to report right away.
You, if your employer asks Form 6A, Worker's Notice to Employer of Injury or Occupational Disease. You give it to your employer, not to WorkSafeBC.
The first aid attendant (or the person who gave first aid) A first aid record for every first aid treatment. WorkSafeBC offers Form 55B23, or the employer can use its own template. Records are kept at least 3 years and are confidential.
The employer Form 7, Employer's Report of Injury or Occupational Disease. The employer must report within 72 hours (three days) if the worker got medical treatment beyond first aid or lost time from work.
The employer An incident investigation if the injury was serious or needed medical treatment: a preliminary investigation and report within 48 hours, and a full investigation report to WorkSafeBC within 30 days. WorkSafeBC's template is Form 52E40.
Anyone who sees a hazard Under section 3.10 of the BC Occupational Health and Safety Regulation, a person who sees what appears to be an unsafe or harmful condition or act must report it as soon as possible to a supervisor or the employer.
When you report to WorkSafeBC, have this ready: your contact information and your employer's, your Personal Health Number if you have one, the date, place and how you were hurt, details of your first medical visit, and, if you missed work, your earnings for the past 12 weeks and your Social Insurance Number.
2. Investigations look for causes
An employer's investigation looks for the unsafe conditions, acts or procedures that led to the incident, so they can be fixed. The BC government's training handbook for joint health and safety committees says the outcome of an investigation should never be the allocation of blame. Write so your report helps find the cause.
3. How to describe what happened
Most injury forms have a box like "Describe how the incident happened." A good description:
follows the order things happened
is in the past tense and active voice: "I slipped", "the board hit my shin"
says what you were doing, with what tool or material, and where
names the body part and the side (left, right, both)
describes conditions you saw: wet, dark, missing guard, missing cleat
names witnesses
leaves out blame and guesses ("the foreman never fixes anything", "I wasn't careful")
Fact Opinion or blame
The ramp was wet. Nobody cares about this ramp.
Two cleats were missing from the lower part of the ramp. The foreman should have fixed it.
I felt pain in my right knee right away. It was my own stupid fault.
4. Protect personal information
Injury forms ask for your Social Insurance Number and Personal Health Number. Give them only on the real form to the right person. In class, use only the fictional details in the case.
Worked example
A weak description:
Was carrying stuff and fell on the ramp. Hurt my leg. Ramp is bad.
A clear description (fictional case, written by the worker):
At about 9:15 am I was walking down the plank ramp at the east entrance, carrying a box of drywall screws in both hands. My right foot slipped on mud on the ramp and I fell onto my left hip and left elbow. I felt pain in my left elbow right away. Kai Larsen was at the bottom of the ramp and saw me fall. I reported it to the first aid attendant at 9:20 am.
Practice
Use this case for Tasks 2 to 5.
Case (fictional). Dakota Joe is an apprentice carpenter with Salmonberry Framing at the Willow Creek duplex site. On 2026-10-28 it had been raining since 7:00 am. At about 10:40 am Dakota was carrying a sheet of 3/4" plywood down the temporary ramp on the north side of the building. Two cleats were missing from the lower part of the ramp. His left boot slipped on the wet ramp. He fell onto his right knee and right hand, and the edge of the plywood hit his left shin. Ana Silva, a carpenter, was cutting at the saw station and saw him fall. At 10:50 am first aid attendant Ray Morin cleaned and bandaged a 3 cm cut on Dakota's left shin and put ice on his right knee. Dakota went back to work on light duty at 11:30 am. By 3:00 pm his right knee was swollen. After work he went to a walk-in clinic. The doctor told him to stay off work the next day.
Task 1 (level 1) Match each report to who writes or does it: W (worker), F (first aid attendant) or E (employer).
a) First aid record ___ b) Form 7 ___ c) Report to WorkSafeBC online or by Teleclaim ___ d) Form 6A, if asked ___ e) Preliminary investigation within 48 hours ___
Task 2 (level 2) Mark each statement F (fact) or O (opinion or blame). For each O, write what you could say instead, or say it should be left out.
It had been raining since 7:00 am. ___
Dakota should have been more careful. ___
Two cleats were missing from the lower part of the ramp. ___
The plywood edge hit Dakota's left shin. ___
This company always cuts corners on safety. ___
Task 3 (level 2 to 3) You are Dakota. Write the answer to "Describe how the incident happened" for Form 6A. Use 80 to 120 words. Write in the first person ("I"), past tense and active voice. Include the time, place, what you were carrying, what you saw about the ramp, the body parts and sides, and the witness.
Task 4 (level 2) You are Ray Morin. Write three short entries for the first aid record:
a) Description of the injury: __________
b) First aid treatment given: __________
c) Actions taken after treatment: __________
Task 5 (level 3) Before Dakota fell, a labourer named Chris had noticed the missing cleats at 8:00 am. Write the message Chris should have sent to the site foreman, Leah Ross, under section 3.10 of the OHS Regulation. Use three to five sentences. Say what the hazard is, where it is, when you saw it, and what you did to warn others.
Check yourself
Who fills in a first aid record?
Within how many hours must an employer report an injury to WorkSafeBC when the worker got medical treatment beyond first aid?
Where do you hand in Form 6A?
Why should an injury description leave out blame?
Give two ways a worker can report an injury to WorkSafeBC.

lessons.title: Text and email a foreman or client
lessons.text:
Choose text or email, lead with the point, write a subject line that says what the message is about, match your tone to the reader, and confirm spoken agreements in writing.
Why this matters on the job
Much of the writing you do in the trades is on your phone. You text your foreman that a delivery is short. You email a homeowner that the install date has moved. You confirm a change the super asked for on the phone. These messages are read fast, often on a small screen, and sometimes forwarded to people you never meant to see them. A clear, polite message gets the answer you need and keeps a record if there is a disagreement later.
Key ideas
1. Pick the right channel
Use When
A text Short, quick, today: "Delivery is here", "Running 10 min late".
An email More detail, attachments, clients, anything you may need a record of later.
A phone call, then a written note Something urgent or complicated. After the call, send a short text or email saying what was agreed.
2. Lead with the point
Put what you need, and by when, in the first line. The reader may only see the first line in a notification.
Weak: "Hey so I got to the site and was looking around and the guys from yesterday..."
Clear: "Need 6 more 2x6x10 by noon. Only 14 of 20 came on today's load."
3. Give the details the reader needs to act
Who, what, where, when, how many. Name the job or address. Keep one topic per message, so replies don't get mixed up.
4. Write a subject line that says what the email is about
Weak: "Question", "Update", "Hi"
Clear: "Job 26-118: drywall delivery moved to Thursday 2026-11-12"
5. Match the tone to the reader
Reader Tone
Your crew or foreman Short is fine. Use the shortcuts your crew already uses. Stay respectful.
A client, inspector or office Greeting, full sentences, no slang, no ALL CAPS, sign with your name and company.
Write as if your message could be forwarded to your boss, the client and a lawyer. If you are angry, wait before you send.
6. Photos need words
A photo of a cracked fitting means nothing without a caption: "Cracked 1/2" tee, kitchen ceiling, Unit 4. Photo taken 9:20 am."
7. Confirm spoken agreements in writing
If someone tells you on the phone or on site to change the work, send a short note: "As we discussed at 2:15 pm today, ... Please reply to confirm." Now there is a record.
8. Never text while you drive
In BC, the Motor Vehicle Act, section 214.2, says a person must not use an electronic device while driving, and must not send text-based messages or email from one. The penalty is a $368 fine and 4 penalty points. Pull over and park safely before you read or write.
Worked example
A vague text to the foreman:
hey no pipe
A clear text:
Hi Marcus, the 3/4" PEX for Unit 4 isn't in the cage. Need it to start rough-in. Can you check with the supplier? I'm on hose bibs at Unit 2 until you let me know.
An email to a client from Cedar Ridge Mechanical (a fictional company):
Subject: Your furnace install at 2214 Birch Lane moved to Tuesday, November 17
Hello Ms. Thomas,
The new furnace for your home will be installed on Tuesday, November 17, instead of Thursday, November 12. The supplier has told us the furnace will not arrive until November 16.
Our installers will arrive between 8:00 and 8:30 am and expect to finish by 4:00 pm. The heat will be off during that time.
Could you please reply by Friday to confirm that someone will be home to let us in?
Thank you, Jordan Paul Service Coordinator, Cedar Ridge Mechanical
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Rewrite each vague text so the reader knows what is needed. Add any details you need and say what you added.
a) "cant make it" b) "the thing is broken again" c) "call me"
Task 2 (level 1 to 2) You are at the Surrey warehouse site (job 26-120). The boom lift you were told to use is there, but its battery is dead and it will not start. Your foreman, Priya, is at another site. Write a text to her. Keep it under 50 words.
Task 3 (level 2) Write an email from you at Cedar Ridge Mechanical to a client, Mr. Ben Arcand, with a subject line. Use these facts:
His water heater replacement at 77 Cedar Court was booked for Monday, November 9, 2026.
The crew lead is sick, so the job has to move. Wednesday, November 11, is Remembrance Day, a statutory holiday in BC, so the office has rebooked the job for Thursday, November 12.
The crew will arrive between 9:00 and 9:30 am. The job takes about 4 hours.
There will be no hot water from about 9:30 am to 1:30 pm.
Ask him to reply to confirm the new date, or to call the office if it doesn't work.
Task 4 (level 3) Today at 2:15 pm, on the phone, the site superintendent, Dan Oakes, asked you to add two extra hose bibs on the north wall of Unit 6 at the Willow Creek duplex. He said to install them at the same height as the existing ones. Write an email to Dan that confirms the change in writing and asks him to reply. Include a clear subject line.
Task 5 (level 2) This email was written in anger. List three problems with it. Then rewrite it so it is polite and still gets the delivery fixed.
Subject: WRONG AGAIN
you guys sent the wrong fittings AGAIN. this is the 3rd time. we ordered 1/2 inch and got 3/4 inch, now my crew is standing around doing nothing. FIX IT.
Check yourself
Why should the first line of a text say what you need?
Rewrite this subject line so it is useful: "Update".
Name two things a client email should have that a quick crew text might not.
What should you do after someone asks you on the phone to change the work?
What does BC's Motor Vehicle Act say about texting while driving?

lessons.title: Check writing made with a phone or AI tool
lessons.text:
Use voice typing and AI writing tools without losing control of your message. Check every word against the facts, keep private information out, and write so any reader or tool keeps the key facts.
Why this matters on the job
On site you might talk a text into your phone with gloves on, or ask an AI tool to clean up an email to a client. These tools save time, but they also mishear words, change trade terms and sometimes make up facts. The message goes out under your name. You are the one who has to check it.
Key ideas
1. You are the author
A tool can draft or fix your writing. You decide what is sent, and you are responsible for it. The Government of Canada's advice to its own staff says the same thing: take responsibility for what you prepare using AI, review it for accuracy, and do not assume the output is correct.
2. Voice typing: say the punctuation, then read it back
Most phones can type what you say.
iPhone Dictation: turn it on in Settings > General > Keyboard > Enable Dictation, then tap the microphone on the keyboard. You can say punctuation such as "comma" or "question mark". In supported languages it also adds some punctuation for you. Apple's guide: https://support.apple.com/guide/iphone/dictate-text-iph2c0651d2/ios
Gboard (Android or iPhone): tap the microphone on the keyboard and speak. You can say "period", "comma", "question mark" and "new line". Google's guide: https://support.google.com/gboard/answer/2781851
Voice typing often gets these wrong. Check them every time:
words that sound alike: tee and tea, two, to and too, four and for, weld and well
sizes and numbers: "three quarter inch" may come out as 3 quarter inch, 3/4 inch or 0.75
names of people, streets and products
trade terms the phone does not know
3. AI writing tools: check every fact against the source
An AI tool can write smooth sentences that are wrong. It may change a date, invent a form number, quote a law that does not say that, or promise something you never agreed to. The BC Information and Privacy Commissioner's tips say to confirm information you get from a generative AI tool before using it, and, if the tool cites a law, to look at the law itself.
Before you send anything an AI tool helped write:
Put your source facts beside the draft.
Check every name, date, time, number, size, address and price.
Check every promise. Remove any you did not agree to.
Check the tone for your reader.
4. Keep private information out of public AI tools
The BC Information and Privacy Commissioner warns that information you type into a generative AI tool may be stored, used or shared by the company that owns it, and you may not be able to get it back or have it deleted. The Government of Canada tells its staff not to put personal, sensitive or protected information into public AI tools.
On the job, that means do not paste in:
anyone's Social Insurance Number, Personal Health Number, address or phone number
details of a co-worker's injury or health
your employer's prices, bids, drawings or client lists, unless your employer has approved the tool for that use
If you want help with wording, replace names and private details with placeholders like [client] or [address] before you paste.
5. Write so the key facts survive
Your email may be read on a small screen, skimmed, forwarded, found later by a search, or summarized by the reader's own AI assistant. A vague message loses its meaning fast. To keep the key facts:
put the main point and date in the subject line and first sentence
name things: "the Unit 4 water heater", not "it"
write full dates: "Thursday, November 12", not "Thursday" or "next week"
write key facts in the message, not only in a photo or attachment
Worked example
What a plumber said into the phone:
"Hi Marcus I need to three quarter inch tees and for elbows for the unit for kitchen can you bring them by ten"
What the phone typed:
Hi Marcus I need to 3 quarter inch teas and for elbows for the unit for kitchen can you bring them by 10
Checked and fixed:
Hi Marcus, I need two 3/4" tees and four elbows for the Unit 4 kitchen. Can you bring them by 10:00 am?
Fixes: "to" to "two", "teas" to "tees", "for" to "four", "unit for" to "Unit 4", the size written as 3/4", punctuation added, and the time made clear.
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) This text was made with voice typing. The plumber meant: two 1/2" ball valves, Unit 6, the north wall, the fitter's name is Kai, needed before lunch. Fix every error.
hey kye can you grab to half inch bowl valves for unit sex north wall before lunch thanks
Task 2 (level 2) A worker asked an AI tool to "write a polite email to the client". Compare the AI draft with the source facts. List every error or added promise, then write the corrected email.
Source facts: - Client: Ms. Grace Thomas. Address: 2214 Birch Lane. - Furnace install moved from Thursday, November 12, to Tuesday, November 17, 2026, because the furnace will arrive on November 16. - Crew arrives 8:00 to 8:30 am, finishes about 4:00 pm. Heat off during the work. - Ask her to reply by Friday to confirm someone will be home.
AI draft:
Dear Ms. Thompson,
We are pleased to confirm your furnace installation at 2214 Birch Lane has been rescheduled to Tuesday, November 18. As required by WorkSafeBC, our licensed crew will arrive at 7:30 am. The installation will be completed by noon, and we will provide a 10% discount for the inconvenience.
Kind regards
Task 3 (level 2) You want an AI tool to help you write a short report about a near miss on site. Sort each item into OK to paste, Remove or replace first, or Do not paste. Explain each choice in a few words.
a) Your own rough notes: "Ladder slid on wet floor in the stairwell, nobody hurt." b) Your co-worker's full name and Personal Health Number. c) The address of the client's house. d) The sentence "Please make this sound more professional." e) Your employer's price list for the job.
Task 4 (level 3) Rewrite this message so that even a one-line summary would keep the key facts. Use the facts in brackets.
Re: stuff
Hey, so about Thursday, it's not going to work because of the thing with the inspector. Can we do it the week after instead? Let me know.
(Facts: the drywall start at the Willow Creek duplex, Unit 6, was set for Thursday, November 12. The framing inspection has not passed yet. You want to move the drywall start to Monday, November 16. You are writing to the drywall subcontractor, Marie.)
Check yourself
Who is responsible for a message that an AI tool helped write?
Name two kinds of words that voice typing often gets wrong.
What should you do if an AI tool tells you a law or form requires something?
Give two kinds of information you should not paste into a public AI tool.
Why is "about Thursday" weaker than "about Thursday, November 12"?

lessons.title: Write a trades résumé and cover letter
lessons.text:
Build a one-page résumé that shows your skills to a trades employer, choose a format that fits your experience, and write a short cover letter tailored to one job posting.
Why this matters on the job
Before a shop or contractor meets you, they meet your résumé. Job Bank, the Government of Canada's job site, says an employer takes an average of 30 seconds to skim a résumé. Many people have the skills a job needs but do not get called, because the résumé does not show those skills clearly, or does not show them at all. A short, tailored résumé and cover letter get you to the interview.
Key ideas
Tool: you can build your résumé and cover letter in the ACCESS Résumé and cover letter builder. It checks your résumé against a job posting and downloads a Word file or a PDF. What you type stays in your browser.
1. The parts of a résumé
Part What goes in it
Contact information Name, phone, email, city
Summary or objective Two or three lines: the job you want and what you bring
Skills Tools, equipment and abilities the job asks for
Tickets and certificates Safety tickets, licences, course certificates, with dates
Work experience Job title, employer, city, dates, then achievement lines
Education and training Programs, schools, courses, with dates
References People who can speak about your work, with their permission. You can write "Available on request" and bring a list to the interview.
Leave out your Social Insurance Number. Service Canada says you do not have to give your SIN to fill out a job application. An employer needs it only after you are hired and start earning income.
2. Choose a format
Three common formats:
Chronological: jobs listed newest first. Good when you have steady work history in the same field. The Government of Manitoba's job tips say a chronological résumé may work best when you are answering an advertised position.
Functional: grouped by skills (for example "Tools and equipment", "Safety", "Teamwork") with a short job list at the end. Useful when you are changing careers or have gaps in your work history.
Combined: a skills section first, then your jobs newest first.
3. Job Bank's do's and don'ts
From Job Bank's "How to write a good resume":
Keep it clear and short.
Quantify your achievements. Use real numbers.
Use simple words and action verbs.
Limit each section to 5 to 7 bullet points.
Don't use "I", "my" or "me".
Don't just list duties. Show what you did well, with examples.
Leave hobbies out unless they relate to the job.
Weak (duty) Strong (achievement)
Responsible for cleaning the kitchen. Cleaned and sanitized a 40-seat kitchen to health inspection standard every closing shift.
I helped with deliveries. Unloaded and checked 3 to 5 supplier deliveries a day against packing slips.
4. Find your hidden skills
Skills from outside paid work count. Fixing your own truck uses troubleshooting and tool skills. Coaching a youth team uses planning, reliability and communication. Helping run a community event uses organizing, timekeeping and teamwork. Write the skill, then one fact that proves it.
5. The cover letter
Job Bank says a cover letter is your introduction to an employer. It should be short, well written and tailored to the company and the job. You may need a different letter for each job. The Government of Manitoba's tips add: name the position and the posting number, and give an email and phone number where you can be reached.
A simple plan, about 150 to 250 words:
Opening: the job you are applying for, the posting number, and where you saw it.
Middle: two or three things the posting asks for, and proof that you have each one.
Closing: when you can start, how to reach you, and thanks.
Some employers invite applicants to self-identify, for example as part of an employment equity program. Whether you do is your choice.
6. Review before you send
Read it aloud. Check every date, phone number and spelling. Ask someone else to read it. A résumé with typing errors can lose you the interview before anyone reads your skills.
Worked example
Two versions of the same person's résumé, for a fictional shop helper job.
Version 1:
Rowan Pierre I am a hard worker looking for any job. Work: Kitchen at Riverside Diner 2022-2026. I did dishes and cleaning and prep. School: high school
Version 2:
Rowan Pierre Langley, BC | 604-555-0182 | rowan.pierre@example.com
Summary Reliable, safety-minded worker with 4 years in a fast-paced kitchen, now training for the metal fabrication trade.
Skills - Measure and cut to 1/16" with a tape measure and chop saw (trades prep program) - Safe use of grinders, drills and hand tools - Follow written procedures and checklists
Work experience Prep Cook, Riverside Diner, Langley, 2022 to 2026 - Prepped food for a 40-seat restaurant on 5 to 6 shifts a week - Trained 3 new dishwashers on safe chemical use - Did not miss a scheduled shift in 2025
Education and training Trades preparation program, 2026 Grade 12, 2021
References Available on request
Rowan, the diner and the contact details are fictional.
Practice
Use this fictional job posting for Tasks 4 and 5.
Fraser Bend Fabrication, Langley: Shop helper (fictional posting FBF-26-14) We are a small structural steel shop. We need a shop helper to move and prepare material, run the band saw and drill press, grind and clean parts, and keep the shop tidy. You have: reliable attendance, the ability to read a tape measure, basic hand and power tool skills, and steel-toed boots. Forklift experience is an asset. Monday to Friday, 7:00 am to 3:30 pm. Start date: December 1.

lessons.title: Use word roots to spell and explain trade words
lessons.text:
Break long trade words into Latin and Greek roots to remember their meaning and spelling, use Canadian spelling, and explain technical words in plain language when the reader needs it.
Why this matters on the job
Trade work is full of long words: hydraulic, pneumatic, perpendicular, circumference, isometric. You have to read them on drawings and in manuals, and spell them on work orders and in reports. If you know the small parts inside a long word, you can often work out what it means, remember how to spell it, and explain it to a client who has never heard it.
Key ideas
1. Long words are built from parts
Many trade words came into English from Latin and Greek, often through French. A root carries the main meaning. A prefix comes at the front. Put the parts together and the word often explains itself.
thermometer = Greek thermos (hot) + Greek metron (measure) = an instrument that measures heat
hydraulic = Greek hydor (water) + Greek aulos (pipe or tube). The Greek word first named a water organ, a musical instrument.
2. Some roots worth knowing
Root or prefix From Meaning Trade words
hydr-, hydro- Greek hydor water hydraulic, hydrogen
pneum- Greek pneuma wind, breath, air pneumatic
therm- Greek thermos hot thermometer
-meter, metr- Greek metron measure diameter, perimeter, isometric
dia- Greek across, through diameter
peri- Greek around perimeter
iso- Greek isos equal isometric
kilo- Greek khilioi thousand kilometre, kilowatt
manu- Latin manus hand manual
plumb- Latin plumbum lead (the metal) plumb, plumber
torqu- Latin torquere to twist torque
ferr- Latin ferrum iron ferrous, non-ferrous
circum- Latin around circumference
tang- Latin tangere to touch tangent
milli- Latin mille thousand, thousandth part millimetre
centi- Latin centum hundred, hundredth part centimetre
Some trade words have a story inside them:
A plumber was first a worker in lead, from Latin plumbum. Lead was used for roofs, gutters and pipes.
Perpendicular comes from Latin perpendiculum, a plumb line. A plumb line hangs straight down, at a right angle to level ground.
Wrench is much older English. It comes from Old English wrencan, "to twist".
3. Use the root to guess, then check
Roots give you a good guess, not a guarantee. Check the meaning in a dictionary. The Language Portal of Canada recommends a reliable Canadian dictionary, such as the Canadian Oxford Dictionary.
4. Canadian spelling
The Language Portal of Canada gives these Canadian preferences:
metre for the unit of length, meter for a measuring device: "The pipe is 3 metres long." "Read the water meter."
litre, not liter
colour, labour (but laborious)
centre, fibre
5. Explain a technical word when the reader needs it
A crew member knows "perpendicular". A homeowner may not. Add a plain explanation the first time: "The pipe runs perpendicular to the joists (at a right angle to them)."
Worked example
A new apprentice sees "isometric" on a piping drawing.
Split the word: iso + metr + ic.
Look up the parts: isos means equal, metron means measure.
Guess: "equal measure", a drawing where measurements along the main directions are shown at the same scale.
Check the dictionary and ask the journeyperson.
Spell it from its parts: i-s-o, m-e-t-r, i-c.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Match each root to its meaning.
Root Meaning
1. hydr- a) around
2. therm- b) iron
3. manu- c) to twist
4. peri- d) water
5. ferr- e) hand
6. torqu- f) hot
Task 2 (level 1 to 2) Split each word into its parts. Write a guess at its meaning from the roots. Then check a dictionary and write the dictionary meaning.
a) perimeter b) pneumatic c) non-ferrous d) manual (as in "manual valve") e) circumference
Task 3 (level 1) Circle the Canadian spelling for each sentence.
a) Cut the conduit to 2.5 (metres / meters). b) Check the reading on the gas (metre / meter). c) The tank holds 40 (litres / liters). d) Mark the (centre / center) of the wall. e) The quote includes (labour / labor) and materials. f) Match the paint (colour / color) to the sample.
Task 4 (level 2) Rewrite this note for a homeowner. Keep the technical words, but add a plain explanation in brackets the first time each one appears.
We'll run the line perpendicular to the joists, put a pneumatic test on it, and set the torque on the flange bolts to spec.
Task 5 (level 2) Choose one root from the table that is used in your trade. Write four words that contain it. Check each word in a dictionary and cross out any that do not really contain that root.
Check yourself
What does the root metron mean? Give two trade words that contain it.
In Canadian spelling, which is the unit of length: metre or meter?
What did the word "plumber" first mean?
Why should you check a dictionary after guessing a meaning from a root?
When should you add a plain explanation after a technical word?

lessons.title: Write a site memo and a short report
lessons.text:
Write a one-page memo that puts the point first and lists who does what by when, then a short report that sets out what you found, two options and a recommendation.
Try it in the visual practice studio
Choose the audience, purpose and key details before writing your memo or report.
Build a clear brief
Why this matters on the job
Texts and emails reach one or two people. A memo goes to a whole crew, a shop or every trade on a site. It gets posted in the site office, pinned to the sign-in board or attached to an email. A short report goes up the chain: your foreman or the shop manager asks you to look into a problem, and you write back what you found and what you think should happen. Lead hands, foremen and estimators write both. If your memo is clear, people do what it asks. If your report is clear, the boss can say yes to your fix.
Key ideas
1. Memo, email or report?
Write a When
Text or email One or two readers, a quick question or update. See Text and email a foreman or client.
Memo Many readers inside the company or on the site. A rule, a change, a reminder everyone must follow. One page.
Short report Someone asked you to look into a problem. You give what you found, the options and what you recommend. One or two pages.
2. The memo heading
Every memo starts with four lines. Readers look here first.
To: who must read it From: your name and job title Date: 2026-11-09 Subject: what it is about and what changes, in a few words
Write the date the same way as in your daily work log: year, month, day.
3. Put the point first
The first sentence says what is changing, who it applies to and from when. Many people read only the first two lines on a sign-in board.
Weak: "As many of you may already be aware, there have been some ongoing concerns lately regarding..."
Clear: "Starting Tuesday, November 10, every crew must put garbage in the new bins by the main gate."
4. Give the reason in one or two sentences
People follow a rule better when they know why. Keep the reason short and true. Leave out blame.
5. Number the actions
Use a numbered list for anything people must do. Each action says who, what and by when.
6. Be specific, not vague
A vague line starts arguments. A specific line gives people the facts.
Vague Specific
"People never clean up." "The lane behind Building B had nails and lunch garbage in it on 3 of 5 days this week."
"Deliveries are always late." "The drywall delivery booked for 7:00 am on November 10 arrived at 10:40 am. Three tapers waited."
7. The short report plan
A short report answers the question someone asked you. Use these headings:
Purpose: who asked, what they asked, when.
What I found: facts, numbers, places and dates.
Options: two choices, each with its cost and what it takes.
Recommendation: which option, and why, in two or three sentences.
Next step: what you need from the reader, and by when.
Use the memo heading (To, From, Date, Subject) at the top. Keep each section short.
Worked example: a memo
Tidewater Builders (a fictional company) has had complaints from neighbours. The superintendent's first try:
Hey all, so it's come to my attention that there's been garbage around and some of it's ending up out back and the neighbours aren't too happy, so let's all try to do better going forward on that, thanks.
The memo she posted instead:
To: All Harbour Lane crews and trades From: Marta Kowal, Site Superintendent Date: 2026-11-09 Subject: New garbage bins and a 10-minute end-of-shift sweep, starting Tuesday, November 10
Starting Tuesday, November 10, every crew must use the new bins by the main gate and sweep its work area at the end of each shift.
Neighbours on Pine Lane phoned the office three times last week about lunch garbage and nails in the lane behind Building B. Nails in the lane can puncture tires, and the complaints hurt our name in this neighbourhood.
Everyone: put food and lunch garbage in the green bins by the main gate. Put offcuts, nails and screws in the metal bin beside them.
Everyone: at the end of each shift, spend 10 minutes picking up your work area, including the lane side of Building B.
Foremen: check your area after the sweep and initial the clean-up sheet in the site office.
Everyone: sign the sign-off sheet in the site office by Friday, November 13, to show you have read this memo.
Questions: see me in the site office.
What changed: a heading, the point first, a short reason with facts, numbered actions with who and when, and a way to ask questions.
Worked example: a short report
Fraser Bend Fabrication (fictional) has been losing tools. The shop manager asked the lead hand to find out why.
To: Dale Okafor, Shop Manager From: Rena Thomas, Lead Hand Date: 2026-11-16 Subject: Missing tools in Bay 2: findings and recommendation
Purpose. On November 2 you asked me to find out why tools keep going missing from Bay 2 and to suggest a fix.
What I found. From September 1 to October 30, six tools went missing from Bay 2: two grinders, one drill, one impact driver and two levels. Replacing them cost $960. Five of the six were last seen on the tool cart at the end of a shift. Bay 2 has no sign-out sheet, and the cart stays outside the tool crib overnight.
Options. A. Put a sign-out sheet on the crib door. The lead hand checks the cart against the sheet at 3:15 pm each day. This takes about 10 minutes a day and costs nothing to buy. B. Buy a lockable cabinet for the cart for $1,450 and use the sign-out sheet as well.
Recommendation. Start option A on Monday, November 23. It costs nothing to buy and deals with the main cause, tools left on the cart overnight. If any tool goes missing before Friday, December 18, buy the cabinet.
Next step. Please tell me by Friday, November 20, if I can start option A.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) These five parts of a memo are out of order. Number them 1 to 5 in the order they should appear.
___ "1. Park in the north lot. 2. Tell anyone who rides with you." ___ "Subject: No parking in the back lane from 7 to 9 am, starting Monday, November 23" ___ "Questions: see Dale in the shop office." ___ "Starting Monday, November 23, nobody may park in the back lane from 7:00 to 9:00 am." ___ "Steel trucks need the whole lane to unload."
Task 2 (level 2) Rewrite each vague line as a specific line. Use only the facts in the brackets.
a) "People keep leaving the gate open." (The gate was found open after 3:30 pm on 4 of 5 days, November 2 to 6.)
b) "The delivery was late again." (Drywall delivery booked for 7:00 am, November 10. Arrived 10:40 am. Three tapers waited.)
c) "We go through way too many grinding discs." (60 discs used in October, 30 in September.)
Task 3 (level 2) This memo from Fraser Bend Fabrication rambles. Rewrite it as a one-page memo with a heading, the point first, a short reason, numbered actions and a contact. Dale Okafor is the Shop Manager. Date it 2026-11-16.
Hi everyone, so as most of you probably know we've been having some issues lately with parking out back, especially in the mornings, because the steel trucks come Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays and they need the whole lane to unload and they've been getting stuck behind people's trucks, which costs us waiting time. So from now on, I mean starting Monday the 23rd, please don't park in the back lane between 7 and 9 in the morning. You can use the north lot instead. And if somebody rides in with you, let them know too. If you have any questions you can come and find me in the office. Thanks!
Task 4 (level 3) You are Sam Ortiz, lead hand on the Harbour Lane townhouses. On November 9, Marta Kowal, the superintendent, asked you to find out why so much drywall is getting damaged on site and to recommend a fix. Write a short report to her, dated 2026-11-23, with the five headings from key idea 7. Use these facts:
Week starting Sheets delivered Sheets damaged
November 2 120 9
November 9 140 12
November 16 100 6
Each sheet costs $18.
The sheets are stored outside at the north end of the site under one tarp. The tarp blew off in the wind twice. It rained in two of the three weeks.
Option A: store the drywall inside the parkade. Moving each delivery in takes 2 labourers 1 hour each. Labour costs $45 an hour per person on this job. There is one delivery a week.
Option B: rent a storage container for $180 a month, plus a one-time $150 delivery fee.
Before you write, find the total sheets damaged, the percent damaged and the cost of the damaged sheets. Show your math.
Check yourself
Name the four lines in a memo heading.
What should the first sentence of a memo say?
Why do memo actions go in a numbered list?
Rewrite as a specific line: "Some of the ladders are in bad shape." Use these facts: 2 of the 8 ladders in the tool crib have cracked side rails, found November 9.
What are the five headings of a short report?

lessons.title: Write a change request before you build it
lessons.text:
Turn a "can you just..." into a written change request that says what is asked, why, and what it does to the scope, days, cost, crew and safety, and get it signed before the work starts.
Why this matters on the job
"While you're here, can you just..." Every trade hears it. A homeowner wants a second set of stairs. A tenant wants two more outlets after the drywall is up. A super wants a wall moved 300 mm. If you say "sure" and start, the extra hours and material often go unpaid, the schedule slips, and nobody can prove later who asked for what. A written change request stops that. It says what is being asked, what it will cost in money and days, and it gets signed by the person who can approve it before anyone picks up a tool.
Key ideas
1. Question, change or normal work?
It is When What you write
Normal work It is already in the drawings, specs or contract. Nothing extra. Build it.
A question (RFI) The drawings are unclear, wrong or missing something. A request for information. See Ask a good RFI question.
A change Someone wants something different from what was agreed. A change request.
An RFI asks a question. A change request asks for approval. On many jobs, an approved change request becomes a change order.
2. Confirming is not the same as approving
In Text and email a foreman or client you confirmed a spoken change by email. That gives you a record. A change request goes further: it puts a price and a number of days on the change and asks for a signature.
3. Find out who can sign
The person asking is not always the person who can approve. A tenant's office manager, a homeowner's neighbour or a crew lead from another trade may ask for a change, but only the person named in the contract, or the person your boss names, can approve it. If you are not sure who that is, ask your foreman before you write.
4. The parts of a change request
Part What goes in it
Heading Job name, change request number (CR-01, CR-02 ...), date, requested by, written by
Description What is being changed, where, how many, what size. Name the drawing or room.
Reason Why the change is wanted, in one or two sentences
Impact on scope What is added, removed or different
Impact on schedule How many working days it adds, and what it pushes back
Impact on cost Labour, material and total, with the math shown
Impact on crew and other trades Who does the work, and which other trade is affected
Safety Any new hazard and how it will be controlled
Approval Name, title, signature, date, approved or rejected
5. Cost the change with BEDMAS
For pricing a change, see Numeracy lessons 22 (Markup, margin and pricing a job) and 26 (What a machine or crew costs per hour).
Labour = people × hours × rate. Then add the material. Multiply before you add.
2 carpenters × 7 h × $80/h + $480 material = $1,120 + $480 = $1,600
Use the labour rate your company gives you for the job. Show the math so the reader can check it. For more practice pricing work, see the Numeracy Hub, Construction Operations tab.
6. No signature, no start
Unless the change is needed right now to make something safe, wait for the signed approval before you start. If something must be made safe, make it safe, tell your foreman, and write up the change the same day.
7. Keep a change log
A change log is a list of every change request on the job, so nothing gets lost.
CR Date Description Amount Status
CR-01 2026-11-12 Add east stairs $1,600 Approved 2026-11-13
CR-02 2026-11-16 Cedar fascia in place of painted fascia $420 Waiting for signature
Worked example
Alder Creek Decks (a fictional company) is building a 12 ft × 16 ft deck at 418 Hemlock Street. The contract includes one set of stairs on the south side. On Thursday, November 12, the homeowner, Carol Grant, asks the carpenter, Jesse Paul, for a second set of stairs on the east side down to the garden.
Jesse does not say "sure". He says, "I can write that up with a price today. We start it once you sign." His change request:
Job: Grant deck, 418 Hemlock Street CR number: CR-01 Date: 2026-11-12 Requested by: Carol Grant, homeowner Written by: Jesse Paul, carpenter, Alder Creek Decks
Description: Add a second set of stairs on the east side of the deck, down to the garden: 4 steps, 36 in wide, with a handrail that matches the south stairs.
Reason: The homeowner wants direct access from the deck to the garden.
Scope: Adds one set of stairs and a handrail. Removes 36 in of the east guard rail for the stair opening.
Schedule: Adds 1 working day. Completion moves from Friday, November 20, to Monday, November 23.
Cost: Labour 2 carpenters × 7 h × $80/h = $1,120. Material $480. Total $1,600.
Crew and other trades: Same 2-person crew. No other trades affected. The office will check whether the permit drawings need to change.
Safety: The east guard rail stays in place until the stair is built, so there is no open edge.
Approval: Name _ Title _ Signature _ Date _ Approved / Rejected
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Mark each item N (normal work), RFI (a question) or CR (a change request).
a) The drawings show a 3-ply beam, but the beam schedule says 2-ply. ___ b) After the wall is drywalled, the client asks to move a light switch to the other side of the door. ___ c) Install the 12 joists shown on the framing plan. ___ d) The owner wants cedar decking in place of the pressure-treated decking in the contract. ___ e) Detail 4 on sheet A3 has no dimension for the stair landing. ___
Task 2 (level 2) Work out the cost of each change. Show each step with BEDMAS.
a) 1 electrician for 5 h at $90/h, plus $160 of material
b) 2 labourers for 3 h at $45/h, plus a $75 dump fee
c) 3 framers for 4 h at $80/h, plus $380 of material

Company: Coastal Spark Electric (fictional). You are the electrician, Mina Cho.
Job: office fit-out, Unit 104, Brightwater Plaza. This is change request CR-03.
On Tuesday, November 17, at 2:00 pm, the tenant's office manager, Priya Nair, asked you to add 4 duplex receptacles on the east wall of the meeting room, spaced evenly, at the same height as the existing receptacles. She wants to plug in a row of laptops at the table.
The east wall is already drywalled and taped.
Labour: 1 electrician, 6 h, at $90/h. Material: $140.
It adds 1 working day for your crew. The drywall trade will need to patch 4 openings. That work is not in your price.
Cutting into finished drywall makes dust. The meeting room carpet is already down.
Only the general contractor's project manager, Leo Brandt, can approve changes on this job.

Job: 5th St reno CR: ___ Date: ___ Description: Move wall a bit. Cost: TBD Requested by: the super Approval: _____

You have priced it at $860 and 1 extra day. Write a text to the superintendent (under 50 words) that keeps the relationship good and gets the change approved before you start. Then write the line you add to your change log.
Check yourself
What is the difference between an RFI and a change request?
Name four things a change request must say about the impact of the change.
Work out: 2 workers × 5 h × $60/h + $250.

lessons.title: Take meeting notes and keep an issue log
lessons.text:
Write meeting notes as decisions and action items with one owner and a due date, move open problems into an issue log, and keep the log up to date until each issue is closed.
Why this matters on the job
On most jobs the trades meet once a week, or every morning, to sort out who goes where and what is in the way. People leave the meeting sure they agreed. Three days later the framer thinks the electrician was calling the inspector, and the electrician thinks the super was. Good notes fix that. They say what was decided, who will do what by when, and which problems are still open. An issue log keeps those open problems on one page until someone closes them. Taking the notes is often a job for an apprentice or a lead hand, and it is a good way to be noticed.
Key ideas
1. Notes are not a word-for-word record
You do not write down everything people say. You listen for three things:
Listen for It sounds like Example
Decision: something agreed "OK, let's do that." "Drywall starts Thursday." Drywall starts Thursday, November 19.
Action item: someone will do something "I'll call them." "Can you book it?" Leo Brandt to call the door supplier today.
Issue: a problem not solved in the meeting "Nobody knows yet." "That's still a problem." The back door does not lock.
Jokes, stories and repeated points do not go in the notes.
2. The header
Meeting: Weekly coordination, Unit 104 fit-out Date and time: 2026-11-16, 7:30 am Place: Site office Present: Leo Brandt (GC project manager), Tasha Bell (framing foreman), Mina Cho (electrician), Kofi Mensah (drywall foreman) Notes by: your name
3. Every action item has one owner and a due date
Weak Clear
Someone will look at the door. Leo Brandt: call the door supplier about the back door lock, by end of day Monday, November 16.
The crew to clean up. Tasha Bell: clear the framing offcuts from Room 105, by noon Tuesday, November 17.
"Everyone", "the crew" and "someone" are not owners. Write a person's name. If nobody takes it, write it as an issue.
4. Open problems go into an issue log
An issue log is a table that lists every open problem on the job:
No. Date raised Issue Raised by Owner Due Status Update
No.: give each issue a number and never reuse it.
Owner: one person who will get it closed.
Status: Open, In progress or Closed.
Update: what changed, and when.
5. Keep the log alive
Update it after every meeting, and when a text or call changes something.
Never erase an issue. When it is fixed, mark it Closed and write the date.
Bring the log to the next meeting and go through the open issues first.
6. Send the notes the same day
Send or post the notes the day of the meeting. End with: "Please tell me by noon tomorrow if anything here is wrong." Now nobody can say later that they did not agree.
Worked example
Weekly coordination meeting, Unit 104 fit-out at Brightwater Plaza (a fictional job). What was said:
Leo (GC project manager): Morning. Three things. First, drywall delivery is Wednesday at 7. Kofi, can your crew start Thursday? Kofi (drywall foreman): Yes, if the framing in Room 105 is done. Tasha (framing foreman): 105 will be done Tuesday by noon. Leo: Good. Second, electrical rough-in inspection. Mina? Mina (electrician): Booked for Tuesday at 1 pm. I need the ceiling in 105 left open till then. Kofi: We won't board 105 before Thursday anyway. Leo: Third, the back door still won't lock. Tasha: That's not ours. The door supplier installed it. Leo: I'll call them today. And coffee's on me Friday.
The notes:
Meeting: Weekly coordination, Unit 104 fit-out Date and time: 2026-11-16, 7:30 am Place: Site office Present: Leo Brandt, Tasha Bell, Mina Cho, Kofi Mensah Notes by: Jordan Paul
Decisions 1. Drywall delivery Wednesday, November 18, at 7:00 am. Drywall starts Thursday, November 19. 2. The Room 105 ceiling stays open until the electrical inspection on Tuesday, November 17.
Action items
Action Owner Due
Finish framing in Room 105 Tasha Bell Tue Nov 17, noon
Electrical rough-in inspection Mina Cho Tue Nov 17, 1:00 pm
Call the door supplier about the back door lock Leo Brandt Mon Nov 16
Open issues: see issue log, No. 1.
Please tell me by noon tomorrow if anything here is wrong.
The issue log:
No. Date raised Issue Raised by Owner Due Status Update
1 2026-11-16 Back door does not lock Leo Brandt Leo Brandt 2026-11-17 Open
The coffee on Friday did not go in the notes.
Practice
Use this second meeting for Tasks 1 to 3.
Weekly coordination, Unit 104 fit-out, Thursday, November 19, 7:30 am, site office. Present: Leo Brandt, Tasha Bell, Mina Cho, Kofi Mensah.
Leo: Drywall is going up in Room 104 today. Kofi, what about 105?
Kofi: We'll start 105 tomorrow, Friday.
Leo: OK, 105 starts Friday.
Mina: The inspector passed rough-in on Tuesday, but he wants a cover plate on the junction box above the back door.
Mina: I'll put it on today.
Tasha: Somebody keeps parking in front of the garbage bin. The bin truck couldn't get in yesterday.
Leo: I'll put up a no-parking sign by the bin by Friday.
Kofi: Did anyone watch the game last night?
Leo: The door supplier says the new lock comes Monday.
Tasha: The header in Room 106 is 50 mm lower than the drawing shows. I need an answer before Monday or my crew stops in 106.
Leo: I'll send an RFI to the architect today.
Task 1 (level 1) Mark each line D (decision), A (action item), I (issue or issue update) or X (does not go in the notes). Some lines can have two letters.
1 ___ 2 ___ 3 ___ 4 ___ 5 ___ 6 ___ 7 ___ 8 ___ 9 ___ 10 ___ 11 ___
Task 2 (level 2) Write the notes for the November 19 meeting: the header, the decisions and an action items table with Action, Owner and Due. Write dates in full.
Task 3 (level 2) Copy the issue log from the worked example. Update issue 1 with the news from the November 19 meeting. Add the new issues from that meeting as issues 2, 3 and 4.
Task 4 (level 2) These messages arrive after the meeting. Update your issue log. Close any issue that is fixed, with the date.
Thursday, November 19, 3:10 pm, text from Mina: "Cover plate is on the back door junction box."
Friday, November 20, 10:00 am, text from Leo: "No-parking sign is up at the bin."
Friday, November 20, 2:30 pm, email from Leo: "Architect replied to the RFI. The Room 106 header is OK where it is. Carry on."
Monday, November 23, 11:00 am, text from Tasha: "New lock is on the back door. It works."
Task 5 (level 1 to 2) Rewrite each action item so it has one owner, a clear action and a due date. Use the names from this lesson. Say what you added.
a) "Someone to sort out the bin." b) "Kofi to check stuff." c) "Order more screws."
Check yourself
Name the three things you listen for when you take meeting notes.
Why is "the crew" not an owner for an action item?
What do you do with an issue in the log once it is fixed?
What should you write at the end of your notes, and why?
Name four columns in an issue log.

lessons.title: Report a near miss in writing
lessons.text:
Know when something counts as a near miss in BC, describe acts and conditions instead of blaming people, and write a near-miss report that helps your employer find and fix the cause before someone gets hurt.
Why this matters on the job
A board slides off a deck and lands a metre from someone. A grinder disc shatters and the pieces hit the wall. Nobody is hurt, so the crew says, "No harm done," and keeps going. But the same thing can happen tomorrow with someone standing a metre closer. A near miss is a free warning. In BC, the law says the employer must investigate a near miss that could have seriously hurt someone, and a clear written report from the people who saw it is where that investigation starts. This lesson builds on Report a workplace injury in BC and on Communication lesson 11, Report up the chain, where you reported a near miss out loud.
Key ideas
1. What counts as a near miss in BC
The BC Workers Compensation Act, section 69, says an employer must investigate an incident that:
did not hurt anyone, or caused only a minor injury that did not need medical treatment,
but could have caused a serious injury to a worker.
That is a near miss. If someone needed medical treatment, it is an injury, and you report it as in lesson 05.
2. Where your report goes
Lesson 05 (Injury report) explains these steps for injuries. The same rules cover a near miss.
Step Who What the law says
1 You, or anyone who sees it Report the unsafe condition or act as soon as possible to your supervisor or employer (OHS Regulation, section 3.10).
2 The person who gets your report Investigates and makes sure it is fixed without delay (section 3.10).
3 Your employer Starts a preliminary investigation right away and completes its report within 48 hours (Act, section 71).
4 Your employer Does a full investigation and sends the report to WorkSafeBC within 30 days (Act, section 72).
Both investigations look for the unsafe conditions, acts or procedures that led to the incident, and the fix. Your written report gives them the facts while they are fresh.
3. What goes in a near-miss report
Box What to write
When Date and time
Where Site, building, floor, room or machine
Who was there Names of the people involved and the witnesses
What was happening The task, the tool or material
What happened Events in time order, past tense, active voice
What could have happened The realistic worst outcome: "The header could have hit Chris on the head."
What was done right away Work stopped, area taped off, tool tagged out, supervisor told at what time
What is needed What would stop it happening again
Reported by Your name, the date and time you wrote it
4. Describe the act, not the person
Name who was there, because the investigators need to talk to them. But describe what was done, not what kind of person did it.
Blame Fact
"Kyle is reckless." "The top limit switch was wedged closed with a wood shim."
"The framers are lazy about safety." "A 2.4 m section of toe board was off the east deck edge from 11:30 am to 1:40 pm."
"Nobody cares here." "I reported the missing toe board to Leah Ross at 1:25 pm on November 3."
5. Safeguards and unsafe equipment
Under the OHS Regulation, section 4.12, a person must not intentionally remove, impair or make ineffective a safeguard that protects workers, except as the Regulation allows. Guards, toe boards, interlocks and limit switches are safeguards.
Under section 12.10, an unsafe tool, machine or piece of equipment must be taken out of service and marked so nobody uses it until it is safe. That is why you tag it out.
6. Hiding it is the real danger
This story is based on a real event that an ACCESS instructor saw as a maintenance technician in a machine shop. The names and some details are changed.
A press operator was setting up a stamping press. The top limit switch kept stopping the machine, so he wedged it closed to keep running. He told no one, because he was afraid of being written up. The press drove the top die past where it should stop. The bolts holding its support pulled out of their threads and the die dropped. Nobody was under it. That was the near miss.
The maintenance technician, Lee, locked out the press and found the threads in the support stripped. Lee wrote a repair report that said the holes had to be properly re-machined before the press ran again. A senior machinist called the report "too theoretical". The supervisor chose a quick fix: new bolts in the damaged threads. The press was running again that afternoon.
Weeks later the bolts pulled out again. A part broke loose, went through the guard, and broke an operator's collarbone.
Two things went wrong in writing. The bypass was never reported. And the written repair report was overruled with no record of why. If the near miss had been written up that day, the investigation would have had to find the wedged switch and the stripped threads.
7. If nothing gets fixed
Follow up in writing with your supervisor. Say what you reported, when, and what is still not fixed. Keep a copy.
Tell the worker member of your joint health and safety committee, or your worker health and safety representative.
Contact WorkSafeBC's Prevention Information Line: 604.276.3100 in the Lower Mainland, or 1.888.621.7233 toll-free. It takes reports of unsafe work conditions 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and you can report anonymously. WorkSafeBC also has an online form for reporting unsafe work.
The Workers Compensation Act protects you. Under section 73, an employer or supervisor must not try to discourage you from reporting a hazardous condition to WorkSafeBC. Under section 48, an employer must not punish or threaten you for using your rights or carrying out your duties under the health and safety rules.
Worked example
A weak near-miss report:
Grinder blew up. Could of been bad. Need better grinders.
A clear one (fictional case at Fraser Bend Fabrication):
When: 2026-11-04, 10:15 am Where: Fraser Bend Fabrication, Bay 1, grinding station Who was there: Rena Thomas (operator), Sam Ortiz (witness, at the saw 3 m away) What was happening: Rena was grinding a weld on a steel bracket with a 4-1/2 in angle grinder. What happened: The grinding disc broke apart. Pieces hit the steel wall behind the station. One piece cracked Rena's face shield. Rena was not injured. What could have happened: A piece could have hit Rena or Sam in the face or neck. What was done right away: Rena stopped work and unplugged the grinder. I tagged the grinder out of service and told Dale Okafor at 10:20 am. The rest of the box of discs was set aside. What is needed: Check the grinder and the box of discs before anyone uses them. Replace Rena's face shield. Reported by: Sam Ortiz, 2026-11-04, 10:40 am
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Mark each one NM (near miss), INJ (injury, report as in lesson 05) or N (not a safety incident).
a) A 2x10 slides off a second-floor deck and lands 1 m from a labourer. Nobody is hurt. ___ b) An apprentice cuts a finger on sheet metal. The first aid attendant cleans and bandages it, and a clinic later puts in stitches. ___ c) A ladder slips 30 cm on a wet floor. The worker on it steps down safely. ___ d) A pipe falls off a rolling cart in a hallway while nobody is near it. It could have hit anyone walking past. ___ e) The microwave in the lunchroom stops working. ___
Task 2 (level 2) Mark each statement F (fact) or O (opinion or blame). Rewrite each O as a fact you could check, or say to leave it out.
The top limit switch was wedged closed. ___
The operator was just being lazy. ___
The die dropped at about 9:40 am. ___
Management never listens to maintenance. ___
The repair report recommended re-machining the holes before restart. ___
Task 3 (level 2 to 3) Read the case. You are Sky Morgan, an apprentice framer with Salmonberry Framing (fictional). Write a near-miss report with the boxes from key idea 3.
Case (fictional). Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at the Harbour Lane townhouses, Building C. At 11:30 am the framers took off a 2.4 m section of toe board from the guardrail at the east edge of the second-floor deck, so they could slide joists up from the ground. Nobody put it back. At 1:20 pm, framer Ana Silva set a 2x10 header down near the east edge. It slid off through the gap and fell about 3 m to the ground. It landed about 1 m from labourer Chris Doyle, who was stacking blocking below. Nobody was hurt. You saw it from the deck. At 1:22 pm you and Ana stopped work at the east edge. Chris moved away and taped off the area below. At 1:25 pm you told the foreman, Leah Ross. Ana put the toe board back at 1:40 pm. You write the report at 2:00 pm.
Task 4 (level 3) It is Friday, November 6, at 8:00 am. The toe board at the north edge of the same deck is off, and nobody is working there. Write a short email to Leah Ross. Say what you saw and where, link it to your November 3 report, say what you did, and ask what will be done and by when. Keep it factual and polite.
Then answer: if the toe boards keep getting left off and nothing changes, name two more steps you can take.
Task 5 (level 3) Use the story in key idea 6.
a) Name three moments when something written down could have stopped the operator from getting hurt.
b) Write the near-miss report Lee could have written the day the die dropped. Use the boxes from key idea 3. Leave out blame. Use no names except Lee's.
Check yourself
In your own words, when does an incident with no injury count as a near miss that a BC employer must investigate?
Within how many hours must the employer complete the preliminary investigation report?
Rewrite as a fact: "That idiot pulled the toe board off and walked away."
What does OHS Regulation section 4.12 say about safeguards?
Give the Lower Mainland number for WorkSafeBC's Prevention Information Line. Can you report anonymously?

lessons.title: Write a site visit report with photos
lessons.text:
Plan a site walk, take photos that show what matters, caption each one, and write a short report with a summary, the visit details, one section per area and a table of who does what by when.
Why this matters on the job
Before a crew starts on a job, someone walks the site to see if it is ready. After a leak, a delivery problem or a bad inspection, someone goes to look. That person writes a site visit report. It records what was there on that day, tells people who were not there what they need to know, and gives the boss what they need to decide: can we start, what needs fixing first, and who fixes it. Photos do a lot of the work, but only if each one has a caption. Lead hands, estimators and foremen write these reports, and a clear one can save a wasted trip for a whole crew.
Key ideas
1. Plan the visit before you go
Answer these on a notepad before you leave:
Question Example
What question does the visit answer? Are the walls in Unit 104 ready to paint?
Who will read the report? The GC's project manager and our office
Which areas will I look at? Reception and hallway, meeting room, washroom
What do I bring? Phone or camera, tape measure, notepad, pen, hard hat, safety boots, vest
Who do I meet? Sign in with the site contact when you arrive.
Ask the site contact before you take photos. Keep people's faces, licence plates and private papers out of your shots.
2. Take photos that show what matters
Wide shot first, so the reader knows where you are. Then a close-up of the problem.
Put a tape measure or another object of known size in the close-up to show scale.
One problem per photo.
Take the photo straight on, in good light. Turn on a work light if you need it.
Number the photos in the order you take them, and note the area for each one in your notepad.
3. Caption every photo
A caption says what, where, which way you are facing, and when.
Weak: "Wall."
Clear: "Photo 3. Drywall patch at the third receptacle from the north end, meeting room east wall, looking east, 2026-11-24, 8:50 am. Tape shows 150 mm."
4. The report skeleton
Cover: project name and address, date of visit, prepared by, prepared for.
Distribution: To the people who must act. CC the people who need to know.
Summary: three or four sentences. Why you went, the overall condition, the main problems, and whether work can start.
Visit details: date and time, weather, who was there, how you got in.
One section per area: the photos with captions, What I saw (facts and measurements), and Steps (a numbered list).
Actions: a table of Action, Who, By when.
Many readers read only the summary. Write it last, after you know what you found, and put it near the top.
5. Write steps as commands
Start each step with a verb, so the reader knows exactly what to do.
Weak Clear
The patches should probably be sanded by somebody. 1. Sand the four patches smooth.
Dust needs dealing with. 2. Vacuum the dust from the floor and the receptacle boxes.
6. Facts, measured where you can
Write what you saw and measured. If you are not sure of a cause, say so: "Possible cause: a door handle hit the corner. Not confirmed."
Worked example
Lakeview Painting (a fictional company) has been hired to paint the office fit-out at Unit 104, Brightwater Plaza. Its lead hand, Nadia Fox, visits on Tuesday, November 24, to see if the painters can start Thursday. Here are parts of her report.
Cover. Site visit report, Unit 104 office fit-out, Brightwater Plaza. Visit date: 2026-11-24. Prepared by: Nadia Fox, Lead Hand, Lakeview Painting. Prepared for: Leo Brandt, Project Manager, general contractor.
Distribution. To: Leo Brandt (GC project manager), Kofi Mensah (drywall foreman). CC: Lakeview Painting office.
Summary. I visited Unit 104 on November 24 to check whether the walls are ready to paint. The reception area and hallway are ready. The meeting room east wall has four drywall patches that are not sanded, and the washroom has a dented corner bead. Painting can start in reception and the hallway on Thursday, November 26. The meeting room and the washroom can start when the drywall fixes are done.
Visit details. 2026-11-24, 8:30 to 9:30 am. Dry, cold. Present: Nadia Fox, Leo Brandt. Signed in at the GC site office. Leo let us in with the front door key.
Area 1: Reception and hallway Photo 1. Reception, looking north from the front door, 2026-11-24, 8:35 am. What I saw: All walls are taped and sanded. No ridges or marks show under a work light. The floor is covered. Steps: 1. Cover the door frames and the front window. 2. Wipe the walls with a damp cloth to remove dust. 3. Prime all walls. 4. Check the primed walls under a work light and mark any flaws. 5. Apply two finish coats. 6. Remove the covers and clean up. 7. Record the paint used against the estimate.
Area 2: Meeting room east wall Photo 2. Meeting room east wall, looking east, 2026-11-24, 8:48 am. Photo 3. Patch at the third receptacle from the north end, looking east, 2026-11-24, 8:50 am. Tape shows 150 mm. What I saw: Four drywall patches around new receptacles, each about 150 mm × 150 mm. The mud is on but not sanded. The edges show as ridges under a work light. Steps: 1. Sand the four patches smooth. 2. Apply a thin finish coat where the edges still show. 3. Sand again when dry. 4. Vacuum the dust from the floor and the receptacle boxes. 5. Tell Lakeview Painting that the wall is ready.
Actions
Action Who By when
Finish and sand the four patches, meeting room east wall Kofi Mensah Fri Nov 27
Fix the dented corner bead, washroom Kofi Mensah Fri Nov 27
Start painting reception and hallway Nadia Fox Thu Nov 26
(Area 3, the washroom, follows the same pattern.)
Practice
Task 1 (level 2) Write a caption for each photo. Use the facts given and the caption pattern from key idea 3.
a) A wide shot of the loading door at Fraser Bend Fabrication, taken from inside the shop looking west, 2026-11-25, 7:40 am.
b) A close-up of a cracked weld on the loading door's top hinge, with a tape showing 40 mm, taken 7:42 am the same day.
c) A wide shot of a stack of steel plate on the floor in front of Bay 3, looking south, 7:50 am the same day.
Task 2 (level 2) Turn these rough notes into a What I saw paragraph with only facts, then a numbered list of Steps that start with a verb.
washroom corner by door is beat up, bead dented maybe 300 mm long at about hip height, someone probably hit it with a cart, needs fixing before paint, also a bit of dust on the floor
Task 3 (level 3) Plan and do a site walk. Your instructor will name three areas at ACCESS, for example the shop, the tool crib and the yard.
a) Fill in the five planning questions from key idea 1. b) In each area, take one wide photo and one close-up of something that matters: a hazard, a repair needed, or something done well. If you cannot take photos, make a quick sketch and label it. c) Write your captions and notes as you go.
Task 4 (level 3) Write your site visit report for the three areas in Task 3. Use the skeleton from key idea 4: cover, distribution, summary, visit details, one section per area with photos, captions, What I saw and Steps, and an actions table. Address it to your instructor, and CC one classmate. Write the summary last.
Task 5 (level 2) Swap reports with a partner. Check their report with this list. Tick each line, and write one thing they should fix.
[ ] The cover has the project, address, date, prepared by and prepared for.
[ ] To and CC are both filled in.
[ ] The summary is three or four sentences and says whether work can start.
[ ] Every photo has a number and a caption with what, where, which way and when.
[ ] What I saw has only facts, with measurements where they help.
[ ] Every step starts with a verb.
[ ] Every action has one person and a date.
One fix: __________
Check yourself
Why do you take a wide shot before a close-up?
What four things does a good caption say?
Who goes on the To line, and who goes on the CC line?
Why do you write the summary last but put it near the top?
Rewrite as a step that starts with a verb: "The floor protection should be put down before anybody starts."

lessons.title: Say no and ask for something in writing
lessons.text:
Turn down a request in writing without losing the relationship, and write a formal request letter that answers the reader's worries and makes it easy for them to say yes.
Why this matters on the job
Some answers are better in writing. A client asks for extra work for free. A supplier wants to send a different size than the drawings call for. You want your employer to pay for a course or give you time to learn estimating. Writing gives you time to get the tone right, and it leaves a record of what was said. In Communication lesson 4, Saying no and setting limits at work, you practised saying no out loud. This lesson puts a no, and a request, on paper.
Key ideas
1. Two plans for two jobs
You need to Use the plan for
Turn down a request, give bad news A written no
Get someone to agree to something A written request
2. The written no: five parts
Thank or acknowledge. Show you read the request.
Give a short, true reason. One or two sentences. No long list of excuses.
Say no clearly. The reader must not finish the message thinking you said "maybe".
Offer an alternative, if there is one you can live with.
Close on a friendly, forward-looking note.
What to avoid:
Burying the no: "We'll see what we can do at some point." The reader hears yes.
Over-explaining. Every extra excuse is something to argue with.
Blame or sarcasm. The message may be forwarded.
When a client asks for extra work for free, the alternative is often to price it. See Write a change request before you build it.
3. The written request: think about the reader first
Before you write, answer four questions:
Question Example
Who is the reader, and what is their job? Dale Okafor, Shop Manager
What do they care about? Cost, keeping the shop running, fewer mistakes
What will they likely object to? "It costs money and you'll miss work on Fridays."
What is in it for them? Fewer remade parts, an apprentice who can check drawings
Then write five short paragraphs:
The request, in the first sentence or two.
Background: why you are asking now.
The details and the benefit to the reader, with numbers.
The objection, answered before they raise it.
The close: the exact decision you need, by when, and an offer to talk.
4. When to send a letter, and how it looks
Use a formal letter for requests that go in a file: training, time off, money, or a request to an organization you do not deal with every day. You can print and sign it, or attach it as a PDF to a short email.
A business letter in block style has every line starting at the left margin, a blank line between paragraphs, and these parts in order:
Your name and title (and your address if you write from outside the company)
The date
The reader's name, title and company (and address if it goes outside the company)
A subject line starting with "Re:"
A greeting: "Dear Mr. Okafor,"
The body
A closing: "Sincerely,"
Your signature, then your typed name and title
Worked example: a written no
Alder Creek Decks (a fictional company) is finishing a deck for Carol Grant. She emails: "While your crew is here, could you also build a small garden shed? I assume it won't cost much since you already have the tools here."
A weak reply:
Hi Carol, hmm, maybe, the guys are pretty busy but we'll see what we can do, I'll let you know.
The reply the owner sent:
Subject: Your garden shed question
Hello Ms. Grant,
Thank you for thinking of us for your garden shed. We're glad you are happy with how the deck is coming along.
Our crew starts another job on Tuesday, November 24, the day after your deck is finished, so we can't add the shed to this job.
We would be glad to price the shed as a separate job for the spring. If you send me the size you have in mind and a photo of the spot, I will send you a price within a week.
Thank you again. We look forward to finishing your deck on Monday.
Lena Paul Owner, Alder Creek Decks
Find the five parts: thanks, reason, the no ("we can't add the shed to this job"), the alternative, the friendly close.
Worked example: a formal request letter
Kai Larsen is an apprentice at Fraser Bend Fabrication (fictional). A local college runs a blueprint reading course on six Fridays, 4:00 to 7:00 pm, from January 8 to February 12, 2027. It costs $395. The shop day ends at 3:30 pm, which is too late to get there. Kai's letter:
Kai Larsen Apprentice, Bay 2, Fraser Bend Fabrication
2026-11-30
Dale Okafor Shop Manager, Fraser Bend Fabrication
Re: Request for course fee and Friday schedule change, January 8 to February 12, 2027
Dear Mr. Okafor,
I am asking the shop to pay the $395 fee for a blueprint reading course, and to let me leave at 2:30 pm instead of 3:30 pm on six Fridays so I can get to the class.
The course runs on Fridays from 4:00 to 7:00 pm, from January 8 to February 12, 2027. In October I misread a dimension on a shop drawing, and two brackets had to be remade. I want to be able to check drawings on my own before I cut.
Reading drawings well means fewer remade parts and less checking time for the lead hands. Over the six weeks I would miss 6 hours of shop time. I will make up all 6 hours by starting 30 minutes early on Tuesdays and Thursdays in those same weeks. Rena Thomas has said that works for Bay 2.
Could you let me know by Friday, December 11, so I can register before the course fills? I am happy to talk about it any time this week.
Sincerely,
(signature)
Kai Larsen Apprentice
The likely objection (cost and missed Fridays) is answered in the third paragraph, with numbers.
Practice
Task 1 (level 1) Number the parts of this written no from 1 to 5 in the order they should go.
___ "We can't take on the extra unit this week." ___ "Thanks for asking us about Unit 6." ___ "Hope the move-in goes well, and thanks again." ___ "We could do it on Monday, November 30, as a separate job." ___ "Our crew is booked on Units 2 to 4 until Friday."
Task 2 (level 2) Kofi Mensah's drywall crew is renovating the hallways of an apartment building. A tenant in Unit 3 asks Kofi to patch four holes in her unit for free while the crew is there. Her unit is not part of the job. Kofi replies:
Hi, yeah maybe, we're pretty slammed right now, and the guys are tired, and I'd have to check with the office and the GC and I'm not sure about the mud, so I'll see if we can squeeze it in sometime.
a) Name three problems with this reply. b) Rewrite it using the five parts of a written no. Offer to give her the drywall company's office number for a price.
Task 3 (level 2 to 3) You work for Fraser Bend Fabrication. A sales rep at Westline Steel Supply (fictional), Marco Diaz, emails: "We can't get your 40 lengths of 2 in square tube for 3 weeks. I can send 1-1/2 in square tube tomorrow instead. Want it?" The shop drawings call for 2 in square tube, and the shop cannot change a size without the customer's approval. Write a reply that says no to the substitute, gives the reason, and asks whether he can send any 2 in tube sooner, from stock or another branch.
Task 4 (level 3) Plan the request in Task 5. Fill in the four reader questions from key idea 3.
Question Your answer
Who is the reader, and what is their job?
What do they care about?
What will they likely object to?
What is in it for them?
Task 5 (level 3) You are Mina Cho's apprentice at Coastal Spark Electric (fictional). You want to learn estimating. Write a formal request letter in block style to Ruth Adeyemi, Operations Manager, dated 2026-11-25. Use these facts:
You want to spend four Wednesday afternoons, 1:00 to 3:30 pm, with the company estimator, Paul Singh, learning to do material takeoffs. The dates are December 2, 9 and 16, 2026, and January 6, 2027.
Paul has said yes if Ruth approves.
That is 4 × 2.5 = 10 hours away from the tools.
On those afternoons your crew is doing trim-out at one site. Mina has said she can cover the work with the rest of the crew.
The company has lost time this fall when material orders came in short. You noticed it on two jobs.
You want an answer by Friday, November 27.
Check yourself
Name the five parts of a written no.
What is wrong with "We'll see what we can do at some point" as an answer you mean as no?
Where in a request letter does the request go?
Why should a request letter answer the reader's objection before they raise it?
Put these letter parts in order: greeting, date, closing, Re: line, reader's name and title.
